items: The earth is not the same all the way through. It is built in layers, and each layer differs in what it is made of and whether it is solid or liquid.
The earth is made of concentric layers (layers one inside another, like the rings of an onion). From the outside in they are the crust, the mantle, the outer core and the inner core.
Density (how much mass is packed into a given volume) and temperature both increase towards the centre of the earth, so the innermost layers are the densest and hottest.
This is why the core, at the centre, is the hottest and densest part, while the thin crust at the surface is the coolest and lightest.
The earth's radius (the distance from the surface to the centre) is about 6,370 km.
Diagram: draw a labelled cross-section of the earth showing every layer and both boundaries between them.
The crust is the thin, solid outer layer of the earth, the part we live on. It exists in two types, which differ in thickness, density and rock type.
Continental crust (the crust that makes up the land) is about 30–70 km thick and is thickest under high mountain ranges.
Continental crust has an average density of about 2.7 g/cm³ (grams per cubic centimetre).
Continental crust is mainly granite-type rock, rich in silica (a mineral made of silicon and oxygen) and aluminium; its old name is sial.
Oceanic crust (the crust under the oceans) is about 5–10 km thick and has an average density of about 3.0 g/cm³.
Oceanic crust is mainly basalt (a dark volcanic rock), rich in silica and magnesium; its old name is sima.
Continental crust is thicker but less dense than oceanic crust, because oceanic crust is thinner but denser; compare 2.7 with 3.0 g/cm³.

No oceanic crust is older than about 200 million years, while some continental rock is billions of years old, because oceanic crust is continually created and destroyed. There is more on this in the plate tectonics model and at plate boundaries.
Where one layer meets the next, the rock changes sharply. These sharp boundaries have names, and exams ask you to tell them apart.
A discontinuity is a sharp boundary between two layers of the earth, where the material changes.
The Moho (Mohorovičić discontinuity) is the boundary between the crust and the mantle, where earthquake waves speed up suddenly.
The Moho is named after Andrija Mohorovičić, a Croatian seismologist (a scientist who studies earthquakes), who identified it in 1909 from earthquake records.
The Gutenberg discontinuity is the boundary between the mantle and the core, at the base of the mantle.
The mantle is the thickest layer. Its upper part contains the layers on which the crust rests and moves.
The mantle extends to about 2,900 km depth and is made of dense rock rich in iron and magnesium.
The mantle has an upper part and a lower part, and it is the upper part that holds the asthenosphere and the base of the lithosphere.
Asthenosphere: the semi-molten (partly melted), plastic (able to flow slowly without breaking) layer in the upper mantle, beneath the lithosphere, on which the plates move. It is not liquid.
Magma is molten rock in the mantle; it is called lava only once it erupts at the surface.
Lithosphere: the rigid outer shell made of the crust plus the solid top of the upper mantle. It is about 100 km thick on average, thinner under the oceans and thicker under the continents.
The lithosphere is broken into tectonic plates (large slabs of rigid rock), which is why the rigid lithosphere can move as separate pieces over the plastic asthenosphere.
The core is the centre of the earth. It is made of iron and nickel and is divided into a liquid outer part and a solid inner part.
Exams ask for the two main metals of the core: iron and nickel.
Outer core: liquid, from about 2,900 km to about 5,150 km depth. Movement of this liquid metal generates the earth's magnetic field (the field that makes a compass needle point north).
Inner core: solid, from about 5,150 km to the centre of the earth. It is the hottest part of the earth, at about 5,500 °C, similar to the surface of the sun.
The inner core is solid despite its heat because the pressure at that depth is enormous, which means the metal cannot melt.
The inside of the earth is hot, and that heat keeps the mantle moving. This movement is what later drives changes in the crust.
Internal heat comes from the decay of radioactive elements (unstable elements that give off heat as they break down) and from heat left over from the earth's formation.
Convection currents are circular movements of semi-molten rock in the mantle, set going by heat from below, so for example hot rock rises while cooler rock sinks.
1. Heated rock near the core becomes less dense and rises.
2. Near the top of the mantle the rock spreads out sideways and cools.
3. Cooled rock becomes denser and sinks again, completing the circle.
The heat inside the earth powers forces that shape the crust. Geographers split the forces that shape the earth into those from inside and those from outside.
Endogenic (internal) forces come from inside the earth and are powered by its internal heat.
Endogenic forces include plate movement, folding (bending of rock layers), faulting (breaking and shifting of rock along cracks), volcanic activity and earthquakes.
Exogenic (external) forces act at the earth's surface, such as weathering (the breakdown of rock where it lies) and erosion (the wearing away and carrying off of rock and soil).
Nobody has drilled through the earth, so its structure is worked out from earthquake (seismic) waves. Their speed and direction change as they pass through layers of different density.
Seismic waves reveal the earth's structure because the changes in their speed and direction at each boundary are how the discontinuities were found.
P-waves (primary waves) pass through both solids and liquids, so they can travel through the liquid outer core as well as through solid layers.
S-waves (secondary waves) pass only through solids, so they are stopped by any liquid layer.
S-waves do not pass through the outer core, which shows that the outer core is liquid.
This leaves an S-wave shadow zone (an area where S-waves are not detected) on the far side of the earth from an earthquake.

The plate tectonics model grew in two stages, and the first was continental drift, the idea that the continents move. Alfred Wegener, a German meteorologist (a scientist who studies weather), proposed it in 1912 and published it in his book The Origin of Continents and Oceans in 1915.
Wegener proposed that the continents were once joined in one supercontinent (a single giant landmass), Pangaea, surrounded by one ocean, Panthalassa, and have since drifted apart.
Pangaea split into Laurasia in the north and Gondwanaland in the south, separated by the Tethys Sea; these broke up further into today's continents, such as South America and Africa.
Pangaea began to break up about 200 million years ago.
Wegener could not explain what force moved the continents, so the theory was rejected at first, because without a cause few accepted that continents could move.
Wegener backed his idea with four kinds of evidence. Each shows that lands now far apart were once joined or lay in different climate zones.
Jigsaw fit: the coastlines of South America and Africa fit together, and the fit is even better at the edge of the continental shelves (the shallow sea floor around a continent's edge).

Fossils: Mesosaurus, a small freshwater reptile, is found in both Brazil and southern Africa. Glossopteris, a fern-like plant, is found in South America, Africa, India, Antarctica and Australia. Neither could have crossed an ocean, so the lands must once have been joined.

Rocks and mountains: the Appalachian Mountains of eastern North America match the Caledonian mountains of Ireland, Scotland and Norway in rock type, age and structure, as if one range had been split by the Atlantic.

Past climates: glacial deposits (material left by ice) and striations (scratches cut into rock by moving ice) about 300 million years old occur in India, Africa, South America and Australia, places now warm or near the equator.
Coal seams in Antarctica formed from plant matter in warm swamps, which shows that Antarctica was once in a much warmer place than it is now.
Continental drift lacked a force to move the continents. The clue came from the ocean floor, which was mapped in detail only after the Second World War.
Detailed mapping of the ocean floor by echo-sounding (sonar, which times sound echoes bounced off the sea bed) followed the Second World War.
The mapping revealed long mid-ocean ridges (underwater mountain chains) with a central rift valley, and deep ocean trenches (long, very deep gashes in the sea floor).
The Mid-Atlantic Ridge is about 16,000 km long.
Sea-floor spreading supplied the mechanism that continental drift lacked, by showing that the ocean floor itself is moving and carrying the continents with it.
Arthur Holmes, a British geologist, suggested in the late 1920s that mantle convection (slow circulation of heated rock in the layer beneath the crust) could move continents.
Harry Hess, an American geologist, proposed sea-floor spreading in the early 1960s, in four stages.
1. Magma (molten rock) rises at mid-ocean ridges.
2. It cools to form new oceanic crust (the crust under the oceans) made of basalt, a dark volcanic rock.
3. The new crust pushes older crust away on both sides of the ridge.
4. Old crust is destroyed again at ocean trenches, so the ocean floor is constantly recycled.
Sea-floor spreading supplied the missing mechanism and turned continental drift into the theory of plate tectonics.
Three pieces of evidence from the ocean floor support Hess: the age of the rocks, the thickness of the sediment and the pattern of magnetism.
Age of rocks: oceanic rocks are youngest at the ridge and get progressively older with distance from it, symmetrically on both sides. This fits new crust forming at the ridge and moving outwards.

Sediment (mud and particles that settle on the sea bed): it is thin or absent at the ridge and thicker further away, because the crust at the ridge is new and the crust further out has had longer to collect it.
Palaeomagnetism (the record of the earth's magnetism in rocks): the earth's magnetic field reverses from time to time. Iron minerals in cooling basalt line up with the field at that moment.
So the ocean floor holds stripes of normal and reversed magnetism that mirror each other on either side of the ridge.
Magnetic striping was explained by Fred Vine and Drummond Matthews in 1963.
Diagram: plan view of a ridge with symmetrical magnetic stripes and arrows showing movement away from the ridge.
Sea-floor spreading showed that the earth's surface is divided into moving pieces called plates. Here you meet the definition of a plate, the main plates by name and the force that moves them.

A plate is a rigid slab of lithosphere (the crust plus the solid upper part of the mantle) that floats and moves on the asthenosphere (the softer, slowly flowing layer beneath). A plate can carry continental crust, oceanic crust or both.
The earth has seven major plates: Pacific, North American, South American, Eurasian, African, Indo-Australian and Antarctic. The Pacific plate is the largest.
Smaller plates include Nazca, Cocos, Caribbean, Juan de Fuca, Philippine, Arabian and Scotia.
Some maps split the Indo-Australian plate into the Indian plate and the Australian plate; both versions are accepted.
Convection currents in the mantle (rising and sinking flows of heated rock) drag the plates along, because the plates sit on top of the moving rock.
Plates move a few centimetres a year, so the map of continents and oceans changes over geological time. The Atlantic is widening by about 2.5 cm a year, roughly the rate a fingernail grows.

Plates meet in three ways: moving apart (constructive, or divergent), moving together (destructive, or convergent), and sliding past (passive, conservative, or transform). There is more on this in the next subsection.
Higher Level students need two more forces that help move plates, one acting at the ridge where a plate forms and one at the edge where it sinks.
Ridge push is new, hot crust at the ridge sliding away from it under gravity, so the plate is shoved away from the ridge.
Slab pull is the cold, dense subducting edge of a plate (the edge sinking back into the mantle) pulling the rest of the plate after it.
Because the crust is mobile, plate movement produces forces from inside the earth, called endogenic forces. These give rise to geological structures such as folds and faults.
Plate movement drives endogenic forces, which, for example, cause folding, faulting, volcanic activity and earthquakes and are concentrated mostly along plate boundaries.
The continental drift and sea-floor spreading evidence above is why the plate tectonics model replaced the earlier theory.
Ireland's position on the plate map determines its present geological activity.
Ireland lies on the Eurasian plate, near its western edge and far from any plate boundary, which means it sits in the interior of a plate.
The nearest plate boundary is the Mid-Atlantic Ridge to the west, which separates the Eurasian and North American plates in the North Atlantic, with Iceland on the ridge.
As the Atlantic widens, Ireland moves slowly away from North America.
Because Ireland is far from a plate boundary, it has no active volcanoes and only rare, minor earthquakes.
Ireland's past position was very different. About 500 million years ago it was split in two by an ocean, and the closing of that ocean built the first set of Irish mountains.

About 500 million years ago, before the Caledonian folding, Ireland was in two parts on opposite sides of the Iapetus Ocean: the north-west part on the North American (Laurentian) side and the south-east part on the European side.

The Iapetus Ocean closed as the plates converged (moved together), and the two parts of Ireland were joined along the Iapetus suture (the line where the two landmasses were welded), which runs across Ireland roughly from the Shannon Estuary to Clogherhead, Co. Louth.
The collision caused the Caledonian folding (the crumpling of rock layers into fold mountains), about 400 million years ago, which built mountains running north-east to south-west.

Caledonian mountains include the mountains of Donegal, Mayo and Connemara, and the Wicklow Mountains. The Leinster granite batholith (a huge mass of granite that cooled underground) was intruded during this period.
As plates carried Ireland north, it passed through different climates, and the rocks that formed record them.
Ireland has drifted north over hundreds of millions of years, which is why rocks formed in very different climates are found there.
Old Red Sandstone (a red sedimentary rock) formed in hot, dry conditions after the Caledonian folding.
Carboniferous limestone formed about 350 million years ago, when Ireland lay near the equator under a warm, shallow tropical sea.
A second collision, further south, built a second set of Irish mountains running in a different direction.
The Armorican (Variscan) folding, about 300 million years ago, came from the collision of Africa, part of Gondwanaland, with Europe as Pangaea came together.
It built east-west mountains across the south of Ireland: Macgillycuddy's Reeks, the Galtee Mountains, the Knockmealdowns and the Caha Mountains, which form the Munster ridge-and-valley landscape.
Armorica is the old name for Brittany, where the same fold belt occurs.
The last events in the story are the splitting of Pangaea, which opened the Atlantic, and Alpine folding, which happened elsewhere.
As North America and Greenland separated from Europe after Pangaea split, magma rose through cracks in north-east Ireland and formed the Antrim basalts about 60 million years ago.
Alpine folding is the most recent period of fold mountain building, producing the Alps and the Himalayas.
Alpine folding did not build Ireland's mountains; the two periods that did are Caledonian and Armorican.
Plates meet in only three ways: they move apart, move together or slide past each other. Each way has a name, and exams use all the synonyms, so learn them together.
Constructive (also called divergent or separating) boundaries: plates move apart and crust is created, because magma fills the gap.
Destructive (also called convergent or colliding) boundaries: plates move together and crust is destroyed, because one plate sinks into the mantle, or modified where two continental plates collide.
Passive (also called conservative or transform) boundaries: plates slide past each other and crust is conserved, meaning it is neither created nor destroyed, so no magma is involved.
At constructive boundaries plates move apart, and new crust is formed in the gap. The process runs in three steps, driven by the mantle (the hot layer beneath the crust).
1. Convection currents (slow circulating flows in the hot mantle) carry the plates apart.
2. Pressure drops as the plates separate, so the mantle partly melts, producing magma (molten rock).
3. Magma rises into the gap and cools to form new basaltic oceanic crust, basalt being a dark, runny volcanic rock.
Where the plates separate under the ocean, the new crust builds up a long underwater mountain chain called a mid-ocean ridge. This is the main oceanic example of a constructive boundary.

A rift valley (a long valley formed where the crust splits and drops) runs along the crest of the ridge, with frequent shallow earthquakes (earthquakes starting close to the surface) and volcanic activity.
Transform faults (cracks where plates slide past each other) cut across the ridge, so it is offset in sections.
Where a mid-ocean ridge rises above sea level it forms volcanic islands, such as Iceland.
The Mid-Atlantic Ridge also separates the South American and African plates in the South Atlantic.
Iceland is a volcanic island on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, and the rift is visible on land at Þingvellir (Thingvellir).
The Azores are also on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, and the East Pacific Rise is another mid-ocean ridge.
Surtsey, a new volcanic island, formed off the south coast of Iceland in an eruption that began in 1963.
Diagram: cross-section of a ridge showing convection currents, rising magma, the rift valley and arrows showing the plates moving apart.
Constructive boundaries can also start under a continent. Here the land is pulled apart instead of the sea floor, and if the process continues a new ocean can open.
Where a continent starts to split, the crust stretches and a block drops between parallel faults (cracks in the crust) to form a rift valley, with volcanoes nearby.
The East African Rift Valley is where the African plate is splitting apart; Mount Kilimanjaro, Tanzania, is a volcano associated with it.
If spreading continues, the sea floods in and a new ocean begins; the Red Sea, between Africa and the Arabian plate, is at this stage.
These are the landforms and activity to name when asked what is found at a constructive boundary. These features are found where plates pull apart.

Features of constructive boundaries, where plates pull apart, are the mid-ocean ridge, rift valley, volcanic islands, fissure eruptions (eruptions from long cracks rather than one vent) of runny basalt lava, and shallow earthquakes.
Where two plates converge, one plate is forced down into the mantle. Which one sinks depends on the density of the crust.
Oceanic crust is denser than continental crust, so where the two meet the oceanic plate is forced down into the mantle.
This process is subduction, and the zone where the plate sinks is the subduction zone.
Crust is destroyed as the subducting plate melts in the hot mantle.
The place where the two plates meet at the surface is an ocean trench, a deep, narrow valley in the sea floor.

When an oceanic plate meets a continental plate, the denser oceanic plate sinks. This one collision produces a trench, fold mountains, volcanoes and earthquakes, which is why such coasts are so active.
An ocean trench forms where the oceanic plate bends down, because the plate is forced into the mantle.
Sediments (loose material laid down on the sea floor) are scraped off the subducting plate and crumpled against the continent into fold mountains.
Melting of the sinking plate produces magma that rises to form a chain of volcanoes on the continent.
Earthquakes occur along the sinking plate because it grinds past the rock around it, shallow near the trench and deeper inland; this inclined zone is the Benioff zone.
The Nazca plate subducts beneath the South American plate: the Peru-Chile Trench lies offshore and the Andes, with many volcanoes, rise on land.
The Juan de Fuca plate subducts beneath the North American plate, producing the Cascade Range volcanoes, including Mount St Helens, Washington, USA.
Diagram: cross-section with ocean trench, subducting plate, melting zone, rising magma, volcano, fold mountains and earthquake foci (the points underground where earthquakes start).

When two oceanic plates meet, neither is light enough to resist sinking, so one is forced under the other. The result is a trench and a curved line of volcanic islands rather than a mountain chain on a continent.
The older, denser oceanic plate subducts beneath the other, because denser crust sinks more easily.
An ocean trench and a curved chain of volcanic islands, called an island arc, form, and earthquakes are frequent.
The Mariana Trench, about 11 km deep, is the deepest place on earth; it lies where the Pacific plate subducts beneath the Philippine plate, and the Mariana Islands form an island arc.
The Aleutian Islands, Alaska, are an island arc where the Pacific plate subducts beneath the North American plate.
Japan lies where the Pacific, Philippine, Eurasian and North American plates meet.
Continental crust is too light to sink into the mantle, so when two continents meet there is no subduction. The crust has nowhere to go but up.
Both plates are too light to subduct, so the crust between them, including sediments from the ocean that once separated them, is crushed, folded and pushed up into high fold mountains.
Earthquakes are common, but there is little or no volcanic activity, because no plate sinks and melts to make magma.
Crust is modified, thickened and folded, rather than destroyed, because it is too light to sink.
The Indo-Australian plate is colliding with the Eurasian plate, forming the Himalayas and the Tibetan Plateau; the collision began about 50 million years ago and continues.
Mount Everest, 8,849 m, is the highest mountain on earth; for example, marine fossils in limestone near its summit show the rocks were once on the floor of the Tethys Sea.
The Alps formed where the African plate is colliding with the Eurasian plate.

Destructive boundaries shape the land and also cause hazards such as powerful earthquakes, tsunamis and explosive volcanic eruptions. For a discussion of their impacts, give landforms and hazards, each with a named example.
Landforms: ocean trenches, fold mountains, volcanic mountain chains and island arcs, such as the Andes and the Mariana Trench.
Earthquakes: Nepal, 25 April 2015, magnitude 7.8 (a measure of earthquake size), killed about 9,000 people on the Himalayan collision boundary.

Undersea earthquakes and tsunamis (huge sea waves caused by earthquakes under the sea): the Tōhoku, Japan, earthquake of 11 March 2011 had magnitude 9.0; its tsunami killed about 18,000 people (dead and missing) and caused the Fukushima Daiichi nuclear disaster.
The Indian Ocean earthquake of 26 December 2004 had magnitude 9.1 off Sumatra, Indonesia, where the Indo-Australian plate subducts; its tsunami killed about 230,000 people in 14 countries.
Volcanic eruptions: Mount St Helens erupted on 18 May 1980, killing 57 people.
At passive (transform) boundaries two plates slide past each other horizontally along a transform fault. Because nothing is pulled apart or pushed under, no crust is made or lost.
Friction locks the plates until stress builds up, and the stress is released suddenly as an earthquake.
No magma is produced, so there is no volcanic activity, and no crust is created or destroyed.
The plates may move in the same direction at different speeds, or in opposite directions, so both count as sliding past.
The San Andreas Fault, California, USA, is a transform boundary where the Pacific plate moves north-west relative to the North American plate.
The San Francisco earthquake of 18 April 1906 had magnitude about 7.8 and was followed by great fires; the Loma Prieta earthquake of 1989, magnitude 6.9, struck near San Francisco.
The North and East Anatolian Faults in Turkey are transform faults; the earthquake of 6 February 2023 on the East Anatolian Fault, magnitude 7.8, killed over 50,000 people in Turkey and Syria.
Diagram: plan view (looking down from above) of two plates with arrows in opposite directions along a fault line.
Putting the boundary types together shows that the ocean floor is constantly being made and used up. This is the tectonic cycle.
Crust is created at ridges, carried across the ocean floor, and destroyed at subduction zones, so the ocean floor is continually recycled.
Continental crust is too light to be subducted, which is why it survives for so long.
Oceans open and close over time: the Iapetus closed and the Atlantic opened.
This summary pairs each boundary type with its plate movement and what happens to the crust. Exams ask for an example of each, so the examples are added here.
Constructive boundaries: plates move apart and crust is created. Examples: the Mid-Atlantic Ridge and the East African Rift Valley.
Destructive boundaries: plates move together and crust is destroyed, or modified where two continental plates collide. Examples: the Andes, the Mariana Trench and the Himalayas.
Transform (passive) boundaries: plates slide past and crust is conserved. Example: the San Andreas Fault.
Earthquakes, volcanoes and fold mountains are concentrated in narrow belts along plate boundaries, with very few in plate interiors. This is how plate tectonics explains where they occur.
The Pacific Ring of Fire is the belt of destructive and some transform boundaries around the edge of the Pacific plate and its neighbours.
The Ring of Fire, because it follows destructive boundaries, contains about 75% of the world's active volcanoes and about 90% of its earthquakes.
Ridges, subduction zones, collision zones and transform faults are the boundaries where these belts form, because plates interact there.
Fold mountains are found only at convergent boundaries, as long chains along the plate edge; the Andes, Himalayas and Alps are examples.

A volcano is an opening (vent) in the Earth's crust, the thin rocky outer layer, through which magma, gases and fragments escape, together with the landform built around it. Magma is molten rock below the surface; lava is magma that has reached the surface.
Magma chamber: the reservoir of magma beneath the volcano, where the molten rock collects before it rises.
Main vent: the pipe (conduit) that carries magma up to the crater.
Secondary (parasitic) vent: a smaller opening on the flanks (sides) of the cone, which lets magma escape away from the summit.
Crater: the hollow at the top of the main vent.
Cone: the hill of the volcano, built up over many eruptions from alternating layers of lava and ash.
Lava flow: lava moving across the surface away from the vent, such as the flows drawn down the side of the cone.

Diagram: draw a labelled cross-section showing the magma chamber, main vent, secondary vent, crater, cone of alternating lava and ash layers, lava flow, ash cloud and volcanic bombs, with the crust around the chamber.
An eruption throws out liquid, gas and solid material. Each one is a hazard in its own right, so you need to know the names and what each does.
Lava: molten rock that flows from the vent, so it can bury land and buildings around the volcano.
Gases: water vapour, carbon dioxide and sulphur dioxide, which are released as the magma rises and the pressure on it falls.
Pyroclastic material (tephra): solid fragments of rock thrown into the air. It includes ash, lapilli (cinders), volcanic bombs and pumice.
Ash: the finest pyroclastic particles, which are light enough to fall over wide areas.
Volcanic bombs: large lumps of lava thrown out of the vent while still partly molten.
Pumice: a light, porous rock (full of tiny holes) formed from frothy lava.
Pyroclastic flows: fast, very hot avalanches of gas, ash and rock moving down the slopes, so they destroy anything in their path.
Lahars: volcanic mudflows of ash and water, for example when an eruption melts snow or ice.
The silica content of magma (silica is the mineral material that makes rock) controls how runny the lava is, how much gas it traps, and so how the volcano erupts.
Basic (basaltic) lava is low in silica and hot, so it is runny (low viscosity, meaning it flows easily).
Gases escape easily from basic lava, so eruptions are gentle (effusive, meaning lava pours out rather than blasting).
Acidic lava is high in silica and cooler, so it is viscous (thick and sticky).
Acidic lava traps gas, so pressure builds up and eruptions are explosive.

Low-viscosity lava spreads widely and builds shield volcanoes (broad, gently sloping); viscous lava piles up into steep cones. The names and shapes of the landform types belong to the volcanic and plutonic landforms notes.
Volcanoes are grouped by how likely they are to erupt again. The groups depend on how long it has been since the last eruption and whether another is expected.
Active: a volcano that has erupted recently and may erupt again soon. Examples: Mount Etna, Sicily, Italy; Kilauea, Hawaii; Stromboli, Italy.
Dormant (sleeping): a volcano that has not erupted for a long time but could erupt again. Example: Mount Fuji, Japan, last erupted in 1707.
Extinct: a volcano not expected ever to erupt again. Example: Slemish, Co. Antrim, the remains of an extinct volcano, linked with St Patrick.
Most volcanoes lie in narrow belts that follow plate boundaries (the lines where the huge slabs of crust, called plates, meet), not at random. Each type of boundary gives a different result.
Constructive (divergent) boundaries: basic magma rises to fill the gap where plates separate, mostly under the sea along mid-ocean ridges (underwater mountain chains).
Iceland is where the Mid-Atlantic Ridge rises above sea level; the North American and Eurasian plates are moving apart there.
Destructive (convergent) boundaries: oceanic crust is subducted (pushed down beneath another plate), the descending plate melts, and acidic magma rises to form explosive volcanoes.
Destructive boundaries form volcanoes in fold-mountain chains (mountains crumpled up where plates collide), such as the Andes where the Nazca plate is subducted beneath the South American plate.
They also form volcanoes in island arcs (curved chains of volcanic islands) such as Japan and Indonesia.
Continental-continental collision and transform (conservative) boundaries, where plates slide past each other, have few or no volcanoes, so magma rarely reaches the surface there.
A belt of volcanoes circles the Pacific Ocean, because most of the plate boundaries around that ocean are destructive.
The Ring of Fire is a belt of volcanoes and earthquakes around the edges of the Pacific Ocean, mainly along destructive boundaries.
It contains about three-quarters of the world's active volcanoes.
Examples: Mount St Helens (Cascade Range, Washington State, USA); Mount Fuji, Japan; Mount Pinatubo, the Philippines; Krakatoa, Indonesia; volcanoes of the Andes.
A hot spot is a plume of magma rising from deep in the mantle (the hot layer beneath the crust), away from plate boundaries. It explains volcanoes in places where no plates meet.
As a plate moves over a stationary hot spot, a chain of volcanoes forms, with the volcanoes getting older with distance from the hot spot, because each one is carried away from the magma supply.
Hawaii sits in the middle of the Pacific plate over a hot spot, so it is not on a plate boundary. The Pacific plate moves north-west, so the islands get older to the north-west.
The active volcanoes Kilauea and Mauna Loa are on the Big Island in the south-east, over the hot spot.
Other hot spots: Yellowstone, USA; Iceland, which is on a constructive boundary and also over a hot spot.
Ireland has no active volcanoes now, but it had huge eruptions in the past. These were linked to the opening of the North Atlantic Ocean, which is the syllabus's national setting.
Ireland lies in the middle of the Eurasian plate, far from a plate boundary, so it has no active volcanoes today.
About 60 million years ago, North America and Greenland separated from Europe as the Atlantic opened. The crust stretched and cracked.
Basic lava poured out of long fissures (cracks in the ground) in north-east Ireland, flow upon flow, in fissure eruptions. These lavas formed the Antrim basalts.
Basalt is an extrusive (volcanic) rock, meaning it formed from lava on the surface. The Antrim basalts came from fissures, not from a single cone volcano.
Landforms from these lavas include the Antrim plateau and the Giant's Causeway.
Eruptions can kill people and damage land, buildings, travel and even the climate. Named examples show how large the damage can be.

Loss of life, and destruction of buildings, farmland and infrastructure by lava, pyroclastic flows and lahars. In AD 79 Vesuvius, near Naples, Italy, buried the Roman towns of Pompeii and Herculaneum under ash and pyroclastic flows.
In 2018, lava from Kilauea's lower East Rift Zone destroyed hundreds of homes in the Leilani Estates area of Hawaii.
Ash fall can collapse roofs under its weight, for example when thick ash builds up on them, destroy crops and contaminate water supplies.
Ash clouds disrupt air travel. In April 2010 an eruption under the Eyjafjallajökull ice cap, Iceland, closed much of European airspace for about a week, and about 100,000 flights were cancelled.
Volcanic tsunamis (huge sea waves): the 1883 eruption of Krakatoa, Indonesia, caused tsunamis that killed about 36,000 people.
The undersea Hunga Tonga-Hunga Ha'apai volcano, Tonga, erupted on 15 January 2022 and caused a tsunami across the Pacific.

Gases and ash can cool the global climate for a year or two. After Mount Pinatubo, the Philippines, erupted in 1991, sulphur dioxide in the upper atmosphere cooled global average temperatures by about 0.5°C over the following year or so.
Economic losses and evacuation of populations, because homes, farms and businesses are lost and people must leave the danger zone.
Volcanoes are dangerous, but they also give people land, energy, income and materials. This is why many people live close to them.
Fertile soils from weathered volcanic ash and lava, which break down into minerals plants can use. On the slopes of Mount Etna and Vesuvius they support vineyards and orchards.
Geothermal energy (heat from underground) and hot water: in Iceland geothermal energy heats about nine in ten homes and generates electricity.
Tourism: volcanoes, geysers (jets of hot water and steam) and hot springs attract visitors, such as the Blue Lagoon and the geysers at Geysir, Iceland.
Minerals and building materials, such as sulphur, pumice and basalt, which can be quarried or mined from volcanic rock.
New land: Surtsey, an island that emerged from the sea off southern Iceland in 1963.
Mount St Helens is the full case study to learn, with date, place, plate setting, events, effects and response. The eruption was sideways, not vertical, which makes it unusual.
Place: Cascade Range, Washington State, USA. The Juan de Fuca plate is subducted beneath the North American plate, a destructive boundary.
For weeks before 18 May 1980, magma pushed the north flank (side) outwards into a bulge.
A magnitude 5.1 earthquake triggered the collapse of the north flank as a huge landslide.
The collapse released a sideways (lateral) blast that flattened forests.
The summit lost about 400 m of height, leaving a horseshoe-shaped crater.
The eruption did great damage, but the number of deaths was low because people had been kept away from the danger zone.
Ash fell across several US states.
Lahars (mudflows of ash and water) flowed down river valleys, including the Toutle River, destroying bridges and homes.
Most people had been kept out of a restricted zone, which kept the death toll low.
Volcanoes usually give warning signs, because magma must move upwards before an eruption. Scientists measure these signs to judge when a volcano is becoming dangerous.
Seismometers (instruments that record earthquakes) pick up swarms of small earthquakes as magma rises.
Ground deformation: tiltmeters (which measure changes in slope), GPS and satellite radar measure swelling or bulging of the cone.
Gas emissions: changes in the amount and type of gas, especially sulphur dioxide.
Temperature: thermal imaging and satellites detect heating of the ground or of crater lakes.
Changes in groundwater and springs, for example because rising magma heats the water underground.
Studying the deposits and records of past eruptions shows how often a volcano erupts and which areas are at risk. Hazard maps show these areas.
Scientists can often forecast that an eruption is likely, but not its exact time, size or style.
Eruptions cannot be stopped, but their effects can be limited. The main approaches are to watch the volcano, keep people out of danger, and sometimes to fight the lava itself.
Monitoring by volcano observatories, so that warning signs are picked up early.
Hazard zoning keeps settlement out of high-risk zones, so fewer people and buildings are in the path of an eruption.
Evacuation plans and warning systems, and public education.
Diverting or slowing lava flows with barriers and channels, or cooling it with water.

Heimaey, Iceland, 1973: the Eldfell eruption on Heimaey, Westman Islands, threatened the harbour. About 5,000 residents were evacuated overnight, mostly by the fishing fleet. Sea water was pumped onto the advancing lava to cool and halt it, saving the harbour.

Pinatubo, the Philippines, 1991: scientists from the US Geological Survey and the Philippine volcano institute monitored earthquakes, gas emissions and swelling, and forecast the eruption. Tens of thousands of people were evacuated, including from the US Clark Air Base, saving thousands of lives.

An earthquake is a sudden shaking of the ground caused by the release of stress (the squeezing, stretching or shearing force) built up in the crust, the Earth's rocky outer layer. It happens in four steps, which together make a repeating cycle.
1. Plates (the huge slabs of crust) moving past, towards or away from each other lock together by friction, because their rough edges grip and cannot slide.
2. Stress builds up in the rocks around the locked boundary, because the plates keep moving while the edges stay stuck.
3. When the stress exceeds the strength of the rock, the rock fractures or slips suddenly along a fault (a crack in the crust along which rock can move).
4. The stored energy is released as seismic waves, which are vibrations that travel through the Earth and shake the ground.
This cycle of locking, stress build-up and sudden release is called elastic rebound: the rock stores energy like a bent stick, then snaps back.
Foreshocks are smaller tremors before the main shock. Aftershocks are tremors after it, and can bring down buildings already weakened by the main shock.
Four key terms describe where an earthquake starts and how its energy spreads. Learn which is underground and which is on the surface.
Focus (hypocentre): the point inside the crust where the rupture begins, so it is always underground.
Epicentre: the point on the surface directly above the focus, where shaking is usually strongest.
Fault (fault line): the fracture along which the rocks move.
Seismic (shock) waves: waves of energy spreading out from the focus in all directions.
Diagram: draw a cross-section showing the fault, the focus below ground, seismic waves spreading out, and the epicentre on the surface directly above the focus.

Depth matters: a shallow-focus earthquake causes more surface damage than a deep-focus one of the same magnitude (the energy released), because the waves have less rock to travel through before reaching the surface.
Seismic waves travel at different speeds and in different ways, so they arrive at a recording station one after another. Each type has a different effect.
P (primary) waves are the fastest seismic waves, so they arrive first.
S (secondary) waves are slower than P waves and arrive second.
Surface waves travel along the surface, arrive last and cause most of the damage, because they shake the ground and the buildings on it.
Scientists can record seismic waves with an instrument and use the records from several places to pinpoint where an earthquake struck.
A seismograph (seismometer) is the instrument that detects and records seismic waves; the record it produces is a seismogram.
A barometer measures air pressure and is not an earthquake instrument.

Seismic stations (places where seismographs are installed) record the arrival times of P and S waves. The gap between the two arrivals shows the distance to the earthquake, because the waves travel at different speeds.
Three or more stations locate the epicentre by triangulation: each station gives a distance, and the epicentre is where the three distances meet.
Earthquakes are measured in two different ways: how much energy they release, and how much damage they do at a particular place. Two different scales do these jobs.
The Richter scale measures magnitude, the energy released, from the size of the waves on a seismogram.
The Richter scale is logarithmic (each step is a multiplication, not an addition): each whole number up means ten times the wave amplitude (the height of the wave) and about 30 times more energy.
The moment magnitude scale is the modern replacement for large earthquakes. Either scale is an accepted answer for a scale that measures magnitude.
The modified Mercalli scale measures intensity, the observed effects and damage at a place, on a scale of I to XII.
Intensity varies from place to place for one earthquake, because shaking is weaker far from the epicentre; magnitude does not vary, because it is the energy released at the source.

Most earthquakes occur in narrow belts along plate boundaries, the lines where plates meet, because that is where plates lock and then slip. Each boundary type produces a different kind of earthquake.
The Pacific Ring of Fire, the horseshoe of plate boundaries around the Pacific Ocean, has about 90% of the world's earthquakes, including most of the most powerful ones.
Ireland lies in the middle of the Eurasian plate, far from a boundary, so it has only rare, minor tremors.
Where plates separate, the crust is pulled apart and rocks fracture.
Earthquakes are frequent, shallow and generally weaker, because the rock is stretched and breaks before much stress can build.
They occur along mid-ocean ridges (underwater mountain chains where plates move apart) and in Iceland, which lies on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge.
Where one plate is subducted (forced down) beneath another, the sinking plate generates earthquakes at a range of depths.
These are the most powerful earthquakes; foci range from shallow to very deep along the sinking plate.
Undersea earthquakes at subduction zones (where one plate sinks under another) can cause tsunamis, which are giant sea waves.
Where continental plates collide, neither sinks easily, so rocks are crushed and folded into fold mountains (mountain ranges formed by crumpled rock).
Collision boundaries produce powerful, shallow earthquakes in fold-mountain belts, such as the Himalayas.

Nepal, 25 April 2015: magnitude 7.8, from the collision of the Indian and Eurasian plates. About 9,000 people died. Kathmandu was severely damaged, and the earthquake triggered avalanches on Mount Everest.
At transform (conservative) boundaries plates slide past each other. The plates stick, then slip suddenly, which is the locking and release of elastic rebound.
These earthquakes are shallow and often very damaging.
San Andreas Fault, California: the Pacific plate and North American plate slide past each other.
San Francisco, 18 April 1906: magnitude about 7.8, with about 3,000 deaths. Fires from broken gas mains burned for days and destroyed much of the city.
Loma Prieta, 1989: magnitude 6.9, near San Francisco, on the San Andreas system.
East Anatolian Fault, Turkey, a transform fault: on 6 February 2023 a magnitude 7.8 earthquake killed over 50,000 people in Turkey and Syria, and many apartment blocks collapsed.
Primary effects are caused directly by the shaking. They happen during the earthquake itself.
Building and bridge collapse, deaths and injuries, and ground rupture (the ground splitting open along the fault).
Broken gas, water and power lines, and damaged roads and railways.
Secondary effects follow from the shaking, as knock-on hazards set off by the damage it causes.
Fires from broken gas mains and power lines, because leaking gas and sparks ignite easily.
Tsunamis: the Tōhoku earthquake of 11 March 2011, magnitude 9.0 off north-east Japan, sent a tsunami that overtopped sea walls. About 18,000 people were killed or are missing.
That tsunami also caused meltdowns at the Fukushima Daiichi nuclear power plant.
Landslides, as shaking brings down loose slopes.
Liquefaction: saturated soft sediment (soil full of water) behaves like a liquid, so buildings sink or topple.
Christchurch, New Zealand, 22 February 2011: magnitude 6.3, 185 deaths, widespread liquefaction, and the cathedral spire collapsed.
Disease from contaminated water, homelessness and economic losses.
Two earthquakes of the same magnitude can do very different damage. The outcome depends on the earthquake itself, on the ground, and on the people and buildings in its path.
Magnitude: larger earthquakes release more energy.
Depth of focus: a shallow-focus earthquake causes more surface damage than a deep-focus one of the same magnitude.
Rock and soil type: soft sediment shakes more and can liquefy.
Population density, and the time of day.
Building quality and building codes (the rules a building must follow).
Level of development and preparedness: wealth to prepare, respond and rebuild.

Haiti, 12 January 2010: magnitude 7.0 near Port-au-Prince. Poorly built concrete buildings collapsed, and the country, a poor one, had little capacity to respond. Estimates of the death toll vary widely, all over 100,000.
Kobe shows how a moderate-magnitude earthquake with a shallow focus, close to a big city, can be devastating. Begin a case-study answer with the date, place, plate setting and magnitude.
Place: the Great Hanshin earthquake, Kobe, Japan, 17 January 1995. Its epicentre was near the northern tip of Awaji Island, and its focus was shallow.
Magnitude 6.9 on the moment magnitude scale.
Kobe lies near where the Philippine Sea plate is subducted beneath the Eurasian plate. The rupture was on a fault close to the city.
The shallow focus and the closeness of the fault to the city meant strong shaking in a built-up area, and weak points in the city's buildings and ground showed up quickly.
Elevated sections of the Hanshin Expressway toppled over, cutting a major road route.
Many older wooden houses with heavy tiled roofs collapsed, because the heavy roofs sat on weak frames.
Fires from broken gas mains burned large areas, because the shaking broke the pipes.
Liquefaction badly damaged the port, which was built on reclaimed land (land made by filling in the sea, so the ground is loose and wet).
About 6,400 people died, and about 300,000 were left homeless.
Response: the government faced criticism for a slow response. Stricter building codes and retrofitting (strengthening existing buildings) followed.
This was an undersea earthquake at a subduction zone, and the seabed movement triggered a tsunami.
Place: off the west coast of northern Sumatra, Indonesia. Magnitude 9.1.
The Indo-Australian plate is subducted beneath the Burma plate. The seabed was thrust upwards, displacing the ocean and causing a tsunami.
There was no tsunami warning system in the Indian Ocean at the time, so coastal people had no advance alert.
The tsunami crossed the ocean and struck many countries, which is why the death toll was so high.
The worst-hit area was Banda Aceh, Sumatra. Sri Lanka, India and Thailand were also badly hit.
Response: an Indian Ocean tsunami warning system was set up afterwards, operational from 2006.
Earthquakes cannot be predicted precisely: their exact time, place and magnitude are not known. Scientists identify where they are likely and estimate how often they occur.
Mapping active faults and plate boundaries, to show where earthquakes are likely.
Studying the history and frequency of past earthquakes, to estimate how often they occur.
Seismic gap theory: a section of an active fault that has not moved for a long time has the most stored stress and is the most likely to slip next.

Monitoring foreshocks, ground deformation (GPS, tiltmeters and laser measurements across faults), radon gas release and changes in well-water levels. Tiltmeters measure small changes in the slope of the ground.
Unusual animal behaviour is anecdotal (based on reports, not tested evidence) and unreliable as a warning.
Three examples show how prediction and warning have worked, failed, and led to legal trouble.
Haicheng, China, 4 February 1975: after foreshocks, the city was evacuated hours before a magnitude 7.3 earthquake, saving many lives.
Tangshan, China, 28 July 1976: no warning was given, and the official death toll was about 240,000.
L'Aquila, Italy, 6 April 2009: magnitude 6.3, about 300 deaths. In 2012 six scientists and an official were convicted of manslaughter for reassuring the public before the quake.
The scientists were acquitted on appeal in 2014.
Prediction cannot give a time, but warning systems can give a short notice once an earthquake has started or a tsunami has been triggered.
Early-warning systems detect the fast P waves, giving seconds of warning before the destructive waves arrive, because P waves outrun the surface waves.
Those seconds are enough to stop trains, shut off gas supplies and take cover.
Japan has a national earthquake early-warning system.
Tsunami warning systems use seabed pressure sensors and buoys, so that a tsunami can be detected at sea, as in the Indian Ocean system set up after 2004.
Buildings can be designed to survive shaking, which limits deaths and damage. Each measure either stops a building from being shaken or lets it move without breaking.
Deep foundations anchored to bedrock (solid rock below the soil), so the building does not sit on soft ground.
Base isolation: rubber and steel bearings or rollers under the building, so the ground moves beneath it.
Flexible steel or reinforced-concrete frames that sway rather than crack, with cross-bracing and shear walls (extra supports that stiffen the structure).
Counterweights (tuned mass dampers) in tall buildings, which swing against the shaking. Taipei 101, Taiwan, has a giant tuned mass damper, a steel ball hung near the top.
Automatic shut-off valves on gas mains, and flexible joints on pipes, so pipes bend rather than break and gas does not leak.
Retrofitting older buildings, which means strengthening them to modern standards.
Preparing people and places before an earthquake reduces harm even when the earthquake itself cannot be stopped or predicted.
Strict building codes, so that new buildings can survive shaking, and land-use planning that avoids soft ground (which shakes more and can liquefy) and fault lines.
Emergency drills, education and emergency supplies.
Tsunami walls and evacuation routes, so that people near the coast can get to safety, for example in Japan, where the Tōhoku tsunami overtopped sea walls.
Japan holds national Disaster Prevention Day drills each 1 September, the anniversary of the 1923 Great Kanto earthquake.
Magma (molten rock) that rises into the crust cools in one of two ways, and the way it cools decides what landform results. Both ways are endogenic (internal) processes, driven from inside the Earth.
Extrusive (volcanic) activity: magma reaches the surface and cools quickly as lava, ash and other material, building landforms on the surface.
Intrusive (plutonic) activity: magma cools slowly underground, forming bodies of rock that become landforms only when the rock above them is eroded away.
Plutonic features are not formed by exogenic processes (surface processes such as weathering and erosion); erosion only reveals them, because the magma had already cooled into rock underground.
Rock is rarely one solid block. Cracks called joints run through it, and they decide where weathering and erosion do their work.
A joint is a crack in rock along which no movement has taken place, which is what separates it from a fault.
In igneous rock (rock formed from cooled magma), joints form by contraction as the rock cools.
In granite, joints also form by expansion when the overlying rock is removed and pressure on the granite is released.
Weathering and erosion work along joints, so the joint pattern shapes the landform.
Not all eruptions come from a single volcano. When lava escapes along a long crack, it can build a wide, high, flat landform instead of a cone.
1. Basic lava (runny lava that flows easily) pours out of long cracks in the crust, called fissures, rather than from a single vent (an opening in the crust).
2. Each lava flow spreads widely before it cools, because the lava is runny.
3. Repeated flows build up, one on top of another, so the plateau grows higher with each eruption.
4. The result is a high, flat-topped plateau with steep edges.
Example: the Antrim plateau, Co. Antrim.
Diagram: cross-section of stacked lava flows forming a flat-topped plateau with steep edges.
The Antrim plateau is an Irish extrusive example, and the granite Mournes are its intrusive neighbour from the same period. Keep the two apart.
The Antrim plateau is made of basalt (a dark volcanic rock) in layers from fissure eruptions about 60 million years ago, linked to the opening of the North Atlantic.
Along the Antrim coast, dark basalt lies on top of white chalk, which the basalt protected from erosion.
The Mourne Mountains, Co. Down, are granite intrusions (granite is a plutonic rock that cooled underground) of the same period as the Antrim basalts, much younger than the Leinster granite.
Slieve Donard is the highest peak of the Mournes.
Basalt columns form in a lava flow as it cools and contracts (shrinks). They are a joint pattern, not a volcano.
Columnar jointing forms when a thick lava flow cools slowly and evenly, so the whole flow shrinks in a regular pattern.
As the flow contracts, cracks form at about 120° to each other, which is why the pattern is regular.
The cracks produce columns at right angles to the cooling surface, mainly six-sided, because cracks meeting at about 120° enclose six-sided shapes.
Sea erosion exposes the columns on the north Antrim coast, where about 40,000 interlocking basalt columns, most of them six-sided, form the Giant's Causeway, a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1986.
Fingal's Cave, Isle of Staffa, Scotland, has columns from the same volcanic period.
The Giant's Causeway is a cooled lava flow, not a volcano, and its columns did not form from growing crystals.
Diagram: labelled sketch of hexagonal columns standing at right angles to the cooling surface of the flow.
A shield volcano is built by runny lava, which is why it is broad and low rather than tall and steep. Viscosity is how thick a liquid is: low viscosity means it flows easily.
1. Low-viscosity (runny) basic lava flows a long way before it cools.
2. Mostly effusive eruptions (lava pours out steadily rather than exploding) build a broad cone with gentle slopes.
3. Successive flows spread out from the central vent, so the volcano is wide rather than steep.
Example: Mauna Loa and Kilauea, Hawaii.
Diagram: cross-section of a broad, low cone with gentle slopes and a summit crater (the bowl-shaped hollow at the top).
Hawaii is the setting to use for shield volcanoes, with its own record-sized examples and two named lava types.
Hawaii's shield volcanoes sit over a hot spot (a hot area under the crust where magma rises), which is why volcanoes form there.
Mauna Loa is the largest active volcano on Earth by volume, for example, which shows how far runny shield-volcano lava can spread.
Mauna Kea is more than 10,000 m high when measured from its base on the sea floor, so most of it lies under the sea.
Pahoehoe lava has a smooth, ropy surface; aa lava has a rough, blocky surface.
A composite volcano is the opposite of a shield. Its magma is too thick to flow far, so it piles up into a steep cone built of alternating layers.
1. Viscous (thick, sticky) acidic or intermediate magma is too thick to flow far.
2. Explosive eruptions alternate with lava flows, so the cone is built of layers of ash and lava.
3. Over time these layers build a steep cone with a crater at the summit.
4. The cone also has a main vent and secondary vents.
Examples: Mount Fuji, Japan; Vesuvius, Italy; Mount Etna, Sicily; Mount St Helens, USA.
Diagram: cross-section of a steep cone showing alternating ash and lava layers, the crater, the main vent and secondary vents.
The smallest volcanic cone is built from loose fragments blown out in short bursts rather than from flowing lava.
A cinder cone is a small, steep cone built mainly of pyroclastic fragments (rock blown out by explosions) during short, explosive eruptions.
Example: Parícutin, Mexico, which began in a farmer's cornfield in 1943.
Diagram: cross-section of a small, steep cone of loose fragments around a central crater.
Some eruptions are so large that they destroy the volcano's own summit. The result is a huge basin called a caldera.
A caldera is a large basin formed when the summit of a volcano collapses into the magma chamber (the underground reservoir of magma) emptied by a huge eruption.
A caldera is much larger than a crater and forms by collapse, not by explosion alone.
A caldera may fill with water to form a crater lake.
Crater Lake, Oregon, USA: Mount Mazama collapsed about 7,700 years ago, and the caldera now holds the lake.
Kilauea, Hawaii, has a summit caldera.
Santorini, Greece, and Krakatoa, Indonesia, are further calderas; Anak Krakatau has grown inside the Krakatoa caldera.
Erosion can leave a volcano's hardened core behind after the rest of the cone has gone, because the core is harder than the cone around it.
1. Magma solidifies in the vent of a volcano.
2. The softer cone around the vent is eroded away.
3. The resistant plug (rock that resists erosion well) is left standing as a steep-sided hill.
Examples: Slemish, Co. Antrim; Castle Rock, Edinburgh, Scotland, a volcanic plug whose crag-and-tail shape was later shaped by ice.
Diagram: cross-section of a plug standing above the eroded cone.
Volcanic heat underground also produces smaller surface features, where hot water, steam and gas escape without any lava.
A geyser erupts hot water and steam from the ground at intervals.
A hot spring is hot water that rises to the surface and flows out without erupting, so it differs from a geyser.
A fumarole is a vent that emits gases and steam.
Example: Old Faithful, Yellowstone, USA, is a geyser.
Iceland is the setting to use for fissure eruptions, geysers and new islands, and it shows how destructive a fissure eruption can be.
The Laki fissure eruption of 1783 poured out huge lava flows; its gases caused crop failure and famine in Iceland, so the harm came from more than the lava.
Geysir and Strokkur are geysers in Iceland, for example.
Surtsey, a new island formed off southern Iceland from 1963.
Hekla and Eyjafjallajökull are also Icelandic volcanoes.
The biggest plutonic landform is the batholith, a mass of rock that cooled deep underground and only becomes a landform once the rock above it has been stripped away.
A batholith is a huge dome-shaped mass of magma that cooled slowly deep underground into granite.
Heat from the magma altered the surrounding rock into a metamorphic aureole (metamorphic means changed by heat), a ring of altered rock around the batholith, for example mica schist.
When the overlying rock is eroded, the granite is exposed and forms upland areas.
The Leinster batholith is Ireland's intrusive case study. It is the largest granite mass in Ireland and forms the Wicklow Mountains.
The granite intruded about 400 million years ago, during the Caledonian mountain-building period.
It is the largest granite mass in Ireland and runs from south Co. Dublin south-west through Wicklow and Carlow.
The overlying slate was eroded, exposing the granite as the Wicklow Mountains.
A band of mica schist, the metamorphic aureole, surrounds the granite.
The granite uplands have rounded summits, such as Lugnaquilla below.
Lugnaquilla, at 925 m, is the highest mountain in Wicklow.
Magma that is forced between layers of rock, rather than rising to the surface, can bend those layers up or down. Which way the layers bend gives the two features their names.
A laccolith forms when magma is forced between layers of rock, arching the layers above into a dome, so a laccolith bulges up.
Henry Mountains, Utah, USA, are laccoliths.
A lopolith is a saucer-shaped intrusion that sags downwards in the centre, so a lopolith sags down.
Two sheet-shaped intrusions differ only in direction. A sill runs along the rock layers, while a dyke cuts across them.
A sill is a horizontal sheet of magma injected between the layers of rock (along a bedding plane, the boundary between layers), parallel to them.
When exposed, a resistant sill forms cliffs, ledges and waterfalls, because it resists erosion better than the layers around it.
Fair Head, Co. Antrim, is a dolerite sill with columnar jointing.
Great Whin Sill, northern England, carries part of Hadrian's Wall along its crest.
A dyke is a vertical or near-vertical sheet of magma cutting across the layers.
A dyke harder than the surrounding rock stands up as a wall-like ridge because the softer rock erodes around it; a softer dyke is eroded into a trench.
The Isle of Arran, Scotland, has a dyke swarm (a group of many dykes).
Plutonic features end up as high ground because of differential erosion, meaning different rocks wear away at different speeds.
Plutonic rocks such as granite are usually more resistant than the rocks around them, so they wear away more slowly.
Once the surrounding cover is removed, the plutonic rock stands as upland while the weaker rock is lowered, because the weaker rock erodes faster.
Diagram: one block of crust showing a batholith, laccolith, lopolith, sill, dyke and volcanic plug, each labelled.
Devon and Cornwall in south-west England are the international example of granite uplands, parts of one exposed batholith.
Dartmoor and Bodmin Moor are granite uplands, parts of one large batholith exposed by erosion, so they are upland for the same reason as the Wicklow Mountains.
Haytor, Dartmoor, is a tor, a granite outcrop rising above the moor.
St Austell, Cornwall, is a centre of china clay (kaolin) quarried from decomposed granite.

Sedimentary rocks are built up in layers, and the boundaries between those layers decide how the rock later breaks and wears away. That is why landforms in layered rock start with strata and bedding planes.

Sedimentary rocks are laid down in layers called strata, or beds, formed by deposition (sediment settling out) followed by compaction (squeezing together) and cementation (minerals gluing the grains).
A bedding plane is the boundary between one layer and the next; when the layers are laid down, bedding planes are roughly horizontal.
A bedding plane marks a pause or change in deposition, which is why neighbouring layers can differ.
Bedding planes divide the rock into layers, and each layer may differ in thickness and resistance (how well it stands up to erosion).
Layers are cut by cracks as well as by planes between them. These cracks give water and ice a way into the rock.
A joint is a crack in rock along which no movement has taken place, so the rock on either side has not slid past.
Joints in sedimentary rock are at right angles to the bedding planes, so they are vertical (across the layers) where the strata are horizontal.
Joints form as sediment dries and shrinks, and by stress and the removal of overlying rock.
Bedding planes and joints together divide the rock into blocks.
Earth movements can tilt layers that were laid down flat. The landform that results depends on how far and in which direction the strata tilt.
Dip is the angle at which strata tilt from the horizontal; the dip direction is the way they tilt.
Strike is the direction along a tilted layer's surface, at right angles to the dip.
Strata are horizontal, gently dipping or steeply dipping, and the landform depends on which, so you must state the attitude (tilt) of the layers when explaining a landform.
Bedding planes and joints are gaps in otherwise solid rock. Erosion does not attack the rock evenly but follows them.
Water, ice and weathering (the breakdown of rock in place) exploit bedding planes and joints as lines of weakness, because they can get into the rock there.
Rock breaks into blocks along these planes, so erosion is concentrated there.
Layers in a rock are not equally tough. Differential erosion means different layers wear away at different rates.
Where resistant layers, such as sandstone and limestone, alternate with weak layers, such as shale and clay, the weak layers are worn away faster.
The resistant layers are left standing out as cliffs and caps, because the soft rock around them has been removed.
Rock layers also differ in whether water can pass through them. This controls where water sinks underground and where it comes back to the surface.
Water passes down joints and bedding planes in permeable (or pervious) rock, which lets water through.
Water flows over impermeable rock instead, because it cannot soak in.
A spring emerges where a permeable layer lies on an impermeable one, because the water sinking through the top layer is stopped by the layer below. The line of springs is a spring line.
A plateau (a flat-topped upland) forms in layered rock. It needs horizontal strata with a tough layer on top.
1. Horizontal strata have a resistant cap rock (the tough top layer) lying above weaker layers.
2. Erosion strips the weaker layers beneath the cap and wears back the edges of the upland, because weak rock wears away faster than the cap.
3. The cap protects the layers beneath, so the top stays flat and the edges stay steep.
Diagram: cross-section of a flat-topped upland with a resistant cap, cliffed edges and weaker strata below.
When horizontal layers of hard and soft rock alternate several times, the plateau edge is not one cliff but a staircase.
Alternating hard and soft horizontal layers erode at different rates, because the hard rock resists erosion and the soft rock does not.
Hard layers form cliffs; soft layers form gentler slopes, often covered by scree (loose broken rock fragments), because the soft rock wears down more easily.
The profile of cliff and slope repeats for each pair of hard and soft layers.

This is the Irish setting for landforms of horizontal strata. Near-horizontal Carboniferous strata (rocks laid down in the geological period of that name) of limestone, shale and sandstone form flat-topped uplands with steep cliffed edges and stepped slopes.
The Dartry Mountains and Cuilcagh span Co. Sligo, Co. Leitrim, Co. Cavan and Co. Fermanagh.
Caves and karst features (the landscape of limestone shaped by water) lie in the limestone beneath the uplands.
Benbulben, part of the Dartry Mountains, shows a resistant cap above weaker rock in one clear profile.
Benbulben, at 526 m, is a flat-topped mountain of near-horizontal strata.
A resistant limestone cap forms its vertical cliffs, because the cap resists erosion.
Weaker shale beneath forms the lower, gentler slopes, partly covered in scree.
Cuilcagh has three rock types stacked on one another, so its profile is stepped rather than a single cliff.
Cuilcagh, at 665 m, is the highest point in both Co. Cavan and Co. Fermanagh.
A resistant sandstone cap lies over shale, which lies over limestone, giving a stepped profile and a flat summit ridge.
The Shannon Pot, the source of the River Shannon, lies at the foot of Cuilcagh in Co. Cavan.
The Marble Arch Caves, Co. Fermanagh, lie in the limestone beneath it.
If erosion keeps working at a plateau, the plateau does not stay in one piece. It is cut into smaller flat-topped hills.
1. Weathering and erosion work back the edges of a plateau.
2. The plateau is broken into separate flat-topped remnants (the parts left behind), each capped by the resistant rock.
3. A mesa is wider than it is high; a butte is a smaller, narrower remnant.
Example: Monument Valley, on the Arizona–Utah border, USA.
Diagram: cross-section of a mesa and a butte, each with a resistant cap.
When strata tilt gently rather than lie flat, a resistant layer makes a ridge with one steep side and one gentle side. This ridge is an escarpment, or cuesta.
1. On gently dipping strata, a resistant layer is exposed at the surface.
2. Erosion cuts a steep scarp slope across the edges of the layers, because the cut ends of the resistant layer are exposed there.
3. The layers continue along the tilt as a long, gentle dip slope.
4. The weaker rock between cuestas is eroded into a vale (a low valley floor).
Example: the Cotswolds, England, a limestone cuesta with a steep west-facing scarp and a long dip slope to the east.
Diagram: cross-section of a cuesta showing scarp slope, dip slope and vale.
If the strata dip steeply instead of gently, the same process gives a different shape.
A hogback forms on steeply dipping strata.
It is a narrow ridge whose scarp and dip slopes are of nearly equal steepness, unlike a cuesta, where one slope is steep and the other gentle.
Example: the Hog's Back, Surrey, England, a narrow chalk ridge.
Bedding planes and joints also shape smaller features. These are named here as effects of the structures; how each forms is taught elsewhere.
Joints and bedding planes in limestone give limestone pavement, with blocks called clints separated by grikes (the gaps between them).
Caves form along bedding planes in limestone.
Waterfalls form over horizontal cap rock.
Sea caves and arches form along joints on the coast.
The Paris Basin is the international example of gently dipping strata. It is a saucer-shaped basin of sedimentary layers of different resistance, dipping gently in towards Paris.
The layers are limestone, chalk and clay.
Paris lies near the centre of the basin.
On the eastern side, resistant layers form outward-facing escarpments (cuestas), with dip slopes facing in towards Paris.
Clay vales lie between the escarpments, because the weaker clay is worn away faster.
The Brecon Beacons are a second international example of gently dipping strata, this time in sandstone.
Gently dipping Old Red Sandstone forms flat-topped summits.
The summits have steep north-facing escarpments and gentle south-facing dip slopes.
Pen y Fan, at 886 m, is the highest peak in southern Britain.
The area was renamed Bannau Brycheiniog National Park in 2023.

Plate movement at boundaries (the lines where the Earth's crustal plates meet) puts the rock of the crust under stress, meaning a force that squeezes, stretches or drags it. Three kinds of stress occur, and each produces a different structure.
Compression (pushing together) produces folds and reverse or thrust faults. It occurs where plates converge, meaning move towards each other.
Tension (pulling apart) produces normal faults. It occurs where plates diverge, meaning move away from each other.
Shearing (sliding past) produces tear, or strike-slip, faults. It occurs where plates slide past each other.
Rock bends into folds when compressed slowly, especially when it is deep, hot and under pressure, because rock in those conditions can flex instead of snapping.
Rock breaks, forming faults (fractures along which rock has moved), when stress is sudden or the rock is brittle, because brittle rock cannot bend without cracking.
Folding is the first of the structures of deformation (changes to rock layers caused by stress). It starts with compression, and the folds that result have named parts you must be able to label.
Compression is horizontal pressure that squeezes layers of rock into a shorter distance, so they buckle into folds. This is the short definition to give if asked.
An anticline is an upfold: layers are pushed upwards into an arch. A helps you remember: A for apex.
A syncline is a downfold: layers are pushed downwards into a trough (a U-shaped dip).
The limbs are the sides of a fold; the axis is the line along its crest (the top of an anticline) or along the bottom of a trough.
Diagram: label the anticline A and the syncline B.
The more strongly rock is compressed, the more the fold is tilted and distorted. Five types are named, from the gentlest to the most extreme.
Simple (symmetrical) fold: the two limbs dip at equal angles, so the fold looks the same on both sides.
Asymmetrical fold: one limb is steeper than the other, because the compression is stronger from one side.
Overfold: one limb is pushed over the other, because the compression is stronger still.
Recumbent fold: the folded layers lie almost flat, because the fold has been pushed right over.
Overthrust fold, or nappe: the fold breaks along a thrust fault (a low-angle fracture) and is pushed far forward over other rocks.
Diagram: one cross-section sketch (a side-on slice through the rock) for each of the five types, in that order.

Fold mountains are the large-scale landform made by folding. They form when two plates converge and the rock between them is crumpled upwards, so this is the answer to a question on how fold mountains are formed.
1. Sediments (layers of mud, sand and other material laid down over time) are deposited in a sea lying between two converging plates.
2. The plates converge, and the sediments are compressed.
3. The sediments are folded into anticlines and synclines.
4. Continued pressure produces overfolds, recumbent folds and nappes.
5. The crust is thickened and uplifted into long, high ranges parallel to the plate edge.
Diagram: before-and-after cross-sections of the sea floor and the resulting fold mountain.

Fold mountains look different depending on their age, because weathering (the breakdown of rock at the surface) and erosion (the wearing away and carrying off of the broken material) lower them over time.
Young fold mountains, such as the Alps, are high, steep and jagged because they have had little time to be worn down.
Old fold mountains have been worn down by hundreds of millions of years of weathering and erosion into lower, rounded mountains.
Ireland's mountains are old fold mountains, formed by Caledonian folding (north-east to south-west trend: Donegal, Mayo, Wicklow) and Armorican folding (east to west trend: Munster).
Other young fold ranges include the Himalayas, the Andes, the Rockies and the Atlas Mountains of north Africa.
Different rocks wear away at different speeds, which is called differential erosion. In folded land this decides which rocks end up as high ground and which as low ground.
The landform depends on which rocks are exposed by erosion, because hard rock resists wearing away and soft rock does not.
In Munster, resistant sandstone survives on the anticlines as ridges.
Weaker limestone survives in the synclines as valleys.
Drainage means the pattern of rivers in an area. Folded rock shapes it because rivers take the easiest route.
Rivers follow the weak rock along the synclines, because weak rock is easiest to cut into.
Where a river breaks through a ridge, it cuts across it, giving trellised drainage (a pattern of main rivers running parallel with tributaries joining at right angles) and sharp right-angled bends.
Armorican folding produced a landscape of east to west ridges and valleys in Munster, the southern province of Ireland. It shows differential erosion and folded drainage in one place.
Ridges of Old Red Sandstone include Macgillycuddy's Reeks, the Galtee Mountains, the Knockmealdown Mountains and the Caha Mountains.
Valleys of Carboniferous limestone include the Blackwater valley and the Lee valley.
The River Blackwater flows east along a limestone valley, then turns sharply south at Cappoquin, Co. Waterford, to reach the sea at Youghal.
The River Lee flows east to Cork Harbour, following its limestone valley, so it too runs along the folds.
The coastal ends of the valleys in Co. Cork and Kerry were drowned by the sea to form rias (long inlets): Bantry Bay, Dingle Bay and the Kenmare River.
Armorican folding was not equally strong everywhere. The Armorican front marks where it changes from strong to gentle.
The Armorican front is the northern limit of strong Armorican folding, running east to west across Munster.
South of the front, rocks were intensely folded and pushed, or thrust, northwards.
North of the front, folding is gentle, so the rocks there are less crumpled.
The Alps are young fold mountains, high and jagged, formed by Alpine folding. Recumbent folds and nappes, two of the most strongly compressed fold types, are characteristic of them.
Alpine folding resulted from the collision of the African plate with the Eurasian plate.
Recumbent folds and nappes are characteristic of the Alps, which fits the very strong compression there.
Mont Blanc is the highest peak of the Alps.
The Appalachians show what old fold mountains look like. They link back to Ireland's own mountains.
The Appalachian Mountains of eastern North America are old fold mountains, so they are worn down rather than steep.
They were folded in the same mountain-building episodes as Ireland's older mountains, when the two continents were joined.
The Ridge-and-Valley Appalachians show long, parallel folded ridges and valleys, with trellised drainage.
Doming is a different kind of upward bending. Instead of a long ridge of folds, the rock is pushed up into a single rounded shape.
Doming pushes rock layers upwards from below into a circular or oval upfold, by compression or by rising magma (molten rock from underground).
Erosion removes the top of the dome first, exposing older rocks in the centre, because the oldest layers lie at the bottom.
Resistant layers form rings of escarpments (long steep slopes) facing inwards towards the centre.
Drainage flows outwards from the centre in a radial pattern, like spokes of a wheel, because the ground slopes away from the middle.
Example: the Lake District, England, with rivers and lakes radiating outwards from the centre.
The Weald is the worked example of an eroded dome. It is a dome, not a basin, and its escarpments face inwards.
Rock layers in Kent, Surrey and Sussex were pushed up into a dome, an elongated anticline (an upfold stretched in one direction).
Erosion removed the chalk from the top, exposing older sandstones and clays.
The chalk now forms the North Downs and the South Downs, two escarpments that face inwards towards the Weald.
Clay vales (low, wide valleys) lie inside the Downs, and sandstone forms the High Weald in the centre.
