Where rock is too brittle to bend, it breaks instead. A break along which the rock moves is a fault, and the way the rock moves is called displacement.
A fault is a fracture in the crust along which rocks have moved.
Displacement may be vertical (rocks move up or down), horizontal (rocks move sideways), or both.
A normal fault is the fault produced when the crust is pulled apart.
One block slides down the fault plane (the sloping surface of the fracture) relative to the other, so the crust is lengthened.
Diagram: a block sliding down along a fault plane, marked as a normal fault.
A reverse fault is the opposite of a normal fault. Compression squeezes the crust, so the movement along the fault is reversed.
Compression pushes one block up the fault plane over the other, so the crust is shortened.
A thrust fault is a low-angle reverse fault that can push rocks a long way forward, linked to nappes.
Diagram: a block pushed up and over the other along a fault plane, marked as a reverse fault.
In a tear fault the rock moves sideways, not up or down. Shearing, where blocks are dragged past each other, causes it.
Shearing makes blocks move horizontally past each other along a tear fault, so there is little up or down movement.
A transform fault is a tear fault at a plate boundary, so it is where plates slide past each other.
Examples of transform faults: the San Andreas Fault, California; the North and East Anatolian Faults, Turkey.
The rock along a tear fault is crushed and weakened. Erosion works on it, and the sideways movement shifts anything that crosses the fault.
The shattered rock of the fault zone is eroded into a straight valley, because crushed rock wears away easily.
Ridges and rivers are offset sideways across the fault, because the blocks have moved horizontally.
Example: the Great Glen Fault, Scotland, where Loch Ness lies in the straight valley eroded along it.
Ireland has its own tear faults, in Donegal. They show how a fault zone becomes a straight valley.
The Donegal tear faults run north-east to south-west.
Rivers and glaciers have eroded long, straight valleys along them, because the broken rock of the fault zone is easier to erode.
The Gweebarra Fault and the Leannan Fault are two of them; the Gweebarra River valley follows the Gweebarra Fault.
Faulting produces landforms when one block ends up higher than its neighbour. Exams ask for two of these landforms by name.
A fault scarp is a steep slope or cliff where one block has been raised above the other.
A horst (block mountain) is a block raised between two parallel faults, or left standing as the land on either side sinks.
A graben, or rift valley, is a block that sinks between two parallel normal faults, forming a long, flat-floored valley with steep walls, often holding lakes.
Diagram: a fault scarp as a steep cliff between two blocks at different heights.
A horst and a graben form together, side by side, when tension stretches the crust. Both come from the same set of normal faults.
1. Tension stretches the crust, producing normal faults on either side of a block.
2. The central block sinks between the faults, forming a graben.
3. The blocks on either side stand higher, forming horsts.
Diagram: horst and graben shown together in one cross-section, with the normal faults labelled.
Three real examples show a graben, with or without its neighbouring horsts.
The Rhine rift valley, a graben, lies between the Vosges, France, and the Black Forest, Germany, which are horsts.
The East African Rift Valley includes a graben in which Lake Tanganyika lies.
The Central Lowlands of Scotland are a rift valley between the Highland Boundary Fault and the Southern Uplands Fault.
Faults affect the landscape beyond the landforms they build directly.
Faults help to guide the lines of coastlines and drainage.
Earthquakes occur along active faults, meaning faults where the rock is still moving.

Rock is never permanent. It is continually formed, modified, destroyed and reconstituted (built again from the broken pieces), so the three rock types are linked in one cycle. Two sets of forces drive it, one working from inside the earth and one at its surface.
Endogenic (internal) forces, driven from within the earth, form and modify rock through magma (molten rock below the surface), heat and pressure.
Exogenic (external) forces, working at the surface, destroy rock through weathering (breakdown of rock in place by weather) and erosion (wearing away and carrying off of rock fragments).
Deposition (dropping of carried sediment, the loose fragments of rock) reconstitutes rock, because the sediment is later turned into new sedimentary rock.

The cycle is easiest to learn as a circular flow chart in which each rock type is reached from another by a named process. Short-cuts across the circle show that rock does not have to follow the full loop.
1. Magma cools and crystallises (forms crystals as it hardens) to make igneous rock.
2. Weathering and erosion break igneous rock down into sediment, because rock at the surface is attacked by weather.
3. Deposition, compaction and cementation turn the sediment into sedimentary rock, because the layers are squeezed and glued together.
4. Heat and pressure change sedimentary rock into metamorphic rock, because buried rock is squeezed and heated without melting.
5. Melting turns the metamorphic rock back into magma, and the cycle starts again.
Short-cuts: any rock can be weathered into sediment, and any rock can be metamorphosed (changed by heat and pressure) or melted, so the arrows do not all follow one loop.
Diagram: draw a circular flow chart with magma and the three rock types as the nodes, and label each arrow with its process, for example crystallisation or compaction and cementation.
The rock cycle does not run at random. It is tied to the moving plates (the large slabs that make up the earth's crust), which decide where each stage happens.
Rock is created at plate boundaries and at hotspots (fixed points of rising magma), because magma reaches the crust there.
Rock is metamorphosed at collision zones, where plates push together and the heat and pressure are great.
Rock is destroyed or recycled at subduction zones, where one plate sinks beneath another and the rock melts back into magma.
Igneous rock forms when molten rock cools and crystallises. Magma is molten rock below the surface; lava is molten rock at the surface. Where the rock cools decides how big its crystals grow.
Crystal size depends on cooling rate: slow cooling gives large crystals because they have time to grow, and fast cooling gives small ones.
Plutonic (intrusive) rock is igneous rock that cools slowly deep in the crust, so its crystals are large.
Volcanic (extrusive) rock is lava that cools quickly at the surface, so its crystals are small.
Uses: granite is used as building stone, kerbs, worktops and headstones; basalt is crushed for road chippings and aggregate (crushed stone used in construction).
Granite is a plutonic rock. When magma pushes into surrounding rock and cools there, it forms masses called intrusions, and their shape gives them different names.
Granite is a plutonic rock built from quartz, feldspar and mica crystals, which are large enough to see because the magma cooled slowly.
Batholiths are huge dome-shaped masses of plutonic rock.
Dykes are vertical intrusions that cut across the beds (layers) of the rock around them.
Sills are horizontal intrusions that lie along bedding planes (the horizontal surfaces between layers).
Plutonic rock reaches the surface only after the rock above it has been eroded away, because it formed deep underground.
Volcanic rock forms at the surface, so it cools fast. Which kind forms depends on the plate setting, the tectonic setting, in which the magma reaches the crust.
Basalt is the commonest volcanic rock and forms from runny lava, which flows easily before it sets.
Basalt forms at constructive (divergent) boundaries, where plates move apart, and at hotspots.
Andesite and granite batholiths form above subduction zones at destructive boundaries, where one plate sinks beneath another.
Sedimentary rock is formed from sediment laid down in layers (strata), usually in seas, lakes, river basins and deserts. Loose sediment then has to be turned into solid rock.
Sediment comes from weathered and eroded fragments of older rock, from the remains of plants and animals, or from minerals precipitated from water (that is, coming out of solution as solids).

Sediment builds up in subsiding basins (areas of sinking land), on continental shelves (the shallow sea floor around a continent) and along trailing (passive) margins, where no plate boundary lies at the coast.
Lithification is the conversion of loose sediment into solid rock by compaction and cementation.
Compaction: the weight of overlying layers squeezes out water and air, packing the grains together.
Cementation: minerals such as silica, calcite and iron oxide, carried by groundwater, bind the grains together like glue.
Because sedimentary rock is laid down in layers from material at the earth's surface, it often contains fossils and shows bedding planes.
Many sedimentary rocks contain fossils, the remains or traces of past life, because living things were buried in the sediment.
Bedding planes are horizontal surfaces separating one layer from the next.
Joints are vertical cracks that cut through the layers.
Many sedimentary rocks are porous, holding water in the spaces between grains. Porous is not the same as permeable (letting water pass through).
Sedimentary rocks are sorted into three groups by the material they are made from.
Clastic rocks are made of broken fragments: sandstone from sand, and shale from mud and clay.
Organic rocks are made of the remains of living things: limestone from the shells and skeletons of sea creatures, and coal from plant remains that accumulated in swamps.
Chemical rocks form from minerals that come out of solution: rock salt and other evaporites form as seawater evaporates and leaves its dissolved minerals behind.
Each Irish sedimentary rock records the conditions in which it formed, such as the climate and the setting at that time. For a longer answer, give the conditions as well as the rock and its place.

Carboniferous limestone (Carboniferous period, about 360 to 300 million years ago) formed when Ireland lay near the equator under a warm, shallow, clear sea, where shells and skeletons built up the deposit. It covers most of the central lowland and forms the Burren, Co. Clare.
Old Red Sandstone (Devonian period) formed in hot, semi-arid (very dry) conditions from sand and pebbles laid down by rivers; its red colour comes from iron oxide.
Old Red Sandstone forms the Macgillycuddy's Reeks, the Galtees and the Comeraghs.
Shale and sandstone of the Cliffs of Moher, Co. Clare, are layers of shale, siltstone and sandstone.
Chalk lies beneath the basalt along the Antrim coast, so the chalk is the older rock and the lava flowed over it.
Coal at Arigna, Co. Roscommon, and Castlecomer, Co. Kilkenny, formed from plant remains in swamps; both are former coal-mining areas.
Rock salt is mined at the Kilroot salt mine, near Carrickfergus, Co. Antrim.
Metamorphic rock forms when existing rock is changed by great heat and/or pressure without melting. The original rock is called the parent rock.
The two factors that cause metamorphism are heat and pressure.
Minerals recrystallise (re-form as new crystals) while the rock stays solid, so the rock usually becomes harder and denser.
The rock may develop banding or cleavage (a tendency to split along flat surfaces).
Metamorphism happens on two scales, depending on whether the heat and pressure come from a single intrusion or from the movement of plates.
Thermal (contact) metamorphism: rock beside an igneous intrusion is baked by its heat, forming a ring of altered rock called a metamorphic aureole; it is small in scale.
Regional metamorphism: heat and pressure act over huge areas during plate collision and mountain building; it is large in scale.
Each metamorphic rock comes from a particular parent rock, and the pairs can be asked either way round.
Limestone becomes marble; Connemara marble is green and is quarried in Connemara, Co. Galway.
Sandstone becomes quartzite, so the parent of quartzite is a sedimentary rock.
Shale (mudstone) becomes slate, and with more heat and pressure becomes schist, so schist is the more strongly altered rock. Slate is quarried on Valentia Island, Co. Kerry.
Granite becomes gneiss, so gneiss is a metamorphic rock formed from an igneous parent.
Quartzite forms Errigal, Co. Donegal; Croagh Patrick, Co. Mayo; the Great Sugar Loaf, Co. Wicklow; and the Twelve Bens, Connemara.
Mica schist is found in Donegal and Connemara, and a metamorphic aureole of mica schist surrounds the Leinster granite.
Gneiss at Inishtrahull, off Co. Donegal, is about 1.7 billion years old and is the oldest rock in Ireland.
Ireland's rock types form a recognisable pattern across the island, and each reflects an event in its geological past.
Limestone floors the central lowland, and Old Red Sandstone forms the ridges of Munster.
Granite outcrops (shows at the surface) in Wicklow, Donegal and the Mournes; basalt covers Co. Antrim; metamorphic rocks lie in Donegal, Connemara and Mayo.
Plutonic example: the Leinster batholith, the granite core of the Wicklow Mountains, is about 400 million years old and is the largest granite mass in Ireland and Britain.
The Mourne granite, in the Mourne Mountains, Co. Down, is much younger, about 56 million years old.
Volcanic example: the Antrim plateau was built by lava flows about 60 million years ago, as the Atlantic began to open. The Giant's Causeway, Co. Antrim, is basalt columns.
The closing of the Iapetus Ocean during Caledonian mountain building produced the Leinster and Donegal granites and regional metamorphism.

North America has two very different edges. The western edge is an active plate margin, where plates are moving and rock is made and changed. The eastern edge is a trailing (passive) margin, where no plate boundary lies at the coast.
Active western margin: Pacific plates subduct (sink) beneath or slide past North America.
Volcanic rock: the Cascade Range volcanoes, including Mount St Helens in Washington state (erupted 1980), lie above a subducting oceanic plate.
Plutonic rock: the Sierra Nevada granite batholith, California.
Regional metamorphism affects the western mountain belts.
The San Andreas Fault, California, is a transform boundary where plates slide past each other.
Trailing eastern margin: there is no plate boundary at the coast, so there are no active volcanoes.
Because the margin is quiet, thick sediments accumulate on the Atlantic coastal plain, on the continental shelf and in the Mississippi delta.
The Appalachians are old, worn-down fold mountains of sedimentary and metamorphic rock.
Rocks can be told apart by what they look like, and photo questions rely on this. Each rock below has one or two clues that separate it from the others.
Granite: speckled, with large interlocking crystals, because it cooled slowly underground.
Basalt: dark and fine-grained because it cooled quickly; it may form columns, as at the Giant's Causeway.
Sandstone: gritty grains, often reddish or buff, and layered, because it is made of cemented sand laid down in beds.
Limestone: pale grey, and it may show fossils because it is made from shells and skeletons.
Marble: white or coloured, with sparkling crystals and no fossils, which separates it from limestone, its parent rock.
Quartzite: pale, very hard and glassy.
Slate: dark grey, and it splits into thin sheets, which is the cleavage (splitting) that metamorphism can produce.

People take rock, minerals and energy out of the earth's crust, and in doing so they become part of the rock cycle. The syllabus asks you to study one of four options: mining, extraction of building materials (quarrying), oil and gas exploitation, or geothermal energy production.
Extraction removes rock far faster than natural weathering (the breakdown of rock in place) and erosion (the wearing away and carrying off of rock) can, and it exposes fresh rock to weathering.
Extraction creates new deposits of waste, which are stored on the surface, for example spoil heaps (piles of waste rock) and tailings (fine waste left after ore is processed).

People therefore act as an exogenic process (one that works on the surface of the crust from outside): removing rock is the human equivalent of erosion, and dumping waste is the human equivalent of deposition.

Mining removes valuable minerals from the crust. The method depends on how deep the ore (rock containing a metal worth extracting) lies, and the ore must then be processed to separate the useful mineral from the rest.
Mined materials include, for example, metal ores (zinc, lead, copper, gold), coal and salt.

Ore bodies form where minerals are concentrated by igneous activity (the movement and cooling of magma) or by hot fluids moving through rock, which is why ore is found in particular places rather than everywhere.
Exploration comes first, so money is not wasted on a poor site: geological surveys and test drilling show whether the ore is worth mining before a mine is developed.
Open-cast (open-pit) mining removes the overburden (the soil and rock lying above the ore) and works ore that lies near the surface, because digging down from above is cheapest there.
Underground (shaft) mining is used because deep ore cannot be reached from the surface; it goes through shafts and tunnels; room and pillar is one underground method.
Processing crushes and grinds the ore and separates the mineral from the waste rock.
Waste rock is stored in spoil heaps, and fine waste, called tailings, is stored in tailings ponds.
A named case study with specific facts carries a mining answer. Learn one Irish mine, one open-pit mine abroad, and Aberfan as an example of what can go wrong with mining waste.

Tara Mines, Navan, Co. Meath: an underground zinc and lead mine, Europe's largest zinc mine, in production since 1977 and owned by the Swedish company Boliden; the ore lies in Carboniferous limestone (limestone formed in the Carboniferous period).
Bingham Canyon copper mine, Utah, USA: one of the largest open-pit mines in the world.
Super Pit gold mine, Kalgoorlie, Western Australia: a large open-pit gold mine.

Aberfan, south Wales, 21 October 1966: a colliery (coal mine) spoil tip built over springs on a hillside collapsed into the village after heavy rain, burying Pantglas Junior School; 144 people were killed, 116 of them children.
Aberfan was a flow slide of saturated waste, a mass movement process (the downhill movement of loose material under gravity).
Mining brings real economic benefits, but it also changes the land and water around the mine. A good answer gives both sides.
Landscape scars and subsidence (the sinking of the ground surface) occur above and around underground workings.
Spoil heaps and tailings take up land, so they remove it from farming or wildlife.

Avoca, Co. Wicklow: centuries of copper mining, now closed, left acid mine drainage (acidic water draining from old workings) that discolours and pollutes the Avoca River with heavy metals (toxic metals such as copper).
Dust, noise and heavy traffic affect people living near the mine, for example on local roads.
Positive impacts are jobs, exports and local spending, so the mine supports the local economy.
Governments and mining companies try to limit the damage, both while the mine runs and after it closes.
Environmental licensing and monitoring control the handling of waste and the quality of water leaving the site, so pollution can be caught and stopped.
Tailings ponds are lined to stop seepage (waste liquid leaking into the ground) and capped (sealed over) when they are closed.
Lisheen, Co. Tipperary: a zinc and lead mine that closed in 2015; the site was rehabilitated (restored to a safe, usable condition).

Quarries work rock and sand close to the surface for cement, aggregate (crushed rock used in concrete), building stone and roofing. This option is called quarrying on the Ordinary Level paper, but it is the same option.
Limestone is quarried, for example, for cement, aggregate and lime for agriculture.
Sand and gravel come from glacial and fluvio-glacial deposits (material dropped by ice and by glacial meltwater) and are used in concrete.
Granite and other dimension stone (stone cut into blocks of a set size) are cut from the rock for building.
Slate is quarried for roofing, such as Valentia slate, and marble for decoration.
Quarrying follows a fixed order, working from the top of the site down into the rock and then preparing the rock for sale.
1. Remove the overburden: the soil and glacial till (the mixed clay and stones left by ice) above the rock.
2. Cut benches (stepped ledges) into the rock face.
4. Crush and screen the rock, grading it by size.
Dimension stone is cut to size rather than blasted, because blasting would shatter the blocks.
Cement is one of the main uses of quarried limestone, and making it links directly back to the rock cycle through the carbon locked in the rock.
Limestone is crushed and mixed with shale, then heated in a kiln (a very hot furnace) to make clinker; the clinker is ground with gypsum to make cement.
Heating limestone releases carbon dioxide, because calcium carbonate gives lime and carbon dioxide.
The carbon dioxide returns to the atmosphere carbon that had been locked in the rock for hundreds of millions of years.
Irish Cement's works at Platin, near Drogheda, Co. Meath, and at Castlemungret, Co. Limerick, are both based on Carboniferous limestone.
Each Irish material has a place you can name. Use these in your answer in place of general statements such as a quarry in Ireland.
Sand and gravel: large pits in glacial deposits around Blessington, Co. Wicklow.
Granite: quarried at Ballyknockan, Co. Wicklow, from the Leinster granite.
Marble: green Connemara marble is quarried in Connemara, Co. Galway.
Slate: quarried on Valentia Island, Co. Kerry.
A quarry sits in the countryside, so its effects fall on neighbours, farmland and water as well as on the rock itself.
Permanent scars, and loss of farmland and habitat, because the ground is removed rather than just covered.
Dust, noise and blasting vibration, and heavy lorries on rural roads.
Lowering of the local water table (the level below which the ground is saturated with water).
Positive impacts are jobs and the materials needed for housing and roads.
Quarries are controlled through the planning system, and the land can be given a new use once the rock is worked out.
Planning permission comes with conditions on working hours, and limits on dust and noise, so neighbours are protected.
Earth banks and trees screen the quarry from view, so it is less of an eyesore.
Worked-out quarries are rehabilitated as lakes, wildlife habitats, landfill or amenity areas (places for public recreation).

Oil and gas are fossil fuels that form from living things buried in sediment, which makes them part of the sedimentary side of the rock cycle. They only become a usable resource where the right rock layers hold them in place.
The remains of tiny marine organisms are buried in sea-floor sediment.
Heat and pressure over millions of years turn these remains into oil and gas.
Oil and gas migrate upward through porous (full of tiny holes), permeable (letting fluids pass through) reservoir rock, such as sandstone.

They are trapped beneath impermeable cap rock (rock that fluids cannot pass through), such as shale, in a trap: an anticline (an upfold of rock layers), a fault (a crack along which rock has moved) or a salt dome (a rising mass of salt that pushes up the layers above).
Finding and producing oil and gas takes several stages. Ireland has two gas fields to use as case studies, and Corrib shows how a project can cause conflict.
Seismic surveys (which use sound waves to map rock layers) locate possible traps, and exploratory wells test them.
Production, which starts once a well finds oil or gas, uses production platforms or subsea wells, with pipelines to an onshore terminal.
Kinsale Head gas field, off the Co. Cork coast: discovered 1971, in production from 1978; Ireland's first commercial gas field; production ended in 2020 when the field was depleted.

Corrib gas field, off the coast of north-west Co. Mayo: discovered 1996, and gas first flowed in December 2015; gas is piped ashore to a processing terminal at Bellanaboy, Co. Mayo, originally operated by Shell.

Opposition at Corrib: the Shell to Sea campaign objected to a high-pressure raw-gas pipeline near homes, and five local men, the Rossport Five, were jailed in 2005 for refusing to obey a court order not to obstruct the pipeline work.
Offshore drilling can go badly wrong. The Deepwater Horizon spill is the international example to learn, alongside the North Sea as a major producing region.
The Deepwater Horizon oil rig, leased by BP in the Gulf of Mexico, exploded on 20 April 2010, killing 11 workers.
About 4.9 million barrels of oil spilled before the well was sealed.
The spill damaged, for example, fishing, tourism and wildlife along the US Gulf coast.
The North Sea, shared by the UK and Norway, is a major oil and gas province (a region with large oil and gas reserves).
Fracking is a newer way of getting gas from rock that does not flow freely, and it is controversial. Like all oil and gas use, it brings benefits and costs that you must weigh.
Hydraulic fracturing (fracking) of shale (a fine-grained rock that traps gas) releases gas; concerns include groundwater pollution and induced earthquakes (quakes caused by human activity).
Ireland banned onshore fracking by law in 2017.
Positive impacts are energy supply and security, revenue and jobs, since a country with its own gas depends less on imports.
Negative impacts are oil spills, damage to marine life and fishing, and conflict with local communities.
Burning fossil fuels returns stored carbon to the atmosphere, contributing to climate change.
Geothermal energy is heat from inside the earth. It is available everywhere deep enough, but it is much easier to use where the heat is close to the surface.
Heat comes from the earth's interior, from radioactive decay (the breakdown of unstable atoms, which gives off heat) and residual heat (heat left over from the earth's formation).
Temperature rises with depth at about 25 to 30 °C per kilometre; this is the geothermal gradient.
Heat is greatest near plate boundaries and hotspots (places where hot rock rises from deep in the earth), where magma (molten rock) lies close to the surface.
Where magma is near the surface, the rock heats groundwater to very high temperatures. This high-temperature (high-enthalpy) system can drive power stations and heat whole towns.
Groundwater is heated by hot rock near magma.
Production wells bring steam and hot water to the surface.
Steam drives turbines (wheels spun by the steam) to generate electricity, and hot water heats buildings through district heating (hot water piped to many buildings from one source).
Cooled water is pumped back down a reinjection well, so the water supply is returned to the ground.
Not every country has hot rock near the surface. Two other approaches use lower heat or create the conditions for heat to be collected.
Ground-source heat pumps use the steady warmth of shallow ground to heat homes. This is the low-temperature type, suited to places far from plate boundaries.
Enhanced geothermal systems pump water into hot dry rock (hot rock with no natural water in it) to fracture it, so that the water picks up heat.
Iceland is the main international case study because geothermal heat is central to its energy supply. Larderello and Wairakei add historical and international examples.
Iceland lies on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge (a plate boundary where plates move apart) above a hotspot, which gives it geothermal heat.
About 9 out of 10 homes in Iceland are heated by geothermal water.
Geothermal power provides between a quarter and a third of Iceland's electricity; most of the rest is hydro (hydroelectric power).
Hellisheiði is Iceland's largest geothermal power station, and Reykjavík has a geothermal district heating system.
The Blue Lagoon is a pool of warm, mineral-rich waste water from the Svartsengi power station, now a tourist attraction.
Larderello, Tuscany, Italy: the world's first geothermal electricity (1904) and first commercial geothermal power station (1913).
Wairakei, New Zealand: geothermal power station opened in 1958.
Ireland is far from a plate boundary, where geothermal heat is greatest, so its geothermal potential is low-temperature only.
Ireland is far from a plate boundary, so it has only low-temperature geothermal potential.
Warm springs at Mallow, Co. Cork, show that heated groundwater exists.
Ground-source heat pumps are the main use, because they need only shallow ground, for example for heating homes.
Geothermal energy is clean and dependable, but it can only be used in suitable places and brings some problems of its own.
Advantages: renewable (it does not run out), low carbon emissions, reliable because it does not depend on the weather, and cheap to run once built.
Disadvantages: it is limited to suitable locations, and drilling costs are high.
Hydrogen sulphide gas is released, giving a rotten-egg smell.
Minerals are deposited in pipes as the hot water cools.
Basel, Switzerland: an enhanced geothermal project triggered small earthquakes in 2006 and was abandoned.
Rock at the surface is attacked by weather, water, plants and animals. Weathering is the first step in wearing landscapes down, and it must be kept separate from erosion.

Weathering is the breakdown of rock in place (in situ) at or near the earth's surface, by weather, water, plants and animals. Erosion is the wearing away and removal of material by a moving agent such as a river, the sea, ice or wind.

Weathering involves no transport: the rock breaks down where it lies, so no moving agent is involved. This prepares the rock for erosion and for mass movement (the downhill movement of loose material under gravity).
Regolith is the layer of loose, weathered rock fragments lying on top of solid bedrock (the unbroken rock beneath).
Physical (mechanical) weathering breaks rock into smaller pieces without changing its minerals (the chemical substances the rock is made of).
Chemical weathering changes or dissolves the minerals in the rock, so the rock itself is altered, not just broken.
Biological weathering by plants and animals works through both physical and chemical means.

Freeze-thaw action, also called frost shattering, is a physical weathering process. It needs temperatures that move above and below 0 °C often, together with water and jointed rock (rock with natural cracks called joints).
1. Water enters cracks and joints in the rock.
2. At night the water freezes and expands by about 9%, which widens the crack.
3. By day the ice thaws, and the water seeps deeper into the crack.
4. Repeated cycles of freezing and thawing split off angular (sharp-edged) fragments.

It is most effective on mountains in upland Ireland, on high mountains and in periglacial areas (cold areas where the ground is frozen for much of the year). Freeze-thaw is active on Irish mountain summits such as Carrauntoohil, Co. Kerry.
Result: scree (talus) slopes of angular fragments at the foot of mountain cliffs, and jagged peaks and blockfields (areas covered in broken angular rock).
In hot deserts the rock surface swings between hot days and cold nights. Both processes here are physical weathering driven by that heating and cooling, called insolation (heating by the sun).
Exfoliation, or onion weathering, is an insolation process in hot deserts such as the Sahara, where the daily temperature range (the gap between day and night temperature) is large.
The outer layer of rock heats and expands by day, and cools and contracts at night more than the interior, because rock conducts heat poorly.
Stress builds up, and curved outer sheets peel off like the layers of an onion, leaving rounded boulders.
Many geographers stress that some moisture, such as dew, must be present for exfoliation to work effectively.
Granular disintegration: dark and light minerals in a rock such as granite heat and expand at different rates, so individual grains loosen and fall away, leaving gravelly sand.
Rock can also break because the forces on it change, or because growing crystals push it apart. Neither process changes the minerals, so both are physical.

Pressure release (also called unloading or sheeting): when the overlying rock is eroded, the weight pressing on buried rock such as granite is removed, so it expands upward and cracks into sheets parallel to the surface.
The sheets peel off to leave domes, such as Half Dome, Yosemite, California, USA, a granite dome shaped by sheeting.
Salt crystallisation: salt water enters pores (tiny holes) and cracks; as it evaporates, salt crystals grow and force the rock apart.
Salt crystallisation is common in hot deserts and on coasts, where salt water is available and evaporates.
Plants and animals break rock down in two ways. Their physical action is a form of physical weathering, and the acids they produce cause chemical weathering.
Physical: plant roots grow into cracks and widen them, and burrowing animals expose fresh rock to weathering.
Chemical: decaying plants produce humic acids, and lichens and mosses release acids that attack rock surfaces.
Carbonation is a chemical weathering process. It dissolves limestone, and it works along joints and bedding planes (the flat surfaces between layers of rock).
Rainwater absorbs carbon dioxide from the air and soil to form weak carbonic acid.
The acid reacts with calcium carbonate in limestone to form calcium bicarbonate, which is soluble, so it is carried away in solution (dissolved in water).
Word equation: calcium carbonate + water + carbon dioxide gives calcium bicarbonate.
Carbonation is the process behind karst (distinctive limestone scenery); it operates on the Carboniferous limestone of the Burren, Co. Clare.
Four more chemical processes each work on different minerals. Each changes or dissolves the mineral, so each is chemical weathering.

Hydrolysis: water reacts with feldspar (a mineral in granite) and turns it into clay (kaolin, or china clay); the quartz grains (another mineral in granite) are left as sand, and the granite crumbles.
China clay from the hydrolysis of granite is quarried around St Austell, Cornwall, England, and on the edge of Dartmoor.
Oxidation: oxygen dissolved in water reacts with iron in the rock to form iron oxide (rust), which gives red, yellow or brown colours and weakens the rock.
Hydration: some minerals absorb water and swell, setting up stress in the rock; anhydrite, for example, becomes gypsum.
Solution: some minerals, such as rock salt, dissolve directly in water.
Weathering does not act at the same speed or in the same way everywhere. Climate decides which type of weathering dominates, and rock type decides how vulnerable the rock is.
Climate: temperature and rainfall decide which type of weathering dominates.
Warm, wet climates favour fast chemical weathering because, by Van 't Hoff's rule, the rate of chemical reactions roughly doubles for every 10 °C rise in temperature.
Cold climates with temperatures around freezing favour freeze-thaw, and hot deserts favour exfoliation and salt crystallisation.
Ireland's mild, wet climate favours chemical weathering, with freeze-thaw on mountain tops.
Rock type (its mineral composition): limestone is vulnerable to carbonation, granite to hydrolysis, and quartzite (a very hard rock) resists both.
Beyond climate and rock type, four more factors affect how quickly rock weathers. Most work by letting water reach the rock or by exposing fresh rock.
Rock structure: joints, bedding planes and faults (breaks in the rock where blocks have moved) let water in, so heavily jointed rock weathers faster.
Vegetation and soil cover: roots and humic acids speed weathering, and soil holds moisture against the rock.
Time: older surfaces are more weathered, because weathering has had longer to act.
Relief (the steepness and shape of the land): steep slopes remove debris and expose fresh rock to weathering.
Aspect (the direction a slope faces): shady slopes stay frozen longer, so freeze-thaw is stronger on them.
Temperature links the processes above. It matters in two different ways, and the type of weathering that results depends on the temperature pattern of the place.
Temperature acts in two ways: as a trigger, through the expansion and contraction that cause stress, and as a control on the rate of chemical reactions.
Freeze-thaw depends on temperature crossing the freezing point, and exfoliation and granular disintegration depend on a large daily range; both need changes in temperature, not just warmth.
Warmth speeds the chemical reactions of carbonation and hydrolysis, so the same temperature can favour chemical weathering in one place and freeze-thaw in another.
Method: name the process and its type, state the temperature condition it needs, explain the stress or rate change it produces, and link this to the result, such as scree from freeze-thaw.

Karst is a landscape on limestone shaped mainly by solution (rock dissolving in water), with few surface streams and many underground features. The name comes from the Kras plateau of Slovenia. Limestone suits this because of its chemistry and the way water moves through it.

Limestone is calcium carbonate, which dissolves in weak acid. Carbonation: rainwater containing carbon dioxide forms weak carbonic acid, which reacts with the rock to form soluble calcium bicarbonate: CaCO3 + H2O + CO2 gives Ca(HCO3)2.
Permeable rock lets water pass through it, mainly along cracks. Porous rock has tiny spaces between its grains that can hold water. Impermeable rock lets no water pass through.
Limestone is permeable because water moves along its bedding planes (horizontal layers) and joints (vertical cracks), not through the solid rock itself.

The ground water table is the upper surface of the zone where all cracks in the rock are saturated (completely full of water). Above it lies the zone of aeration (where cracks hold air). The table rises in wet weather and falls in dry weather.
Percolation is the downward movement of water through soil and rock, which is how rainwater reaches the limestone's cracks.
Limestone pavement is a bare, flat limestone surface. It exists because glacial ice scraped away the soil, leaving jointed rock open to the rain.
Stage 1: ice removes the soil cover, exposing the jointed and bedded rock (rock with horizontal layers and vertical cracks) to rain.
Stage 2: carbonation, the reaction of the rock with carbonic acid in rainwater, widens the joints into grikes.
Stage 3: the blocks left standing between the grikes are clints, because the rock there was not dissolved away.
Burren, Co. Clare: Ireland's best-known karst landscape, of Carboniferous limestone with extensive pavement of clints and grikes. Its name comes from the Irish 'Boireann', meaning rocky place.
Mullaghmore is a Burren hill with folded, terraced limestone.
A pavement is made of a few small features, and exam photographs ask you to name each one.
Grikes: deep, narrow vertical cracks, because carbonation widens the rock along joints, where water collects.
Clints: flat-topped blocks of limestone between grikes, so together they look like paving.
Karren (runnels): small grooves cut into clint surfaces because rainwater running across them slowly dissolves the rock.
Solution hollows (kamenitza or solution pans): small enclosed hollows on clint surfaces where rainwater collects and dissolves the rock.
Diagram: plan of clints and grikes; cross-section showing bedding planes and joints in the rock.
Once water can sink into limestone, the surface develops holes and hollows where streams vanish or the ground dissolves or collapses.
Swallow hole (slugga): a surface stream flowing off impermeable rock reaches limestone and disappears underground down a hole widened by carbonation along a joint.
Doline (sinkhole): a hollow formed by solution of the surface, or by collapse of a cave roof. A doline formed by cave collapse is still a doline.
Uvala: several dolines merged into one larger hollow, as their edges dissolve or collapse into each other.
Polje: a large, flat-floored depression that floods seasonally, for example when water cannot drain away fast enough. Poljes occur in Slovenia.
Dry valley: a valley cut by a surface river when the ground was frozen (and so impermeable, letting water run over it) or the water table was higher. It now carries no stream.
Water that sinks underground can also come back, and in Irish limestone the water table rising and falling makes lakes appear and vanish.
Turlough: a seasonal lake in a hollow in limestone. It fills in winter when the water table rises and drains through the floor in summer.
Turloughs are common in the Burren and east Co. Galway. Rahasane turlough, near Craughwell, Co. Galway, is one of the largest.

River of resurgence: an underground river that re-emerges at the surface, usually where limestone meets impermeable rock below. It is the reverse of a swallow hole, which takes a surface stream underground.
Diagram: cross-section from impermeable rock, through a swallow hole, underground to the resurgence.
Below the surface, the same solution widens cracks in the limestone into hollow spaces that can be large enough to walk through.
Caves and caverns: water dissolves passages along bedding planes and joints, and underground rivers enlarge them by erosion (wearing away rock). A cavern is a very large cave.
Caves occur where limestone is dissolved, for example: Aillwee Cave, Co. Clare (Burren); Mitchelstown Cave, Co. Tipperary.
Doolin Cave, Co. Clare, holds the Great Stalactite, about 7.3 m long, one of the longest free-hanging stalactites in the world.
Cave water carries dissolved limestone, and when it drips it leaves some behind as solid calcite. Over time this builds the decorations seen in caves.
Dripstone formation: water dripping from the roof carries dissolved calcium bicarbonate. When it loses carbon dioxide and evaporates, it deposits calcite (calcium carbonate).
Stalactites hang from the roof and grow downward. Stalactite: C for ceiling.
Stalagmites grow upward from the floor beneath, where the drips land, and are usually thicker and blunter. Stalagmite: G for ground.
Pillars (columns) form where a stalactite and a stalagmite join, so the drip has built a solid link from roof to floor.
Curtains are sheets of calcite formed where water trickles along a crack in the roof.
Diagram: labelled cross-section of a cave showing stalactites, stalagmites, a pillar, a swallow hole and an underground river.
A karst landscape develops through three stages.
Youth: surface drainage begins to sink, so swallow holes form.
Maturity: most drainage goes underground because the swallow holes now take it, with caves, dolines and uvalas.
Old age: cave roofs collapse because so much rock below has dissolved, the limestone is mostly removed, and isolated residual hills (left standing as the rest wears away) remain.
Ireland has three named karst settings in the syllabus. Besides the Burren, they show streams sinking into limestone and water travelling through it unseen.
Marble Arch upland: the Marble Arch Caves lie on the slopes of Cuilcagh Mountain, Co. Fermanagh. They are part of the cross-border Marble Arch Caves Global Geopark with Co. Cavan.
Streams flowing off the impermeable shale and sandstone of Cuilcagh sink into swallow holes where they reach the limestone, flow through the caves and re-emerge as the Cladagh River.
The Marble Arch is a natural limestone arch over the Cladagh. The Shannon Pot, the source of the River Shannon, is on the slopes of Cuilcagh in Co. Cavan.
Mask-Corrib lowland: water from Lough Mask flows underground through the limestone to Lough Corrib near Cong, Co. Mayo.
The Cong Canal, built in the mid-1800s to link the two lakes, never held water because it leaked into the permeable limestone. It became known as the dry canal.
Karst occurs wherever limestone is dissolved, and each international setting is known for a different feature.
Slovenia: Postojna Cave and the Škocjan Caves, a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Poljes occur here.
South-west China: Guilin and the Li River have tower karst, steep-sided limestone hills. The South China Karst is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
Kentucky, USA: Mammoth Cave is the longest known cave system in the world.
Jamaica: Cockpit Country has cockpit karst, steep conical hills separated by deep, star-shaped hollows.
Granite is hard, crystalline and resistant to erosion, and its landscapes reflect how it drains and weathers. Unlike limestone, it keeps water on the surface.
Granite is impermeable: water cannot enter it and runs off, so it has many surface streams and boggy ground.
Granite is jointed (cracked). It weathers mainly by hydrolysis (a chemical reaction with water) of its feldspar, a mineral in granite, which forms clay.
China clay (kaolin) is the clay that results. It is quarried at Lee Moor, on the south-west edge of Dartmoor.
The Leinster batholith, the largest granite mass in Ireland and Britain, forms the Wicklow Mountains.
Its rounded, dome-shaped uplands are worn down from rock that once covered the granite.
Impermeable granite with high rainfall gives thin, acidic soils and blanket bog (a deep cover of wet peat), e.g. on the Sally Gap area of Co. Wicklow.
Ice cut deep valleys into the granite. There is more on this in Glacial processes, patterns and associated landforms (Glaciation).
Tors are the best-known granite landform. The main explanation is that they formed in two stages, with weathering underground first and stripping of the loose material afterwards.
Tor: a block of granite standing on a hilltop.

Two-stage formation, put forward by D. L. Linton in 1955. Stage 1: under warm, wet conditions, deep chemical weathering (hydrolysis) attacked the granite along its joints, rotting it most where the joints were closest together.

Stage 2: the rotted material was later stripped away, e.g. by mass movement (downslope movement of material) under periglacial conditions (cold conditions beside ice), leaving solid, widely jointed blocks standing as tors.
An alternative theory explains tors by freeze-thaw and solifluction alone. Solifluction is the slow flow of waterlogged soil down a slope.
Clitter: blockfields of boulders on the slopes below tors, which is where the stripped blocks ended up.
Dartmoor, Devon, England: a granite upland with tors such as Haytor and Hound Tor, clitter on its slopes and blanket bog.
Diagram: cross-section showing the rotted zone along joints and the standing tor after stripping.
Rock type changes across Ireland, and the landscape changes with it. Resistant rock stands up, weaker rock is worn low, and permeability decides whether water flows on the surface or underground.
Ireland's saucer shape: a low central lowland of Carboniferous limestone is ringed by uplands of harder, more resistant rocks such as granite, quartzite and sandstone.
Differential erosion (different rocks wearing away at different rates): resistant rock forms uplands, headlands and peaks, while weaker rock forms lowlands, valleys and bays.
Quartzite peaks stand above the surrounding rock: Errigal, Co. Donegal; Croagh Patrick, Co. Mayo; the Great Sugar Loaf, Co. Wicklow.
Rock type and drainage: impermeable granite and shale give many surface streams and bog. Permeable limestone takes drainage underground, leaving few rivers and dry surfaces.
Lough Corrib roughly divides the limestone lowland of east Co. Galway from the granite and metamorphic uplands of Connemara to the west.

Slopes are never completely still. Mass movement is the way weathered material shifts downhill, and everything else in this subsection (the processes, the factors and the case studies) is a variation on it.

Mass movement (also called mass wasting) is the downslope movement of weathered material, such as regolith (the loose broken rock and soil that covers solid rock), soil, rock, mud, peat or snow, under the influence of gravity.
No transporting agent such as a river, glacier or wind is needed, because gravity does the work. Weathering (the breakdown of rock where it lies) supplies the material that moves.
Gravity pulls material downslope. Friction (grip between surfaces), cohesion (particles sticking together) and plant roots resist it. Movement happens when the downslope force exceeds the resistance.
Processes are classed, so that they can be compared, by speed (slow or fast), by water content (dry or wet) and by type of movement (heave, slide, flow or fall).

Mass movement is not even across the landscape or through the year. It varies in space and in time, which is the syllabus idea of processes differing in intensity (how strong) and frequency (how often).
In space, it is most intense on steep, wet and unvegetated slopes, because steepness increases the pull downslope while water and bare ground reduce the resistance.
In time, its frequency rises after heavy rain, snowmelt, earthquakes and seasonal freeze-thaw (the repeated freezing and thawing of water in rock cracks).
The slowest mass movement, moving soil by a few millimetres to centimetres a year. It is too slow to watch, so you recognise it from its effects.
Soil particles are lifted at right angles to the slope by wetting (swelling) or by freezing (frost heave, the upward push of freezing ground).
On drying or thawing, the particles drop vertically under gravity, so each cycle moves them a little further downslope.
Evidence: terracettes (small steps on grassy slopes), bent tree trunks, tilted fences, walls and poles, soil piled up behind walls, and cracked roads.
Diagram: draw the zigzag path of a particle, lifted at right angles to the slope and dropped vertically.
Solifluction is a slow flow of waterlogged soil in cold regions near ice. It works because frozen ground below stops water draining away.
In periglacial areas (cold areas bordering ice sheets and glaciers) the surface layer thaws in summer above permanently frozen ground, called permafrost.
The saturated layer cannot drain, because the frozen ground beneath is impermeable, so it flows slowly downhill, forming lobes (tongue-shaped bulges) and terraces.
Solifluction was widespread in Ireland at the end of the last glaciation, when the climate was periglacial.
Rockfall and landslide both move solid rock quickly. The difference is that rockfall is a free fall from a cliff, while a landslide is a slide along a plane.
Rockfall: blocks loosened by freeze-thaw, or undercut by the sea or a river (worn away at the base), fall freely from a steep cliff. They collect as scree (also called talus) at the foot.

Landslide (rockslide): a mass of rock or debris slides suddenly along a flat plane, such as a bedding plane (a layer boundary in sedimentary rock) or joint (a crack) sloping in the same direction as the slope.
Landslides often follow heavy rain, which lubricates the plane so the rock slips more easily, or an earthquake, which shakes it loose.
A slump is a fast slide in which the moving mass turns as it goes, because the surface it slides on is curved rather than flat.
Saturated material, often clay over or under permeable rock (rock that lets water through), slides along a curved (concave) slip plane and rotates backward.
The slump leaves a crescent-shaped scar (scarp) at the top, a back-tilted block and a bulging toe at the foot.
Slumps are common on clay cliffs undercut by the sea, because the sea removes the support at the base, for example on the Antrim coast.
A slump moves on a curved plane. A landslide moves on a flat plane.
These three fast flows each carry a wet or loose mass downhill: mud, volcanic mud, or snow and ice. All are triggered by a sudden supply of water or by disturbance.
Mudflow: fine material (clay, silt, weathered rock or volcanic ash) saturated by heavy rain or snowmelt flows rapidly downhill like a liquid, often along valleys. It can bury settlements.
Lahar: a volcanic mudflow of ash and water, from rain or from melted snow and ice on the volcano. It can travel very fast and far. The word is from Indonesia.
Avalanche: a sudden, rapid slide of snow and ice down a steep mountain slope, triggered by heavy snowfall, rapid thaw or disturbance.
Ice avalanches occur when part of a glacier collapses, such as at Marmolada in 2022.
A bog burst is a fast mass movement of peat, common in the uplands of Ireland. Peat (partly rotted plant matter that builds up in waterlogged ground) on a slope fills with water and then slides.
Blanket bog (a thick layer of peat covering a hillside) on a slope becomes saturated after prolonged or intense rain.
The peat gains weight, and its base loses grip on the underlying mineral soil or rock. The peat bursts and flows downhill as a black slurry.
A bog burst blocks rivers, kills fish, and destroys roads, bridges and land.
Bog bursts are common in the uplands of western and north-western Ireland.
Whether a slope moves, and how fast, depends on a set of factors. The first three are the slope angle, the water in the ground and what the slope is made of.
Gradient (slope angle): the steeper the slope, the greater the downslope pull of gravity and the faster the movement. Gentle slopes favour creep; steep slopes favour falls and slides.
Water content: some water adds cohesion, but saturation fills the pores (the tiny gaps between particles), adds weight, reduces friction and acts as a lubricant, so material flows.
Heavy or prolonged rain and snowmelt trigger most fast movements, because they saturate the slope.
Clay becomes slippery and plastic (easily moulded) when wet. Jointed or bedded rock dipping towards the slope slides.
Permeable rock over impermeable clay or shale (rock that water cannot pass through) concentrates water at the junction, as on the Antrim coast.
The remaining factors either hold a slope together or remove what supports it. Some are natural, some come from the climate, and one is human.
Vegetation: roots bind soil and plants absorb water, so bare slopes move more easily.
Climate and weathering: freeze-thaw loosens rock, heavy seasonal rainfall adds water, and periglacial climates produce solifluction.
Undercutting: erosion by the sea or a river at the base of a slope removes support, so the material above is left unsupported.
Loading: extra weight at the top of a slope, from rock, buildings or spoil (waste rock), increases the downslope force.
Tectonic activity: earthquakes and volcanic eruptions shake loose material and trigger landslides and lahars.
Human activity also affects slope stability. There is more on this in Human interaction: mass movement.
The Antrim coast is an Irish example of landslides and slumps. Its layers of rock, hard on top of soft, explain why the slopes fail.
Location: the Antrim coast between Larne and Cushendall, along the Antrim Coast Road (A2).
Geology: hard basalt lies on chalk, which lies on soft Lias clay with other mudstones.
Rainwater soaks through the jointed basalt and chalk and saturates the clay, which becomes slippery and plastic.
The rock above slumps and rotates seaward in rotational slides, and clay flows out as mudflows. These have repeatedly blocked the coast road.
Garron Point is a classic landslip site on this coast.
Responses, so that the road stays open: engineers have built retaining walls and drainage, and fitted rock-catch fences and netting to protect the road.
Two Irish bog bursts show how rain-soaked peat can fail, one recent and one historic.
Pollatomish (Dooncarton Mountain), Co. Mayo, 19 September 2003: an intense thunderstorm with very heavy rain triggered about 40 landslides and peat slides in a few hours.
At Pollatomish, houses, roads, a bridge and a graveyard were damaged, and several families were evacuated.
Knocknageeha, near Rathmore, Co. Kerry, December 1896: a bog burst swept away a house, killing a family of eight. It is the classic Irish bog burst.
Italy gives two international examples: mudflows after heavy rain at Sarno, and a landslide into a reservoir at Vajont.

Sarno and neighbouring towns, Campania, southern Italy, 5-6 May 1998: after prolonged heavy rain, loose volcanic ash and soil on steep limestone slopes became saturated and slid off as fast mudflows into the towns below. About 160 people were killed.

Vajont Dam, northern Italy, 9 October 1963: a huge landslide from Monte Toc slid into the reservoir (the lake held back by the dam). The wave it sent over the dam destroyed the town of Longarone, killing about 2,000 people. The dam itself survived.
Weak clay layers in the valley side, and the filling of the reservoir which saturated the slope, caused the Vajont slide.
South America gives a lahar triggered by a volcano and mudslides triggered by torrential rain.
Nevado del Ruiz, Colombia, 13 November 1985: a small eruption melted part of the summit ice cap. Lahars rushed down river valleys and buried the town of Armero, killing about 23,000 people.
Warnings had been given, but Armero was not evacuated.
Vargas state, on the coast of Venezuela, December 1999: days of torrential rain triggered mudslides and debris flows on the steep mountains above coastal towns, killing thousands of people.
Recent glacier collapses in the Alps are mass movements of ice, rock and mud. They show glacier retreat acting as a new cause.
Blatten, Lötschental, canton of Valais, Switzerland, 28 May 2025: the Birch Glacier collapsed, sending a huge mass of ice, rock and mud onto the village and burying most of it.
The village had been evacuated days earlier, after geologists detected rockfalls onto the glacier.
The debris blocked the River Lonza, forming a lake upstream, which means a flood risk.
Marmolada glacier, Dolomites, Italy, 3 July 2022: during a heatwave a large section of the glacier collapsed as an ice avalanche, killing 11 people.

Aeolian processes are the work of the wind: it erodes (wears away) rock and soil, transports the material and deposits it elsewhere. Wind only does much work where the ground gives it something to pick up.
Wind erosion is most effective in hot and cold deserts and on coasts. These places have loose, dry, fine material, little vegetation to bind (hold together) the surface, and strong winds.
Air is far less dense than water or ice, so wind can move only sand and finer particles, and mostly close to the ground. Rivers, waves and glaciers can carry far heavier loads.
Wind wears the land down in three ways: it lifts material away, it uses the sand it carries as a tool to cut rock, and it breaks the carried grains down.
Deflation: wind lifts and blows away loose, dry, fine particles (dust, silt and sand), so the land surface is lowered. It works best where there is no vegetation to hold the particles down.
Abrasion (sandblasting): sand grains carried by the wind strike rock surfaces and wear them away. It is most effective within a metre or two of the ground, because that is where most sand is carried.
Attrition: wind-blown grains collide with each other and with rock, so they become smaller, rounder and frosted (dull and scratched, like frosted glass).
How the wind carries material depends on the size of the particles. The finest are lifted high, sand hops along the ground and the largest grains are shoved along the surface.
Suspension: fine dust is carried high in the air, sometimes for thousands of kilometres in dust storms, because the grains are light enough to stay airborne.
Saltation: sand grains bounce along the surface in short hops. Most wind-blown sand moves this way, which is why it stays close to the ground.
Surface creep: larger grains, too heavy to lift, are pushed and rolled along by the impact of saltating grains landing on them.
Deflation lowers the ground and leaves behind whatever the wind cannot lift. Abrasion then cuts at the stones that remain. Together they produce three landforms.

Deflation hollow: a depression formed where deflation removes loose material down to the water table (the level below which the ground is saturated) or to a resistant layer that the wind cannot lower further.
Example: the Qattara Depression, Egypt, lies below sea level and is attributed mainly to deflation down to the water table.
Desert pavement (reg): a surface of closely packed stones left after deflation has blown away the fine material between them. The stones protect the ground below from further deflation.
Ventifacts: stones with flat, polished faces and sharp edges, cut by sandblasting from the prevailing wind direction (the direction the wind blows from most often).
Diagram: plan (view from above) of a deflation hollow; cross-section (a slice through it) of a desert pavement.
Abrasion by wind-blown sand carves larger rock landforms as well. Their shapes depend on how hard the rock is, how it is layered and where the sand is concentrated.
Yardangs: long, streamlined ridges of rock lying parallel to the prevailing wind, separated by grooves abraded in softer rock.
Zeugens: tabular (table-like), flat-topped ridges where a hard cap rock overlies softer rock. They form where the rock layers are horizontal and the joints (cracks in the rock) run across the wind.
Zeugen stages: 1. Abrasion cuts down along joints in the cap rock. 2. The soft rock beneath is undercut. 3. A flat-topped ridge remains.
Mushroom (pedestal) rocks: rock pillars undercut near the base by sandblasting, which is concentrated near the ground.
Mushroom rock stages: 1. A pillar of rock stands on the desert floor. 2. Sandblasting undercuts its base. 3. The top, above the zone of abrasion, stays wide, leaving a mushroom shape.
Diagram: plan of yardangs aligned with the wind; cross-sections of a zeugen and a mushroom rock.
Wind drops its load when it loses energy. This builds the sand and stone surfaces and the dunes of deserts, and in some places thick layers of fertile dust.
Deposition occurs when wind speed drops or the wind meets an obstacle, because slower air can no longer carry the same load.
Desert landscapes: erg (sand sea), reg (stony desert) and hamada (bare rock). The Sahara Desert, North Africa, has all three.
Barchan dunes: crescent-shaped dunes with horns pointing downwind. They have a gentle windward slope (facing the wind) and a steep slip face on the lee (sheltered) side, and they migrate downwind.
Seif (linear) dunes: long ridges roughly parallel to the dominant wind, formed where winds blow from two directions. The Sahara has barchan and seif dunes.
Loess: fine wind-blown dust, often from the edges of former ice sheets or deserts, which forms very fertile soils. Example: the Loess Plateau of northern China.
Diagram: cross-section of a barchan dune showing the windward slope and slip face.
Wind erosion becomes a serious problem when people remove the vegetation that protects the soil. In Ireland the climate limits it.

The Dust Bowl, Great Plains of the USA (including Oklahoma and Kansas), 1930s: ploughing up the natural grassland for wheat, followed by severe drought, left bare, dry soil that strong winds blew away in huge dust storms, known as black blizzards.

Many farming families were forced to leave. The US Soil Conservation Service was set up in 1935 and shelter belts of trees were planted. There is more on this in the notes on Human interaction: mass movement.
In Ireland, the damp climate and vegetation cover limit wind erosion. The main aeolian landforms are coastal sand dunes and blowouts (hollows) where dune vegetation is damaged.
Mass movement is the downhill movement of soil and rock under gravity. People can make it happen more often and faster, or reduce it, depending on how they treat slopes.

Humans make mass movement more frequent and faster in three ways: by removing the vegetation that binds soil and absorbs water, by adding water or weight to slopes, and by removing support at the base of slopes.
Managing slopes can reduce the risk, because the same three factors can be reversed: keep vegetation, keep water out and keep the base supported.

Removing vegetation also exposes soil to rain splash (raindrops knocking soil particles loose), sheet wash (thin water flow over the whole surface), gullying (water cutting channels) and wind, which strip it away. Slopes then become prone to creep, slides and mudflows.
Answers may cover soil erosion as well as mass movement, provided the link to slopes and gravity is made.
Overgrazing means keeping more animals on land than it can feed. It removes the plant cover that holds a slope together, so it is one of the three human activities the syllabus names.
Too many animals for the land's carrying capacity (the number it can support without damage) eat the vegetation down to the roots and trample the ground.
Hooves compact the soil and break the surface of peat, leaving bare patches.
Without roots, soil and peat lose cohesion (the way the particles stick together). Rain runs off the compacted surface or saturates the broken peat, so the ground is both weaker and wetter.
Sheet and gully erosion increase, soil creep (slow downhill movement of soil) speeds up as terracettes (small step-like ridges on a slope) deepen, and peat slides occur.
Sediment from the eroded slopes silts up rivers and damages fish spawning beds.
In Ireland, overgrazing occurred on the hill commonage of the west, where grazing land is shared. A payment system encouraged farmers to keep far more sheep than the hills could carry.

From the 1980s, EU (CAP) headage payments paid farmers per animal, so sheep numbers rose sharply on hill commonage (shared mountain grazing) in western Ireland, including Connemara, Co. Galway, and the mountains of Co. Mayo, Co. Donegal and Co. Kerry.
Overgrazing stripped heather and grass and exposed and eroded blanket peat (a thick layer of peat covering upland ground). Silt then entered rivers, harming salmon and trout spawning grounds.
Response 1: payments were changed from per-head to per-area, so farmers no longer gained by adding animals.
Response 2: Commonage Framework Plans, from the early 2000s, set lower stocking rates (fewer animals per area).
Response 3: REPS (the Rural Environment Protection Scheme, introduced in 1994) paid farmers to farm in environmentally friendly ways.
Each management method tackles the cause of overgrazing: too many animals, or animals staying too long in one place.
Destocking: reducing the number of animals to the land's carrying capacity, so the vegetation is no longer eaten down to the roots.
Rotational grazing, moving animals between areas so that vegetation can recover.
Fencing off degraded ground to let vegetation recover, because the roots can then bind the soil again.
Overcropping means growing crops on the same land too intensively, so the soil is worn out. Weak, bare soil is then easily carried away.
The same land is cropped year after year without fallow periods (rest years with no crop) or fertiliser. Soil nutrients and organic matter are used up, and soil structure breaks down.
Crops grow poorly, the ground is left bare between harvests, and marginal (poor-quality) and sloping land is ploughed.
Loose, dry, structureless soil is washed downslope by rain or blown away by wind, forming rills (tiny channels) and gullies (larger, deeper channels).
On slopes, ploughing up and down the slope channels water and soil downhill, because the furrows act like drains.
The Dust Bowl shows how ploughing up natural cover and then meeting a drought can strip a whole region of its soil.
On the Great Plains of the USA, including Oklahoma and Kansas, natural grassland was ploughed up for wheat in the 1930s.
Severe drought then left bare, dry soil, which wind erosion removed in huge dust storms, because there were no grass roots to hold it.
Many farming families were forced to leave, because the land could no longer grow crops.

The US Soil Conservation Service was set up in 1935. Shelter belts of trees (rows of trees that break the wind), contour ploughing (ploughing along the slope) and crop rotation (changing the crop grown each year) were promoted.
The Sahel is an international example in which overgrazing and overcropping act together, with fuelwood cutting added.
The Sahel is the semi-arid (very dry) belt along the southern edge of the Sahara.
Population growth led to more cattle, goats and sheep concentrated around wells and boreholes, so the land around the water was grazed bare.
Population growth also led to shorter fallow periods and more cash crops (crops grown to sell), which is overcropping, and to more fuelwood cutting.
With droughts, notably in the 1970s and 1980s, the bare soil was eroded by wind and by the heavy rain of the short wet season. This process is called desertification (land turning into desert).
Management either keeps the soil fed and covered, or stops water and wind from carrying it away.
Crop rotation and fallow periods, so that soil nutrients recover.
Contour ploughing, ploughing along the slope rather than up and down it, so furrows hold water instead of channelling it downhill.
Strip cropping (growing crops in alternate strips), terracing of steep slopes (cutting level steps into them), and shelter belts against wind.
Mulching (covering the soil with plant material) and cover crops keep the soil covered between harvests.
Example: the rice terraces of Banaue, Luzon, Philippines, show terracing of steep slopes that is over 2,000 years old.
Deforestation is the clearing of forest. Trees hold a slope together and manage the water that falls on it, so removing them makes slopes much less stable.
Trees are removed for farmland, timber, fuelwood, roads and building, so forest is replaced by bare or thinly covered ground.

Tree roots bind soil and anchor it to bedrock. The canopy breaks the force of rain, and trees take up water (interception, where leaves catch rain, and transpiration, where plants release water vapour).
Without trees, more rain reaches and saturates the soil. Roots rot and no longer hold the slope.
Landslides and mudflows become more frequent, especially in heavy tropical rain. More sediment and faster run-off reach rivers.
Two international examples show how deforested slopes turn heavy rain into deadly floods and mudflows.
Haiti has lost almost all its natural forest, mainly for farmland and charcoal. Neighbouring Dominican Republic has far more forest cover.
In September 2004 Tropical Storm Jeanne caused floods and mudslides off the bare hills around Gonaïves, killing about 3,000 people.
Hurricane Mitch, October 1998: torrential rain over Honduras and Nicaragua caused floods and landslides, made worse by deforested slopes. About 11,000 people were killed.
A mudflow from the Casita volcano, Nicaragua, buried villages during Hurricane Mitch.
Ireland has little woodland left after centuries of clearance, and modern forestry can still destabilise upland slopes.
Historic forest clearance left Ireland with very little woodland. About 1% of Ireland was forested around 1900.
Forest cover is now about 11%, so it has risen since 1900, mostly in conifer plantations.
Clear-felling (cutting down all the trees in an area at once) of conifer plantations on upland peat, and building forestry and wind-farm roads, can destabilise peat slopes.
These methods keep tree roots and canopy in place on the slopes that need them most.
Afforestation (planting trees where there were none) and reforestation (replanting where trees were cut) of steep slopes, so roots bind the soil again.
Buffer strips of trees beside rivers, so that roots hold the banks and trap sediment.
Selective felling (removing only some trees) instead of clear-felling, and restricting felling on steep or peaty slopes.
Building on upland blanket bog can cause peat slides, because the work disturbs a wet, weak slope. Exams accept this as a human cause of mass movement.
Wind farms and roads on upland blanket bog involve excavation, dumping of spoil (waste material dug out) on the bog surface and interference with drainage.

Derrybrien, Slieve Aughty Mountains, Co. Galway, 16 October 2003: during construction of a wind farm on a forested blanket-bog hillside, a peat slide of about 450,000 cubic metres moved into the Owendalulleegh River, killing large numbers of fish.

In 2019 the EU Court of Justice fined Ireland, a lump sum of €5 million plus €15,000 a day, because no proper environmental impact assessment (a study of likely damage before building) had been carried out.

Meenbog wind farm, near Ballybofey, Co. Donegal, November 2020: a peat slide during construction flowed into the Mourne Beg River and crossed into Northern Ireland, polluting a river system important for salmon.
Anything that steepens a slope, loads it, wets it or removes its support raises the risk of mass movement.
Road and rail cuttings steepen slopes or remove support at their base, so the slope above is left unsupported.
Building weight on top of a slope adds to the downslope force.
Leaking pipes, drainage and irrigation saturate slopes, because extra water adds weight and reduces friction between particles.
Reservoirs saturate valley sides. Vajont is the example.
Mining spoil heaps (piles of waste rock) are unstable. Aberfan is the example.
Slope risk can be cut by physically strengthening slopes, and by planning so that people avoid or are warned about the danger.
Slope engineering: retaining walls, gabions (wire cages of stones), rock bolts, wire netting and rock-catch fences on cliffs, all of which hold or catch loose material.
Regrading slopes to a gentler angle, and drainage pipes to lower the water content.
Planning: hazard mapping, avoiding building on unstable slopes, and environmental impact assessments before building on peat.
Monitoring and warning systems, so that people can leave before a slope fails.

Ireland was glaciated (covered by moving ice) during the Pleistocene, the geological period of repeated ice ages. The landforms in this subsection were shaped by ice in its two main cold stages, and the type of ice involved decides what it can shape.
The older cold stage is the Munsterian; the more recent is the Midlandian. Their names are the ones to use when you are asked to date Irish glaciation.
Munsterian ice covered almost all of the island, so it was more extensive than the Midlandian ice, which left the far south free.
Midlandian glaciation ended about 10,000 years ago, and its ice did not cover the far south of Ireland, so the south kept land the Midlandian ice never reached.
An ice sheet is a continental mass of ice covering whole landscapes, buried hills and all, as in Antarctica and Greenland today.
A valley glacier is confined to a valley, so its path is set by the landscape. It is fed by snow and ice from corries (armchair-shaped hollows high on the mountainside).
Glacier ice is not frozen water poured into a valley. It is built up slowly from snow that never melts away.
Snow that survives the summer is compacted into firn (granular snow, also called nevé), because each year's new snow presses down on the older snow beneath.
Firn becomes glacier ice as the weight of overlying snow squeezes out the air and the ice crystals grow larger and interlock, producing dense solid ice.
A glacier gains ice at its head and loses it at its snout (its lower end), and the balance between these determines its behaviour. Geographers compare this to a budget of income against spending.
Accumulation zone: the upper part of the glacier, where snow and ice are gained, because more snow falls there than melts.
Ablation zone: the lower part, including the snout, where ice is lost by melting. Ablation simply means loss of ice.
Equilibrium line: the boundary between the two zones, where gain and loss are equal over a year, so above it the glacier gains and below it the glacier loses.
A glacier is not frozen in place. Gravity and the weight of the ice make it creep downhill by three different mechanisms, and friction makes some parts move faster than others.
Basal slip: meltwater at the base lubricates the bed (the rock floor beneath the ice), so the whole glacier slides over the rock.
Internal deformation (plastic flow): ice crystals slip past one another under the weight of the ice, so the glacier flows downhill.
Rotational movement: ice in a corrie (the hollow where a glacier begins) rotates within the hollow instead of moving straight down the valley.
Ice moves fastest at the centre of the surface and slowest at the sides and base, where friction with the valley walls and bed is greatest.
The snout's position depends on whether more ice arrives from the accumulation zone than melts at the snout. This balance decides whether the glacier is getting longer or shorter.
Advance: when more ice arrives from the accumulation zone than melts, the snout moves forward.
Retreat: when melting exceeds the ice arriving, the snout moves back up the valley, although the ice is still flowing forward. The snout retreats because it melts back faster than the ice feeds it.
Heavier snowfall or cooler summers, which reduce melting, cause the glacier to advance.
Less snowfall or warmer summers, which increase melting, cause the glacier to retreat.
Average rate of movement is found by dividing the distance moved by the number of years. The figures below are illustrative, invented for practice.
Average rate = distance moved ÷ number of years, given in metres per year.
Illustrative: a snout that retreats 600 m over 20 years has moved an average of 600 ÷ 20 = 30 m per year.
Illustrative: a snout that advances 450 m over 9 years has moved an average of 450 ÷ 9 = 50 m per year.
Glaciers erode mainly by plucking and abrasion, while freeze-thaw supplies rock debris at the edges of the ice. Together these processes carve the corries, valleys and lakes of glaciated uplands.

Plucking (quarrying): meltwater enters joints (cracks) in the bedrock and freezes, bonding the ice to the rock; as the glacier moves on, it tears out blocks, mainly on the downhill side of rock obstacles.
Abrasion: rock fragments frozen into the base of the ice scrape and polish the bedrock, like sandpaper on wood. It produces striations (scratches), polished rock and rock flour.
Rock flour: fine powder ground from the bedrock by abrasion, which meltwater carries away, giving glacial lakes a milky colour.
Freeze-thaw on the rock above and beside the ice: water freezing in cracks expands and breaks off fragments, which fall onto the ice and are carried away.
A corrie (also called a cirque) is the armchair-shaped hollow where a mountain glacier begins. Corrie ice feeds valley glaciers, so corries are linked to the valleys below them.
1. Snow collects in a hollow on the mountainside; nivation (erosion by snow patches) and freeze-thaw enlarge the hollow.
2. The snow turns to ice, and the rotating glacier plucks and abrades the back wall and floor, deepening the hollow and steepening the back wall.
3. The result is a bowl with a steep back wall and a rock lip, called the threshold, at its lower edge, because the ice erodes the floor more deeply than the rim.
4. When the ice melts, water collects behind the lip, because the lip dams the hollow, and forms a lake called a tarn.
Examples: Coumshingaun, Comeragh Mountains, Co. Waterford; the Devil's Punchbowl, Mangerton, Co. Kerry.
Diagram: cross-section of a corrie with steep back wall, rock lip and tarn; plan view of the bowl-shaped hollow.
