Corries do not only deepen hollows; they also eat into the mountain around them. Where corries meet, they leave sharp ridges and peaks standing between them.
1. Two corries cut back into the mountainside from opposite sides of a ridge.
2. Their back walls retreat, so the ridge between them is sharpened into a thin, knife-edged arête.
3. Three or more corries erode back around one summit from different directions.
4. The summit is left as a sharp, pointed pyramidal peak, also called a horn, because erosion has cut away every side of it.
Arête example: Striding Edge, Helvellyn, Lake District, England.
Pyramidal peak examples: Carrauntoohil, Macgillycuddy's Reeks, Co. Kerry, Ireland's highest mountain; the Matterhorn, Swiss-Italian Alps.
Diagram: plan view of two corries backing onto an arête; plan view of a horn ringed by three corries.
A glacier reshapes the river valley it occupies. It turns a narrow V-shaped valley into a wide trough, which is why glaciated valleys look so different from river valleys.
1. Before glaciation the valley is V-shaped, cut by a river.
2. A glacier fills the valley and deepens and widens its floor by plucking and abrasion.
3. The glacier cuts off the river's interlocking spurs (ridges that overlap from alternate sides of a river valley), leaving blunt cliff faces called truncated spurs.
4. The result is a broad, flat-floored trough with steep sides, which gives the valley its U-shape because the ice cuts down and sideways at once. It is also called a glacial trough.
Examples: Glendalough and Glenmalure, Co. Wicklow.
Diagram: cross-sections of a V-shaped valley beside a U-shaped valley, with truncated spurs labelled.
When a small glacier joins a large one, the two do not cut to the same depth. This leaves the smaller valley stranded high above the main one.
1. A smaller tributary glacier joins the larger glacier that is filling the main valley.
2. Because the tributary glacier is smaller, it erodes less deeply, so its valley is left hanging above the main valley floor.
3. When the ice melts, the tributary stream falls over the edge of the hanging valley as a waterfall.
Example: Poulanass Waterfall, falling from a hanging valley into the Glendalough valley, Co. Wicklow.
Diagram: long profile (side view along the valley) of a hanging valley and its waterfall above the main valley floor.
A glacier does not erode its valley floor evenly. Where it cuts deeper, it leaves a rock basin (a hollow in the bedrock) that fills with water as a lake.
1. Plucking and abrasion overdeepen a section of the valley floor more than the rest, leaving a rock basin.
2. When the ice melts, the basin fills with water, forming a long, narrow ribbon lake, because the lake takes the shape of the valley floor.
Example: Upper Lake, Glendalough, Co. Wicklow.
Paternoster lakes: a chain of rock-basin lakes along a valley floor, separated by bars of harder rock.
Tarns, ribbon lakes and kettle lakes are all glacial lakes.
Diagram: long profile of an overdeepened valley with a ribbon lake.
A fjord is a glaciated valley on the coast that the sea has flooded after the ice melted. It forms only where a glacier cut the valley floor below sea level.
1. A glacier overdeepens a coastal valley so that its floor lies well below sea level.
2. When the ice melts, the sea floods the valley, leaving a fjord with steep sides.
Examples: Killary Harbour, on the Co. Galway-Co. Mayo border; Sognefjord, Norway.
Diagram: plan view of a fjord with steep sides and the sea at its mouth.
Where ice flows over a bump of hard bedrock, it treats the two sides differently. Abrasion smooths the side it climbs and plucking roughens the side it leaves.
1. Ice flows over a bedrock outcrop (rock exposed at the surface), and abrasion smooths and polishes its upstream (stoss) side.
2. On the downstream (lee) side, plucking tears blocks from the rock, leaving a steep, rough face.
3. The result is a rounded hill with a smooth stoss side and a rough lee side.
Example: Lembert Dome, Yosemite, California, USA.
Striations: fine parallel scratches cut into bedrock by rock fragments held in the base of the ice; they are carved by the ice and show the direction of ice flow.
Diagram: cross-section of a roche moutonnee showing the stoss side, lee side and direction of ice flow; plan view of striations on bedrock.
A glacier carries rock debris, called its load, in three positions. Where the load sits decides how much work it does and what it looks like when dropped.
Supraglacial load: debris resting on the surface of the glacier, such as rock falling from the valley sides.
Englacial load: debris trapped within the ice, so it is carried inside the glacier, away from the surface and base.
Subglacial load: debris dragged along the base; it is the most abrasive part of the load and does most of the erosion, because it is pressed against the bedrock.
Glacial load is angular and unsorted: ice does not sort it by size, and it is not rounded by water as river load is, so sharp edges and mixed sizes survive.
Deposition means dropping the load. Ice that deposits material directly leaves a jumble, and this jumble also affects how water drains across the land afterwards.
Till (boulder clay) is unsorted and unstratified (not laid down in layers), angular material ranging from clay to boulders, deposited directly by ice.
Boulder clay plains of the Irish Midlands are formed where till is left across the land, for example when ice melts and drops its load over a wide area.
Deranged drainage: no clear pattern, with many lakes and marshes, forms on poorly drained glacial deposits such as till.
A moraine is a ridge or sheet of till. Its name depends on where in or around the glacier it was left.
Lateral moraine: a ridge of till along the side of a glacier, built from debris falling from the valley walls, such as frost-shattered rock.
Medial moraine: formed where two glaciers join, as their lateral moraines merge and run down the middle of the combined ice.
Terminal (end) moraine: an arc-shaped ridge of till at the snout, marking the furthest advance or a long pause in retreat, because the snout dumps its load where it stays still.
Recessional moraine: a ridge of till built at the snout during a pause while the glacier retreats.
Ground moraine: a sheet of till left on the bed as the glacier melts back.
Southern Irish End Moraine: marks the southern limit of the Midlandian ice sheet.
Diagram: cross-section of a valley glacier with lateral, medial and terminal moraines labelled; plan view of an arc-shaped terminal moraine.
Drumlins are smooth, oval hills of till, moulded by the ice that flowed over them. Their shape records which way the ice was moving.
1. Ice deposits or overrides an accumulation of till on the bed, building an irregular mass of material.
2. Ice flowing over the mass moulds it into an elongated, streamlined hill lying parallel to the direction of ice flow.
3. The blunt, steep end faces up-ice, and the tapered end points down-ice.
4. Drumlins occur in swarms, all aligned in one direction, forming a basket of eggs landscape.
5. Where the sea floods low ground, drumlins become islands, forming drowned drumlins, as in Clew Bay, Co. Mayo, and Strangford Lough, Co. Down.
Example: the drumlin belt across Co. Cavan, Co. Monaghan and Co. Leitrim.
Diagram: plan view of a drumlin swarm with an ice-flow arrow; side profile showing the blunt up-ice end and tapered down-ice end.
Ice can carry very large rocks over long distances. When it melts it drops them, so they end up in places where they do not belong geologically.
Erratic: a boulder carried by ice and dropped far from its source, with a rock type unlike the bedrock beneath it.
Example: granite erratics from Connemara resting on the limestone of the Burren, Co. Clare.
Fluvio-glacial material is laid down by meltwater rather than directly by ice, so it differs from till. Exams ask you to sort landforms into three groups, listed here.
Meltwater sorts material by size, so fluvio-glacial deposits are sorted, and layers are stratified (laid down in layers); till is neither.
Exam classification, glacial erosion: corrie, arete, pyramidal peak, U-shaped valley, hanging valley, ribbon lake, fjord, roche moutonnee, striations.
Exam classification, glacial deposition: till, moraines, drumlins, erratics.
Exam classification, fluvio-glacial: eskers, outwash plains, kames, kettle holes.
An esker is a long ridge built by a meltwater stream that once flowed through a tunnel in the ice. The ridge is what is left once the ice around it has gone.
1. Meltwater flows in a tunnel within or beneath the glacier.
2. The stream deposits sorted sand and gravel on the tunnel floor as its velocity falls, because slower water can no longer carry its load.
3. When the ice melts, the deposit is left as a long, winding ridge called an esker.
Example: Esker Riada, a series of eskers across the Midlands from roughly Dublin to Galway, used as an ancient routeway (the Slí Mhór); Clonmacnoise, Co. Offaly, is built beside it.
Diagram: plan view of a winding esker ridge; cross-section of a ridge of sorted gravel.
Meltwater leaves the glacier carrying sand and gravel and drops it beyond the ice limit. It builds a broad, flat plain, also called a sandur.
1. Meltwater spreads sand and gravel beyond the terminal moraine (the ridge of till marking the furthest ice advance) onto flat ground.
2. The deposit forms a flat, sorted outwash plain.
Example: The Curragh, Co. Kildare, a plain of sand and gravel; it is well-drained grassland used for horse training and an army camp.
Diagram: plan view of an outwash plain lying beyond a terminal moraine.
Meltwater also dumps sand and gravel on and around the ice itself. When the ice is gone, mounds and hollows are left behind.
1. Meltwater deposits sand and gravel in a hollow on the ice surface or at its margin.
2. When the ice melts, the deposit is left as a mound called a kame; where it lies against a valley side it forms a kame terrace.
3. A block of ice buried in outwash melts, leaving a hollow called a kettle hole. When water fills the hollow it becomes a kettle lake.
Diagram: cross-section of a kame beside a kettle hole.
Landforms are shaped by forces that build up the land and by forces that wear it down. The landscape you see reflects the balance between the two.
Endogenetic (endogenic) forces come from within the earth and raise the land, for example through crustal uplift (the rising of the earth's outer rocky layer, the crust).

Exogenetic (exogenic) forces act at the surface: weathering (breakdown of rock in place), erosion (wearing away and carrying off of material) and deposition (dropping of material) wear the land down and move material.
All landforms represent a balance between endogenetic and exogenetic forces, and this balance may change through time, so a landscape can shift as one force gains on the other.
The crust is not fixed in height. It sits on the layer beneath it and settles to a level that depends on the weight it carries, and isostasy is the name for that balance.
Isostasy is the state of balance between the crust and the denser mantle (the thick layer of hot rock under the crust) beneath it.
The crust floats on the mantle, as a block of wood floats in water. The mantle beneath the crust is called the asthenosphere.
Isostatic change is the adjustment of the crust's height that restores this balance when the load on the crust changes, so adding weight lowers the crust and removing weight lets it rise.
Ice sheets add a heavy load to the crust, and melting removes it. The crust responds slowly in both directions.
Isostatic depression: the weight of an ice sheet presses the crust down into the mantle, as a heavy load pushes a floating block lower in water.
Isostatic rebound (also called recovery or uplift): when the ice melts and the load is removed, the crust slowly rises.
Rebound lags far behind melting, because the crust adjusts slowly, so land can still be rising long after the ice has gone.
Rebound is still continuing in some places: Scandinavia around the Gulf of Bothnia, Hudson Bay in Canada, and Scotland.
Ice is not the only thing that changes the load on the crust. Surface processes do it too, by moving material from one place to another.
Denudation (the wearing away and lowering of the land surface by weathering and erosion) removes material from the land. Removing weight through erosion causes the crust to rise.
Heavy deposition adds weight to the crust, so it sinks; a delta (a landform built where a river drops its load at the sea) is one place where a large load builds up.
The land and the sea can each change height, and the two must not be confused. Isostatic change moves the land. Eustatic change moves the sea.
Isostatic change is a local change in the height of the land relative to the sea.
Eustatic change is a worldwide change in sea level.
During glaciation, water locked up in ice sheets lowered sea level worldwide, because less water was left in the oceans.
When the ice melted, the meltwater returned to the oceans and raised sea level again.
The level of the land relative to the sea is the combined result of isostatic and eustatic change, so the coast can rise or sink depending on which effect is stronger.
Base level is the lowest level to which a river can erode, normally sea level. A relative change between land and sea alters it.
A river cannot erode its channel below base level, so sea level controls the lower course of every river.
Uplift faster than denudation: the land rises but is not worn down quickly enough to match, so features are left high above the present sea.
Sea level rising faster than the land: the sea reaches features that were cut when it stood lower.
Such landscapes show features that do not match present conditions, because the balance between endogenetic and exogenetic forces is temporarily out of balance.
Where the land rises relative to sea level, the coast is emergent (rising out of the sea) and former shore features stand above the present tide reach.
Isostatic uplift lifts a former beach, its cliffs and its rock platform above present high tide, which is how a raised beach forms.
An old cliff line marks the position of the former sea cliffs, now inland of the sea.
A wave-cut notch is cut into the old cliff at the former sea level, where waves once undercut the rock.
Sea caves and stacks (pillars of rock left standing when waves cut away the land around them) stand above the present tide reach.
Beach shingle (rounded pebbles) lies on the raised beach.
A flat former wave-cut platform is a level rock shelf cut by waves at the former sea level.
Examples: raised beaches at Malin Head, Inishowen, Co. Donegal, and on the Isle of Jura, Scotland.
Where the sea stands higher relative to the land, the coast is submergent (sinking under the sea) and valleys and lowlands are flooded.
A ria is a drowned river valley. It has a V-shaped cross-section and a winding outline, because it was cut by a river.
Examples of rias: Bantry Bay, the Kenmare River and Dingle Bay (Co. Cork and Co. Kerry), and Cork Harbour. They are drowned river valleys of the Munster ridge-and-valley landscape.
A fjord is a drowned glacial trough (a valley deepened by a glacier). It is deep and U-shaped, often with a shallow threshold (a raised rock lip) at its mouth.
Examples of fjords: Killary Harbour, on the Co. Galway and Co. Mayo border, and the Norwegian fjords.
Drowned drumlins: a drumlin is an oval hill of glacial deposit, and when the lowland between drumlins floods, the crests of the drumlins stand as islands in the sea.
Examples of drowned drumlins: Clew Bay, Co. Mayo, and Strangford Lough, Co. Down.
Ireland shows both kinds of coast, because the amount of ice, and so the amount of rebound, differed from north to south.
The north of Ireland had thicker ice, so it was depressed more and has undergone more isostatic rebound. Its coast shows raised beaches, as at Malin Head in Co. Donegal.
The south-west has the opposite pattern: its coast is drowned, with rias and related submerged features, as in Cork and Kerry.
A fall in base level, caused by the land rising relative to the sea, gives a river renewed erosive power. This renewal is called rejuvenation.
The river erodes downwards again to the new, lower base level, and the renewed erosion works upstream from the mouth.
Knickpoint: a sudden steepening in the long profile (the line of the river's slope from source to mouth) of the river, which can form a waterfall.
Incised meanders: the river cuts down into its old meanders (bends), leaving them entrenched (cut deep) in steep-sided valleys.
River terraces: the old valley floor is left as a step above the new, lowered channel.
The opposite change drowns rivers instead of renewing them. When the sea rises relative to the land, base level rises too.
A rise in base level, caused by the sea rising relative to the land, drowns the lower course of a river.
The drowned lower course becomes an estuary (the wide tidal mouth of a river) or a ria, a drowned river valley with a V-shaped cross-section and a winding outline.
Before looking at how rivers shape the land, you need the vocabulary for the parts of a river system. These words are used to label maps and diagrams.
Source: where the river rises, meaning where it begins. The River Shannon, Ireland's longest river, rises at the Shannon Pot, Co. Cavan.
Mouth: where the river ends by entering the sea, a lake or another river, so it is the opposite end from the source.
Tributary: a smaller river that flows into a larger river, so it adds its water to the main river.
Confluence: the point where a tributary joins the main river.
Drainage basin (catchment): the whole area of land drained by a river and its tributaries, so all rain falling in it ends up in that river system.
Watershed: the high ground that separates one drainage basin from the next, so water on either side flows to a different river.
Distributary: a channel that leaves the main river and flows away from it, found on deltas (fan-shaped landforms of deposited material at a river mouth).
Estuary: the tidal lower course of a river, where fresh water meets salt water. The Shannon enters the Atlantic through the Shannon Estuary below Limerick.

The long profile is the smooth, concave slope of a river from its source to its mouth. Because the slope changes along the way, the river is divided into three courses, and each course has its own landforms.
The gradient (steepness of the river's slope) is steep near the source and gentle near the mouth, which is what makes the profile concave.
Upper (youthful) course: steep, with V-shaped valleys, interlocking spurs (ridges that overlap like the teeth of a zip), waterfalls, rapids and potholes.
Middle (mature) course: meanders (looping bends) develop as the valley widens, because the gentler gradient lets the river swing from side to side.
Lower (old) course: a wide floodplain (flat land beside the river), levees (natural banks built up beside the channel), meanders with oxbow lakes (cut-off loops), and a delta or estuary at the mouth.
A river can only erode or carry material if it has energy. How much it has, and where it uses it, explains why the upper course looks so different from the lower course.
A river's energy depends on its volume (discharge, the amount of water flowing past a point) and its gradient.
Energy left after overcoming friction with the bed and banks is used for erosion (wearing away the land) and transport (carrying material, called the load).
Volume increases downstream because tributaries keep joining the main river.
Vertical erosion (deepening the bed) dominates in the upper course, so valleys there are cut downwards.
Lateral erosion (widening the valley sideways) dominates in the middle and lower courses, so the valley floor there becomes wide.
Headward erosion lengthens a valley at its source, cutting back upstream.
Rivers wear away their bed and banks in four ways. Each works differently, and each is a named process you may be asked to explain.
Hydraulic action: the force of moving water dislodges loose material and forces air into cracks in the bed and banks, widening them until rock breaks away.
Abrasion (corrasion): the load scrapes and grinds the bed and banks like sandpaper. Pebbles swirled in eddies (small whirlpools) drill potholes into the bed.
Attrition: particles of the load collide with each other and with the bed, so they become smaller and more rounded downstream.
Solution (corrosion): slightly acidic water dissolves soluble rock such as limestone, carrying it away in solution (dissolved in the water).
Once material has been eroded, the river carries it downstream. The method depends on the size of the particles and the speed of the flow.
Traction: the largest boulders are rolled along the bed, mainly during floods when the flow is strongest.
Saltation: pebbles and sand are too heavy to stay in the flow, so they bounce along the bed in a series of hops.
Suspension: fine silt and clay are carried within the flow, giving the water its brown colour.
Solution: dissolved minerals are carried invisibly in the water.
Competence: the largest particle a river can carry. It rises sharply in flood because the faster, bigger flow can move larger particles.
Capacity: the total load a river can carry. It also rises sharply in flood, so a flooded river carries far more material overall.
A river drops its load when it no longer has the energy to carry it. Understanding why it drops it, and in what order, explains the shape of most depositional landforms.
Deposition (dropping of the load) happens when velocity (speed of flow) falls: on entering a lake or the sea, on the inside of a bend, when floodwater recedes, or on a gentler gradient.
Deposition also happens when the load becomes too great for the river's energy to carry, so the excess is dropped even if the flow has not slowed.
Heavier material is deposited first and the finest last, so deposits are sorted by size. This contrasts with glacial till (material dropped by ice), which is unsorted and angular.

A drainage pattern is the arrangement of a river and its tributaries, shaped by the underlying rock and relief (the height and shape of the land). Each pattern tells you something about the rock or land beneath it.
Dendritic: tree-like, with tributaries joining at acute angles (sharp angles); forms on rock of uniform resistance, so the rivers have no reason to favour any direction.

Trellised: tributaries meet the main rivers at right angles; forms where bands of hard and soft rock alternate. In the ridge-and-valley landscape of Munster, rivers follow the soft limestone valleys and tributaries flow off the sandstone ridges at right angles.
Radial: rivers flow outward from a central high point like the spokes of a wheel, because the ground slopes away in every direction from the high point.
Deranged: no clear pattern; forms on poorly drained glacial deposits (material left by ice), e.g. the drumlin belt of Co. Cavan, with many small lakes and marshes between the drumlins.
Centripetal: rivers flow inward to a central lake or basin, e.g. Lough Neagh, into which rivers drain from all sides.

On an Ordnance Survey map, dendritic streams branch like a tree at sharp angles, trellised streams run parallel with tributaries meeting them at right angles, radial streams spread out from a high point, and centripetal streams converge on a lake.
In the upper course the river is steep and powerful, so it cuts downwards into its bed. This shapes a narrow valley with a V-shaped cross-section.
1. The steep gradient gives the river high energy, so it erodes vertically by hydraulic action and abrasion.
2. Weathering (breakdown of rock in place) and mass movement (downhill movement of loose material) loosen the valley sides and move material into the channel, widening the top of the valley.
3. The result is a narrow floor and steep sides in a V-shape, because the river cuts down faster than it widens the valley.
4. The river swings around areas of harder rock, leaving spurs (ridges of land) that interlock like the teeth of a zip.
Interlocking spurs are fluvial (made by rivers) and are not to be confused with truncated spurs, which are glacial.
On an Ordnance Survey map, the contours (lines joining points of equal height) form a V that points upstream.
Example: the upper course of the River Liffey in the Wicklow Mountains.
Diagram: cross-section of a V-shaped valley; plan view of interlocking spurs with the river winding between them.
A waterfall forms where a river crosses rock of different hardness. Two erosion processes, hydraulic action and abrasion, do the work in the undercutting and plunge-pool stages.
1. A waterfall forms where a band of resistant rock (rock that wears away slowly) lies over less resistant rock.
2. Hydraulic action and abrasion erode the soft rock below faster, undercutting the hard rock and leaving an overhang.
3. Falling water and its load scour a deep plunge pool at the base by hydraulic action and abrasion.
4. The unsupported overhang collapses, and the waterfall retreats upstream.
5. Repeated retreat leaves a steep-sided gorge downstream of the falls, because the river has cut back through the rock the falls once occupied.
Example: Niagara Falls, USA-Canada border, with a resistant cap of dolomite over weaker shale; the retreat of the falls has cut the Niagara Gorge below them.
Irish waterfalls: Powerscourt Waterfall, River Dargle, Co. Wicklow, Ireland's highest waterfall at about 121 m; and Torc Waterfall, near Killarney, Co. Kerry.
Diagram: cross-section showing hard rock cap, soft rock beneath, overhang, plunge pool and direction of retreat.
Rapids and potholes are smaller features of the steep upper course, both made by erosion of the river bed.
1. Rapids form where alternating bands of hard and soft rock lie across the river bed.
2. Hydraulic action and abrasion erode the soft bands faster, leaving the hard bands standing as steps.
3. Fast, turbulent water tumbles over the steps, so the surface is broken and white, forming rapids.
Potholes: hollows drilled into the bed by pebbles swirled in eddies, the grinding action of abrasion.
A meander is a looping bend in a river. It is formed by both erosion and deposition, so it is classified under both.
1. Water flows fastest on the outside of a bend, where it erodes the bank by hydraulic action and abrasion, forming a steep river cliff.
2. Water is slowest on the inside of the bend, where it deposits sand and gravel, forming a gently sloping point bar (slip-off slope).
3. Helicoidal (corkscrew-shaped) flow carries eroded material from the outer bank to the inner bank of the next bend.
4. Continued lateral erosion makes the bends more pronounced, so that only a narrow neck of land eventually separates them.
Example: meanders on the River Shannon's floodplain, the Shannon Callows, between Athlone and Portumna.
Diagram: plan view of a meander with the fastest-flow line, river cliff and point bar.
If meanders keep growing, the loops can eventually be cut off from the river. This leaves a lake that later disappears.
1. During a flood the river cuts through the neck of a meander and takes the straighter, shorter course.
2. Deposition seals off the old bend, so the water left behind forms a crescent-shaped oxbow lake.
3. The oxbow lake slowly fills with silt and becomes a meander scar (a dry, curved hollow where the loop used to be).
Example: oxbow lakes on the lower Mississippi, USA.
Diagram: plan sequence showing the cut-off and the formation of the oxbow lake.
Floodplains and levees are built by deposition during floods. They are among the main depositional landforms of the lower course.
Lateral erosion by migrating meanders widens the valley floor, so there is a broad flat area for floodwater to spread over.
When the river floods, it spreads across the valley, loses velocity and deposits a layer of fine silt called alluvium.
Repeated floods build a wide, flat, fertile floodplain; on an Ordnance Survey map, widely spaced contours show it. Example: the Shannon Callows, a wide floodplain of seasonally flooded meadows.
Levees: the coarsest material is dropped first, right beside the channel, because the water slows as soon as it leaves it. Each flood therefore raises the banks a little.
Over time these build into natural embankments called levees, and the river bed itself may rise above the level of the floodplain.
Example: levees along the lower Mississippi, USA, which have been artificially raised for flood control.
Diagram: cross-section of a floodplain showing alluvium layers, levees and the raised channel.
A delta is a landform of deposition at a river mouth. It builds up when the river drops its load faster than the sea or lake can remove it.
A delta forms where a river carrying a heavy load enters a sea or lake and its velocity drops sharply.
In salt water, fine clay particles clump together (flocculation) and sink faster.
Deposits build up until they block the channel, forcing the river to split into smaller channels called distributaries.
Conditions needed: a large load, and calm water with a small tidal range and weak currents, so that deposits are not removed.
A delta is built up in layers, and deltas take different shapes depending on how the deposits spread. You should know the layers and the named types.
Topset beds: flat, coarser deposits laid down on top of the delta, because the heavier material drops first.
Foreset beds: steeply sloping deposits at the front of the delta, built out into the water so the delta grows forward.
Bottomset beds: fine, flat layers laid down beyond the front of the delta, because the finest material is carried furthest.
Arcuate (fan-shaped) delta, e.g. the Nile delta, Egypt.
Bird's-foot delta: long fingers of deposits along distributaries, e.g. the Mississippi delta, USA.
Estuarine delta: fills a drowned river mouth (a river mouth flooded by the sea).
Lake delta, e.g. the delta between the Upper and Lower Lakes at Glendalough, Co. Wicklow, which divided what was once a single lake.
Diagram: plan view of a delta with distributaries; cross-section showing topset, foreset and bottomset beds.
Two more depositional features occur near the mouth, or where the load is large: the estuary and the braided channel.
Estuary: in the tidal river mouth, fresh and salt water meet, and deposition builds mudflats and salt marsh.
Example: the Shannon Estuary below Limerick, where the Shannon enters the Atlantic.
Braided channel: the river splits into several channels around islands of deposited sand and gravel, called eyots or braid bars.
Braided channels form where the load is large and discharge varies, so the river cannot carry all its sediment and drops it as islands in the channel.
Every fluvial landform is formed by erosion, by deposition, or by both. Sorting them this way is a skill that exams test.
Erosion: V-shaped valley, interlocking spurs, waterfall, gorge, potholes, rapids.
Erosion and deposition: meander, oxbow lake.
Deposition: floodplain, levee, delta, point bar, estuary mudflats.

A river can erode no lower than its base level, the lowest point it can cut down to. Sea level is the ultimate base level, and a river that has settled into balance with its base level has a smooth, predictable shape.

A lake, a band of resistant rock or a main river (for its tributary, the smaller stream that joins it) acts as a temporary, local base level, because the river cannot cut below that point until it is removed.

A graded (equilibrium) profile is a smooth, concave long profile (the river's slope from source to mouth, steep at the top and flattening downstream) where the river's energy is just enough to carry its load (the material it transports), so erosion and deposition (dropping of load) are balanced.
A change in base level upsets this balance, so the river adjusts its profile to the new level.
Rejuvenation is renewed vertical erosion (cutting downwards) caused by a fall in base level relative to the land. It gives the river renewed energy and interrupts a cycle of erosion.

Cause 1, a eustatic fall in sea level (the sea itself moves): during a glacial period, water is locked up in ice sheets, so sea level falls worldwide and the river has further to fall to reach the sea.

Cause 2, isostatic uplift (the land itself moves): land depressed under the weight of an ice sheet rises, or rebounds, when the ice melts, raising it relative to sea level. There is more on this in Glaciation.
Cause 3, tectonic uplift of the land by earth movements, which raises the land above its old base level so the river cuts down again.

Cause 4, an increase in discharge (the volume of water flowing in the river), e.g. from a wetter climate or by river capture (one river taking over the water of another), gives the river more energy; this is a less common cause.
A fall in base level is felt first at the river's mouth (where it meets the sea), and the effect then travels up the valley. This leaves a river made of two parts.
Rejuvenation begins at the mouth and works upstream by headward erosion (erosion that cuts back towards the source), because the extra energy is first available at the lowest point.
For a long time the river has two graded sections: a new, steeper lower section and the old, gentler upper section.
This is the landscape that is temporarily out of balance, because the two sections reflect two different base levels.
A knickpoint is where the new, rejuvenated river meets the old one. It is the key feature of a rejuvenated long profile (the river's slope from source to mouth).
1. Rejuvenation cuts down at the mouth, creating a new graded section below the old one.
2. Where the new and old graded profiles meet, the long profile has a break of slope: this is the knickpoint.
3. A waterfall or rapids is often found at the knickpoint, because the river drops steeply there. The knickpoint is the break of slope itself, not the waterfall.
4. The knickpoint retreats upstream over time, and the new profile extends behind it.
5. Once the whole river has graded to the new base level, the knickpoint disappears.
Diagram: long profile showing the old and new graded sections and the knickpoint at their junction.

Renewed vertical erosion cuts existing meanders (bends in the river) down into the land, rather than forming them on a floodplain (the flat land beside a river). This leaves meanders set deep in a valley with steep sides.
Ingrown meanders have an asymmetrical cross-section (a slice across the valley), with one gentle and one steep side, because downcutting is slower and there is some lateral (sideways) erosion.
Entrenched meanders have a symmetrical cross-section with steep sides, forming a gorge (a deep, narrow, steep-sided valley), because downcutting is rapid.
Example of entrenched meanders: the Goosenecks of the San Juan River, Utah, USA.
Example of incised meanders: the River Wye, Wales-England border.
Diagram: cross-section showing a meander cut down into the land, with steep sides and no floodplain.

When a river cuts down into its old floodplain, the old floodplain is left stranded above the river. River terraces are remnants of an old floodplain, left as flat steps above the new floodplain after the river has cut down.
Paired terraces are at the same height on both sides of the valley; they form where the river downcuts rapidly, so it has little time to move sideways.
Unpaired terraces are at different heights on each side; they form while the river downcuts and migrates (moves) sideways.
Example: the river terraces of the River Thames in and around London, England.
Diagram: cross-section of a valley showing paired terraces above the present floodplain.
Uplift of the land gives a river renewed cutting power, and deep incision (cutting down) can produce a gorge, a deep, narrow valley with steep sides.
A gorge can be cut by deep incision of a river into an uplifted landscape.
Example: the Grand Canyon, cut by the Colorado River in Arizona, USA, as the Colorado Plateau was uplifted.
Each episode of rejuvenation leaves a mark, so a diagram can be read like a record. Counting the marks tells you how many times the river has been rejuvenated.
The number of rejuvenations equals the number of knickpoints on a long profile, because each fall in base level creates one.
On a cross-section, the number of rejuvenations equals the number of terrace levels above the present floodplain, because each rejuvenation leaves a terrace behind.
Rejuvenation features not shown in a diagram are knickpoints, waterfalls or rapids at knickpoints, incised meanders, river terraces and gorges.
A rise in base level, from sea level rising or land sinking, reduces the river's energy. This is the opposite of rejuvenation, so it drowns rather than cuts.

The lower course is drowned and deposition (dropping of load) increases because the river has less energy; the mouth becomes a ria (a drowned river valley) or an estuary (the wide tidal mouth of a river). There is more on rias in Glaciation.
Coastal landforms caused by a change in base level are raised beaches (from a fall in base level) and rias (from a rise).

Setting: rivers of north-west Ireland were rejuvenated as the land rose isostatically after the Midlandian ice melted about 10,000 years ago; the north, under thicker ice, rose more, with raised beaches at Malin Head, Co. Donegal.

A landscape is shaped by two opposing sets of forces acting over very long periods. Endogenetic forces come from inside the Earth and push the land up (uplift). Exogenetic forces act at the surface and wear it down (denudation, the lowering of land by weathering, erosion and transport).
When uplift stops, denudation slowly lowers the land towards base level (the lowest level to which rivers can cut down, usually sea level), so the land is gradually worn down.
Cyclic landscape development means the landscape passes through a sequence of stages, from uplift to near-flatness.
A new uplift, or a fall in base level, gives the rivers fresh cutting power and so starts the sequence again.
One model of cyclic development is the geographical cycle, also called the cycle of erosion. It was set out by William Morris Davis, an American geographer, who published it in 1899.

Davis's model assumes rapid uplift followed by a long period of stability, during which rivers and weathering wear the land down. The uplift is treated as a single quick event so that the wearing down can be followed stage by stage.
Davis held that the landscape depends on structure (the type and arrangement of the rocks), process (what is wearing the land down) and stage (time, how far through the cycle it is).
Davis's stages describe a whole landscape changing through time: youth, maturity and old age. Do not confuse them with the upper, middle and lower courses of one river, though the landforms overlap.
Youth is the first stage, just after uplift. The land is high and the rivers have plenty of energy to cut downwards.
The landscape is an uplifted plateau with high relief (a large height difference between hills and valley floors). Gradients are steep, so rivers cut vertically downwards (vertical erosion).
Valleys are deep and V-shaped, with waterfalls and rapids, because the rivers are still cutting down through uneven rock.
Wide, flat interfluves (the areas between rivers) are not yet eroded, and there are few tributaries (small rivers that join a bigger one) because the drainage network has had little time to develop.
In maturity the rivers have cut down as far as they usefully can in places and begin to work sideways. The landscape is at its most dissected.
Relief is at its maximum, meaning the difference in height between the highest ground and the valley floors is greatest.
Valleys widen by lateral erosion (sideways cutting into the banks), so meanders (bends in the river) and floodplains (flat land beside the river that floods) develop.
The drainage network (the pattern of the main river and its tributaries) is fully developed, and interfluves are reduced to ridges because streams have cut into them from both sides.
In old age the land has been worn down almost to base level, and the rivers have little energy left to cut. The end product of the whole cycle is the peneplain.
Relief is low, with very wide floodplains, large meanders, oxbow lakes (curved lakes left when a meander is cut off) and levees (natural raised banks built up along the river by floods).
Rivers flow sluggishly close to base level, because they have almost no slope left to flow down. Divides (the high ground separating one river basin from the next) are lowered to gentle rises.
A peneplain is the end product: a gently undulating surface of low relief close to base level, almost a plain. Its name means 'almost a plain'.
Erosion does not always lower every part of the land equally. Harder rock can survive as a high point on an otherwise flat surface.
Monadnocks are isolated residual hills (hills left standing after the land around them was worn away) of more resistant rock rising above the peneplain.
The term comes from Mount Monadnock, New Hampshire, USA.
Davis's cycle does not always run to its end. If the land is raised again or sea level falls, the rivers have a steeper slope to cut down, and the cycle restarts.
Uplift, isostatic rebound (the land rising as the weight of ice or eroded material is removed) or a fall in sea level rejuvenates the rivers (gives them renewed cutting power).
This starts a new cycle before the old one is finished. There is more on this in Fluvial adjustment to base level (Rivers).
A landscape with remnants of more than one cycle is polycyclic, because surfaces from earlier cycles survive beside the newer ones.
Long-continued erosion can leave behind a distinctive flat surface. If that surface is later raised, it can still be recognised in the landscape.
A planation surface is a flat erosion surface cut across rocks of different types and structures, so its flatness is not controlled by the rock beneath.
An uplifted peneplain survives as a plateau, or as summits at similar heights (accordant summits) that cut across folded rock.
An uplifted peneplain is no longer near base level, because the land has been raised since it formed.
Davis's model is useful, but geomorphologists (scientists who study landforms) have questioned several of its assumptions. Know both the criticisms and the strength.
Walther Penck, a German geomorphologist, argued that uplift and denudation happen at the same time, not one after the other as Davis assumed.
The time needed for the cycle is far too long to observe, so the model cannot be tested directly.
The model ignores climate change, glaciation and the isostatic response to erosion (the land rising as material is removed).
Few, if any, true peneplains exist today at sea level.
In its favour, the model gives a simple, useful framework for describing landscapes by stage.
Munster is the Irish case study for planation surfaces. First the rocks were folded, then a long period of denudation cut across the folds to leave a near-level surface.

Folding about 300 million years ago (Variscan, also called Armorican) formed east-west ridges of Old Red Sandstone (anticlines, the upfolds) and valleys of softer Carboniferous limestone (synclines, the downfolds).
Over a very long period of denudation, the region was worn down towards a near-level surface cutting across the folds.
Evidence: flat or gently sloping upland surfaces, and summit levels at similar heights, cut across folded rocks of different types.
Diagram cue: a cross-section of folded rock with a flat planation surface cutting across the ridges and valleys.

The Munster surface was not left at base level. It was uplifted, and the rivers began cutting down again, which re-exposed the ridges and valleys. The odd course of the rivers has a usual explanation, but it is not a proven fact.
Later uplift raised the planation surface, and the rivers were rejuvenated (given new cutting power) and cut down again.

Renewed erosion removed the softer limestone faster than the sandstone, so the ridge-and-valley relief was re-exposed. This is differential erosion (rocks of different hardness wearing away at different rates).
The Munster Blackwater flows east through Mallow, Fermoy and Lismore, then turns sharply south at Cappoquin, Co. Waterford, to reach the sea at Youghal.

The usual explanation for the southward turn is superimposed drainage: the river first flowed south across an older surface above the present rocks, and kept its course as it cut down into the folded rocks below. This is the usual explanation, not a proven fact.
The Munster landscape is temporarily out of balance: uplift has outpaced denudation, so an old surface survives at height while the rivers are still adjusting.

Rivers are useful, so people change them. Every change alters how the river's processes work: its velocity (speed of flow), erosion (wearing away of bed and banks), transport (carrying of material), deposition (dropping of material) and flooding.
Reasons for interfering include making electricity, supplying water, irrigation (watering crops), navigation (letting boats travel), draining farmland and protecting towns from flooding.
The three measures studied here are hydro-electric dams, canalisation and flood control, each with Irish and international examples.
A hydro-electric dam turns the energy of falling water into electricity. It does this by holding the river back and then releasing it in a controlled way.
The dam stores water in a reservoir (an artificial lake behind the dam), and the water is then released so that it falls through turbines (wheels that spin and drive generators).
The drop in height of the water (the head) gives the power, so a greater drop means more energy from the same water.
Upstream of a dam the river meets still water in the reservoir. This changes its processes completely, because a river can only carry material while it keeps moving.
Velocity falls to near zero in the reservoir, so the river deposits its load (the sand, silt and stones it was carrying) there.
The reservoir slowly fills with sediment, a process called sedimentation, which reduces its capacity (how much water it can hold).
A delta (a fan of deposited sediment) can build where the river enters the reservoir, because that is where the flow slows and drops its load.
Below the dam the river has lost its sediment and its natural rhythm of floods and low flows. Both changes alter erosion and deposition.
Water released from the dam is clear of sediment, so it has spare energy and erodes the bed and banks below the dam. This is called clear-water erosion.
The floodplain (the flat land beside the river) and delta receive no new silt, so deltas and coasts erode because nothing replaces the material lost.
Discharge (the volume of water flowing past a point) is regulated, so natural floods and low flows are evened out.
Less flooding means less deposition on the floodplain, because floodwater is what normally lays down silt there.
Where water is diverted out of the old channel, the bypassed channel carries much less water.
Dams block migrating salmon and eels, which cannot pass the wall. Fish passes (routes around the dam) and trapping and transporting fish around dams are responses.
The Shannon Scheme is one power station at Ardnacrusha, near Limerick, fed by a weir and a canal. It is not a series of dams.
It was built 1925–1929 by the German firm Siemens for the Irish Free State, and it was Ireland's first large hydro-electric station.

Parteen Weir (a low barrier across the river) diverts most of the Shannon's water into a headrace canal to Ardnacrusha. A tailrace (the channel carrying used water away) returns it to the river near Limerick.
Lough Derg's level is controlled by Parteen Weir, so the lough acts as the scheme's reservoir.
The original channel between Parteen and Limerick, the Old River Shannon, carries much less water because most of it is diverted.
Salmon and eel stocks declined. The ESB built a fish pass, and it traps silver eels (adult eels migrating downstream) upstream and transports them past the dam.
Ardnacrusha is not the only Irish example. Four more dams and power stations can be named in an answer.
Poulaphouca dam, River Liffey: created the Blessington Lakes reservoir, Co. Wicklow. It generates electricity and supplies drinking water to Dublin.
Inniscarra and Carrigadrohid dams, River Lee, Co. Cork.
Cathaleen's Fall power station, River Erne, at Ballyshannon, Co. Donegal.
The Aswan High Dam is the main international case study. It holds back the Nile in a huge reservoir to give Egypt control over a river that once flooded and shrank unpredictably.
Aswan High Dam, River Nile, Egypt, was completed in 1970. Its reservoir is Lake Nasser, which extends into Sudan.
Benefits are flood control, year-round irrigation (which allows more than one crop a year), hydro-electricity, and protection from drought.
The dam's effects follow from the same processes as any dam: trapped sediment, clear-water erosion and regulated flow. They then spread into farming, fishing, health and settlement.
Silt is trapped in Lake Nasser, so farmers downstream rely on artificial fertilisers instead of the natural silt that floods once left.
The river bed below the dam is scoured (worn away) by clear water, which has spare energy to erode.
The Nile delta coast is eroding, e.g. at the Rosetta promontory (a headland on the delta coast), because no new sediment arrives to replace what the sea removes.
The sardine fishery off the delta in the Mediterranean declined sharply.
Irrigated land suffers waterlogging (soil saturated with water) and salinisation (a build-up of salt in the soil).
Perennial irrigation canals (canals that hold water all year) spread the disease schistosomiasis (bilharzia).
Nubian people were displaced, and the temples of Abu Simbel were moved to higher ground.
The Three Gorges Dam is a second international example, built on the Yangtze to produce power and to reduce floods.
Three Gorges Dam, Hubei province, China, is the world's largest power station by installed capacity.
It was completed in 2006 and fully operational in 2012, and over one million people were relocated.
It aims to reduce flood peaks downstream, because the Yangtze floods of 1998 killed thousands.
It traps sediment that once reached the river's lower course and delta, so those areas receive less of the sediment they depended on.
Canalisation modifies an existing river channel. It is not the same as building a canal.

Methods are straightening, deepening and widening the channel, sometimes lining it with concrete, cutting through meanders (bends in the river), dredging (scooping sediment from the bed) and building locks and weirs for navigation.
Purposes are navigation, faster drainage of land, and flood control.
Making a river straighter and smoother makes the water move faster. Almost every other effect follows from that rise in velocity.
A straighter, shorter course has a steeper gradient (slope) and less friction (drag from the bed and banks), so velocity rises.
Water and floods are passed downstream faster, so flood peaks downstream are higher and arrive sooner.
Faster flow has more energy, so it erodes the bed and banks.
Where the channel widens or the flow slows again, deposition increases and dredging is needed to keep the channel clear.
Meanders, oxbow lakes (cut-off loops of old meander), pools and riffles (deeper and shallower stretches of the bed) are lost, and the river is cut off from its floodplain.
Canalisation has been used for drainage and navigation in Ireland and for shortening and straightening big rivers abroad.

Arterial drainage (deepening and straightening main rivers to drain land) was carried out by the Office of Public Works (OPW) under the Arterial Drainage Act 1945, e.g. the Moy and Boyne schemes. Rivers were deepened and straightened mainly to drain farmland, not to protect towns.
Arterial drainage effects were changes to fish spawning beds, bank erosion and downstream flooding.
Mississippi: cut-offs (new short channels across bends) made by the US Army Corps of Engineers shortened the river.
Rhine: the Upper Rhine was straightened in the 19th century under Johann Gottfried Tulla, which sped flood waves downstream and caused the bed to erode downward.
Navigation in Ireland: locks and weirs on the Shannon Navigation control water levels and slow the flow.
Flood control measures respond to the causes of river flooding, so it helps to know what those causes are.
Prolonged or intense rain, and saturated ground (soil that is already full of water and cannot absorb more), send water into rivers faster than they can carry it.
Urban surfaces and drains speed runoff (water flowing over land into rivers). Deforestation and drainage of bogs and farmland upstream add to it.
Building on floodplains puts homes in the path of floodwater.
Hard engineering uses built structures to hold floodwater back or move it away. Each one changes river processes, and some pass the problem on downstream.
Embankments and levees (raised banks) confine flow to the channel, so deposition raises the bed and the banks must be raised again.
With embankments and levees the floodplain gets no silt, and failure gives sudden, severe floods.
Flood walls and demountable (removable) barriers protect towns.
Dredging and deepening increase channel capacity, but the flow is faster and downstream flooding can increase.
Relief (bypass) channels take floodwater around the town.
Soft engineering works with the river instead of against it. It slows water or gives it space, so natural processes carry on.
Floodplain zoning uses planning controls on building, so that homes are kept off land that floods.
Afforestation (planting trees) upstream works through interception (leaves catching rain), which slows runoff.
Wetlands and bogs can be restored, and washlands (land that is allowed to flood) give the river more room.
Flood forecasting and warning give people time to prepare.
Effect on processes: natural flooding and floodplain deposition continue.
Irish floods show hard engineering, dam management and flood-risk planning in practice.
Cork, November 2009: the River Lee flooded when the ESB released large volumes from Inniscarra dam during very heavy rain because the reservoir was full.
The releases were not the sole cause, because the rain was exceptional. The University College Cork and the city water treatment works were flooded, and many homes lost their water supply.
Clonmel, Co. Tipperary: an OPW flood relief scheme on the River Suir uses demountable barriers that are put in place when floods are forecast.
December 2015: Storm Desmond caused prolonged flooding on the Shannon, in towns such as Athlone.
CFRAM (Catchment Flood Risk Assessment and Management) is the OPW programme that maps flood risk.
The Mississippi is the international case study for levees. It shows both what they protect and how they can fail.
The Great Mississippi Flood of 1927 led to the US federal levee and floodway system run by the US Army Corps of Engineers.
The 1993 flood breached many levees along the upper Mississippi and Missouri.
In August 2005 Hurricane Katrina caused levee and floodwall failures in New Orleans, and about 80% of the city flooded.
Levees stop flood silt reaching the delta, which contributes to the loss of Louisiana's coastal wetlands.
The Netherlands shows a soft-engineering response to flooding: instead of building higher walls, it gives the river space.
Room for the River (Ruimte voor de Rivier), Netherlands, started after near-disastrous high water on the Rhine and Maas in 1993 and 1995.
Measures include moving dykes (embankments) back, lowering floodplains and digging side channels so the river can spread out safely.
Exams expect a judgement, so weigh what these measures achieve against what they cost.
Benefits are protection of homes, electricity, navigation and water supply.
Costs are problems moved downstream, sediment starvation (rivers and deltas losing the sediment they need), habitat loss, high cost, and a false sense of security.
There is a trend towards working with natural processes.
Waves take their energy from the wind, and the water itself stays in place as the wave passes. Knowing how a wave forms and breaks explains everything the sea later does to the coast.
Wind blowing over the sea surface transfers energy to the water, raising waves.
Wave size depends on wind speed, the length of time the wind blows, and fetch.
Fetch is the distance of open water over which the wind blows; a longer fetch allows bigger waves because the wind has more distance in which to pass energy to the water.
Water particles move in circles as a wave passes, so it is the energy that travels, not the water; the water does not travel forward until the wave breaks.
A wave's crest is its highest point and its trough the lowest; wave height is the vertical distance between them, and wavelength is the distance between successive crests.
A wave breaks in shallow water: friction with the sea bed slows its base while the crest keeps moving, so the crest topples forward.
Swash is the water rushing up the beach after a wave breaks, carrying sand and shingle with it.
Backwash is the water draining back down the beach under gravity, so it can pull material back down with it, which is why the swash and backwash balance matters.

The balance between swash (water running up the beach) and backwash (water draining back down) decides whether a beach is built up or cut back. Waves fall into two types according to which of the two is stronger.
Constructive waves are low, gentle, long-wavelength (far apart) and low-frequency (few waves per minute), and they spill onto the beach.
Constructive waves are typical of calm weather; their swash is stronger than their backwash, so they carry material up the beach and build it up.
Destructive waves are high, steep, short-wavelength (close together) and high-frequency (many waves per minute), and they plunge down onto the beach.
Destructive waves are typical of storms; their backwash is stronger than their swash, so they drag material out to sea and erode the beach.
Real coasts are not straight, so waves do not hit them evenly. Refraction (the bending of waves) shows why some parts of a coast erode while others receive sediment.
Refraction: waves approaching an indented coast slow down first in shallow water off headlands (points of land jutting into the sea), so the wave fronts bend.
Energy converges on headlands, causing more erosion there, and spreads out in bays (curved inlets of the sea), where it is weaker and deposition (the dropping of material) is favoured.
Refraction turns wave fronts until they are roughly parallel to the shore.
Waves do not always strike the same part of the coast, because the level of the sea changes. Tides and storm surges change where the waves do their work.
Tides are the twice-daily rise and fall of sea level, caused mainly by the pull of the moon, with the sun also contributing.
Tidal range (the difference between high and low tide) sets the vertical band of coast on which the waves work, so a larger range spreads wave attack over a wider band.
A storm surge (a temporary rise in sea level during a storm) lets waves reach higher up cliffs and beaches.
Longer-term changes in land and sea level also change coasts: raised beaches (old beaches left above sea level) form emergent coasts.

Rias (drowned river valleys), fjords (flooded glacial valleys) and drowned drumlins (flooded egg-shaped hills of glacial deposit) form submergent coasts. There is more on this in the glaciation chapter, under isostasy (the rising or sinking of land).
Waves wear away rock by four processes, and abrasion is the most effective at the foot of a cliff. Each works differently, so you need to name them and say how they work.

Hydraulic action: the force of breaking waves forces air and water into joints (natural cracks in rock) and cracks; the trapped air and water are compressed, then released as the wave retreats, weakening and shattering the rock.
Abrasion (corrasion): waves hurl sand, shingle and boulders against the cliff, grinding and undercutting it. It is the most effective process at the cliff base.
Attrition: rocks carried by the waves collide with each other and break into smaller, rounder pieces; attrition wears down the load (the material the waves carry) rather than the cliff.
Solution (corrosion): sea water dissolves soluble rock such as limestone.
Waves are not the only thing that wears a cliff back, and they do not erode every coast at the same speed. Processes above the waves and several controls on the rate of erosion also matter.
Above the waves, weathering (the breakdown of rock in place, by freeze-thaw and salt crystallisation) and mass movement (rockfalls, and slumping on soft clay cliffs) wear the cliff back.
Waves then remove the debris that falls from the cliff face, so the cliff is exposed to further attack.

Soft glacial deposits such as boulder clay (a soft mix of clay and stones left by ice) erode fastest; on the Holderness coast of Yorkshire, England, cliffs of soft boulder clay are among the fastest-eroding coastlines in Europe.
Rock structure matters: joints, faults (breaks in the rock where it has moved) and bedding (the layers in sedimentary rock) give waves lines of weakness to exploit.
Wave energy depends on fetch, storms and refraction, so a coast with a long fetch or frequent storms is eroded faster.
A beach at the foot of a cliff can absorb wave energy and protect the cliff; human activity, such as the removal of beach material, can change the rate of erosion.
Exposure to the Atlantic or the Irish Sea decides whether a coast is eroding or depositing. The rock pattern along the coast then shapes headlands and bays.
The west coast faces the long Atlantic fetch and the prevailing (most common) south-westerly winds, so high-energy waves produce rugged, cliffed, erosional coasts.
The east coast faces the narrow Irish Sea, which gives a short fetch; its lower-energy waves and soft glacial deposits favour depositional features such as beaches, spits, lagoons and dunes.
Storms do most of the erosion, in short episodes; this is the temporal variation (variation over time) in coastal processes.
Where bands of hard and soft rock meet the coast at right angles (a discordant coast), the soft rock is eroded back into bays and the hard rock is left as headlands.
A concordant coast, where the rock bands run parallel to the shore, stays straighter because the outer band protects the softer rock behind it.

Headland and bay: the two landforms that result from this differential (uneven) erosion; Downpatrick Head, Co. Mayo, is a headland, and the chalk headland of Handfast Point, Dorset, England, lies between Studland Bay and Swanage Bay, which are cut into softer sands and clays.
A cliff retreats inland as its base is undercut, leaving a platform of rock at its foot. Learn the stages in order, because exams ask you to describe how one landform of erosion forms.
1. Waves erode a notch in the cliff base, between high and low tide, by hydraulic action and abrasion.
2. The rock above the notch becomes an overhang, which collapses because nothing supports it.
3. Waves remove the debris, and the cliff retreats inland, remaining steep.
4. The gently sloping rock surface left at the foot of the retreating cliff is the wave-cut platform, exposed at low tide.
5. The platform widens as the cliff retreats, until waves lose most of their energy crossing it, which slows erosion.
Example: Cliffs of Moher, Co. Clare, rise to 214 m at their highest and are made of layers of shale and sandstone.
Diagram: side view of a cliff with the notch, overhang, arrow showing retreat, and the wave-cut platform exposed at low tide.
These four features form one sequence as a headland is cut back. Each stage grows out of the one before it, so keep the order cave, arch, stack, stump.
1. Waves exploit a line of weakness, a joint or fault, at the base of a headland, enlarging it by hydraulic action and abrasion to form a sea cave.
2. Caves on opposite sides of a headland meet, or one cave cuts right through, forming a sea arch.
3. The arch roof is weakened from below by wave erosion and from above by weathering, then collapses, leaving an isolated pillar called a sea stack.
4. The stack is undercut at its base and collapses into a low sea stump, which is covered at high tide.
Examples of arches: Bridges of Ross, Co. Clare, were originally three sea arches, and only one still stands; Durdle Door, Dorset, England, is a sea arch.
Examples of stacks: Dún Briste, a sea stack off Downpatrick Head, Co. Mayo; Old Harry Rocks, chalk stacks off Handfast Point, Dorset, England.
Diagram: four-stage sequence of cave, arch, stack and stump, with the joint or fault marked at the cave.
A blowhole is a cave that has been enlarged upward until it opens at the cliff top. It forms where a vertical joint runs up from the cave.
1. A cave is enlarged upward along a vertical joint by hydraulic action, with compressed air, until it breaks through to the cliff top, forming a blowhole.
2. In storms, spray is forced up through the hole, because the waves push water and air into the cave below.
3. If the roof between the blowhole and the sea collapses, a narrow inlet called a geo forms.
Blowholes are classified as erosional features, because the sea forms them by wearing rock away.
Diagram: vertical section of a cave connected to a vertical joint that opens at the cliff top.
Waves do not only erode; they also carry material along the shore. This movement supplies the sediment that builds depositional landforms.

Waves carry load in the same four ways as rivers, so the river transport terms apply here too: traction (rolling along the sea bed), saltation (bouncing along it), suspension (carried within the water) and solution (dissolved in the water).
Longshore drift: waves approach the beach at an angle set by the prevailing wind; swash carries material up the beach at that angle, and backwash drags it straight back down the slope under gravity.
Repeated over time, longshore drift moves sand and shingle along the coast in a zigzag.
Longshore drift is the transport process behind spits, bars, lagoons and tombolos.
Example: on the Holderness coast, longshore drift moves eroded material southward to Spurn Head.
Deposition is the dropping of material that the sea has been carrying. It happens when waves lose energy and there is plenty of sediment to drop.
Waves deposit material when they lose energy: in constructive wave conditions, in sheltered bays, in shallow water, or after refraction has reduced their energy.
Deposition also happens where the coast changes direction, such as at a river mouth or bay.
A large supply of sediment is needed, from rivers, cliff erosion or glacial deposits offshore.
A beach is sand and shingle deposited between low tide and the highest storm waves.
Finer sand is deposited lower down the beach, and coarser shingle higher up, for example on a storm beach.
A storm beach is a ridge of large shingle thrown above normal high tide by storm waves.
Berms are ridges marking successive high-tide levels, because each tide leaves a ridge where it reached.
Examples: Tramore, Co. Waterford; Curracloe, Co. Wexford.
Longshore drift keeps moving sand along the coast until the coast bends away, and there it builds a ridge. Whether the ridge is a spit or a bar depends on how far across the bay it grows.
1. Longshore drift carries material past a point where the coast changes direction, such as a bay or river mouth.
2. The material is deposited in calmer, deeper water, building a ridge out from the land; a spit is attached to the land at one end only.
3. Wave refraction or a change in wind direction curves the tip, forming a recurved end.
4. Sheltered water behind the spit fills with silt, forming salt marsh or mudflat.
A sand bar (barrier beach) is a spit that grows right across the mouth of a bay, joining two headlands.

Examples: Inch and Rossbeigh, Co. Kerry, are two sand spits growing out from opposite sides of Dingle Bay; Spurn Head, at the mouth of the Humber estuary (where a river meets the sea), England, is a spit.
Diagram: plan view of a recurved spit showing the drift direction, the ridge attached to the land, the recurved tip and the salt marsh behind.
Two more depositional landforms follow from longshore drift: a lagoon forms when a bar cuts off part of the sea, and a tombolo forms when a ridge reaches an island.
A lagoon is the body of water trapped behind a sand bar; it is a depositional feature, because the bar that traps it is built from deposited sediment.
A lagoon slowly fills with sediment and vegetation because it is sheltered from the waves, and it may become marsh.
Examples: Lady's Island Lake and Tacumshin Lake, Co. Wexford, are coastal lagoons behind sand-and-gravel barriers; the Back Strand at Tramore, Co. Waterford, is another.
A tombolo is a ridge of sand or shingle joining an island to the mainland.
It is built by longshore drift and by waves refracting around the island and meeting in its shelter.
Example: Sutton, Co. Dublin, where a tombolo joins Howth Head, once an island, to the mainland.
Where there is a wide, sandy beach, the wind carries dry sand inland and builds dunes. Plants, especially marram grass, are what turn loose sand into stable dunes.
1. Wind blows dry sand from a wide beach at low tide inland, where it piles up against obstacles such as driftwood, seaweed and plants above high tide.
2. Marram grass colonises the sand; its long roots bind the sand, and its growth keeps pace with burial.
3. Embryo (newly forming) dunes grow into fore dunes, and further inland, as soil develops and other plants arrive, grey (fixed) dunes form.
Dune slacks are damp hollows between the dune ridges.
Damage to dunes by people is covered with the human impacts on coasts.
Examples: Brittas Bay, Co. Wicklow; Curracloe, Co. Wexford; North Bull Island, Dublin Bay.
Diagram: cross-section from beach to inland showing embryo, fore and grey dunes, and a dune slack.
Every coastal landform is either erosional (made by wearing rock away) or depositional (made by dropping material). Sorting them correctly is a quick way to win marks.
Erosional features: cliff, wave-cut notch, wave-cut platform, cave, sea arch, sea stack, sea stump, blowhole and headland.
Depositional features: beach, storm beach, sand spit, sand bar, lagoon, tombolo, sand dunes and salt marsh.
Matching a photograph, aerial photograph or diagram to these features uses the same two classes.
The average annual rate of coastal erosion is the total distance retreated divided by the number of years. It is a short calculation that needs the years counted correctly.
Step 1: subtract the earlier year from the later year to find the number of years.
Step 2: divide the total distance the cliff retreated by the number of years, so the answer is a distance per year.
Illustrative figures (invented): a cliff retreats 50 m between 1990 and 2015.
Rate: 50 m divided by 25 years gives an average of 2 m per year.

Coasts are a balance between erosion (wearing land away), transport (moving the material) and deposition (dropping it). Human activity can upset that balance, which is why this option looks at how people change coastal processes.

Human activity can interrupt longshore drift (the movement of sand and shingle along the shore by waves hitting at an angle), remove sediment (the sand and stones that make up beaches), destroy the vegetation that holds dunes together, or reflect wave energy back out to sea.

The effects often appear further along the coast, downdrift (in the direction the sediment travels), rather than where the work was done. This is because the sediment supply is cut off or changed for everywhere further along.
Sand dunes are held in place by plants, so anything that kills the plants lets the wind start to remove the dune. Recreation is one of the main ways people do this.
Trampling of sand dunes by walkers and sunbathers kills marram grass, the tough grass whose roots bind dune sand together.
With no roots binding it, the sand is removed by the wind, cutting blowouts (hollows) into the dunes.
A blowout can breach (break through) the dune ridge, letting the sea reach the land behind, which the dunes had been protecting.
Vehicles and parking on dunes and beaches destroy vegetation and compact the sand (press it down hard); caravan parks and holiday homes built on dunes do the same.
Heavy use of a coast, even for quiet recreation, damages both the land surface and the wildlife that depends on it.
Golf courses on dunes (links) stabilise some dunes, but replace natural habitats and lead to demands for defences to protect the course.
Footpath erosion and cliff-edge damage occur at busy viewing points, because so many feet wear away the surface.
Litter, pollution and disturbance of nesting and feeding birds follow heavy use.
Building a resort right at the shore does more than take up space. It removes the natural store of sand and leaves the beach with nowhere to move.
Hotels, apartments and promenades built on the beach or dune line remove the natural sediment store, the sand that would normally feed the beach.

They block the natural landward movement of dunes and beaches, so the beach narrows and defences become necessary; this is called coastal squeeze (the beach is squeezed between the sea and the buildings).
Example: the Spanish Mediterranean coast, including the Costa del Sol and Benidorm on the Costa Blanca, where high-rise resorts have been built along the shore since mass tourism grew in the 1960s.
Once people build on a coast, they often try to protect it from the sea. Coastal defences fall into two types, and the difference decides how they affect coastal processes.
Hard engineering builds structures to resist the sea; soft engineering works with natural processes.
Hard engineering is usually expensive and effective locally, and it can increase erosion elsewhere, because it changes how waves and sediment move along the rest of the coast.
A sea wall protects the land behind it but changes the processes in front of it.
Sea walls are concrete or stone walls, often curved (recurved) to throw waves back.
They reflect wave energy, so backwash (the water running back down the beach) scours (digs out) the beach in front, lowering and narrowing it, and the wall itself is undermined.
Erosion often increases at the ends of a sea wall, because the unprotected land beside it still takes the full force of the waves.
Sea walls are expensive to build and maintain, so they are usually used only where valuable land or buildings need protecting.
Rock armour is a cheaper alternative to a wall. Instead of reflecting waves, it uses gaps to soak up their energy.
Rock armour (rip-rap) is large boulders piled at the foot of a cliff or in front of a sea wall.
The gaps between the boulders absorb and break up wave energy.
It is cheaper than a sea wall and quick to place, because the boulders are simply piled up rather than built into a structure.
It can be unsightly and hard to walk over, and big storms may move the boulders.
In photographs, rock armour appears as a pile of loose boulders at the cliff foot or wall.
Groynes work by catching the sand that longshore drift carries along the beach. This helps the beach in one place but harms it further along.
Groynes are low wooden, rock or concrete barriers built out from the shore at right angles, across the beach.
They trap sand moving by longshore drift on their updrift side (the side the sand arrives from), widening the beach, which absorbs wave energy.
Effect on processes: the beach downdrift is starved of sediment, so erosion increases there.
Unlike rock armour, which lies along the foot of a cliff or wall, groynes run out across the beach at right angles to the shore.
Several other structures are used on coasts. Each either breaks up waves or interrupts the movement of sediment.
Gabions are wire cages filled with stones, which are stacked to form a protective barrier.
Revetments are sloping wooden, concrete or rock structures that break waves.
Offshore breakwaters and reefs are structures parallel to the shore, just offshore, that make waves break before they reach the beach.

Training walls and harbour piers (walls built to guide water or protect a harbour entrance) interrupt longshore drift and cause deposition in new places; the North Bull Wall, Dublin Bay, is an example.
Soft engineering rebuilds the natural defences of the coast, the beach and the dunes, instead of building against the sea.
Beach nourishment pumps or trucks sand or shingle onto a beach to widen it.
It looks natural and keeps the beach for tourism, so visitors still have sand to use.
It must be repeated, as waves remove the sand, and dredging (digging up) the source can harm the sea bed.
Dune regeneration uses sand fencing or brushwood to trap blown sand, replants marram grass, and fences off damaged areas.
It is cheap and natural, but takes years because the plants must grow, and it needs visitors to keep off the dunes so the new growth is not trampled.
Sometimes the cheapest option is to stop fighting the sea. Managed retreat gives up some land in a planned way.
In managed retreat (managed realignment), or 'do nothing', defences are removed or not replaced, and the sea is allowed to flood low-value land.
The flooded land becomes salt marsh (a muddy, plant-covered area flooded by the tide), which absorbs wave energy and provides habitat.
It is cheap and sustainable because natural salt marsh needs no upkeep, but landowners lose land.
The Mappleton scheme shows how a defence can move erosion downdrift.
At Mappleton, on the Holderness coast, England, a 1991 scheme of two rock groynes and rock armour at the cliff foot protected the village and the main coast road.
The scheme cost about £2 million, which shows how expensive hard engineering can be.
Result: the beach built up between the groynes, but the cliffs immediately south of the scheme, starved of sediment, eroded faster than before.
This is the textbook example of defence moving the problem downdrift.
In Dublin Bay a wall built for shipping changed where sand was deposited, and a whole island grew as a result.
The North Bull Wall was built in the 1820s to stop sand silting up the entrance to Dublin Port.
Sand then built up against and beside the wall, and North Bull Island grew from a sandbank into an island with dunes, salt marsh and mudflats.
It is an example of a human structure causing deposition, because the wall slowed the moving sand so it settled beside it.
Rosslare Strand is an Irish example of a resort coast that needs defending.
Rosslare Strand is a sandy resort coast on an eroding shoreline, so the resort needs defences to protect it.
It is protected by groynes and rock armour.
After the 1953 storm surge, the Dutch built defences that were balanced with conservation.
The North Sea storm surge of 1953 (a rise in sea level driven by storm winds) flooded the south-west of the Netherlands and killed about 1,800 people there.
The response was the Delta Works: dams, sluices (gates that control water flow) and storm-surge barriers that shortened and sealed the coast of Zeeland.
The Oosterschelde (Eastern Scheldt) barrier, completed in 1986, has movable gates that stay open in normal weather.
Because the tides still flow in, the estuary's ecosystem and shellfish industry are kept, which makes this defence balanced with conservation.
