Defences protect single places, but a coast is one connected system. Management looks at the whole coast and balances competing needs.
Coasts are under pressure from erosion, development, tourism and rising sea levels.
Management tries to protect people and property while keeping natural processes and habitats working.
Integrated coastal zone management (ICZM) plans a whole stretch of coast, a sediment cell (a length of coast where sediment moves as a closed system), as one unit.
ICZM balances defence, tourism, development and conservation, because work in one place affects places downdrift.
Laws and awards are tools for managing the coast. Laws limit what can be built or damaged, and awards encourage good management.

The EU Habitats and Birds Directives protect coastal sites through Special Areas of Conservation (SACs) for habitats and Special Protection Areas (SPAs) for birds, which together form the Natura 2000 network.
In Ireland, the National Parks and Wildlife Service oversees these sites, so there is a state body responsible for enforcing the protection.
Planning controls restrict building close to the shore.
Spain's Ley de Costas (Coastal Law) of 1988 was passed in response to overdevelopment and restricts building on the shore zone.
Blue Flag is an international beach award run by the Foundation for Environmental Education and administered in Ireland by An Taisce.
Its criteria cover water quality, environmental education and information, environmental management, and safety and services, encouraging councils to manage beaches well.
Popular dunes and cliffs can be kept open to visitors if the visitors are guided, so that trampling does less damage and people stay safe.
Dune management at busy beaches uses boardwalks and marked paths, fencing off eroded areas, marram replanting, moving car parks back from the dunes, information signs and seasonal wardens.

Example: Brittas Bay, Co. Wicklow, is a dune system heavily used by day-trippers from Dublin in summer; trampling and parking damaged the dunes, which are part of a protected Special Area of Conservation.
Cliffs of Moher, Co. Clare: a visitor centre, built into the hillside, opened in 2007.
Paths and a wall or barrier are set back from the cliff edge to control trampling and keep people safe.
North Bull Island, first met as a landform made by a wall, is also a protected site, with recreation and conservation pressing on the same place.
North Bull Island, Dublin Bay, has been a UNESCO Biosphere Reserve since 1981, and was extended in 2015 as the Dublin Bay Biosphere.
Its salt marsh and mudflats are a major wintering ground for Brent geese and other wildfowl (water birds) and waders (long-legged shore birds).
Pressures include the Royal Dublin and St Anne's golf courses on the island, cars driving onto the beach, and many visitors from the city.
It shows recreation, conservation and a human-made landform in one place.
Medmerry is the example of managed retreat used as a management measure, where the sea is let in on purpose.
Medmerry, West Sussex, England, was completed in 2013 as a managed realignment scheme.
The shingle bank was no longer maintained, a new embankment was built further inland, and the sea was let in to create intertidal habitat (land flooded and exposed by the tide).
This intertidal habitat absorbs wave energy, so it acts as a natural defence for the land behind the new embankment.
For a long answer you need to weigh the options against each other. Each type of measure has strengths and limits.
Hard defences protect a place, but they move erosion downdrift and are costly, so the problem is shifted rather than solved.
Soft measures are cheaper and more sustainable because they work with natural processes, but they are slower and less certain.
The best management works with the sediment system along a whole coast, because work in one place affects places downdrift.
An aerial photograph is taken from the air, and its type depends on the angle of the camera. A vertical photograph is the first type: the camera points straight down.
A vertical photograph is taken with the camera pointing straight down, so it shows only roofs and the tops of features, with no horizon (the line where land meets sky).
The scale of a vertical photograph (how much real distance is shrunk onto the picture) is roughly constant across the picture, so it looks like a map and can be used for measuring and mapping.
Features are harder to recognise on a vertical photograph because their sides and heights are hidden, so you must identify them from the shape of the roof.
An oblique photograph is taken with the camera tilted at an angle to the ground, like a photograph taken from a hilltop or aircraft window. This gives depth but changes how the picture can be used.
An oblique photograph is taken with the camera at an angle to the ground, so the sides as well as the roofs of buildings are visible.

The scale of an oblique photograph is not constant: foreground features (those nearest the camera) look larger than identical features in the background, and the area covered widens towards the background.
Features are easier to recognise on an oblique photograph because you can see their sides, but distance and area cannot be measured directly from it.
A low oblique photograph does not show the horizon; a high oblique photograph shows the horizon or skyline.
To say which type you have, look for the clues below and quote them as your reason.
Oblique clues: the sides of buildings are visible, foreground features look larger than background features, and depth or a horizon is shown.
Vertical clues: only roofs are visible, the scale looks even, and the picture looks like a map.

To say where a feature is on an oblique photograph, imagine the picture divided into nine areas and name the area it lies in. This is called relative location, because it gives the position within the photograph.
Three strips run across the picture: left, centre and right, so every feature falls in one of three columns.
Three strips run into the picture: foreground at the bottom, nearest the camera; middleground in the centre; background at the top, furthest from the camera.
Accepted notation gives one term from each set, across-term first: left foreground, centre middleground, right background. Both parts must be correct to score.
Use the exam spelling foreground, middleground and background, and use centre, not middle, for the across strip.
Method: draw the grid lightly on the photo in pencil (or fold the picture into thirds in your head), find the feature, and state its zone.
The same method answers true or false statements about what lies in a zone, and matches cropped sections of the photo to zones.
The nine-area grid applies to oblique photographs. A vertical photograph looks straight down, so there is no near or far.
On a vertical photograph foreground and background have no meaning, because the camera looks straight down and nothing is nearer to it than anything else.
Use top, centre or bottom with left, centre or right instead, or compass directions such as north-east and south-west if the orientation is known.
Rivertown is an invented market town on an invented oblique photograph. Every worked example here uses it and is labelled illustrative.
Illustrative: a river flows from the left foreground to the right background, and a stone bridge crosses it in the centre middleground.
Illustrative: a church with a spire stands in the left middleground, with a graveyard beside it.
Illustrative: a main street and a square lie in the centre middleground.
Illustrative: an industrial estate lies in the right foreground, and a housing estate of semi-detached houses lies in the left background.
Illustrative: fields with hedgerows lie in the right background, and a GAA pitch lies in the centre background.
Illustrative: waste ground lies in the centre foreground.
Illustrative true or false: there is waste ground in the centre foreground. This is true, because the waste ground is in the centre foreground.
Each feature has a clue that identifies it on the photograph. Use the clue to name the feature, then give its zone.
Church: a spire or tower, a cross-shaped plan, and a graveyard beside it.
School: a large building with a playground, pitches and a car park.
Shopping centre: a very large flat roof and an extensive car park, because many shoppers arrive by car.
Factory or warehouse: a large flat or sawtooth roof (a row of angled ridges like saw teeth), with yards and lorries but no gardens.
Apartments: a large multi-storey block with communal parking, meaning parking shared by all residents.
Houses are told apart by how they are joined, and open land by its markings or lack of them.
Housing estate: rows of similar houses with gardens, often arranged in cul-de-sacs (dead-end streets).
Terraced houses share side walls; semi-detached houses share one wall; detached houses stand alone. This is how you tell the three apart.
Car park: marked bays with vehicles in them, so you can tell it from waste ground.
Sports pitch: a rectangle with lines and goalposts. Running track: an oval with lanes.
Waste or derelict ground: rough, unused land with no clear use.
Transport routes and water have their own shapes and surfaces, which make them easy to pick out.
Railway: gentle curves, no cars, and crossings of roads by bridges.
River and lake: smooth, dark water with a natural outline.
Bridge: a structure carrying a road or railway across water or another route; its parapet (the low wall along its edge) is a clue.
Harbour, pier or quay: boats moored alongside a structure that projects into the water or lines it.
Roundabout: a circular junction with roads leading off it, such as the one at the end of a bridge.
A street map, satellite image or street-view images (ground-level photographs) may show the same features, labelled A to E, in a different orientation from the photograph.

Find two features common to both, because they give you fixed reference points; such as the river, a bridge, the railway or a large church, and turn the second source mentally until they match. This is needed because it may be oriented differently from the photo.
Identify each feature by a distinctive clue: a spire, a cruciform (cross-shaped) roof, pitch markings, a large flat roof beside a car park, a bridge parapet, or shopfronts.
Give each feature's zone on the photograph in accepted notation.
There are two ways to say where something is. Absolute location uses the map's grid, and relative location uses the photograph itself or neighbouring features.

Absolute location is a grid reference read from the OS (Ordnance Survey) map. Relative location is a zone in the nine-area notation, or a position relative to other features, such as beside the bridge, north of the river.

To give a grid reference for a feature seen on the photograph, find it on the photograph, locate it on the map from its position relative to roads, the river and junctions, then give a four- or six-figure grid reference as taught in Map interpretation.
On a 1:50 000 map individual buildings are often not drawn, so locate the feature from the surrounding road pattern; churches are shown by map symbols.
To name a road or river seen on the photograph, trace it on the photograph, find the same route on the map, and read its number (N, R or M) or its name from the map.
The map can tell you which way the camera was facing when the photograph was taken. This is also what lets you turn left and right on the photo into compass directions.
The direction from a foreground feature to a background feature on the map is the direction the camera was pointing, because the background is the part furthest in front of the camera.
Identify one foreground feature and one background feature on the photograph, find both on the map, and state the direction in an eight-point compass term such as north-east.
Check the camera direction with a third feature, so that one wrongly identified feature does not mislead you.
Illustrative: on the map the bridge (centre middleground) lies due south of the pitch (centre background), and the waste ground (centre foreground) lies south of the bridge.
Illustrative: foreground to background runs south to north, so the camera was pointing north.
The photograph and the map record different things, so each answers questions the other cannot.
The photograph shows what the map does not: individual buildings, land-use type, crops and field use, building height and age, car parks, traffic, temporary features and recent developments.

The map shows what the photograph does not: names, road numbers, height and contours (lines joining places of equal height), the grid, labelled antiquities (ancient monuments), boundaries, and features hidden by trees or lying beyond the frame.
The map covers the whole area at a constant scale; an oblique photograph gives a partial view with changing scale.
The photograph and map were usually made on different dates, so differences between them can reveal change.
Whether you can work out a scale depends on the type of photograph.
An oblique photograph has no single scale, so measure distances on the map instead.
The scale of a vertical photograph is found by comparing a distance on the photograph with the real ground distance, which is read from the map. The map-scale method is taught in Map interpretation.
Illustrative: two road junctions are 5 cm apart on a vertical photograph and 2 cm apart on the 1:50 000 map.
Illustrative: 2 cm on the 1:50 000 map equals 1 km, which is 100 000 cm on the ground.
Illustrative: the photograph scale is 5 cm to 100 000 cm, which is 1:20 000.
A sketch map is a drawn copy of the photograph's main features, not a tracing. Following the rules for size, shapes and labels is where the marks are won.
Draw a frame with four ruled sides, the same shape as the photograph.
The exam usually asks for half the length and half the breadth: each side is halved, so the sketch has a quarter of the photograph's area.
Measure the photograph and calculate the sketch size before drawing.
Divide the photograph and the frame into the nine-area grid lightly in pencil, so that you can place features accurately.
Show only the features asked for, in approximately the correct position, shape and proportion, because a sketch is a simplified copy and not a tracing.
Different kinds of feature are drawn in different ways, and every one must be labelled.

Draw rivers, roads and railways as lines, with the river as a broad double line; draw areas such as housing, industry, farmland, car parks and lakes as closed outlined shapes; draw single buildings as small blocks or symbols.
Label every feature on or beside it, or in a key (a list explaining the symbols), and give the sketch a title. An unlabelled feature scores nothing.
A feature specified with a position, such as a car park in the centre foreground, must be drawn in that zone.

Common requests to practise: river, coastline, lake, bridge, railway, two connecting streets (two streets drawn meeting at a junction), car park, church, ecclesiastical land use, housing estate, residential land use, industrial building or estate, warehouse, agricultural land, recreational land use, sports ground, waste ground, a historic ruin, and the CBD.
This shows the rules applied to the invented Rivertown photograph.
Illustrative: a photograph 22 cm by 16 cm gives a sketch frame of 11 cm by 8 cm, because each side is halved.
Illustrative request: the river, a bridge, a church, an industrial area in the foreground, and agricultural land in the background.
Illustrative: draw the river as a broad double line from the left foreground to the right background.
Illustrative: draw the bridge as a short line crossing the river in the centre middleground, and label it.
Illustrative: draw the church as a small cross-shaped symbol in the left middleground, and label it.
Illustrative: draw the industrial area as a closed outlined shape in the right foreground, because the request places it there, and label it.
Illustrative: draw the agricultural land as field outlines with hedgerows in the background of the right side, and label it.
Land use means what an area of land is used for. Sorting what you see into categories is the first step in describing a town.
Land-use categories: residential, commercial or retail, industrial, ecclesiastical, educational, recreational, transport, agricultural, open space, and waste or derelict ground.
Ecclesiastical land use is religious land use: churches, their grounds and graveyards. Schools are educational land use.
Agricultural land around the town shows field patterns with hedgerows, and is either pasture (grass, often with livestock) or tillage (ploughed or cropped fields).
Industry needs space and good transport, so it sits in particular places in a town.

Industrial land is usually on the edge of town: large flat-roofed buildings in an industrial estate, near main roads, a bypass (a road built round a town to take traffic away from its centre), a railway or a port, with space for parking and lorries.
Older industry, such as mills, may be found beside the river or quays.
Density means how many homes fit into an area. It changes from the centre of a town outwards, and the centre itself has a distinctive look.
Older terraced housing near the centre has high density, with small or no gardens, because the houses share walls and are packed together.
Suburban estates of semi-detached and detached houses lie further out, at lower density, with gardens and cul-de-sacs.
Apartments are high density, because many homes are stacked in one multi-storey block.
Residential density usually falls outward from the centre.
The CBD (central business district) is the commercial core of the town, found at the centre where roads converge.
CBD clues: the tallest and most densely packed buildings, no gardens, shops fronting onto main streets, car parks and heavy traffic, and often a square or main street.
A function is a purpose a town serves, such as trade, worship or transport. Each function can be seen on a photograph.
Functions visible on photographs: residential; commercial or retail; industrial or manufacturing; ecclesiastical or religious; educational; recreational or leisure; medical, such as a hospital.
Further functions: transport (bridge, railway station, converging roads, harbour); port or fishing (piers, boats); tourism (hotels, caravan parks, marinas, beaches, historic sites).

Further functions: market (a square, a market house); administrative (courthouse, council offices, Garda station, which is often hard to confirm from a photograph alone); defensive (a historic castle or town walls).
A function question wants evidence, a location and a reason. Following the same four steps each time gives a full answer.
Answer formula for describing and explaining a function: name the function, give the photograph evidence, give its location in accepted notation, and explain why the town performs it.
Explain the reason using its site (the land it stands on), situation (its position relative to surroundings), size or hinterland (the area around it that it serves).
Give several pieces of evidence for each function, so that one doubtful clue does not weaken the answer.
Illustrative ecclesiastical function: a church with a spire and graveyard in the left middleground.
Illustrative industrial function: large flat-roofed units and lorry yards in the right foreground, beside the main road.
Illustrative market or commercial function: a square and a main street of shops in the centre middleground, where roads converge at the bridge.
A town's history is visible in its buildings and layout, so the photograph can show which parts are old and which are new.
Older features show early growth: a castle, tower house or other ruin; an old church or abbey ruin with an old graveyard; town walls or gates.
A market square, fair green or market house shows the town's role as a market centre.
Old stone bridges, quays and warehouses on the river, and mills and weirs (low dams across a river) show the town's use of the river.
A railway line and station show growth in the 19th century.
Modern housing estates and industrial estates on the edge of town show recent growth.
Towns grow where a site offers an advantage, and many of those advantages can be seen on the photograph.

Reasons for the town's location seen on the photograph: a bridging point, a river or coastal site, converging routes, flat land, a harbour, surrounding farmland for a market town, or a defensive site.
The layout of the streets shows whether a town was designed or grew bit by bit, and the pattern can be named.
A planned town has wide, straight streets, a regular grid, a central square or diamond, and uniform terraces.
An unplanned town has narrow, winding, irregular streets, often of medieval origin.
Wide streets on their own do not show that a town is unplanned, because planned towns also have wide, straight streets.
Linear growth: development along a main road, for example houses strung out beside it.
Nucleated growth: development clustered around a centre or junction.
Radial pattern: streets radiating from a bridge or square.
Grid pattern: streets laid out at right angles in regular blocks.
Name the pattern on the photograph and use it as evidence for the type of town.
Congestion means roads so full that traffic slows or stops. Several causes can be spotted on a photograph.
Narrow streets in the old core of the town, which cannot carry many vehicles.
On-street parking that narrows the road.
Routes converging on one bridge or junction, so all traffic must squeeze through one point.
Through-traffic passing the town centre, meaning vehicles that are only passing through and do not stop there.
Delivery vehicles, and limited off-street parking.
Schools and shopping centres that generate peak traffic.
Traffic management means the measures used to keep traffic moving and safe. Many can be spotted on the photograph.

Measures visible on photographs: roundabouts, traffic lights, pedestrian crossings, one-way streets (all parked cars face one way, with arrows on the road), double yellow lines (no parking), bus lanes and cycle lanes.

Further measures: off-street and multi-storey car parks, pedestrianised streets (closed to vehicles), bypasses, relief roads and ring roads, bollards (short posts that block vehicles) and traffic-calming ramps.
Answer formula for a measure: name it, give its location in accepted notation, and explain how it reduces congestion or improves safety.
Answer formula for a problem: name it, locate it, and explain why it causes congestion.
A suggested solution, such as a bypass to remove through-traffic, a car park on waste ground, a one-way system or pedestrianisation, must be justified with photograph evidence.
This applies the formulas to the invented Rivertown photograph.
Illustrative problem: all routes converge on the single bridge in the centre middleground, and on-street parking on the main street narrows the road.
Illustrative measures: a roundabout at the end of the bridge, and a car park beside the square.
Illustrative solution: a relief road crossing the river further downstream, using the open fields.
Land use changes as a town grows. The photograph can be compared with the map to show what a place used to be.
Land-use change is found by comparing the map with the photograph, which are dated differently, or by comparing a location's present use with a listed change.
Listed changes include agricultural to housing, industrial to residential, green space to recreation, open space to residential, farmland to relief road, and green space to waste ground.
Method: find the location, identify its present use, then infer its earlier use from the map or from surrounding clues.
Clues to earlier use: new estates on the edge with fields beyond, cleared sites, and new roads cutting across field patterns.
Illustrative: the map shows fields where the photograph shows the left background housing estate, so the change is agricultural to residential.
Second pair, same method: a site shown as industrial on the map and as housing on the photograph is recorded as industrial to residential.
A growing town leaves signs on its edges, which the photograph can show.
New estates on the edge of the town.
Ribbon development (houses built in a line along a road) along approach roads.
Industrial estates and retail parks on the outskirts.
Sprawl is the spreading of a town into the countryside. There is more on this wider urban issue in the Urban Geography chapter.
A site is chosen or rejected on evidence from the photograph.
Choose a site on the photograph for a proposed development, such as a shopping centre, factory, car park or playground, and give three reasons, each with photograph evidence.
For example, reasons to look for: available flat land; access to main roads; nearness to the population served; space for parking; a position away from a flood-prone river bank.
For industry, a site away from housing is suitable.
To show a given site is unsuitable, name the reason it fails these tests and give the photograph evidence for it.
The season can be worked out from what plants, animals and people are doing. Reason from the evidence rather than guessing a month.
Deciduous trees (trees that lose their leaves in autumn) in full leaf indicate summer; bare trees indicate winter.
Crops growing or ripening, golden fields and harvested stubble (the short stalks left after harvest) indicate late summer to autumn.
Ploughed fields indicate autumn or spring.
Silage or hay bales in fields indicate summer.
Cattle grazing outdoors indicate the grazing season, roughly spring to autumn, because Irish cattle are usually housed indoors over winter.
People in light clothing, and outdoor activity on beaches or pitches, indicate warm weather.
Give two or three pieces of evidence and reason from them, without guessing exact months.
Illustrative: trees in full leaf and silage bales in the right background fields indicate summer.
Shadows point away from the sun. Use the camera direction from the map to turn a shadow direction into a compass direction.
Ireland is in the northern hemisphere, so the midday sun is due south and midday shadows point north, where they are at their shortest.
The sun rises in the east and sets in the west, roughly. Morning shadows point west; evening shadows point east.
Long shadows mean a low sun, which occurs early or late in the day, or in winter, so long shadows alone do not give the hour.
Other clues: busy streets and full car parks in business hours, school car parks full or empty, rush-hour traffic, and street lights on.
Illustrative: the camera points north, so left is west and right is east. Building shadows fall to the left, which is west, so the sun is in the east: morning.
Illustrative: the shadows are long, so the sun is low and it is early morning.

Exam map questions are set on an Ordnance Survey (OS) map, the official survey map of Ireland. To answer them you need to know what the map shows and how its scale (the link between a distance on paper and the real distance on the ground) works. Worked examples use an invented town called Rivertown and are labelled illustrative.

The exam map is a 1:50 000 Ordnance Survey (Discovery Series) extract, meaning a cut-out piece of the national map, and questions say 'examine the map and legend'. The legend is the key that explains the symbols.
Every symbol, colour and road-class answer comes from the legend, so read it before answering instead of guessing from memory.
A ratio (representative fraction) of 1:50 000 means 1 unit on the map equals 50 000 of the same units on the ground, for example 1 cm on the map stands for 50 000 cm on the ground.
A linear scale (scale bar, a ruler-like line printed on the map) and a statement scale ('2 cm to 1 km', written in words) express the same scale in different forms.
On 1:50 000, 1 cm = 0.5 km and 2 cm = 1 km, so a grid square (one square of the printed grid) of 2 cm × 2 cm is 1 km × 1 km = 1 km².
A large-scale map (e.g. 1:1 000) shows a small area in great detail; a small-scale map (e.g. 1:1 000 000) shows a large area with little detail. The bigger the ratio number, the smaller the scale.
1:50 000 is a medium scale, suited to a town and its surroundings because it shows buildings, roads and relief clearly while still covering a useful area.
A grid reference is a short code that pins a place on the map. Learn the two types, because a four-figure reference names a whole square and a six-figure reference names a point inside it.

The Irish Grid divides Ireland into 25 sub-zones, each 100 km × 100 km, lettered A to Z with I omitted. The sub-zone letter is printed on the map and starts every grid reference, so that the code points to one place only.
Eastings are the vertical grid lines, numbered along the top and bottom, and the numbers increase eastward. Read them first, because the grid reference runs across before it runs up.
Northings are the horizontal grid lines, numbered up the sides, and the numbers increase northward. Read them second, so that the reference reads across then up.
Memory aid for the order: along the corridor, then up the stairs.

A four-figure reference identifies a whole 1 km square by the easting and northing of its bottom-left (south-west) corner. Use it for areas such as a lake, a forest or a slope, which cover a whole square rather than a single point.
A six-figure reference identifies a point to the nearest 100 m. Mentally divide the square into tenths, then read the tenths east of the easting line and the tenths north of the northing line.

Six-figure references locate point features such as a building symbol, a road junction, a spot height (a dot marking an exact height) or the point where a road leaves the map. Give the reference for the centre of the symbol.

Illustrative: the square containing the ringfort (an early Christian farmstead) in Rivertown is the four-figure reference R 25 43, easting 25 first and then northing 43, with R as the sub-zone letter.

Questions use grid references in two directions: you are given a reference and asked what is there, or told a feature and asked to locate it. Position can also be given in words, relative to other things.
To name a feature at a grid reference, find the sub-zone letter, then the easting, then the northing, and name what the map or legend labels at that point exactly.
A common Ordinary task is naming the feature at three or four grid references, such as an antiquity (a historic monument), a Garda station, a post office or a tourist feature.
Illustrative: the bridge over the River Dallow is at six-figure reference R 268 441, so the easting 268 is read before the northing 441; the feature at R 280 436 is a motte (a Norman earth mound).
Absolute location is a precise position given by a grid reference or by latitude and longitude (degrees measured from fixed lines on the globe), so it can be checked exactly.
Relative location describes a position against other features or directions, so it is approximate, e.g. 'north-west of the town, beside the river'.
Exams ask which area of the map (north-west, south-east and so on) a named feature lies in, for example the north-east.
Latitude and longitude give a global position in degrees from two fixed reference lines, which makes them useful for any place on Earth, not only places on one OS map.

Latitude is the angular distance north or south of the Equator (0°, the line round the middle of the Earth), up to 90°N and 90°S at the poles. Lines of latitude (parallels) run east–west, parallel to each other.
Longitude is the angular distance east or west of the Prime Meridian (0°), which passes through Greenwich, London, up to 180°. Lines of longitude (meridians) run north–south and meet at the poles.
Each degree is divided into 60 minutes (′). Write latitude first with N or S, then longitude with E or W, e.g. 53°20′N, 6°15′W.

Key lines: the Equator (0°); the Tropics of Cancer and Capricorn at about 23.5°N and 23.5°S; the Arctic and Antarctic Circles at about 66.5°N and 66.5°S; the International Date Line roughly follows 180°.

One degree of latitude is about 111 km everywhere, because parallels are evenly spaced. One degree of longitude is about 111 km at the Equator and shrinks to zero at the poles, because the meridians meet there.
Longitude is linked to time, and it also lets you describe where Ireland sits on the globe. Each coordinate system has its own best use.
The earth turns 360° in 24 hours, so 15° of longitude equals 1 hour of time. Places to the east are ahead.
Illustrative: a place 30° east of Greenwich is 2 hours ahead, since 30 ÷ 15 = 2.

Ireland's position is fixed by coordinates: it lies between about 51.5°N and 55.5°N and about 5.5°W and 10.5°W, so it is in the northern hemisphere (north of the Equator) and the western hemisphere (west of Greenwich).
Example: Dublin lies at about 53°20′N, 6°15′W, which puts it north of the Equator and west of Greenwich.
Grid references are used on OS maps because they are quicker and more precise at local scale; latitude and longitude are used for global location.
Distance questions ask for a length in km between two points. A straight-line distance is measured directly; a curved distance has to follow the bends of a road, railway, river or walk.

Straight-line distance: measure with a ruler in cm and multiply by 0.5 to get km, or lay a paper edge between the two points and read it against the scale bar. Give the answer in km to one decimal place.
From two grid references: find the difference in eastings (ΔE) and the difference in northings (ΔN) in km, then distance = √(ΔE² + ΔN²). This is Pythagoras' theorem applied to the grid.

Curved distance (a road, railway, river or walk): mark the start on the straight edge of a strip of paper, pivot the strip at each bend and mark as you go, then straighten it and measure against the scale bar. A string laid along the route also works.
Start and stop exactly at the points named, such as where the road enters the map, a junction or a roundabout, so that the length is not too long or too short.
Illustrative: the bridge at R 268 441 to the summit pillar at R 240 405 measures 9.1 cm, or 4.6 km (rounded); by grid, ΔE = 2.8 km and ΔN = 3.6 km, so √(2.8² + 3.6²) = √20.8 ≈ 4.6 km.
Illustrative: the R990 from the town to the crossroads village measures 9.0 cm along its bends, or 4.5 km.
Area is found by counting grid squares, because each 1 km square on a 1:50 000 map is 1 km². The method depends on whether the shape is a neat rectangle or irregular.
Rectangular areas (the whole map, or the part north of a named northing or west of a named easting): count kilometres east–west × kilometres north–south; each 1 km square is 1 km².

Irregular features (a lake, a bay, land above a contour): count the full squares; count squares more than half covered as full; ignore squares less than half covered, or estimate part-squares as fractions.
Give the answer in km² and state that it is approximate, since counting part-squares is an estimate.
Land on one side of a road or railway: count the squares on that side and estimate partly covered squares; exclude sea where the question asks for land.
Illustrative: the whole extract is 14 km × 8 km = 112 km²; the land north of northing 44 is 14 km × 4 km = 56 km².
Illustrative: an invented lake covering 3 full squares and 4 squares more than half covered is about 7 km².
Direction questions ask which way you would travel between two places, or which way a feature runs. The map has a fixed north, so every answer is read against it.
North is the top of the OS map (grid north). The eight compass points are N, NE, E, SE, S, SW, W and NW; sixteen points add NNE, ENE, ESE, SSE, SSW, WSW, WNW and NNW.
Method: draw a line from the start point to the destination, imagine a compass centred on the start, and read the direction of travel.
'From A to B' means the direction of travel, read at A. Quick check: is B above or below A (north or south), and to the left or right (west or east)?

Direction along a route (a walk, a road, a river's flow) is the overall direction from its start to its end. A river flows from its source on high ground to its mouth on low ground, which spot heights and contours show.
Bearings (optional for Higher): the angle measured clockwise from north, from 0° to 360°; E = 090°, S = 180°, W = 270°.

Illustrative: from the bridge at R 268 441 to the summit pillar at R 240 405, the pillar is 2.8 km west and 3.6 km south, so the direction of travel is south-west; from the pillar to the bridge it is north-east. The River Dallow flows towards the north-east.
The OS map shows height with several devices. Contours are the main one, and you must be able to read a height from each.

Contours are lines joining places of equal height above sea level. On the Discovery Series the vertical interval (the height difference between neighbouring contours) is 10 m, and some contours are numbered with their height.

Spot heights are dots with the height in metres, which is useful for exact heights; triangulation pillars are survey points with their height; layer colouring (colour bands for ranges of height) is shown in the legend.
Height of a point: read the spot height or pillar beside it, or the nearest numbered contour, and count contours up or down at 10 m each.
The highest point on the map is the highest spot height or pillar; check the upland areas, because high ground is where the top height will be.
The spacing of contours shows how steep the ground is, and the pattern of spacing gives the shape of the slope. This is how you recognise a slope type on the map.

Contours close together mean a steep slope, because the ground rises 10 m over a short distance; contours far apart mean a gentle slope; a wide area with no contours is flat ground, such as a floodplain or coastal lowland.
Even slope: contours are evenly spaced, so the gradient stays constant, as on a straight ramp.
Concave slope: contours close together near the top and widely spaced near the bottom, so the slope is steep above and gentle below, and the whole slope can be seen from the top.
Convex slope: contours widely spaced near the top and close together near the bottom, so the slope is gentle above and steep below, and the foot cannot be seen from the top.
Stepped slope, for example a terraced hillside: alternating bands of close and wide contour spacing, which gives steep sections and flat sections in turn.
Different relief features make distinct contour shapes. Learn the shape of each and you can name the feature from the contours alone.
Valley: contours form V or U shapes pointing upstream (towards higher ground, where the river rises), with a river along the floor.
Spur: a ridge of land sticking out from a hill, so water runs off it either side, with contours forming V shapes pointing downhill, towards lower ground.
Plateau: a high, flat or gently sloping top with steep edges; contours crowd round the edge and are few on the top.
Ridge: a long, narrow stretch of high ground, shown by elongated contours along its crest (the top line).
Col or saddle: a low pass between two summits, shown as a dip between two high points, so it is a natural route across a range.
Escarpment: a steep slope on one side and a gentle slope on the other, so contours are close on one side and wide on the other.
Knoll or isolated hill: a closed ring of contours, because the ground falls away on every side.
Gradient measures steepness as a number, aspect says which way a slope faces, and intervisibility asks whether two points can see each other. All three use the heights and distances on the map.

Gradient is the steepness of a slope: vertical interval (VI, the difference in height) ÷ horizontal equivalent (HE, the ground distance), both in the same units, written as 1 in x or 1:x. A larger x means a gentler slope.

Method: find the height of each point and subtract to get the VI; measure the distance on the map and convert it to metres for the HE; divide HE by VI. The result is an average gradient between the two points.
Aspect is the direction a slope faces, which is the direction you look when facing downhill, not the uphill direction: a slope falling towards the south is south-facing, with a southerly aspect.
In Ireland, south-facing slopes receive more sunshine and are warmer.
Intervisibility: whether one point can be seen from another. A convex slope or intervening high ground blocks the view, so check with a cross-section (a side-on drawing of the ground between them).
Illustrative: the summit at 512 m to the bridge at 52 m gives VI = 460 m; HE = 4.6 km = 4 600 m; gradient = 4 600 ÷ 460 = 1 in 10.
A cross-section is a side-on view of the ground along a line between two points, built from the contours the line crosses. It shows the shape of the relief and lets you test slopes and views.
1. Join the two points with a straight line on the map.
2. Lay a straight paper edge along the line and mark where every contour crosses it, with its height, plus rivers, roads and other features.
3. Draw a horizontal axis the same length as the line (horizontal scale = map scale) and a vertical axis with a chosen height scale.
4. Plot each height above its mark and join the points with a smooth curve.
5. Label the rivers, roads, the summit, the slope types and the ends (X and Y, with grid references); give a title and both scales.

Vertical exaggeration: the vertical scale is stretched so that relief shows, since otherwise the hills would look almost flat. It equals the horizontal scale distance ÷ the vertical scale distance for the same map length, and is stated in the title or key.

Illustrative: a cross-section north from the summit to the river uses a horizontal scale of 1:50 000 (1 cm = 500 m) and a vertical scale of 1 cm = 50 m (1:5 000); vertical exaggeration = 500 m ÷ 50 m = ×10.
Illustrative: the slope from the summit is concave, with contours crowded near the top and widely spaced near the river.
In some questions the profile is already drawn for you. Your job is to match each labelled point on it to the map, then read facts off the map at that spot.
A printed profile runs along a named easting or northing between points X and Y, with features labelled A to E; match each labelled point to the map by its distance along the line and its height.
A river crossing is a dip in the profile, because the land falls to the river, with a blue line on the map at that spot.
A road is identified by its number on the map, for example the N99 in the illustrative example below.
The height at a point is read from the vertical axis or from the map, so cross-check one against the other.
The slope type between two points (concave, convex, even, steep, gentle, flat) is read from the profile curve and the contours.
Land use or forestry type is read from the map symbol at that point.
A named walk, cycle route or tourist attraction crossing the line, and the townland (the smallest Irish land division) or place name at a point, are read from the map labels.

Illustrative: along northing 42 from X (R 200 420) to Y (R 300 420), point A is a dip where the River Dallow crosses, B is on the N99, C is on coniferous plantation, and the slope between D and E is concave.

Symbols are drawn or named by copying them from the legend, in proportion and in the legend's colour where colour is used. The legend is provided in the exam, so the skill is knowing its groups and reading it quickly.
Legend groups: roads; railways and stations; water features; height; vegetation; antiquities; tourist and leisure information; public services; boundaries.
Road letters: M = motorway; N = national road (national primary and national secondary routes); R = regional road. N stands for National and R for Regional, not 'route' or 'rural'.
Vegetation: coniferous plantation (pointed, conifer-shaped tree symbols), deciduous woodland (rounded tree symbols) and mixed woodland (both); use the legend's terms.

Symbols exams have asked students to draw or name: viewpoint, picnic site, parking, boating activities, triangulation pillar, ringfort, county boundary, wind farm, post office, youth or independent holiday hostel, golf course, camping site, electricity transmission line, waymarked walk and cycle route. Learn them from the legend.
Antiquities are historic monuments, and the map labels each one. Some maps also mark a cultural area, so you should know how to spot it.
Antiquities are grouped in the legend; name one exactly as the map labels it, e.g. 'Castle (in ruins)', 'Ringfort', 'Standing Stone', 'Megalithic Tomb', 'Church (in ruins)', 'Holy Well' or 'Motte'.
Cultural areas: some maps mark a Gaeltacht (Irish-speaking area) boundary, which the legend identifies.
Irish-language place names on the map are further evidence of a cultural area.
A sketch is a ruled, labelled drawing of the features asked for, placed accurately on a frame. It is never a tracing.

Higher asks for a sketch to half scale (20 marks): half the length and half the breadth of the extract. Ordinary asks for a sketch map of the area shown (30 marks); a frame of similar shape, about half size, is safest.
Measure the extract, or count squares (each 2 cm square becomes 1 cm), and draw a frame with four ruled sides.
Draw light pencil grid lines on the frame at the same eastings and northings (every 1 cm at half scale, or every second line) and label the edge numbers. These let you place features accurately.

Draw a coastline as a firm line, so that it stands out from the grid lines; draw a river as a line between the named grid references, or along its entire course; draw broad rivers and lakes as outlined shapes.

Draw roads and railways as lines along their entire route where asked; draw areas (land above a contour, plantation, built-up area, golf course) as shaded closed shapes; draw point features (post office, triangulation pillar, viewpoint, camping site) as a symbol or dot.
'Land above 300 m': follow the 300 m contour accurately round every part of the area asked for. 'Entire area' means all of it; 'at' or 'in the south-west of the map' means only that part.
Label every feature on the sketch or in a key; an unlabelled feature earns nothing. Add a title, a north arrow and the words 'half scale'.
Never trace the map. Draw only the features asked for, in the correct part of the frame, since a feature placed in the wrong part loses marks.
Illustrative: the extract is 28 cm × 16 cm, so the frame is 14 cm × 8 cm, with grid lines every 1 cm. Here is how each requested feature of the invented Rivertown map is drawn and labelled.
River Dallow, entire course: a line from its entry at R 200 402 in the south-west to its exit at R 340 470 in the north-east, following its meanders across the floodplain east of the town; label it.
N99, entire route: a road line from the south-west to the north-east through the town; label it N99.
Railway: a line with its station at R 272 445; label it.
Built-up area of Rivertown: a shaded closed shape around the town centre and the housing estates on the northern edge, with the industrial estate on the N99 at the north-eastern edge; label it.
Area above 300 m at Slievenagh: a shaded closed shape following the 300 m contour round the summit triangulation pillar at R 240 405; label it.

A drainage pattern is the shape that a river and its tributaries (the smaller streams that join it) make on the map. Each pattern has a recognisable look, and the shape hints at the rock or land beneath.
Dendritic: tree-like, with tributaries joining the main river at acute angles, on rock of uniform resistance (rock that wears away at the same rate everywhere).
Trellised: tributaries join the main river at right angles, on alternating bands of hard and soft rock, so the streams follow the soft bands.
Radial: streams flow outward in all directions from a central hill or mountain, because the water runs downhill every way, as the small streams do around the summit of Slievenagh.
Centripetal: streams flow inward to a central lake or lowland, because that is the lowest ground.
Deranged: no clear pattern, with many small lakes and marshes, on glacial deposits (material left by ice).
Real examples, one clause each: trellised in the Munster ridge and valley; deranged in the Co. Cavan drumlin belt; centripetal at Lough Neagh.
Fluvial landforms are those made by rivers. On the map each one has a clue, such as a loop, a flat area with no contours, or contours crowded across the river.
V-shaped valley: the upland valley pattern given under landforms read from contours, with sharp contour Vs pointing upstream; the river runs along the floor.
Meander: a river swinging in loops, such as those on a flat floodplain. Oxbow lake: a crescent-shaped lake beside a meandering river.
Floodplain: wide and flat, with no contours, along a lowland river; often marshy.
Levees: embankments (raised banks) along the channel, where the map shows them.
Braiding: the river splits, so it looks like a plait, into several channels around islands.
Confluence: the point where a tributary joins the main river, which you can see as a Y-shaped junction of blue lines.
Delta: deposits where a river enters a lake or the sea.
Waterfall: shown by a symbol or name, with contours crowded across the river.
Glacial landforms were shaped by ice. They show up on the map as hollows, narrow ridges and groups of small hills, each with a distinctive contour shape.
Corrie: an armchair-shaped hollow (the shape ice carves, with a steep back wall), with contours close on three sides and open downhill.
Tarn: a small, round lake in a corrie, often high up.
Arête: a narrow ridge with very close contours on both sides, because the ground falls steeply away either side.
U-shaped valley: a broad, flat floor with steep sides, and contours close together on the valley sides.
Ribbon lake: a long, narrow lake on the floor of a U-shaped valley.
Drumlins: many small oval closed contour rings, often with small lakes between them.
Esker: a long, narrow, winding ridge on lowland, so it stands out from the flat ground around it.
Coastal landforms are found where land meets sea. Karst landforms belong to limestone country, where water drains underground. Both are recognised by their shapes, symbols and names.
Beach: for example sand or shingle (small rounded stones) shading along the shore.
Cliff: a cliff symbol, or contours crowded together at the coast, because the land drops steeply to the sea.
Headland: land projecting into the sea, often high.
Bay: a curved inlet of the sea, so the coastline bends inland.

Sand spit (a narrow strip of sand built out from the coast), tombolo (a ridge joining an island to the mainland) and lagoon (a shallow pool cut off from the sea): identified by their shapes and names on the map.
Sand dunes: shown by dune shading or a name.
Swallow hole: a stream ends abruptly where it disappears underground; limestone areas have few surface streams.
A lake's origin can usually be read from its shape and setting on the map, so questions ask you to give the type at a grid reference.
Lake type at a grid reference: glacial (tarn or ribbon lake), fluvial (oxbow), coastal (lagoon) or artificial (reservoir, shown by a straight dam edge, a dam symbol or a 'Reservoir' label).
Some Higher questions link the map to mass movement (the downhill movement of rock and soil), and ask you to find extremes of slope. Steepness comes from contour spacing.
A very steep area is shown by crowded contours or cliffs; locate it with a six-figure grid reference.
A very gentle area is shown by widely spaced contours; locate it with a six-figure grid reference.
There is more on mass movement on steep ground in the rocks and weathering chapter.
Settlement pattern means how buildings are arranged on the land. Three patterns appear on OS maps, and each has a look and a reason.
Nucleated: buildings clustered at a crossroads, bridge, church or village, such as the crossroads village on the invented Rivertown map.
Linear (ribbon): buildings strung along a road, sometimes a coast road or a valley floor, such as the houses along the R990 north of Rivertown.
Dispersed: individual farmhouses scattered across farmland, each on its own land, so there is no cluster.

Nucleated settlement forms around a route focus (where routes meet) or a service; linear settlement forms where a road gives access to services; dispersed settlement reflects farming and land consolidation (joining small plots into larger farms).
Ribbon development on the approach roads to a town: linear housing spreads out along the main roads, because of cheaper rural sites, road access and services along the road.
Houses are not spread evenly. Map evidence shows where people avoided building and where they chose to cluster, and each reason must be backed by that evidence.
Absence from high land above about 200–300 m, which is cold, wet, exposed and has thin soils; give a four-figure grid reference and the map evidence.
Absence on steep slopes, shown by crowded contours, because building and farming are difficult there.
Absence on poorly drained land, shown by a marsh or bog symbol, and on floodplains liable to flooding, because houses there would be damp or flooded.
Absence where forestry plantations cover the land, since the land is used for trees, and on lakes, because they cannot be built on.
High density of settlement: give a four-figure grid reference for lowland, gently sloping, well-drained land near roads, a town or the coast.
Explain each factor that favours high density: flat or gently sloping land, good drainage, road access, and nearness to a town or the coast.
A variations question asks you to compare how settlement is spread in two parts of the map. Use the same set of factors for both parts so that the comparison is fair.
A variations question (Higher, 30 marks) usually compares two contrasting parts of the map, e.g. north and south of a named northing.
For each part, compare relief and height, drainage, the soils implied by the land use, communications (roads and rail), and the pull of a town or the coast.
State each factor with a grid reference and explain it for both areas.

Illustrative: settlement is nucleated at the crossroads village, linear along the R990 north of the town and dispersed in the north-west of the lowland; there is no settlement on Slievenagh above 300 m (R 23 40: high, steep, exposed, forestry) or on the floodplain east of the town (flood risk).
Historic settlement questions ask you to name monuments on the map and say what period they belong to. The prehistoric period runs from the Stone Age to the Iron Age.
Stone Age to Iron Age sites, such as megalithic tombs (stone-built burial monuments: court, portal or dolmen, passage and wedge tombs), standing stones, stone circles and cists (stone-lined graves).
Also prehistoric: fulachta fia (Bronze Age cooking sites), promontory forts (forts on land jutting out into water) and crannógs (lake dwellings).
Who lived there: early farming communities. Why the site was chosen: defence (promontory forts) and a lake (crannógs). What it shows: farming economy, and burial and ritual sites for religion.
Illustrative: a megalithic tomb at R 225 412 and a standing stone at R 231 418.
The early Christian (early medieval) period left many farmsteads and church sites. Several different map names point to the same kind of site.

Early Christian (early medieval) sites include ringforts, also named rath, lios, dún, caher or cashel on the map; souterrains (underground passages); ecclesiastical (church-related) sites with churches and graveyards; holy wells; round towers; and high crosses.
Ringforts were the farmsteads of the period, enclosed by an earth bank (stone in a cashel or caher).
Ringforts belong to the early Christian period, not to the prehistoric or Norman periods.
What it shows: a farming society, and the spread of Christianity, seen in churches, round towers and high crosses.
Illustrative: a ringfort at R 255 430 and a church in ruins with its graveyard at R 262 446.
The Normans were medieval invaders who built castles to hold land. Their sites are usually placed to guard something, such as a river crossing.
Norman (medieval) sites include mottes and motte-and-bailey sites (earth mounds, with a walled yard in the second type), castles, town walls, abbeys and friaries, and towns at bridging points.
Mottes are Norman sites; fulachta fia are Bronze Age, and ringforts are early Christian, so check the label before dating a site.
Why the site was chosen: defence, and control of a river crossing, so that the Normans could hold the land around it.
What it shows: Norman military control, and the religious life of the abbeys and friaries.
Illustrative: a motte at R 280 436 and a castle in ruins at R 269 439, beside the bridge.
The later periods leave planned towns, large estates and industrial and transport remains. Each tells you about how the country was organised and how it developed.
Tower houses are fortified stone houses, built for protection; planned towns have a regular layout with a square or wide main street; demesnes are large houses with estate woodland.
19th and 20th century sites include canals, railways and stations, mills, coastguard stations, later housing and industrial estates.
What it shows: the growth of planned towns and estates, and of transport and industry.
Many Irish place names are built from Irish words that describe the land or what stood there. Knowing the elements helps you read the history and site of a place from its name.

Settlement and building elements: baile/bally (townland or settlement), cill/kil (church), ráth/rath and lios/lis (ringfort), dún/dun (fort), cathair/caher (stone fort), áth/ath (ford), droichead (bridge).
Land elements: cnoc/knock (hill), sliabh/slieve (mountain), ard (height), drom/drum (ridge), gleann/glen (valley), mullach/mullagh (summit).
Water, vegetation and other elements: loch/lough (lake), inis/inch (island), cluain/clon (meadow), doire (oak wood), carraig/carrick (rock).
Townlands are the smallest land division in Ireland; townland names are printed on OS maps, and exams ask which townland a point lies in.
A 30-mark question asks for three reasons, each named, evidenced from the map with a grid reference and explained. Choose the three for which the map gives the clearest evidence.
Bridging point: the town grew where a river could be crossed, and bridges and roads converge on it.
Route focus: several N and R roads and a railway meet, so the town became a market and service centre.
Defence: a castle, town walls, a hill or a river bend guards the site.
River or coastal site: water supply, transport, power for mills, and a harbour or pier for trade and fishing.
Flat or gently sloping lowland: easy to build on, with widely spaced contours.
Fertile surrounding farmland: dispersed farms and no marsh, so the town serves as a market town for its hinterland (the area around it that it serves).
Ecclesiastical origin: an abbey or early church site. Tourism: a coast, beaches, lakes or uplands attract visitors to the town.

Illustrative: the bridging point is the bridge at R 268 441, with roads converging on it; the route focus is the N99, the R990 and the railway station at R 272 445; defence is the castle at R 269 439 and the motte at R 280 436, guarding the crossing.
A function is a job a town does for its people and surroundings. Name each function, give the symbol or label and its grid reference, and explain it.
Residential: built-up area and housing estates, because they show where people live.
Market and retail: a route focus and a central square, because people gather where routes meet to buy and sell.
Services: hospital, Garda station, post office, schools and courthouse, where labelled.
Transport: railway station, bus routes and motorway junction, such as the Rivertown station at R 272 445.
Industrial: industrial estate or factory labels, because they show where goods are made.
Tourist and recreational: tourist information office, golf course, hostels, camping and caravan sites, marinas, viewpoints and walks.
Port or fishing: pier, harbour and slipway, because boats land and load there.
Ecclesiastical: churches and abbeys. Defensive in the past: castle.
A town's layout records its history, with the oldest parts near the crossing point and newer parts at the edge.
Old core, the first part to be built: narrow streets, a square, and a castle or abbey near the bridge.
Newer edge, where there is more space: housing estates, industrial estates, a bypass or motorway with junctions, and ribbon development.
Choose a site with a six-figure grid reference and give three reasons, each supported by map evidence.
Flat land: widely spaced contours, because it is cheaper and easier to build on.
Access: an N road, a motorway junction, a railway or a port, so that goods and workers can reach the site.
Nearness to a town for labour, services and markets; space to expand; a site off the floodplain and away from protected or scenic areas.
Wind farms need exposed high ground away from houses; hotels need to be near tourist attractions.
State a disadvantage when asked, e.g. visual impact, traffic, loss of farmland or conflict with residents.

Economic activities are the ways people earn a living, grouped as primary, secondary and tertiary. The map shows each through symbols and labels, and tourism can be judged from what the map offers visitors.
Primary activity (using natural resources): forestry plantations, farming (shown by dispersed farms and field land), quarries and fishing piers.
Secondary activity (making goods): industrial estates and factories, such as the industrial estate on the N99 at the north-eastern edge of Rivertown.
Tertiary activity (providing services): services, tourism and transport, such as shops, hotels and railways.
Each activity is evidenced by a map symbol or label and its grid reference.
Tourism potential, accessibility and services, so that visitors can get there and stay: road access, parking, accommodation and tourist information.
Tourism potential, attractions that draw visitors, such as antiquities, viewpoints, walks, cycle routes, beaches, lakes and golf courses.
Each factor is evidenced with grid references and explained.
Statistical maps show numbers on a map. The OS map links to them through its contours and its key.

Contours are isolines (lines joining places of equal value), so they work like the lines on a weather map, the same kind of line used on isoline statistical maps, where the value is a statistic instead of height.
Choropleth, dot, isoline, proportional-symbol and flow-line maps are taught in Graph skills; there is more on them there.
Map questions fall into short questions, matching questions, sketch maps and long map-evidence questions. Short questions are worth Higher 2 marks each; Ordinary 3–5 marks, often tick-box.

Short questions: a six-figure reference for a named building, road junction or exit point; the antiquity, public service or feature at a grid reference; the height of a spot height, pillar or highest point; the length of a road, motorway or railway; the straight-line distance between two points.
Short questions also ask for the area of the whole map, of a lake or bay, of land above a contour, or of land east, west, north or south of a grid line or railway.
More short questions ask for the direction of travel; the part of the map a feature lies in; the type of forestry; what N or R stands for; a legend symbol; a cultural area (Gaeltacht).

Matching questions give features (such as a meander, a drumlin or a headland) to grid references, and ask for two drainage patterns, the type of lake or the aspect of a slope at a grid reference; elevation profile questions and true or false profile statements (Higher).
Sketch maps: Higher 20 marks at half scale; Ordinary 30 marks; typically four or five features.
15-mark map-and-process question (Higher): name and locate two landforms with six-figure grid references and explain one; locate a very steep and a very gentle slope.
30-mark map-evidence questions: three reasons a town developed at its location; three rural settlement patterns; variations in settlement distribution; absence and high density of settlement.
More 30-mark map-evidence questions: three phases of historic settlement; site suitability with a six-figure reference; economic activity and tourism potential.

Every piece of geographical information comes either from first-hand collection or from material someone else has already gathered. Textual sources are written secondary sources, so you need to know where they sit.

Primary data is information the student collects first-hand, such as measurements, observations, questionnaires (written sets of questions given to people), counts, field sketches and the student's own photographs.
Secondary data is information already collected or published by someone else, so the student did not gather it personally.
A questionnaire the student designs and carries out is primary, because the student collected the answers; a published survey is secondary, because someone else did.
Old maps and the census (the official count of the population) are secondary sources.
Secondary sources give background, past data and comparisons that fieldwork cannot provide, so being secondary does not make them less useful.

In the geographical investigation (the student's own research project), secondary sources supply the background and the published studies used for comparison in the conclusion. There is more on this in The Geographical Investigation (20%).
Textual and secondary sources come in many forms. Present-day ones are the ones a student can find and use now.
Textbooks and reference books, which give established background knowledge on a topic.
Newspapers and magazines, which report current events and issues.
Official statistics and reports from state bodies (government organisations), such as census reports, weather and climate records and environmental reports.
Local authority documents (those of the county or city council), such as county or city development plans and planning notices.
Academic articles, which are written by researchers and scholars.
Current maps, aerial photographs (photographs taken from the air) and satellite images (pictures taken from space).
Official data comes from named state bodies, and knowing which body produces which kind of data tells you where to look and how far to trust it.
Central Statistics Office (CSO): conducts the census and publishes official statistics.
Met Éireann: the Irish national meteorological service (the body that forecasts and records the weather), which supplies weather data.
Environmental Protection Agency (EPA): reports on environmental quality, including water and air.
Tailte Éireann: now responsible for national mapping. Ordnance Survey Ireland became part of it in 2023, and it now publishes the Ordnance Survey (OS) maps.
Local authorities: publish development plans, which set out how land in the county or city is to be used.
Comparing an old source with a present-day one shows change in land use, settlement, transport, the coastline or a river course. This is why sources from the past matter.
Sources from the past include historical maps (earlier editions of OS maps, old town plans, estate maps), old photographs and postcards, old newspapers and earlier census returns.
Other past sources include local histories, parish and school records, directories (lists of residents and businesses), travel accounts and archive documents in libraries and county archives.
The first Ordnance Survey of Ireland mapped the whole country at six inches to one mile in the 1830s and 1840s, so it gives a record of the country from that time.
Early and later map editions show field patterns, town plans, mills, demesnes (the grounds of large estates), railways and features since lost.
Old maps may use different scales, symbols and place-name spellings, and can be inaccurate or out of date, so state these limits when using them.
To show change you compare the two maps in a set order. Following the steps keeps the comparison fair and lets you explain what you find.
1. Match the scale and orientation of the two maps, so that distances and directions on one can be compared with the other.
2. Find fixed points, such as a bridge, church, castle or main street, that appear on both, because they let you line the maps up.
3. List what has appeared, what has disappeared and what has stayed the same.

4. Describe the change, e.g. growth along approach roads, a new bypass (a road built to take traffic around a town), the loss of a mill, reclaimed land (land made from sea or marsh) or a straightened river.
5. Explain each change, saying why it happened.
Illustrative: a Rivertown map of the 1840s shows a mill and weir on the River Dallow, a market square, the castle and fields to the north.
Illustrative, today: the OS map shows the mill gone, housing estates on those northern fields, the railway and station, an industrial estate on the N99 (a national road) and the GAA pitch.
Illustrative explanations: growth after the railway arrived, suburban expansion (building on the edge of the town), and the decline of water-powered industry, which explains why the mill has gone.
Old photographs and written accounts record how a place once looked, so they can be compared with the place today in the same way as old maps.
Describe what has changed between an old photograph or written account and the present day.
Note its limits: it records a single moment, a chosen viewpoint, or the writer's own view, so it may not show the whole picture.
The Higher paper can ask for a sketch map of a historical map, worth 20 marks. The method follows the OS sketch-map rules in the notes on Map interpretation.
Rule a frame of the same shape as the map, with a title and a north arrow.
Historical maps usually have no grid, so divide the map and the frame into a light pencil grid of equal sections. This lets you place features accurately.
Place each requested feature by its grid section, draw it in the correct position and label it.
Show and label only the features the question asks for, because extra features are not wanted.
Illustrative: an old Rivertown town plan, 20 cm × 15 cm, is to be sketched showing the River Dallow, two connecting streets drawn meeting, the market house and the church.
A text is only useful once you have pulled the geography out of it. Read it for the main idea, then turn it into geographical terms and usable forms.
Identify the main idea of the text, then pick out its facts, figures, places and dates.
Translate everyday language into geographical terms: "the town keeps spreading into the fields" describes urban sprawl (a town growing outwards over farmland).
Use the correct term in answers and reports, e.g. hinterland (the area a town serves), nucleated settlement (houses clustered around a centre) or discharge (the volume of water a river carries).
Other correct terms are prevailing wind (the direction the wind blows from most of the time) and dependency ratio (the number of dependants compared with the working-age population).
Exam stimulus texts (the extracts given on the paper) often contain the clue term, so underline it.
Take notes under headings that match the objectives, and summarise them in bullet points.
Turn figures in a text into a table or graph, and plot places named in a text on a sketch map, so the information is easier to use.
Two sources on the same place or topic may agree, disagree or cover different dates, so cross-checking with a second source, or with primary data, increases reliability.
A fact can be checked against a measurement, a date or a statistic. An opinion is a view or judgement. Being able to tell them apart is a key skill for evaluating a source.

Illustrative extract from a Rivertown community newsletter: “Traffic on Main Street has doubled since the new industrial estate opened in 2015. The council's plan for a relief road is a disaster for the town.” The date 2015 is invented.
The first sentence is a fact: it can be checked with traffic counts or council data.
The second sentence is an opinion: it is a judgement, shown by the emotive word “disaster” (a word chosen to stir feeling rather than to inform).
Not every source can be trusted equally. Asking who wrote it, why and with what evidence lets you judge how far to rely on it.
Bias: ask who wrote the source and why, since a developer's brochure, a campaign group's leaflet, a political leaflet or an advertisement may be one-sided.
Bias shows in one-sided arguments, emotive language and selective figures (only the figures that suit the writer).
Reliability checklist, author or organisation: an official body or expert is more reliable than an anonymous author.
Reliability checklist, date: is the source current, or is it a past source useful for comparison?
Reliability checklist, purpose: does it inform, persuade or sell?
Reliability checklist, evidence: are sources cited and data given?
Reliability checklist, scale and area: national figures may not apply to the local area.
Reliability checklist, agreement: does it match other sources?
Even a reliable secondary source has limits, because it was not collected for your study. Applying the checklist to an example shows how this works.
Limitations of secondary data: it may be out of date, collected for another purpose, not covering the exact study area, defined differently between sources or dates, or, if online, unverified.
Illustrative: an invented property developer's brochure praising a new Rivertown housing estate is written to sell, so its purpose is persuasion.
The brochure is one-sided and gives unsourced figures, so it fails the evidence check.
To judge it, check it against the county development plan and an own land-use survey (the student's own record of how land is used).
Using someone else's work without saying so is dishonest, so every secondary source in a report must be credited.
List every secondary source used in a report with its author or organisation, title and date.
For online sources, also give the web address and the date accessed, because web pages can change or disappear.
Never copy text and present it as one's own.
The authenticity of the investigation is verified by the teacher and principal. There is more on this in The Geographical Investigation (20%).
In the written exam, textual sources appear as stimulus material (items given on the paper for you to use). Questions test whether you can use them.
Exam questions use stimulus material: a short text, a table, a cartoon or a newspaper-style extract.
Questions ask students to extract information, identify the issue, distinguish fact from opinion, or use the information in an answer.
Method: read the question first, so you know what to look for, then underline the key terms and figures in the text, then answer using the text's evidence plus your own knowledge.
Pictures, including cartoons, are an information source: identify the message, the issue, who is shown and the viewpoint.

The investigation is an individual study of a geographical question, carried out under the teacher's supervision and written up in the SEC report booklet. It is worth 20% of the total mark, so it is a large part of your grade even though it is not sat in the exam hall.
It is compulsory at Higher and Ordinary level, and is assessed outside the written examination, so it does not appear as a question on the written paper.
The topic is chosen from the prescribed list that the State Examinations Commission (SEC, the body that runs the Leaving Cert) issues for each year's examination.

Typical topic areas are physical (rivers, coasts, glacial or karst landscapes, weather, soils, rocks) and human (urban land use, traffic, settlement, economic activity), but only the year's own list applies.
The SEC sets the completion date each year: for 2027 the completed report goes to the teacher by 16 April 2027, and the school then submits it to the SEC.
A class may work on one investigation and collect data together, but each student must write a full and complete report of their own. Group reports are not accepted.

Primary sources (first-hand fieldwork data you collect yourself) must make up at least 60% of the information gathered, and every source must be referenced, including any material generated using AI. Unreferenced material counts as plagiarism (passing off someone else's work as your own).

The report is authenticated (confirmed as your own work) by the candidate and by the teacher. Copying from classmates, textbooks or websites, other than essential references such as definitions, makes the report invalid.

The report is completed in the official SEC Reporting Booklet, which has been completed and submitted digitally since the 2025 examination. The typed text is no more than 1,000 words, and examiners mark only what is in the booklet.
The booklet divides the report into five stages, each with its own marks. Stages 1 to 4 also have word limits that add up to 1,000 words, so every sentence has to earn its place.
Stage 1, Introduction: 5 marks, no more than 50 words.
Stage 2, Planning: 5 marks, no more than 100 words.
Stage 3, Gathering of information: 40 marks, no more than 450 words.
Stage 4, Results, conclusions and evaluation: 30 marks, no more than 400 words.
Stage 5, Presentation of results: 20 marks, for hand-drawn graphs and diagrams added to the booklet's image pages.

The marks are the same at Higher and Ordinary level, but Higher Level answers are expected to develop each heading fully, with detailed analysis and comparison with theory (the established models geographers use, such as those in the Conclusion block).
The introduction states a hypothesis to test or the aims of the study, in no more than 50 words. Everything later in the report traces back to this statement.
Hypothesis: a precise, testable statement that the data can prove or disprove, for example a measurable claim about change with distance downstream.
Aim: a statement of what the investigation sets out to find out. Use a hypothesis or an aim, as the booklet asks.
A hypothesis is a testable statement, not a question or a topic title.
Fifty words is room for one hypothesis or two or three short aims, so leave the detail of tasks and methods to Stage 2.
Write the statement so that Stage 4 can say it is accepted, rejected or partly accepted, and so every later stage traces back to it.
Good practice: keep the hypothesis narrow enough to test in a day or two of fieldwork (data collection outdoors), avoid vague words such as "better" or "nice", and include the place studied.
Illustrative hypothesis for a river study of the River Dallow upstream of Rivertown: "The velocity of the River Dallow increases downstream." Velocity means how fast the water flows.
Planning identifies the information required and the methods or tasks for gathering it, in no more than 100 words. It also separates primary sources from secondary ones.

Types of information required: primary (measurements, observations, counts, questionnaire answers) and secondary (maps, statistics, texts that someone else produced), with a note of how each secondary source will be accessed.
Objectives: specific, measurable tasks that together test the hypothesis, each naming what will be measured and where.

Illustrative tasks for the River Dallow: measure channel width, average depth and velocity at five sites 500 m apart; calculate cross-sectional area and discharge at each site; measure the size of ten pebbles at each site.
