Illustrative information required: primary measurements, and a secondary OS map (Ordnance Survey map) and aerial photograph of the river.

Within 100 words the stage names the methods, says why each suits the hypothesis, and mentions the design of the recording sheet or questionnaire. The fuller preparation (maps, sites, equipment, safety) is done but not all written up.
Good practice: explain why each method suits its objective, and describe the method clearly enough for someone else to repeat it.
Good fieldwork is decided before you leave school. Careful preparation means the data are consistent and the day runs safely.
Before fieldwork, study OS maps and aerial photographs of the area, so you know where the river or town can be reached.
Choose and justify sites, for example evenly spaced along a river, or sample points across a town.
Choose the date and time, gather the equipment, divide tasks within the group and arrange landowner permission where needed.
Recording sheet: a table prepared in advance, with columns for site, time, each measurement and repeat readings, so that data are recorded consistently.
Illustrative planning for the River Dallow: sites on the OS map where the river is accessible and safe.

Illustrative River Dallow recording sheet: columns for site, width, depths at five points, three float times over 10 m and pebble lengths; a risk assessment of low river level, wellingtons and groups of four.
Human topics gather information by asking people, so the questionnaire must be designed well. Whatever the topic, fieldwork must be safe and fair to others.
Questionnaire design: keep it short, with closed questions (tick boxes, yes/no, rating scales) for easy analysis and a few open questions, which let people answer in their own words.
Questionnaire wording must be neutral and unbiased, with no unnecessary personal questions. Pilot it (test it) with a few people first.
Sampling plan for a questionnaire: who is asked, where, when and how many.

Safety and ethics: complete a risk assessment (a list of hazards and how you will reduce them), never work alone, supervise near water or traffic, wear suitable clothing and footwear, check the weather and river level, and respect property and the environment.
Questionnaires are anonymous and voluntary, so nobody is named and nobody is forced to answer.
The gathering stage describes the tasks or methods used, the equipment and how information was recorded, in no more than 450 words. It carries 40 marks, the most of any stage.
The examiner's marking boxes cover two methods plus coherence, so two methods described fully earn more than many described thinly.
Each method says what was done, where, with which equipment, how results were recorded, and how many sites, readings or responses were taken, so that someone else could repeat it.

Field observations (what you record by looking rather than measuring): labelled field sketches, land-use mapping on a base map (an outline map you add to), traffic or pedestrian counts at set times, and environmental quality surveys using scored criteria.
Each instrument measures one thing, so match the instrument to the objective and say how you used it.
Measuring tape or ranging poles (tall marker poles): channel width, beach width and distances.
Metre stick: depth at regular intervals across a channel.
Float and stopwatch, or a flow meter: velocity. Time a float over a measured distance, repeat the timing and average the results.
Clinometer (an instrument that measures angles): the slope angle of a beach or valley side.
Callipers or a ruler measure pebble size; a roundness chart measures pebble shape.
Compass: orientation, aspect (the direction a slope faces) and wind direction.
Weather instruments: thermometer, rain gauge, anemometer (measures wind speed) and wind vane (shows wind direction).
Camera: a photographic record, dated and located. GPS or a smartphone mapping app locates sites.
Secondary sources add information you could not collect yourself, and careful technique makes your own readings trustworthy.

Secondary sources used in investigations include OS maps and aerial photographs, census data (the national population count), weather records, local authority plans, textbooks and websites. There is more on this in Textual sources, which covers how to evaluate them.
Record full details of each secondary source when you collect it, so you can acknowledge it in the report.
Take repeat readings and average them, so one odd reading does not distort the result.
Use the same method and the same people at every site, so differences in results come from the sites and not from the way they were measured.
Record units, and note the conditions: weather, time and river level.
Real fieldwork never goes perfectly, and the report must discuss the problems you met and how you overcame them.

Problems to name in the report: bad weather or high water that makes measurement unsafe, equipment faults, a float caught in vegetation, people refusing questionnaires, restricted access to a site, and time limits.
For each problem, state the problem, its effect on the data and the solution.
Illustrative: at site 3 the float snagged on reeds twice; the group discarded those runs and took three clean timings.
Velocity is how fast the water flows. Discharge is the volume of water passing a point each second. Illustrative values from the River Dallow study show how both are calculated for the results.
Velocity = distance ÷ time, using the average of the repeated float timings.
Cross-sectional area = width × average depth (m²), the area of the face of water you would see if you cut across the channel.
Discharge = cross-sectional area × velocity (m³ per second).
Illustrative site 1: width 3.0 m; average depth 0.20 m; average float time over 10 m of 25 s, so velocity 0.4 m/s; cross-sectional area 0.6 m²; discharge 0.24 m³/s.
Illustrative site 5: width 6.0 m; average depth 0.40 m; average float time over 10 m of 10 s, so velocity 1.0 m/s; cross-sectional area 2.4 m²; discharge 2.4 m³/s.
Stage 4 covers results, conclusions and evaluation together, in no more than 400 words, for 30 marks. Results come first and state what the data show, with figures.
State each finding in words with its key figures, and refer to the graph or table that shows it.
Higher Level statistical analysis: averages (mean and median), range (highest minus lowest value) and percentages.
Results can be calculated with a calculator or spreadsheet, but no software may be used to create the graphs, charts, tables, maps or diagrams in the booklet.
Describe trends with figures, for example "velocity rose from site 1 to site 5", note anomalies (results that do not fit the pattern) and suggest their causes.
Keep results separate from conclusions, so the data are reported first and explained afterwards.
The conclusion tests the hypothesis against the results, explains the pattern and compares the findings with established theory (a well-known model from textbooks or published work).
State whether the hypothesis is accepted, rejected or partly accepted, using the evidence from each objective.
Explain the findings geographically: say why the pattern occurs.
Bradshaw model: downstream, a river's discharge, channel width, depth and velocity tend to increase, while gradient and load particle size decrease.
Burgess concentric zone model (Chicago, 1925): describes urban land use in zones around a central business district, so it suits an urban study as the Bradshaw model suits a river study.
Compare results with the textbook model or published work, and explain any differences, such as local geology, human interference or a small sample.

Illustrative conclusion: the hypothesis is accepted because velocity rose from 0.4 m/s to 1.0 m/s; this matches the Bradshaw model, which is explained by greater depth reducing friction and more water from tributaries (smaller streams that join the river).
The evaluation judges how reliable the data are, names the limits of the study and proposes specific improvements.
Evaluate the reliability and accuracy of the data, and say what went well.
Name the limits of the study: one day's data, few sites, a small questionnaire sample, measurement error and the weather on the day.
A surface float overestimates average velocity, so float results are estimates, not exact values.
Improvements: more sites, repeat visits in different seasons or conditions, better equipment such as a flow meter, larger samples and a longer stretch of river.
Suggest further investigation that the findings point towards.

Skills gained (optional): teamwork, fieldwork skills, ICT (information and communication technology) and report writing, which the syllabus links to working conditions similar to those likely to be encountered in the world of work.
Results are presented in graphic form on the booklet's image pages and discussed in Stage 4. Presentation is marked out of 20.
Illustrations include tables of raw and averaged data, sketch maps locating sites, annotated photographs (photographs with labels added) and field sketches.
The examiner's boxes cover two presentation methods plus coherence, so results are shown in at least two clearly different graphic forms.

Choose the graph that suits the data: a line graph for change with distance or time, a bar chart for comparison between sites, a pie chart for shares, a scatter graph for a relationship, and channel cross-sections for showing a river channel's shape.
Every illustration is titled, labelled, has units and a key, and is referred to in the text. There is more on this in Figure interpretation, which covers graph-drawing technique.
Every sketch, map, diagram, graph, chart and table is the student's own hand-drawn work, inserted into the digital booklet as an image such as a photo or scan.
Illustrations go only on the booklet's image pages, because examiners mark only what is in the booklet.
For the River Dallow study, the illustrations are: a line graph of velocity against distance downstream; channel cross-sections drawn to scale for sites 1 and 5; and a sketch map of the five sites.
The investigation is assessed only through the report, marked section by section in the SEC booklet. Knowing what earns and loses marks tells you where to spend your words.
Within each stage, marks are awarded for significant relevant points (SRPs, specific points that answer the section), and Stage 5 is marked on the graphic illustrations.
Marks are earned by a clear, testable hypothesis or aim within the word limit.
Marks are earned by methods described step by step, with equipment named and justified.
Marks are earned by accurate data presented in varied, well-labelled illustrations, and by results that refer to the actual figures.
Marks are earned by conclusions that answer the hypothesis and are supported by the results, comparison with theory, and an honest evaluation with specific improvements.
Marks are lost for vague or untestable hypotheses, methods listed without explanation, and results given without figures.
Marks are lost for generic evaluations such as "it went well", for writing outside the space provided, and for material copied from others or the internet.

Weather and climate describe the atmosphere (the layer of air around the Earth) over different lengths of time, and every weather map and table uses fixed units. Knowing the units lets you read a value correctly and give it with its unit.
Weather is the state of the atmosphere at a place at a given time, measured over hours and days. For example, a wet, windy afternoon is weather.
Climate is the average weather of a place over a long period, usually calculated over 30 years. A single wet day does not change a place's climate.
Pressure (the weight of the air pressing down on a surface) is measured in hectopascals (hPa); 1 hPa equals 1 millibar (mb), so the two units give the same value and are never converted.
Average sea-level pressure is about 1013 hPa, which gives a reference point for judging whether a pressure reading is high or low.
Units on weather charts and tables: temperature in °C, rainfall in mm, wind speed in km/h or knots (nautical miles per hour), sunshine in hours, cloud cover in oktas (eighths of the sky covered).
A synoptic chart shows the weather over a large area at one moment, giving a general view of the whole (this is what 'synoptic' means).

Observations are taken at the same time from many weather stations, ships, buoys (floating instrument platforms at sea) and satellites, and plotted onto one map, so the chart is a snapshot of one moment.
A surface analysis chart shows the observed situation at a given time; a forecast chart shows the expected situation at a later time.
Charts are issued at fixed times, stated in UTC (Coordinated Universal Time, the standard world time used so that observations from everywhere match).

Met Éireann, Ireland's national meteorological (weather) service, produces Irish weather maps from its network of stations, combined with satellite and radar data. Forecasters combine charts with satellite and radar data to build up a full picture.
Met Éireann stations include Valentia Observatory (Co. Kerry), Malin Head (Co. Donegal), Belmullet (Co. Mayo), Dublin Airport and Shannon Airport.
An isoline joins places of equal value. Read the name of the line before its interval, because each name refers to one quantity and the names are easily swapped.
Isobars join places of equal atmospheric pressure; they are usually drawn at fixed intervals, commonly every 4 hPa, so read the labels to confirm the interval.
Isotherms join places of equal temperature, so they show where it is warmer or colder.
Isohyets join places of equal rainfall.
Isohels join places of equal sunshine.
Isonephs join places of equal cloud cover, so a line labelled with a cloud amount is an isoneph.

Shaded or banded maps, such as rainfall, sunshine, UV or temperature maps, use a colour key: read the class from the key and give the range it states when the map shows a band rather than a single value.

To read a value between isolines, find the two lines either side of the point, note their values and the interval between them, then estimate in proportion to distance. A point halfway between two lines is about halfway between their values.
A value at a closed centre (where an isoline forms a complete loop) is the figure written on it, such as 'L 976', or lies beyond the innermost isobar.
High and low pressure are relative to the surrounding air, so no fixed value marks the boundary between them. Each system has its own marking on the chart and its own typical weather.

A depression (also called a low or cyclone) is marked L or Low with a pressure figure; it has closed isobars with pressure falling towards the centre, and usually has fronts attached. Its isobars are usually tightly packed.
Air rises in a depression, cools and condenses (turns from vapour into water droplets), so rain, cloud and strong winds are associated with depressions.
An anticyclone (also called a high) is marked H or High; it has closed isobars with pressure rising towards the centre, widely spaced isobars, and no fronts.
Air sinks in an anticyclone and warms, so clouds rarely form: summer brings warm, sunny days, and winter brings cold, clear nights with frost and fog.
A trough is an elongated area of low pressure, often unsettled because air rises along it, sometimes drawn as a line.
A ridge is an elongated extension of high pressure, bringing a short settled spell.
A col is a slack area between two highs and two lows, with light winds, uncertain weather, and possible fog or thunderstorms.

An air mass is a large body of air with fairly uniform temperature and humidity (moisture content), named from its source region (polar or tropical; maritime or continental). Ireland's usual air mass is maritime, from the Atlantic. There is more on this in Atmospheric and oceanic circulation.
The values in this example are invented for illustration and are not taken from any real chart. It shows how to answer the usual questions on pressure and wind from isobars.
A depression marked 'L 976' is centred in the Atlantic about 500 km west of Ireland, with closed isobars at 980, 984, 988, 992, 996 and 1000 hPa packed closely over the west coast.
An anticyclone marked 'H 1036' lies over central Europe, with widely spaced isobars at 1032, 1028 and 1024 hPa.
Pressure at the depression's centre is 976 hPa, the figure written on the L, and the isobar interval is 4 hPa, the gap between neighbouring isobars such as 980 and 984.
A point midway between the 988 and 992 hPa isobars is about 990 hPa, because it lies halfway between the two values.
Winds are stronger over the west of Ireland than over central Europe, because the isobars are closer together over the west.
Ireland lies under the depression, so it is likely to be wet and windy; central Europe lies under the high, so it is likely to be calm and dry.
Wind is named from the direction it blows from, and its strength follows the spacing of the isobars. Once you know these rules you can judge the wind anywhere on a chart.
Wind direction is named by the direction the wind blows from: a westerly blows from the west.

Air moves from high to low pressure; closely spaced isobars mean a steep pressure gradient (a big pressure change over a short distance) and strong winds, while widely spaced isobars mean light winds or calm.
In the northern hemisphere the wind blows anticlockwise around a depression and clockwise around an anticyclone. There is more on the cause of this pattern in Atmospheric and oceanic circulation.
Near the surface the wind blows nearly parallel to the isobars, angled slightly in towards a low and out from a high.
Buys Ballot's law: stand with your back to the wind, and low pressure is on your left in the northern hemisphere.
The prevailing wind is the wind that blows most frequently over an area; in Ireland it is south-westerly, from the Atlantic.
The Beaufort scale rates wind force from 0 (calm) to 12 (hurricane force), based on observed effects, such as how trees and the sea look.
A front is the boundary between two air masses of different temperature and humidity. Frontal symbols point in the direction the front is moving.

Warm front: a line with semicircles on the side it moves towards (red on colour charts). Warm air rises gently over cold air, bringing a long period of steady rain and thickening cloud, then rising temperature after it passes.

Cold front: a line with triangles on the side it moves towards (blue on colour charts). Cold air undercuts warm air (pushes underneath it), bringing short heavy showers, possible thunder and falling temperature; clearer, brighter showery weather follows.

Occluded front: triangles and semicircles alternating on the same side (purple on colour charts). It forms where a cold front catches up with a warm front, lifting the warm air off the ground, and it brings cloud and rain.
An occluded front is usually found near the centre of a mature depression (one that is fully developed).
Stationary (quasi-stationary) front: triangles and semicircles alternating on opposite sides.
Worked example W3 (drawing practice): in a box, draw each of the four symbols above, placing the symbol on the side the front moves towards.
Draw a curved line with three triangles for cold and three semicircles for warm. Alternate them on one side for occluded and on opposite sides for stationary.
Diagram cue: a plan of a depression shows the warm front ahead, the warm sector (the area of warm air between the fronts), the cold front behind and the occlusion near the centre.
The isobars are kinked where they cross the fronts. There is more on the weather as a depression passes in Atmospheric and oceanic circulation.

A station model is the cluster of symbols plotted at each weather station on a synoptic chart. Each part gives one reading, so you can pull the cloud, wind, temperature and weather out of one small drawing.
The circle at the station shows cloud cover in oktas: one okta is one eighth of the sky covered by cloud, so an empty circle is clear sky (0 oktas) and a fully shaded circle is overcast (8 oktas).
The wind arrow's shaft points from the station towards the direction the wind is coming from, not where it is going.
Barbs (the short lines on the shaft) give wind speed: a half barb is 5 knots, a full barb 10 knots and a pennant (filled triangle) 50 knots; add them together.
A circle around the station with no shaft means calm, because there is no wind to point from.

Other values around the circle are temperature (°C), dew point (the temperature at which the air is saturated and water vapour condenses), pressure and a present-weather symbol such as rain, drizzle, showers, snow, fog or thunderstorm; read them from the chart's key.

Worked example W2 (illustrative): a circle three-quarters shaded is 6 oktas (three-quarters of 8); a shaft pointing towards the south-west with two full barbs and one half barb is a south-westerly wind of 25 knots (20 + 5); the temperature is 12 °C and the present weather is rain.
Television, websites and apps use simplified symbols for the same features that appear on a synoptic chart. A series of maps at set times can then show how the weather moves.
Media weather symbols include the sun, cloud, sun-and-cloud, rain drops, showers, snow, thunder (a lightning bolt) and fog.
Wind arrows on media maps show speed in km/h, for example 20 km/h, and temperatures appear in coloured boxes.
On rainfall radar (which detects rain in the air), heavier rain is shown in darker or warmer colours.

A rainfall forecast sequence is a series of maps at set times; compare the position of the rain band on successive maps to give its direction of movement, and read each map rather than assuming a direction.

Worked example W5 (illustrative): at 06:00 a rain band covers Munster and Connacht; at 12:00 it covers the midlands; at 18:00 it is over Leinster and the east coast. The rain moves from west to east, and Leinster's rain arrives last.
Forecasts and warnings turn the charts into advice for the public. Knowing what a forecast contains and what the warning colours mean lets you read and use them.
Met Éireann forecasts reach viewers through TV, radio, the website and app, as national, regional and city forecasts.
Sea area and coastal forecasts give wind and sea state for shipping and fishing; farming, UV and pollen forecasts are also issued.

A forecast describes the synoptic situation (what pressure systems and fronts are doing), expected rain, the highs and lows of temperature, wind direction and speed, cloud and sunshine, and how conditions change across the country and through the day.
Warnings are colour-coded Yellow, Orange and Red by expected impact; Red is the most severe, and people should act to protect themselves and property.
Warning types include wind, rain, snow-ice, low temperature, high temperature, fog and thunderstorm.
Naming storms makes warnings easier to communicate, and the UV index gives a simple scale for the strength of the sun. Both appear in media reports.
Storms have been named jointly by Met Éireann and the UK Met Office since 2015, and by the Dutch service KNMI since 2019; names make warnings easier to communicate.

Ex-hurricane Ophelia reached Ireland on 16 October 2017. It had been a major hurricane south of the Azores, unusually far east for an Atlantic hurricane, and arrived as a post-tropical storm; Met Éireann issued Red warnings and three people died in Ireland.
Storm Éowyn, a named storm, crossed Ireland on 24 January 2025, when Met Éireann issued Red wind warnings.

The UV index measures the strength of the sun's ultraviolet radiation (the part of sunlight that burns skin); World Health Organization categories are Low 1-2, Moderate 3-5, High 6-7, Very high 8-10 and Extreme 11 and above.
UV maps are read with isolines or a colour key, like any other map, so give the class or range the key states.
Station tables and graphs record daily, hourly or monthly figures, and each figure comes from a particular instrument. Here you need to name each instrument and say what it measures.
Rain gauge: measures rainfall in mm, so it is the instrument to name for rainfall.

Thermometer: measures air temperature in °C (the instrument to name for temperature), and is kept in a Stevenson screen (a white, louvred box about 1.25 m above the ground) so that it measures shaded air temperature.
Maximum-minimum thermometer: records the highest and lowest temperature in a period.
Barometer: measures pressure in hPa; barograph: gives a continuous record of pressure.
Anemometer: measures wind speed; wind vane: shows wind direction.
Hygrometer or wet-and-dry bulb thermometer: measures humidity (the amount of water vapour in the air); sunshine recorder: measures hours of sunshine.
Once you can name the instrument and read the value, you calculate with the figures in the units given. Exams set a table or graph of a station's daily, hourly or monthly figures.
Total: add the values, for example rainfall over three days or three months.
Mean (the average): total divided by the number of values; mean daily temperature = (maximum + minimum) ÷ 2.
Range: highest minus lowest, for a day or for a year, such as 14 minus 6 for one day.
Other tasks: find the difference between two places; count the months or days above a threshold; find the highest or lowest month. Always give units.
Hourly graphs: read times carefully on the horizontal axis (00:00 is midnight), read the value at a given hour, and count the hours with rain.
Climate graphs (a temperature line with rainfall bars by month) at an Irish station typically show mild winters, cool summers and rain all year, with the wettest months usually in autumn and winter.
This links to the cool temperate oceanic climate in The Concept of a Region. There is more on the graph method in Figure interpretation.
The figures in this example are invented for illustration. Each result is worked out from the values stated.
Monday: maximum 14 °C, minimum 6 °C, rainfall 4 mm, mean wind 20 km/h.
Tuesday: maximum 12 °C, minimum 5 °C, rainfall 11 mm, mean wind 32 km/h.
Wednesday: maximum 15 °C, minimum 8 °C, rainfall 0 mm, mean wind 14 km/h.
Total rainfall over the three days is 15 mm (4 + 11 + 0); Monday's temperature range is 8 °C (14 - 6); Monday's mean temperature is 10 °C ((14 + 6) ÷ 2).
Mean wind speed over the three days is 22 km/h ((20 + 32 + 14) ÷ 3); the wettest day is Tuesday and the driest is Wednesday.
Illustrative monthly rainfall: January 120, February 95, March 80, April 60, May 55 and June 70 mm. The total for April to June is 185 mm; one month (January) is over 100 mm; May is the lowest month.
A two-mark 'state one reason' answer links the pattern to the moist Atlantic air and to the relief (the height and shape) of the land.

The west is wetter than the east: moist air from the Atlantic is forced to rise over the western mountains, where it cools and condenses, producing relief (orographic) rain. There is more on this in Exchanges of water between oceans and atmosphere.

The east and south-east are sunnier and drier because they lie in the rain shadow of the western and central uplands: descending air warms and its cloud evaporates. The south-east is the sunniest part of Ireland.
Coastal areas are milder in winter than the interior, because the sea warms the coast, including through the North Atlantic Drift (a warm ocean current); inland areas have a larger temperature range.
Long-term averages from Met Éireann: most of the east gets about 750-1,000 mm of rain a year, the west about 1,000-1,250 mm, and many mountain areas over 2,000 mm.
The highest rainfall totals are on mountains near the west coast, because that is where the Atlantic air is forced to rise, and the lowest are around Dublin and the east.

Satellite imagery is remote sensing: information about the earth's surface gathered from a distance, without contact, by sensors that record reflected or emitted energy. It lets geographers study large areas that nobody could survey on foot.
Sensors on satellites or aircraft record energy in several wavebands (separate bands of the energy spectrum), such as visible light, infrared (heat energy) and microwaves (radar).

Each picture element, or pixel (one tiny square of the image), stores a number for each waveband, and a computer turns these numbers into an image. A satellite image is therefore not a photograph in the ordinary sense.
Resolution is the size of the ground area one pixel covers. High resolution shows individual buildings, while low resolution shows only large patterns such as cloud systems.

A satellite image is taken from far higher than an aerial photograph (a photo taken from an aircraft), covers a much larger area, is repeated on a schedule and can record wavebands the eye cannot see.
An aerial photograph shows more detail of a small area and is vertical (taken straight down) or oblique (taken at a slant). There is more on this in Aerial photograph interpretation.
The height and path of a satellite's orbit decide how much of the earth it sees, how often, and in how much detail. There are two main types, and they trade coverage against detail.

Geostationary satellites orbit about 36,000 km above the equator at the same speed as the earth turns, so they stay over one point and view the same large area, a whole hemisphere (half the globe), continuously.

Geostationary images have low detail and are used for weather, because the satellite can watch cloud systems continuously. Meteosat weather satellites are operated by EUMETSAT, of which Ireland is a member state.
Polar-orbiting satellites fly in much lower orbits of hundreds of km, passing near both poles while the earth turns beneath them, so they cover the whole surface strip by strip over days.

Polar-orbiting images have much greater detail and are used for land use, mapping and environmental monitoring. Landsat (USA) has imaged the earth since 1972, and the Sentinel satellites belong to the EU's Copernicus earth-observation programme.
Different sensors record different energy, so the same place looks different on each type of image. Knowing which type you have tells you what the colours mean.
Visible image: records reflected sunlight, like a photograph, so it works in daytime only. Thick cloud appears bright white.
Infrared image: records heat, so it works day and night. Cold, high cloud tops appear white and warm land and sea appear darker, which is why it is used to show cloud height and sea temperature.
False-colour image: near-infrared (infrared just beyond visible red) is shown as red, so healthy vegetation appears red and towns appear blue-grey. It is used to study crops and forests.
Radar image: the satellite sends microwaves and records the echo. It sees through cloud and works at night, so it is useful for mapping floods in cloudy weather.
Work through the same five steps for any image, then give the answer in geographical terms.
Step 1: read the caption, date, scale or area covered, and check whether the image is true colour (natural colours), false colour or infrared, because this decides what each colour means.
Step 2: find north (usually the top) and any coastline or river to orient yourself.
Step 3: identify features by colour or tone, texture, shape, size, pattern and association, meaning what lies next to what.
Step 4: describe the distribution and pattern, such as linear, clustered or regular, or lying along rivers or coasts.
Step 5: explain the pattern using geographical knowledge.
In a true-colour image each surface has a typical colour. White is the confusing one, because several very different things appear white.
In true colour, water is dark blue to black, and muddy or shallow water is brown or turquoise.
Vegetation is green, because plants reflect green light: forest is dark green, and crops and grass are lighter.
Bare ground and desert are yellow, brown, orange or red; urban areas are grey.
Snow, ice, cloud and salt flats (flat areas of dried salt) all appear white, so decide between them using shape, texture and location.
Cloud is fluffy, streaky or swirling, casts shadows and changes position between images, because it is moving.
Snow and ice follow the shape of the land, filling valleys and lying along mountain ridges and the coastline.
Matching questions depend on recognition clues. Each feature below has a look that identifies it, and you only need to know what the image shows, not how the feature forms.
Depression (mid-latitude storm, a low-pressure system): a large comma-shaped or spiral band of white cloud, with a long trailing cloud band, the front (the boundary between air masses).
Hurricane (tropical cyclone): a huge circular spiral of thick white cloud with a clear, dark eye (the calm centre) at the middle, over the ocean.
Anticyclone (a high-pressure system): a large cloud-free area in which land and sea are clearly visible.

Glacier: a long white or grey-blue river of ice in a valley between dark mountains, with dark stripes of moraine (rock debris carried by the ice) along it and a cracked (crevassed) texture. It may end in the sea or a lake with icebergs.
Ice sheet: a vast, smooth white surface with no visible land.
Hazards change the surface suddenly, and the change shows up in colour. Before-and-after comparison is often the clearest way to spot the damage.
Volcano: a circular cone with a crater at the summit and radial gullies (channels running outward) down its sides.
During an eruption a grey or white ash plume is blown in one direction, and dark lava flows spread downslope.
Wildfire: grey or brown smoke plumes drift downwind from bright red-orange fire fronts.
After a wildfire a dark brown or black burn scar (the burnt ground) lies among green vegetation.
Flood: brown, muddy water spread over land outside the river channel, covering fields and roads. Compare with an image taken before the flood.
Hot desert: a yellow, orange or red-brown surface with no vegetation, sand-dune patterns of ripples or ridges, and dry river beds.
Human land use leaves patterns that nature rarely makes: straight lines, circles and regular grids. These shapes are the main clue.

Irrigated farming (artificial watering of crops) in a dry region: bright green geometric fields, often perfect circles from centre-pivot irrigation (a rotating watering arm) or rectangles, sharply set against brown desert; or a green strip along a river.
Centre-pivot circles are well known in Saudi Arabia and on the Great Plains of the USA. The Nile valley and delta, Egypt, shows as a green strip and fan of farmland through the desert.
Commercial crop farming in temperate lowlands: a regular chequerboard of rectangular fields of different colours, showing crops at different stages, with straight roads on a grid.
Forest: a uniform dark green texture. Deforestation (clearing of forest) shows as light-brown cleared patches, often in a fishbone pattern along new roads, as in Rondônia, Brazil (Amazon).
Urban area: a grey or purple-grey patch with fine texture, a street grid, and roads and railways converging. Parks show as green.
Airport: long straight runways, often crossing, beside large paved areas and terminal buildings.
Coasts and large landforms are recognised by outline, shape and tone. Here you only name what the image shows.

Coastal features: spits, tombolos and sandbars show as narrow pale strips of sand joining or extending from the coast. A spit is a sand strip attached at one end, and a tombolo joins an island to the mainland.
Deltas show as fan-shaped land with branching channels and sediment plumes (clouds of suspended mud) in the sea. Islands, bays and headlands are recognised by outline.
Large landforms: river valleys and meanders (bends in a river), and mountain ranges shown by ridges, shadows and snow.
Canyons appear as deep, branching, steep-sided valleys in bare rock, and salt pans as dazzling white geometric patches in deserts.

Night-time lights images: bright areas show cities and population density; dark areas are sparsely populated. There is more on coastal landform formation in Coastal processes, patterns and associated landforms (The Sea at Work).
For a 'state one use' question, name the use and say what the image shows. These first uses cover forecasting, mapping, farming and long-term change.

Weather forecasting: tracking depressions, fronts and cloud, issuing storm warnings and tracking hurricanes so that coasts can be evacuated. Ex-hurricane Ophelia (October 2017) was tracked by satellite as it approached Ireland.
Mapping: mapping remote or inaccessible areas and updating maps with new roads and housing.
Agriculture: monitoring crop health and yields, irrigation and land-use change, and checking farm area claims.
Environmental change: tracking deforestation, desertification (land turning to desert), shrinking lakes, glacier and ice-sheet retreat, sea-ice extent and sea surface temperature.

The Aral Sea (Kazakhstan-Uzbekistan) has shrunk greatly since the 1960s because the rivers feeding it, the Amu Darya and Syr Darya, were diverted for irrigation. Satellite images from different decades show the shrinkage.
Satellite images also help in emergencies and in planning, and some satellites that people link with 'satellite' do not take images at all.
Natural hazards: tracking volcanic ash plumes, mapping earthquake and flood damage to direct emergency relief, and monitoring wildfires.
Pollution: detecting oil spills at sea, smog and algal blooms (dense growths of algae in water).

Urban growth: measuring urban sprawl (the spread of a city into the countryside) over time, which is a GIS (geographic information system) study. There is more on this in Geographical information systems (GIS).
Navigation (GPS and Galileo) and communications satellites do not take images; they provide positioning and relay signals.
Satellite images are a source for the rest of the course. They show whole landscapes at once, which suits both physical and human geography.

Physical landscape: plate boundaries (where crustal plates meet) and fold mountains (long parallel ranges), volcanoes, rift valleys, glaciated valleys and ice sheets, river basins and deltas, and coastlines.

Regions: images of Ireland and Europe show regional contrasts, such as the mountainous, wetter, greener west against the flatter, more cultivated east, and cloud-cover patterns. Regional detail is in the regional chapters.
Human landscape: settlement patterns, urban growth, transport routes, field patterns, land-use change and deforestation.
Satellite imagery is powerful for large areas and change over time, but it has weaknesses that affect what it can tell you.
Advantage: one image covers a very large area in a single view, so patterns too big to see on the ground become clear.
Advantage: regular repeat coverage shows change over time, such as a shrinking lake, and archives go back decades.
Advantage: remote and dangerous areas can be reached without a visit, and invisible wavebands such as infrared and radar are recorded.
Advantage: images can be produced quickly, so they are useful in emergencies.
Limitation: cloud blocks visible and infrared images, so the ground beneath cannot be seen.
Limitation: many images have limited resolution, and interpreting them needs skill and software.
Limitation: images carry no names or labels, and relief (the height and shape of the land) is hard to judge on a flat image unless shadows show it.
Limitation: high-resolution imagery can be costly, so not every user can afford it.

A geographical information system (GIS) is a computer system that combines data linked to places on the earth's surface, so that data sources for one area can be studied together. Its power comes from combining: one map or photo on its own is not a GIS.

A GIS captures, stores, analyses and displays spatial (geo-referenced) data, meaning data tied to a location, from maps, aerial photographs, satellite images, census and other statistics, and field surveys.

Each data set is stored as a separate layer, such as roads, rivers, land use, population or protected sites, over the same base map (the common background map). Layers can be switched on and off and overlaid to reveal relationships.

Geo-referencing ties every item to coordinates, such as latitude and longitude or a national grid, so layers from different sources line up. Irish maps use the Irish Transverse Mercator (ITM) grid and the older Irish Grid.
Vector data are points, lines and polygons (closed shapes enclosing an area): a monument is shown as a point, a road as a line and a forest as a polygon.
Raster data are a grid of cells or pixels (tiny squares, each holding one value), such as a satellite image or an aerial photograph.
Each feature can carry attribute data, a table of information about it, such as a house's year of building or a field's crop.
A GIS is useful because of what it can do with the layers once they are lined up. Every study follows the same sequence, so the analysis tools below are used in whichever option is chosen.
Overlay combines layers to show where things coincide, such as new housing on former farmland.
Buffering draws a zone of set distance around a feature, such as a zone around a river or monument.
Querying selects the features that meet a condition, such as all Small Areas (the small census districts) whose population grew by more than a set amount.
Change detection compares the same layer at different dates, so you can see what has altered.
Network analysis finds the shortest or fastest route along roads or other links, such as for an ambulance.
Choropleth maps shade each area by a statistic, such as census figures, so high and low areas stand out.

Steps: 1. define the problem and area; 2. collect data layers; 3. geo-reference them to one base map; 4. overlay and analyse; 5. map and present the results; 6. draw conclusions and recommend planning action (decisions about how land should be used).
Beyond the four studies, GIS is used across planning and services. Knowing its strengths, its limits and where Irish data come from lets you judge any GIS study.

Wider uses of GIS: local authority planning and zoning, flood-risk mapping, emergency services, water and electricity networks, retail and service location, environmental monitoring and census mapping.

Advantages: handles very large data sets, combines many sources, analyses and re-analyses quickly, updates easily, gives clear map output and models 'what if' scenarios (testing the effect of a possible change before it happens).

Limitations: software and data are costly and need training; results are only as good as the data, which may be out of date or inaccurate; layers at different scales or dates may not match; personal data raise privacy issues.

Tailte Éireann, set up in 2023 by bringing together Ordnance Survey Ireland, the Property Registration Authority and the Valuation Office, supplies maps and aerial photography. Either name for the mapping body is acceptable.
The Central Statistics Office (CSO) supplies census data by area. Tailte Éireann is not a census body.
Satellite images, such as Landsat and Copernicus Sentinel, are another source; government departments and agencies supply sector statistics. There is more on satellite images in Satellite imagery.

Urban sprawl is the uncontrolled outward spread of low-density urban development, such as housing estates, retail parks and business parks, into the surrounding countryside, often along roads and into commuter towns (towns from which people travel to work in a city) and villages. This study uses aerial photographs, census material and maps.

Aerial photographs of the same area at different dates show farmland replaced by housing estates, new roads, roundabouts and business parks, and ribbon development (building in a line along approach roads). Overlaying them shows exactly where and when land changed.
Census material: population and housing counts by small area show where population grew fastest, the age of the housing stock, household size and commuting (distance and mode of travel to work).
The CSO publishes census results for Small Areas, each generally of 50–200 dwellings, so growth can be mapped in fine detail.

Ireland's censuses were held in 2011, 2016 and 2022; the 2021 census was postponed to 2022 because of COVID-19. Census 2022 counted about 5.1 million people in Ireland and about 1.45 million in Dublin county.

Maps: Ordnance Survey and historic maps of different editions show the built-up area expanding; development plan zoning maps show land zoned (officially set aside) for housing; transport maps show new motorways and rail lines that encouraged growth.
Once the layers are lined up, the analysis tests how and why the city spread. The Dublin findings then show the problems and the planning responses.
Overlay the built-up area at each date to measure how much land was urbanised (turned into built-up land), then overlay census growth on it.
Buffer motorways and rail stations to test whether growth followed transport, and link commuting data to show dependence on the car.

Findings for Dublin: the city and its suburbs spread into the surrounding counties; commuter towns such as Navan, Drogheda, Naas, Newbridge and Portlaoise grew rapidly; many residents commute long distances into Dublin. The Greater Dublin Area comprises Dublin, Meath, Kildare and Wicklow.
Problems shown by the study: loss of farmland and green space; car dependence, long commutes and traffic congestion; services such as schools, transport and shops lagging behind new housing.

Further problems: high cost of extending water, sewerage and public transport to low-density areas, and weakened community life in dormitory settlements (places where people mainly sleep and travel out to work).
Responses: compact growth and higher density near public transport, promoted by the National Planning Framework (2018).

Other responses: planned new communities with services built alongside housing, such as Adamstown, Co. Dublin, a planned Strategic Development Zone (SDZ); and greenbelts (protected rings of open land around a city).
This study combines satellite images with statistics to measure how farmland has changed between dates.
Satellite images from different years show changes in crops and grassland, field size, drainage, reclaimed marginal land (poorer land brought into use), and land lost to housing or forestry.
Satellite images repeat regularly, so changes can be tracked within a single season.

CORINE land cover is an EU inventory (a mapped record) made from satellite images that shows agricultural, forest, wetland and urban land at each date, so change can be measured. Ireland has been mapped for 1990, 2000, 2006, 2012 and 2018.

Statistical information: the CSO Census of Agriculture (about 135,000 farms counted in 2020) and annual crop and livestock surveys give farm numbers, farm size, crop areas and livestock numbers by county.
Department of Agriculture data on farm payments add the financial side of land use.
The satellite layers are overlaid and joined to the statistics, so the pattern of change can be explained by soils, relief and rainfall.
Overlay satellite-derived land use from two dates to map where tillage (growing crops), grassland, forestry and built land changed.

Join county statistics to the map, then relate the change to soils, relief and rainfall layers. For example, tillage is concentrated on the drier, flatter, better-drained land of the east and south-east.
Most Irish farmland is grassland for cattle and sheep; tillage is concentrated in the east and south-east.
Dairy farming expanded after EU milk quotas (limits on how much milk farms could produce) ended in 2015.
Some marginal land in the west has been planted with forestry, and farmland on the edge of cities has been lost to urban growth.

Uses: checking farmers' land-use claims under the EU's Common Agricultural Policy (CAP, the EU farm payment scheme) by satellite, monitoring crop health and forecasting yields, and tracking wetland drainage, hedgerow loss and nitrate pressure on water.

International illustration: satellite images of irrigated desert farming (centre-pivot circles) and of Amazon clearance show agricultural change on a large scale. There is more on this in Satellite imagery.
This study combines aerial photographs, maps and forestry statistics to show where forest has been planted and cleared, and why planting went where it did.

Aerial photographs of different dates show new plantations as dark, uniform blocks with straight edges and firebreaks (gaps that stop fire spreading), clear-felled areas as bare brown patches with brash (leftover branches), and replanting. Species and age can be distinguished by tone and texture.
OS maps show forest areas by symbol (coniferous, deciduous or mixed) and can be compared across editions.
Soil, peat and relief maps show where planting took place, on marginal upland, wet mineral soils and peat.
Maps of protected areas, Special Areas of Conservation and Special Protection Areas (sites protected for habitats and birds), show where planting conflicts with conservation.

Statistical information: the Forest Service's National Forest Inventory (forest area, species, ownership and age by county), annual afforestation (planting new forest) and felling figures, and grant data.
GIS analysis: overlay forest cover at successive dates to map expansion; overlay soils, slope and altitude to explain where planting happened.
GIS analysis, continued: overlay protected sites, rivers and archaeological sites, with buffers, to identify conflicts; query which counties had the largest increase.
The study shows how much forest Ireland has gained, who planted it and what it has cost the environment.
Forest cover was about 1% of Ireland at the start of the 20th century and is about 11% today (National Forest Inventory, 2022).
Most planting has been of conifers, mainly Sitka spruce, which makes up about half of all forest area, largely on marginal land.
Coillte, the state forestry company set up in 1988, manages most public forest; private, largely farm-based, planting grew with grants.
Benefits: timber and jobs, farm income diversification (more than one source of farm income), carbon storage and recreation.

Problems: dense conifer blocks change the landscape and reduce biodiversity; acidification and sediment in streams harm fish and the freshwater pearl mussel; open upland habitat for birds such as the hen harrier is lost.
Further problems: planting on peat releases carbon; clear-felling (cutting all trees in an area) causes erosion; forestry replacing farms has caused local opposition, for example in Co. Leitrim.
Ash dieback, a tree disease first found in Ireland in 2012, is a disease risk.

Management: more broadleaf planting, buffer zones along rivers, environmental assessment of planting, and continuous-cover forestry (harvesting without clear-felling, so the ground is always covered by trees).
The archaeological study uses the official record of known sites, old and new maps, and aerial photographs. The record is the starting point because it says which sites are known and protected.

The Record of Monuments and Places (RMP) is the statutory (legally established) list of known archaeological monuments in each county, set up under section 12 of the National Monuments (Amendment) Act 1994.

It is published as a written list with OS maps on which each site is circled; the database behind it, the Sites and Monuments Record, is viewable in the National Monuments Service's online Historic Environment Viewer.
Anyone intending works at or near a recorded monument must give two months' notice before the works begin, so the site can be assessed.

Types of site: ringforts (about 45,000 in Ireland, the most common field monument), megalithic tombs, standing stones, ecclesiastical (church) sites, castles and tower houses, crannógs (lake dwellings), fulachta fiadh (burnt-mound cooking sites), and buried sites known only from below-ground remains.
Old maps show where sites once stood and aerial photographs reveal what survives, so overlaying them shows what has been lost.

First edition OS six-inch maps of Ireland date from the 1830s–1840s and later editions record sites, for example ringforts drawn as circles. Comparing old maps, modern maps and the RMP shows which sites have disappeared.

Aerial photographs reveal sites that are invisible on the ground. Cropmarks: crops over buried ditches grow taller and greener from extra moisture, while over buried walls they are stunted and parched.
Other marks: parchmarks (dry patches) in dry summers; soil marks in ploughed fields; and shadow marks, where low sun shows earthworks (banks and mounds).
Comparing photographs from different dates shows sites that have been levelled; LiDAR (laser scanning from an aircraft) reveals earthworks under trees.
GIS analysis: overlay the RMP point layer on old and new maps and aerial photographs to record which sites survive, are damaged or are destroyed.
Overlay development layers (new roads, housing, quarries, forestry and land drainage), buffer each monument to predict threats, and map destruction rates by area.
The study identifies what destroys sites, uses named cases to show it, and supports the measures that protect monuments.
Agricultural improvement (land reclamation, drainage, ploughing and removal of field boundaries) causes destruction.

Other causes: road building, urban and housing development, quarrying, afforestation (ploughing, drains and tree roots), and natural erosion such as coastal erosion of promontory forts and middens (ancient rubbish heaps).
Wood Quay, Dublin: a Viking-age site, excavated and largely removed for Dublin Corporation's civic offices after protests in the late 1970s.

M3 motorway through the Tara–Skryne valley, Co. Meath: opened 2010, and passes through the valley near the Hill of Tara; a henge (a circular earthwork) was found at Lismullin during construction in 2007.
Carrickmines Castle on the M50 route, Co. Dublin: a dispute in the early 2000s.
July 2018 drought: a henge at Brú na Bóinne, Co. Meath, was spotted from the air (by drone).

Protection the study supports: the RMP and its notification system; archaeological assessment and excavation before development, which means preservation by record (recording the site before it is removed) or preservation in situ (keeping it in place).
Further protection: planning conditions; rerouting roads; public awareness; and farm schemes that protect monuments.

Every figure question starts the same way: read the labels and units before reading any value. Most lost marks come from a wrong unit, year or column, because a correct reading of the wrong one still scores nothing.

Check the title, both axis labels (the words along the horizontal and vertical lines), the key or legend (the box explaining colours or symbols), the units (%, thousands, millions, €m, hectares, mm, °C, per 1,000), the years shown and the source line. Each one changes what a number means.
Read a bar or line value by running a ruler from the top of the bar or point across to the vertical axis, estimating between gridlines, and quoting the value with its unit.
In a table, find the row and the column and read the cell where they meet. Check the totals row before using a figure, so you know whether a number is a part or the whole.
Compare two years by reading neighbouring columns. To spot the one that did not change, read across the whole row, because the unchanged value is the one that stays the same between years.
For highest and lowest, scan every value, not just the first and last, because the extreme can sit in the middle. For a ranking, list the values from largest to smallest.
To count how many items are above an average line, count the bars or points whose tops lie above it.
For 'twice as much', double the smaller value and look for the value that matches it.

An infographic (a single page combining headline numbers, icons, small charts and county maps) has several panels. Read each panel's own label and unit: headline figures are often totals, while panels may show percentages.
A description states what the figure shows. Using exact trend words and quoting numbers turns a vague answer into a complete one.

Trend vocabulary: increase, rise or growth; decrease, fall or decline; steady, constant or no change; fluctuate (go up and down); peak (highest point); trough (lowest point); gradual or rapid (sharp); levelling off (the change slows and flattens).
The overall trend is the long-term direction. A short-term change, such as a single year's dip, is described separately so it does not hide the main pattern.
To describe a trend, state the overall direction, the start and end values with their years and units, and the period of fastest change.
Name any peak, trough or reversal (a change of direction), and quantify the change as the difference, the percentage change, or both.
Point out anomalies: values that break the pattern of the others.
Once a trend is described, the next marks come from comparing it with another, saying why it happened and judging whether the figure can be trusted.

To compare two series (two lines or two sets of bars), say which is higher, when the lines cross, whether the gap widens or narrows, and the difference in a given year. For example, net migration = immigration minus emigration.
To explain a trend, link the pattern to one cause from the relevant chapter, in one clause. Explaining means saying why the figure looks as it does, not just what it shows.
To evaluate a figure, check whether an axis that does not start at zero or has uneven intervals exaggerates change, because a small rise then looks large.
Also check whether unevenly spaced dates distort the trend, whether the sample (the group measured) is small, and whether the source is reliable and recent.
Percentages can hide small totals: a large percentage rise may be a small change in numbers, because a small starting number is easy to double.

These worked values come from the invented (illustrative) population of six towns, in thousands: Town A 18, Town B 32, Town C 25, Town D 41, Town E 12, Town F 29. Each statistic has a short method that you can repeat on any data set.
Difference: subtract the smaller value from the larger and say which is larger. Town B (32) exceeds Town C (25) by 7 thousand (illustrative).
Mean (average) = total of the values ÷ number of values: 157 ÷ 6 = 26.2 thousand, to one decimal place (illustrative).
Median (the middle value): put the values in order (12, 18, 25, 29, 32, 41); with an even number of values, average the middle two: (25 + 29) ÷ 2 = 27 thousand (illustrative).
Mode: the most frequent value. The six towns have no mode because no value repeats.
Range = highest value minus lowest value: 41 − 12 = 29 thousand (illustrative), which shows how spread out the values are.
Percentages let you compare parts of different-sized wholes, but the method matters: dividing by the wrong number, or mixing up a percentage with a percentage point, gives a wrong answer.
Percentage of a total = part ÷ total × 100. Illustrative: Town D's share of the six towns is 41 ÷ 157 × 100 = 26.1%.
Percentage change = (new value − old value) ÷ old value × 100. A positive result is an increase; a negative result is a decrease.

Always divide by the old (earlier) value, because the change is measured against where you started. Illustrative Country P, broadband households: 20% in 2000 and 90% in 2025, so the percentage change is (90 − 20) ÷ 20 × 100 = 350%.

Percentage points: when both values are already percentages, the change is a difference in percentage points. A rise from 20% to 30% is a 10 percentage-point increase, but a 50% increase in the percentage change, (30 − 20) ÷ 20 × 100.

When a question asks by what percentage a percentage changed, the subtraction is the usual reading: give the answer in percentage points and add the percentage change if unsure. Use the percentage-change formula when the values are numbers rather than percentages.

Missing value X: parts of a whole add to 100% (pie chart or percentage table) or to a stated total (stacked bar, a bar split into parts, or a total row), so X = total minus the sum of the known parts.
Illustrative Country Q: if all segments except 'other' total 85%, then other = 100 − 85 = 15%, because the parts of a pie chart must reach 100%.
To find a number from a percentage: number = percentage ÷ 100 × total.
Raw numbers are hard to compare between places of different size, so geographers use rates, densities and ratios. How you present the answer matters too.
Rate per 1,000 = number ÷ population × 1,000, which lets places of different size be compared. A birth rate is births ÷ population × 1,000.
Density = number ÷ area, given as people per km².
Ratio: compare two values as a ratio, e.g. 2 : 1. Illustrative: Town D (41) is more than three times the size of Town E (12), a ratio of about 3.4 : 1.
'Twice as much' means two times the other value; 'half' means divided by two.
Round to the precision the data uses, or to one decimal place where needed, and keep the unit and the multiplier (thousands, millions) in every answer.
In a calculation question, show the working: a correct answer with working is safe, and the working can earn marks if the answer slips.
When you are asked to draw a graph from a small table of data, marks are given for each of these rules, so each one is worth doing even when the shape of the graph is easy.
Use graph paper, a sharp pencil and a ruler; draw the graph large enough to fill most of the space.
The title says what the data is, where and when, taken from the wording of the question.
The horizontal (x) axis shows categories or time; the vertical (y) axis shows values. Label both axes with units.
The scale starts at zero, is evenly divided, and its interval is chosen so the largest value fits (e.g. steps of 5 or 10 units).
On a line graph, time intervals are spaced in proportion to the years. If the data is for 1990, 2000, 2010 and 2015, the last gap is half the others.
Plot every value accurately. Bars have equal widths and equal gaps; points are joined with ruled straight lines.
Use a key or legend (a box saying what each colour or shading means) whenever more than one colour or shading is used, and shade or colour each category distinctly.
Illustrative data: population of six towns, in thousands, from the totals block above. Following the rules in order shows how each mark is earned.
Graph choice: a bar chart, because the values are one measure for separate towns.
x-axis: 'Town', with Towns A to F in order.
y-axis: 'Population (thousands)', from 0 to 45 in steps of 5, so the largest value (41) fits.
Six bars of equal width with equal gaps, each drawn to its value: A 18, B 32, C 25, D 41, E 12, F 29.
A single data series (one set of values) needs no key; check each bar top against the scale before finishing.
The question 'draw a suitable graph' is answered by naming the graph type, then giving one sentence of justification. The type depends on what the data is. Each example below is illustrative.
Values for separate categories, e.g. the populations of six towns: bar chart.
Change over time, e.g. the percentage of an urban population from 1980 to 2020: line graph (a bar chart is usually also accepted).
Parts of a whole, or percentage shares adding to 100%, e.g. car sales by fuel type in one year: pie chart or divided bar.
Two related variables for the same places, e.g. income and birth rate for twenty countries: scatter graph.
Three components that add to 100%, e.g. sand, silt and clay at a soil site: triangular graph.
Age and sex structure of a population: population pyramid.
Monthly temperature and rainfall for one place: climate graph.
Values for areas on a map, e.g. population density by region: choropleth map (a map with areas shaded by value).
Bar charts show amounts for separate categories. They come in several forms, depending on whether you are comparing categories, groups within a category, or parts of a total.
Simple bar chart: separate categories, one bar per category, equal widths and equal gaps; vertical or horizontal.
Multiple (clustered or comparative) bar chart: two or more bars side by side per category, e.g. males and females, or two years; a key is needed to tell the bars apart.
Compound (stacked or divided) bar chart: each bar is split into components, and the top of the whole bar is the total.
To read a component in a compound bar, take the top of its segment minus the bottom of its segment.
Percentage compound bar: every bar reaches 100%, so the segments show shares rather than totals.
Illustrative Region R, tree planting: total 2,000 hectares, of which conifers 1,350 ha. Broadleaf = 2,000 − 1,350 = 650 ha, a share of 650 ÷ 2,000 × 100 = 32.5%.
A histogram looks like a bar chart but is used for continuous data, while a line graph is the standard way to show one variable changing over time.
Histogram: like a bar chart but for continuous data grouped in classes (e.g. age groups or rainfall amounts), drawn with no gaps between bars because one class runs straight into the next.
Line graph (trend graph): one variable over time; plot the points at the correct years and join them with ruled lines.
Multiple line graph: two or more series on the same axes, with a key so each line can be identified.
The gradient (steepness) of a line shows the rate of change: a steeper section means faster change.

Illustrative Country P, households with broadband: 2000 20%, 2005 38%, 2010 61%, 2015 74%, 2020 86%, 2025 90%. The rise is continuous; the fastest change is 2005 to 2010 (+23 percentage points), and the rise slows to +4 points from 2020 to 2025 as the line levels off.

Illustrative Country P: the change from 2000 to 2025 is +70 percentage points, which is not the same as the 350% percentage change above, because one is a subtraction and the other is measured against the old value.
A pie chart shows how a whole is split into parts. Because a full circle is 360° and the parts add to 100%, each 1% takes up 3.6° of the circle.
Pie chart: parts of a whole. Degrees = percentage × 3.6, because 360° ÷ 100 = 3.6.
For raw numbers rather than percentages: degrees = value ÷ total × 360. Do not multiply raw numbers by 3.6.
Drawing steps: draw a circle with a compass, draw a radius (a line from the centre to the edge) to 12 o'clock, then measure each angle clockwise with a protractor, largest segment first.
Shade, key or label each segment with its percentage, and check that the angles add to 360°.
Illustrative Country Q, electricity sources (gas 40%, wind 25%, solar 10%, coal 5%, hydro 5%, other 15%): angles 144°, 90°, 36°, 18°, 18° and 54°, totalling 360°.
Two pie charts compare the shares in two years, not the totals, unless the circles are drawn in proportion to the totals.
Divided (percentage) bar: a single bar split into shares that add to 100%, an alternative to a pie chart.
A pictogram uses icons to stand for quantities. A population pyramid is a special graph showing how many people of each age and sex a country has.
Pictogram: each icon stands for a fixed quantity stated in the key, so check the key first; a part-icon is a fraction of that quantity.
Population pyramid: a back-to-back horizontal bar chart, which is a histogram on its side.
Age groups, usually in 5-year bands, sit on the central vertical axis: 0 to 4 at the bottom and the oldest group at the top.
Males are drawn on the left and females on the right. The horizontal axis shows the percentage (or number) of the population, not age, scaled outward from zero on both sides.

Reading a pyramid: a wide base means a high birth rate; a narrow top means low life expectancy; a narrowing base means a falling birth rate; bulges and indentations suggest baby booms, migration, war or famine.
Describe the dependent groups (the young and the old, who rely on others) and the working-age group when reading a pyramid.

Drawing one band (illustrative, Country Z): males aged 20 to 24 are 3.5% and females 3.4%, so at the 20 to 24 level draw a bar 3.5 units long left of the centre axis and one 3.4 units long to the right.

The shapes of pyramids and the stages of demographic transition (how a country's birth and death rates change over time) are taught fully elsewhere. There is more on this in Changing population characteristics.
A climate graph combines two kinds of data for one place on a single set of axes: rainfall as bars and temperature as a line, across 12 months.
Months J to D run along the bottom axis. Rainfall is shown as bars against a left-hand axis in mm.
Mean (average) monthly temperature is shown as a line, plotted at the middle of each month, against a right-hand axis in °C.
From the graph, read the hottest and coldest months, the wettest and driest months, and the seasonal pattern (rain all year, or a wet and dry season).

Calculations from the graph: annual temperature range = maximum mean monthly temperature minus minimum; mean annual temperature = sum of the 12 monthly means ÷ 12; total annual rainfall = sum of the 12 bars.
Illustrative Station M, mean monthly temperature (°C) J to D: 5, 5, 7, 9, 12, 14, 16, 16, 14, 11, 8, 6. Rainfall (mm) J to D: 110, 80, 85, 60, 65, 70, 70, 85, 90, 115, 110, 120.
Illustrative Station M results: warmest in July and August (16°C); coldest in January and February (5°C); annual range 16 − 5 = 11°C; mean annual temperature 123 ÷ 12 = 10.3°C.

Illustrative Station M: total rainfall 1,060 mm; wettest month December (120 mm); driest month April (60 mm). Rain falls in every month with a winter maximum, and the mild winters and cool summers resemble a cool temperate oceanic pattern.
Identifying a climate type from a climate graph is taught elsewhere. There is more on this in Physical regions and Climatic environments and climate change.
A scatter graph tests whether two measurements for the same set of places are related, for example whether land value changes with distance from a city centre.

Scatter graph: two variables for the same set of places. The independent variable (the one that may cause the change) goes on the x-axis; each place is plotted as a point, and the points are not joined.
Draw a line of best fit by eye through the middle of the points, so it shows the general direction.
Positive correlation: both variables rise together. Negative correlation: one rises as the other falls. No correlation: no clear pattern. Strength is described as strong or weak.
Outliers, or anomalies, are points that lie away from the pattern of the others.
Correlation does not prove cause: two things can move together without one causing the other.
Illustrative distance from a city centre and land value at eight sites: 1 km €900 per m²; 2 km €700; 3 km €620; 4 km €450; 5 km €400; 6 km €250; 7 km €260; 8 km €150.

Illustrative: the result is a strong negative correlation, with the 7 km site a slight anomaly because it is higher than the 6 km site. A one-clause explanation: accessibility falls with distance from the centre.
A triangular graph is used when a total is split into exactly three parts. Each point is placed using all three values at once.
Triangular graph: shows three components that always total 100%, e.g. the percentage employed in the primary, secondary and tertiary sectors.
Each side is a 0 to 100% scale. Read each component along the gridlines parallel to the side where its 0 is, following the direction in which its numbers run.
Check that the three readings add to 100, which confirms you have read the scales correctly.
To plot a point: find the first value on its scale, follow its gridline in, and mark where it meets the second value's gridline; check the point with the third value.
A point clustered near a corner is dominated by the component that corner represents.

Illustrative employment structure: Country X is primary 10%, secondary 25%, tertiary 65%; it sits near the tertiary corner, typical of a developed economy. Country Y is primary 60%, secondary 15%, tertiary 25%; it sits near the primary corner, typical of a less developed economy.
Statistical maps put values onto a map so you can see how they vary from place to place. The choropleth is the main one; four other types each show a different kind of data.
Choropleth map: areas (counties, regions or countries) shaded by value class; darker shading means a higher value.
Classes must not overlap and must cover every value, e.g. 0 to 49, 50 to 99, 100 to 149, 150 and over. A key is essential.
Choropleth maps suit densities and percentages. Their weakness is that they imply the value is even across each area and hide variation inside it, and the boundaries look like sudden changes.

Illustrative regional population densities (people per km²): North 35, East 160, South 85, West 40, Midlands 60. North and West are the lightest shade and East the darkest; the empty 100 to 149 class still appears in the key.
Dot map: each dot stands for a fixed number, showing the distribution of a value.
Isoline map: lines join places of equal value, e.g. isobars, isotherms, isohyets or contours.
Flow-line map: arrow width is proportional to the amount moving, e.g. migration, traffic or trade.
Proportional symbols: circles or bars sized in proportion to the value, placed on the map.
Sometimes a table is a better way to present data than a graph, and tables, graphs and maps all feed into the Geographical Investigation.
Use a table rather than a graph when many exact values must be given. A table cannot show a trend at a glance.
Graphs, maps and tables are expected in the presentation of results in the Geographical Investigation report. There is more on this in The Geographical Investigation (20%).

A census of population is an official count of every person in the country on one night, with information collected on each person and household. Because everyone is counted on the same night, the results give a comparable picture of the whole country.
In Ireland the census is carried out by the Central Statistics Office (CSO, the State's statistics agency), and taking part is required by law, so every household must complete the form.

Ireland's census is de facto (based on where people are on the night): it counts everyone present in the State on census night, including visitors, wherever they usually live. The form also records each person's usual residence, so results can be given both ways.
The census is normally held every five years on a Sunday night in April. It used to fall in years ending in 1 and 6, but the 2021 census was postponed to 2022, so the next is in 2027.
The 2001 census was postponed to 2002 because of foot-and-mouth disease (an animal disease outbreak).
The 2021 census was postponed to 2022 because of COVID-19. The next census is planned for 2027.
The first census of the Irish Free State (the State as it was from 1922) was held in 1926.
Counting a whole country on one night needs a careful system for delivering and collecting forms, and people will only answer honestly if their details are protected.
Enumerators (field staff who visit homes) deliver a household form to every dwelling before census night and collect it afterwards.
One form is completed per household, with a page for each person in it, so each person's details are recorded separately.

Communal establishments (places where people live together) such as hotels, hospitals and prisons are covered separately, and vacant dwellings (empty homes) are recorded, so that every building is accounted for.
Information is used only for statistics, and personal forms are kept closed for 100 years, which protects people's privacy.
After 100 years the returns become historical records. The 1901 and 1911 census returns are freely available online from the National Archives of Ireland and are used for family history.
The form asks about people, work, housing and the household, which gives planners the information they need on how people live.
Personal topics: age, sex and marital status; relationships within the household; place of birth, citizenship, ethnicity and religion; ability to speak Irish; other languages; education level.
Work topics: occupation, industry and unemployment; commuting (the daily journey to work or school), covering means of travel and journey time.
Housing topics: type, age and tenure of the home (tenure means how it is held: owned with or without a mortgage, or rented); rent paid; heating; vacancy.
Household topics: internet access, car ownership, health and disability, and carers (people who look after others).
Census 2022 asked for the first time about working from home and about renewable energy sources at the home, such as solar panels.
Census 2022 included an optional time capsule page whose contents will be released after 100 years.
Only a few national totals are needed, and each must be tied to the census it comes from. Take care to keep the Republic's figures apart from Northern Ireland's.
Census 2016, held on 24 April 2016: about 4.76 million people.
Census 2022, held on 3 April 2022: 5,149,139, about 5.15 million people.
Between the 2016 and 2022 censuses the population rose by about 387,000, about 8%.
Northern Ireland has its own census, run by NISRA (Northern Ireland Statistics and Research Agency). Its latest was held on 21 March 2021 and counted about 1.9 million people.
Ireland's census figures cover the State, not the island. The Republic's latest census was 2022 and Northern Ireland's was 2021, so their figures must not be merged.
Results come out in stages and at several scales, from the whole State down to a few streets, so that users can find the level of detail they need.
Preliminary results are published within months of census night, because they are quick to produce; detailed results by theme follow over the next year or two.
Results are published for the State, the provinces, counties, cities, towns, Electoral Divisions (EDs, small local administrative areas) and Small Areas.
Small Areas are the smallest units, roughly a street or estate.
Results appear in online tables, interactive maps on the CSO website, county profiles and infographics (pictures and charts that summarise figures).
Governments and businesses plan ahead using census numbers, because the data shows how many people of each kind live where.
Schools: the number of young children shows how many school places are needed, so new schools can be built where children live.
Healthcare and nursing homes: the size of the older population shows the places needed, because older people use these services most.
Housing: household numbers and vacancy show how many homes are needed, so planners can tell whether to build more.
Transport: commuting flows (how many people travel from where to where) show where roads and public transport are needed, because they reveal busy routes.
Pensions and social welfare: the age structure shows future demand, because more older people means more pensions to be paid.
Government targets resources at disadvantaged areas, which the figures help to identify, and plans regional and county development.
Businesses use the figures to choose where to locate shops and services, so that they open where there are enough customers.
Researchers and students use the data; tracking the Irish language and historical and genealogical (family history) research use census returns.
The census also decides how Ireland's Dáil (the lower house of parliament) is divided into constituencies, the areas whose voters elect TDs (Teachtaí Dála, members of the Dáil).
