Dáil constituencies are reviewed after each census so that each TD represents roughly the same number of people, which keeps votes fair across the country.
The Constitution requires one TD for every 20,000 to 30,000 people.
Constituencies must be revised at least once every 12 years, with regard to census figures.
The Electoral Commission (An Coimisiún Toghcháin) carries out the review after each census.
A census is a powerful source but not a perfect one, so any conclusions drawn from it need to be treated with care. Other sources fill the gaps between censuses.
A census is a snapshot of one night, so it is out of date between censuses, and detailed results take a long time to appear.
There may be an undercount (fewer people recorded than really live there): homeless people and people avoiding the count can be missed.
Answers are self-reported (people fill in the form themselves) and may be inaccurate.
A census is very expensive and raises privacy concerns, because it collects personal details about every household.
Electoral Divisions and Small Areas change over time, which makes comparisons between censuses difficult because the areas are no longer the same.

Between censuses, civil registration (the official recording of life events) records births, deaths and marriages; the CSO publishes annual population and migration estimates; the Labour Force Survey (a regular sample survey of work and employment) gives other population data.

Demographic structure is the make-up of a population by age, sex and other characteristics, such as marital status, nationality or ethnicity, religion, language, education, occupation, household size and urban or rural location.
Age structure has three groups: young dependents (0 to 14), working age (15 to 64) and old dependents (65 and over). Dependents are people who are mostly supported by the working-age group.
Dependency ratio = (0 to 14 plus 65 and over) ÷ (15 to 64) × 100. It divides by the working-age group, not by the total population.
A high young dependency ratio means many schools are needed; a high old dependency ratio means many pensions and healthcare places are needed.
Illustrative Rivertown ED, later census: 0 to 14 = 1,050; 15 to 64 = 3,120; 65 and over = 660; total 4,830.
Illustrative dependency ratio = (1,050 + 660) ÷ 3,120 × 100 = 54.8, about 55 dependents per 100 people of working age.

Census data is drawn as a population pyramid (a bar chart of age and sex groups) in the way taught in the notes on Figure interpretation; the meaning of pyramid shapes is taught in the notes on Changing population characteristics.
Sex structure compares the numbers of males and females. It is measured with a ratio, and it can show the effects of life expectancy and migration.
Sex ratio = males ÷ females × 100, giving the number of males per 100 females.
Women outnumber men in the older age groups because of longer life expectancy (women tend to live longer).
Local imbalances arise from migration, e.g. young women moving to cities for work.
Illustrative Rivertown ED, later census: males 2,390 and females 2,440 (total 4,830); sex ratio = 2,390 ÷ 2,440 × 100 = 98 males per 100 females.
A population changes in two ways: people are born and die, and people move in and out. Splitting the change into these two parts shows which is driving it.
Population change = natural increase + net migration.
Natural increase = births minus deaths, so it is positive when more babies are born than people die.
Net migration = immigrants (people moving in) minus emigrants (people moving out).

Comparing two censuses, with births and deaths from civil registration (the official record of births and deaths), gives the estimated net migration: net migration = total change minus natural increase.
Illustrative Rivertown ED, six years apart: population 4,200 at the earlier census and 4,830 at the later census, a change of +630.
Illustrative: births 380 and deaths 210 give a natural increase of 170, so net migration = 630 − 170 = +460, meaning more people moved in than out.
Raw totals are hard to compare between places of different size, so geographers also use measures that scale the figures, such as rates per 1,000 people.
Crude birth rate and crude death rate are the births and deaths per 1,000 people per year. They are called crude because they use the whole population without adjusting for age.
Population density is the number of people per km², so it shows how crowded an area is.
Percentage of the population in an age group = people in the group ÷ total population × 100.
Illustrative Rivertown ED, census year: 65 births; crude birth rate = 65 ÷ 4,830 × 1,000 = 13.5 per 1,000.
The census totals show a long-term pattern for the State: a fall, a low point and then growth. Only the headline trend is given here.
The State's population fell steeply after the Great Famine (the potato failure of the 1840s) and was at its lowest in the 1961 census, at about 2.8 million.
For comparison, the population of the whole island was about 8.2 million in 1841.
After 1961 the population grew, and Census 2022 was the first to show it passing 5 million since the 1851 census.
Present features: growth driven by both natural increase and immigration; an ageing population, with a growing share aged 65 and over; rising cultural diversity, with many non-Irish citizens.

Demographic transition (the shift in birth and death rates as a country develops), fertility and mortality change and Ireland's twentieth-century history are in the notes on Changing population characteristics and the notes on Changing migration patterns in Ireland.
Migration patterns, policy and reasons are in the migration notes, from Changing migration patterns in Ireland to Rural-to-urban migration.
A local-area study applies the census to a place you know, by following a fixed sequence from choosing the area to judging the data. Following the steps in order keeps the study complete.
Step 1: choose the area, an Electoral Division, Small Area, town or county.
Step 2: find its census tables for two or more censuses on the CSO website or interactive map, so that you can compare change over time.
Step 3: record the total population, age groups, sex, households, nationality and commuting, because these are the figures the calculations in step 4 need.
Step 4: calculate the changes (number and percentage), the dependency ratio, the sex ratio and the share in each age group.

Step 5: present the results with graphs: a line graph of population over several censuses, bar or pie charts of age groups, a population pyramid if five-year age bands are available, or a choropleth map (a map shaded by value) of Electoral Divisions.
Step 6: describe the trends; step 7: explain them; step 8: note the limitations of the data.

Illustrative Rivertown: a line graph of population over several censuses (any earlier values are invented and must be labelled illustrative), a bar or pie chart of the three age groups, and a pyramid only if five-year bands are available.
Once a trend is described, the next step is to give reasons for it. Local trends usually come from housing, jobs and migration.
New housing estates and commuter growth near cities and along motorways bring rising population, young families and a high young dependency ratio.
Rural decline in remote areas brings a falling population, an ageing population and more single-person households, because younger people tend to leave.
Other causes include immigration, the closure or opening of a major employer, and town-centre decline set against suburban growth.

Illustrative Rivertown: the population growth and high young dependency fit a new housing estate on the edge of town (the aerial photograph of Rivertown shows one; see the notes on Aerial photograph interpretation) that attracts young families who commute, together with positive net migration.
There is more on this in the notes on Rural-to-urban migration in developed and developing regions and the Urban Geography chapter.
Two further uses of the census link to other parts of the course: language and the study of how cities spread.

The census records ability to speak Irish and how often it is spoken: daily within the education system, daily outside it, weekly, less often, or never. The cultural detail is in the notes on Language as a cultural indicator.

Census data is also used in the GIS (geographical information systems, computer mapping) study of urban sprawl (the outward spread of a city into the countryside); there is more on this in the notes on Geographical information systems (GIS).

Geographers divide the earth into regions so that places can be studied as groups instead of one by one. A region is an area of the earth's surface that shares one or more characteristics, called criteria, which make it different from the areas around it.
Physical criteria: climate (the usual weather of a place), relief (the height and shape of the land) and rock type, such as limestone.
Administrative criteria: the boundaries set by government, such as county lines.
Cultural criteria: language and religion, which separate groups of people.
Socio-economic criteria: wealth, employment and development (how advanced a place's economy and living standards are).
Urban criteria: a city and its hinterland (the surrounding area that depends on the city for services and jobs).
These five types of region are the five subsections of this chapter, and this subsection deals with physical regions.
Regions can be big or small, and they can be defined by one criterion or by several. Their edges also differ: some are fixed by law, others fade gradually.

Regions exist at different scales. A local region is a county or a city's hinterland, e.g. Co. Clare; a national region is the West of Ireland; a continental region is North West Europe; a global region is the Islamic world.
A single index (one measurable criterion) defines a region by that one thing: rock type alone gives a karst region (a limestone landscape shaped by water dissolving the rock).

Multiple indices combine several criteria. For example, a peripheral region (one on the edge of a country's economic activity, far from its centre) can be defined by income, unemployment and out-migration (people leaving the area) together.
Physical and cultural regions usually merge into their neighbours through transition zones (a gradual belt of change) rather than ending at a sharp line.
Administrative regions have exact boundaries, fixed by law, so you can say precisely which side of the line a place lies on.
Regions also change over time as their criteria change.

Climate is the usual pattern of weather in a place over many years. A climatic region is a large area with similar temperature, precipitation (rain, snow and other moisture falling from the sky) and seasonal pattern, usually with similar natural vegetation and soils.
The world can be divided into climatic regions. This subsection studies the cool temperate oceanic type in detail.
Cool temperate oceanic: Ireland and North West Europe, which is why Ireland is the case studied here.
Warm temperate oceanic: the Mediterranean type, with hot, dry summers and mild, wet winters, so it differs from Ireland.
The cool temperate oceanic climate is mild and wet, with no extremes of heat or cold. These are the features to describe, with the Irish figures (Met Éireann long-term averages).
Mild winters, because of the warm sea: mean January (coldest month) temperatures are about 4-7°C.
Cool summers, so it is never hot: mean July (warmest month) temperatures are about 14-16°C.
The annual range of temperature (the gap between the warmest and coldest month) is small, only about 10°C, and snow is rare on low ground.
Rain falls in every month, so there is no dry season.
The weather is changeable, with prevailing (most frequent) south-westerly winds.
Ireland's climate comes from several causes working together: where it sits on the globe, the ocean beside it and the winds that cross it. Each cause explains one feature of the climate.
Latitude: Ireland lies between about 51.5°N and 55.5°N, in the mid-latitudes, where the sun's angle is moderate, so it is neither very hot nor very cold.
North Atlantic Drift: a warm ocean current, the extension of the Gulf Stream, keeps winters mild and coasts free of ice.
Maritime influence (the effect of being close to the sea): the sea heats and cools slowly, so the annual temperature range is small.
Prevailing south-westerly winds blow off the Atlantic, carrying its mild, moist air over Ireland.

Frequent Atlantic depressions (areas of low pressure that bring wind and rain) and their fronts (the boundaries between warm and cold air) bring rain. These weather systems are taught in the Weather and Climate chapter.
Relief rainfall: moist air is forced up the western mountains, cools and releases its rain on their western slopes.
The climate is not the same everywhere in Ireland. Because the wet south-westerly winds arrive from the Atlantic, the west gets the most rain and the east the least.
The west is wetter than the east: about 1,000-1,250 mm of rain a year across much of the west, against about 750 mm in the driest parts of the east, around Dublin.
Over 2,000 mm a year falls on many western mountains, because moist air is forced to rise over them.
The east lies in a rain shadow (a drier area on the sheltered side of high ground), protected from the south-westerly winds by the western uplands.
Wet days (days with measurable rain): about 150 a year on the east and south-east coasts, rising to about 225 a year in parts of the west.
The south-east is the sunniest region, because it is sheltered from the wet south-westerlies.
The north is slightly cooler than the south, and coasts are milder in winter than the inland Midlands, because the sea warms them.
North West Europe is the international setting for this climate, because the same conditions that affect Ireland affect its neighbours. Further east the climate changes step by step.
The same climate covers Ireland, Britain, north-west France (Brittany), Belgium, the Netherlands, Denmark and coastal Norway.
All of these face the Atlantic, share the North Atlantic Drift and lie in the path of westerly depressions, which is why they have the same climate.

Moving east, away from the Atlantic, winters become colder, summers warmer, the annual range larger and rainfall lower, with a summer maximum (most rain falls in summer). This is the continental influence (the effect of being far from the sea).
The change is gradual, so the boundary of a climatic region is a transition zone, not a line.
Climate shapes more than the weather. In a cool temperate oceanic region it also influences what grows naturally and how the land is farmed.
Natural vegetation is deciduous forest (trees that lose their leaves in winter), mainly oak and ash.
Soils are brown earth, the typical soil under deciduous forest.
Grass grows for most of the year, because winters are mild and rain falls in every month. This favours pastoral farming (rearing animals on grass) in Ireland, mainly cattle and dairying.

Geomorphology is the study of landforms (natural features of the land) and how they formed. A geomorphological region is an area with a distinctive landscape produced by the same rock type, geological structure (how rocks are arranged and folded) or landforming processes.
Three settings are studied here: the Burren (a karst region), Munster ridge and valley (South Munster) and the Northern European Plain.

The Burren in north-west Co. Clare is a karst region on Carboniferous limestone, a rock that water slowly dissolves. Formation of its landforms is taught in the notes on Landforms associated with particular rock types; here each landform is only named.
The name comes from the Irish Boireann, meaning rocky place.
Limestone pavement (a bare, flat expanse of rock): blocks called clints, separated by fissures (cracks) called grikes.
Turloughs: seasonal lakes in hollows, which fill in winter and drain in summer.
Caves: Aillwee Cave and Doolin Cave, which holds the Great Stalactite, about 7.3 m long.
Mullaghmore: a hill of folded, terraced limestone, an example of how the rock forms stepped slopes.
Very few surface rivers, because drainage is underground: water sinks through the cracks in the limestone.
Glaciation: granite erratics (boulders carried by ice and dropped far from their source) from Connemara rest on the limestone, showing that ice scraped off the soil and exposed the pavement.
The limestone shapes life on the Burren as well as its landforms: it affects which plants grow, how farmers use the land and why visitors come.
Plants from Arctic-alpine and Mediterranean environments grow side by side, for example the spring gentian and mountain avens.
Winterage: cattle graze the upland limestone in winter, because the rock stores heat and the ground is dry.
Poulnabrone, a Neolithic (New Stone Age) portal tomb (dolmen, a stone tomb of upright stones with a large capstone), stands on the limestone pavement.
Burren National Park protects part of the area near Mullaghmore.
The Burren and Cliffs of Moher UNESCO Global Geopark (an area recognised internationally for its geological heritage): tourism is a major activity.
South Munster is a region of Old Red Sandstone ridges alternating with Carboniferous limestone valleys. Its parallel pattern comes from folding of the rocks and then erosion.
Armorican folding (a period of crustal folding) about 300 million years ago, on an east-west trend, produced anticlines (upfolds) and synclines (downfolds).
Differential erosion (different rocks wearing away at different rates) left the harder sandstone standing as ridges and wore the softer limestone down into valleys.
Ridges (anticlines of sandstone): Macgillycuddy's Reeks, the Galtee Mountains, the Knockmealdown Mountains and the Caha Mountains.
Valleys (synclines of limestone): the Blackwater valley and the Lee valley.

Trellised drainage (a pattern of rivers following parallel valleys, with short links across them): rivers flow east along the valleys. The River Blackwater then turns sharply south at Cappoquin, Co. Waterford, and reaches the sea at Youghal. The Lee flows east to Cork Harbour.
Drowned valleys at the coast, flooded by the sea, form rias (long, narrow inlets): Bantry Bay, Dingle Bay and the Kenmare River.
Human consequences: towns, routes and fertile farmland lie in the valleys, while the ridges carry rough grazing, forestry and bog.

The Northern European Plain is a vast lowland, mostly low, flat or gently rolling, stretching from western France into Russia. Ice and wind shaped its surface, and its flat, fertile land supports many people.
Countries crossed: France (north), Belgium, the Netherlands, northern Germany, Denmark and Poland, and into Russia.
Glacial deposits (material left by ice sheets), including moraines (ridges of rock debris), outwash sands (sand washed out from melting ice) and lakes, shape the north of the plain.
A belt of loess, a wind-blown silt, forms fertile soils along the southern edge.
Loess soils are fertile, so they support crops such as wheat and sugar beet.
The Rhine and Elbe flow north to the North Sea; the Oder and Vistula flow north to the Baltic, which shows the plain slopes gently north.
Polders: land reclaimed from the sea in the Netherlands. The Afsluitdijk, completed in 1932, closed off the Zuiderzee.
Human consequences: fertile farmland, easy movement for transport because the land is flat, dense population and major cities, including Berlin, Warsaw, Hamburg and Amsterdam.
Each of the three regions is defined by a different criterion, which shows how geomorphology can be used to define regions.
The Burren is defined by its rock type, Carboniferous limestone, because that rock produces its karst landforms.
Munster ridge and valley is defined by its geological structure, folded sandstone and limestone, because the folds gave alternating ridges and valleys.
The Northern European Plain is defined by its relief and its surface deposits, glacial and loess, because it is flat and its surface is made of these materials.

The Wicklow Mountains and the Leinster batholith (a huge mass of granite) are granite uplands, also classed as geomorphological regions; their landforms are taught in the notes on Landforms associated with particular rock types.

Physical and cultural regions fade gradually into their neighbours, but governments need clear lines to know who is responsible for what. An administrative region is an area with fixed, legally defined boundaries, set up by a government to organise services, elections and decision-making.
Its boundaries are exact lines on a map, unlike the transition zones (gradual border areas where one region shades into the next) of physical and cultural regions.
Governments create administrative regions to deliver services close to people, such as housing, roads and planning (deciding where and what can be built).
They also organise elections fairly, collect statistics and channel funding, including EU regional funds (money the European Union gives to particular regions).
In other words, an administrative region is one involved in governing the functions and organisation of an area.
Administrative regions exist at several scales, from tiny local units up to a union of countries. The list below runs in order from the local scale to the supranational scale.
Townland and electoral division: the smallest units (a townland is a very small traditional land area), used for census (the national count of the population) and local purposes.
Local authority area: a county or city council, the body that runs services in that area.
Constituency: an electoral region, the area whose voters elect representatives.
Regional assembly area: a group of counties that plans at regional level, covered below.
The State: the national scale, meaning the whole of the Republic of Ireland.
The European Union: a supranational scale (above the level of individual countries) of 27 member states, since the United Kingdom left in 2020.
The county is the main traditional unit of Irish administration. Matching questions on administrative regions, set in most years, often use a named county as one of the examples.
Counties are the main traditional administrative unit (the unit used to organise local government): 26 in the Republic of Ireland and 32 on the island.
Four provinces: Leinster, Munster, Connacht and Ulster. They are historic and have no administrative function today, so they have no councils and no functions to list.
A county is not always a single administrative area. Where a county was large or heavily populated, it could be split for administration, and in one case later joined back together.
Some counties were divided for administration because of their size or population, which made one council hard to run.
In 1994 County Dublin was divided into Fingal, South Dublin and Dún Laoghaire-Rathdown county councils, alongside Dublin City Council. This is why Dublin has four councils.
North Tipperary and South Tipperary merged in 2014 to form Tipperary County Council, so the county has one council again.
Local councils are the bodies that actually run local services. Their structure was reorganised in 2014, and the old city 'corporations' were renamed.
Corporations were the old name for city governments, e.g. Dublin Corporation, which became Dublin City Council in 2002 under the Local Government Act 2001.
Local Government Reform Act 2014: 31 local authorities, made up of 26 county councils, 3 city councils (Dublin, Cork, Galway) and 2 city and county councils (Limerick, Waterford).
The same Act abolished town councils and replaced them with municipal districts (smaller local divisions within a county). There are 949 councillors (elected local representatives) in total.
Councils handle housing, roads and traffic, planning permission and development plans, libraries, the fire service, environment and waste, and parks and amenities.
Councils are funded partly by the Local Property Tax (a yearly tax on homes) and commercial rates (a tax on businesses).
Local elections, which choose the councillors, are held every five years, most recently in 2019 and 2024.
Administrative boundaries are fixed by law but not permanent. When a city's built-up area spreads past its boundary, the boundary can be moved.
Cork City's boundary was extended in 2019 to take in the growing suburbs of Ballincollig, Blarney and Glanmire, and Cork Airport.
There is more on this in the European Regions chapter, which covers growing city regions.
Between the county and the State there is a regional level, used mainly to plan regionally and to handle EU money, which is given out by region.
Three regional assemblies were set up in 2015: Northern and Western; Southern; and Eastern and Midland. They prepare regional plans and manage EU regional funds.
From 2000 to 2006 Ireland was divided into two regions for EU funding: the Border, Midland and Western (BMW) region and the Southern and Eastern region.
The BMW region held Objective 1 status, the highest level of EU aid, which was given to the regions that most needed support.
There is more on the BMW region's status as a peripheral region (one far from the centre of economic activity) in the notes on Socio-economic regions.

A Dáil constituency is an electoral region that elects TDs (members of the Dáil, the lower house of the Irish parliament) by proportional representation (PR-STV, a voting system in which seats are shared out in proportion to votes). It is an electoral region, not a council area.
The Constitution requires roughly equal representation, between one TD for every 20,000 and one for every 30,000 people. Boundaries are therefore redrawn after each census as population shifts.
The Electoral Commission, established in 2023, reviews the boundaries. Before it, constituency commissions did this work.
The 2023 review created 43 constituencies electing 174 TDs, first used in the 2024 general election.
Constituencies often cross county boundaries, because a county's population may not fit a 3-to-5-seat constituency. Sligo-Leitrim is an example.

Growing areas, such as Dublin and its commuter belt (the surrounding towns whose people travel into the city for work), gain seats; declining areas lose them. This shows administrative boundaries changing over time.
Other electoral regions: local electoral areas for council elections, and three European Parliament constituencies in Ireland: Dublin, Midlands-North-West and South.

For the international setting, the syllabus names the French département. It sits between the commune (the smallest unit of local government) and the region, and exams call it an administrative region in France.
Origin: created in 1790 during the French Revolution to replace the old provinces, weaken regional loyalties and centralise power in Paris.
Each was drawn so that every place could reach its main town (chef-lieu) within about a day's ride on horseback, which kept government reachable.
There are 101 départements: 96 in metropolitan France (the mainland and Corsica) and 5 overseas.

Each has a number, originally allocated alphabetically, which forms the first two digits of its postcodes; Paris is 75. Corsica has two départements, numbered 2A and 2B, though its postcodes begin with 20.
Many are named after natural features such as rivers and mountains, e.g. Bouches-du-Rhône (mouths of the Rhône), Haute-Garonne, Seine-Maritime and Pyrénées-Atlantiques.
Government: each has a prefect (préfet), appointed by the national government, and an elected departmental council responsible for social welfare, roads and lower secondary schools (collèges).
France has its own hierarchy of administrative scales, and the top tier was reorganised in 2016.
France has three tiers of local and regional government: about 35,000 communes, the smallest units, each with a mayor; the départements; and the regions.
In 2016 the number of metropolitan regions was cut from 22 to 13 by merging, to create larger regions able to compete in Europe.
Regions handle economic development, regional transport and upper secondary schools (lycées).
Île-de-France is the region around Paris.
Setting the two countries side by side shows how much power sits at local and regional level in each.
France has three tiers of local and regional government (communes, départements and regions), while Ireland is highly centralised, with weaker local government than France's three tiers allow.
A cultural region is an area where people share one or more cultural traits that set them apart from neighbouring areas. Language and religion are the traits the syllabus uses to define them.
Culture is the shared way of life of a group: its language, religion, customs, music, sport and sense of identity (feeling that you belong to that group).
Language and religion are the two cultural traits the syllabus uses. Both are easy to map because census data (the official count of the population, taken every few years) records them.

Cultural regions rarely match political borders (the lines between states). One state can contain several, as Belgium and Switzerland do, and one region can cross several states, as the Basque Country and the Islamic world do.
Their edges are usually transition zones, where the shared trait gradually thins out rather than stopping at a line, because people and customs mix across any boundary.
The Gaeltacht is the officially recognised area where Irish is, or was, the community language (the language people use in everyday life). It is not one continuous region.
It lies in seven counties: Donegal, Mayo, Galway, Kerry, Cork, Waterford and Meath.

Main areas: Gaoth Dobhair (Gweedore), Co. Donegal; Conamara and the Aran Islands (Oileáin Árann), Co. Galway, the largest Gaeltacht area; Corca Dhuibhne (the Dingle Peninsula), Co. Kerry; Múscraí and Oileán Chléire (Cape Clear), Co. Cork; An Rinn (Ring), Co. Waterford; Ráth Chairn and Baile Ghib, Co. Meath.
The pockets are scattered, mainly along the western seaboard (the Atlantic coast), rather than joined into one block.

Remote, mountainous areas with poor farmland and poor communications (roads and transport links) had the least contact with English-speaking trade, towns and administration, which is why Irish survived there.

The Gaeltacht therefore overlaps with the peripheral West of Ireland (the outlying, less developed area far from the main centres of population and wealth). There is more on this in the socio-economic regions subsection.
The State created a cultural region deliberately: the two Meath Gaeltachtaí (Gaeltacht areas) were formed in the 1930s by resettling Irish-speaking families from Connemara, Ráth Chairn among them.
The State backs the Irish language with laws, institutions and media, because the Gaeltacht is small and under pressure. Several trends still threaten it.
Irish is the first official language under Article 8 of the 1937 Constitution, which gives the language legal standing.
Údarás na Gaeltachta, set up in 1980, promotes employment and the language in the Gaeltacht, so that people have jobs and can stay in their communities.
Raidió na Gaeltachta (1972) and TG4 (first broadcast in 1996 as Teilifís na Gaeilge) broadcast in Irish, so people can hear and watch their language daily.
State language policy is also set out in the Official Languages Act 2003.
Irish-medium schools (where lessons are taught in Irish) and summer colleges bring learners into the Gaeltacht and sustain the language there.
Threats: out-migration of young people (leaving to find work), in-migration of English speakers and holiday homes, and English-language media and tourism, all of which bring English into daily life.

Census 2022 (whole State): about 1.9 million people said they could speak Irish, but only about 72,000 spoke it daily outside the education system. This shows a big gap between ability and everyday use.
The Gaeltacht has shrunk and been redrawn since 1850, so its boundaries have changed. There is more on this in the European Regions chapter.
Belgium is split by a language border that runs east to west across the country, creating three language areas and a bilingual capital.
Flanders, in the north: Dutch-speaking. Flemish is the Dutch spoken in Flanders.
Wallonia, in the south: French-speaking, because it lies on the Latin-speaking side of the border.
A small German-speaking community in the east, around Eupen, so Belgium has three language areas in all.
The Brussels-Capital Region is officially bilingual (French and Dutch). It lies inside Flanders but is mostly French-speaking.
The border marks the old boundary between Germanic-speaking and Latin-speaking peoples (the two language families of northern and southern Europe), and was fixed by law in 1962–63.
More than half of Belgians live in Flanders.
Because the two main language groups live in separate areas, language shapes how Belgium is governed and how its people live. It also lines up with a difference in wealth.
Belgium became a federal state in 1993, which means power is shared between a central government and regional and community governments.
It has three regions (Flanders, Wallonia, Brussels-Capital) and three language communities (Flemish, French, German-speaking), each with its own parliament.
Schools, media and political parties are divided by language, so the two main groups have separate public lives.
In 1968 the university at Leuven split: its French-speaking section moved to a new town, Louvain-la-Neuve, in Wallonia.
After the 2010 election Belgium went 541 days without a new government, because Flemish and French-speaking parties could not agree.

The language divide matches an economic divide: Flanders, with the port of Antwerp and newer industries, became the wealthier region, and many Flemish people resent money transferred to Wallonia, whose coal and steel industries in the Sambre–Meuse valley declined.
Several other European regions are defined mainly by language. Exams use them in matching questions, so know what marks each one out.
The Basque Country (Euskara): Basque is unrelated to any other European language, and the region crosses the border of Spain and France, so one cultural region lies in two states.
Catalonia, north-east Spain: Catalan is the language and Barcelona is the capital. An unofficial independence referendum (a public vote on breaking away from Spain) was held there on 1 October 2017.
Wales (Welsh) and Brittany (Breton) are Celtic-language regions, so each is defined by a Celtic language such as Welsh or Breton.
Switzerland has four national languages: German, French, Italian and Romansh, so it holds several language regions within one state.
Religion divides Ireland in two ways. In the Republic it is changing as the Catholic share falls, and in Northern Ireland it is tied to politics and to where people live.
The Republic is mainly Roman Catholic, but in Census 2022 about 69% were Roman Catholic, down from about 78% in Census 2016.
About 14% said they had no religion in Census 2022, and that share is rising.
Immigration has added other religions, such as Orthodox Christians and Muslims, because people bring their faith with them.
The Plantation of Ulster (the settling of Ulster with colonists), begun in 1609, brought Protestant settlers from Britain and created a Protestant majority in much of the north-east of Ulster.
Religion became tied to political identity: mostly Catholic nationalists (who want a united Ireland) and mostly Protestant unionists (who want to stay in the United Kingdom).
In Belfast, religion defines segregated residential areas, separated in places by peace walls (peace lines), barriers built between the neighbourhoods.
Census 2021 showed, for the first time, more Catholics than Protestants in Northern Ireland.
The partition (the division of Ireland), the Troubles and the Good Friday Agreement shaped this situation. There is more on this in the European Regions chapter.
The Islamic world is a region defined by religion that stretches from Morocco to Indonesia. To explain it, you need to know where Islam began, how far it reaches and how it spread.
Islam was founded by the Prophet Muhammad in Arabia in the 7th century. Mecca and Medina, in present-day Saudi Arabia, are its holiest cities.
The Islamic calendar begins with the Hijra, Muhammad's move from Mecca to Medina, in 622.
The Islamic world stretches from Morocco in North Africa, through the Middle East and Central Asia, to Pakistan, Bangladesh and Indonesia.
Indonesia has the largest Muslim population of any country, so Islam is not confined to the Arab world.
Muslims are almost a quarter of the world's population, so Islam is the second-largest religion after Christianity.

Arab conquest carried Islam across North Africa and into Spain, beginning in 711; trade routes carried it to South and South-East Asia; the Ottoman Turks later carried it into the Balkans (the region of south-east Europe).
A religion makes a region when shared beliefs and practices leave visible and lasting marks on the lives and landscape of the people. In the Islamic world these are the following.

A shared faith built on the Five Pillars (the five duties of a Muslim): declaration of faith; prayer five times a day, facing Mecca; giving to charity; fasting in Ramadan; and the pilgrimage to Mecca (the Hajj).
Arabic is the language of the Qur'an (the holy book of Islam), read across the region, so it unites people who speak different everyday languages.
Mosques (places of worship) and minarets (the towers beside them) mark the landscape.
Islamic law (Sharia) shapes the laws of some states, so religion affects government as well as worship.
Shared customs of dress, food and calendar, such as the Islamic calendar that begins with the Hijra, make everyday life similar across the region.
Sunni Muslims are the large majority overall. Shia Muslims are the majority in Iran and Iraq, and rivalry between the two branches of Islam adds to conflict in the Middle East.
The edges of the Islamic world are not fixed. History and migration have left Muslim communities beyond its core, and in some places Muslim rule has ended.
Ottoman rule (rule by the Ottoman Turks) left Muslim communities in Bosnia and Herzegovina, Albania and Kosovo, in the Balkans.
Spain was under Muslim (Moorish) rule until Granada fell to the Christian kingdoms in 1492.
Migration has created large Muslim communities in western Europe: North Africans in France, Turks in Germany, and Pakistanis and Bangladeshis in Britain.
Europe divides into three broad Christian regions. Each has its roots in a split within the Church, and the divisions have sometimes led to conflict.
Roman Catholic south and centre: Italy, Spain, Portugal, Poland, Ireland and southern Germany.
Protestant north, so a region shaped by the Reformation: Scandinavia, northern Germany and Britain.
Orthodox east and south-east: Greece, Russia, Romania and Serbia.
The Catholic and Orthodox churches split, which is why Europe has two eastern and western Christian traditions, with Rome and Constantinople at the centre of the two traditions.
The Protestant Reformation (the movement that broke away from the Catholic Church) began in Germany in 1517, with Martin Luther. Vatican City, in Rome, is the centre of the Catholic Church.
The break-up of Yugoslavia in the 1990s set Orthodox Serbs, Catholic Croats and Muslim Bosniaks against each other in war in Bosnia, showing how religious differences can fuel conflict.

Geographers group places into regions by how wealthy and developed they are, not just by landscape. A socio-economic region is defined by its level of wealth and development, judged by several indicators at once, because no single figure tells the whole story.

The indicators include income or GDP per head (the value of what an area produces, divided by its population), unemployment, the mix of primary, secondary and tertiary jobs, migration, age structure, education and services.

Primary jobs take materials from the land and sea (farming, fishing, forestry, mining); secondary jobs make goods in factories; tertiary jobs provide services. The mix of these three is a clue to how developed a region is.

The core–periphery idea: wealth, people and investment (money put into businesses and infrastructure) concentrate in a core, while the periphery (the outer, distant area) loses people and capital to it.
Cumulative causation means each advantage in the core attracts more, so the gap tends to widen unless governments or the EU intervene.
A core region has a strong, growing economy, high incomes, and a concentration of population, investment and decision-making. Everything else about it follows from that economic strength.
It has high GDP per head and low unemployment, because jobs are plentiful.
It has a large tertiary (services) sector, including finance, company headquarters and high-tech industry.
Most foreign investment goes to the core, because firms from abroad want its markets, workers and transport links.
Net in-migration (more people arriving than leaving) of young, educated workers gives it a young population, because they move to where the jobs are.
It has dense, well-developed infrastructure (the transport networks that move people and goods): motorways, airports, ports and rail lines.
It has universities and research institutions, which supply skilled workers, and usually the capital city with the seat of government.

Causes: accessibility, a large market and labour force, an early start, government and capital functions, and agglomeration, where firms attract more firms to the same place because they gain from being near suppliers, customers and workers.
Problems of success: congestion, high house prices, urban sprawl (the city spreading outwards over farmland) and pressure on services.
Three examples show what a core looks like at national and European scale. Each is a place where population, government and business cluster.
Greater Dublin Area: Dublin, Kildare, Meath and Wicklow. County Dublin had about 1.45 million people in Census 2022, when the State's population was about 5.1 million.

Dublin, the capital, has the seat of government, Ireland's main port (Dublin Port) and busiest airport (Dublin Airport). Its docklands host the European headquarters of many technology firms, e.g. Google. There is more on this in the Irish Regions chapter.
Paris Basin, France: Île-de-France, the region around Paris at the basin's core, has about 12 million people. There is more on this in the European Regions chapter.

The Blue Banana: the curved belt of Europe's main core, running from south-east England and London through the Benelux countries (Belgium, the Netherlands and Luxembourg) and the Rhine valley to northern Italy (Milan).

A peripheral region is distant, physically or economically, from the core, with a weaker economy and fewer opportunities. Its problems tend to feed each other, so people leave and the region falls further behind.
Remote location and poor access to markets and services, so it is costly to sell goods or reach shops, hospitals and schools.
Difficult physical conditions: mountains, high rainfall, poor soils and a short growing season, which limit what farmers can produce.
Dependence on primary activity (taking materials from land and sea): small farms, fishing and forestry.
Low incomes and higher unemployment, so people look elsewhere for work, or underemployment (people working fewer hours or in lower-skilled jobs than they want).
Net out-migration of young adults, so the people left behind are older and rural populations fall.
Fewer services, and small, scattered settlements, which means services costly to provide.
Because the periphery tends to fall further behind, governments and the EU act to slow the loss of people and jobs.
EU regional and cohesion funds (money meant to narrow the gap between richer and poorer regions) and state agencies channel investment into the periphery.
Better roads and broadband, and decentralisation of government offices (moving them out of the capital), help peripheral areas keep people and jobs.
Tourism builds on the scenery and culture of peripheral areas, so it brings jobs without needing a nearby core.
There is more on each example in the case-study chapters.
These four examples are far from their country's or Europe's core, in the west, south and far north.
West of Ireland: the Northern and Western regional assembly area. Co. Leitrim has the smallest population of any Irish county.
The Mezzogiorno, southern Italy. There is more on this in the European Regions chapter.
Northern Norway: Arctic, remote and reliant on fishing.
North-west Scotland: the Highlands and Islands.
A less-developed region is defined by how far its development falls below an average, and the EU uses a precise cut-off to decide which regions get the most help.
A less-developed region is one whose level of development is well below the national or EU average.
In EU regional policy, a less-developed region has GDP per head below 75% of the EU average, and receives the most EU aid.
Most less-developed regions in Europe are also peripheral: the Mezzogiorno, and much of eastern Europe such as Romania and Bulgaria.
Peripheral is not the same as less-developed, because a peripheral region can lie in a rich country, such as the West of Ireland or northern Norway.
Ireland was a single Objective 1 region (the category receiving the highest level of EU aid) until 1999. From 2000 to 2006 only the BMW (Border, Midland and Western) region kept Objective 1 status.
At a global scale, less-developed regions are developing countries. India is the continental example. There is more on India in its own chapter.
The Mezzogiorno's development history began with the Cassa per il Mezzogiorno (Fund for the South) in 1950.
A region of industrial decline grew on heavy, traditional industry and has since lost much of it. The loss then spreads through the local economy.
Its traditional industries include coal mining, iron and steel, shipbuilding and textiles.

Causes: coal seams exhausted or too costly to work; cheaper imports and competition from newly industrialised countries (countries that built up their factory industry more recently, often with lower costs).
Further causes: coal replaced by oil and gas; out-of-date plant (old machinery and factories); and automation (machines doing work people once did), which needs fewer workers.
Effects: high unemployment, especially among older male workers; derelict factories, mines and spoil heaps (waste rock dumped from mining); and polluted land.
Further effects: out-migration, falling services, and a poor image that deters new investment.

Responses: retraining; clearing and cleaning derelict land; attracting new light industry and services; universities and technology parks; reuse of industrial heritage for tourism and culture; EU funds.
Most examples are old coal and steel regions of north-west Europe. The Irish examples are port and shipbuilding areas.
Sambre–Meuse valley, Wallonia, Belgium: coal mining and steel along the Sambre and Meuse, e.g. Charleroi on the Sambre and Liège on the Meuse.
Ruhr, Germany (North Rhine-Westphalia): Europe's largest coal and steel region, so its decline was large, with cities such as Essen, Dortmund and Duisburg.

Prosper-Haniel in Bottrop, the last hard-coal mine in Germany, closed in 2018. The Zollverein coal mine complex in Essen became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2001 and is now a cultural centre, an example of reusing industrial heritage.
South Wales coalfield, including the Rhondda valleys: coal mining collapsed in the late 20th century.
Nord–Pas-de-Calais, France, is a further European example.
Belfast, for example: the Harland and Wolff shipyard, which built the Titanic (launched 1911), declined greatly in the late 20th century.

Dublin docklands: port jobs fell with containerisation (goods shipped in standard metal containers, which need far fewer dock workers). The International Financial Services Centre (IFSC), established in 1987 on derelict dockland, regenerated the area.
There is more on Irish economic evidence in the Primary, Secondary and Tertiary Economic Activities chapter.
The clearest difference between the two region types is the kind of work people do. Compare them sector by sector: primary, secondary and tertiary.
Primary, for example: large, commercial, efficient farms on good land in the core; small, fragmented farms on poor land in the periphery, with more fishing and forestry.

Secondary: concentrations of manufacturing and multinational investment (factories owned by firms based in other countries) in the core; few, small and often grant-aided (helped by state money) factories in the periphery.
Tertiary: finance, headquarters, government, universities, and major ports and airports in the core; tourism and public services in the periphery.

A nodal region is a city together with the surrounding area linked to it by flows of people, goods, services and information. Unlike the other regions in this chapter, it is defined by connections, not by uniform features.
A node is a central point where routes meet by road, rail, sea or air, usually a town or city. Think of it as the hub that the surrounding area is connected to.
A nodal region is also called a functional, city or urban region. It is functional because it is defined by what the links to the centre do, not by everything in it being the same.
A hinterland is the area around a town or city that it serves and depends on for jobs, shopping, services and markets. It is also called its sphere of influence or urban field.
The urban area is the continuously built-up part of the city, with houses and streets running on without a break. The hinterland extends far beyond it, into countryside and smaller towns.
The commuter belt is the part of the hinterland from which people travel daily to work in the city (commuting means making that regular journey).
A city and its hinterland depend on each other. Four kinds of flow tie them together: jobs, services, goods and information.
Jobs: commuters travel in from the hinterland every day, because the city has the workplaces and the hinterland has many of the workers.

Services: the city provides shops, hospitals, third-level colleges (universities and similar colleges), entertainment and offices that smaller places cannot support, and people from the hinterland travel in to use them.
Goods: the hinterland supplies food, water, raw materials and labour (workers); the city supplies manufactured goods and services in return.
A port's hinterland is the area whose trade passes through it, so goods from that area are exported, and goods for it imported, through that port.
Information: local newspapers, radio and TV stations based in the city serve the hinterland around it.
A hinterland has no marked border, so geographers work out where it ends by tracing where a city's services and links reach. Each method below gives a picture of the area.
Commuting data from the census (the official count of the population, which records where people travel to work) show how far workers come from.
The catchment area of a hospital, college or secondary school is the area from which it draws its patients or students.
The circulation area of a local newspaper (where it is sold) or the reach of a local radio station (where it can be heard) shows where the city's information flows.
Bus and rail routes and timetables show which places are linked to the city and how often.
The delivery areas of businesses, and the home addresses of shoppers or of members of a sports club, show who uses the city's shops and clubs and where they live.
The edge of a hinterland is not a sharp line: neighbouring hinterlands overlap, and different services give different boundaries, since a hospital and a newspaper do not reach the same distance.
Larger cities have larger hinterlands. A capital city's hinterland for some services is the whole country.
Hinterlands are not fixed. Changes in transport, work and shopping can stretch them or squeeze them.
Motorways, car ownership, faster rail and remote working (working from home, so fewer daily trips) extend commuter belts outwards, because people can live further from the city and still reach it.
New shopping centres or services in smaller towns can shrink a city's hinterland, because people no longer need to travel to the city to use them.

A primate city is the largest city in a country, far larger than any other. Dublin is Ireland's primate city and capital: County Dublin has about 1.45 million people out of a State total of about 5.1 million (Census 2022).

It is the focus of the national motorway network: radial routes (roads spreading out from the centre like spokes) meet at the M50 ring road, which circles the city. The main rail lines also meet there.
Dublin Port and Dublin Airport, Ireland's busiest airport, make the city the main national gateway (entry and exit point) for trade and travel.

The commuter belt extends into Meath, Kildare, Wicklow and Louth, with fast-growing commuter towns (towns where many residents work in the city): Navan (Co. Meath), Naas and Newbridge (Co. Kildare), Bray (Co. Wicklow) and Drogheda (Co. Louth).
For government, national media, specialist hospitals and the main airport, Dublin's hinterland is the whole country, because these functions exist in Dublin and nowhere else on the same scale.
Problems of its urban region: urban sprawl (the built-up area spreading outwards into the countryside), long commutes and congestion, and high house prices.
There is more on the growth of city regions and Dublin's council structures in the European Regions chapter, and on land use and planning in the Urban Geography chapter.
Outside Dublin, Ireland's other cities act as smaller nodes, each serving its own hinterland.
Cork: Ireland's second city, at the head of Cork Harbour on the River Lee.
Cork Harbour has a port and a pharmaceutical industry (making medicines), with plants at Ringaskiddy. Cork's hinterland covers much of Munster, with commuter towns Carrigaline, Midleton and Cobh.
Galway: the main city of the West, serving a large rural hinterland that includes Connemara.
Galway is a centre of the medical devices industry (making equipment used in healthcare) and of higher education (study after secondary school), home to the University of Galway.
Limerick and Waterford are regional cities serving the Mid-West and the South-East.
Dublin is so much larger than every other Irish city that national planning tries to even things out.

The National Planning Framework, part of Project Ireland 2040 and published in 2018, aims to direct more growth to Cork, Limerick, Galway and Waterford to counterbalance Dublin (to offset its dominance by building up the other cities).
Cities across Europe are nodes with hinterlands of different sizes. Some reach across a whole country, and one crosses national borders.
Paris is the primate city of France, at the centre of the Paris Basin. Radial motorways and TGV (high-speed train) lines meet there, so its hinterland reaches across France.
The first TGV line, Paris to Lyon, opened in 1981. Charles de Gaulle Airport serves the city, and its region, Ile-de-France, has about 12 million people.

London is the capital of the United Kingdom and a global financial centre, through the City of London. Greater London has about 9 million people (Census 2021), and its commuter belt covers much of south-east England.
Brussels is the capital of Belgium and seat of the European Commission and the Council of the EU, so its influence extends across the EU. NATO headquarters is also there.
The European Parliament meets both in Brussels and in Strasbourg, its official seat, so not all EU institutions are in Brussels.
Rotterdam is Europe's largest port, at the mouth of the Rhine (Europoort). Its hinterland is the whole Rhine basin, linked by river barges, rail and pipelines, so it crosses national borders.
Milan is the main city of Lombardy, the core of northern Italy, and Italy's financial centre, home to the Borsa Italiana stock exchange (where company shares are traded).
Other urban regions named in exam matching include Munich (capital of Bavaria), Berlin (capital of Germany) and Rome (capital of Italy).
Most city regions have one dominant centre, but the Netherlands has a region built around several cities of similar importance.
The Randstad in the Netherlands is a ring of cities (Amsterdam, Rotterdam, The Hague and Utrecht) forming one large urban region around a rural area called the Green Heart (Groene Hart).
It is polycentric, meaning it has many centres, in contrast to the single-centre city regions of Paris and Dublin.

The Greater Dublin Area (GDA) is the core region of Ireland's east coast, facing Britain and Europe across the Irish Sea. Knowing exactly which counties it includes is the starting point for every question on it.
The GDA is Dublin City and County Dublin, plus Counties Meath, Kildare and Wicklow. Louth, including Drogheda, is not part of it, so do not count it.

Dublin City, Fingal, South Dublin and Dún Laoghaire–Rathdown are the four local authorities (the councils that run local services) of Dublin; the single Co. Dublin county council was split into the last three in 1994.
A core region is one that concentrates people, wealth and services, in contrast to peripheral regions (remote areas with fewer of these). The GDA fits this description in several ways.
Its large, dense and growing population is the largest in the State, which gives firms customers and workers.
It holds most of the State's wealth, jobs, multinational investment, government and services, which means firms and workers want to be there.
It has the best infrastructure in the State, including the main port, airport and motorway network, so goods and people move easily.
It attracts in-migrants (people moving in) from the rest of Ireland and from abroad.
Cumulative causation (growth that feeds more growth): growth attracts firms and workers, which attracts further investment and widens the gap with peripheral regions such as the West.
A sketch map of the region is set as a question, and it is marked on a handful of simple features. Draw these, each clearly labelled.
Outline the four counties: Dublin and Wicklow on the coast, Meath to the north (with a short coastline south of the Boyne estuary), Kildare to the west.
Draw the River Liffey from the Wicklow Mountains, through Kildare, to Dublin Bay.
Draw the River Boyne through Trim and Navan, reaching the sea at Drogheda, just outside the GDA.
Mark Dublin city, and the towns of Navan, Naas and Bray.
Show relief (the height and shape of the land): the Wicklow Mountains in the south and the lowland plain of Meath and Kildare, so the map shows both upland and lowland.

The GDA has a cool temperate oceanic climate (mild and wet because of the nearby ocean), with prevailing south-westerly winds bringing moist Atlantic air. Because of where the mountains sit, the east is drier than the west.

Rain shadow (the dry area on the sheltered side of high ground): the Wicklow Mountains and the uplands further west force moist air to drop its rain on the western slopes, so the east is the driest part of Ireland.
Rainfall in the east is about 750–1,000 mm a year, so it is much drier than the west; Dublin Airport records about 750 mm.
By contrast, the west receives 1,000–1,250 mm a year and some mountains exceed 2,000 mm.
The south-east is the sunniest part of Ireland, which adds to the east's value for crops.
Mean January temperatures in Ireland are about 4–7 °C and mean July temperatures about 14–16 °C, so winters are mild and summers cool.
Being farther from the Atlantic than the west gives a slightly greater temperature range: warmer summers, colder winters and more frost.
Heavier rain and snow fall on the Wicklow uplands than on the lowlands, because rising air cools and drops its moisture.
Climate decides what the land can be used for. The dry east and the wet uplands are used in different ways.
Effect on farming: the dry, relatively sunny lowlands suit tillage (growing crops such as cereals and vegetables) and horticulture (growing vegetables, fruit and flowers).
Effect on land use: heavy upland rain supports conifer forestry and reservoirs, because the rain feeds fast-growing trees and fills water stores.
Relief means the height and shape of the land. The GDA has a wide lowland to the north and west and a mountain block to the south, and each is used differently.
A low-lying, gently undulating lowland covers most of Meath, Kildare and north Co. Dublin, part of the Central Lowlands.
The Central Lowlands are underlain by Carboniferous limestone (a sedimentary rock), covered by glacial deposits.

The Wicklow and Dublin Mountains lie to the south, with a core of the Leinster granite batholith (a huge mass of granite that cooled underground), about 400 million years old (Caledonian, the mountain-building episode that made it).
Lugnaquilla, 925 m, in Co. Wicklow, is the highest peak in Leinster, so it is a good example of the region's upland relief.
Kippure, about 757 m, stands on the Dublin–Wicklow border, so the mountains are close enough to the city to be used for recreation.
The Great Sugar Loaf, Co. Wicklow, is a quartzite peak (quartzite is a very hard rock) that stands out from the granite.
Effect: the lowland is easy to farm, build on and cross with roads and rail; the uplands suit forestry, water supply and recreation.
Ice sheets and the sea have both shaped the region. These named landforms are the examples to use.
The U-shaped valleys (steep-sided, flat-floored valleys) of Glendalough and Glenmalure were carved by glacial erosion, which is why their sides are steep and their floors flat.
Esker Riada is a long ridge of sand and gravel deposited by glacial meltwater, which is why it is made of loose, rounded material.
Howth Head is joined to the mainland by the Sutton tombolo (a bar of sand or shingle linking an island or headland to the land).
North Bull Island lies in Dublin Bay, so it is an example of a coastal feature there.
Soil follows the rock and drainage beneath it. The lowlands have deep, fertile soils, while the granite uplands and bogs have poor ones, so soil sets how land is used.

Deep, fertile brown earths (a well-developed soil rich in nutrients) on limestone boulder clay (stony clay left by ice sheets) cover Meath, Kildare and north Co. Dublin, among the best farmland in Ireland.
Brown earths are well drained, which suits both tillage and grassland.
The Curragh, Co. Kildare, has free-draining sand and gravel from glacial outwash (material washed out from the ice by meltwater), with well-drained grassland used for horse training.
The Bog of Allen, Co. Kildare, is a raised bog (a dome of peat built up from dead plants) of deep peat, which is unsuitable for farming unless drained.
Blanket bog (peat covering the ground like a blanket) on granite at the Sally Gap, Co. Wicklow, is waterlogged and acidic, so it is of little use for farming.
Acidic, leached podzols (grey soils with nutrients washed out of the top layer) cover the granite uplands of Wicklow, poor for farming but suitable for conifers.
Effect on land use: fertile lowland soils support farming; thin, acidic upland soils and bog are used for forestry, recreation and water catchment (land that collects rain for a river or reservoir).
Drainage covers the rivers, canals and reservoirs of the region. In the GDA they matter because a large city needs a reliable water supply.
The River Liffey rises in the Wicklow Mountains, flows through Kildare and enters the sea at Dublin Bay, so it links upland to city.
The Poulaphouca dam on the Liffey created the Blessington Lakes reservoir, used for hydro-electricity and for Dublin's drinking water.
The Vartry Reservoir at Roundwood, Co. Wicklow, supplies Dublin with water, so the uplands serve the city.
The River Boyne flows through Trim and Navan, Co. Meath, and reaches the sea near Drogheda, outside the GDA, so its mouth is not in the region.
The smaller Dublin rivers, the Dodder and the Tolka, flow through the city to Dublin Bay, so they drain urban areas.
The Royal and Grand Canals link Dublin to the River Shannon, so they connect the east coast to the interior.
Uisce Éireann (Irish Water) has proposed a pipeline to bring water from the River Shannon to the Dublin region, because demand on local supplies is growing.
Paved surfaces in the city let rain run off quickly into rivers, raising urban flood risk.
Farming does well in the GDA because physical and human advantages come together. Each factor below can be developed as a separate point in an answer.
Climate: the dry, relatively sunny east suits tillage (growing crops) and horticulture (growing vegetables and similar crops).
Relief: flat lowland allows large fields and mechanised farming, which cuts the cost of each crop.
Soils: deep, fertile brown earths in Meath and Kildare give high-quality land for crops and grass.
Market: Dublin, the largest urban area in the State, lies on the farms' doorstep, so produce has a short journey to many buyers.
Transport: Dublin Port and Dublin Airport export farm produce and livestock, so farmers can sell abroad.
Policy and technology: EU and Irish agricultural policy and modern machinery support large, productive farms.
Farming here is large-scale and commercial, but each county specialises in something different, shaped by its soil, relief and nearness to Dublin.
Large, commercial and highly productive farms dominate the lowlands, because the flat, fertile land suits them.
Meath, for example: beef cattle fattening (raising cattle to slaughter weight) and tillage on large farms.
Kildare: bloodstock (breeding of racehorses) and racehorse training, centred on the Curragh racecourse and the Irish National Stud at Tully, Kildare town.
Fingal, for example: horticulture, with field vegetables and glasshouse crops centred on Rush and Lusk.
Wicklow: sheep grazing on the upland pasture of the Wicklow Mountains, because the steep, poor land suits sheep better than crops.
The pressure of a huge city next door is the main problem for farmers in the GDA, along with market and policy pressures.
Urban sprawl (spread of housing and industry outward from the city) takes farmland for housing and industry.
High land prices, especially near Dublin, push farmers to sell land to developers.
Part-time farming is common near the city, where farm owners depend on jobs off the farm, because farm income alone is not enough.
Horticulture needs seasonal labour, which is costly and sometimes in short supply.
Growers face competition from imported vegetables, which can undercut their prices.
Changes to the rules of the EU Common Agricultural Policy (CAP, the EU's farm support scheme) alter farm incomes and force farmers to adapt.
Forestry uses the land that is too poor to farm. In the GDA that means the Wicklow uplands, though forests cover only a small share of Ireland.
Wicklow is among Ireland's most forested counties and is known as the Garden of Ireland, because so much of its upland is wooded.
Conifer plantations, mainly Sitka spruce (native to western North America), grow on poor upland soils unsuited to farming.
Coillte, the State forestry company set up in 1988, has its head office at Newtownmountkennedy, Co. Wicklow.
Wicklow Mountains National Park, set up in 1991, protects the upland landscape and provides recreation, so it serves both conservation and visitors.
Forest recreation areas near Dublin are used by city residents for walking and cycling, because they are close to the city.
Ireland's forest cover is about 11% (2020s), one of the lowest in the EU, so forestry covers a small share of the land.
Fishing is only a small part of the region's economy. The main facts are Howth, the quota rules and the shrinking fleet.
Fishing is a small part of the region's economy, so the region depends little on it.
Howth, Co. Dublin, is one of Ireland's six State-owned Fishery Harbour Centres (harbours run by the State for the fishing industry).
The other five are Killybegs, Castletownbere, Dingle, Rossaveel and Dunmore East; none is in the GDA.
Dublin Bay prawns and whitefish, for example, are landed at Howth.
EU Common Fisheries Policy quotas (limits on the amount of each fish species that may be caught) limit how much Irish boats can catch.
The 2020 EU–UK Brexit trade agreement reduced Irish fishing quotas.
The fishing fleet has been falling in size, which is partly a result of the quota limits.
The region's rocks and glacial deposits supply minerals and building materials. Tara Mines at Navan is the largest operation.
Tara Mines at Navan, Co. Meath, is an underground zinc and lead mine, opened in 1977 (paused from July 2023, restarted at the end of 2024).
Tara Mines is Europe's largest zinc mine, and is owned by Boliden.
Sand and gravel are quarried from glacial deposits for construction, because the ice sheets left large amounts of them.
Granite is quarried at Ballyknockan, Co. Wicklow.
Bord na Móna has ended peat harvesting in the Bog of Allen, Co. Kildare, where peat was once cut for fuel.
A big population and many businesses make the GDA Ireland's largest energy market. Its power comes from several sources.
The GDA is Ireland's largest energy market, because it has the most people and businesses.
Poolbeg, Ringsend, has gas-fired power generation on Dublin Bay.
The Dublin Waste-to-Energy incinerator, operating since 2017, generates electricity by burning waste.
Turlough Hill, Co. Wicklow, is an ESB pumped-storage station built in 1974: water is pumped uphill at night and released to generate power at peak demand.
Arklow Bank Wind Park off Co. Wicklow is Ireland's first offshore wind farm, so it uses wind over the sea rather than land.
Data centres (buildings full of computer servers) used about a fifth of Ireland's metered electricity in 2023 (CSO), most of them in the Dublin region.
The East–West Interconnector carries electricity by cable to Wales from near Rush, Co. Dublin.
The GDA is where most Irish manufacturing is found, but the location of factories within it has shifted outward over time.
The GDA is Ireland's largest manufacturing region, which is why its factory locations matter for exams.
Older industries near Dublin Port and in the inner city, such as brewing, food and port-related industry, declined as older plants closed.
Newer high-tech and pharmaceutical plants are in suburban business parks and towns near the M50 (the orbital motorway around Dublin) and motorways.
Examples of these locations are Grange Castle near Clondalkin, Leixlip and Blanchardstown.
Production has moved from the inner city to edge-of-city sites because they offer space and road access.
Three firms show the pattern: two modern plants on the edge of the city and one old brewery still working in the inner city.
Intel at Leixlip, Co. Kildare, opened in 1989 and is Ireland's largest private-sector investment, worth billions of euro.
Intel's high-tech plant lies near the M4, which links it to Dublin Airport and Dublin Port, so products can be exported quickly.
Pfizer's biopharmaceutical (medicine-making) plant is at Grange Castle Business Park, Clondalkin.
Guinness's St James's Gate Brewery was founded in 1759 on a 9,000-year lease.
Guinness at St James's Gate shows, for example, that an older inner-city industry can survive beside newer high-tech plants.
A market is a group of customers. The GDA has a large one on its doorstep and easy routes to larger ones abroad.
The GDA has about 2.1 million people, the largest concentration of consumers in the State.
Dublin Port and Dublin Airport give access to the EU single market (the EU area where goods move without trade barriers).
Ferries from Dublin Port to Holyhead, Wales, give access to the British market, which is the nearest large foreign market.
Dublin Airport allows high-value products to be shipped quickly by air to customers across Europe and beyond.
Together, the port and airport link the region to foreign markets for exports.
Modern plants need skilled workers. The GDA has the largest and best-educated pool of labour in the State.
The GDA has a large, young, educated workforce, so firms can fill technical jobs.
Trinity College Dublin, University College Dublin, Dublin City University, Technological University Dublin and Maynooth University (Co. Kildare) produce graduates for technical and research jobs.
Immigrant workers add skills and languages to the workforce, which helps firms that sell abroad.
Commuters from Meath, Kildare and Wicklow widen the pool of workers, so firms can recruit from beyond the city.
A concentration of skilled workers attracts firms that need specialist staff, so labour reinforces the other factors.
Infrastructure means the transport, power and communications systems that firms depend on. The GDA's is the best in the State.
Dublin Port and Dublin Airport provide the sea and air freight links that move components in and products out.
Motorways radiate from the M50 orbital motorway to the port, the airport and industrial sites, so lorries can reach them quickly.
Reliable, high-capacity electricity and broadband supply suit data-intensive plants.
Rail and bus links bring commuters to business parks and industrial estates, so workers can reach jobs without a car.
Government and EU decisions have made Ireland attractive to foreign multinational companies, which choose where to build plants partly on taxes and grants.
IDA Ireland, the State agency that attracts foreign investment, promotes the GDA to foreign multinationals and offers sites and grants.
Corporation tax (the tax firms pay on their profits) is 12.5% for most firms.
From 2024, corporation tax rises to 15% for very large multinational groups (turnover over €750 million), under the OECD agreement.
Ireland joined the EEC (the forerunner of the EU) in 1973, giving firms access to European markets.
Raw materials are the inputs a factory processes. The GDA has few of its own, so its industries are of two kinds.
The GDA has few local raw materials for manufacturing.
High-tech industries import components and ship light, high-value products by air, so distance from raw materials matters little to them.
Food and drink firms process farm produce from the region's hinterland (the surrounding farming area), including the farms of Meath and Kildare.
Agglomeration means firms clustering together in one place. Once a cluster starts, it tends to keep growing.
Firms cluster together because they can share suppliers, services, skilled workers and transport links.
Once a cluster forms, it attracts further investment and suppliers, which reinforces growth.
Large, concentrated production lowers the cost of each unit produced.
The same size and success that attract industry also create costs and risks for firms in the GDA.
High costs of land, housing and wages make the GDA expensive for firms.
Traffic congestion delays deliveries and the movement of workers, which raises costs.
A shortage of housing for workers makes recruitment harder.
Manufacturing faces competition from lower-cost countries, because the GDA's wages and land are expensive.
Dependence on multinational firms, which can relocate or cut jobs, leaves the economy exposed.
Global corporation tax changes reduce Ireland's tax advantage, so firms have less reason to choose the GDA.
Strain on electricity and water supply from data centres and growing demand.
Tourism is a tertiary (service) activity. Dublin is Ireland's main gateway for visitors and has many attractions in the city itself.
Dublin Airport and Dublin Port are Ireland's main gateway for visitors, so most tourists arrive through them.
The Guinness Storehouse, opened in 2000, is Ireland's most visited fee-paying attraction.
The Book of Kells is displayed at Trinity College Dublin.
Croke Park, the headquarters of the GAA (Gaelic Athletic Association), draws visitors to matches and tours, for example.
The Convention Centre Dublin, opened in 2010, supports conference and business tourism (visitors who come for meetings and events).
Good accommodation and transport links support visitors, because tourists need somewhere to stay and ways to get around.
Beyond the city, ancient and early Christian sites in Meath and Wicklow draw visitors, and a regional brand promotes them together.
Brú na Bóinne, Co. Meath (Newgrange, Knowth and Dowth), has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site (a place protected as important to all humanity) since 1993.
Newgrange is a passage tomb (a burial chamber reached by a stone passage) about 5,000 years old (about 3200 BC).
Glendalough, a monastic site founded by St Kevin in the 6th century, lies in the Wicklow Mountains National Park.
Powerscourt, Enniskerry, Co. Wicklow, is a historic estate.
Ireland's Ancient East, a Fáilte Ireland brand launched in 2015, promotes the region's heritage.
Success brings pressure. Tourism in the GDA faces problems of capacity and competition.
Shortages of hotel rooms keep prices high, because demand is greater than supply.
Overcrowding at the most popular sites, such as the Book of Kells, spoils the visitor experience, because crowds make visits slow and uncomfortable.
Traffic congestion in the city centre makes getting between attractions difficult.
The region competes with other European city-break destinations.
Transport is both a service industry and an advantage for the region. Dublin's port and airport are the busiest in the State and connect it to Britain and beyond.
Dublin Port is Ireland's busiest port, so it is the State's main sea gateway.
Ferries from Dublin Port run to Holyhead, Wales.
Dublin Airport is Ireland's busiest airport, handling over 30 million passengers in 2023.
A north runway opened at Dublin Airport in 2022, adding capacity.
Within the region, roads and rail link the city to its commuter counties. Most routes radiate from Dublin like the spokes of a wheel.
Radial motorways (M1, M3, M4, M7 and M11) run out from the city and are joined by the M50 orbital motorway.
The Dublin Port Tunnel, opened in 2006, takes freight traffic from the port directly onto the motorway network, which keeps lorries off city streets.
DART, the electrified coastal commuter rail line, opened in 1984, so commuters can travel along Dublin Bay without a car.
The Luas tram network, opened in 2004, has Red and Green lines.
Dublin Bus and BusConnects, a redesign of the bus network, provide city and suburban bus services.
MetroLink is a planned rail line from the city centre to Dublin Airport and Swords.
Heavy use of transport brings problems, and the authorities have responded with new public transport and a long-term plan.
Traffic congestion on radial roads and the M50 slows journeys, because so many commuters use the same routes.
Long commutes from Meath, Kildare and Wicklow into the city add to congestion.
Low-density sprawl makes households car-dependent, because homes are too spread out for frequent public transport.
Responses include investment in public transport, such as DART, Luas and planned MetroLink.
Cycle lanes encourage travel by bicycle, so fewer people need to drive.
The National Transport Authority (NTA) sets out the Greater Dublin Area Transport Strategy 2022–2042.
Besides tourism and transport, the GDA holds the State's main financial, technology and public services, concentrated in the capital.
The International Financial Services Centre (IFSC), a district for banking and finance firms, in Custom House Docks, was set up in 1987.
Google's European headquarters, on Barrow Street in Grand Canal Dock, is part of 'Silicon Docks'.
