The Dublin Docklands Development Authority, set up in 1997, regenerated the docklands for offices and tech firms.
Government, health and education services are concentrated in the capital, because Dublin is the seat of national government.
Census 2022 shows how large the GDA's population is and how it is shared between the counties. The State total was about 5.1 million.
Census 2022 counted about 2.1 million people in the GDA, about 40% of the State's population of about 5.1 million.
Co. Dublin had about 1.45 million people; Kildare about 250,000; Meath about 220,000; Wicklow about 156,000.
Dublin city and suburbs had about 1.26 million people; the Dublin City Council area about 590,000.
Co. Dublin has a density of about 1,600 people per km², against a State average of about 73.
Population is not spread evenly across the region. Each high-density or low-density area has its own reason, and exam questions ask for those reasons.
The highest densities are in Dublin city and suburbs, then in commuter towns along motorways and rail lines.
The lowest densities are on the Wicklow uplands, because steep relief and poor soils limit settlement and farming.
Jobs concentrated in Dublin draw population to the city and its commuter belt.
Lowland relief and fertile soils in Meath and Kildare make settlement and building easier than on the uplands.
Transport routes along motorways and rail lines make commuter towns accessible to Dublin jobs.
Population dynamics means how a population changes over time. The GDA is growing steadily, and the growth has a pattern.
Growth comes mainly from natural increase (births minus deaths): the population is young, with more births than deaths.
In-migration comes from the rest of Ireland and from abroad, because people move for jobs.
The age structure is young and has low dependency (few children and old people compared with working adults) compared with the West.
The population is increasingly multicultural, because immigrants have settled in the region.
Growth is spreading outward into the commuter counties of Meath, Kildare and Wicklow, because people move out to find cheaper housing.
Dublin's growth began over a thousand years ago and was shaped by successive rulers. Georgian Dublin added the planned streets that still define the centre.
Dublin was founded as a Viking settlement in 841, which makes it a very old city.
Norman rule expanded the town in medieval times.
The Wide Streets Commissioners, set up in 1757, widened and laid out Georgian streets; squares such as Merrion Square were developed by private estates.
Georgian Dublin grew into a planned capital with wide streets and squares.
A question on how one urban area developed asks for factors. For Dublin, these are site, route focus, port, capital-city functions, industry and planning.
Site: Dublin grew at the lowest bridging point of the Liffey (the lowest place the river could be crossed by a bridge), sheltered by Dublin Bay.
Route focus: roads and routeways radiate from the city, linking it to the rest of the region, so people and goods pass through it.
Port: the harbour on the Liffey gave the settlement a trading role, so the city grew by trade.
Capital-city functions: national government, administration and services concentrate in the city, which creates jobs.
Industry: brewing and food processing grew near the port, because ships brought in materials and carried out products.
Planning: the Wide Streets Commissioners, the Wright Report and the Docklands Development Authority shaped the city's growth.
In the 20th century the city spread outward, while its inner areas were rebuilt. Planning and regeneration (renewing run-down areas) drove both changes.
Suburban expansion spread the city outward during the 20th century, because more people needed housing.
The Wright Report, 1967, proposed new towns at Tallaght, Clondalkin and Lucan.
Ballymun high-rise flats, built in the 1960s, were demolished during regeneration from the 2000s.
Temple Bar was regenerated in the 1990s as a cultural quarter, so a run-down inner-city area gained new uses.
The Docklands and IFSC renewed the inner city, drawing offices and tech firms.
Commuter towns have expanded: Navan and Ashbourne (Meath); Naas, Newbridge and Maynooth (Kildare); Bray and Greystones (Wicklow).
Rapid growth has left Dublin with problems that affect both the city and the commuter towns around it.
Urban sprawl spreads low-density housing into farmland and commuter towns.
A housing shortage pushes up rents and house prices, because demand is greater than supply.
Homelessness is a serious problem in the city.
Commuting traffic causes congestion on the city's roads, because so many workers travel in at the same time.
Growing demand puts pressure on the water supply.
In the West, rural areas are losing people. In the counties around Dublin the opposite is true: the countryside is under pressure from the city.
Rural areas of Meath, Kildare and Wicklow are under urban pressure, not decline.
Commuter villages grow as city workers move out to live in the countryside, for example in Meath and Kildare.
One-off houses (single houses built in the countryside) and urban-generated housing (housing built for people who work in the city) are built in rural areas.
Rising land prices lead to the loss of farmland to housing.
Growing populations need new schools and services in rural towns and villages, so rural areas are building rather than closing.
Contrast: the West faces rural decline and depopulation.
English is the everyday language of the GDA, but Irish and many other languages are also spoken there.
English is the dominant language of the GDA, so most daily life is in English.
Nationally, about 1.9 million people (about 40%) said they could speak Irish in Census 2022; about 72,000 spoke it daily outside the education system.
Gaelscoileanna (Irish-medium schools) are growing in number in the region, so more children are learning through Irish.
Ráth Chairn, Co. Meath, is a Gaeltacht (an area where Irish is the community language) founded in 1935 by families resettled from Connemara by the Land Commission.
Immigration has made the region multilingual; Polish is the most common foreign language spoken at home in Ireland (Census 2022).
The GDA is mostly Roman Catholic, as is Ireland as a whole, but Dublin is less Catholic than the national figure.
Nationally, about 69% of people are Roman Catholic and about 14% have no religion (Census 2022).
Dublin has a lower Catholic share and a higher no-religion share than the national figure, so it is more secular than the State as a whole.
The Church of Ireland has a historic presence, shown by Christ Church and St Patrick's cathedrals in Dublin.
Immigration has added Muslim, Orthodox and other communities; the Islamic Cultural Centre of Ireland is in Clonskeagh.
Secularisation (the decline in the role of religion in society) has weakened the role of organised religion in the city.

This case study uses the West Region, made up of Counties Galway (including Galway city), Mayo and Roscommon. It is a peripheral region, meaning it lies far from the country's economic core around Dublin and from European markets.
Galway and Mayo lie on the Atlantic coast, so they face the ocean that shapes the region's weather, while Roscommon is inland.
Galway city is the region's only city, so it dominates the region's services and jobs, and Castlebar is the largest town in Mayo.
The three counties together form the State's West regional unit for statistics, so this is the standard definition of the region to use throughout.

A region is peripheral when several disadvantages add up and keep it behind the core. In the West they reinforce each other: distance and a harsh physical environment lead to a weak economy, and that drives people away.
Remote location: long distances to Dublin and to European markets raise transport costs for goods.
Difficult physical conditions: high rainfall, poor soils and rugged relief (the shape and height of the land) limit farming and building.
The population is small, scattered and ageing, after a long history of out-migration (people leaving the region) since the Great Famine of the late 1840s.
The economy depends on primary activities (farming, forestry, fishing) and the public sector, with lower incomes than the core.

Infrastructure (roads, rail, broadband) is weaker than in the core, with Galway city as the main exception, because it is a growth centre (a place planned and chosen to attract investment and population).
A sketch map of the region is set as a question. Build it in layers: the outline first, then water, then towns, then relief (upland and lowland).
Outline Galway, Mayo and Roscommon, with the Atlantic coast along the western edge of Galway and Mayo.
Draw the River Corrib flowing from Lough Corrib through Galway city to Galway Bay.
Draw the River Moy reaching Killala Bay at Ballina, and the River Shannon along Roscommon's eastern edge.
Mark the urban centres, such as Galway city, Castlebar, Westport and Ballina.
Mark one upland: the Twelve Bens in Connemara, or Mweelrea in west Mayo.
Shade the limestone lowland (low, flat to rolling land on limestone rock) of east Galway and Roscommon.
Mark the Aran Islands offshore from Galway, for example as a small group of islands in the Atlantic.
The West faces the Atlantic Ocean, which controls its weather. Moist, mild air arrives from the south-west and meets the western mountains, so the region is wet, windy, mild and cloudy.
The climate is cool temperate oceanic (mild and wet all year, with no extremes), strongly influenced by the Atlantic Ocean.
Prevailing south-westerly winds (the winds that blow most often) bring frequent depressions (low-pressure weather systems that bring rain and wind) and gales from the Atlantic.
Relief rainfall: moist Atlantic air is forced up over the western mountains, where it cools and drops its rain.
Annual rainfall is about 1,000 to 1,250 mm on lowlands and over 2,000 mm on some mountains, against about 750 to 1,000 mm in the east.
Winters are mild: mean January temperatures are about 4 to 7 °C, warmed by the North Atlantic Drift (a warm ocean current), so frost and snow are rare at the coast.
Summers are cool: mean July temperatures are about 14 to 16 °C, so the annual temperature range (the gap between winter and summer) is small.
The west is cloudier and less sunny than the east, because the moist Atlantic air arrives there first.
The wet, windy climate shapes what the land can be used for. It suits grass but works against almost everything else.
Grass grows well, but waterlogged land and wet weather make tillage (growing crops) difficult and hay hard to save, because it needs dry spells to dry.
Exposure to Atlantic gales limits the land that can be farmed and the crops that can be grown.
Gales and storms damage forests and power lines, because both stand exposed to the wind.
For example, Storm Éowyn, January 2025, caused widespread damage and power cuts across the West.

Relief (the shape and height of the land) divides the West in two: rugged, hard-rock uplands in the west and low limestone land in the east. Between them lies an ice-scoured lowland, and the coast is cut up by the sea.
Rugged uplands in the west: the Twelve Bens and Maumturks in Connemara, and Mweelrea, Nephin and Croagh Patrick in Co. Mayo.
Mweelrea, 814 m, is the highest peak in Connacht (the province containing the West), so it is the tallest of these; Nephin is 806 m and Croagh Patrick is 764 m.
These are hard rocks, which resist erosion and so form the high ground: quartzite forms the Twelve Bens and Croagh Patrick; granite and mica schist form the uplands of Connemara.
The ice-scoured Connemara lowland has bare rock and many small lakes, because glaciers scraped away the soil and left hollows.
A low, flat to rolling limestone lowland lies in east Galway and Roscommon; Lough Corrib roughly divides it from the Connemara uplands.
Clew Bay's drowned drumlins are glacial hills (low hills of glacial deposit) that the sea now covers in part.
The Atlantic coast is heavily indented (cut by many inlets): Killary Harbour, a fjord (a long narrow inlet carved by a glacier) on the Galway–Mayo border, Clew Bay, and Achill Island.
Achill Island is the largest island off the Irish coast, so it is the biggest of Ireland's offshore islands; the Aran Islands are Carboniferous limestone, a continuation of the Burren limestone.
Soils follow relief and rainfall. Wet, steep, acidic ground gives poor soils in the west, and only the limestone lowland in the east has good ones. This is why most of the region suits only grazing.
Blanket bog (peat, a thick wet layer of partly rotted plants) covers much of west Mayo, around Bellacorick, and Connemara, where high rainfall keeps the ground waterlogged.
Leached, acidic podzols (soils with nutrients washed out of the top layer) with an iron pan (a hard, iron-rich layer) lie on the uplands.
Heavy, poorly drained gley soils (sticky, waterlogged clay soils) lie on the drumlins and clay lowlands.
Better-drained, more fertile brown earths lie on the limestone of east Galway and Roscommon.
Thin, rocky soils cover the limestone pavement (bare, flat limestone rock) of the Aran Islands, where islanders made soil from layers of sand and seaweed on bare rock.
Drainage means how water leaves the land through rivers, lakes and underground. In the West, limestone sends some water underground, while poor natural drainage elsewhere leaves land liable to flood.
The River Corrib flows only a few kilometres from Lough Corrib through Galway city to Galway Bay.
Lough Corrib is the largest lake in the Republic of Ireland, so it is a major feature of the drainage.
Lough Mask's water flows underground to Lough Corrib near Cong, through the Cong 'dry canal', because limestone lets water drain through it.
Turloughs, seasonal lakes on limestone, such as Rahasane turlough near Craughwell, Co. Galway, flood in winter and drain away underground.
The River Moy reaches Killala Bay at Ballina, so Ballina lies on the river near its mouth.
The River Shannon and Lough Ree form much of Roscommon's eastern boundary; the River Suck flows through Ballinasloe to the Shannon.
Poor natural drainage leaves low land beside the Shannon liable to flooding.
The Moy arterial drainage scheme (deepening and straightening a river), run by the Office of Public Works under the Arterial Drainage Act 1945, was built to reduce flooding on the Moy.
Physical factors give the West a short effective grazing season (the part of the year when grass can actually be grazed) and restrict farming to grazing on most of the land.
High rainfall, waterlogged and leached soils, steep uplands and exposure give a short effective grazing season.
Tillage is restricted to the better-drained limestone soils of east Galway and Roscommon, because crops need drained soil.
Brown earths on the limestone of east Galway and Roscommon are the region's most fertile farmland, so this is where the best farming is.
Blanket bog and gley soils restrict most of the rest of the region to grazing, because they are too wet and poorly drained for crops.
Human and economic factors add to the physical limits. Farms are small, incomes are low and the region is far from the buyers of its produce.
Farms are small and often fragmented (split into several separate plots), a legacy of the pre-Famine rundale system (shared land held in scattered strips) and of population pressure on the land.
The Congested Districts Board, set up in 1891, improved conditions in the poor western districts through land consolidation (joining scattered plots), piers and cottage industries.
The Land Commission later consolidated holdings, which reduced fragmentation further.
Part-time farming, with off-farm jobs supplementing low farm incomes, because farm income alone is not enough.
Income depends heavily on subsidies and EU payments, which come from the EU's Common Agricultural Policy (CAP).
Distance from markets and ports adds to the cost of moving livestock and produce.
Because most of the land suits only grass, the West's farming is based on animals, mainly cattle and sheep.

Cattle rearing is the main enterprise: suckler herds (cows that rear their own calves) rear calves, and young store cattle (young animals not yet ready for slaughter) are sold through local marts (livestock markets) to farmers in the east to be fattened.
Sheep graze the hill commonage (shared hill land) of Connemara and the Mayo mountains.
There is little tillage or dairying compared with the south and east, because the wet, poorly drained land is poorly suited to both.
The October Fair at Ballinasloe, Co. Galway, is one of Europe's oldest horse fairs, an example of the West's animal-based farming.
The Connemara pony is Ireland's native pony breed, another example of the region's livestock.
Low farm incomes and the pressure of subsidy-driven sheep farming brought two kinds of problem: people leaving the land and damage to the hills. Schemes then tried to put these right.
Low incomes, ageing farmers and few young successors lead to land abandonment, because no one is left to work the farm.
CAP headage payments (payments per animal kept) from the 1980s raised sheep numbers on the hill commonage of Connemara and the Mayo mountains.
Overgrazing stripped vegetation from the hills and eroded the peat.
The Rural Environment Protection Scheme (REPS), from 1994, was a response to the damage.
Commonage Framework Plans, from the early 2000s, set out how shared hill land is to be managed.
Area-based payments paid farmers on the area of land they farm, not per animal, so there was no reward for keeping more sheep.
Diversification (adding new income sources) into agri-tourism and forestry.
Forestry is a primary activity (using natural resources) that suits land too poor for farming. Trees can be grown on wet, acidic ground where grazing pays badly.
Conifer plantations, mainly Sitka spruce (native to western North America), cover marginal land (poor land where farming barely pays) and blanket bog where farming pays poorly.
Coillte, founded in 1988, is the State forestry company, so it is the main planter and manager of State forests.
Planting grants and premiums (payments to landowners) encourage forestry on farmland and bog.
Benefits: income from timber, jobs, and carbon storage in the trees.
Forest cover in Ireland is about 11% (2020s), which is low, so there is room for more planting.
Forestry on this scale has costs for water, landscape and the stability of the ground.
Acidification of streams from conifer plantations, which harms the water for fish.
Monoculture (one species grown over a large area) and landscape impact of large blocks of single-species forest.
Peat slide (a mass of wet peat slipping downhill) at Derrybrien, Slieve Aughty Mountains, Co. Galway, on 16 October 2003: about 450,000 m³ of peat slid during wind-farm construction on forested bog.
The EU Court of Justice fined Ireland in 2019 over Derrybrien, so the slide had legal consequences.

The Atlantic coast and the inland lakes and rivers give the West fishing, fish farming (aquaculture), seaweed harvesting and angling (fishing with rod and line). The sheltered bays are used for farming the sea.
Rossaveel, Co. Galway, is one of six State Fishery Harbour Centres (State-supported fishing ports) and the ferry port for the Aran Islands.
Killary Harbour: rope-grown mussels are farmed on mussel rafts.
Salmon farms in Connemara bays raise concerns over sea lice (parasites on the fish) and pollution.
Seaweed, a resource of the shore, is harvested and processed by Arramara Teoranta at Kilkieran, Connemara.
Angling: salmon on the River Moy at Ballina, including the Ridge Pool, and brown trout on Lough Corrib and Lough Mask.
Problems: EU fishing quotas (limits on the catch), loss of quota after Brexit (the UK's departure from the EU), small boats and distance from markets.
Bellacorick shows the West's energy changing from peat to wind. The region's exposure to the Atlantic, a problem for farming, is an advantage for renewable energy.
Bellacorick, Co. Mayo, had a peat-fired power station, which closed in 2003.
Bellacorick wind farm (1992) was Ireland's first commercial wind farm, so it began wind energy in the same place as the peat station.
The Oweninny wind farm is on cutaway bog (bog where the peat has been removed) nearby, so worked-out land is reused for energy.
Strong Atlantic winds and waves give the region high renewable energy potential.
The Atlantic Marine Energy Test Site off Belmullet, Co. Mayo, tests wave energy.
The West has had gas, coal, marble and gold. Some projects went ahead, one caused conflict and one was refused.
The Corrib gas field, off north-west Mayo, was discovered in 1996.
Gas first flowed in December 2015, many years after discovery; gas is processed at the Bellanaboy terminal.
The Shell to Sea campaign opposed the project, for example through protest, and the 'Rossport Five' were jailed in 2005.
Arigna, Co. Roscommon: coal mining ended in 1990; the site is now the Arigna Mining Experience, a visitor attraction.
Connemara marble is quarried, using the region's hard metamorphic rock.
Croagh Patrick: gold was found in the 1980s, but mining was not allowed after public opposition.
Manufacturing (making goods in factories) is a secondary activity. In the West it is thin and clustered in a few places, which reflects the region's peripheral position.
Manufacturing is limited and concentrated in Galway city and a few towns: Castlebar, Westport and Ballina.
There are few heavy industries, so most rural areas have little manufacturing.
Small food-processing and craft firms are the main rural manufacturers, for example firms using local produce.
A cluster is a group of related firms in one place that support each other. Galway's medical-technology cluster grew from a factory closure that left skilled workers looking for jobs.
Digital Equipment Corporation (DEC) closed its Galway manufacturing plant in 1993, leaving a skilled workforce.
Boston Scientific opened in Galway in 1994, and Medtronic followed at Parkmore.
Suppliers and start-ups clustered around the multinationals (large firms that operate in many countries), with links to the University of Galway.
Galway is now one of Europe's leading medical-technology clusters.
Mayo has no large city, but several multinationals have set up in its towns. Each is a named example of foreign investment in the West.
Allergan, now part of AbbVie, Westport, which makes Botox, a medical product.
Hollister, Ballina, which spreads manufacturing beyond Galway.
Coca-Cola concentrate plant, Ballina, an example of a multinational that does not make medical products.
State and EU policy tries to steer industry towards the peripheral West with grants, designated centres and agencies. Exams ask for any two factors, and this is one of the five.
IDA Ireland (the State agency that attracts foreign firms) and regional incentives attract foreign manufacturing firms to the region.
Údarás na Gaeltachta, set up in 1980 with its head office at Na Forbacha, Co. Galway, gives grants to firms in Gaeltacht areas (the Irish-speaking districts).
The National Spatial Strategy (2002) named Galway a gateway (a major centre intended to drive regional growth) and Castlebar–Ballina a linked hub (a smaller centre working together as one unit).
The National Planning Framework (Project Ireland 2040), 2018, requires Galway, Cork, Limerick and Waterford each to grow by at least 50% by 2040.
The Western Development Commission, a statutory body (set up by law) under the Western Development Commission Act 1998, promotes development in the west.
Firms locate where they can find skilled workers. Galway has a supply, but the rest of the region loses its skilled young people.
The University of Galway, founded in 1845 as Queen's College Galway and given its present name in 2022, supplies graduates, so firms can recruit trained staff locally.
Atlantic Technological University (ATU), with campuses in Galway and Mayo, supplies graduates and skilled workers, so firms in both counties can recruit trained staff.
Outside Galway, the pool of skilled workers is small, because skilled young people leave the region.
A market is where the firm's customers are. The West's market is small and far from its largest buyers.
The local market is small and scattered, with low population density across much of the region, so few customers live near any one factory.
Galway city provides the largest local market, because it is the biggest concentration of people in the region.
Exports must travel long distances to ports and airports, which raises costs.
Infrastructure (roads, rail, broadband) lets firms move goods and information, and raw materials are the inputs that factories use. Both vary across the region.
Good road links to Galway city, so firms there can move goods, but weaker roads and broadband in rural areas.
EU Structural Funds (EU money for poorer regions) have paid for roads and broadband.
Local farm and fish produce supplies the food-processing firms.
Medtech firms import the materials they use, so local raw materials matter less to them.
The same peripheral position that limits the pattern of industry also creates problems for firms already in the West. Most of these come back to distance and small size.
Peripheral location adds to transport costs for goods, because firms ship over long distances.
The labour pool outside Galway city is small, so firms have fewer workers to choose from.
Dependence on a few multinationals, and closures such as DEC's in 1993, which show the risk when one large employer leaves.
Difficulty attracting investment away from Galway, so the rest of the region gets less of it.
Poor rural infrastructure, which makes it hard for firms to locate in rural towns.
Tourism is a tertiary activity (a service). The West's main selling point is its Atlantic landscape of mountains, islands and coast.
Connemara National Park, at Letterfrack, protects the Connemara landscape, so visitors can see it unspoilt.
Killary Harbour, Croagh Patrick, Achill Island and Clew Bay draw visitors to the coast and mountains, because of their scenery.
For example, Dún Aonghasa, a prehistoric stone fort on a cliff edge on Inis Mór, Aran Islands.
The Atlantic coast and beaches are used for surfing and water sports.
The Wild Atlantic Way, a Fáilte Ireland touring route launched in 2014, runs about 2,500 km from Inishowen, Co. Donegal, to Kinsale, Co. Cork.
Culture and history give visitors reasons to come beyond the scenery. They include language, ancient sites, historic houses and festivals.
Gaeltacht culture and the Irish language, with Irish summer colleges, which attract students to the Gaeltacht.
Céide Fields, north Co. Mayo: Stone Age (Neolithic) field systems over 5,000 years old, preserved under blanket bog.
Kylemore Abbey, Connemara, a Benedictine abbey, is a heritage attraction.
Westport House, a historic house, is a heritage attraction.
Strokestown Park and the National Famine Museum, Co. Roscommon.
Rathcroghan, Co. Roscommon: the ancient royal site of Connacht, which draws visitors interested in early history.
Lough Key Forest Park, near Boyle, offers outdoor recreation.
Galway International Arts Festival (July); Galway was European Capital of Culture in 2020, a year disrupted by COVID-19.
Active holidays and events make use of the landscape and of Galway city.
Angling, walking and cycling, which use the region's rivers, lakes and countryside.
For example, the Great Western Greenway, about 42 km from Westport to Achill, first opened in 2010.
Galway city's festivals, nightlife and the Galway Races at Ballybrit in summer.
Tourism brings income, but it has weaknesses that come from the West's weather, distance and size.
The season is short and depends on the weather, because most visitors come in good weather.
Seasonal and low-paid jobs, because tourism work is only available for part of the year.
Distance and weaker access than the east, which make the journey harder for visitors.
Pressure on fragile landscapes and on the Irish language, because large numbers of visitors wear the land and bring English into Gaeltacht areas.
Over-reliance on Galway city, so the rest of the region gains less.
Better transport reduces the effects of distance. The West has gained motorways, an airport and rail links, though not every link is open.
M6 Dublin–Galway motorway, completed in 2009, which shortens the journey to the capital.
M17/M18 Galway–Tuam motorway, 2017, which links Galway with Tuam.
Ireland West Airport Knock opened in 1986, promoted by Monsignor James Horan, and it gives air access to the north of the region.
Rail lines run from Galway, Westport and Ballina to Dublin, which link the main towns to the capital.
The Western Rail Corridor's Ennis–Athenry section reopened in 2010; the line north of Athenry to Claremorris has not reopened.
Ferries link the islands to the mainland, because the islands have no road link.
Even with improvements, transport in the West has weaknesses that come from its thin population. Good transport still matters for the region's economy.
Low population density makes public transport uneconomic outside the towns, because there are too few passengers.
Poor minor roads and heavy dependence on the car, because buses and trains are too few.
Congestion in Galway city: the Galway City Ring Road has been proposed for many years but not built.
Long journey times to Dublin, which adds to peripherality.
Transport supports tourism and industry and reduces peripherality.
Services besides tourism and transport also provide jobs, and most are based in Galway city.
A major hospital in Galway city serves as a regional centre for the west, so patients from the three counties travel there.
Public-sector jobs, including decentralised government offices (offices moved out of Dublin).
Galway is the West's only city and the urban area to use for a question on one urban area. Its location where a river meets the sea explains why it began.
Galway city lies where the River Corrib reaches Galway Bay.
It began as an Anglo-Norman walled town, from the 13th century, so the walls protected the settlement.
The Spanish Arch recalls medieval trade with Spain, so it shows Galway's past as a trading port.
'City of the Tribes' is the city's name for the 14 merchant families who ran its trade.
Eyre Square is the city's central open space, so it is a landmark of the city centre.
Galway has grown into the region's centre for education, industry, health and planning. Growth has also brought urban problems.
Galway city had about 85,000 people in the Galway City Council area in Census 2022.
The University of Galway has been in the city since 1845, which gives the city graduates and research.
Galway is a designated growth centre in national planning policy, named a gateway in 2002 and set to grow by at least 50% by 2040 under the National Planning Framework.
Galway is a medical-technology cluster, which shows its industrial growth since DEC and the medtech firms.
For example, Oranmore is a growing satellite town (a smaller settlement near a city that takes some of its growth).
Suburban sprawl (the spread of housing over the edge of the city) and housing costs in the growing city.
Traffic congestion, because the Galway City Ring Road is still not built.
Beyond Galway, the West's towns are small. They serve local areas rather than forming a strong network of larger towns.
Castlebar is the county town of Mayo, so it is the administrative centre of the county.
Westport is an 18th-century planned town laid out for the Browne family of Westport House.
Westport's Octagon and the Mall, along the Carrowbeg River, show its planned layout.
Ballina lies on the River Moy; Tuam is the seat of the Catholic Archdiocese of Tuam.
Ballinasloe, Co. Galway, and Boyle, near Lough Key Forest Park, are small towns, for example serving their local areas.
The towns form a weak urban hierarchy (the ranking of settlements by size and services): few large towns and no large city beyond Galway.
The West has a small share of the State's people, and they are spread very unevenly. Exams ask you to account for the distribution, which means explaining each pattern with a reason.
The region had about 486,000 people in Census 2022, about 9% of the State's 5.1 million.
Galway (including Galway city) about 278,000, Mayo about 138,000 and Roscommon about 70,000 in Census 2022.
Mayo has about 25 people per km² (area about 5,590 km², Ireland's third-largest county); Roscommon has under 30 per km².
The State average is about 73 per km², and Co. Dublin has about 1,600 per km², which shows how thinly the West is settled.
Concentration in Galway city and its suburbs and satellite towns, where jobs, services and transport are.
Moderate densities on the east Galway, Roscommon and east Mayo lowlands and in the towns, where land and roads are better.
Very low densities on the uplands and blanket bogs of west Mayo (Erris) and Connemara, where soils are poor, slopes steep and the land exposed.
Coastal and island settlement, linked to fishing and the Gaeltacht, as on the Aran Islands.
Population dynamics means how a population changes over time. The West's history of loss is now partly reversed in places.
The Great Famine of the late 1840s hit the West hard, because many people depended on small farms.
A long history of emigration has left populations far below pre-Famine levels, so the West has not recovered its earlier numbers.
Continuing out-migration of young adults to Dublin and abroad, known as brain drain (the loss of educated, skilled people).
An ageing population with fewer births and many empty houses, because the young have left.
Recent growth from return migration (emigrants coming home), immigration and the expansion of Galway city.
The population of every county grew between 2016 and 2022 (Census 2022).
Rural settlement in the West has changed from old clustered and scattered forms to housing strung along roads. Rural life has also declined as people have left.
Traditional dispersed settlement (houses spread out across the land) and clachans, small clusters of houses shared by families under rundale.
Later ribbon development (houses in a line along roads) and one-off housing, because roads give access to services.
Rural decline, which follows from out-migration: depopulation, an ageing population, and closures of schools, post offices and Garda stations.
Island depopulation, especially on the Aran Islands, where fewer people stay.
Governments and the EU have launched programmes to support rural areas. Some invest in places that have lost population and some bring in jobs and services.
CLÁR programme (2001): investment in depopulated rural areas, to slow the decline.
LEADER, the EU rural development programme, which funds local projects.
National Broadband Plan: contract signed in 2019 with National Broadband Ireland, to bring broadband to rural areas.
Our Rural Future (2021): rural development policy.
Remote-working hubs and digital hubs bring work to rural towns, so people can work there without commuting to the city.
The Western Development Commission covers seven counties, including Galway, Mayo and Roscommon, which is wider than the three-county region used here.
The Congested Districts Board of 1891 was an earlier response, and Údarás na Gaeltachta supports Gaeltacht areas by giving grants to firms.
The West holds Ireland's largest Gaeltacht areas, the districts where Irish is the main community language.
The Galway Gaeltacht is the largest; it includes Connemara and the Aran Islands.
The Mayo Gaeltacht: Erris (Iorras), Achill (Acaill) and Tourmakeady (Tuar Mhic Éadaigh).
Roscommon has no Gaeltacht area, so Irish-speaking districts lie only in Galway and Mayo.
The Census 2022 Gaeltacht population was about 106,000.
Fewer people now use Irish every day, even inside the Gaeltacht. Several forces push the language back.
About 20,000 people speak Irish daily outside the education system in the Gaeltacht; about 72,000 do so nationally (Census 2022).
Emigration of young speakers from the Gaeltacht, which removes the next generation of speakers.
English-language media and English spoken in the home, which reduce daily use of Irish.
Tourism and the in-migration of English speakers into Gaeltacht areas, which makes English the common language locally.
Institutions and strategies try to protect Irish in the Gaeltacht. They include State bodies, media, laws and plans, schooling and housing.
Údarás na Gaeltachta (1980), head office at Na Forbacha, Co. Galway, is the State body responsible for the Gaeltacht's development.
TG4, launched in 1996 as Teilifís na Gaeilge, with its headquarters at Baile na hAbhann, Co. Galway.
RTÉ Raidió na Gaeltachta, from 1972, with its headquarters at Casla (Costelloe), Co. Galway.
Irish-medium schools (where lessons are taught in Irish) and summer colleges, so young people use Irish regularly.
Planning conditions that reserve new houses for Irish speakers, so that new housing goes to Irish speakers.
Údarás jobs to keep young people in the Gaeltacht, which counters emigration.
The West is strongly Roman Catholic, and its religion shows in pilgrimage sites and old church centres. Religion also draws tourists.
The West has a higher Roman Catholic share than Dublin; nationally, about 69% of people are Roman Catholic and about 14% have no religion (Census 2022).
For example, Knock Shrine, Co. Mayo: an apparition was reported in 1879; Pope John Paul II visited in 1979 and Pope Francis in 2018.
Croagh Patrick pilgrimage on Reek Sunday, the last Sunday in July, for example, draws pilgrims to the mountain.
Ballintubber Abbey, Co. Mayo, was founded in 1216, and Mass has been celebrated there continuously since.
Tuam is the seat of the Catholic Archdiocese of Tuam, so it is a church centre for the region.
Religious practice and vocations (people entering the priesthood) are declining, but religion remains important in community life.

The Paris Basin is a large, low sedimentary lowland (a basin floored by layers of rock laid down as sediment) in northern France, centred on Paris. Knowing exactly where it starts and stops matters, because the edging hills are not part of it.
It is open to the English Channel in the north-west, so the basin has a sea outlet on one side and is closed in by higher land elsewhere.
Older uplands ring the basin and mark its edge, and they are not part of the lowland: the Armorican Massif (west), the Massif Central (south), the Vosges (east) and the Ardennes (north-east).
The basin covers several French administrative regions (the main divisions used to govern France). Île-de-France, the region containing Paris, is its core.
France has 13 regions in mainland France (since 2016); Île-de-France is one of them.

A core region is one where people, wealth and decision-making are concentrated. The Paris Basin earns that status from the concentration of people, wealth and functions around Paris, and from the links that radiate out from it.
Paris is the capital, so government, finance and head offices (the headquarters of large firms) are concentrated there.
The region holds the largest concentration of population, wealth, industry and services in France.
Fertile farmland surrounds the city and supplies its food, so the city does not depend on distant supplies.
The national transport network is focused on the region, so routes across France lead in and out of it.
The basin has a central position in the EU.
The reasons reinforce each other: the large market draws industry and services, these draw migrants, and the transport links carry goods and people in and out.
Exams ask for an outline map of a European region with named features on it. These are the items you can draw and name, and where each one belongs.
River: draw the Seine and name it; the Marne, Oise and Loire may be added as named rivers.
Urban centres: name Paris with two others from Rouen, Le Havre, Reims, Orléans, Troyes, Chartres or Amiens.

Placement on rivers: Paris, Rouen and Le Havre lie on the Seine, with Le Havre at its mouth and Rouen upstream of it. Troyes is on the Seine upstream of Paris. Orléans is on the Loire. Épernay, not Reims, is on the Marne.
Placement elsewhere: Chartres lies in the Beauce (a lowland plain) and Amiens is on the Somme.
Relief: shade the Beauce (lowland plain) and the Brie plateau, and mark the edging uplands on the rim, labelled as bounding the region.
Agricultural area: the Beauce for cereals, and Champagne for vines.
Industrial area: the Lower Seine between Rouen and Le Havre.

The climate is transitional, between cool temperate oceanic conditions in the west (mild, wet, moderated by the sea) and more continental conditions in the east (bigger swings between summer and winter). This shapes what can be grown.
The annual temperature range (the gap between the warmest and coldest month) increases from west to east, so inland winters are colder and summers warmer.
Paris: average January temperature about 5°C; average July temperature about 20°C.
Paris: annual rainfall about 600–650 mm, spread fairly evenly through the year, so rainfall is moderate and there is no dry season.
Champagne lies near the northern limit of commercial vine growing, so its warm summers are essential to the crop.
The basin is a saucer of sedimentary rock layers, with the youngest rocks at the centre and the oldest at the rim. The resulting low, gentle relief matters for land use.
Layers of limestone, chalk, clay and sand dip (slope) gently towards Paris, which sits near the centre on the youngest rocks.
The land is mostly below about 300 m, so the relief is low and gently rolling, which suits large-scale farming.
On the eastern side, resistant layers form escarpments (long ridges with a steep face) that face outwards (east), while their dip slopes (the gentle back slopes) fall back in towards Paris.
Clay vales (low, wet valleys cut in soft clay) lie between the escarpments.
Only the relief and its effect on land use are needed here. There is more on how cuestas (escarpments) form in Landforms from sedimentary structures.
Soil type decides what a farmer can grow, and the basin has a clear pattern: rich loam on the plateaux, thin chalk soil in Champagne, and heavy clay in the vales.
Limon, a fine, wind-blown loam, covers the Beauce, Brie and Picardy plateaux.
Limon is deep, fine, well-drained, fertile and easily worked, so it is among the most fertile soils in Europe.
Champagne's chalk gives thin calcareous (lime-rich) soils. The dry chalk plain east of Reims was once called 'Champagne pouilleuse' (poor Champagne).
Fertilisers and modern farming turned that dry chalk plain into productive cereal land, so soil weakness was overcome by human effort.
Heavier, wetter clay soils in the vales and in the west are suited to grass rather than crops, because they are hard to work and waterlogged.
The Seine and its tributaries (rivers that flow into it) form the main drainage system, and they converge on Paris. The gentle land that makes them useful also makes them a flood risk.
The Seine rises on the Langres plateau in Burgundy and flows about 775 km north-west through Troyes, Paris and Rouen to the English Channel at Le Havre.
Its tributaries are the Aube, Yonne, Marne and Oise.
Gentle gradients make the rivers navigable, so boats and barges can use them.
The lower Seine meanders (winds in loops) between Paris and Rouen.
The Loire crosses the south of the region and flows through Orléans.
Permeable chalk and limestone (rock that lets water soak in) store groundwater in aquifers (underground water stores) and give dry valleys, which are valleys with no river in them now.

The gentle gradient and low relief let floodwater spread slowly across the flat valley floor. The Great Flood of Paris (January 1910) and a major flood in June 2016 (which closed the lower galleries of the Louvre) both show this risk.
Upstream reservoirs regulate the flow of the rivers; Lac du Der-Chantecoq regulates the Marne.
The Paris Basin is the main arable region (growing crops rather than keeping animals) of France, and its physical conditions give it a head start in farming.
France is the EU's largest agricultural producer and its largest wheat producer.
Low, gently rolling relief allows large fields to be worked with machinery.
Limon soils are fertile and easily worked, giving high yields.
Warm summers ripen cereals and grapes, and the long growing season extends the time crops have to develop.
Dry harvest weather lets crops be gathered in good condition, because wet grain is harder to store.
The Beauce is the best example of the basin's arable farming, where flat land and limon soil are put to full use.
The Beauce, south-west of Paris around Chartres, is known as the granary of France (a granary is a store for grain).
Crops: wheat, barley and maize, with sugar beet and oilseed rape grown on the plateaux.
Many cereal farms exceed 100 hectares, which is large enough for big machines to work efficiently.
Large, highly mechanised farms achieve high yields on the flat limon land, because flat ground suits big machines.
Viticulture (growing grapes for wine) is the basin's best-known specialist farming. It depends on chalk soils, slopes and a protected name.
Vineyards lie on the chalk slopes around Reims and Épernay; Épernay is on the Marne.
The vines grow on the slopes of the escarpment, on thin chalk soils.
Only sparkling wine from this protected (AOC) area may be called Champagne. AOC is a legal label that protects a product's name and place of origin.
The Champagne houses (the firms that make and sell the wine) store wine in chalk cellars. Moët & Chandon is based in Épernay.
The houses add value: grapes grown on the slopes become a branded product sold under the protected name, which links farming to manufacturing.
Where the soil is too wet and heavy for crops, farmers turn to grass and animals. Near Paris, the huge city market favours fresh produce instead.
Wetter clay soils and grassland support dairy farming (milk production) in Normandy (west), which produces Camembert cheese.
Brie, east of Paris, is also a dairy area, so it gives its name to Brie cheese.
Market gardening (growing vegetables and flowers for sale) is practised on the edge of Paris.
Proximity to Paris lets fresh produce reach a very large urban market quickly, which matters because fresh goods spoil.
Physical conditions are only part of the story. Changes to farm layout, organisation and EU money also explain why the basin farms so productively.
Remembrement: after the Second World War, fragmented holdings (many small scattered plots) were consolidated into larger farms.
Mechanisation allows fewer workers to farm larger areas, which is also why the rural population falls.
Farm co-operatives (farmers' groups) and agribusiness firms (large commercial food companies) buy, process and market farm produce.
France receives the largest share of CAP spending (the EU's Common Agricultural Policy) of any member state, which supports French farm incomes.
The Paris market is a large outlet for farm produce within reach of the basin.
Forestry and fishing are small activities here compared with farming.

Large forests grow on the poorer sandy soils near Paris, which are less useful for crops, so trees took the land. They include the Forests of Fontainebleau (on sands and sandstone), Compiègne and Rambouillet.
These state forests are used for timber and recreation.
Fishing is minor in this region and no port is named for it.
France has few local fossil fuels (coal, oil and gas), so it relies on nuclear power, and the basin's rivers and coast host many of the stations.
Nuclear power supplies about two-thirds of France's electricity (recent years).

Nuclear stations sit on rivers and the coast, which supply the cooling water they need: Nogent-sur-Seine on the Seine; Dampierre and Saint-Laurent on the Loire near Orléans; Paluel and Penly on the Normandy Channel coast.
France has few local fossil fuels, so oil is imported as crude (unrefined) and refined on the Seine estuary.
Oil refining and petrochemicals (chemicals made from oil) are located at Gonfreville-l'Orcher near Le Havre.
The largest market and labour force in France drew manufacturing to Paris, and firms with head offices and research staff stayed close to it.
Market: the Paris region is the largest market in France, so firms locate close to their customers.
Labour: it has the largest labour force in France, so factories can find workers.
Capital: the head offices of large firms and their finance are based in Paris.
Research: universities and research institutes provide the skills and ideas that industry needs.
Food and drink processing is manufacturing that turns farm output into products. It sits close to the farms that supply it.
Food and drink processing uses local farm output: sugar beet and cereals from the plateaux, and grapes from the Champagne vineyards.
Processing close to the source saves the cost of moving bulky crops such as sugar beet to distant factories.
Infrastructure (the roads, rails, ports and other networks that support industry) is a major reason firms locate here. Paris sits at the centre of the network.
Paris is the hub of road, rail, river and air transport in France, so firms there are well connected.
Firms can move raw materials and finished goods by road, rail, river and air from a single location.
The Seine and the Lower Seine allow bulk goods to reach factories by water.
Good transport lowers the cost of getting inputs in and products out, so transport links reinforce the location advantage of the region.
Car making shows both the strength of Paris as an industrial region and a shift in where factories are built.
Renault has a plant at Flins, and PSA (now Stellantis) has a plant at Poissy; both are west of Paris.
Renault's Boulogne-Billancourt plant, on Île Seguin in the Seine, closed in 1992.
The closure is an example of industry leaving the inner city for suburban and provincial sites.
Between Rouen and Le Havre, the Seine becomes a corridor of ports and heavy industry. It links the basin to overseas markets.
The Lower Seine, between Rouen and Le Havre, is an industrial area built around its ports, oil refining and petrochemicals.
Le Havre is France's largest container port, and it sits at the mouth of the Seine where the river meets the English Channel.
Rouen is France's main grain-exporting port, so it links the basin's cereal surplus to overseas markets.
Since 2021 the ports of Le Havre, Rouen and Paris form one body, HAROPA.
Modern industry here is based on research and knowledge, and Paris-Saclay is the named example.
Paris-Saclay is a research and high-technology cluster (a group of related firms and institutions in one place) on the Saclay plateau, south-west of Paris.
It combines universities, research institutes and company laboratories.
Its research base, such as its universities and laboratories, supports the high-technology firms located in the cluster.
Decentralisation means moving activity out of the capital. From the 1950s the French state tried to limit Paris's dominance and spread industry to the provinces (regions outside Paris).
Decentralisation from the 1950s–60s restricted new industry in Paris and steered it to the provinces.
DATAR, the regional planning agency, was set up in 1963.
Eight métropoles d'équilibre (balancing metropolises) were named in 1964, including Lyon, Marseille and Lille, to counter the pull of Paris.
The 1965 regional plan (schéma directeur) for Paris led to five new towns: Cergy-Pontoise, Évry, Marne-la-Vallée, Melun-Sénart and Saint-Quentin-en-Yvelines.
Result: because factories were steered away, Paris lost its share of manufacturing but kept its head offices and research.
Paris is the primate city of France (a city far larger and more important than any other), and its services are the basis of its economic dominance in the region.
Government, finance, head offices, universities and international organisations are concentrated in Paris.
The OECD and UNESCO have their headquarters in Paris, as international organisations that add to its service role.
La Défense, west of the city, is one of Europe's largest purpose-built business districts.
Île-de-France has about 12 million people (2020s), about 18% of France's population (France about 68 million, 2024).
Île-de-France produces about 30% of France's GDP (the total value of goods and services produced).
Concentrated services draw international business, which in turn needs more of the same services, so the centre keeps growing.
Rungis shows how farming (primary activity) and services such as trade and distribution (tertiary activity) connect.
Rungis International Market, south of Paris, opened in 1969, replacing Les Halles in central Paris.
It is one of the world's largest wholesale fresh-food markets.
It links primary and tertiary activity: farm produce from the basin is sold wholesale there and then distributed to the city's shops and restaurants.
Tourism is a major tertiary activity in the region, with attractions to suit many interests. Heavy visitor numbers also create problems.
Visitors come for heritage, culture, shopping, events, theme parks, Champagne and the countryside.
The Eiffel Tower was built for the 1889 Exposition Universelle. The Louvre is the world's most visited art museum.
Notre-Dame Cathedral was damaged by fire in April 2019 and reopened in December 2024. The Palace of Versailles is a major heritage attraction in the region.
Disneyland Paris, at Marne-la-Vallée, opened in 1992 and is Europe's most visited theme park, so it is a major draw for visitors.
Paris hosted the 2024 Olympic and Paralympic Games.
Champagne Hillsides, Houses and Cellars became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2015; the Champagne houses in Reims and Épernay offer cellar tours.
Problems: congestion, seasonal pressure on sites (crowding in peak months), and wear on heritage sites from large visitor numbers.
Transport is central to the region's development. The network is built around Paris, with new lines extending it.
The road and rail network is radial (star-shaped), centred on Paris, so routes spread out from the capital like spokes.
The Boulevard Périphérique ring road, completed in 1973, encircles the city and carries traffic around it, so through traffic can avoid the centre.
The TGV's first high-speed line, Paris–Lyon, opened in 1981.
The Channel Tunnel opened in 1994; Eurostar links Paris with London, so the region is joined to Britain by rail.
The RER is the regional express rail network across the city region, so suburbs are linked to the centre.
The Grand Paris Express is about 200 km of new automatic metro lines with 68 new stations.
Line 14 was extended north to Saint-Denis Pleyel and south to Orly airport in 2024.
Air and river links add to the road and rail network, and together they keep Paris attractive for business.
Charles de Gaulle Airport (Roissy, opened 1974) is France's busiest airport; Orly is the second Paris airport, so air links serve the whole region.
The Port of Paris at Gennevilliers is one of Europe's largest river ports.
Transport links let firms in the region reach markets and suppliers quickly, which sustains the concentration of head offices and services.
The same network connects the basin to the Channel ports and to the rest of Europe, so the region gains from both road and river access.
The language of the region is tied to Paris's history as a centre of power.
The language of the region is French.
Standard French developed from the dialect of the Paris region, which became the standard because Paris was the centre of government.
Immigrant languages are spoken in the suburbs, because of post-war migration.
Religion in the region has changed from a Catholic tradition to a mixed and largely secular society.
The region is traditionally Roman Catholic, but church attendance is now low.
The 1905 law separating church and state (laïcité) keeps religion out of government and public institutions.
There is a large Muslim minority, mainly of North African origin.
Secularisation (the decline of religion's role in society) has reduced the role of the church in public life.
Culture covers more than religion and language. Politics, sport and the arts all reflect Paris's role as the centre of France.
Politics: France is a highly centralised state run from Paris.
Paris Saint-Germain won the UEFA Champions League in 2025.
Stade de France, in Saint-Denis, was built for the 1998 FIFA World Cup.
The French Open tennis is played at Roland-Garros, Paris.
The Tour de France traditionally finishes on the Champs-Élysées.
Paris is a centre of art, fashion and cuisine, which also draws tourists.
Exams ask for the factors that influenced the development of one urban area. Here each factor is matched to Paris.
Site: Paris began on the Île de la Cité, an island at a crossing point of the Seine.

Situation: Paris lies near the centre of the Paris Basin, where the Seine's main tributaries, the Marne, Oise, Aube and Yonne, converge (the Marne joins just upstream of the city and the Oise just downstream).
Transport: the city is the hub of a radial road and rail network and of the river port at Gennevilliers.
Administration: as capital and seat of a centralised state, Paris concentrates government, finance and head offices.
Primary activity: the rich limon plateaux around the city supplied food to a growing population.
Industry and services: the largest market and labour force attracted manufacturing and services, including the business district of La Défense.
Planning: the 1853–1870 rebuilding, the post-war estates and the new towns each shaped the city's growth.
Paris grew in stages, from planned rebuilding in the nineteenth century to suburban estates and regional planning in the twentieth.
Haussmann rebuilt central Paris between 1853 and 1870 under Napoleon III, so the city gained wide boulevards, uniform apartment blocks, parks and sewers.
Grands ensembles, large high-rise social housing estates built in the suburbs (banlieues) in the 1950s–70s, housed a growing population; Sarcelles is an example.
Growth spread beyond the Périphérique ring road into the surrounding suburbs.
The five new towns built under the 1965 plan are Cergy-Pontoise, Évry, Marne-la-Vallée, Melun-Sénart and Saint-Quentin-en-Yvelines.
Métropole du Grand Paris was created on 1 January 2016, joining Paris with about 130 surrounding communes (the smallest units of local government in France).
The Grand Paris Express metro network is the latest large-scale project for the city region.
Rapid growth and concentration have brought serious problems to Paris and its suburbs.
Congestion on roads into and around the city, because so many people and jobs are concentrated there.
High housing costs, which push people out to the suburbs.

Social segregation (different groups living apart) and deprivation in the banlieues: Seine-Saint-Denis, north-east of Paris, is the poorest département (a French county-sized administrative area) in mainland France.
Riots in the banlieues began in Clichy-sous-Bois in October 2005 and spread across France.
Urban sprawl: development spreads outward into the surrounding countryside, because high housing costs push people out.
Away from Paris, the countryside has changed as farming has mechanised and as the city's influence has spread outward.
Fewer farmers on larger holdings leave the outer basin with a declining rural population.
Rural depopulation in the outer basin forms part of the 'diagonale du vide' (empty diagonal), a band of low population density from north-east to south-west France.
Commuter villages near Paris are growing as residents travel to jobs in the city.
Second homes and rural tourism bring visitors and money to villages in the Champagne and countryside areas.
Population is very unevenly spread: packed into Paris and its region, thinly spread across the outer basin.
Île-de-France has about 1,000 people per km² (2020s).
The City of Paris has about 2.1 million people (2020s) on about 105 km², about 20,000 people per km²; it is divided into 20 arrondissements (administrative districts of the city).
Densities are much lower in rural Champagne and across the outer basin, where mechanised farming needs few workers.
The dense core exists because jobs, services and transport access are concentrated in and around Paris.
Population change in the basin has been driven by movement of people into Paris, from the French countryside and from abroad.
Jean-François Gravier's Paris et le désert français (Paris and the French desert), 1947, argued that Paris drained people and wealth from the rest of France.
Rural-to-urban migration into Paris continued because jobs and services concentrated there.
The Paris region has a young age structure, because in-migrants are mostly young adults seeking work.
Older residents move out of the region on retirement, so the age structure stays young.
After the Second World War, immigrant labour arrived from Algeria, Morocco, Tunisia and Portugal.

The Mezzogiorno is the Mediterranean, peripheral region you can study as a contrast to the core Paris Basin. It is southern Italy and its islands, which together form the peripheral south of the country.

It is made up of eight regions: Abruzzo, Molise, Campania, Puglia (Apulia), Basilicata, Calabria, Sicily and Sardinia. This is why the region is described as the South and its islands, not one single area.
The name Mezzogiorno means midday, a reference to the strong midday sun of the south.
It covers about 40% of Italy's area but holds only about one-third of its population: about 20 million people (2020s), out of an Italian population of about 59 million (2024).
Rome and the region of Lazio lie north of the Mezzogiorno and are not part of it, so never include them when you describe the region.
Sicily and Sardinia are autonomous regions with a special statute (their own legal status), which gives their regional governments extra powers. This reflects their separate island identity.

Peripheral means far from the economic core, where the main markets, industry and wealth are. Distance, relief (the shape and height of the land), history and politics combine to keep the South behind the North.
Distance: the South is far from the EU's core markets and from the industrial North of Italy, which raises the cost of moving goods.
Relief and climate: the land is mostly mountainous or hilly and summers are dry, which limits farming, transport and settlement.

History: the South, formerly the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies, became part of a united Italy in 1861, and the North–South gap widened after unification. Land stayed in large estates, which kept farming backward.
Organised crime and emigration drain investment and people from the South, so the region loses both money and workers.

The North–South divide is known as the questione meridionale (the southern question). The Mezzogiorno produces only about 22% of Italy's GDP (the value of all goods and services made), and its GDP per head is a little over half that of the Centre-North (recent years).
Unemployment in the South is roughly two to three times the North's rate (recent years).
Contrast: the Paris Basin, studied in region s1, is a core European region; the Mezzogiorno is the peripheral counterpart.
You may be asked to draw an outline map of a European region and mark named features. These are the Mezzogiorno features you can draw and name.
Rivers: the Volturno in Campania, the longest river of the southern mainland; the Ofanto in Puglia; the Basento in Basilicata.
Urban centres: Naples, Bari, Taranto, Brindisi, Palermo, Catania and Reggio Calabria.
Relief: the Apennines (the mountain chain down the peninsula), the Sila in Calabria, Mount Etna and Vesuvius.
Lowlands: the Tavoliere di Puglia around Foggia, the Campanian plain and the plain of Catania.
Agricultural and industrial areas: the Tavoliere (durum wheat) and the Bari–Brindisi–Taranto industrial triangle, which is the South's own industrial area.
The climate has hot, dry summers and mild, wet winters, with rain concentrated in the cooler months. This pattern drives the region's water problems and its farming.
Summers are hot and dry because the subtropical high-pressure belt (a zone of sinking, dry air) moves north over the region.
Lowland summer (July) averages around 25°C or more. This heat is why summers need irrigation.
Winters are mild and wet, with rain brought by Atlantic depressions (low-pressure weather systems); most rain falls between October and March.
Annual rainfall is under 600 mm on parts of the Puglia lowlands and Sicily, but much higher on the Apennines. This is why irrigation is needed on the lowlands, while the high Apennines are wetter.
The sirocco is a hot, dry, dusty wind from the Sahara that adds to the dryness of summer.
Summer drought causes water shortage, while intense autumn and winter downpours cause flash floods (sudden floods after heavy rain).
Farmers respond with irrigation (supplying water to crops) and drought-tolerant crops.
Mountains and hills cover most of the region, and the lowlands are small and mostly coastal. This shapes where people farm and live.
The Apennines run the length of the peninsula, forming its spine.
The highest point of the Apennines is Corno Grande (Gran Sasso, Abruzzo), at 2,912 m. This is why the interior is so hard to farm or cross.
The Calabrian uplands are dominated by high ground, including the Sila plateau. Because the high ground leaves little flat land, farming and settlement are limited.
The Tavoliere di Puglia, around Foggia, is the largest plain of peninsular southern Italy. Because it is flat, it suits large-scale farming, such as durum wheat.
The Campanian plain around Naples and the plain of Catania, Sicily's largest plain, are the other main lowlands.
Mount Etna in Sicily, about 3,300 m, is Europe's highest active volcano. This is why the island has both a volcanic hazard and fertile volcanic soil.
Steep slopes limit farming, transport and settlement to small areas and push villages onto hilltops.
The region is geologically restless, so earthquakes and volcanoes are part of life in the South. Here are the local examples; they are also a source of fertile soil.
The region lies where the African and Eurasian plates meet, which is why it has earthquakes and volcanoes.
Messina and Reggio Calabria were destroyed by the earthquake and tsunami of 28 December 1908, with tens of thousands killed.
L'Aquila, Abruzzo, 6 April 2009: magnitude 6.3, about 300 deaths.
Vesuvius buried Pompeii and Herculaneum in AD 79 and last erupted in 1944. Because it is still active, it remains a hazard to nearby Naples.
Etna and Stromboli are active volcanoes. This is another sign of the plate boundary beneath the region.
Campi Flegrei is a volcanic caldera (a large crater formed by collapse) west of Naples, where the ground rises and falls, called bradyseism, around Pozzuoli.
Soils vary sharply with bedrock (the solid rock under the soil) and slope, and this decides which land can be farmed well.
Thin, stony soils cover much of the upland, where the bedrock is close to the surface. This is why upland farming is poor.
Terra rossa is red clay soil that forms on limestone, for example in Puglia.
Fertile volcanic soils on Vesuvius and Etna, in Campania and Sicily, support vineyards and orchards.
Alluvial soils (soils deposited by rivers) on the lowlands are used for intensive farming. Because rivers deposit fresh fertile material, these soils suit intensive farming.
Calanchi are gullied badland slopes on clay, for example in Basilicata. Because clay erodes easily in heavy rain, it forms gullies, so the land is of little farming use.
Soil erosion is worsened by deforestation, overgrazing and the winter downpours that wash bare soil away.
Sarno, Campania, 5–6 May 1998: saturated volcanic ash slid as mudflows, killing about 160 people.
Rivers follow the climate: they carry water in the wet winter and shrink in the dry summer. This makes them poor sources of water and transport.
Rivers are short and steep, so they flood quickly after rain.
Winter: heavy rain turns the rivers into torrents. This is why rivers flood so quickly.
Summer: many channels run dry. This is why rivers cannot supply irrigation water in the season crops need it most.
Fiumare are wide, dry, stony riverbeds in Calabria and Sicily that flood after heavy rain.
Few rivers are navigable (deep and steady enough for boats), so they are of little use for transport.
The Apulian Aqueduct (Acquedotto Pugliese), built in the early 20th century, carries water from the Sele river springs in Campania across the Apennines to Puglia, which has little water of its own.
Before reform, most land was held in large estates, which kept productivity (output per worker or hectare) low.
Latifundia are large estates owned by absentee landlords, who lived away from them.
The latifundia were worked by landless day labourers (braccianti) paid wages.
The main uses of the estates were extensive wheat growing (low output per hectare) and sheep grazing.
Small hill farms were fragmented into scattered plots, which were hard to farm efficiently. So the farmers could not use their land efficiently.
Productivity was low on both the estates and the small hill farms.
After the Second World War the state tried to fix the old estate system and develop the South. It did this through land reform and a development fund.
Land reform laws of 1950 expropriated (took by law) parts of the large estates and gave plots to peasants.
The Cassa per il Mezzogiorno (Fund for the South) ran from 1950 to 1984. Its aim was to develop the South with state money.
Its work included land reclamation (making wet or unusable land farmable), drainage, irrigation dams, aqueducts and roads. These works improved land and water supply for farming.
It built new settlements on reclaimed lowlands for the new smallholders (small farm owners).
Malaria was eradicated from the lowlands after the Second World War, which made them safe to settle.
From the late 1950s the Cassa also funded industry.
Modern farming in the South is specialised: it grows Mediterranean crops suited to the climate and soils, often for markets beyond the region.
Durum wheat is grown on the Tavoliere di Puglia around Foggia, Italy's main durum wheat area, for pasta. The dry summers and flat land suit it.
Puglia is Italy's leading olive-oil region. Olives are drought-tolerant, so they suit the dry climate.
Sicilian blood oranges are grown on the plain of Catania near Etna.
Lemons are grown on the Amalfi coast and around Sorrento. These crops are specialised and sold beyond the region.
Irrigated market gardening (growing vegetables for sale) on the Campanian plain includes San Marzano tomatoes grown near Vesuvius.
Puglia and Sicily are major wine producers. Vines are drought-tolerant, so they suit the dry summers.
Specialised Mediterranean produce is grown for markets, and agri-food firms (food-processing businesses) process it.
Despite reform, southern farming faces natural, economic and social problems.
Drought and water shortage reduce yields where land is not irrigated. This is why irrigation matters.
Soil erosion removes topsoil from the hills. Steep slopes and winter downpours make this worse.
Xylella fastidiosa, a bacterial disease of olive trees, was detected in the Salento (southern Puglia) in 2013 and has killed millions of olive trees.
Ageing farmers and rural depopulation leave fewer people to work the farms. This is why farms are harder to keep going.
Caporalato is illegal gangmaster hiring and exploitation of farm labourers, many of them migrants. This is why farm work can be unsafe and underpaid.
Many farms depend on EU Common Agricultural Policy (CAP) support (payments to farmers), so they are exposed if it changes.
Forests were cut down in the past, and the dry climate still threatens what remains.
Historic deforestation of the Apennines has left slopes exposed to erosion. Without tree roots to hold the soil, rain washes it away.
Reafforestation (replanting trees) of the Sila plateau in Calabria was carried out under the Cassa per il Mezzogiorno.
Summer wildfires destroy woodland in the dry season. The dry heat makes fires spread easily.
Fishing in the South is based on Mediterranean ports such as Mazara del Vallo in Sicily, and overfishing now limits catches.
Mazara del Vallo, Sicily, is one of Italy's main fishing ports.
Traditional tuna trapping, the mattanza, took place in Sicily at Favignana; it has now largely ended.
Overfishing (catching fish faster than stocks recover) in the Mediterranean reduces catches.
The South has some energy resources and is also a landing point for imported gas, with growing renewable power.
The Val d'Agri oilfield in Basilicata is Italy's largest onshore oilfield and one of the largest onshore oilfields in western Europe. This makes Basilicata a significant energy source.
Gas pipelines from Algeria land at Mazara del Vallo, and gas from Libya lands at Gela, both in Sicily.
The Trans Adriatic Pipeline (TAP), carrying gas from Azerbaijan, lands in Puglia and began flowing in 2020.
Puglia and Sicily are among Italy's leading regions for wind and solar power, which suit their sunny, open land.
Industry in the South has stayed weak compared with the North. Several causes reinforce each other.
Distance from markets raises the cost of transporting goods to buyers. This is why firms in the South struggle to compete.
Poor infrastructure: weak roads, railways and ports make transport slow and costly. This is why firms find it costly to move goods.
Small local market and low incomes: local demand is too small to support many firms.
Lack of capital and enterprise: few local firms have the funds or entrepreneurs to start up.
Organised crime: extortion payments, known as pizzo, deter investment because firms must pay criminals to operate.
Lack of raw materials: few are available locally for heavy industry.
The Cassa used state investment to build large growth poles, plants intended to spark industrial growth around them.
The Taranto steelworks was built by the state firm Italsider in the 1960s; it became one of Europe's largest steelworks, later called Ilva and now Acciaierie d'Italia.

Petrochemical plants (making chemicals from oil and gas) were built at Brindisi and at the Priolo–Augusta complex near Siracusa in Sicily, and a refinery at Gela in Sicily. These plants were state-led, part of the growth-pole policy.
The Bari–Brindisi–Taranto triangle is the South's own industrial area, not the industrial triangle of the North.
Cathedrals in the desert is the name for large, capital-intensive (needing huge investment but few workers) state plants that created few jobs and few local spin-off firms.
Car plants were another attempt to bring large-scale manufacturing to the South.
The Alfasud plant at Pomigliano d'Arco near Naples opened in 1972 and now builds the Fiat Panda. It brought car making close to Naples, a large city with workers.
Fiat's Melfi plant in Basilicata opened in the early 1990s and is now part of Stellantis. It brought a major car plant to inland Basilicata.
Fiat's plant at Termini Imerese, Sicily, closed in 2011. The closure shows how fragile southern manufacturing jobs are.
Some of the South's industry has brought serious problems as well as jobs.
In 2012 a court ordered parts of the Taranto steelworks seized because of pollution linked to illness in Taranto.
Lavoro nero is undeclared work in the informal, or black, economy, outside tax and labour rules, so workers lack protection and the state loses tax.
Current policy tries to close the North–South gap using EU and Italian funds and new growth sectors.

For EU cohesion policy (EU funding to reduce regional inequality) 2021–27, most of the South, including Campania, Puglia, Basilicata, Calabria and Sicily, is classed as less developed regions, with GDP per head below 75% of the EU average.
A single Special Economic Zone for the South (ZES Unica) began in January 2024, offering tax credits and simplified permits.
Italy's post-Covid National Recovery and Resilience Plan reserves at least 40% of its territorially allocated funds for the South.
Aerospace is a growth sector: Leonardo builds Boeing 787 fuselage sections at Grottaglie, near Taranto. This shows the South moving beyond heavy industry.
Agri-food is also a growth sector, building on the region's specialised produce. This is because local produce can be processed locally for added value.
Exams ask you to explain secondary activity (manufacturing) using factors such as labour and markets. For each factor, give the fact and the challenge it creates in the Mezzogiorno.
Labour: there is a large pool of unemployed workers, but low incomes limit local spending.
Raw materials: heavy industry depends on inputs brought in from outside, such as gas by pipeline.
Markets: the small local market and distant European markets mean firms face high transport costs.
Infrastructure: slow motorway upgrading and limited high-speed rail make transport costly and slow.
Government policy: the Cassa's growth poles and the ZES Unica attract investment, but capital-intensive plants create few jobs.
Tourism is a tertiary (service) activity that suits the South's sun, scenery and history.
Visitors come for the climate, the coast, the volcanoes of Vesuvius and Etna, the heritage sites and the food.

UNESCO sites (World Heritage Sites): Pompeii and Herculaneum (1997); the Amalfi Coast (1997); the Valley of the Temples, Agrigento (1997); the trulli of Alberobello, Puglia (1996); the sassi of Matera (1993); the historic centre of Naples (1995).
Taormina, Sicily, is a coastal tourist town. It is a coastal town, so it draws visitors for the sea and scenery.
The Costa Smeralda in north-east Sardinia was developed as a luxury resort from the 1960s by the Aga Khan. This was planned luxury tourism, so it differs from the mass tourism elsewhere.
Agriturismo is farm-stay tourism, bringing visitors into the countryside. This is why it suits the countryside, such as farms in hill areas.
Tourism brings benefits, but it also creates problems.
Seasonality: most visitors come in the summer months, leaving tourist jobs short-term. This is why tourism gives uneven year-round income.
Coastal overdevelopment: abusivismo, illegal building including on coasts, damages the landscape.
Crime: organised crime can affect businesses and tourist areas.
Poor transport: slow road and rail links limit access to the South's attractions.
Transport links open markets and bring investors and tourists, so poor links keep the region remote. The region's remoteness is partly a transport problem.
The Autostrada del Sole (A1, Milan–Rome–Naples) was completed in 1964. It linked the South to the industrial North, which opened routes for goods and people.
The A2 Salerno–Reggio Calabria motorway has been notorious for decades of slow, costly upgrading. This slow progress is why it counts as a transport problem.
High-speed rail reaches Naples and Salerno; the Naples–Bari line is being upgraded.
Gioia Tauro, Calabria, is Italy's largest container transhipment port (where containers are moved between ships). Because ships transfer cargo there, it is a hub for sea trade.
Ferries cross the Strait of Messina between Villa San Giovanni/Reggio Calabria and Messina. They link Sicily to the mainland, so island goods and visitors can move.
Ferries sail from Bari and Brindisi to Greece and Albania. This is why these ports matter for trade with Greece and Albania.
