A bridge across the Strait of Messina has been proposed, approved and challenged repeatedly over many years, so do not assume it is built.
Services provide jobs in the South, but not the same kind as in the North.
Public-sector employment (jobs paid by the state) is a large source of jobs in the South. This is because private industry is weak.
Informal employment, such as lavoro nero (undeclared work), is also large.
Private services are weaker than in the North.
Population is concentrated on the coastal lowlands and in cities, and thins out in the interior.
Campania has about 400 people per km², one of Italy's most densely populated regions. This is because of its fertile volcanic lowlands and the city of Naples.
Basilicata has about 55 people per km² and only about 540,000 people (2020s). This is because it is largely mountainous and remote.
Dense coastal lowlands and cities contrast with sparse interior uplands.
Fertile volcanic lowlands attract settlement; thin, stony soils and dry uplands do not.
Cities offer jobs in services and industry, drawing people from the interior.
Poverty and lack of jobs have pushed people out of the South for well over a century.
Large-scale emigration from the late 19th century went to the USA and Argentina. People left because of poverty and lack of work.
After the Second World War, emigration went to the industrial cities of northern Italy (Turin, Milan) and to Germany, Switzerland and Belgium.
Out-migration continues, as young graduates leave the region for work elsewhere in Italy and abroad. This is because jobs in the South are limited.
Fewer births and continued departures mean the population is ageing, while some migrants arrive across the sea.
Fertility (births per woman) was once high but is now very low: Italy's rate is about 1.2 children per woman (2023), among the lowest in the EU. This is why the population is ageing.
Sardinia's fertility rate is among the lowest in Italy.
Inland villages are ageing and depopulating, with few young residents. This is because young people leave and few children are born.
€1 house schemes in depopulating villages, for example Sambuca di Sicilia, sell houses for €1 to attract new residents.
Lampedusa, an Italian island south of Sicily, is a main landing point for migrants crossing the Mediterranean. It lies south of Sicily, so it is close to the sea route from Africa.
Standard Italian is shared across the country, but the South also has strong dialects and minority languages.
Standard Italian is the official language.
Strong regional dialects include Neapolitan and Sicilian.
Arbëreshë is spoken by Albanian-speaking communities in Calabria and Sicily, settled from the 15th century. This is why Albanian is still spoken there.
Griko is a Greek dialect spoken in the Salento (Puglia) and southern Calabria.
Catalan is spoken in Alghero, Sardinia.
Religion remains an important part of southern life.
The population is mainly Roman Catholic, with strong traditional practice.
The Feast of San Gennaro, patron saint of Naples, includes the ritual of the liquefaction of his blood.
Culture in the South combines folk traditions, regional identity and football. Religion and language, covered above, are part of it too.
The tarantella is a fast folk dance of southern Italy, named after Taranto.
SSC Napoli won Serie A (Italy's top football league) in 1987, 1990, 2023 and 2025.
The art of the Neapolitan pizza maker was added to UNESCO's intangible heritage list in 2017.
Sicily and Sardinia are autonomous regions with a special statute, giving their regional governments extra powers.
Clientelism, the exchange of votes for favours, and organised crime both influence local politics.
Naples is the South's largest city. Its rapid, unplanned growth left serious problems.
Naples is the South's largest city, with about 900,000 people in the city and about 3 million in the metropolitan city (2020s).
The Spanish Quarter (Quartieri Spagnoli) is a dense, overcrowded historic district. Overcrowding there followed rapid growth.
The Vele di Scampia are large 1960s–70s public housing blocks on the northern edge of Naples, linked with Camorra (Naples organised crime) drug dealing; several have been demolished.
The Naples waste crisis of 2007–08 left rubbish piled in the streets after landfills filled. This shows how rapid growth overwhelmed city services.
The Camorra was involved in illegal dumping and burning of waste in the Terra dei Fuochi (land of fires), between Naples and Caserta. This is why the area is called the land of fires.
Rapid, unplanned growth fed by rural migration produced overcrowding and illegal building.
Several advantages explain why Naples grew into the South's largest city.
Site: the city lies on the Bay of Naples beside Vesuvius.
Port: the harbour gave access to sea trade. Trade through the port helped the city grow.
Capital: Naples was the capital of the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies until 1861, a centre of government.
Fertile volcanic hinterland (the surrounding area) supports farming and markets around the city.
Rural in-migration: people moved from the countryside to the city for work and services.
Rural settlement reflects the region's history of danger and poverty, and today many villages are emptying.
Hilltop villages were built for defence and to avoid the malarial coastal lowlands. This is why many villages sit high up and far from the farmland.
Matera's sassi (cave dwellings) were evacuated in the 1950s, and their residents moved to new housing; the sassi became a UNESCO site in 1993.
Matera was European Capital of Culture in 2019. This shows how a once-evacuated town was revived as a cultural attraction.
Depopulation and abandonment of interior villages continue as young people leave.

Ireland is a single island but two political regions: the Republic of Ireland and Northern Ireland. Their economic, political and cultural activities interact across a border. Both regions exist because of the 1921 partition (the division of the island into two political units), and their cultural groups are not evenly matched, so it helps to know the starting facts about each.

Northern Ireland was established in 1921 with six counties: Antrim, Armagh, Down, Fermanagh, Londonderry (Derry) and Tyrone. It is part of the United Kingdom, so it is governed within the UK, not by the Irish state.
The Irish Free State was established in 1922. Ireland left the Commonwealth (the association of former British territories) and was declared a republic in 1949.
The Republic has about 5.15 million people (Census 2022, the official population count) and Northern Ireland about 1.9 million (Census 2021), so the two regions differ greatly in size.
Northern Ireland's population is divided into two main cultural groups. Their identity, religion, schooling and language differ, and this is the background to the political interaction that follows.

Nationalists, mostly Catholic, identify as Irish. Unionists (people who want Northern Ireland to stay in the UK), mostly Protestant, identify as British. Some people identify as Northern Irish instead.
In Census 2021, by religion (or religion brought up in), Catholic was about 46% and Protestant and other Christian about 43%. This was the first census in which Catholics outnumbered Protestants.
In the Republic, Census 2022 gave Catholic about 69% and no religion about 14%, which shows the Republic's population is far more uniformly Catholic.

Most children in Northern Ireland attend schools of their own community, and housing is often segregated by community (the two groups live in separate areas), so everyday contact between the groups is limited.
Irish and Ulster-Scots (a Scots-based language tradition of Ulster) are officially recognised under the Identity and Language (Northern Ireland) Act 2022.

The two communities disagreed about whether Northern Ireland should be in the UK or united with the Republic, and the disagreement turned violent. The Good Friday Agreement of 1998 set up a new way for them to share power.
The Troubles, from the late 1960s to 1998, killed over 3,500 people and left the two communities divided by violence and political deadlock (no side able to make decisions).
The Good Friday (Belfast) Agreement was signed on 10 April 1998. A referendum (a public vote) approved it on 22 May 1998: about 71% Yes in Northern Ireland and about 94% Yes in the Republic.
The Republic changed Articles 2 and 3 of its Constitution, which had claimed Northern Ireland as part of the national territory, so the Republic gave up that claim.
Power-sharing: a Northern Ireland Assembly (its elected parliament) in which ministers from both communities share government, so neither side can govern alone.
The North/South Ministerial Council and other cross-border bodies link the Irish government with the Northern Ireland executive (its government), so the two regions co-operate on shared issues.
Consent principle: Northern Ireland remains in the UK unless a majority of its people vote otherwise. Under the Agreement, people may hold Irish or British citizenship or both.
Power-sharing needs both communities to take part, so it is fragile. The Assembly shows how political interaction can break down and recover.
The Assembly has been suspended several times, meaning it stopped working and its powers were paused, for example in the two-year collapse before 2024.
After a two-year collapse it was restored in February 2024, when Michelle O'Neill became the first nationalist First Minister.
After 1998, the border mattered less in economic life and the two regions worked together more. Conflict had held this back, so peace let activity grow across the whole island.
Conflict deterred investment and tourism; after 1998, falling violence allowed both to recover on the island as a whole.
Cross-border bodies include InterTradeIreland and Waterways Ireland. Tourism Ireland markets the whole island abroad, so visitors see one destination, not two.
A Single Electricity Market for the whole island has operated since 2007, so electricity is bought and sold as one all-island market.
The Dublin–Belfast Enterprise rail service and the M1/A1 road corridor link the two main cities, which makes cross-border travel and trade easier.

The International Fund for Ireland was set up in 1986. The EU PEACE programme began in 1995 as PEACE I; the current PEACE PLUS programme runs from 2021 to 2027. Both fund peace-building and co-operation.
Culture and sport do not follow the border either. Several organisations cover the whole island, although some cultural symbols still divide communities.
The GAA (Gaelic Athletic Association), the Irish rugby team, the Catholic Church and the Church of Ireland are organised on an all-island basis, so they treat Ireland as one unit.
The Catholic and Church of Ireland archbishops of Armagh are each Primate of All Ireland (the senior bishop of their church across the island).
The Irish language and Irish sport cross the border, while parades and flags remain sources of tension between communities, because they express one community's identity.
Brexit (the UK leaving the EU) shows the three processes interacting at the border. It affected trade, politics and identity on the island all at once.
In the UK referendum on EU membership, 23 June 2016, about 52% voted Leave overall; about 56% voted Remain in Northern Ireland and about 62% Remain in Scotland.
The UK left the EU on 31 January 2020; the transition period (when old rules still applied) ended on 31 December 2020. The 2016 referendum did not itself end membership.
The Irish–Northern Irish land border is about 499 km long and became the UK–EU land border, which raised the question of customs checks between the two regions.

The Northern Ireland Protocol kept Northern Ireland aligned with many EU single-market rules for goods, avoiding checks at the land border (a hard border). The Windsor Framework (February 2023) revised it.
The Common Travel Area between Ireland and the UK has existed since 1923. Irish passport holders in Northern Ireland keep EU free movement, the right to live and work in the EU.

In Belgium the language communities and the political regions do not coincide, so politics is organised around language. Belgium is the main European example of cultural groups and political regions interacting.
Belgium became independent in 1830. Its population is about 11.8 million (2024).

Flanders (about 6.8 million) is Dutch-speaking in the north. Wallonia (about 3.7 million) is French-speaking in the south. Brussels-Capital (about 1.2 million) is officially bilingual, so both languages are used there.
A German-speaking community in the east has fewer than 80,000 people.
Dutch speakers are about 6 in 10 of the population and French speakers about 4 in 10.
French was long the language of government, courts and universities, so the language of the minority (French, about 4 in 10) once held the main public institutions.
Language differences in Belgium were sharpened by a shift in wealth between north and south. Politics then split along language lines.

Economic reversal: Wallonia's coal and steel industries (Liège, Charleroi and the Sambre–Meuse valley) declined, while Flanders grew through the port of Antwerp, Europe's second-largest port, and modern industry.
The Catholic University of Leuven split in 1968; its French-speaking section moved to a new town, Louvain-la-Neuve, in Wallonia, so even education separated by language.
There are no nationwide parties: each party stands in one language community only, so no party represents voters in all of Belgium.
Political consequences: Belgium went 541 days without a new government in 2010–11, which shows how hard it is to form a government when each party stands in one language community only.
The Flemish nationalist N-VA has been the largest party since 2010, and its leader Bart De Wever became Prime Minister in February 2025.
Belgium's federal solution (power divided between a national government and regional ones) gives its language communities and regions considerable self-government.
Brussels hosts the main institutions of the EU and the headquarters of NATO (a military alliance).
Other European countries also have cultural groups tied to regions. Some share power peacefully, while others have faced independence movements.
Switzerland has four national languages: German (about 6 in 10), French (about 2 in 10), Italian (under 1 in 10) and Romansh (under 1%).
Switzerland has 26 cantons (its regional units) with wide powers. Power is shared between language groups and cantons, which keeps the country stable.
Basque (Euskara) is unrelated to any other European language. The Basque Country lies in both Spain and France.
ETA, a Basque separatist group, declared a definitive end to violence in 2011 and dissolved in 2018.

Catalonia has its own language, Catalan. It held an independence referendum on 1 October 2017 that Spain's courts declared illegal. Spain imposed direct rule (control from the central government) using Article 155 of its constitution.
The Basque Country and Catalonia are autonomous communities of Spain (regions with self-government) and among its wealthiest regions.
Scottish independence referendum, 18 September 2014: about 55% voted No.
The examples above share one pattern, and a general statement of it can round off a 30-mark answer.
Where cultural and political regions do not match, tension arises.

Outcomes range from devolution or federalism (Belgium, Spain) and power-sharing (Northern Ireland) to violent conflict (the Troubles). Devolution means a central government passes some powers to a region.
Political union is the EU's move beyond economic co-operation towards shared political institutions and decisions.
The Maastricht Treaty created the EU and planned the single currency (its dates are in the s4 notes).
The draft EU Constitution was rejected by French and Dutch voters in 2005, so it did not come into force.
The Lisbon Treaty created a permanent President of the European Council and a High Representative for Foreign Affairs. It extended qualified majority voting and the powers of the European Parliament.

Qualified majority voting: a decision passes when enough member states, representing enough of the EU population, support it. Unanimity requires every member state to agree, so one state can block a decision.
European Parliament: 720 MEPs (Members of the European Parliament, elected by voters) after the 2024 elections; Ireland elects 14.
Competing visions: a federal Europe with stronger central power, or a Europe of nation states co-operating on shared aims.
Eurosceptic parties (parties sceptical of the EU) have grown across Europe, opposing further political integration.
Economic union is the EU's shared market and shared currency. Not every member state takes part in both.
The single market removes barriers to trade, services, capital and labour between member states, so goods, services, money and workers can move freely.
21 member states use the euro in 2026. Bulgaria joined on 1 January 2026, replacing the lev. Croatia joined in 2023.

Euro countries: Austria, Belgium, Bulgaria, Croatia, Cyprus, Estonia, Finland, France, Germany, Greece, Ireland, Italy, Latvia, Lithuania, Luxembourg, Malta, the Netherlands, Portugal, Slovakia, Slovenia and Spain.
Not in the euro: Denmark (legal opt-out, a formal exemption); Sweden (voted No in a 2003 referendum and stays out by not joining the exchange-rate mechanism); Poland, Czechia, Hungary and Romania.
The European Central Bank in Frankfurt sets one interest rate for the euro area. Since November 2014 its Single Supervisory Mechanism has supervised the big banks.
A state must meet set economic tests before joining the euro, which keeps weaker economies from harming the shared currency. Once in, people gain several benefits.

Convergence (Maastricht) criteria: low inflation (slow price rises); government deficit (spending above income in a year) no more than 3% of GDP (the value of a country's output); government debt no more than 60% of GDP.
Two more criteria: a stable exchange rate, held for two years in ERM II (a system that keeps a currency steady against the euro); and low long-term interest rates.
Benefits for people in the eurozone: no currency exchange costs; easy price comparison between countries; no exchange-rate risk in trade and travel; generally low interest rates and inflation.
The euro area met serious financial trouble after 2010. A bailout (emergency loans to a government) was needed in some countries.
Ireland's EU/IMF bailout of about €85 billion was agreed in November 2010 and exited in December 2013.
Greece received three bailouts (2010, 2012 and 2015), ending in 2018, which shows the crisis there lasted longer than in Ireland.
NextGenerationEU, agreed in 2020, is a recovery fund of about €750 billion financed by joint EU borrowing, so member states borrow together.
Sovereignty is the power to make decisions for a state. Membership pools some of it; some areas stay national.
Pooling sovereignty means member states share decision-making in areas such as trade and the single market.
Taxation, defence and foreign policy remain largely national, and decisions in these areas are mostly made by unanimity.
Brexit is an example of national sovereignty being reasserted against pooled decision-making.

Article 7 procedures, which could suspend a member's voting rights, were opened against Poland (2017) and Hungary (2018) over rule-of-law concerns (whether governments respect courts and legal limits).
Ireland's own history in the EU gives specific examples of sovereignty being pooled, tested and defended.
Crotty v An Taoiseach (1987): Ireland's Supreme Court ruled that significant EU treaty changes need a referendum.
Irish voters rejected the Nice Treaty (2001) and approved it in 2002. They rejected the Lisbon Treaty in June 2008 and approved it in October 2009.
Ireland's corporation tax (tax on company profits) rate is 12.5%. Under the OECD agreement, a 15% minimum rate applies to large firms (turnover over €750 million) from 2024.

Apple ruling: on 10 September 2024 the EU Court of Justice ruled that Ireland must recover €13 billion, plus interest, in unpaid tax from Apple as illegal state aid (help from a state that unfairly favours one company).
Ireland is militarily neutral and not in NATO. It is outside the Schengen area (the EU zone without passport checks), linked to its Common Travel Area with the UK.
The EU faces a mix of social and economic challenges, and exams ask for both kinds.

Social challenges: an ageing population; migration and asylum pressures; youth unemployment; rising populism (politics that claims to speak for ordinary people against elites) and euroscepticism; regional inequality.
Economic challenges: public debt; competitiveness; energy security; the cost of enlargement; the economic effects of Brexit.
Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine began on 24 February 2022. It caused an energy price shock and a large refugee movement into the EU.
The challenges of political union and sovereignty include disagreement over how far to deepen integration, and the slowness of decisions that need unanimity.
Enlargement means admitting new member states, and it is debated for and against. The benefits of further expansion are in the s4 notes.

Candidate countries (officially recognised as being on the path to join, so they are the likely future members):Ukraine and Moldova (June 2022); Bosnia and Herzegovina (December 2022); Georgia (December 2023).
Other candidates: Albania, Montenegro, North Macedonia and Serbia; Turkey (candidate since 1999, with talks frozen).
Arguments against enlargement: the cost of accession (joining) and of EU funding, slower decision-making with more members, and doubts over whether candidates are ready.
The Gaeltacht is the area where Irish is the community language, the language people use in everyday life. Its extent has shrunk as speakers have declined, and the decline began in the 1800s.

Census 1851 (a count of the whole population) was the first census to count Irish speakers. It found about 1.5 million Irish speakers, about 23% of the population, and Irish-speaking areas then covered much of the west and south.
The Great Famine (1845–49) and emigration (people leaving the country) hit the poor, western, Irish-speaking areas hardest, so the Irish-speaking population fell fastest where Irish was strongest.
National schools, set up in 1831, taught through English, so children learned to read and write in a language that was not their home language.
English became the language of law, trade, politics, the Church and emigration. Parents saw English as the route to work, so many chose not to pass Irish on to their children.
Census 1891 shows the result: about 680,000 Irish speakers, about 14% of the population, down from about 23% in 1851.
From the 1890s people tried to reverse the decline. The new state then gave the Gaeltacht its first official boundaries, and later redrew them.
The Gaelic League (Conradh na Gaeilge), a revival movement, founded in 1893 by Douglas Hyde and Eoin MacNeill, promoted the language, to stop its decline.
The new state's language policy made Irish compulsory in schools and required for some public jobs, so that the state itself supported the language.

Coimisiún na Gaeltachta (the commission set up to define the Gaeltacht) reported in 1926 and defined two types of Gaeltacht. Fíor-Ghaeltacht ('true' Gaeltacht): districts where 80% or more spoke Irish.
Breac-Ghaeltacht ('partly' Gaeltacht): districts with 25–79% Irish speakers. The 1926 definitions together covered a large area across many western and southern counties.

The Gaeltacht Areas Order 1956 (a government order, not a new law) shrank the official Gaeltacht to areas where Irish was still the community language, because Irish had weakened in the Breac-Ghaeltacht districts.
The Department of the Gaeltacht (Roinn na Gaeltachta) was set up in 1956. Gaeltarra Éireann, the Gaeltacht industry body, followed in 1957. Later small extensions were made by order.
Today's Gaeltacht lies in seven counties, and one of them, Meath, is an unusual case because its Gaeltacht was planned by the state.
Gaeltacht areas lie in seven counties: Donegal, Mayo, Galway, Kerry, Cork, Waterford and Meath.

The Meath Gaeltacht was built by planned colonies (settlements created by the state, not areas where Irish had survived): Ráth Chairn, settled in 1935 by families moved from Connemara, and Baile Ghib, settled in 1937.
Galway (Conamara) has the largest Gaeltacht population; Donegal is second.
Census 2022: the Gaeltacht population was about 106,000, and about 20,000 Gaeltacht residents speak Irish daily outside the education system, so only a minority use it as an everyday language.
Nationally (Census 2022): about 1.87 million people (about 40%) said they could speak Irish, but only about 72,000 spoke it daily outside the education system.
The state and communities have built institutions to protect Irish, from development agencies to broadcasting and official recognition.

Údarás na Gaeltachta, the Gaeltacht development authority, was set up in 1980 to replace Gaeltarra Éireann. It creates jobs so people can stay in the Gaeltacht. The Gaoth Dobhair (Gweedore) industrial estate in Co. Donegal is an example of Gaeltacht industry.
Raidió na Gaeltachta began broadcasting in 1972. TG4 (originally Teilifís na Gaeilge) launched on 31 October 1996. Both give Irish a presence in the media.
The Official Languages Act 2003 (amended 2021) gives Irish official status, which means public bodies must provide services in it.
Irish became an official EU language in 2007 and gained full working-language status on 1 January 2022.
The 20-Year Strategy for the Irish Language, a long-term state plan, covers 2010 to 2030.
Gaeltacht summer colleges give young people intensive immersion in Irish, so they use the language all day.
The 2012 Act changed how the Gaeltacht is defined. Instead of a fixed map, boundaries now depend on how much Irish is actually spoken.
The Gaeltacht Act 2012 defined the Gaeltacht by language use rather than by a fixed map, so boundaries now depend on language use.
Gaeltacht Language Planning Areas: 26, so the Gaeltacht is now a set of planning units, each needing a language plan (a local plan to strengthen the use of Irish).
Gaeltacht Service Towns, and Irish Language Networks outside the Gaeltacht, extend Irish use beyond the core areas.
Even with these supports, the use of Irish as a daily language in the Gaeltacht has kept falling. A 2007 study set out how much daily use is needed to keep it alive.
The Comprehensive Linguistic Study of the Use of Irish in the Gaeltacht (2007) found that Irish is viable as a community language only where at least 67% of people speak it daily.
Its 2015 update warned that Irish could cease to be the community language in most Gaeltacht districts within about ten years.
In-migration of English speakers (people moving in from outside) weakens Irish, because English becomes the language of daily life in the area.
Suburban growth, such as Galway city's spread west, brings the Gaeltacht edge into contact with English-speaking suburbs.
Tourism, emigration of young people and English-language media add further pressure on Irish as the language of the community.
Responses target the pressures above, by keeping Irish speakers in the Gaeltacht and giving them reasons and ways to use the language.
Housing with language conditions, so that Irish speakers can afford to stay in Gaeltacht areas.
Jobs through Údarás na Gaeltachta and Gaeltacht industry, so that people do not have to leave to find work.
Irish-medium schooling (teaching through Irish) and preschools, so children learn the language early.
Language plans in each Language Planning Area.
Family supports for Irish-speaking households, and Irish-language media such as TG4 and Raidió na Gaeltachta.
Belgium is a brief comparison from outside Ireland: a language boundary fixed in law. There is more on its present-day relations in the notes on the next part of this topic.
The language border between Dutch- and French-speaking areas was fixed by laws of 1962 and 1963, so the boundary between language regions became official.

The first state reform came in 1970. Belgium became a federal state in 1993 (power shared between central and regional governments), with Flanders, Wallonia and Brussels-Capital as its regions. Brussels is officially bilingual.
Dublin's growth has spread from the city into the surrounding counties, creating a city region (a city and the area that depends on it).

Suburban expansion (new housing on the edge of the city) from the 1950s and 1960s led to the Advisory Regional Plan for Dublin (Myles Wright, 1967), which proposed new towns west of the city: Tallaght, Clondalkin, Lucan and Blanchardstown.
Ballymun, an example of high-rise housing: seven 15-storey tower blocks built 1966–69 and demolished between 2004 and 2015 under a regeneration plan (a plan to rebuild and improve a run-down area).
Census 2022: County Dublin had about 1.46 million people.
The Greater Dublin Area (Dublin, Meath, Kildare and Wicklow) had about 2.1 million people in Census 2022, about 40% of the State's population.
Commuter towns (towns whose residents travel to work in the city) in the surrounding counties, such as Navan, Drogheda, Naas and Newbridge.
As Dublin grew, the areas that govern it were redrawn several times, from adding townships to splitting the county council.
Rathmines and Pembroke townships were added to Dublin city in 1930, extending the city boundary.

Local Government (Dublin) Act 1993: from 1 January 1994, Dublin County Council was replaced by Fingal, South Dublin and Dún Laoghaire–Rathdown County Councils. The county had grown too large to govern as one unit, and local government needed to be closer to the people.
Dublin Corporation was renamed Dublin City Council in 2002 under the Local Government Act 2001.
Census 2022 populations of the four Dublin local authorities: Dublin City about 590,000; Fingal about 330,000; South Dublin about 300,000; Dún Laoghaire–Rathdown about 235,000.
The Dublin Regional Authority was set up in 1994.

The Local Government Reform Act 2014 replaced the regional authorities, including the Dublin Regional Authority, with three regional assemblies from 2015: Northern and Western; Eastern and Midland; Southern.
A growing city region brings problems, and the state has responded with planning, transport, regeneration and new forms of governance.

Problems: urban sprawl (a city spreading outwards over farmland), long commutes, congestion, housing costs, one-off housing (single houses built in the countryside) and dormitory growth (towns that people sleep in but work elsewhere).

The National Planning Framework (Project Ireland 2040), published in 2018, aims for half of future population growth in the five cities (Dublin, Cork, Limerick, Galway and Waterford) and to limit sprawl.
Transport: the M50 orbital motorway (a ring road around the city) was built in stages from 1990, the Luas light rail opened in 2004, and DART serves the suburbs by rail.
Regeneration: the IFSC (International Financial Services Centre) was set up in the Docklands in 1987; the Docklands and Ballymun are regeneration areas.
The Citizens' Assembly reported in 2023, recommending a directly elected mayor (a mayor chosen by voters, not by councillors) for Dublin.
Limerick elected Ireland's first directly elected mayor in June 2024, after a plebiscite (a public vote on one question) in 2019.
Dublin is not the only place where boundaries moved. Other cities were extended or merged, and the EU divided Ireland into economic regions for funding.
Cork city boundary extended on 31 May 2019, taking in suburbs such as Ballincollig, Glanmire and Blarney from the county.
Limerick City and County Council and Waterford City and County Council were formed by merger in 2014.
From 1999/2000 Ireland was divided for EU purposes into two NUTS 2 regions (the EU's standard statistical regions): the Border, Midland and Western (BMW) region, and the Southern and Eastern region.
The BMW region kept Objective 1 (poorest-region) funding status for 2000–06, which meant it qualified for the highest level of EU support.
The economic regions were drawn for EU funding, so their boundaries follow economic need rather than language or identity.
The European Union began as a way to make war between European states impossible, by tying their economies together after the Second World War.

Reasons: peace after two world wars; rebuilding after the war; coal and steel placed under shared control, so no state could secretly build up weapons; economic growth; the Cold War (the rivalry between the communist East and the capitalist West).
Schuman Declaration, 9 May 1950 (now Europe Day), proposed pooling coal and steel production.
The Treaty of Paris (1951) put the shared control of coal and steel into practice, because it set up the European Coal and Steel Community (ECSC).
The Treaty of Rome (1957, in force 1958) set up the European Economic Community (EEC) and Euratom (the European Atomic Energy Community).
The six founders ('the Six') were Belgium, France, West Germany, Italy, Luxembourg and the Netherlands.
Deepening means the members drew closer together, with more shared rules and institutions. Only the dates are given here; the issues each step raised come later.
Single market (one market with free movement of goods, services, people and money, so trade between members is easier): from 1 January 1993.
Maastricht Treaty: signed 7 February 1992; in force 1 November 1993, creating the European Union.
Euro (the shared currency): launched 1 January 1999 for banks and electronic payments; notes and coins from 1 January 2002.
Widening means adding new member states. Each enlargement is listed by date, with the countries that joined.
1973: Ireland, the UK and Denmark, the first enlargement. 1981: Greece. 1986: Spain and Portugal.
1990: East Germany joined through reunification with West Germany, not as a new member state.
2004: ten countries joined: Cyprus, Czech Republic, Estonia, Hungary, Latvia, Lithuania, Malta, Poland, Slovakia and Slovenia.
2007: Bulgaria and Romania, not 2004. 2013: Croatia, the most recent member.
The UK left on 31 January 2020, so it is now a former member, leaving 27 members with about 450 million people (2024).
The end of communism in Eastern Europe made the biggest enlargement possible, and it changed the EU for both new and old members.
The Berlin Wall fell on 9 November 1989, opening the way for former communist states to seek EU membership.

Copenhagen criteria (1993), the conditions for joining: stable democracy, rule of law, human rights and protection of minorities; a working market economy able to cope with competition; and the ability to take on the obligations of membership.
Most of the 2004 entrants (such as Poland and Hungary), and both 2007 entrants, were former communist states, which is why the fall of communism led to this enlargement.
Effects on newer members: economic growth, EU funds and emigration (workers leaving for richer members).
Effects on older members: competition for jobs and investment, and migration from the newer members.
Croatia joined the Schengen area (the area of passport-free travel between member states) in 2023. Bulgaria and Romania joined it fully on 1 January 2025.
Enlargement brought Ireland both opportunities and competition. Ireland opened its doors early in 2004, which shaped who came and what followed.
In 2004 Ireland, the UK and Sweden were the only existing members to give the new members' citizens immediate access to their labour markets.
Polish was the most common language other than English and Irish spoken at home in Census 2016 and Census 2022, showing the size of the Polish community.
Advantages: a larger market; a labour supply for the Celtic Tiger economy (Ireland's period of rapid growth); cultural diversity; export opportunities.

Disadvantages: competition for foreign direct investment (companies from abroad setting up factories and offices) from lower-cost states; less EU regional funding for Ireland; pressure on wages and services.
Example of investment competition: Dell announced in January 2009 that it would move its manufacturing from Limerick to Łódź, Poland, with the loss of about 1,900 jobs.
Further expansion would affect both the EU and the countries waiting to join. The current candidate countries are named in a separate subsection.
Benefits of further expansion for the EU: a larger single market with more consumers, which means more trade, and greater stability on its borders.
Benefits for candidates: access to the single market and to EU funding, and, because they must meet the Copenhagen criteria, reforms to meet the Copenhagen criteria (the conditions for joining).

Partition of Ireland (dividing the island into two political units) redrew a political boundary across a single island. Its present-day effects, including the Good Friday Agreement and Brexit, are in the next subsection.
The Government of Ireland Act 1920 partitioned the island. Northern Ireland was established in 1921 with six of Ulster's nine counties, so Ulster itself was divided.
Cavan, Donegal and Monaghan went to the Irish Free State.
The Anglo-Irish Treaty was signed in December 1921.
Boundary Commission (1925), the body set up to review the border: its report was not published, and the border was left unchanged.
The border created a nationalist minority in the north (people who wanted a united Ireland) and a small Protestant minority in the south.
Impact: nationalists in Northern Ireland faced discrimination, which fuelled the civil rights movement from 1968 and then the Troubles (the conflict in Northern Ireland).
Communities, parishes and farms were divided by the border, so everyday life was cut across.
Yugoslavia was a multi-ethnic federal state that fell apart in the 1990s. Its break-up shows how new borders can leave cultural groups on the wrong side.
Yugoslavia was a multi-ethnic federal state. Its new borders followed the old internal republic lines, leaving Serb, Croat and Bosniak minorities on the 'wrong' side of them.
Slovenia and Croatia declared independence in 1991, breaking away from the federal state; Bosnia and Herzegovina followed in 1992.
War and ethnic cleansing (forcing a group out of an area by violence) followed in Bosnia and Herzegovina.
Srebrenica, July 1995: about 8,000 Bosniak men and boys were killed by Bosnian Serb forces.
The Dayton Agreement (1995) divided Bosnia and Herzegovina into two entities: the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina and Republika Srpska.
Montenegro became independent in 2006, a further split of the old state. Kosovo declared independence on 17 February 2008; Serbia does not recognise it.
After the Second World War, borders in central Europe were moved by the victorious powers, and millions of people moved with them.
In 1945 Poland's western border moved to the Oder–Neisse line. The USSR took Poland's eastern lands, so Poland shifted westward.
Millions of Germans were expelled westwards, and Poles were resettled from the east into the lands Germany had lost.
The Berlin Wall was built in 1961, dividing Germany and Berlin, so the city was split in two.
Germany was reunified on 3 October 1990, so the division ended, after the Berlin Wall fell in 1989.
The collapse of communism also split two multi-national states. One split left minorities behind; the other was peaceful.
The USSR (the Soviet Union) broke up in 1991 into 15 independent states, such as Estonia and Latvia.
Ethnic Russians became minorities in newly independent states. In Estonia and Latvia they make up roughly a fifth to a quarter of the population.
Czechoslovakia split peacefully into the Czech Republic and Slovakia on 1 January 1993, the 'Velvet Divorce'.
Cyprus is a divided island that is also an EU member, so a political boundary there has a direct effect on how EU law applies.
The Turkish invasion of July 1974 divided Cyprus between Greek Cypriots in the south and Turkish Cypriots in the north.
The UN buffer zone, the Green Line (a strip that keeps the two sides apart), runs through Nicosia.
The 'Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus' is recognised only by Turkey, so almost no other state accepts it.
2004 Annan Plan referendum: about 65% of Turkish Cypriots voted Yes, and about 76% of Greek Cypriots voted No.
Cyprus joined the EU in 2004, one of ten countries that year,, but EU law is suspended in the north, so the division continues inside the EU.
A non-European example of a political boundary redrawn along religious lines.
Partition of India, August 1947: India and Pakistan (including East Pakistan, now Bangladesh) were created along religious lines.
Around 15 million people were displaced, and hundreds of thousands were killed in communal violence (violence between religious communities).
The examples can be pulled together into three conclusions, which are useful for ending a 30-mark answer.
Boundaries drawn across cultural groups create minorities, displacement and conflict, as in Ireland, Yugoslavia and India.
Boundaries drawn around cultural groups, as in Belgium, can reduce conflict but can harden division.
Shared institutions, such as power-sharing and EU membership, can soften the effect of a border.
The region studied is the Republic of India. Pakistan, Bangladesh and Nepal are referred to only as neighbours, so keep them out of your answers as parts of the region.

India is part of South Asia, a subcontinent (a large landmass that is part of a continent but distinct from the rest of it), bounded by the Himalayas to the north, the Arabian Sea to the west and the Bay of Bengal to the east.
India is the world's seventh-largest country by area, about 3.3 million km².
The Tropic of Cancer (the line of latitude north of the equator, marking the northern edge of the tropics) crosses central India, so much of the country lies in the tropics.
Neighbours, which are not part of the region studied: Pakistan to the west, China and Nepal to the north, Bangladesh to the east.
The republic has 28 states and 8 union territories (areas ruled more directly by the central government); its capital is New Delhi.
India is treated as a subcontinental region because of its size, the Himalayan barrier that gives it physical unity, and its own cultural and economic identity.

A sketch map earns marks for an accurate outline and for showing and naming each feature asked for. Names may go on the map itself or in a key, so choose one named example of each feature and learn where it goes.
Outline: a triangular peninsula (land almost surrounded by sea) tapering to the south, with a north-eastern lobe around Bangladesh.

Relief (the shape of the land), one option: outline the Himalayas as a band along the northern border, or outline the Deccan Plateau as the peninsula south of the Narmada, between the Western and Eastern Ghats.

River: the Ganges, drawn from the Himalayas in Uttarakhand south-east across the northern plain, past Varanasi, to its delta (the fan of land where a river splits and meets the sea) on the Bay of Bengal. Show it within India, ending at the delta.

Urban centres as dots on the correct river or coast: Mumbai on the west coast; Kolkata on the Hooghly near the Bay of Bengal; Delhi on the Yamuna in the north; Chennai on the east coast; Bengaluru on the southern Deccan.
Agricultural region as an outlined area: Punjab in the north-west (wheat and the Green Revolution, the introduction of high-yielding crops and modern inputs), or Assam (tea, Brahmaputra valley).
Industrial region as an outlined area: the Chota Nagpur Plateau and Damodar valley, north-east of the Deccan around Jamshedpur, or Mumbai–Pune.
India's climate is dominated by the monsoon, which divides the year into three seasons. Understanding the monsoon explains most of India's farming, rivers and hazards.
India has a tropical monsoon climate. A monsoon is a seasonal reversal of wind direction, not simply a wet period, so the winds blow from a different direction in summer and in winter.
The word monsoon comes from the Arabic word for season.
Hot season: March to May, with the hottest conditions on the northern plains, because they are far inland and the land heats strongly before the rains.
Wet south-west monsoon: June to September, bringing most of the year's rain, because moist winds from the ocean blow onto the land.
Cool dry season: October to February, when most of India is dry because the winds blow off the land.
The monsoon retreats in October and November, marking the change between the wet and dry seasons.
The summer monsoon is driven by heating of the land and by the movement of global wind belts. Follow the steps in order, because each one causes the next.
1. Intense heating of the land in early summer creates low pressure (rising warm air) over north-west India and the Tibetan Plateau, which draws in air from the cooler ocean.
2. The Intertropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ, the belt near the equator where trade winds from both hemispheres meet) shifts north over India.

3. South-east trade winds (steady winds blowing towards the equator) cross the equator and are deflected by the Coriolis force (the effect of the Earth's spin, which bends winds) into south-west winds.
4. These winds pick up moisture over the Indian Ocean and reach the land as the monsoon.
5. The subtropical westerly jet stream (a fast, high-altitude river of air) moves north of the Himalayas in early summer, and the monsoon arrives suddenly, a 'burst'.
6. The jet stream returns south of the Himalayas in winter, when the monsoon withdraws.
The monsoon does not arrive everywhere at once. It sweeps north in two branches, which hit different parts of India first.
The south-west monsoon normally reaches Kerala around 1 June and covers all of India by mid-July.
It brings about three-quarters of India's annual rainfall, falling mainly in June to September, so the other eight months share the remaining quarter.
The Arabian Sea branch strikes the Western Ghats (the mountain range along the west coast) first, dropping heavy rain on the windward side, the side facing the wind.
The Bay of Bengal branch strikes the north-east hills, then is turned west along the Ganges plain by the Himalayas, bringing rain eastwards and along the plain.
Rainfall in India depends on where the monsoon winds meet high ground. Mountains force moist air up, making one side very wet and the other dry.
Relief (orographic) rain: moist air is forced up the windward slopes of the Western Ghats, cools and drops its rain, giving heavy rain on the Konkan and Malabar coasts.
The Deccan Plateau behind the Western Ghats lies in their rain shadow (the dry area on the sheltered side of mountains, where the air has already lost its moisture) and is much drier.
Mawsynram and Cherrapunji, in the Khasi Hills of Meghalaya, are among the wettest places on earth, due to relief rain from the Bay of Bengal branch.
Rainfall falls off westwards along the Ganges plain: Kolkata in the east is wetter than Delhi in the north-west, because the winds lose moisture as they travel inland.
The Thar Desert in Rajasthan is the driest region, because the Arabian Sea branch passes parallel to the Aravalli Range and has no barrier to force it upwards.
In winter the wind pattern reverses and India is mostly dry, but there are two regional exceptions. Both matter for farming.
High pressure over Central Asia gives north-east winds that blow off the land, so most of India is dry in winter, because air from land carries little moisture.
The Himalayas shelter India from cold air from Central Asia.
Exception: the Tamil Nadu (Coromandel) coast receives most of its rain from the north-east monsoon, as these winds pick up moisture over the Bay of Bengal.
Western disturbances (depressions from the west, areas of low pressure that move in) bring light winter rain to the north-west, which is important for wheat.
India lies mostly in the tropics, so heat is the norm. Only height above sea level and the season change it much.
The hot season brings high temperatures to the northern plains, often above 40°C, with hot, dry winds called loo.
The south stays hot all year.
The Himalayas are cold, so temperatures fall with altitude (height above sea level).
The monsoon is not reliable, and both too little and too much rain cause disasters. Climate change is adding to the risk.
A late, weak or broken monsoon (one with long dry breaks) causes drought, because crops and reservoirs depend on its rain.
A heavy monsoon causes floods, because rivers receive more water than their channels can carry.
Tropical cyclones (violent rotating storms that form over warm seas) strike the east coast, mainly in the pre-monsoon and retreating-monsoon periods.
Odisha super cyclone, October 1999: about 10,000 deaths, an example of how deadly a storm on the east coast can be.
Climate change is making the monsoon more erratic (so drought and flood risks both rise) and heatwaves more severe.
Because most Indians depend on farming, the timing and strength of the monsoon shape the whole economy.
Its timing decides the farming calendar, so a late monsoon delays sowing, with kharif crops (sown with the monsoon) and rabi crops (sown after it), which are covered under the farming calendar below.
It refills reservoirs and groundwater, which supply irrigation and drinking water.
Because farming is a large part of the economy, a poor monsoon affects GDP (the total value of what the country produces).
Soil type follows the parent material (the rock or sediment the soil forms from) and the climate. Alluvial soil is India's most extensive soil type.
Alluvial soils (soils made of silt and sand laid down by rivers) are the most extensive and most fertile, found on the Indo-Gangetic Plain and the eastern deltas.
They are deposited by Himalayan rivers, which carry silt down from the mountains, forming newer khadar (floodplain) soils and older bhangar (higher terraces).
Desert soils in the Thar, Rajasthan, are sandy, so they hold little water, low in humus (decayed plant matter that feeds soil) and sometimes saline (salty).
Desert soils are productive only where canal irrigation reaches them: the Indira Gandhi Canal, Rajasthan, brings water from Punjab's rivers into the Thar Desert.
Black soils form on volcanic rock and are among the best soils of the Deccan for one particular crop.
Black soils (regur, or black cotton soil) are weathered (broken down) from the basalt lava (dark volcanic rock) of the Deccan Traps in north-west Deccan, Maharashtra.
They are clay-rich, so they hold moisture well.
They crack deeply when dry, a feature sometimes called self-ploughing, because the cracks let air and water into the soil.
They are ideal for cotton, the main crop on the Deccan Traps, because cotton needs soil that keeps moisture.
Red soils form on old, hard rock and are poorer than black soils.
Red soils are weathered from ancient crystalline rocks (hard rocks made of interlocking crystals, here granite and gneiss) of the south and east Deccan.
They are red because of iron oxide (rust), and are low in nitrogen and humus.
They support millets (small-seeded drought-tolerant cereals), groundnuts and pulses (beans, peas and lentils), and give better yields with fertiliser and irrigation.
Laterite forms where heat and heavy rain wash goodness out of the ground. It is a poor soil for farming, though it has a use in building.
Laterite forms under high temperatures and heavy rainfall, which leach out (wash away) silica and nutrients, leaving iron and aluminium oxides behind.
Laterite is found on the Western Ghats and in Kerala.
It is infertile because the leaching removed the nutrients, but with fertiliser it supports tea, coffee and cashew.
It hardens when exposed to air, so it is cut into building bricks.
On steep Himalayan slopes soil cannot build up, so farming depends on cutting flat steps into the hillside.
Mountain soils on the Himalayan slopes are thin and immature (not yet developed into deep, layered soil).
On the terraces (flat steps cut into the slopes, which give level ground on steep land) tea and fruit are grown.
Farming and the monsoon together damage India's soils in three main ways.
Erosion (the wearing away of soil): monsoon downpours and deforestation create gullies and ravines, such as the Chambal ravines of Madhya Pradesh and Rajasthan.
Salinisation (salt build-up in the soil) and waterlogging (soil saturated with water) occur under canal irrigation in Punjab and Haryana.
Nutrient exhaustion results from intensive Green Revolution farming, which takes crop after crop from the same land.
Two Indian soils show how rock type and weathering link to soil.
Basalt weathers to black soil, so black soils are tied to soils to the Deccan Traps, the thick basalt layers covered under the relief notes below.
Laterite is the product of intense chemical weathering (rock broken down by chemical reactions) in hot, wet conditions.
Relief means the shape and height of the land. India has three main relief divisions, with the Thar Desert, the coastal plains and the islands added to them.
The Himalayas lie to the north, forming India's mountain wall.
The Northern Plains, the Indo-Gangetic Plain, lie in front of the Himalayas, where the rivers spread their silt.
The Peninsular Plateau, the Deccan, forms the southern peninsula.
Coastal plains and islands lie along the coasts.
The Himalayas form India's northern wall. They are the youngest and highest of its landforms.

The Himalayas are young fold mountains (formed when rock layers are crumpled up by collision) formed by the collision of the Indian (Indo-Australian) plate with the Eurasian plate. The collision began about 50 million years ago and continues.
Three parallel ranges run west to east: the Greater Himalaya (Himadri), the Lesser Himalaya and the Shiwaliks.
Kangchenjunga, 8,586 m, on the India (Sikkim)–Nepal border, is India's highest peak and the world's third highest.
Mount Everest (8,849 m) is on the Nepal–China border, not in India.
The Himalayas shape India's climate, rivers and settlement. Their effects are both helpful and harmful.
The mountains are a barrier to cold air from Central Asia.
They trigger monsoon rain, as the monsoon is forced upwards by the mountain wall.
Perennial rivers (rivers that flow all year) fed by snow melt rise in the Himalayas.
The rivers have hydroelectric potential (power from falling water) because they drop steeply.
The mountains are a barrier to transport and are prone to earthquakes and landslides.
Settlement is sparse because of the steep, cold terrain, which makes farming and building hard.
South of the Himalayas lies the flattest and most useful land in India.
The Northern Plains are vast, flat and low.
They are built from alluvium (silt and sand laid down by rivers) deposited by the Indus, Ganges and Brahmaputra river systems in a trough (a long hollow) in front of the Himalayas.
They are the agricultural and population heartland of India.
The Deccan is an old, stable upland that covers most of southern India. Part of it is covered by lava from ancient eruptions.
The Deccan Plateau is very old, made of hard crystalline rock, so it forms a stable shield (a block of ancient rock that is no longer folded or moved much).
It was once part of the ancient Gondwanaland landmass, the supercontinent that later broke apart.
The plateau tilts from west to east, so most of its rivers flow east.
The Chota Nagpur Plateau in the north-east of the plateau is rich in minerals, such as coal and iron ore.

The Deccan Traps are thick layers of basalt from huge fissure eruptions (lava pouring from long cracks) about 66 million years ago, covering much of the north-west Deccan (the source of the black soils).
Two mountain ranges edge the Deccan Plateau, one on each coast. They differ in height and continuity.
The Western Ghats, also called the Sahyadri, form a steep, continuous escarpment (a long steep slope) along the west coast.
The Western Ghats are a UNESCO World Heritage Site (2012) for their biodiversity (the variety of living things).
Anamudi, 2,695 m, in Kerala, is the highest peak in India south of the Himalayas.
The Eastern Ghats are lower and broken into separate hills, because east-flowing rivers cut through them.
Between the plains and the plateau, and in the north-west, are older ranges that also shape drainage and rainfall.
The Vindhya and Satpura ranges separate the plains from the Deccan, forming a divide between north and south.
The Narmada flows west between the Vindhya and Satpura ranges.
The Aravalli Range, Rajasthan, is among the oldest fold mountains on earth.
The Thar Desert lies west of the Aravalli Range, on the dry side where the monsoon winds are not forced upwards.
Narrow plains run along both coasts, but the west and east differ in width and in what the rivers have built.

The narrow western plain includes the Konkan coast (Maharashtra, Goa) in the north and the Malabar coast (Kerala) in the south, with backwaters and lagoons (shallow coastal waters partly cut off from the sea).
The wider eastern plain is the Coromandel coast (Tamil Nadu), with large river deltas, because the Deccan's rivers flow east and deposit silt there.
Each relief division supports a different way of life, which is why people and industry are spread unevenly.
The plains support dense population, intensive farming and easy transport, because the land is flat and fertile.
The plateau is rich in minerals, so it supports industry.
The mountains support tourism and hydroelectricity, with sparse settlement because the land is steep and cold.
India's rivers fall into two groups. The Himalayan and peninsular rivers differ in their source, flow and seasonal regime (how their flow changes through the year).
Himalayan rivers are perennial, because they are fed by snow and glacier melt plus monsoon rain, and are large, with high flows in summer.
Peninsular rivers are seasonal, because they are rain-fed, so they are low in the dry season, and shorter.
Peninsular rivers flow in older, harder rock, with fixed valleys, so they cannot easily shift course.
The Ganges is India's most important river. It drains the largest basin in the country and feeds the Northern Plains.
The Ganges rises as the Bhagirathi at Gaumukh, the snout of the Gangotri Glacier in Uttarakhand.
It becomes the Ganga where the Bhagirathi meets the Alaknanda at Devprayag.
It flows past Haridwar, Kanpur, Prayagraj (Allahabad), Varanasi and Patna.
The Yamuna, a tributary (a river that joins a larger one) which flows past Delhi and Agra, joins it at Prayagraj.
The river is about 2,500 km long and its basin (the area drained by it and its tributaries) covers about a quarter of India, the largest basin in India.
It enters Bangladesh and joins the Brahmaputra to form the Ganges–Brahmaputra delta, the world's largest delta; the delta is shared with Bangladesh.
The Sundarbans mangrove forest (trees that grow in salty coastal mud), home of the Bengal tiger, lies on the delta across India and Bangladesh.
The Hooghly, a distributary (a branch that leaves the main river), flows through Kolkata, which is why the city is a river port.
The Brahmaputra drains the north-east and carries so much sediment that it floods the same area every year.
The Brahmaputra rises in Tibet as the Yarlung Tsangpo.
It enters India in Arunachal Pradesh and flows west through Assam.
It joins the Ganges in Bangladesh.
It is braided (split into many shifting channels around sandbanks) and carries huge loads of silt, so its channels clog and it floods Assam annually.
The Indus is a Himalayan river that mostly flows outside India, yet its tributaries water India's wheat belt.
The Indus rises in Tibet and flows through Ladakh into Pakistan, mostly through Pakistan.
Its five Punjab tributaries are the Jhelum, Chenab, Ravi, Beas and Sutlej.
Its waters irrigate India's wheat belt in the Punjab, which is why the Indus matters to India even though it flows mostly through Pakistan.
The Indus Waters Treaty with Pakistan, 1960, brokered by the World Bank, divides its waters.
Because the Deccan Plateau tilts eastwards, its main rivers cross it to reach the Bay of Bengal.
The Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna and Kaveri flow east to the Bay of Bengal.
The Godavari is the longest river of peninsular India, which is the name for the southern triangle of the country.
They build deltas on the Bay of Bengal coast, which are fertile rice lands because of the silt they deposit.
The Kaveri (Cauvery) water dispute is between Karnataka and Tamil Nadu, two states that both want the river's water.
Two peninsular rivers run against the general eastward tilt and reach the Arabian Sea.
The Narmada and the Tapi flow west into the Arabian Sea.
They flow through rift valleys (long valleys formed where land has dropped between faults) and end in estuaries (wide river mouths affected by the tide), not deltas.
Rivers on the flat plains both create and destroy. Their floods bring fertile silt but also loss.
Monsoon floods occur on the Ganges plain and in Bihar and Assam, because the rivers swell with monsoon rain and snow melt.
Silt deposition renews soils, but floods destroy crops and homes.
The Kosi, a Ganges tributary in Bihar, is called the 'Sorrow of Bihar' because of its floods and shifting course; it broke its embankment in 2008.
Rivers shift course on the flat plains, because there is little slope to hold them in one channel.
People try to control the rivers so that water is available all year and floods are reduced. This brings benefits and conflict.
Multipurpose dams (dams built for several uses at once) provide irrigation, hydroelectricity and flood control.
Bhakra Dam on the Sutlej, Himachal Pradesh, supplies irrigation water and power to Punjab and Haryana.
Sardar Sarovar Dam on the Narmada, Gujarat, brings irrigation and drinking water to Gujarat but displaced many thousands of villagers.
The displacement led to the Narmada Bachao Andolan ('Save the Narmada') protest movement.
Canal irrigation spreads water beyond the river valleys, so dry land far from a river can be farmed.
Water is disputed between states, as in the Kaveri dispute, and with neighbouring countries, as in the Indus Waters Treaty.
The same river that millions depend on is heavily polluted, and governments have launched clean-up programmes.
The Ganges is polluted by sewage, industrial waste and cremations.
Ritual bathing and cremation take place along the river at Varanasi, which adds to the pollution because ashes and waste enter the water.
The Ganga Action Plan was launched in 1985.
The Namami Gange programme followed in 2014.
Rivers are central to religion and daily life as well as to the economy.
The Ganges is sacred to Hindus, so millions bathe in it and visit it.
Rivers provide water for drinking, irrigation and transport, such as boats on the Ganges.
The rivers' floods deposit fertile alluvium on the plains, sustaining farming and settlement.
Agriculture is the biggest employer in India but contributes far less to the economy than its workforce suggests.
Agriculture employs the largest share of workers: in Census 2011, about 55% of workers were cultivators or agricultural labourers.
It produces a much smaller share of GDP, under a fifth in the early 2020s, which shows low productivity (little output per worker).
Its share of employment is falling, as more people move into industry and services.
Indian farming ranges from tiny family plots to large commercial farms. Each type suits a particular region and climate.
Subsistence farming (growing food mainly for the farmer's own family) on small plots, so little is left to sell.
Intensive wet-rice (paddy) farming in the wet east, the south and the deltas, where rain and flooded fields suit rice.
Commercial irrigated wheat farming (growing for sale, using canal or well water) in the north-west, in Punjab and Haryana.
Plantation farming (large estates growing one crop for sale): tea in Assam and Darjeeling (West Bengal), and in the Nilgiri Hills (Tamil Nadu); coffee in Karnataka.
Cash crops (crops grown to sell): cotton on black soils in Maharashtra and Gujarat, sugar cane, and jute in West Bengal.
Dairy farming, such as the co-operatives described under the White Revolution, and pastoralism (herding animals) in dry areas.
The monsoon splits the farming year into two main cropping seasons, kharif and rabi.
Kharif crops are sown with the monsoon in June and July, so they use its rain, and harvested in autumn: rice, cotton, maize and millets.
Rabi crops are sown in October and November and harvested in March and April: wheat, mustard and gram.
Rabi crops depend on irrigation and on the rain from western disturbances, because the main monsoon has ended.
Kharif means monsoon (summer) crops such as rice; rabi means winter crops such as wheat.
India's climate, soils and rivers give farmers several natural advantages.
Tropical temperatures allow two or three crops a year, because there is no cold season long enough to stop growth.
Fertile alluvium covers the plains, and black soil covers the Deccan, so both regions grow crops well.
The land is flat across the plains, easing cultivation and transport.
Perennial Himalayan rivers supply water for irrigation, so crops can be watered in the dry season.
The same physical setting also limits farming in many places.
The monsoon is unreliable, so farmers face drought in some years and floods in others.
Laterite and desert soils are poor, because they are infertile or short of water.
Steep slopes limit cultivation, because soil is thin and machines cannot work them.
Soil erosion and salinisation reduce yields, since the soil loses its fertility.
Water tables (the level below which the ground is saturated) are falling, as more water is pumped out than the rain refills.
Irrigation (supplying water to crops by artificial means) makes farming possible in dry areas and in the dry season.
Canals in Punjab and the Indira Gandhi Canal in Rajasthan, which brings river water into the Thar Desert, supply water.
Tubewells (deep pumped wells) draw groundwater for irrigation, which makes farming possible where there is no canal.
Irrigation was essential to the Green Revolution, because the new crop varieties needed reliable water.
Groundwater is overused in Punjab, lowering the water table.
From the mid-1960s, a package of new methods raised food-grain output. It made India self-sufficient but brought costs.
High-yielding wheat varieties were developed in Mexico by Norman Borlaug; Indian scientist M. S. Swaminathan led their introduction in India.
The package included high-yielding varieties of wheat and rice, chemical fertilisers, pesticides, irrigation and machinery.
Food-grain output rose from about 51 million tonnes (1950–51) to about 330 million tonnes (2022–23).
India became self-sufficient in food, meaning it could feed itself without relying on imports.
The core areas were Punjab, Haryana and western Uttar Pradesh, where irrigation was already available.
Benefits were concentrated in these areas and among larger farmers, because they could afford seed, fertiliser and machinery.
Costs: groundwater depletion, soil degradation, chemical pollution and farmer debt.
A similar push in dairying made India the world's largest producer of milk, using co-operatives (businesses owned and run by their farmer members).
Operation Flood, launched in 1970 by the National Dairy Development Board under Verghese Kurien, built co-operative dairying.
The Amul co-operative, based at Anand, Gujarat, is a model of the system.
Operation Flood made India the world's largest milk producer, because co-operatives gave small farmers a market for their milk.
Religion supports dairying: the cow is sacred to Hindus, so cattle are kept for milk and draught (pulling ploughs and carts), not beef.
Beyond the weather, many of farming's problems come from how land is owned and how farmers are paid.
Holdings are very small and fragmented: in the Agriculture Census 2015–16, the average holding was about 1.1 hectares, and about 86% of holdings were small or marginal (under 2 hectares).
Holdings are subdivided at each inheritance, because land is divided among heirs.
Landless labourers have little land of their own, so they depend on wages and are very poor.
Farmers lack capital and credit, so debt is common.
Middlemen (traders between farmer and buyer) take a share of the profit, so farmers receive less.
Poor storage and roads cause post-harvest losses, because crops spoil or cannot reach markets.
Government policy and a large home market give Indian farmers some security.
India has a huge domestic market of over 1.4 billion people, so there is strong demand for food.
The government sets minimum support prices (guaranteed prices) and buys grain, which is stored by the Food Corporation of India.
PM-KISAN, launched in 2019, gives income support: it pays ₹6,000 a year directly to landholding farm families.
India is the world's largest rice exporter (early 2020s).
Farming also causes distress, pollution and political conflict.
Drought and farmer distress, including farmer suicides, are persistent problems, because debt and crop failure leave farmers with no safety net.
Stubble burning (burning the straw left after harvest) in Punjab and Haryana, October to November, after the rice harvest, worsens Delhi's winter smog.
The 2020–21 farmers' protests, mainly by Punjab and Haryana farmers camped on Delhi's borders, opposed three farm laws.
The farm laws were repealed (withdrawn) in November 2021, after the protests.
These rankings back up answers on the importance of Indian agriculture.
India is the world's second-largest producer of rice and of wheat, after China.
India is the second-largest producer of tea, after China.
India is the largest producer of jute.
India is the largest producer of milk, thanks to the White Revolution, so dairying is a major strength.
Bt (genetically modified) cotton, a variety changed to resist pests, was approved in 2002.
Forests cover only part of India and are under pressure from people, so protection is needed.
Forests cover about one-fifth of India's area (early 2020s).
Tropical monsoon (deciduous, leaf-shedding) forests cover much of the country.
Wet evergreen forest grows on the Western Ghats and in the north-east.
Mangroves grow in the Sundarbans, West Bengal, a UNESCO site.
Fuelwood use (burning wood for cooking and heating) and deforestation reduce forest cover, because trees are cut faster than they regrow.
Afforestation (planting new forest) and protected areas respond to these losses; Project Tiger began in 1973.
India's long coast and large rivers support both sea and inland fishing.
India has a long coastline and large rivers, which give it both sea and freshwater fishing.
Marine fishing is important in Kerala, Gujarat and West Bengal.
Inland aquaculture (fish and prawn ponds) is growing fast, because it does not depend on the sea.
India is one of the world's largest fish producers.
India's minerals are concentrated in one upland region, which became the base of its steel industry.
The Chota Nagpur Plateau covers Jharkhand, Odisha, Chhattisgarh and West Bengal.
It holds most of India's coal and iron ore, so it is the basis of the steel industry.
Coal is mined in the Jharia coalfield and the Damodar valley coalfields in Jharkhand.
Iron ore is also mined in Karnataka and Goa, and in Odisha, Jharkhand and Chhattisgarh.
India relies on coal for most of its electricity, which brings economic gain and environmental cost.
India is the world's second-largest coal producer, after China.
Coal generates about 70% of India's electricity (early 2020s), which makes it the main source of power.
Coal's environmental costs include air pollution and the displacement of tribal people, who lose land where mines are opened.
India has some oil but not enough for its needs.
The Mumbai High offshore oil field (drilled from the sea bed), in the Arabian Sea, was discovered in 1974.
India imports most of its crude oil, because its own output is small compared with demand.
India is expanding sources of power that do not burn coal.
Hydroelectricity (power from flowing water) comes from the Himalayan rivers, which fall steeply, and from large dams.
Solar energy is expanding fastest in Rajasthan, a sunny dry state, where the Bhadla Solar Park is one of the world's largest.
Wind energy is developing in Tamil Nadu and Gujarat, so power can come from sources other than coal.
India's target, announced at COP26 in Glasgow in 2021, is 500 GW of non-fossil electricity capacity by 2030.
This is background only. It explains where Indian industry first grew.
Britain used India as a source of raw materials and as a market for its manufactures, so Indian industry grew to serve Britain's needs.
Early industry was cotton textiles in Bombay (Mumbai) and Ahmedabad, called the 'Manchester of India', from the 19th century.
Jute mills were built along the Hooghly near Calcutta (Kolkata), close to the jute-growing delta and a port.
The Tata Iron and Steel Company, founded in 1907 at Jamshedpur, Jharkhand, was India's first large steel works, sited on Chota Nagpur coal and iron ore.
After independence the government planned and owned much of industry, and also controlled it tightly.
The First Five-Year Plan began in 1951; Jawaharlal Nehru was the first Prime Minister, from 1947 to 1964.
Industrialisation was state-led: the state built steel plants at Bhilai (with Soviet Union help), Rourkela (West Germany) and Durgapur (Britain).
Imports were protected from foreign competition, so Indian firms were sheltered from rivals.
The Licence Raj required permits to start or expand a factory, which made industry inefficient.
In 1991 India changed course and opened its economy, which sped up growth.
A balance-of-payments crisis (when a country cannot pay for its imports) led to reform in 1991, under Prime Minister P. V. Narasimha Rao and Finance Minister Manmohan Singh.
Most licences were removed, tariffs (taxes on imports) were cut and India opened to foreign investment, so firms could grow and compete.
Manufacturing and services grew rapidly after 1991, because firms were freer to expand.
Export markets grew after 1991, because trade barriers were lowered.
More recent policies try to attract firms and boost factory output.
Make in India was launched in 2014 to attract firms to make goods in India.
The Special Economic Zones Act was passed in 2005; Special Economic Zones offer incentives to firms, so firms are drawn to them.
Production-Linked Incentive schemes, from 2020, pay subsidies per unit produced for electronics, cars and pharmaceuticals.
Industrial corridors (planned belts of industry and transport), such as the Delhi–Mumbai Industrial Corridor, link manufacturing sites.
A location factor is a reason a factory is sited in one place. Raw materials were decisive for India's oldest industries.
Coal, iron ore, limestone and manganese of the Chota Nagpur Plateau support iron and steel, at Jamshedpur and in the state plants.
Cotton grown on black soils supports textiles in Mumbai and Ahmedabad, because mills sit near their raw material.
Jute grown in the Ganges delta supports jute mills in Kolkata, which is close by.
India's people are one of its main advantages for industry.
India has a huge, young, low-cost labour force, so wage bills are low.
It has a large pool of engineers and graduates from the Indian Institutes of Technology (IITs); the first opened at Kharagpur in 1951.
Most workers are in the informal sector (jobs with no contract, regular wage or legal protection).
Firms locate where there are customers, and India has many.
The domestic market of over 1.4 billion people is growing, with a rising middle class that buys cars, phones and consumer goods.
Export markets have been open to Indian manufacturers since 1991, so firms can sell abroad.
Infrastructure means the transport and power systems that firms rely on. It is good in some places and weak in others.
Ports at Mumbai, Chennai and Kolkata handle trade, so goods can be exported and raw materials imported.
Jawaharlal Nehru Port, Navi Mumbai, is one of India's main container ports.
Railways and the Golden Quadrilateral road network link factories to markets, so goods reach customers.
Infrastructure is weak in many areas, with power cuts and congestion raising costs.
Policy, not just geography, decides where industry grows.
Policy changed location as well as scale: licensing shaped where firms could expand, and incentive schemes now steer firms to chosen sites.
Special Economic Zones and production-linked incentives are offered by policy, not by natural resources.
Manufacturing is concentrated in the west and south, in a few named industrial regions.
The Hooghly belt around Kolkata, in the east.
The Chota Nagpur and Damodar valley region, around Jamshedpur.
The Delhi National Capital Region, including Gurugram and Noida.
The southern cluster of Bengaluru, Chennai and Coimbatore.
The north and east (Bihar, Uttar Pradesh, Odisha) are less industrialised, in contrast with the west and south.
Each major industry has named firms and centres you can use as examples.
Iron and steel: India is the world's second-largest crude steel producer (since 2018).
Cotton textiles and garments: Tiruppur, Tamil Nadu, is known for knitwear exports.
Cars: Maruti Suzuki, a joint venture with Suzuki of Japan, began in 1983 with the Maruti 800; its plants are at Gurugram and Manesar, Haryana. Chennai has a car cluster that includes Hyundai.

Pharmaceuticals: India is a leading maker of generic medicines (cheaper copies of branded drugs), called the 'pharmacy of the world'; Hyderabad is a major centre. The Serum Institute of India in Pune is the world's largest vaccine maker by number of doses and made the Covishield (AstraZeneca) COVID-19 vaccine.
Electronics assembly: Foxconn assembles Apple iPhones at Sriperumbudur, near Chennai.
Aerospace and defence: Hindustan Aeronautics Limited (HAL) and the headquarters of the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) are in Bengaluru.
Indian manufacturing faces obstacles that have held its share of the economy down.
Poor infrastructure and power supply raise costs.
Land acquisition causes conflict: in Singur, West Bengal, in 2008, protests over farmland taken for Tata's Nano car factory forced Tata to move the plant to Sanand, Gujarat.
Bureaucracy and complex regulation slow investment, because approvals take time.
Competition from China is strong, because Chinese manufacturing is larger.
Pollution and industrial accidents: the Bhopal gas leak of December 1984, from the Union Carbide pesticide plant, killed thousands.
Old industries have declined: the Great Bombay textile strike of 1982 led to the closure of most of Mumbai's cotton mills, whose land was later redeveloped.
Manufacturing's share of the economy has stayed low compared with China.
Tertiary activities (services such as IT, tourism and transport) now dominate the Indian economy.
Services are now the largest sector, so they matter more than farming or industry, producing over half of India's GDP (early 2020s).
India is among the world's five largest economies by GDP (early 2020s).
Outsourcing means a foreign firm pays an Indian company to do work such as software or call-centre tasks. India's IT industry is centred on Bengaluru.
Bengaluru, called the 'Silicon Valley of India' after the US technology centre, is the leading IT centre.
Other IT centres are Hyderabad, Pune, Chennai, Gurugram and Noida.
