Indigenous peoples (the original inhabitants of a region) lose land to mining, ranching and logging, as in the Amazon example in the Brazil section of Case study of a developing economy.
Pressure to improve conditions comes from consumers, from the law and from workers themselves.
Ethical consumer campaigns and company codes of conduct (a company's own rules for how suppliers must treat workers) put pressure on brands.
The EU Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive, adopted in 2024, requires very large companies to identify and address human-rights and environmental harm in their supply chains.
Trade unions represent workers and campaign for safer conditions and better wages.
Climate change is an injustice because the countries that caused it least suffer most from it.
The poorest countries have contributed least to greenhouse gas emissions (the gases that cause global warming) but suffer most from climate change.
Bangladesh is a low-lying delta vulnerable to cyclones, floods and sea-level rise, because so much of its land is barely above the sea.
Small island states such as Tuvalu, Kiribati and the Maldives are threatened by sea-level rise, because their land is low.
Sub-Saharan Africa has produced only a small share of historical emissions, yet its dry regions suffer drought.

Responses include climate finance (money from rich countries to help poorer ones cope) and the Loss and Damage Fund, agreed at COP27 in Sharm el-Sheikh, Egypt (2022) and made operational at COP28 in Dubai (2023).
The Mary Robinson Foundation - Climate Justice was set up in 2010 by Mary Robinson, who was President of Ireland from 1990 to 1997 and UN High Commissioner for Human Rights from 1997 to 2002.
A justice evaluation weighs real progress against the problems that remain.
Extreme poverty has fallen greatly since 1990, especially in China. Child mortality has fallen, and more children attend school.
Sub-Saharan Africa lags behind other regions.
Inequality within and between countries is high, so gains are not shared equally.
Conflict, such as the war in Sudan, and climate change are reversing gains. There is more on this in Case study of a developing economy.
The COVID-19 pandemic in 2020 caused the first rise in global extreme poverty in about a generation (World Bank).
Justice is not only for governments. Individuals and Ireland can act.
Individuals can buy fair trade, campaign, and support NGOs. Ireland can press governments on aid, trade and debt policy.

Economic activities (the ways people earn a living) are grouped into three sectors by what they do with raw materials or with people's needs. Knowing which sector a job belongs to is the first step in describing any economy.

Primary activity is extracting raw materials from nature, such as farming, fishing, forestry, mining, quarrying and energy extraction. Nothing is made yet, so the resource is simply taken from the land or sea.
Secondary activity is processing raw materials or assembling components (parts) into goods, such as manufacturing, food processing and construction.
Tertiary activity is services, which provide help or access rather than goods, such as retail, banking, tourism, teaching, health, transport and IT (information technology).
Classifying jobs: a miner or forester is primary; a builder is secondary, because construction is secondary; a teacher, banker or tour guide is tertiary.
Some writers add a quaternary sector for research and information, but the three-sector model is used here.
The share of workers in each sector changes as a country becomes richer. Ireland shows the end result of that shift.
As an economy develops, employment moves from primary to secondary and then to tertiary activity. This is why primary employment falls as countries develop.
Services employ about three-quarters of Irish workers (2020s), which means Ireland is a tertiary economy; agriculture, forestry and fishing employ about 4–5%.
Census 2022 counted a State population of about 5.1 million; the CSO (Central Statistics Office) Labour Force Survey (2024) recorded over 2.7 million people in employment.
In a developing economy, by contrast, primary employment is high. There is more on this in the Economic Development notes.
For its first decades as an independent State, Ireland tried to shelter its own firms from foreign competition. This is the starting point of the timeline of how Ireland became a developed economy.
The Control of Manufactures Acts, 1932 and 1934, restricted foreign ownership of Irish firms, so industry stayed in Irish hands.
High tariffs (taxes on imported goods) protected small Irish firms serving the home market, so they had little pressure to become efficient or to export.
The 1950s brought high unemployment and heavy emigration (people leaving the country to live abroad), which showed that protection had not created enough jobs.
From the late 1950s Ireland reversed its policy and opened up to trade and foreign companies. Each step below was meant to bring in jobs and exports.
The Industrial Development Authority (IDA) was set up in 1949 to attract industry, so Ireland had an agency for winning new firms.
Export Profits Tax Relief, 1956, removed tax on profits from exports, so firms had a reason to sell abroad.

T.K. Whitaker's Economic Development and the First Programme for Economic Expansion (1958) set the policy of free trade, foreign investment and export-led growth (growth driven by selling abroad), carried out under Seán Lemass as Taoiseach from 1959.
The Anglo-Irish Free Trade Agreement (1965) reduced trade barriers with Britain, Ireland's nearest and biggest market.
Ireland joined the EEC (European Economic Community, the forerunner of the EU) on 1 January 1973, together with the UK and Denmark.
Attracting foreign firms also needed people with the right skills. Free schooling was the policy that built them.
Free second-level education was announced in 1966 by Donogh O'Malley and introduced in 1967.
A better-educated workforce made Ireland attractive to firms that needed skilled labour in the decades that followed.
The IDA became an independent agency under the Industrial Development Act 1969, so it could pursue foreign investment in its own right.
Later steps tied Ireland more closely to Europe and set the tax rates that attract multinational companies. Corporation tax is the tax a company pays on its profits.
The EU Single Market began in 1993, giving Irish firms and foreign investors access to the wider EU market without trade barriers.
The euro was adopted in 1999, with notes and coins introduced in 2002, which means Irish firms trade with the eurozone (the countries using the euro) without exchange-rate costs.
Corporation tax on trading profits was 12.5% from 2003. This low rate is a main reason multinationals locate in Ireland.
From 2024 very large multinational groups (global turnover over €750 million) pay a 15% minimum rate under the OECD (Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development) agreement.
The Celtic Tiger is the name for Ireland's period of very rapid growth. It followed from the earlier policies of free trade, investment and education.

Rapid growth from the mid-1990s to 2007 was driven first by exports and foreign direct investment (FDI, money invested by foreign firms in Irish plants), especially from US technology and pharmaceutical firms.
A property and construction boom added to growth later in the period, because rising prices encouraged more building.
Unemployment fell to about 4–5% by the mid-2000s, because so many new jobs were created.
Net immigration (more people arriving than leaving) replaced emigration, with large inflows from the new EU states after the 2004 enlargement.
The property boom ended in a crash that put Irish banks in danger. The State stepped in to protect them.
The property bubble (a rise in prices that could not last) burst in 2007–2008, leaving banks with large bad loans (loans unlikely to be repaid) secured on property that had lost value.
On 30 September 2008 the government guaranteed Irish bank liabilities, promising that the banks' debts would be covered.
Anglo Irish Bank was nationalised (taken into State ownership) in January 2009.
The National Asset Management Agency (NAMA), set up in 2009, took over property loans from the banks.
The cost of rescuing the banks left the State unable to borrow normally, so it needed outside help. The crash also hit jobs and population.
An EU–IMF (International Monetary Fund) programme was agreed in November 2010, providing €67.5 billion in external loans.
Ireland left the programme in December 2013, which means the State could borrow on normal markets again.
Unemployment peaked at about 16% in early 2012, so net emigration resumed from 2009 to 2014.

Government debt peaked at about 120% of GDP (the value of everything produced in the country in a year) in 2012: the state borrowed to rescue the banks while its tax base (the income and spending that can be taxed) collapsed with the economy.
After 2013 the economy recovered strongly. Jobs returned and public finances improved.
Unemployment was about 4–5% in 2023–2024, near full employment (almost everyone who wants work has it).
Budget surpluses (tax income greater than spending) in the 2020s came largely from corporation tax paid by a small number of large multinationals, so public finances depend on them.
COVID-19 lockdowns in 2020–2021 hit tourism, hospitality and retail hardest.
When most people who want work have it, the whole economy gains, not only the workers. Each benefit below follows from people earning and spending.
Employed people pay income tax, and their spending pays VAT (value-added tax, a tax on goods and services), so tax revenue rises.
Welfare spending falls because fewer people need unemployment payments, so the State has more to spend elsewhere.
Consumer spending by employed people supports jobs in other sectors, such as shops and cafes.
Less emigration keeps skilled people in the economy, so firms can find the workers they need.
Government revenue can pay for investment in infrastructure (roads, rail, utilities) and services.
Because so many multinationals are based in Ireland, their profits can distort the national figures. This makes GDP a poor guide to how well Irish people are doing.
In 2015 Irish GDP grew by about 26% after multinationals moved intellectual property assets (such as patents and software rights) to Ireland; the effect was nicknamed 'leprechaun economics'.
Because GDP is inflated by these profits, the CSO introduced modified gross national income (GNI*) in 2017 to strip out their effects.
Farming is Ireland's main primary activity, and its pattern follows the climate. Mild, wet weather suits grass, so animals matter more than crops.
The Census of Agriculture 2020 counted about 135,000 farms, averaging about 33 hectares.
Grass grows for most of the year because winters are mild and rain is reliable, so grass-based livestock farming dominates.
Pastoral farming is livestock farming: beef and dairy cattle, sheep and pigs. The national cattle herd is about 7 million (2020s), which is why beef and dairy cattle are central to farming.
Arable (tillage) farming grows crops: barley is the largest tillage crop, with wheat, oats and potatoes also grown.
Tillage is concentrated in the south and east, in Counties Wexford, Carlow, Kildare, Meath and Cork.
Livestock farming earns money abroad, but a large herd also damages the environment. Exams ask for a benefit and a problem.
EU milk quotas (limits on how much milk each country could produce) ended on 1 April 2015, and dairy cow numbers and milk output rose strongly afterwards.
About 90% of Irish beef and dairy output is exported (Bord Bia, 2020s).
A large cattle herd brings exports, food-processing jobs and incomes to rural areas.
Agriculture is the largest single source of Ireland's greenhouse gas emissions (gases that warm the atmosphere), about 38% (EPA, 2022 data), with methane from livestock a main part of this.
Nitrate and phosphate runoff (fertiliser and slurry washed from fields) pollutes rivers and lakes, and livestock release ammonia.
Agri-food means food and drink made from farm produce. Irish brands turn farm output into exports, and exams ask for one food and one drink product.
Kerrygold butter is exported by Ornua, the dairy co-operatives' export company; the brand was launched in 1962.
Kerry Group (headquarters Tralee, Co. Kerry) and Glanbia (headquarters Kilkenny) are major food companies, such as those that process Irish farm output.
Tayto crisps were first made in 1954 by Joe 'Spud' Murphy.
Bord Bia, the Irish food board, promotes Irish food, so its exports are better known abroad.
Guinness is made at St James's Gate Brewery, Dublin, a site dating from 1759.
Jameson Irish whiskey is made at Midleton Distillery, Co. Cork; its producer, Irish Distillers, is owned by Pernod Ricard.
Baileys Irish Cream was launched in 1974.
Ireland's geography gives it good conditions for fishing. Several harbours are officially designated as fishing centres.
Ireland has a long, indented coastline with sheltered harbours, so boats can land fish safely, and a wide continental shelf (shallow seabed around the coast where fish feed).
Plankton-rich waters and the North Atlantic Drift (a warm ocean current) support productive stocks, especially pelagic (surface-swimming) fish such as mackerel.
Six State Fishery Harbour Centres: Killybegs (Co. Donegal), Castletownbere (Co. Cork), Dingle (Co. Kerry), Rossaveel (Co. Galway), Dunmore East (Co. Waterford) and Howth (Co. Dublin).
Killybegs is Ireland's largest fishing port and lands mainly pelagic fish, such as mackerel.
Bord Iascaigh Mhara (BIM) is the Irish sea fisheries board, so it is the State body for the industry.
Irish fishing is limited by EU rules, but it still matters to the coastal places that depend on it.
The EU Common Fisheries Policy (1983) sets fishing quotas (limits on the catch) for member states, so Irish boats cannot catch as much as they wish.
The 2020 EU–UK Brexit trade agreement reduced Irish quotas, which means Irish fishers may catch less.
Mackerel is the most valuable species landed in Ireland, which is why pelagic waters matter so much.
Fishing earns export income, provides jobs in remote coastal communities and supports fish processing.
Ireland has little forest, which limits how much wood can be processed. This also explains why the wood industry employs few people.
Forest cover is about 11% (2020s), among the lowest in the EU, so there is little timber to process.
Coillte, the State forestry company, was set up in 1988; Sitka spruce is the main plantation tree.

Wood processing employs few people because the forest area is small, plantations are young, sawmills and board mills (which make boards from wood) are highly mechanised (done by machines), and timber is partly exported unprocessed.
Coillte's board mills are Medite, making MDF (medium-density fibreboard) at Clonmel, Co. Tipperary, and SmartPly, making oriented strand board at Belview, Co. Kilkenny, on Waterford Port.
Ireland also takes metal and energy from the ground. The examples below are the named ones to know, one for each.
Tara Mines, Navan, Co. Meath, is Europe's largest zinc mine; it opened in 1977 and is owned by Boliden. Production was paused from July 2023 and restarted at the end of 2024.
The Corrib gas field off Co. Mayo first flowed in December 2015, so it is Ireland's example of gas extraction.
ESB's peat-fired power stations at Shannonbridge (West Offaly) and Lanesborough (Lough Ree) closed in December 2020.
Bord na Móna's peat harvesting for electricity has ended, because the peat stations it supplied have closed.
Manufacturing in Ireland is driven by foreign companies. The reasons they come are also the answer to 'factors that attract industry to Ireland'.
Foreign direct investment (FDI) is investment by foreign companies that set up or expand plants and offices in Ireland.
IDA client companies, mostly foreign-owned, employ about 300,000 people (2023), which shows how much jobs depend on FDI.
Low corporation tax, IDA grants and serviced sites (land already supplied with roads, power and water) attract firms to Ireland.
A young, educated, English-speaking workforce gives firms access to skilled labour.
Access to the EU single market and clusters of similar firms add to the attraction, since suppliers and skills are nearby.
Ireland's time zone, between the USA and Asia, suits firms that serve both.
Pharmaceuticals (medicines) and chemicals are the biggest manufacturing sector in Ireland. Cork Harbour is the main centre.
Cork Harbour, especially Ringaskiddy and Little Island, is one of the world's largest concentrations of pharmaceutical and chemical plants.
Pfizer, Janssen (Johnson & Johnson) and Novartis have plants at Ringaskiddy; Eli Lilly is at Kinsale, Co. Cork; Pfizer also has a site at Grange Castle, Clondalkin, Dublin.
Pharmaceuticals and chemicals are Ireland's largest goods exports, about half or more of the total (2020s).
Medical technology and electronics are the other main manufacturing sectors, each centred on named places.
Galway is one of Europe's leading medical-technology clusters: Boston Scientific opened there in 1994 and Medtronic is at Parkmore.
Intel at Leixlip, Co. Kildare, opened in 1989 and is Ireland's largest private-sector investment, worth billions of euro.
Fab 34 at Leixlip opened in 2023 and makes advanced chips using extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography (printing very fine circuits with a short-wavelength light).
Apple's European headquarters at Hollyhill, Cork, opened in 1980 and employs about 6,000 staff (2020s), so it is a major employer in the city.
Not all Irish industry is foreign-owned. Indigenous (Irish-owned) firms get State support, and some have become multinationals themselves.
Enterprise Ireland, set up in 1998, supports Irish-owned firms, so they can grow as well as the foreign ones.
Irish-founded firms that grew into multinationals include CRH (building materials) and Smurfit Kappa (paper packaging), which merged with WestRock in 2024 as Smurfit Westrock.
Ryanair, an Irish-founded airline, is a tertiary firm because it provides a transport service.
Ireland has a dual economy: a highly productive foreign-owned sector sits beside a smaller, lower-productivity Irish-owned sector.
Ireland's industrial success rests on a few foreign firms and favourable conditions. Each challenge below puts one of those at risk.
Dependence on a few large US multinationals means that a single firm's decisions can change output and jobs.
The 15% global minimum tax for very large groups reduces the advantage of Ireland's low rate. There is more on this in the block on the Single Market, euro and corporation tax.
In September 2024 the EU Court of Justice ruled that Apple must pay Ireland about €13 billion plus interest in back taxes; the case had been begun by the European Commission in 2016.
US trade and tax policy changes: the USA raised tariffs on EU goods in 2025.
Brexit: the UK left the EU on 31 January 2020 and the transition ended on 31 December 2020, changing trade, supply chains and access to the UK market.
High housing and living costs make it hard to attract staff, because workers cannot afford to live near the jobs.
Electricity grid and water constraints, and high energy costs, limit expansion.
Competition from lower-cost countries, because they can make goods more cheaply.
A footloose industry is not tied to a location by raw materials or power, so it can locate almost anywhere. This freedom is why governments compete to attract it.
Footloose firms choose places with skilled labour, good communications, quality of life and government incentives, because none of these is fixed by nature.
Services such as software, internet and data processing are the most footloose, since their product is information that needs no bulky raw materials.
The Dublin region is Ireland's main example of an area dominated by services and footloose industry. Its best-known cluster is Silicon Docks.
Silicon Docks is the Grand Canal Dock area, south of the River Liffey, where digital firms cluster.
Microsoft has been in Ireland since 1985; Google has had its European headquarters in Dublin since 2003, at Barrow Street on Grand Canal Dock.
Meta (Facebook), LinkedIn and Salesforce also have large Dublin offices.
The Dublin Docklands Development Authority, set up in 1997, was created to plan and regenerate the docklands.
Service firms are footloose, so they go where conditions suit them. Dublin offers several at once.
Skilled graduates come from Trinity College Dublin, UCD, DCU, TU Dublin and Maynooth University.
Firms recruit staff from across the EU for offices serving Europe, so language and skills are not limited to Ireland.
Dublin Airport, with over 30 million passengers a year (2023), and fibre connectivity (high-speed internet cables) link the region to the world.
A low tax rate and government incentives attract firms, because they cut costs.
Agglomeration: firms gain from being close to each other, sharing skills and suppliers, so one firm attracts others.
Clustering brings both gains and strains to the Dublin region.
The cluster provides high-paid jobs in offices and related services.
Demand for offices and housing has pushed rents up, because supply cannot keep pace.
The concentration of firms and workers adds to congestion (crowded roads and transport) in Dublin.
Data centres are buildings full of computers that store and process internet data. They are a newer footloose service, and they put heavy demand on the electricity supply.
Data centres used about a fifth (about 21%) of Ireland's metered electricity in 2023 (CSO), and most are in the Dublin region.
A cool climate reduces cooling costs, so running the machines is cheaper; fibre links connect them to global networks; firms cluster near each other; and tax is favourable.
The problem is electricity demand: EirGrid (the national electricity grid operator) stated in 2022 that it would not connect new data centres in the Dublin region until about 2028.
Shannon was an early planned zone for footloose industry. Its duty-free shop (1947) came before the Free Zone (1959).
Brendan O'Regan opened the world's first duty-free airport shop at Shannon in 1947.
The Shannon Free Airport Development Company (SFADCo) was set up in 1959, and the Shannon Free Zone that year offered firms tax relief and duty-free import of components, which cut their costs.
Aircraft leasing (renting planes to airlines) grew from Shannon after Guinness Peat Aviation (GPA) was founded there in 1975 by Tony Ryan, who co-founded Ryanair in the 1980s.
Ireland now manages about half of the world's leased commercial aircraft (2020s, approximately).
Silicon Valley is the original region of footloose high-technology and service industry. It is the global comparison for Dublin.
It covers the Santa Clara Valley and the southern San Francisco Bay Area; the name comes from the silicon used in microchips.
Stanford University at Palo Alto encouraged spin-off firms (new firms started by its staff and graduates) and set up Stanford Research Park in 1951.
Hewlett-Packard was founded in a Palo Alto garage in 1939; Intel was founded in Mountain View in 1968 and is now headquartered in Santa Clara.
Apple is based in Cupertino and Google in Mountain View, which shows how the valley hosts the biggest firms.
Problems: very high house prices and rents, traffic congestion, and homelessness alongside great wealth.
Financial services are a highly footloose, high-value tertiary activity. They deal in money rather than goods.
They include banking, insurance, fund administration, asset management (looking after investments for clients), aircraft leasing, payments and fintech (technology used to deliver financial services).
The International Financial Services Centre (IFSC) is Ireland's main financial services case study. It was set up to bring in finance and to revive a run-down area.
The IFSC was set up in 1987 by the Charles Haughey government on the derelict Custom House Docks, on the north bank of the Liffey.
Approved firms paid a 10% corporation tax rate, so the IFSC was cheaper than elsewhere, later replaced by the 12.5% national rate.
Firms were attracted by the low tax rate, government incentives, an educated English-speaking workforce, EU access, the time zone, and the chance to regenerate a declining dock area.
The IFSC grew into a major international centre and changed the area around it.
The IFSC became one of the world's largest centres for investment funds (pooled savings invested for clients); Irish-domiciled funds held over €3 trillion in assets (2020s, Central Bank of Ireland).
Aircraft leasing is a second specialism. There is more on this in the block on the Shannon Free Zone and aircraft leasing.
Effects: high-value jobs and the regeneration of the north docklands, served by the Luas Red Line from 2004, with new housing nearby.
Finance brings risks as well as gains, but Brexit also created an opening for Dublin.
The 2008 banking crisis damaged confidence in Irish finance, and the Central Bank of Ireland regulates the sector.
After the 2016 Brexit vote, Bank of America and Barclays moved their main EU operations to Dublin, an opportunity for Ireland.
London is the older and larger financial centre against which Dublin can be compared.
The City of London (the Square Mile) was deregulated (its rules relaxed) by the 'Big Bang' of the London Stock Exchange in October 1986.
Canary Wharf, built on derelict London docks from the late 1980s, became a second financial district.
After Brexit, some banks moved EU operations from London to Dublin, Frankfurt and Paris.
Tourism is a tertiary activity, and whether an area develops it depends on a mix of natural and human factors.
Physical attractions: climate, coast, scenery, mountains and lakes.
Cultural and historic attractions: heritage sites, language, music, festivals and sport.
Access: airports, ports, roads and low-cost airlines.
Accommodation and services, and marketing by government agencies.
Cost and exchange rates, and safety and political stability.
Tourism brings overseas visitors and supports jobs. State agencies develop it and market it abroad.
About 11 million overseas visits were made to the Republic of Ireland in 2019 (CSO).
Tourism supported about a quarter of a million jobs in 2019 (industry estimate), which means it is a major employer.
Britain, the USA and continental Europe (Germany, France) are the main source markets, so most visitors come from these.
Fáilte Ireland, set up in 2003, develops tourism in the Republic; Tourism Ireland, an all-island marketing body created under the Good Friday Agreement (1998), markets the island abroad.
The Wild Atlantic Way, launched in 2014, runs about 2,500 km from Inishowen to Kinsale; Ireland's Ancient East was launched in 2015.
Tourism depends on people being free to travel, so it is exposed to sudden shocks.
Overseas visits collapsed in 2020–2021 during COVID-19 travel restrictions, because people could not travel.
Job losses, closed hotels and lost revenue hit remote areas that depend on visitors.
Visitors arrive by air or sea, so access is a main factor in tourism. Exams ask you to name an airport and a ferry port.
International airports: Dublin, Shannon, Cork, Ireland West Airport Knock (opened 1986) and Kerry Airport at Farranfore.
Ferry ports: Dublin Port (to Holyhead), Rosslare Europort (to Fishguard and Pembroke, and since Brexit more direct routes to France) and Port of Cork at Ringaskiddy (to Roscoff, France).
Ryanair, Europe's largest airline by passengers (2020s), is headquartered in Swords, Co. Dublin.
More overseas visitors arrive on the east coast than anywhere else. The reasons all come back to Dublin.
Dublin Airport and Dublin Port are the main entry points for overseas visitors.
Dublin is the capital, with the most attractions, hotels and events.
Short trips, such as city breaks, suit visitors who arrive in Dublin.
Good motorway and rail links radiate from Dublin, so visitors can reach other places easily.
These are named east-coast attractions you can use when asked for two Irish tourist attractions.
The Guinness Storehouse, opened in 2000, is Ireland's most visited fee-paying attraction.
The Book of Kells is at Trinity College Dublin; Dublin Zoo is in the Phoenix Park.
Brú na Bóinne (Newgrange), Co. Meath, has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site (a place listed by the United Nations as of world importance) since 1993.
The Glendalough monastic site and Powerscourt are both in Co. Wicklow.
The west and north coasts have scenic attractions for visitors.
The Cliffs of Moher, Co. Clare, are part of the Burren and Cliffs of Moher UNESCO Global Geopark.
Kylemore Abbey is in Connemara, for example as a west-coast attraction.
The Giant's Causeway, Co. Antrim, in Northern Ireland, has been a UNESCO site since 1986.
Co. Kerry, centred on Killarney and the Ring of Kerry, is a mass-tourism region, meaning large numbers of visitors come there. Its scenery, heritage and access combine to draw them.
Killarney National Park, created in 1932 from the Muckross estate, was Ireland's first national park; the estate was given to the State by the Bourn Vincent family.
Attractions include Muckross House, the Lakes of Killarney, Torc Waterfall, the Gap of Dunloe and Ross Castle.
Carrauntoohil (1,038 m), in the Macgillycuddy's Reeks, is Ireland's highest mountain.
The Ring of Kerry is a circular route of about 180 km around the Iveragh Peninsula.

Skellig Michael, an early Christian monastery on a rocky island, has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1996 and was a film location for Star Wars: The Force Awakens (2015) and The Last Jedi (2017).
The Dingle Peninsula, with the Slea Head drive and the Dingle Gaeltacht (an Irish-speaking area), adds to the county's attractions.
Kerry has attracted visitors for a long time, and better transport helped.
Tourism in Killarney dates from the 18th and 19th centuries.
The railway reached Killarney in 1853, bringing more visitors by making travel easier.
Queen Victoria visited Killarney in 1861, which helped publicise it.
Tourism changes a region in good and bad ways. Exams ask for positive and negative impacts in a named region.
Positive: jobs and income in a peripheral region (one far from the main centres), services kept open in rural areas, and heritage protected through tourism income.
Negative: seasonal jobs, with work concentrated in the summer months.
Negative: traffic and coach congestion on the narrow roads of the Ring of Kerry.
Negative: erosion on the Carrauntoohil paths and litter on popular trails.
Negative: holiday homes push up house prices and make affordable housing scarce for local workers.
Spain is the European example of mass tourism on a large scale. Its growth had specific causes.
Spain received about 84 million international tourists in 2019 and about 94 million in 2024, a record (INE, the Spanish statistics office).
Tourism provides over a tenth of Spain's GDP (2020s, approximate).
Mass tourism grew from the 1960s under the Franco regime, which promoted it with the 'Spain is different' slogan to earn foreign currency.
Causes: sun and beaches; package holidays and jet aircraft; cheap flights; low costs; and proximity to northern Europe.
Spain's Mediterranean coasts and islands hold the main resorts.
Benidorm, on the Costa Blanca, was a small fishing village transformed in the 1950s and 1960s by mayor Pedro Zaragoza's plan for high-rise buildings close to the beach.
The Gran Hotel Bali (186 m, opened 2002) was then Europe's tallest hotel.
The Costa del Sol has Málaga airport, so visitors arrive by air at Torremolinos and Marbella.
The Balearic Islands, in the Mediterranean, include Mallorca (Palma, Magaluf) and Ibiza.
Mass tourism brought money to Spain, but it also caused problems, now met with protest.
Effects: jobs, foreign earnings and infrastructure, such as airports and roads.
Problems: 'ribbon development' (a strip of concrete buildings along the coast), and high-rise overdevelopment.
Water shortages: Catalonia declared a drought emergency in early 2024.
Low-paid seasonal jobs, and rising rents as short-term tourist lets spread.
Large anti-overtourism protests took place in 2024 in Barcelona, Mallorca and the Canary Islands.
Governments in Spain have started to limit the effects of tourism.
The Balearic and Catalan governments charge tourist taxes.
Barcelona plans to end licences for about 10,000 tourist apartments by 2028.
Industries do not last forever. Industrial decline is a downward trend, and it leaves visible signs.
Industrial decline is the long-term fall in the number of firms and jobs in a traditional industry or region.
Evidence: plant closures, derelict sites and buildings, high unemployment, emigration (out-migration), falling population in industrial towns, and social problems.
Irish industry declined for several reasons. Each reason is illustrated by the dated examples that follow.
The end of protection and the opening to free trade exposed small, inefficient protected firms, through the Anglo-Irish Free Trade Agreement (1965) and EEC membership (1973).
Competition from low-wage countries, because they can sell more cheaply.
Recessions (periods when the economy shrinks), such as those of the 1980s and 2008.
New technology replacing labour, so fewer workers are needed.
EU policy reform, such as the reform of the EU sugar regime.
Corporate decisions to move production to lower-cost locations, as with Dell in Limerick. There is more on this in the Irish examples blocks.
Cork lost several large employers in the 1980s, during a recession.
The Dunlop tyre factory in Cork closed in 1983.
Ford's Marina plant in Cork closed in 1984; Ford's Cork company was founded in 1917.
Verolme Cork Dockyard at Rushbrooke closed in 1984.
Further closures followed in the 2000s, each with a different cause. Dates matter here.
Irish Steel (later Ispat) closed on Haulbowline Island, Cork Harbour, in 2001; the site needed a costly clean-up of contaminated waste.
Irish Sugar (Greencore) closed its Carlow beet factory in 2005 and its Mallow factory in 2006, ending Irish sugar production after EU sugar-regime reform.
Waterford Crystal's Kilbarry factory closed in January 2009 when the company went into receivership (when an outside manager takes control of a company that cannot pay its debts).
Dell opened at Raheen, Limerick, in 1990; in January 2009 it announced that manufacturing would move to Łódź, Poland, with the loss of about 1,900 jobs, while sales and service stayed in Ireland.
Energy industries also declined as Ireland moved away from fossil fuels (fuels such as coal and peat, formed from ancient plants).
Moneypoint, Co. Clare, a coal-fired power station built in the 1980s, was Ireland's last coal-burning power station.
Coal burning at Moneypoint ended in 2025, so Ireland no longer burns coal for power, part of the move away from fossil fuels that also closed the peat stations.
When industries close, the damage spreads from the workers to the whole town.
Unemployment reached about 17% in the mid-1980s.
Heavy emigration in the 1980s drew skilled people away from the affected towns, because there were no jobs for them.
Derelict docklands and empty factories were left in city and town centres.
Local towns lost skills and spending as jobs disappeared.
Governments and agencies tried to replace lost jobs and reuse empty sites.
Replacement investment: the IDA and Enterprise Ireland sought new firms to replace lost jobs.
Regeneration (rebuilding and renewing run-down areas) of the Dublin Docklands and the IFSC. There is more on this in the IFSC blocks.
Regeneration of Cork Docklands, through a city plan to redevelop the old port quays.
Heritage reuse: a smaller House of Waterford Crystal factory and visitor centre opened in Waterford city centre (the Mall) in 2010.
Retraining for displaced workers, so they can move into new jobs.
The EU Just Transition Fund supports the Midlands peat region, because peat jobs have ended.
Ireland is not alone in losing traditional industry.
There is more on coalfield and steel regions of decline elsewhere in Europe in the Socio-economic regions notes.
Economic activity is unevenly spread across Ireland. Some regions have far more jobs and income than others.
The Greater Dublin Area had about 2.1 million people in Census 2022, about 40% of the State's population, and holds most multinational and service jobs, along with Cork, Galway and Limerick.
The Border, Midlands and West have more small farms, fewer FDI jobs and lower incomes.
The Border, Midland and Western (BMW) region was designated for EU funding in 1999 (Objective 1 for 2000–2006); the rest of the State was the Southern and Eastern region.
The National Planning Framework (Project Ireland 2040, 2018) aims for Galway, Cork, Limerick and Waterford to each grow by at least 50% by 2040, to balance growth away from Dublin.

Firms try to locate where total transport costs are lowest. This least-cost principle of industrial location was set out by Alfred Weber in 1909, and it depends on whether processing makes the materials lighter or heavier.

Bulk-reducing industries are those where the raw material loses weight in processing, so the plant locates near the raw material because carrying the heavy input a long way would waste money. Examples: alumina refining, dairy processing, fish processing, mining.

Bulk-gaining industries are those where the product gains weight or bulk in production, so the plant locates near the market because the finished product is the costly thing to move. Examples: brewing, soft drinks bottling, bakeries.

Test for an exam location question: if the inputs lose weight in processing, the plant is pulled towards the raw material; if the finished product is heavier or bulkier, it is pulled towards the market.
Location questions use a set of working terms. Knowing them makes the location factors easier to follow.
Footloose industry: one that is not tied to a raw material or a market, so it is free to choose its location. The factors below explain where footloose activities choose to locate.
Branch plant: a factory or office owned by a company headquartered elsewhere, usually carrying out routine production.
Headquarters (HQ): the head office where a company's main decisions are made. Research and development (R&D): the work of designing new products and processes.
Greenfield site: undeveloped land on which a new plant is built. Brownfield site: land already built on, often a former industrial site that may need clearing before reuse.
Industrial estate or business park: a serviced area of land set aside for firms, with roads and utilities already in place.
Cluster, or agglomeration: firms in the same or related industries grouped together, sharing skills, suppliers and research.
Backward linkages are links to a firm's suppliers; forward linkages are links to its customers.
Infrastructure: the transport, energy, water, communications and waste systems that firms depend on.
A location factor is any condition that makes one place more suitable than another for an activity. The first three are the inputs a firm needs to make its product.
Raw materials: weight-losing raw materials pull processing towards their source or towards a port where they arrive, which keeps the cost of moving heavy loads down.

Energy: industry once clustered on coalfields, where the fuel was. National electricity grids freed most industry from this, but energy-hungry activities such as alumina refining and data centres still need large, reliable and affordable power.
Labour: the quantity, skills and education, cost, productivity and flexibility of the workforce.
High-technology and service firms seek graduates because their work needs advanced skills; standardised assembly (repeating the same simple steps) seeks low wages.
Irish examples for labour: the Intel plant at Leixlip and the Galway cluster, both described below.
Once a product is made it has to reach its customers, and firms need to receive inputs. Markets, transport links and communications decide how cheaply and quickly that happens.

Markets: the size and wealth of the market, and access to the EU single market (the EU area with no trade barriers between members). Bulk-gaining and perishable goods locate near the market; services locate near their customers.
Ports: deep water lets bulk carriers (large ships carrying loose cargo) berth. Dublin Port is Ireland's busiest port. Port of Cork and Shannon Foynes Port are also major ports.
Rosslare Europort: direct ferry routes to France grew after Brexit (2021) to avoid the UK land bridge, the route across Britain to continental Europe.
Whitegate, Cork Harbour: Ireland's only oil refinery, opened 1959.

Airports: air freight suits light, high-value, time-sensitive goods such as pharmaceuticals, medical devices and microchips, because the high price of the goods can bear the high cost of air transport.
Dublin Airport handled over 30 million passengers in 2023; its North Runway opened in 2022.

Freight modes: road offers door-to-door flexibility over short and medium distances; rail carries heavy loads on fixed routes; sea is the cheapest way to move bulk over long distances; air is the fastest but the most expensive.

Motorways, rail, broadband and fibre (fibre-optic cable) connect firms to markets and suppliers; for services, broadband and fibre matter most. One environmental challenge of air transport is its CO2 emissions.
A firm also needs money and a welcoming policy environment. Governments, and the EU above them, can make a location more or less attractive through money, tax and rules.
Capital: investment money comes from banks, shareholders, government grants and venture capital (money from investors who back new, risky businesses).

IDA Ireland was set up in 1949 and became an independent agency in 1969. It attracts firms by offering grants, serviced sites (land with utilities already supplied) and advance factories (buildings built ready for a firm to move into).
Corporation tax (the tax on company profits) was 12.5% from 2003. Very large groups pay 15% from 2024.
Enterprise Ireland (1998) supports Irish-owned firms. Údarás na Gaeltachta (1980) supports enterprise in Gaeltacht areas.
Regional policy steers firms towards less-developed areas through grants and incentives.
Planning permission (official approval from the local authority) is needed before a site can be built on.
EU state-aid rules limit the subsidies governments may give firms, while EU funds support regional development.
Trade agreements reduce the barriers that firms face when selling across borders, which makes a location inside the agreement more attractive.

After a firm picks a general area it must find a suitable piece of land, and workers and the plant both need services. The site and its services decide whether the plant can actually be built and run.
Site: flat, well-drained land, large enough for expansion, at a cheap price, so that building is easy and the plant can grow later.
Site: a water supply, and facilities for effluent (liquid waste) and waste disposal.
Site: hazardous industry needs distance from homes, so that accidents or pollution do not harm residents.
Services: water, electricity, gas, broadband, waste treatment, housing and schools. Workers must be able to live near the plant, which is why housing and schools count as location factors.
Some location factors are about people and history rather than land and transport. Firms gather together, stay put out of habit, or follow the pull of a pleasant place to live.
Agglomeration: firms in the same industry gather to share skilled workers, suppliers, research and universities, so each firm gains from the others being nearby.
Cork Harbour (pharmaceuticals) and Galway (medical technology) grew into clusters in this way.
Personal and historical factors: the choices of founders and the history of a site can decide a location, whatever the economics of the place.
Industrial inertia: an industry stays where it is after the original reason for locating there has gone.
Quality of life: attractive places to live help firms recruit skilled staff, because graduates can choose where to work.
Local opposition and environmental regulation can stop or delay a project. Corrib gas shows how long a delay can be.
Corrib gas was discovered in 1996. Its terminal (the plant that receives and processes the gas) is at Bellanaboy, Co. Mayo.
The Shell to Sea campaign opposed the project, and the Rossport Five were jailed in 2005.
Gas first flowed in December 2015, after a long delay caused by local opposition and changes to planning.
The weight of each factor has changed over time as transport, energy supply and technology have changed. The pattern runs from resources, to customers, to skills and quality of life.
In the 19th century, raw materials and power were the main location factors, so industry sat on or near coalfields and sources of materials.
In the 20th century, markets and labour became the main factors.
Today, footloose activities (those free to choose a location) chase skills, tax, connectivity and quality of life.
A bulk-reducing heavy industry located on a deep-water estuary, where imported raw material arrives by sea.
Aughinish Alumina opened in 1983 on Aughinish Island near Askeaton, Co. Limerick, on the south shore of the Shannon Estuary. It is Europe's largest alumina refinery.
Bulk-reducing: about two to three tonnes of bauxite (the ore, or raw rock, that alumina is made from) make one tonne of alumina, so the refinery sits at the raw material's port.
Bauxite is imported by sea, mainly from Guinea and Brazil. The alumina (aluminium oxide) is shipped to aluminium smelters elsewhere; the refinery does not make aluminium.
Deep, sheltered water in the Shannon Estuary, Ireland's deepest natural sheltered water, allows large bulk carriers to berth.
The site is a flat island location away from towns, which suits a large heavy industry.
Government support for heavy industry is a further factor in its siting.
Problems: bauxite residue, known as red mud, is stored in large disposal areas on site.
The company has been owned by the Russian company Rusal since 2007.
The same estuary that serves Aughinish has also been used for energy, because deep water lets fuel arrive by ship.
Moneypoint power station, Co. Clare, is on the Shannon Estuary and imported coal by sea.
Coal burning at Moneypoint ended in 2025, so the estuary's energy role has changed.

Intel is footloose in the sense that its products are not tied to a raw material or a market, so it chose Leixlip from many possible sites. Its choice shows which factors matter to a high-technology firm.
Intel's Leixlip plant opened in 1989. It is Ireland's largest private-sector investment, worth billions of euro.
Skilled graduates are available, so with Maynooth University nearby, which meets the plant's need for a skilled workforce.
IDA support and low corporation tax attracted the investment. There is more on this in Capital, government and EU policy.
Access to the EU single market from an English-speaking base.
The plant lies beside the M4 motorway and close to Dublin Airport, so goods and staff can move easily.
It occupies a large greenfield site (undeveloped land) with a supply of electricity and water.
Footloose does not mean likely to leave: the large fixed investment makes relocation unlikely.
Global job cuts announced in 2024 and 2025 affected Leixlip, showing that even a large plant depends on parent-company decisions.
Cork Harbour combines deep water, industrial land and skilled graduates, so pharmaceutical firms have gathered there. Their closeness to each other reinforces the pattern.
Pfizer, Janssen (Johnson & Johnson) and Novartis are at Ringaskiddy; Eli Lilly is at Kinsale, Co. Cork.
The Port of Cork has deep-water berths at Ringaskiddy, which suits the import and export of pharmaceutical goods.
Large flat sites are zoned for industry (set aside for it in the local plan), with water supply and waste facilities.
Skilled labour comes from University College Cork (UCC) and Munster Technological University (MTU). MTU was formed in 2021 from Cork IT and IT Tralee.
IDA support, tax and clustering reinforce the pattern.
Pharmaceuticals and chemicals are Ireland's largest goods exports.
Older heavy industry in the same harbour: Irish Steel at Haulbowline closed in 2001.
Galway shows how the closure of one firm can feed the growth of another industry. Skilled people left behind became the base for a cluster making medical devices.
Boston Scientific opened in Galway in 1994. Medtronic, Parkmore, Galway followed.
The cluster draws on skilled engineers left by the closure of DEC's plant. The Dell and DEC block below gives the date.
University of Galway research (renamed in 2022) supports the cluster, and a network of suppliers has grown around the firms.
There is more on this in Irish Regions — Core and Peripheral, in the peripheral Irish region subsection.
Food and drink show both sides of Weber's idea. Processing that makes the product lighter stays at the source, while brewing, which makes the product heavier, stays near its customers.
Kerry Group grew from the North Kerry Milk Products co-operative at Listowel, founded in 1972. Its headquarters are in Tralee, Co. Kerry.
Dairy processing is bulk-reducing: plants at Listowel and Tralee sit near the supply of milk.
Killybegs, Co. Donegal, is Ireland's largest fishing port.
Fish processing plants at Killybegs handle pelagic fish (fish that live near the surface) such as mackerel and herring, a bulk-reducing process that locates at the port.
Guinness at St James's Gate, Dublin, was founded in 1759 by Arthur Guinness on a 9,000-year lease.
Brewing is bulk-gaining because water is added to the product, so the brewery sits near its market.
Industrial inertia: Guinness still brews at St James's Gate today, long after the original reasons for the site have gone.

Data centres (buildings full of computers that store and process online data) are a modern footloose activity, but they use huge amounts of electricity. For them the power grid has become a limit on location.
Data centres used about 21% of Ireland's metered electricity in 2023 (CSO).
EirGrid (the electricity grid operator) stated in 2022 that it would not connect new data centres in the Dublin region until about 2028, so the electricity grid now limits their location.
Amazon Web Services, Microsoft, Google and Meta operate data centres in Ireland.
Why Ireland: a cool, mild climate reduces cooling costs; fibre links to the USA and Europe; existing clusters of technology firms; tax.
Modern economic activities can move more easily than older ones. Five changes have loosened the link between an activity and a fixed place.
Lower transport costs, through containerisation (goods packed in standard boxes that move easily between ship, rail and lorry) and air freight, let goods move cheaply over long distances.
Instant communications, through the internet, fibre and video calls, let firms manage plants at a distance.
Standardised production can be done by low-skilled workers, so the work can go anywhere with a cheap labour supply.
The removal of trade barriers, through the EU single market and the World Trade Organization, makes it easier to sell across borders from any member location.
Multinationals (firms operating in many countries) can compare countries and move capital quickly.
A country that hosts a branch plant gains quickly, but its gains are not secure. The same mobility that brings the plant can take it away.
Investment brings rapid job creation, but jobs can leave just as quickly.
Branch plants are vulnerable because the decisions are made at a distant headquarters, not in the host country.
Countries compete for investment by offering tax and grants.
A company opens a branch plant in another country when the move helps its own plans. These are the strategies behind such decisions.
Expansion into new markets, for example, so that customers are served from nearby.
Getting inside a trade bloc (a group of countries trading freely together), which gives tariff-free access to the EU. A tariff is a tax on imports.
Lower costs, because cheaper land, labour or tax raises profit.
Access to skilled labour, because some work cannot be done without trained staff.
Following competitors into a cluster, so as to share the skills and suppliers already there.
Tax planning, because a low-tax country leaves the firm more profit.
The strategies that open plants have opposites that close them. A parent company closes a branch plant when the plant no longer suits its plans.
Rationalisation: cutting surplus capacity after a fall in demand or a merger.
Relocation to lower-cost countries, because production costs are lower there.
Outsourcing: contract manufacturers make the goods instead of the company's own plant.
Automation (machines replacing workers) reduces the number of workers needed.
Mergers and takeovers, after which a parent firm may close a duplicate plant.
A product reaching the end of its life cycle, because falling demand leaves the plant with no future output.
A branch plant does not have to close when its routine work moves away. It can survive by changing what it does.
A plant can survive by moving up the value chain (the steps that add more value to a product) into more R&D, advanced products and services.
Intel's continuing investment at Leixlip is the example: Fab 34, opened in 2023, makes advanced chips using extreme ultraviolet lithography, a chip-making technique.
Dell and DEC are two short examples of plants that closed or moved, and of how a closure can affect a region.
In January 2009 Dell announced that manufacturing would move to Łódź, Poland, with about 1,900 jobs lost in Limerick. It kept sales and service functions in Ireland.
Poland joined the EU on 1 May 2004, with nine other states, so its plants lay inside the enlarged EU with lower costs.
DEC closed its Galway plant in 1993, and its skilled workforce later helped attract the medtech cluster.
There is more on Dell in The MNC and change subsection of The Global Economy — Multinationals and Globalisation.
A product passes through stages from launch to decline, and its best production location changes at each stage. This is how the product life cycle shapes where plants are found.
Introduction: the product is developed near headquarters and R&D, in a core region with highly skilled labour.
Growth: branch plants are opened in other developed countries near large markets; Ireland gained many.
Maturity: the standardised product is mass-produced in low-wage locations, because it no longer needs high skills.
Decline: the plant closes or production is concentrated in the cheapest plant.
Apple's Cork site shows a plant changing its role as the company's production methods change, rather than closing.
Apple opened at Hollyhill, Cork, in 1980 and first made computers there.
As Apple's manufacturing moved to contract manufacturers in Asia, the Cork site shifted mainly to operations, support and services.
The Cork site is now Apple's European headquarters, with about 6,000 staff (2020s).
A host country is not helpless against mobile firms. It can aim to make its jobs harder to move.
Attract firms early in new life cycles, for example in pharmaceuticals, medical technology and software, so the country has the work while it is new and growing.

Invest in education and research so that jobs are harder to move: Science Foundation Ireland, set up in 2000 and made a statutory body (one created by law) in 2003, funds research; it merged into Research Ireland in 2024.
Universities supply the graduates that keep high-technology firms in place.
Computing and the internet have freed many services from a fixed place. Delivering a service at a distance means it can be located almost anywhere.
Computing and the internet have made many services footloose, and Ireland became a European base for software and internet firms.
Teleservices are services delivered at a distance by phone or internet, such as customer support, technical support and remote data processing.
Teleservices can locate anywhere with broadband, including peripheral areas (those far from the main centres).
Low-skilled teleservice work moves easily to cheaper countries or is automated.
There is more on IT and teleservices in The MNC and change subsection of The Global Economy — Multinationals and Globalisation.
E-commerce has three effects on where activities locate: on warehouses, on town-centre shops and on bank branches, because customers no longer need to travel.
E-commerce is buying and selling goods and services over the internet.
Warehouses and delivery depots locate near motorways and airports, so that parcels can be moved quickly.
Pressure on town-centre shops, and bank branch closures, follow the growth of online trade.
There is more on e-commerce and an MNC's operations in The MNC and change subsection of The Global Economy — Multinationals and Globalisation.
After COVID-19 many jobs could be done away from a city office. This gives rural areas a chance to attract work, but only if they have good broadband.
Remote and hybrid working (part at home, part in the office) grew after COVID-19, so some jobs can be done from home or a local hub rather than a city office.
National Broadband Plan: the contract was signed in 2019 with National Broadband Ireland to bring high-speed broadband to rural premises.
Connected Hubs: a national network of remote-working hubs launched in 2021.
Our Rural Future, rural development policy, 2021.
Broadband availability differs from region to region, and a region's coverage affects whether it can attract remote-working jobs.
New technology continues to change where work is done and how many people are needed.
Artificial intelligence and automation are future drivers of location and job change.
Automation can reduce the labour-cost advantage of low-wage locations, favouring places with skills and research, because machines make cheap labour less important.
Map and photograph questions ask why an activity might or might not locate at a point, using evidence from the map or photograph.
Name the factor, then give evidence from the map or photograph: a grid reference, or the photograph's location in accepted notation.
Explain why the factor matters to the activity.
Give three to five significant relevant points (SRPs) for each reason.
Use the same structure for a reason why the activity might not locate there.
For a factory or multinational, look on the map for the features that supply land, transport, workers and services.
Flat land and an edge-of-town site, where there is room and land is cheaper.
A national primary road or motorway, a railway, and a port or airport, for moving goods.
A town labour force and services: schools, hospital and housing.
Water and an existing industrial estate, because services and planning approval for industry are already in place.
A fish processing plant needs to be close to where fish are landed, because fish is a bulk-reducing, perishable raw material.
A pier, harbour or fishing port, on the coast.
Roads to markets, so that fresh fish reaches buyers quickly.
Water and a labour force, because processing needs both.
Low-lying land, because it is flat enough to build on and close to the coast.
A hotel depends on attractions that draw visitors, together with the services that let them reach and use the hotel.
Coast, beach and scenery; lakes or mountains; antiquities (ancient sites and monuments).
A golf course, and water sports, because these give guests activities.
Nearby town services and road access, so guests and staff can reach the hotel.
Tourist information, which helps visitors plan trips.
The one reason against in your answer comes from the map features that make a site unsuitable.
Steep or high land, which is hard and costly to build on.
A protected or scenic area, where planning conflict is likely.
Poor roads, remoteness from labour, distance from services, and impact on residents, because each makes the plant harder to run or provokes opposition.
The invented town of Ballyglas lies beside an invented N-road and river. All grid references in this example are illustrative.
Reason for locating: the flat land beside the N-road at illustrative grid reference M 142 335 gives room for a factory and its expansion.
Why it matters: a factory needs a large flat site, and the road gives access to markets.
Reason against: the river floodplain at illustrative grid reference M 140 333 would flood, so a plant there would be at risk.
Ordinary Level aerial photograph questions ask you to judge a proposed factory site and an alternative location.
Give advantages and disadvantages of the proposed factory site and of an alternative location, using accepted notation for the photograph.
Refer to features by their position in the photograph, such as foreground, background, left or right, so the examiner can tell exactly what you mean.

A resource is anything in the environment that people use to meet their needs. Resources are classed by whether nature can replace them, and this decides whether a country can keep using them for ever.
Resources include energy, minerals, water, soil, forests, fish, land and scenery, so the word covers far more than fuels.

Non-renewable (stock, finite) resources formed over millions of years, so they are used up far faster than they form and will eventually run out. Examples are coal, oil, natural gas, peat, metal ores and uranium.

Renewable (flow) resources are replaced naturally, so they will not run out however much is used. Examples are wind, solar, hydro (running water), wave, tidal and geothermal heat (heat from inside the Earth).

Some resources are renewable only if managed sustainably (used no faster than they are replaced): forests, fish stocks, soils, groundwater and biomass (plant material used as fuel). Overuse turns them into exhausted resources, as happens with fish stocks. There is more on this in Sustainable economic development.
Three kinds of fuel are non-renewable. Fossil fuels and peat formed from once-living material, and uranium is a finite mineral.
Fossil fuels (coal, oil, natural gas and peat) formed from the remains of plants or marine organisms buried and compressed over millions of years. Burning them releases the carbon they stored.
Peat is non-renewable because a bog (wet ground where dead plants build up as peat) grows only about 1 mm a year, far slower than it is cut.
Nuclear energy from uranium is an alternative to fossil fuels with low carbon emissions, but it is not renewable because uranium is finite.
Energy is the resource that the rest of the economy runs on. This is why a country's energy supply matters so much to its wealth and security.
Primary energy is energy in its raw form, such as oil, gas or wind. Electricity is a secondary form made from primary sources, for example by burning gas or by turning turbines with wind.
Renewables give a far larger share of electricity than of total energy, because much of total energy is oil used for transport and heating, which renewables supply little of.
Energy powers industry, transport, farming and homes, so resources are central to the economy.
Energy security means a secure and affordable supply that is not disrupted by price shocks (sudden large rises in price) or supply cuts.
A country that imports its energy pays a large import bill (the money spent buying energy from abroad) and is exposed to price shocks and supply cuts.
Ireland has few fossil fuels of its own, so it depends heavily on imported energy. The mix of fuels it uses shows where that dependence lies.
Import dependence (the share of energy bought from abroad): Ireland imported close to 90% of its energy in the years before Corrib gas came ashore in 2015.

The share fell after Corrib began and has risen again as Corrib's output declines. In the early 2020s Ireland still imported about three-quarters of its energy (SEAI, the Sustainable Energy Authority of Ireland).
Early 2020s primary energy mix (SEAI): oil just under half and the largest single source; natural gas about a third; renewables a little over a tenth; coal and peat small and falling.
Adding oil, gas, coal and peat shows that fossil fuels still supply most of Ireland's primary energy, while renewables are growing.
Oil is Ireland's largest single source of primary energy, and Ireland produces none of it.
All of Ireland's oil is imported, which adds to the import bill and leaves the country exposed to price shocks.
Oil is used mainly for transport and home heating.
Whitegate, Co. Cork, is Ireland's only oil refinery (the plant that turns crude oil into fuels).
Natural gas is Ireland's second-largest primary energy source and its largest source of electricity. Home gas fields supplied it for decades but are now running down.

Kinsale Head gas field, off Co. Cork, was discovered in 1971 and began production in 1978 as Ireland's first commercial gas field. Production ended in 2020 when the field was depleted (used up), so it is no longer a working field.
Corrib gas field, off north-west Co. Mayo, was discovered in 1996 and first flowed in December 2015. Its gas is processed at Bellanaboy, Co. Mayo.
For a time after 2015 Corrib supplied over half of Ireland's gas. Its output is now declining, which is why import dependence has risen again.
Most of Ireland's gas now comes from Britain through interconnector pipelines (cross-border links) from Moffat, Scotland.
Gas is the largest single source of Irish electricity, because gas-fired power stations generate more of it than any other fuel.
Ireland's own coal fields are small and long closed. Moneypoint, the big coal-burning station, ran on imported coal and has now stopped burning coal.
Ireland's native coalfields are small and long closed. They are Arigna, Co. Roscommon, where mining ended in 1990 and which is now the Arigna Mining Experience, and Castlecomer, Co. Kilkenny.

Moneypoint, Co. Clare, on the Shannon Estuary, is an ESB (Electricity Supply Board) coal-fired station opened in 1985. At about 900 MW (megawatts, a measure of power output) it is Ireland's largest power station.
Moneypoint burned imported coal, brought in by large ships to its deep-water jetty (a landing pier where water is deep enough for big ships).

Peat, cut from the bogs of the Midlands, was Ireland's own fuel and powered stations for decades. It has now ended, and the cutaway bogs (bogs from which the peat has been removed) are being given new uses.
Bord na Móna, the State peat company, was founded in 1946.
Peat-fired stations at Lanesborough (Lough Ree) and Shannonbridge (West Offaly) closed in December 2020. Bord na Móna ended all peat harvesting in January 2021.
Edenderry, Co. Offaly, switched from peat to biomass, a renewable fuel of wood and energy crops.
Bellacorick, Co. Mayo: the peat station closed in 2003 and was replaced by wind farms on the cutaway bog.
Cutaway bogs are reused. Lough Boora Discovery Park, Co. Offaly, has turned a cutaway bog into parkland, wetlands and walking and cycling trails.
Hydroelectric power uses falling water to turn turbines (machines that spin to drive generators). The Shannon Scheme at Ardnacrusha was an early large scheme, and little potential is left for more.

Ardnacrusha, on the River Shannon near Limerick, was built by the German firm Siemens and opened in 1929 as the Shannon Scheme. The ESB was set up in 1927 to run it, and for some years it supplied most of the country's electricity.
Other stations: Poulaphouca on the River Liffey, Co. Wicklow; Inniscarra and Carrigadrohid on the River Lee, Co. Cork; and Cathaleen's Fall at Ballyshannon on the River Erne, Co. Donegal.

Turlough Hill, Co. Wicklow, opened in 1974 as an ESB pumped-storage station. Water is pumped uphill when demand is low and released through turbines at peak times, so it stores energy for when it is needed.
Little potential is left for large new hydro schemes, because the best sites were already used.
Wind is Ireland's main renewable source. The country's position on the Atlantic edge of Europe gives it an advantage.
Wind supplied about a third of Irish electricity in the early 2020s. Renewables, mostly wind, supplied about two-fifths.
Strong, frequent Atlantic winds make the western coasts and uplands the best sites for wind farms.
Bellacorick wind farm, Co. Mayo (1992), was Ireland's first commercial wind farm. Oweninny wind farm was built on the same cutaway bog.
Galway Wind Park, Connemara, completed in 2017, is one of Ireland's largest onshore (on land) wind farms.

Arklow Bank Wind Park, off Co. Wicklow, opened in 2004 as Ireland's first offshore (at sea) wind farm, with seven turbines. Offshore wind is planned to grow strongly, with at least 5 GW targeted by 2030.
Ireland's other renewable sources are smaller than wind. Some are growing quickly and some are still at an early stage.
Solar power has grown rapidly since the early 2020s, through large solar farms on farmland and panels on rooftops. SEAI grants support home installations.
The Atlantic Marine Energy Test Site off Belmullet, Co. Mayo, is Ireland's wave-energy test site, where wave machines are trialled.
Geothermal energy is limited to low-temperature ground-source heat pumps (devices that take heat from the ground to warm buildings).
Tidal energy harnesses the rise and fall of the sea, and it is at an early stage in Ireland.
Biomass (wood and energy crops) and biofuels (fuels made from plant material) are the remaining renewable sources.
Governments set targets to push renewables up and cut emissions. Ireland missed its 2020 target and has set tougher ones for 2030 and 2050.
Ireland's 2020 EU target was 16% of gross final energy consumption (all the energy used by final users such as homes, industry and transport) from renewables.
Ireland reached only about 13.5% and missed the target. It was one of the furthest from its target of any EU member state.
Climate Action Plan: 80% of electricity from renewables by 2030, and at least 5 GW (gigawatts) of offshore wind by 2030.

Climate Action and Low Carbon Development (Amendment) Act 2021: cut greenhouse gas emissions by 51% by 2030, compared with 2018, and reach climate neutrality (net zero, meaning emissions no higher than what is removed) by 2050.
Ireland's renewable share fell short of its 2020 target for six linked reasons. Several come from how Irish people live and travel, and some from delays in building.
Heavy dependence on cars and road freight for transport, which runs on oil, so renewables supply little of it.
Oil used for home heating in a dispersed rural settlement pattern (homes spread out, so gas networks and shared heating are hard to provide).
Slow planning and grid connection for wind farms, which delayed new capacity.
No large hydro potential left for new schemes, because the best sites were already used.
A late start on offshore wind, which left Ireland with less renewable capacity.
Strong economic and population growth raising energy demand, which made the renewable share harder to raise.
Interconnectors are cables or pipelines that link Ireland's energy network to other countries. They help security of supply because power and gas can flow in when Ireland needs them.
The East-West Interconnector, opened in 2012, links Co. Dublin to north Wales by electricity cable.
The Celtic Interconnector, from Co. Cork to Brittany, France, is under construction and due to link Ireland to the EU mainland grid in the late 2020s.
Gas also arrives by interconnector pipelines from Scotland, which is how most of Ireland's gas now reaches it.
Knowing which sectors use most energy shows where demand is highest and where savings or renewables matter most.
Transport is the largest energy-using sector in Ireland (SEAI).
Heat for homes and businesses comes next, then electricity generation for industry and services.
Data centres (buildings full of computer servers) used about a fifth of Ireland's metered electricity in 2023 (CSO, the Central Statistics Office). Most are in the Dublin region.
Europe depends heavily on imported energy, and its main oil and gas comes from the North Sea and from suppliers outside the EU.
The EU imports close to three-fifths of its energy (early 2020s, Eurostat, the EU's statistics office).
The North Sea, shared by the UK and Norway, is Europe's main oil and gas province (an area rich in oil and gas).
Norway is not an EU member but is one of the EU's main gas suppliers, by pipeline.
Relying on one supplier for a vital fuel is risky. Europe learned this when Russia, its biggest gas supplier, invaded Ukraine.
Before 2022 Russia supplied about two-fifths of the EU's imported gas.
Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022. Gas and electricity prices soared across Europe.

REPowerEU plan, May 2022: cut dependence on Russian fossil fuels by saving energy, importing more liquefied natural gas (LNG, gas cooled to a liquid so ships can carry it, much of it from the USA) and speeding up renewables.
Russia's share of EU gas imports has since fallen sharply.
National energy mixes differ widely across Europe. France relies on nuclear power.
Nuclear power (electricity made from splitting uranium atoms) supplies about two-thirds of France's electricity.
Germany is changing its energy mix by moving to renewables and ending nuclear power, though it still burns coal.
The Energiewende (energy transition) is Germany's long-term switch to renewables.
After the Fukushima disaster in Japan in March 2011 (a nuclear accident), Germany decided to phase out nuclear power. Its last three reactors closed on 15 April 2023.
Germany still burns lignite (brown coal) from huge open-cast mines (mines dug from the surface) in the Rhineland. A 2020 law sets 2038 at the latest as the end of coal-fired power.
Poland shows a country whose power still rests on coal.
Coal generates well over half of Poland's electricity (early 2020s).
Denmark shows a country that has built its electricity supply around wind.
Wind supplies about half of Denmark's electricity (2020s).
Denmark was an early leader in wind power and is home to the turbine maker Vestas.
Two European countries that are not EU members get nearly all their electricity from renewable sources, thanks to their landscapes.
Hydroelectric power supplies about 90% of Norway's electricity, from its mountains, high rainfall and glacial lakes, which give plenty of falling water.
Geothermal and hydro supply almost all of Iceland's electricity, and about 9 in 10 Icelandic homes are heated geothermally.
The EU sets renewable targets for all its members. It met its 2020 target and has raised the goal for 2030.
The EU target of 20% renewable energy by 2020 was achieved, at about 22%.
The revised Renewable Energy Directive (2023, an EU law binding on member states) requires at least 42.5% renewable energy by 2030.
Renewables supplied about a quarter of EU gross final energy consumption in 2023, so the EU still has far to go to reach 42.5%.
Despite the growth of renewables, fossil fuels still supply most of the EU's energy. Final energy (the energy used by consumers) is spread across several sectors.
Fossil fuels (oil, gas and coal) still supply most of the EU's energy. Oil is the largest single source, mainly for transport.
Transport, households and industry each take roughly a quarter to a third of final energy. Services take a smaller share.
Energy production and consumption are not spread evenly across Europe. Which role a country plays depends on its industry and its natural resources.
Core industrial countries, such as Germany and France, consume most of the energy, because their large industry and populations need so much.
Resource-rich countries, such as Norway, export energy, because they produce more than they need.
Peripheral countries, such as Ireland, depend on imports, because they have few fuels of their own.

Fossil fuels (coal, oil and gas formed from ancient living things) supply about four-fifths of the world's primary energy (the energy taken straight from nature before conversion) in the 2020s. Their production is concentrated in a few places, so most countries must import them.
The Middle East (e.g. Saudi Arabia, Iran, Iraq) holds about half the world's proven oil reserves (oil known to be recoverable). Venezuela has the largest proven reserves of any single country.
The USA has been the world's largest oil producer since the late 2010s, through shale oil and gas (trapped in rock and released by fracking, which fractures the rock with pressurised liquid).
Russia is one of the largest gas exporters. Qatar is a leading exporter of liquefied natural gas (LNG, gas cooled to a liquid so that ships can carry it).
China produces and consumes about half the world's coal.
Fossil fuels are traded over long distances by tanker, pipeline and LNG ship, so importers depend on exporters for their energy security (a steady, affordable supply of energy).
Energy use is very uneven across the world. It follows wealth and industry, and the pattern is shifting towards Asia.
Developed countries use far more energy per person than developing countries. Demand is now growing fastest in Asia, notably China and India, because their economies and populations are growing.
The USA, Canada and Australia use many times more energy per person than India or most of sub-Saharan Africa.
China has been the world's largest CO2 (carbon dioxide) emitter in total since the mid-2000s, but the USA emits far more CO2 per person.
Burning a fossil fuel releases the carbon and impurities locked inside it. Each pollutant causes a different problem, so keep them apart.
Carbon dioxide (CO2) is the main greenhouse gas released, and it drives global warming.
Sulphur dioxide (SO2), mainly from coal and heavy oil (thick, impure oil), is a cause of acid rain.
Nitrogen oxides (NOx), mainly from vehicles and power stations, are also a cause of acid rain.
Smoke, fine particles (soot, tiny solid specks that can be breathed deep into the lungs) and carbon monoxide are released as well.
The greenhouse effect is the natural trapping of heat by gases in the atmosphere. Burning fossil fuels adds extra gas to it.
CO2 traps heat in the atmosphere, so extra CO2 from burning fossil fuels enhances the greenhouse effect and causes global warming. There is more on this in Environmental pollution.
Acid rain is a transboundary problem (one that crosses national borders): the countries that cause it are often not the ones that suffer.
Normal rain is slightly acidic, at about pH 5.6, because CO2 dissolves in it naturally. Acid rain is rain with a pH below 5.6, not below pH 7.
SO2 and NOx dissolve in water vapour to form sulphuric and nitric acids. These fall as wet deposition in rain, or as dry deposition of acidic particles and gases.
Sources include coal-fired power stations, heavy industry and vehicles, because all of them burn fuels that contain sulphur or release nitrogen oxides.

Emissions from Britain and Germany were carried by the prevailing south-westerly winds (the usual wind direction) to Norway and Sweden, which is why Scandinavia suffered from other countries' pollution.

The Black Triangle, the border region of former East Germany, Poland and Czechia, had lignite-burning power stations (lignite is a low-grade, smoky coal) that caused severe forest death in the 1970s and 1980s.
Acid rain harms living things, buildings and people. The damage can appear far from the source, because the wind carries the pollution across borders.
