Forest damage: needle and leaf loss, and nutrients leached (washed out) from the soil. German forests, such as the Black Forest, were reported dying in the 1980s (Waldsterben, meaning forest death).
Lake acidification: thousands of Scandinavian lakes were acidified and lost their fish. Aluminium released from the soil by the acid kills fish.
Limestone and marble buildings and statues dissolve, through the same process as the chemical weathering of limestone (carbonation, where weak acid reacts with the rock).
Corrosion of metal, for example, and respiratory (breathing) problems in people.
Because acid rain crosses borders, responses had to be international as well as national. They work either by cutting emissions or by repairing the damage.

The 1979 Convention on Long-Range Transboundary Air Pollution, signed at UNECE (the United Nations Economic Commission for Europe) in Geneva, was an international agreement on air pollution that crosses borders.
EU directives (laws binding on member states) limit emissions from large power stations.

Flue-gas desulphurisation (scrubbers, which remove SO2 from the smoke before it leaves the chimney) is used at power stations. Moneypoint, Co. Clare, opened in 1985 and had scrubbers fitted in the late 2000s.
Low-sulphur fuels cut SO2 at source. Catalytic converters (exhaust devices that reduce NOx) became compulsory on new petrol cars in the EU in 1993.
Sweden and Norway have limed acidified lakes (added lime to neutralise the acid) since the 1970s and 1980s.
Countries switched from coal to gas and renewables, which release little or no SO2.
Outcome: European SO2 emissions have fallen by well over three-quarters since 1990, and many lakes are recovering.
Smog is smoke mixed with fog. It builds up when smoke from home fires cannot escape upwards.
Burning coal and turf in homes releases smoke and fine particles, because the fuel burns incompletely in an open fire.
In calm, cold winter weather an anticyclone (a high-pressure system with settled air) creates a temperature inversion, where a layer of warm air sits above cold air near the ground.
The inversion traps the smoke near the ground, because the warm layer stops it rising and blowing away. This forms smog.
Smog causes bronchitis, asthma, heart and lung disease, and extra deaths, because the smoke and fine particles are breathed in.
Smog led governments to ban smoky fuels in city areas. London's disaster in 1952 was the earlier precedent, and Dublin's ban is the Irish case study.
London's Great Smog, in December 1952, caused about 4,000 deaths at the time. Later estimates are far higher.
The Great Smog led to the UK Clean Air Act 1956, which created smokeless zones (areas where smoky fuel may not be burned).
Dublin suffered severe winter smogs in the early 1980s from household coal burning, which led to the ban.
The sale of smoky (bituminous) coal was banned in Dublin from 1 September 1990. Black smoke levels fell by about 70%.
The ban covered smoky coal only, so smokeless fuel and turf could still be burned in Dublin at first.
A study published in The Lancet in 2002 estimated that the ban was linked to about 350 fewer deaths a year in Dublin from respiratory and heart disease.
The ban was extended to Cork in 1995, and in stages to other cities and large towns as low-smoke zones. National rules from 2022 further restrict the sale of smoky solid fuels and wet wood.
Beyond the air pollutants, getting and using fossil fuels harms land, water and rivers.
Oil spills during transport, for example from tankers, pollute the sea and coasts. There is more on this in Environmental pollution.
Landscape damage comes from coal mining and peat cutting, which scar and strip the land.
Thermal pollution of rivers is caused by the cooling water of power stations, which is returned to the river warmer than it was taken.
Wind turns turbine blades that drive a generator. Turbines are built onshore on land and offshore at sea.

Ireland: wind supplied about a third of Irish electricity in the early 2020s, from onshore farms such as Galway Wind Park, Connemara (2017), and from Arklow Bank Wind Park, off Co. Wicklow (2004), Ireland's first offshore wind farm.
Denmark: wind supplies about half of Denmark's electricity.
Advantage: strong, frequent Atlantic winds give Ireland a good wind resource, and wind is the main renewable source in Irish electricity.
Disadvantage: output varies with the wind, and local residents object on grounds of noise, shadow flicker (flickering shadows cast by moving blades) and visual impact.

Disadvantage: Derrybrien, Co. Galway, suffered a peat slide of about 450,000 m³ on 16 October 2003 during construction of a wind farm on bog. The EU Court of Justice fined Ireland in 2019 for the lack of a proper environmental impact assessment (a study of the likely harm before building).
Hydroelectric power uses falling water to turn turbines, through three main methods.
Dams and reservoirs release stored water through turbines at a controlled rate.
Run-of-river schemes use the river's natural flow, so they need little or no stored water.
Pumped storage pumps water uphill at times of low demand and releases it at peak times, so it acts like a store of energy.

Ireland: Ardnacrusha on the River Shannon (Shannon Scheme, opened 1929, built by Siemens) and Turlough Hill, Co. Wicklow (1974), the country's pumped-storage station. Poulaphouca on the Liffey, Inniscarra and Carrigadrohid on the Lee, and Cathaleen's Fall at Ballyshannon on the Erne also generate power.
Advantage: output can be raised quickly at peak times (when demand is highest), as at Turlough Hill.
Disadvantage: Ireland has little hydro potential left for large new schemes.
Norway: hydroelectric power supplies about 90% of its electricity, for example.

Three Gorges Dam, Yangtze River, China: the world's largest power station by installed capacity. It was completed in 2006, fully operational in 2012, and over one million people were relocated. It gives flood control downstream but traps sediment (silt that would otherwise travel downriver).
Photovoltaic panels convert sunlight into electricity, and solar thermal panels use sunlight to heat water.

Ireland: solar power has grown rapidly since the early 2020s, through large solar farms on farmland and panels on rooftops. SEAI (Sustainable Energy Authority of Ireland) grants help homes to install panels.
Disadvantage: Ireland's cloud cover and short winter days limit output, because panels need strong daylight.
Waves and tides drive turbines or barrages (dams built across an estuary). The three technologies are different, so do not mix them up.
Wave: the Atlantic Marine Energy Test Site off Belmullet, Co. Mayo, is a wave test site.
Tidal barrage: La Rance, Brittany, France, a barrage across the Rance estuary, opened in 1966. It was one of the first and largest tidal power stations.

Tidal stream: SeaGen in Strangford Lough, Co. Down, was installed in 2008 as the world's first commercial-scale tidal-stream turbine, using the fast tidal flow through the narrows. It has since been removed.
Advantage: tides are predictable, because they follow the moon's cycle. Disadvantages: high cost and marine impacts (harm to sea life and habitats).
Geothermal energy uses heat from the Earth's interior, to heat water or to generate steam.

Iceland lies on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge (a plate boundary where the crust is thin) over a hotspot (a rising plume of hot rock). The Hellisheiði power station generates electricity from geothermal water, and about 9 in 10 Icelandic homes are heated by it.
Ireland uses low-temperature heat pumps only, which draw modest heat from the ground.
Advantage: output does not depend on the weather. Disadvantage: high-temperature sources are found only where the crust is hot, as in Iceland.
Biomass is organic material (from plants or animal waste) burned or converted to energy.
Sources: wood chip, energy crops such as willow and miscanthus, and biogas from slurry and food waste produced by anaerobic digestion (rotting without oxygen).
Biofuels (fuels made from plants) are blended into petrol and diesel, by law in Ireland.
Edenderry, Co. Offaly, was converted from peat to biomass, an example of a power station switching fuel.
Advantage: carbon-neutral in principle, because the crops absorb as much CO2 as they release when burned. Disadvantage: energy crops compete with food production for land.
Nuclear power uses fission, the splitting of uranium atoms, to release heat that makes steam to drive turbines. Nuclear is not renewable.
France: nuclear power supplies about two-thirds of its electricity.
Advantages: low carbon emissions, so little CO2, plus reliable and large output.
Disadvantages, such as radioactive waste, accident risk, very high cost, and the cost of decommissioning (safely shutting down and dismantling) old reactors.
Chernobyl, Ukraine (then USSR), 26 April 1986: a reactor exploded, and radioactive fallout spread across Europe, including Ireland. A 30 km exclusion zone remains.
Fukushima Daiichi, Japan, 11 March 2011: an earthquake and tsunami knocked out cooling and caused meltdowns.
Ireland has never had a nuclear power station. A combination of law, public opinion and practical limits explains why.
The Electricity Regulation Act 1999 bans the use of nuclear fission to generate electricity in Ireland.
The ESB (Electricity Supply Board) planned a nuclear power station at Carnsore Point, Co. Wexford, in the 1970s. It was abandoned after large public protests and was never built.
Other reasons: Ireland's small electricity grid, the high cost, the problem of waste disposal, and fears raised by Chernobyl.
Sellafield, Cumbria, England, a nuclear reprocessing site on the Irish Sea coast, has discharges that Irish governments have long objected to, which adds to Irish unease about nuclear power.
Renewable energy comes from sources that are naturally replaced. These advantages apply to wind, hydro, solar, wave, tidal and geothermal power.
Renewables are inexhaustible, so supply is secure: the sun, wind, water and tides will not run out.
They produce little or no CO2, SO2 or NOx, so they cause less global warming and acid rain.
They reduce the fossil-fuel import bill and improve energy security.
They create jobs, often in rural areas.
Once a plant is built, the fuel is free.
They help meet EU and national targets and avoid penalties for missing them.
Renewables also have costs and limits, and these explain why fossil fuels are still widely used.
Renewables are intermittent (not constant), because wind and sun vary, so backup or storage is needed.
The initial cost of building a plant is high.
Turbines and dams have visual impact, and cause noise and local objections.
Remote sites need grid connections (cables linking them to the electricity network).
Some habitats are damaged: birds are killed by turbines, and dams flood valleys. Peat slides can also happen at wind farms on bog.
Ireland imports a large share of its energy, so renewable energy matters for both its environment and its economy.

Ireland imported about three-quarters of its energy in the early 2020s, at a cost of billions of euro a year. Renewables reduce this import bill and the exposure to price shocks (sudden rises in world fuel prices).

Ireland must meet its 2030 targets for renewable electricity and emissions. The Climate Action Plan aims for 80% renewable electricity by 2030, and missing EU targets exposes Ireland to the cost of buying compliance.
Energy security improves through interconnectors (cables that link electricity grids): the East-West Interconnector to Wales (2012) and the Celtic Interconnector to France (due in the late 2020s).
Renewables provide jobs and income in rural areas, because wind farms, solar farms and dams are built there.
Green power attracts multinational companies that want renewable electricity.
Cleaner air and water follow from burning less fossil fuel.
Map questions ask you to choose and justify a wind-farm site on an Ordnance Survey map, and to explain how conflict may arise. Match each feature of the site to a need of the wind farm.
A wind farm needs a high, exposed upland or coastal site with strong winds, because output depends on wind speed.
It should be away from houses, to limit noise and shadow flicker.
It needs an access road close by for construction, and a connection close to the electricity grid, by transmission line (the high-voltage cable that carries power).
It should avoid protected areas and deep peat, because peat can slide when disturbed. It is best placed on land of low farming value.
Conflict arises when a site lies near homes or in a protected or scenic area, so the site must balance wind strength against these constraints.
Pollution is a problem caused by people, and it can be small or enormous in scale. Knowing how to define it, classify it and place it on a scale lets you tackle any pollution question.

Pollution is the release by human activity of substances or energy (heat, noise, light) into the environment in amounts that harm living things, health or property. Harm is what makes a release pollution.
Types of pollution: air, water (fresh and marine), land and soil, noise and visual. For example, oil in the sea is water pollution and a motorway's roar is noise pollution.
Scales: local (one river or town), national (a country's water quality) and global (the whole atmosphere or ocean). The scale tells you how many people and places are affected.

Transboundary pollution (pollution that crosses national borders) means the place it harms may be far from its source. Acid rain, rain made acidic by gases from burning fuels, is the European example, taught in the note Burning fossil fuels and using alternative energy sources.

Pollution can be traced back to its source in two ways, depending on whether it leaves from one spot or from many. This matters because a single outlet is easier to find and control than thousands of small ones.
Point sources come from one identifiable place, such as a factory pipe or a sewage outfall (the pipe where sewage enters a river or the sea).
Diffuse sources come from many places at once, such as runoff (rainwater washing substances off the land) from many farms, or traffic.
Economic activities that pollute include agriculture, manufacturing, energy generation, transport, mining, tourism, households and urban waste.
Global warming is the main global-scale example of pollution. It starts with a natural process that human activity has strengthened.

The natural greenhouse effect: greenhouse gases (gases in the atmosphere that trap heat) let incoming short-wave solar radiation through but absorb outgoing long-wave radiation (heat given off by the earth), which keeps the earth habitable.
The enhanced greenhouse effect: human activity adds greenhouse gases to the atmosphere, which trap more heat and so warm the planet further.
Each greenhouse gas has its own human sources, and many of them are economic activities. Knowing which activity gives which gas lets you explain the causes of warming.
CO2 (carbon dioxide) comes from burning fossil fuels (coal, oil and gas), deforestation (clearing forests, which removes trees that absorb CO2) and cement production.
Methane comes from cattle and sheep, rice paddies, landfill (rubbish buried in the ground) and gas leaks.
Nitrous oxide comes from nitrogen fertilisers and slurry (liquid animal manure).
CFCs (chlorofluorocarbons, man-made gases) and other fluorinated gases are also greenhouse gases.
Scientists measure warming in several independent ways, and they all point the same way. Each measurement below is a piece of evidence you can quote.

Atmospheric CO2 was about 280 ppm (parts per million) before the Industrial Revolution. It passed 400 ppm in the mid-2010s and was over 420 ppm by the mid-2020s. These readings are measured at Mauna Loa, Hawaii, which has recorded them since 1958.
Global average surface temperature has risen by about 1.1 to 1.2 °C since the late 1800s (IPCC, the UN's climate science panel).
2024 was the warmest year on record and the first calendar year more than 1.5 °C above pre-industrial levels (Copernicus, the EU's Earth observation programme).
Arctic summer sea ice has shrunk by about 13% per decade since satellite records began in 1979.
Global sea level rose by about 20 cm between 1901 and 2018 (IPCC).
Glaciers (large masses of ice on land) are retreating worldwide, which is a visible sign that temperatures are rising.
A warmer atmosphere changes oceans, ice, weather and ecosystems, and these changes harm people and wildlife. The effects are worst for places that are low-lying or already vulnerable.

Sea-level rise, from thermal expansion of seawater (water expands as it warms) and melting land ice, threatens low-lying countries and deltas: Bangladesh (the Ganges-Brahmaputra delta), the Maldives, Tuvalu and Kiribati.
More intense heatwaves, droughts, floods and storms. The Sahel (the dry belt south of the Sahara) has suffered droughts.
Glacier retreat threatens water supplies, because many places depend on meltwater from glaciers.
Coral bleaching (corals losing their colour and dying when seas get too warm): the Great Barrier Reef, Australia, has suffered repeated mass bleaching since the late 1990s.
Species shifts and extinctions, crop failures in vulnerable regions, and climate refugees (people forced to leave their homes because of climate change).
Ireland is not exempt from global warming. Its temperature has risen, and the effects are felt on land, at the coast and at sea.
Ireland's average temperature has risen by about 0.9 °C since 1900 (EPA and Met Éireann, the national weather service).
Warmer temperatures bring wetter winters and more flooding, a risk of summer drought, stronger storms and coastal erosion (the sea wearing away the coast).
Effects also include changes to farming and to marine species, and a threat to low-lying coastal towns.
Storm Éowyn, in January 2025, caused record damage and power cuts.
Ireland's emissions come mainly from a few sectors, and farming dominates. This is why so many Irish climate measures target agriculture.
Agriculture produces over a third of Ireland's greenhouse gas emissions, the largest share, mainly methane and nitrous oxide from cattle, slurry and fertiliser.
Transport, mainly fuel burned by vehicles, is the next largest source, at about a fifth of emissions (EPA, early 2020s), followed by energy.
Ireland's emissions per person are high for an EU country, which is largely because of its large farming sector.
Warming is a global problem, so governments have tried to answer it through international agreements. Each one built on the one before.
The United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) was agreed at the Earth Summit in Rio de Janeiro in 1992.

The Kyoto Protocol, agreed in 1997 and in force from 2005, set legally binding cuts for developed countries only. The USA never ratified it (it signed but did not formally approve it), so it was not a full party.
The Paris Agreement, 2015, aims to keep warming well below 2 °C and to pursue efforts to limit it to 1.5 °C. Each country sets its own national plan (nationally determined contribution).
Countries meet every year at COP meetings (conferences of the countries that signed the UNFCCC). COP30 was held at Belém, Brazil, in November 2025.
The EU and Ireland have turned the global agreements into laws, targets and charges. Together they put a price on emissions and set deadlines for cutting them.
The EU Emissions Trading System began in 2005. Power stations and heavy industry must hold an allowance (a permit) for each tonne of CO2 they emit, which gives them a cost reason to cut emissions.
The European Green Deal (2019) aims for a climate-neutral EU by 2050 (no net emissions). Its Fit for 55 package aims to cut net emissions by at least 55% by 2030, compared with 1990.
Ireland's Climate Action and Low Carbon Development (Amendment) Act 2021 requires a 51% cut in emissions by 2030, compared with 2018, and net zero by 2050.
Sectoral ceilings (limits on each sector's emissions, set in 2022) require agriculture to cut its emissions by 25% by 2030.
An Irish carbon tax (a charge on fuels based on their CO2) was introduced in 2010 and is rising in stages towards €100 a tonne by 2030.
The Climate Action Plan aims to retrofit (upgrade with insulation and heating) 500,000 homes to a B2 energy rating by 2030, and includes renewables, electric vehicles and measures for agriculture.
Governments cannot cut emissions alone, because homes, transport and food are all household choices. Everyday changes add up.
Improve energy efficiency and insulate homes, so less fuel is burned for heating.
Use public transport, cycling and walking in place of car journeys, so fewer fossil fuels are burned.
Reduce food waste, because rotting food in landfill gives off methane.
Switch to renewable heating, because it does not burn fossil fuels such as oil and gas, so it gives off less CO2.
Agricultural water pollution is the Irish national case study of water pollution. Nutrients meant to grow crops end up in rivers and lakes, where they set off a chain of events called eutrophication.

Cause: nitrogen and phosphorus from slurry, manure and chemical fertilisers wash off fields into rivers and lakes, especially after heavy rain or when spread on wet or frozen ground. Silage effluent (liquid from stored grass) and sewage from towns and septic tanks (private sewage tanks) add more.
Eutrophication (water becoming overloaded with nutrients): the nutrients feed rapid algal growth, forming algal blooms (dense layers of algae).
When the algae die, bacteria decomposing them use up the dissolved oxygen, so fish and other life suffocate in fish kills.
The water turns green and smells. Some blue-green algae are toxic.
Polluted water harms wildlife first, and then the people and businesses that rely on clean water.
Loss of fish and other wildlife, such as in a fish kill, and damage to angling and tourism, because few people visit or fish in green, smelly water.
Drinking water needs costly treatment, and nitrates (nitrogen compounds from fertiliser) contaminate groundwater (water held underground).
Coastal waters, including estuaries (where rivers meet the sea), are affected by algal mats, because rivers carry the nutrients downstream.
The EPA, which monitors water quality, shows that pollution is a national problem and not only a local one. Farming is the main pressure.
An EPA assessment for 2016 to 2021 found that only about half of Ireland's rivers, lakes and estuaries were in good or high ecological status.
Agriculture is the most common pressure on water quality, followed by urban wastewater (sewage from towns), because fertiliser and slurry wash into streams.
Milk quotas (limits on how much milk farms could produce) were abolished on 1 April 2015. The dairy herd then grew strongly, especially in the south and east, and raised nitrogen levels there.
Lough Neagh is a real example of eutrophication, and the 2023 bloom shows the processes above in action. Treat it as a single event, and do not claim it has been solved.
Lough Neagh, Northern Ireland, is the largest lake on the island of Ireland. In summer 2023 a huge toxic blue-green algal bloom covered much of it.
The bloom was blamed on nutrient pollution from farm runoff, sewage and septic tanks, together with warm weather and invasive zebra mussels that clear the water, letting more light reach the algae.
Lough Neagh supplies a large share of Northern Ireland's drinking water, so a toxic bloom threatens a key water supply.
Reducing the pollution means keeping nutrients on the land and out of water. Most of the rules limit when, where and how much farmers spread.

The EU Nitrates Directive (1991) and Ireland's Nitrates Action Programme set closed periods each winter when slurry and fertiliser may not be spread, because rain would wash them straight into rivers.

The Nitrates Action Programme also limits nitrogen per hectare, requires slurry storage, and requires buffer strips (strips of vegetation) beside watercourses, which trap nutrients before they reach the water.
The EU Water Framework Directive (2000) aims for good status for all waters, which gives countries a target to work towards.
Other measures: upgrading urban wastewater treatment, EPA monitoring of water quality, and farm advisory programmes.
Oil in the sea comes from accidents and from deliberate or careless releases. It is a global pollution problem because oil is moved and drilled for all over the world.
Tanker accidents, drilling blow-outs (uncontrolled releases of oil from a well), illegal tank washing at sea, and pipeline leaks release oil into the sea.
The Exxon Valdez is a tanker accident that caused huge damage to a wild coast and led to a change in law. Remember it is in Alaska, not the Gulf of Mexico.
The tanker ran aground on Bligh Reef, Prince William Sound, Alaska, on 24 March 1989.
About 11 million US gallons (about 37,000 tonnes) of crude oil were spilled, and about 2,000 km of coastline was oiled.
Hundreds of thousands of seabirds and thousands of sea otters were killed, and the herring fishery collapsed.
The response was the US Oil Pollution Act 1990, which required double-hulled tankers (tankers with two layers of steel, so a hit is less likely to leak) in US waters.
The Prestige shows that a tanker accident can damage the coasts of several countries and the fishing that depends on them.
The single-hulled tanker Prestige broke in two and sank off Galicia, north-west Spain, in November 2002. It spilled tens of thousands of tonnes of heavy fuel oil.
Oil reached the Costa da Morte and the coasts of Spain, Portugal and France. Galician shellfish and fishing industries were closed for months.
The disaster sped up the EU's phase-out of single-hulled tankers, because a single hull is more likely to leak after damage.
Deepwater Horizon is an example of oil pollution from drilling, and not from a tanker. It is in the Gulf of Mexico.
The Deepwater Horizon rig (an offshore drilling platform), operated by BP, exploded on 20 April 2010 in the Gulf of Mexico. Eleven workers were killed.
About 4.9 million barrels of oil were spilled.
Whatever the cause, oil spills have similar effects, and the same responses are used in each. Know the effects first, then the clean-up and the prevention.
Effects: oiled seabirds and mammals, smothered shorelines, fishing bans and lost tourism, because beaches and catches are unusable.
Clean-up: booms (floating barriers) to contain the oil, skimmers (machines that scoop oil off the surface) to remove it, and dispersants (chemicals) to break it up.
Prevention: double-hulled tankers, and routing ships away from coasts, so that any accident happens far from the shore.
Plastic is cheap and lasts a very long time, which is why it is a problem once it is thrown away. It pollutes at local and global scale.
Causes: single-use packaging that is thrown away after one use, litter, illegal dumping and landfill (burying rubbish in the ground).
Plastics take hundreds of years to break down, and they fragment into microplastics (tiny pieces of plastic).
Effects: litter in towns and countryside, and wildlife entangled in or eating plastic, which can injure or kill animals.
Ocean garbage patches: the Great Pacific Garbage Patch is a large area of the North Pacific where floating plastic collects in an ocean gyre (a large circling ocean current).
Microplastics enter food chains, as animals eat them. Landfill produces leachate (polluted liquid that drains from rubbish) and methane.
Ireland has tried to cut plastic and waste by putting a price on it, by rewarding returns, and by ranking how waste should be handled.

The plastic bag levy (a charge on each bag) was introduced in March 2002 at 15 cent a bag, raised to 22 cent in 2007. Plastic bag use fell by over 90% almost at once, and the money funds environmental projects.
The Deposit Return Scheme (Re-turn) began on 1 February 2024 for plastic drinks bottles and cans.
The waste hierarchy ranks reduce, reuse, recycle, recover and dispose. The EPA licenses waste facilities.
The Dublin Waste-to-Energy incinerator at Poolbeg (a plant that burns waste to make energy) has operated since 2017.
Ozone depletion is a different problem from global warming, with a different cause and a different treaty. It is also a success story.
CFCs, from aerosols, fridges and air conditioning, destroy stratospheric ozone (the ozone in the upper atmosphere), which absorbs harmful ultraviolet radiation.
British Antarctic Survey scientists reported the Antarctic ozone hole (a thin area in the ozone layer over Antarctica) in 1985.
More ultraviolet radiation causes skin cancer and eye cataracts, and damages plankton and crops.
The Montreal Protocol, agreed in 1987, phased out CFCs. Every UN member state has ratified it, and it is often cited as the most successful global environmental agreement.
The Antarctic ozone layer is expected to recover to 1980 levels around the 2060s (UN assessment, 2023).
Pollution also occurs closer to home, from traffic, old mines and large structures. Each of these is a local example.

Air pollution in towns: traffic produces nitrogen dioxide and fine particles. Home burning of solid fuel adds smoke, which is why smoke-free zones exist in some towns (see the note Burning fossil fuels and using alternative energy sources for smoke-free zones).
Mining pollution: acid mine drainage (acidic water flowing out of old mines) from old copper mines at Avoca, Co. Wicklow, discolours and pollutes the Avoca River.
Noise and visual pollution (unwanted sound and ugly views) from airports, motorways, quarries, wind farms and pylons.
Economic activity such as farming, fishing, mining and industry always affects the environment. Sustainable development is the framework within which that environmental impact is controlled.

The Brundtland Report, "Our Common Future" (UN World Commission on Environment and Development, 1987), defined it as development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs.

It has three pillars: environmental protection, economic growth and social fairness. Sustainable development balances all three rather than maximising one, so a plan that boosts profit but wrecks the environment is not sustainable.
Five working rules turn the definition into practice. Each one protects the environment so that it can keep supporting people in the future.
Renewable resources (ones that regrow or refill naturally) such as fish, forests and water should be used no faster than they regenerate, otherwise they are used up.
Non-renewable resources (ones that cannot be replaced once used) should be used efficiently and recycled, so that they last longer.
Pollution should be kept within what the environment can absorb, so that air, water and soil are not overloaded.
The polluter pays: those who cause environmental damage bear the cost of it, which gives them a reason to cause less.
The precautionary principle: act to prevent serious harm even before the harm is proven, because waiting for proof may be too late.
Sustainable development became an international aim, with world meetings setting out plans for governments to follow.
The Earth Summit in Rio de Janeiro (1992) was a later, separate event from the Brundtland Report. It produced Agenda 21, an action plan for sustainable development.
The UN Sustainable Development Goals were adopted in 2015: 17 goals with a target year of 2030.

In Ireland, the main body that controls the environmental impact of industry is the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA). It was created by law and works independently of the government departments it advises.
It was set up under the Environmental Protection Agency Act 1992, and the EPA began work in 1993.
It is an independent public body (a State organisation not run by a government minister) with headquarters at Johnstown Castle, Co. Wexford.
The EPA's most important power is licensing. Activities with a high risk of pollution may not operate unless the EPA allows it and sets the conditions.
Large industries need an EPA licence: pharmaceutical and chemical plants, power stations, intensive pig and poultry farms, cement works and mines. Waste facilities also need one.
The licence sets emission limits for the activity, which means the maximum pollution it may release into air, water or land.
Integrated pollution control means one licence covers air, water, waste and noise, instead of separate permits for each. This lets the EPA look at the whole impact of a site at once.
To control pollution, the EPA first has to measure it. It tracks the state of the environment and reports what it finds.
The EPA monitors water quality in rivers, lakes, estuaries (where rivers meet the sea), groundwater (water held underground in rock and soil) and bathing waters.
It runs a national air quality network and produces a greenhouse gas inventory (a count of emissions of gases that cause climate change) and projections of future emissions.
Drinking water is supplied by Uisce Éireann.
The State of the Environment report is published every four years, so the public and government can see whether things are improving.
The EPA advises government and the public and funds environmental research.
The EPA took over radiological protection in 2014, including the control of radon (a natural radioactive gas that can seep up from the ground).
A licence is only useful if it is obeyed, so the EPA checks and punishes breaches.
Inspections check that licensed activities keep within their emission limits.
The Office of Environmental Enforcement, set up within the EPA in 2003, prosecutes polluters (takes them to court).
The EPA oversees the environmental work carried out by local authorities (the county and city councils).
The EPA cannot solve every problem alone. Some pollution is hard to see, track or assign to one source.
The EPA cannot inspect everywhere, so some breaches go unchecked.
Diffuse pollution (pollution that comes from many scattered sources rather than one pipe or chimney) from thousands of farms is hard to police.
Local authorities and other bodies share responsibility for environmental control, so the EPA is one part of a wider system.
Control is best done before a project starts. An environmental impact assessment is the study that looks at a project's likely effects in advance.
An environmental impact assessment is a study, required before planning permission is decided for large projects, that predicts a project's effects on the environment and how to reduce them.
The developer's report (the developer is the company or body proposing the project) was called an Environmental Impact Statement (EIS). It is now an Environmental Impact Assessment Report (EIAR).
Environmental impact assessment is not optional for big projects. It comes from EU law and is built into Irish planning rules.
The EU Environmental Impact Assessment Directive, 1985, is applied in Irish planning law.

Assessment is required for projects above set sizes, such as motorways, power stations, wind farms, mines and quarries, large intensive farms, pipelines, ports and airports. Small projects below the set sizes do not need one.
An EIAR has to describe the project, the place it will be built and every kind of effect it could have, then say how harm will be reduced.
A description of the project and of the existing environment (the baseline, meaning the condition of the site before anything is built, which later effects are measured against).
Likely effects on people, plants and animals, soil, water, air, climate, landscape, archaeology and heritage, traffic and noise.
Alternatives considered, such as other designs or sites, and the mitigation measures (steps to reduce or prevent harm) proposed to reduce effects.
A non-technical summary for the public, so ordinary people can understand the report.
The developer writes the report, often with consultants. Neither the EPA nor the planning authority writes it.
The assessment follows a set order. It ends with a decision-maker who weighs the report against what the public and experts say.
2. The public and bodies such as the National Parks and Wildlife Service make submissions (written comments and objections).

3. The planning authority or An Coimisiún Pleanála decides whether to grant permission, often with conditions. The board was renamed in 2025 from An Bord Pleanála, the national planning appeals board.
Short questions ask why environmental impact studies are needed. There are four reasons, and Ireland's experience at Derrybrien shows what happens when the law is not followed.
They prevent damage before it happens, which is cheaper than paying for clean-up afterwards.
They require developers to consider alternatives, so a less harmful design or site may be chosen.
They give the public a say in decisions, through submissions.

At Derrybrien, Co. Galway, a peat slide on 16 October 2003 occurred during wind-farm construction. In 2019 the EU Court of Justice fined Ireland a lump sum of €5 million plus €15,000 a day because no proper environmental impact assessment had been carried out.
Fish are a renewable resource, but only if people leave enough of them to breed. This idea is the basis of sustainable fishing.
Fish are renewable only while catches stay below the rate at which the stock (the population of one kind of fish) breeds and grows.
The maximum sustainable yield is the largest catch that can be taken year after year without reducing the stock.
Overfishing means taking fish faster than stocks can replace themselves. Several causes push fleets to do this.

Modern technology, including sonar (finds fish using sound), satellite navigation, factory ships (which process the catch at sea) and huge nets, lets fleets find and take fish faster than stocks can recover.
Too many boats chase the same stock, so the catch is shared out among more boats and each one fishes harder.
Subsidies (payments from government) keep fleets fishing when stocks are falling.
Young fish are caught before they have had the chance to breed, so the stock cannot renew itself.
Discards: dead or unwanted fish are thrown back into the sea, which wastes the catch.
Illegal fishing takes fish outside the quota system (the limits on how much each country or boat may catch).
The Grand Banks is the classic example of a fishery destroyed by overfishing. It shows how both fish stocks and jobs can be lost.
The Grand Banks, off Newfoundland, Canada, were one of the world's richest cod fisheries for centuries.
Catches rose sharply with factory trawlers (large boats that fish with nets and process the catch on board) from the 1960s, and the stock collapsed.
Canada declared a moratorium (ban) on northern cod fishing on 2 July 1992.
About 30,000 people in Newfoundland lost their jobs, the largest single lay-off in Canadian history.
The stock has recovered only slowly, and partly, in the decades since.
North Sea herring is a second example, with a happier ending. It shows that a stock can recover when fishing is stopped and then tightly limited.
North Sea herring was overfished in the 1960s and 1970s.
The fishery was closed from 1977 to the early 1980s, which gave the stock time to breed.
The stock recovered after the fishery reopened under strict quotas.
In EU waters, fish stocks are managed through the Common Fisheries Policy (CFP). Here it matters as a conservation tool that tries to keep catches sustainable.
The EU Common Fisheries Policy, 1983, sets total allowable catches (TACs, the maximum amount of each stock that may be caught) and divides them into national quotas.
Conservation rules include minimum mesh sizes (so small fish escape the net), minimum landing sizes, closed areas and seasons, and vessel decommissioning (scrapping boats to reduce fleet size).
The CFP reform of 2013 aims to fish at maximum sustainable yield and introduces a landing obligation that ends discards, phased in from 2015 to 2019.
Monitoring uses satellite tracking, the Sea-Fisheries Protection Authority (set up in 2007) and fishery protection patrols by the Irish Naval Service.
Ireland's exclusive economic zone (the sea area over which a country controls resources) extends 200 nautical miles from the coast, within which these rules apply.
Further measures include marine protected areas (areas of sea where fishing is restricted) and aquaculture (fish farming) as an alternative to wild catch.
Fishing matters to Irish coastal communities, which depend on the fish stocks around the coast for their living.
Mackerel is the most valuable Irish catch, landed mainly at Killybegs, Co. Donegal, Ireland's largest fishing port.
Killybegs is the base of the pelagic fleet (boats that fish species living in open water, not on the seabed) that catches mackerel and herring.
Ireland has six State Fishery Harbour Centres: Killybegs, Castletownbere, Dingle, Rossaveel, Dunmore East and Howth.
Irish fishing communities depend on these stocks, so conservation limits cause hardship. There is more on this in Conflicts between economic interests and environmental interests.
Mining that happened before modern controls can go on polluting for generations. Avoca is the Irish example.
Copper mining at Avoca, Co. Wicklow, over centuries left acid mine drainage (acidic water that runs out of old mine workings) when mining ended.
The acid drainage still discolours and pollutes the Avoca River long after the mines closed, which shows why closure plans are needed.
Today a mine has to work within licence rules. Tara Mines shows what controlled mining looks like.
Tara Mines, Navan, Co. Meath, is an underground zinc and lead mine, Europe's largest zinc mine, producing since 1977 and owned by Boliden.
It operates under an EPA licence, which sets limits on its emissions.
Tailings (the waste left after the metal has been extracted) are stored in a lined tailings facility, so they do not leak into the ground, and the water is monitored.
Restoration plans are in place for the site.
A responsible mine plans for its end before it opens. Lisheen shows rehabilitation (restoring a site to a safe, useful condition) after closure.
Lisheen, Co. Tipperary, a zinc and lead mine, closed in 2015 and the site has been rehabilitated.

A new mine needs an environmental impact assessment report (EIAR) and a closure and restoration plan backed by a financial bond (money set aside in advance) before it opens, so the clean-up is paid for even if the company fails.
Peat was long treated as a fuel to be dug out. The scale of that harvesting damaged Ireland's bogs.
Bord na Móna, founded in 1946, carried out large-scale industrial harvesting of peat for power stations and fuel.
Harvesting removed raised bogs (domed peatlands formed over thousands of years), released the carbon they had stored and destroyed their habitats.
Peat harvesting has ended, and the focus has moved to repairing the damage and finding new uses for the land.
The Lanesborough and Shannonbridge peat stations closed in December 2020, and Bord na Móna ended peat harvesting in January 2021.
Cutaway bogs (bogs where the peat has been removed) are being rehabilitated and rewetted, meaning water is returned to them.
Lough Boora Discovery Park, Co. Offaly: a cutaway bog turned into parkland, wetlands and trails.
Bellacorick, Co. Mayo: the peat station closed in 2003 and wind farms now stand on the cutaway bog.
A just transition (a change that is fair to the workers affected) is needed for Midland workers who lost jobs in peat.
The Aral Sea shows how diverting water for farming can destroy a whole environment and the livelihoods that depended on it.
The Amu Darya and Syr Darya, which feed the Aral Sea in Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan, were diverted from the 1960s to irrigate (water by channels) cotton in the Soviet Union.
The sea shrank to a fraction of its size and split into separate lakes, and its salinity (salt content) rose.
The fishing industry collapsed, and ports such as Moynaq (Uzbekistan) were left stranded far from the water.
Dust storms spread salt and pesticides from the exposed seabed, harming local health.
The Kok-Aral dam (Kazakhstan, 2005) raised the level of the small northern sea, and fishing there has partly revived.
Burning fossil fuels pollutes the air and adds to climate change, so a sustainable approach changes the energy source.

Switching to renewable energy (energy from sources that do not run out, such as wind) reduces the environmental impact of power generation. There is more on this in Burning fossil fuels and using alternative energy sources.
Farming can be paid and encouraged to protect the environment, not just to produce food.
Agri-environment schemes pay farmers for conservation: REPS (Rural Environment Protection Scheme, 1994), now succeeded by ACRES.
Origin Green, Bord Bia's sustainability programme for Irish food and drink, was launched in 2012.
Nitrates rules limit the amount of nitrogen fertiliser and manure that farms can apply, because the excess can run off and pollute water.
BurrenLIFE (2005 to 2010) paid Burren farmers to manage species-rich limestone grassland through winter grazing (winterage); it continued as the Burren Programme.
Results-based farming in the Burren rewards farmers for measured environmental outcomes, not just for following set practices.
Forests and tourist sites can be used without being destroyed if how they are used is controlled.
Forests are replanted after felling, using mixed native broadleaves (a variety of native trees such as oak, rather than one species).
Forests are not planted on deep peat.
Visitor limits and ecotourism (tourism designed to protect nature) reduce pressure on fragile sites.
At Skellig Michael, Co. Kerry, access is controlled through licensed boats and visitor limits.
The best way to deal with waste is to create less of it, which is why there is an order of priority.
Reduce, reuse and recycle, in that order of priority.
Levies (charges) and deposit schemes (a refundable payment on containers) give people and businesses an incentive to reduce waste.
A circular economy keeps products and materials in use for as long as possible, instead of using them once and throwing them away.
The polluter pays principle is put into effect through taxes and charges that put a price on pollution.
Plastic bag levy, introduced in March 2002, a charge on plastic bags, so shoppers have a reason to use fewer.
Landfill levy, charged on waste sent to landfill, so dumping costs more than reducing waste.
EU Emissions Trading System, from 2005: companies pay for the emissions they release.
Governments have set targets for cutting emissions, and the future of sustainable development depends on meeting them.
The EU and Ireland aim for climate neutrality by 2050 (releasing no more greenhouse gases than are removed).
Ireland's Climate Act 2021 sets a 51% cut in emissions by 2030.
The Climate Action Plan sets 80% renewable electricity by 2030 and a retrofit (upgrading insulation and heating) of 500,000 homes to B2 energy rating by 2030.
Offshore wind, electric vehicles, public transport and the circular economy are the main routes to lower emissions.
Cutting agricultural emissions, restoring bogs and planting forests as carbon sinks (places that absorb and store carbon).
Meeting these targets will not be easy. Several obstacles stand in the way.
Cost: clean technology, retrofitting and rehabilitation are expensive.
Short-term economic pressure favours quick profit over long-term protection.
Jobs in traditional industries, such as peat and fishing, are at risk.
Global cooperation is needed, because pollution and climate change do not stop at borders.

Land, sea and resources can be used to make money or can be protected, and often they cannot do both at once. A conflict starts when people with economic interests and people with environmental interests want different things from the same place.

Economic interests are jobs, profit, energy supply, tax revenue, regional development (bringing investment to a poorer area) and infrastructure (roads, pipelines, power lines and similar). These are the reasons a project is proposed.
Environmental interests are habitats, landscape, heritage (historic and archaeological sites), water and air quality, health, safety and the climate. These are the reasons people object.
Interests conflict at local, national and global scales: a local community may oppose a project that the State or the world supports, or the reverse.
Each conflict has several groups, called stakeholders (people or bodies affected by a decision), and they rarely agree. Knowing who they are lets you explain who wants what.
Developers and companies want to build or extract, and government and State agencies decide, regulate or sometimes carry out the project themselves.
Local communities are often divided among themselves, because some residents gain jobs or income while others lose quiet, safety or their way of life.
Environmental groups, farmers and fishermen, tourists, the EU and the courts are also involved. Farmers and fishermen depend on the land or sea, and the EU and the courts set and enforce the rules.
Conflicts are settled through legal and planning systems, through payment, or through a deal that gives each side part of what it wants.

Planning permission (official approval to build) is needed for most developments, and decisions can be appealed to An Coimisiún Pleanála (formerly An Bord Pleanála), the national planning appeals body.
An environmental impact assessment (a study of a project's likely effects on the environment) is carried out before approval, and court cases follow where decisions are challenged.
EU law, such as the Habitats and Birds Directives, protects habitats and species, so a member state must protect them even when it would prefer to develop.
Compensation can be paid, such as payments to turf cutters or to fishermen who give up fishing, to make a restriction acceptable to those who lose by it.
Compromise includes route changes, limits on activity, conditions attached to permission and sustainable management (using a resource so that it lasts).
The Corrib gas project is a national example of a conflict. Gas from a field under the sea promised energy and money, but bringing it ashore caused a long local dispute.
The Corrib gas field lies about 80 km off north-west Co. Mayo and was discovered in 1996.
Gas first flowed in December 2015 and, so that it could be used, was processed at the Bellanaboy terminal (the onshore plant that treats the gas); for a time it supplied over half of Ireland's gas.
Economic arguments were energy security (less reliance on imported gas), a domestic gas supply, revenue for the State and the companies, and construction jobs.
Opposition came from how and where the gas would be brought ashore, not from the field itself.
The original plan piped high-pressure, unprocessed gas onshore near homes at Rossport, creating a safety risk for residents because raw gas at high pressure is dangerous close to houses.
The Shell to Sea campaign, from 2005, argued that the gas should be processed at sea rather than onshore, which would keep the hazardous raw gas away from people.
Sruwaddacon Bay, a protected estuary (a Special Area of Conservation, a site protected under EU law for its habitats), lay on the route of the pipeline.
The dispute escalated into jailings and years of protest before the project was altered and completed.
The Rossport Five were jailed in June 2005 for refusing to obey a court order not to obstruct pipeline work; they were released after 94 days.
Protests were policed heavily for years, and the dispute divided the local community, because some residents backed the project and others opposed it.
The onshore route was changed to keep the pipeline further from houses, and a tunnel was bored under Sruwaddacon Bay to carry it, so the protected estuary was not dug up.
Shell sold its share in the project in 2018.
Fish in Irish waters are a shared resource. Fishing communities want a bigger catch, while conservation rules limit how much can be taken.

Killybegs, Co. Donegal, is Ireland's largest fishing port, so it matters most for jobs; the six State Fishery Harbour Centres are Killybegs, Castletownbere, Dingle, Rossaveel, Dunmore East and Howth. Coastal jobs depend on these harbours.
Under the Common Fisheries Policy (1983), total allowable catches (the maximum amount of each species that may be caught) are set by the EU and divided into national quotas.
Irish fishermen have long argued that Ireland's share of the catch in its own rich waters is too small, and much of that catch is taken by other EU fleets.
Ireland's exclusive economic zone (the sea area where the State has the rights to the resources) extends 200 nautical miles from the coast.
Political change after Brexit (the UK leaving the EU) shrank what Irish boats could catch, which hurt fishing incomes.
The EU-UK Brexit trade agreement (December 2020) reduced Irish quotas, so Irish boats were allowed to catch less.
A scheme paid vessel owners to decommission (scrap) their boats, which cut the size of the fleet to match the smaller quota.
When wild salmon numbers collapsed, the State banned a fishing method, which set commercial fishermen against anglers and conservationists.
Ireland banned drift-net fishing (fishing with nets left floating in the open sea) for wild salmon at sea from 2007, because wild salmon returning to Irish rivers had fallen sharply.
Commercial salmon fishermen received compensation, so that they were not left without income, for losing their livelihood.
Anglers (people who fish with rods) and conservation groups supported the ban, because wild salmon sustain angling tourism.
Fish stocks cross borders and farms share water with wild fish, so conflicts reach beyond Ireland and affect the sea and the bays.
From 2010 Iceland and the Faroe Islands set large mackerel quotas as mackerel moved north-west into their waters, taking a bigger share of a stock Irish boats also fish.

The EU, with strong support from Irish fishermen, protested; in 2013 it imposed trade measures on the Faroe Islands over its herring catches, banning imports of Faroese herring and mackerel; the dispute eased in 2014.
Salmon farms in western bays are blamed by anglers for harming wild salmon and sea trout, because sea lice (parasites that attach to fish) from the farms spread to wild fish.
Mullaghmore is a main national case of tourism against a fragile landscape. A visitor centre was meant to help tourism but was planned in a place valued for being unspoilt.

The Burren, Co. Clare, has Carboniferous limestone pavement (a bare, flat surface of limestone), with rare Arctic-alpine and Mediterranean plants growing side by side, such as spring gentian and mountain avens.
Mullaghmore is a hill of folded, terraced limestone; the Burren National Park protects the area near it.

In the early 1990s the Office of Public Works (OPW, the State body that manages heritage sites and public buildings) began building an interpretative centre (a visitor centre with displays) and car park near Mullaghmore.
The two sides disagreed on whether a visitor centre at Mullaghmore would help or harm the Burren, because one side focused on jobs and income and the other on the fragile landscape.
Supporters wanted tourism jobs and visitor spending in a poor rural area, and better visitor management, which means directing visitors to one place instead of leaving them to wander.
The Burren Action Group argued that traffic, sewage and visitor pressure would damage a fragile, unspoilt landscape, and that any centre should be in nearby villages.
The case was settled in the courts and the planning system, so it shows how legal challenge can stop a State project.

In 1993 the Supreme Court (Ireland's highest court) ruled that the State had to obtain planning permission like any other developer, so the State was not exempt from the planning rules, and work stopped.
In 2000 An Bord Pleanála refused permission, and the partly built site was cleared and restored.
Skellig Michael is a remote island of great heritage and wildlife value, which is why increased tourism there is a problem.
Skellig Michael, about 12 km off the Iveragh Peninsula, Co. Kerry, has an early Christian monastery of stone beehive huts on a steep rocky island.
It has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site (a place recognised by the United Nations as being of outstanding value to humanity) since 1996 and is managed by the OPW.
Seabirds, including puffins, Manx shearwaters and storm petrels, breed on the island; Little Skellig holds one of the world's largest gannet colonies.
Film fame brought more demand for visits than a fragile island can easily take, so access is controlled.
Filming for the Star Wars films (from 2014) greatly increased demand for visits.
Boat operators and local businesses want more access, because visitors bring them income; conservationists object to the filming and to rising visitor numbers.
Access is only by licensed boats in summer, with visitor numbers capped at about 180 a day; landings depend on the weather.
Steep steps and the weather make landing a safety issue, which is why landings are limited.
The Hill of Tara is a heritage site of national importance, and the land around it is rich in archaeology. This is the heritage side of the conflict over the M3 motorway.
The Hill of Tara, Co. Meath, is an ancient ceremonial site and the traditional seat of the High Kings of Ireland.

The Tara-Skryne valley around the hill is an archaeological landscape (an area where the sites and the land together tell the story of the past); excavation along the planned road route found dozens of sites.
The road was meant to solve a transport problem for fast-growing towns, and the best route crossed an important archaeological area.
The M3 runs from Clonee to north of Kells, relieving congestion on the N3 for the fast-growing commuter towns of Meath (towns whose residents travel to work elsewhere), such as Navan and Kells.
It cuts journey times to Dublin, so commuters save time, which helps regional access and commuters.
The route passes through the Tara-Skryne valley, about 2 km from the Hill of Tara.
Opponents said the road would destroy archaeology. The road was built, but only after a major find was recorded.
Campaign groups, archaeologists and protesters camped on the route argued that the road would destroy an archaeological landscape.
In 2007 a large prehistoric ceremonial enclosure was found at Lismullin and declared a national monument; it was excavated and recorded, and then the road was built over it.
The M3 opened in 2010, so the road was completed despite the protests.
Turf (dried peat cut from bogs) is a traditional fuel, but the bogs it comes from are rare habitats protected by EU law.
Turf cutting gives rural families a traditional right and a cheap source of fuel.
Raised bogs are rare in Europe and store large amounts of carbon; Ireland holds a large share of the EU's remaining active raised bog (bog that is still growing).
The EU Habitats Directive (1992) required Ireland to designate raised bogs as Special Areas of Conservation (SACs), sites protected for their habitats.
The ban took away a traditional way of life, so the State offered compensation. Even so, some people protested.
After a ten-year derogation (a temporary exemption from the rules) ended, turf cutting was banned on 53 raised-bog SACs from 2011.
Compensation: about €1,500 a year for 15 years per turf cutter, or relocation to a bog that is not protected.
The Turf Cutters and Contractors Association organised protests, because the ban ended a traditional right, and some cutting continued on some bogs.
Wind power helps with climate targets, but turbines are built in places where people live and wildlife lives, so wind farms cause conflict at local and national level.
Economic and renewable case: renewable energy targets, income for landowners and community funds. The Climate Action Plan aims for 80% renewable electricity by 2030.
Local objections: visual impact, noise, shadow flicker (the flickering shadow cast by rotating blades), falling property values, effects on birds, and peat stability.
Derrybrien, Slieve Aughty Mountains, Co. Galway: a peat slide of about 450,000 m³ on 16 October 2003, during wind-farm construction, killed fish in the Owendalulleegh River.
In 2019 the EU Court of Justice fined Ireland €5 million plus €15,000 a day because no proper environmental impact assessment (a study of effects before approval) had been carried out.
Offshore wind: the Climate Action Plan sets at least 5 GW (gigawatts, a measure of generating capacity) of offshore wind, which can conflict with fishing grounds and seascapes.
Ending milk quotas let farmers produce more milk. The economic gain came with costs for rivers and for the climate.
Milk quotas (EU limits on how much milk each farmer could produce) were abolished on 1 April 2015, and the dairy herd grew strongly afterwards.
Economic case: farm incomes and food exports, because more milk means more to sell.
Environmental case: nitrates (chemicals from fertiliser and slurry) reaching water damage water quality; agriculture produces over a third of Ireland's greenhouse gas emissions.

EPA (the Environmental Protection Agency, 2016-2021): only about half of Irish rivers, lakes and estuaries were in good or high ecological status (a measure of water health), with agriculture the main pressure.
Sectoral ceilings (limits on emissions set for each sector of the economy, 2022) require agriculture to cut emissions by 25% by 2030.
Data centres (buildings full of computers that store and process online data) bring investment, but they use so much electricity that they conflict with climate goals.
Economic case: investment, multinational jobs and Ireland's technology economy, because the centres bring in big companies.
Data centres used about a fifth of Ireland's metered electricity in 2023 (CSO, the Central Statistics Office), and most are in the Dublin region.
Environmental and grid case: huge electricity demand strains the grid (the national network that carries electricity) and works against climate targets.
In 2022 EirGrid (the operator of the electricity grid) said it would not connect new data centres in the Dublin area until about 2028, because the grid could not supply them.
The Amazon is the main global example. Brazil's economic activities clear the forest for farming, timber, mining, roads and power.
The Amazon is the world's largest tropical rainforest, with about 60% of it in Brazil.
Cattle ranching is the main driver of clearing, and most cleared land becomes pasture; soya farming spreads in the south.
Logging removes timber from the forest, so the trees are cut for sale, for example.
The Trans-Amazonian Highway, begun in 1970, opened the forest to settlers; clearings along the roads form a fishbone pattern (a central road with side tracks branching off), as in Rondônia.
Carajás, Pará, has the world's largest iron-ore mine, run by Vale.
The Belo Monte dam on the Xingu River, completed in 2019, was opposed by indigenous groups including the Kayapó.
The forest matters to people far from Brazil, so protecting it is a global interest as well as a Brazilian one.
The forest holds biodiversity (a huge variety of species), stores large amounts of carbon, recycles rainfall and is home to indigenous peoples.
Global interest: clearing the forest releases carbon that adds to climate change, while Brazil's development needs drive clearing.
Satellite figures show how clearing fell when protection was strong and rose when it weakened. These are rounded figures for the Brazilian Amazon only.
Satellite monitoring by PRODES (Brazil's official programme for measuring deforestation): about 27,800 km² of the Brazilian Amazon was cleared in 2004.
Clearing was cut by over 80%, to about 4,600 km², by 2012, showing that protection can work.
Clearing rose again to about 13,000 km² in 2021, so the gains were not permanent.
Brazil and other countries have tried several ways to slow clearing, but results have depended on which government is in power.
Brazil's Forest Code, a law to protect the forest, requires landowners in the Amazon to keep 80% of their land as forest, though this is often not enforced.
The soy moratorium (an agreed pause) of 2006: major traders agreed not to buy soya from newly cleared Amazon land.
The Amazon Fund of 2008: donors, mainly Norway and also Germany, pay for reduced deforestation.
Deforestation rose under President Bolsonaro (2019-2022) and fell under President Lula (2003-2010, and again from 2023), showing that government policy matters.
The Amazon conflict was also a conflict between people, sometimes with deadly results.
Chico Mendes, a rubber tapper (a worker who collects rubber from trees without felling them) and union leader who campaigned to protect the forest, was murdered at Xapuri, Acre, on 22 December 1988.
His murder shows that the conflict over clearing was one between people, not only between economic and environmental interests.
Germany is a European example of a global conflict: mining a fuel that heats the climate against protecting a forest and villages.
RWE's Hambach open-cast lignite mine (a surface mine for lignite, a soft brown coal) in North Rhine-Westphalia expands into the ancient Hambach Forest.
Economic side: the mine supplies power and jobs in the Rhineland. Environmental side: the forest, the villages and the carbon released by burning lignite.
Protesters occupied tree houses in the forest for years, to stop the trees being felled; in October 2018 a German court halted the clearing.
The remaining forest was later spared under the coal phase-out (the planned ending of coal use).
Even after the Hambach ruling, mining continued elsewhere, until national law set an end date for coal.
The village of Lützerath was cleared of protesters in January 2023 to extend the Garzweiler lignite mine.
Germany's 2020 law ends coal-fired power by 2038 at the latest, so the mines have a fixed end date.
The Three Gorges Dam is a huge project that shows the economic case for damming a river.
The Three Gorges Dam on the Yangtze River is the world's largest power station by installed capacity (the most electricity it can generate).
It provides clean electricity, flood control downstream and improved navigation (easier passage for ships).
The dam was completed in 2006 and became fully operational in 2012.
The same dam brought heavy costs for people, heritage and the river itself.
Over one million people were relocated, because the reservoir flooded their homes.
Farmland, towns and archaeological sites were flooded by the reservoir (the lake formed behind the dam).
The dam traps sediment that would otherwise reach the river downstream, and the ecology of the river has changed.
The conflict between economy and environment also shows up between countries, in the argument over who should cut emissions.
Developing countries argue for their right to develop with cheap energy, while the global need is to cut emissions.
Fossil-fuel exporting countries protect their revenue from coal, oil and gas, which they would lose if the world used less of them.
Belém, Pará, hosted the COP30 climate conference in November 2025.
On an Ordnance Survey map question you are asked to show how conflict could arise from where a development is placed. Work through the same steps each time.
Identify the development and the features of the site it needs, such as a wind farm on high ground with open views, or a quarry close to a village.
Read the map for relevant features, because they show who would be affected: contour lines for height, settlements, roads for access, rivers, and protected areas.
Identify the groups for and against: developers and landowners usually support a site, while residents, environmental groups and tourism businesses may object.
Conflict arises when a site serves one group's interests while threatening another group's interests; give the reasons for each side.

A trading bloc is a group of countries that remove trade barriers between themselves and act together in trade with the rest of the world. The EU is the biggest example, and its two founding trade tools are a customs union and the single market.

The EU accounted for about 13% of world goods trade in 2024, second to China in goods. Counting goods and services together, the EU is the world's largest trader, with China and the USA as the other two of the three largest.

Customs union: completed on 1 July 1968 (as the EEC, the European Economic Community, the EU's earlier name), it removes tariffs (taxes on imports) between members and applies a common external tariff to imports from outside the EU, so every member charges the same rate.

The single market, in force from 1 January 1993 and set up by the Single European Act of 1986, goes beyond the customs union. A customs union only deals with tariffs, whereas the single market also tackles every other obstacle to trade.
It guarantees the four freedoms: free movement of goods, services, capital (money and investment) and people.

It removes non-tariff barriers (obstacles to trade other than taxes): border checks, different national product standards and national preference in public contracts (governments favouring their own firms).
Common standards, such as the CE mark (a label showing a product meets EU rules), replace those barriers, so one product can be sold in every member state.

The single market extends beyond the 27 members: the European Economic Area (EEA) brings in Norway, Iceland and Liechtenstein, while Switzerland, which is in neither the EU nor the EEA, trades under bilateral agreements (separate deals made with the EU).
Trade questions use a small set of terms, and examiners expect you to define them precisely.
Imports are goods or services bought from abroad; exports are goods or services sold abroad.
Visible trade is trade in goods, things you can see and touch; invisible trade is trade in services, such as finance, tourism and transport.
Balance of trade: the value of exports minus the value of imports. A positive balance is a surplus (the country sells more than it buys); a negative balance is a deficit (it buys more than it sells).
A tariff is a tax on imports; a quota is a limit on the quantity of imports allowed. Both make imports harder to sell.
Intra-EU (internal) trade is trade between member states; extra-EU (external) trade is trade with countries outside the EU.
Most member states trade mainly with each other, because the single market makes it the easiest and cheapest option. The share, though, varies a great deal from country to country.
In 2024 intra-EU goods exports were about €4.0 trillion, against about €2.6 trillion of extra-EU goods exports. So about three-fifths (about 60%) of members' goods exports stayed within the EU.
Germany is by far the largest intra-EU trader, with intra-EU goods exports of about €845 billion in 2024; Cyprus is the smallest, at about €1 billion.

The core of the EU, the Blue Banana (a curved band of dense industry and population) from south-east England through the Benelux countries and the Rhine valley to northern Italy, together with the Paris Basin, dominates internal trade.
Peripheral members (those on the edge of the EU, far from the core), such as Cyprus and Greece, trade much less within the EU.

Eastern members depend most on intra-EU trade. Intra-EU trade was about 81% of Czechia's goods trade in 2024, compared with about 30% for Cyprus, because of their proximity to Germany and their integration into its supply chains (the linked steps in making a product, spread across countries).
The goods that cross borders inside the EU are mostly high-value manufactures. The pattern of trade takes three forms: swapping similar goods, linked production chains, and swapping different goods.
Manufactured goods dominate: machinery, vehicles and parts, and chemicals and pharmaceuticals. Food and farm produce come next, and services such as finance, tourism and transport add to the total.
Intra-industry trade: members swap similar goods, such as cars for cars, and components cross borders several times in supply chains before the finished product is sold.

Since the 2004 enlargement the car industry has linked Germany with Czechia, Slovakia, Hungary and Poland, where assembly plants supply the German-centred industry. Volkswagen took over Škoda (Czechia) in stages from 1991 and has fully owned it since 2000.
Slovakia makes more cars per head of population than any other country.

Complementary trade (members swapping goods the other lacks): greenhouse fruit and vegetables from Almería in southern Spain are trucked north to northern Europe, while northern manufactured goods flow south and east.
Some trade figures look larger than the country's own economy would suggest, because goods pass through its ports on the way to somewhere else.
Rotterdam in the Netherlands is Europe's largest port and Antwerp in Belgium is the second largest; both sit at the mouth of the Rhine-Meuse-Scheldt delta, where the Rhine reaches the sea.
Goods entering and leaving the single market through these ports are counted as trade with the Netherlands and Belgium, which gives both countries very large trade totals.
The Rotterdam effect: goods recorded as trade with the Netherlands may be going on to other member states, so the figure overstates what the Netherlands itself buys or sells.
Trade inside the EU is high because several things lower its costs and widen its market. Exams ask you to explain these factors, so give each with its reason.
Removal of tariffs and border controls: the customs union, the single market and Schengen border-free travel for most members cut costs and delays.
The euro: 21 countries used it from 1 January 2026, with Bulgaria the newest. Trade among them has no exchange costs or exchange-rate risk, and prices are easy to compare.
The euro is not the currency of the whole EU, which has 27 members. The euro's history is in The complexity of regions (i).

Proximity and transport: short distances, dense motorway and rail networks, the Rhine (navigable to Basel in Switzerland), the Channel Tunnel (opened 1994) and the Øresund Bridge between Copenhagen and Malmö (opened 2000).
EU-funded Trans-European Transport Networks (TEN-T) also add links, so goods move quickly and cheaply between member states.

Common policies: the CAP (Common Agricultural Policy, the EU's farm policy) and common food standards make farm and food trade easy within the EU. There is more on the CAP in How the EU influences the Irish economy.
The size of the market and changes in membership also shape internal trade.
A large, wealthy market: about 450 million people in 2024, with high incomes and broadly similar tastes, so a product made for one country sells easily in others.
Enlargement widened the single market: ten countries joined in 2004, Bulgaria and Romania in 2007 and Croatia in 2013. New members opened new markets and lower-cost production sites in the east.

Brexit moved the UK from internal to external partner. The UK left on 31 January 2020; the Trade and Cooperation Agreement has applied since 1 January 2021, with zero tariffs and zero quotas on qualifying goods (those meeting rules of origin).
Trade with the UK nonetheless became more costly because of customs declarations, checks and rules-of-origin paperwork.
In trade with the outside world the EU does not act as 27 separate countries. Its common trade policy gives it a single negotiating position.

The European Commission (the EU's executive body) negotiates trade for all 27 members under the Common Commercial Policy, so the EU speaks with one voice in the World Trade Organization (WTO, the body that sets global trade rules).
All members apply the same common external tariff, so the EU bargains as one bloc rather than as 27 separate countries, which gives it more weight.
Outside the EU, a handful of big economies take most of the EU's goods and supply most of its imports. The EU sells more to them than it buys overall.
Export partners for extra-EU goods: the USA is the largest at about 21%, then the UK at about 13%, China at about 8%, Switzerland at about 7-8% and Turkey at about 4%.
Import partners for extra-EU goods: China is the largest at about a fifth (about 20-21%), then the USA at about 13-14%, the UK at about 7%, Switzerland at about 6% and Turkey at about 4%.
Overall, extra-EU goods exports were about €2.58 trillion and imports about €2.43 trillion, a goods surplus (exports exceed imports) of about €150 billion.
The EU had a surplus with the USA and a large deficit with China, meaning it bought far more from China than it sold there. It also had a surplus with the UK.
The EU sells high-value manufactured goods and buys energy, raw materials and cheaper manufactured goods, because it has little energy of its own.

Exports: machinery and vehicles were about €1.0 trillion (about 39% of extra-EU exports); chemicals and related products, including pharmaceuticals, were about €560 billion (about 22%). Food, drink and services are also exported.
Imports: energy products, mainly oil and gas, were about 15% of EU imports by value in 2024, down from about 23% in 2022.

Imports also include raw materials, consumer electronics and other manufactured goods from China and Asia, and tropical foods such as coffee, cocoa and bananas, which cannot be grown in the EU's climate.
Political events change trade patterns quickly, as the change in energy imports shows.
Russia was a major gas supplier before its full-scale invasion of Ukraine began on 24 February 2022.

Russian gas fell from about 45% of EU gas imports in 2021 to about 19% in 2024, through sanctions (penalties that restrict trade with a country) and the REPowerEU plan (the EU's plan to cut energy dependence on Russia, launched May 2022).
The USA supplied almost half of EU liquefied natural gas (LNG, gas cooled to a liquid so ships can carry it) imports in 2024, replacing much of the lost Russian gas.
The EU plans to end Russian gas imports by the end of 2027.
The EU widens its external trade by signing agreements with other countries. It also gives poorer countries easier access to its market, though critics say its past policies hurt them.

Trade agreements widen external trade: CETA with Canada has been provisionally applied (in use before final approval) since September 2017; the EU-Japan Economic Partnership Agreement has been in force since February 2019; the EU-South Korea agreement has applied since 2011.
EU-Mercosur negotiations with Brazil, Argentina, Uruguay and Paraguay concluded in December 2024. Irish farm organisations strongly opposed the deal because of competition from South American beef.

The Lomé Convention (1975, with African, Caribbean and Pacific (ACP) countries) and the Cotonou Agreement (2000) gave preferential access (easier, lower-tariff entry to the EU market) to poorer countries.
Everything But Arms (2001) gives the least developed countries duty-free, quota-free access for all goods except arms.

Critics argue that tariffs on processed goods (tariff escalation, where the tariff rises as a product is processed further) and past subsidised farm exports (sold cheaply with EU government support) harmed producers in the developing world.
The EU also uses tariffs to protect its industries, and it is on the receiving end of other countries' tariffs. In each case it acts as a single bloc.
