The EU-USA agreement of July 2025 capped the US tariff on most EU goods at 15%, including pharmaceuticals; Irish pharmaceutical exports to the USA are among the goods it covers. Steel and aluminium remained at 50%.
EU definitive duties (lasting tariffs, not temporary ones) on Chinese-made electric cars, from October 2024, reached up to about 35%.
In both disputes the EU acted as one bloc, so one set of duties or one deal applies to all 27 members.
Several factors explain why the EU trades with the outside world as it does. Exams ask you to explain them after describing the patterns.
The size and wealth of the single market gives the EU bargaining power in trade negotiations, because other countries want access to its consumers.
High-tech, high-value industry makes manufactured goods the main exports.
A lack of energy and some raw materials makes the EU dependent on imports, especially of fuels.
Historical and colonial links, including former colonies in Africa, the Caribbean and the Pacific and the Commonwealth ties of the former UK member, shaped the preferential agreements.
Globalisation (the growing worldwide linking of economies): low-cost manufacturing in China and Asia draws in imports.

The trading triad is the three main trading regions, the USA, the EU and the Pacific Rim (the countries around the Pacific Ocean). There is more on the trading triad in Patterns in world trade, in The Global Economy.
Politics redirects trade: sanctions on Russia, US tariff disputes and Brexit each changed the direction of trade flows.
Exam data questions give export and import shares for each partner. Use the invented values below only to practise the method.
Identify the largest partner: the biggest slice or the highest value.
Calculate a missing share: subtract the known shares from 100. Illustrative: exports to Country A 25% and Country B 15% leave 100 minus 25 minus 15 = 60% for all other partners.
Compare exports and imports with one partner. If the value sent to it is higher than the value received, the EU has a surplus with that partner; if it is lower, a deficit.

Irish trading patterns changed enormously after 1973, so you need to know the starting point. Before Ireland joined the EEC (the European Economic Community, the forerunner of the EU), its trade depended on one neighbour, the UK.

Before 1973 Irish trade depended on the UK. In 1960 about three-quarters (74%) of Irish exports went to the UK, mainly live cattle and other farm produce, so Ireland sold mostly raw farm output to a single customer.
The Anglo-Irish Free Trade Agreement, signed in 1965, governed trade with the UK (free trade means few or no tariffs, the taxes charged on imports).
Protectionism, meaning taxes and limits on imports to shield home industry, was dismantled from the late 1950s, which opened the Irish economy to outside trade.
Membership of the EEC gave Ireland a way to trade beyond the UK. The decision was put to the people first.
Ireland joined the EEC on 1 January 1973, together with the UK and Denmark.
A referendum (a public vote on one question) on 10 May 1972 returned about 83% Yes, which shows strong public support for joining.
Diversification means spreading sales across more customers instead of relying on one. After 1973 Ireland did this, and the UK's role shrank.

The UK's share of Irish exports fell from about three-quarters in 1960 to a small fraction today. In February 2024 Great Britain took about 8% of Irish goods exports in that month alone, which is under a tenth.
As the UK's share fell, the rest of the EU and the USA became far more important, so Ireland is no longer tied to a single market.
It is not only where Ireland sells that changed but what it sells. Exports moved from raw farm produce to goods and services of much higher value.

Exports moved from mainly agricultural goods and live animals to high-value manufactured goods (goods that sell for a lot relative to their size). Pharmaceuticals and chemicals, medical devices, and computers and electronics grew strongly in the 1990s and 2000s.
Processed food and drink replaced live animals as the main farm exports, and services (such as software and finance, rather than physical goods) became a larger part of the economy's trade.

Exports far exceed imports. Ireland has a very large goods trade surplus (exports worth more than imports), mainly because foreign multinationals (companies that operate in several countries) export most of what they make in Ireland.
Use 2024 as the main current year: it is a normal year, unlike 2025, when exports surged. These three figures show the size of Ireland's trade and its surplus.
Goods exports were about €224 billion in 2024, a record and up about 14% on 2023.
Goods imports were about €135 billion in 2024, giving a goods surplus (exports minus imports) of about €89 billion.
A trading bloc is a group of countries that trade freely together. Ireland sells most to two destinations, the EU 27 (the 27 member states) as a bloc and the USA as a single country.
The EU 27 took about €88 billion of Irish goods exports in 2024, about 40%, making it the largest bloc.
The USA took about €73 billion, about one-third of exports, and is Ireland's largest single export market, ahead of any one EU country.
The main EU markets in 2024 were the Netherlands (about €23 billion), Germany (about €20 billion), Belgium (about €17 billion) and then France.
Imports are the goods Ireland buys from abroad. The EU is again the biggest source, but the pattern is more spread out than for exports.
The EU 27 supplied about €50 billion of Irish imports in 2024, about 37%, making it the largest bloc.
Asia supplied about €31 billion, the USA about €23 billion and the UK about €22 billion. The USA and the UK are the largest single countries.
Asia, especially China, is growing as a source of imports.
A few product groups make up most of what Ireland sells abroad. One of them dominates.
Medical and pharmaceutical products are the largest export group, at about €100 billion in 2024 (about 45% of goods exports), roughly half the total.
Organic chemicals, medical devices, and food and drink follow as the other main exports.
What Ireland buys reflects what it lacks and what its industries and consumers need.
Fuels, because Ireland imports most of its energy.
Machinery and transport equipment, including aircraft for the leasing industry (firms that buy aircraft and rent them to airlines).
2025 was an unusual year. Preliminary CSO (Central Statistics Office) figures show a record, driven by firms moving exports forward to beat US tariffs (taxes on imported goods).

Preliminary CSO figures show goods exports of about €260 billion in 2025, up about 16% and a record. Pharmaceutical exports to the USA were brought forward (front-loaded) before threatened US tariffs.
Medical and pharmaceutical products were about €139 billion in 2025, about 53% of goods exports.
The USA took about 43% of exports in 2025. Imports were about €144 billion.
Exports to the USA fell sharply at the end of 2025. The EU-USA deal of July 2025 capped US tariffs on most EU goods, including pharmaceuticals, at 15%.
The surge shows how dependent the totals are on one product and one market, so 2024 is the better guide to a typical year.
Ireland sells services as well as goods. Many are sold by multinationals based in Dublin, and much of this trade goes to EU customers.
Ireland is a major exporter of services, especially computer and software services sold by multinationals such as Google, Meta and Microsoft, whose European headquarters are in Dublin.
Financial services are based at the International Financial Services Centre (IFSC) in Dublin Docklands, which opened in 1987. Aircraft leasing is another major service.
Much of this services trade is sold into EU markets from an Irish base.
Farming is still central to Irish trade. Ireland produces far more food than it needs, so the surplus must be sold abroad.
Ireland exports about 90% of its beef and dairy output, and produces far more food than its population eats.
Food, drink and horticulture (growing fruit, vegetables and flowers) exports were about €17 billion in 2024, a record and up about 5% (Bord Bia, the Irish food board).
Of these exports, about 35% (about €5.9 billion) went to the EU and about €5.2 billion to markets outside the EU and UK; the UK took the remainder, about a third.
Dairy, at about €6.3 billion, was the largest category.
Food exports show how Ireland sells to both the EU and the UK, and Irish brands carry the products into those markets.
The UK remains the largest single market for Irish food, though not for Irish goods overall.
Meat and livestock exports in 2024 went about 44% to the EU and about 42% to the UK, so they are split almost equally.
Kerrygold butter, marketed by Ornua (formerly the Irish Dairy Board), sells in Germany, one of its biggest markets, and other EU countries.
Irish beef is sold through EU retailers, and Irish whiskey and Baileys are sold internationally.
Several features of EU membership make the EU the natural market for Irish firms. Each one lowers the cost or risk of selling there.
Single market access: the single market lets goods move tariff-free and barrier-free among member states, giving Irish firms access to about 450 million consumers in 2024.
The euro: Ireland adopted it in 1999 and notes and coins followed in 2002. Trade with eurozone countries (those using the euro) carries no exchange-rate risk, because there is no currency to change.
Sterling (the British pound) fell sharply after the UK referendum of 23 June 2016, which hurt Irish food exporters to the UK because sterling earnings bought fewer euros. This makes UK trade riskier.
CAP (the Common Agricultural Policy) access and common standards opened EU food markets to Irish farm produce. There is more on this in How the EU influences the Irish economy.
Foreign direct investment (FDI) means a foreign company setting up operations in Ireland. It is another reason Irish trade with the EU is so large.
US and other multinationals locate in Ireland to supply the EU market from inside it. Examples include Intel at Leixlip, Co. Kildare (since 1989), Apple in Cork (since 1980) and Pfizer.

Ireland attracts them with an English-speaking, educated workforce, a corporation tax (tax on company profits) rate of 12.5%, and support from IDA Ireland, the state agency that attracts foreign investment.
From 2024 firms with turnover over €750 million pay a minimum tax of 15%. There is more on the multinationals in The Global Economy notes.
Ireland's position shapes how goods leave and arrive. Being an island makes sea links the main route to Europe.
Ireland is an island on the periphery (the edge) of Europe, so most trade goes by sea.
Dublin Port is Ireland's largest port. Rosslare Europort in Co. Wexford is the main port for direct ferries to continental Europe. Cork and Shannon Foynes also handle trade.
High-value, light goods such as pharmaceuticals and electronics go by air.
Brexit, the UK's departure from the EU, changed the rules for Ireland's trade with its nearest neighbour. It pushed Irish trade further towards the rest of the EU.
The UK left the EU on 31 January 2020. The transition ended on 31 December 2020, and the Trade and Cooperation Agreement has applied since 1 January 2021.
Trade with Great Britain now crosses an EU external border, with customs declarations (forms listing goods crossing the border) and checks on food and animals.

The UK landbridge, trucks crossing Britain to reach the continent, became slower. From 2 January 2021 DFDS ran a direct Rosslare-Dunkirk freight ferry, six times a week. By April 2021 there were about 36 direct weekly sailings from Rosslare to continental Europe.
Rosslare also has direct sailings to Cherbourg, Saint-Malo and Roscoff in France, and to Bilbao in Spain.

Imports from Great Britain fell after 2021 as some importers switched to EU suppliers. Cross-border trade with Northern Ireland grew, because Northern Ireland stays in the EU single market for goods under the Windsor Framework of February 2023. There is more on this in The complexity of regions (i).
Brexit raised the share of Irish trade with the rest of the EU and reduced Ireland's dependence on the UK further.
The pattern has weaknesses as well as strengths. Concentrating trade in a few places leaves Ireland exposed.
Over-reliance on a few multinationals, one sector (pharmaceuticals) and one market (the USA) leaves exports exposed to US tariffs and to corporate decisions, such as a firm moving production.
Ireland's peripheral location adds transport costs, so sea links to the continent are vital.

Every member state pays into the EU budget and receives money back. Whether a country gets out more than it puts in (a net recipient) or puts in more than it gets (a net contributor) shows how its place in the EU has changed.

Ireland was a net recipient of EU budget money from joining on 1 January 1973 until about 2014, receiving over €40 billion more than it paid in, mostly through the CAP (the Common Agricultural Policy, the EU's farm policy).
Ireland became a net contributor in 2014, the first time since joining, because its economic growth meant it was now a richer member paying more in than it received.
Membership brings Ireland benefits and costs. Exams ask for one or two advantages, so learn the short list and the matching costs.

Advantages: access to the single market (the EU area of about 450 million people in 2024, where goods and services move freely), foreign direct investment (FDI, money invested in Irish operations by overseas firms), and CAP payments.
More advantages: structural funds (EU money for poorer regions and for people) that pay for infrastructure, social and equality laws, and free movement to work and study anywhere in the EU.
Costs: loss of control over some policies, such as fishing and farm prices, because these are set at EU level rather than by Ireland alone.
Further costs: net contributions to the EU budget since 2014, and competition from lower-cost members, whose firms and workers can sell and work in Ireland.
FDI examples are Intel, Leixlip (since 1989) and Apple, Cork (since 1980). Ireland's 2010 EU/IMF bailout of about €85 billion may be named as an EU-related support.
There is more on this in The complexity of regions (ii), which covers the effects of enlargement (the EU taking in new member states).
The Common Agricultural Policy was launched in 1962 to run farming for all EU members as one system.

Its aims, set out in the Treaty of Rome (the founding treaty of the EEC, the forerunner of the EU), were to raise farm productivity, give farmers a fair standard of living, stabilise markets, secure food supplies and provide reasonable prices for consumers.
The CAP was once the largest part of the EU budget. It still takes about a third of the budget (2021-27), which shows how central farming remains to EU spending.
To meet its aims, the early CAP guaranteed farmers a price for what they produced. This worked too well for producers and created problems for everyone else.

Guaranteed (intervention) prices were set above world levels, so farmers were sure of a good price, and intervention buying (the EU buying up produce) took up surpluses that the market could not absorb.
Export subsidies (payments to sell abroad) and import levies (taxes on food imported from outside the EU) supported the system by keeping EU prices above world prices.

Results: overproduction, shown by the butter mountains and wine lakes of the 1970s and 1980s (huge stored surpluses), high cost, and dumping of surpluses on world markets (selling them abroad cheaply).
Ireland joined in 1973, so its farmers suddenly gained access to CAP guaranteed prices. For Irish farming this was a major boost.
Farm prices and incomes rose sharply, because Irish farmers now received the higher EU guaranteed prices.
A guaranteed market opened for beef and dairy, so farmers knew they could sell what they produced.
Farms modernised with machinery, fertiliser, silage (stored grass for winter feed), land drainage and farm buildings, in what is remembered as the golden age of the 1970s.
Because the CAP caused surpluses, the EU limited how much milk each farm could produce. Irish dairying was held back until the limit was removed.
Milk quotas, introduced in 1984, capped each farm's milk output to cut surpluses. They held back Irish dairying for 30 years.
The quotas were abolished on 1 April 2015; the last quota year ended on 31 March 2015.
Once the cap went, output rose: Irish milk output went from about 5.5 billion litres in 2014 to about 8.3 billion litres in 2020.
From 2013 to 2023 dairy cow numbers rose about 41% and milk output about 56% (EPA, from CSO data).
Expansion was strongest in the south, especially Munster.
Surpluses and high costs forced the CAP to change. Each reform moved support away from guaranteed prices and towards payments tied to other goals.

The MacSharry reform of 1992, led by Ray MacSharry, EU Agriculture Commissioner from Sligo, replaced price cuts with direct payments (money paid straight to farmers) and introduced set-aside (paying farmers to leave some land unused to cut output).
Agenda 2000 made rural development (support for the wider countryside, not only farm output) the second pillar of the CAP.
The Fischler reform, agreed in 2003, decoupled payments from production, so farmers were no longer paid according to how much they produced.
The Single Farm Payment began in 2005 and was replaced by the Basic Payment Scheme from 2015.
Cross-compliance links payments to environmental and animal-welfare rules, so a farmer who breaks the rules can lose payment.
The current CAP period is run in Ireland through a national plan that puts a large share of the money towards the environment.
Ireland's CAP Strategic Plan (its national plan for the CAP) is worth about €9.8 billion from EU and national funds, with about 45% for environmental and climate measures.

Basic Income Support for Sustainability (BISS, the main direct payment to farmers) is worth about €3.6 billion. The eco-scheme (a payment for environmentally friendly farming) is worth about €1.5 billion, 25% of direct payments.
Convergence (moving payments towards the national average) raises every payment entitlement to at least 85% of the national average.
Payments for young farmers and the ACRES agri-environment scheme (paying farmers for farming that protects nature) are included in the plan.
Areas of Natural Constraint (ANC) payments support farms on disadvantaged land, where farming is harder because of natural conditions.
Under the CAP's second pillar, money also goes to protecting the environment and keeping the countryside economically alive, not just to farm output.
REPS, the Rural Environment Protection Scheme, ran from 1994 to 2009 as an agri-environment scheme, paying farmers to farm in ways that protect the environment.
LEADER, from 1991, funds local rural enterprise such as farm diversification (farmers earning from new activities), rural tourism and crafts.
Grants support forestry and young farmers, such as those taking over family farms.
Exams ask you to name types of farm and may ask about the number and size of farms. The Census of Agriculture 2020 (CSO) gives the picture.
The Census of Agriculture 2020 counted 135,037 farms, down about 3% on 2010, with an average size of about 33 hectares.
On a third (33%) of farms the holder was aged 65 or over; only 7% of holders were under 35, which shows the farming population is ageing.
The main farm types are dairy, cattle (beef) rearing, sheep, tillage (growing crops) and mixed. Specialist beef is the most common type.
For Ireland the CAP has brought security and support to farming and the countryside. These points suit questions on the positive effects of EU policies.
Stable farm incomes and a guaranteed market, so farmers can plan with confidence.
Modernisation of farms and food quality standards, so Irish produce meets EU rules and sells in the single market.
Environmental schemes and support for rural communities, such as LEADER and REPS, so the countryside keeps people and income.
Dependence on direct payments is high for many beef and sheep farms, which is a limit as well as a support, because those farms struggle if payments change.
The same policy also has costs. To get full marks, pair each positive effect with a negative one.
Payments have historically favoured bigger farmers, so most of the money went to a minority.
Dependence on subsidies (payments from the state or EU) and heavy bureaucracy and inspections.
Intensification (farming more intensively, with more animals and inputs) has damaged water quality through nitrates and raised greenhouse gas emissions as the dairy herd grew.
The number of farms has fallen and farmers are ageing; small western farms remain uneconomic, meaning they cannot make a viable living.
Trade deals such as EU-Mercosur, which concluded in December 2024 and was opposed by Irish farm organisations, are feared to undercut Irish beef.
Intensive farming puts nitrogen into water, so the EU limits it. This shows EU environmental rules shaping Irish farming.
The Nitrates Directive of 1991 limits the organic nitrogen (for example from slurry and manure) that can be spread per hectare.

Ireland has a derogation (a permitted exception) that allows higher stocking (more animals per hectare) on intensive farms, conditional on water quality. EU environmental rules therefore shape farming directly.
The Common Fisheries Policy treats EU seas as shared resources. This suited countries with big fleets more than Ireland.
The Common Fisheries Policy (CFP) was agreed in full in 1983. It creates a common pond of EU waters, giving all members' fleets equal access beyond coastal limits.
Its aim is to conserve fish stocks (the numbers of fish in the sea) for the long term.
Ireland had to share its rich waters with much larger fleets, notably those of Spain, France and the Netherlands. Spain and Portugal joined in 1986.
The CFP controls how much fish can be taken and how, through quotas and rules on fishing effort.
Total Allowable Catches (TACs, the maximum amount of each species that can be caught) are set each December by EU fisheries ministers and divided into national quotas using fixed shares.
A coastal band of 12 nautical miles is reserved mainly for local boats.
Days-at-sea limits, mesh sizes (net hole size, so young fish escape), closed areas and closed seasons control fishing effort.
The Hague Preferences, agreed in 1976, give Ireland a smaller cut when TACs fall, in recognition of its coastal communities' dependence on fishing.
Irish fishing is centred on a small number of ports on the coast, and a state agency supports it.
Killybegs, Co. Donegal, is Ireland's largest fishing port by volume and value, specialising in pelagic fish (species living near the surface or mid-water): mackerel, herring and blue whiting.
The other Fishery Harbour Centres are Castletownbere (Co. Cork), Ros an Mhíl (Rossaveel, Co. Galway), Dingle (Co. Kerry), Howth (Co. Dublin) and Dunmore East (Co. Waterford).
Bord Iascaigh Mhara (BIM) is the state seafood development agency.
Processing and fishing jobs sustain peripheral coastal areas, which have few other sources of employment.
For Ireland the CFP has brought funding, protection for stocks and market access.
EU funding for boats, harbours and processing plants, now through the European Maritime, Fisheries and Aquaculture Fund.
Conservation aims protect stocks over the long term, so there are fish left for future catches.
Access to EU seafood markets, so Irish fish can be sold across the EU.
The Hague Preferences protect Ireland's share when quotas are cut.
The CFP has costs for Ireland as well as benefits, because its quota share is small and stocks have not always been protected.
Ireland's quota share is small relative to the size and richness of its waters.
Overfishing and stock collapses have occurred despite the CFP, so its conservation aim has not always been met.
Discards, the throwing back of dead fish, were common until the landing obligation, which wasted fish.
Decommissioning of boats (paying owners to take boats out of service) and job losses in coastal communities.
The 2013 reform tackled two weaknesses: wasteful discarding and overfishing.
The reform was agreed in 2013. It introduced a landing obligation, which bans discarding, phased in between 2015 and 2019.
It aims to fish at maximum sustainable yield, the largest catch that can be taken without running down stocks.
There is more on this in Conflicts between economic interests and environmental interests, which covers depletion of fish stocks as an economic and environmental conflict.
Brexit (the UK's leaving of the EU) hit Irish fishing hard because EU fishing quota was handed to the UK.
The EU-UK Trade and Cooperation Agreement from 1 January 2021 transferred EU quota to the UK.
Ireland lost about 26% of its mackerel quota. The government's Seafood Task Force valued the annual quota loss at about €43 million by 2026.
Irish ministers said Ireland's losses were about double those of other EU fleets in proportion.
The Brexit Adjustment Reserve (an EU fund to help countries hit by Brexit) gave Ireland about €1 billion, the largest share of the EU-wide reserve.
A €25.6 million pelagic support scheme was funded from the reserve, and a voluntary permanent cessation (decommissioning) scheme ran in 2022-23.
The EU has rich and poor regions, and Ireland began as one of the poor ones. Regional funds exist to narrow that gap.
The EU has regional inequality, and Ireland was a poor, peripheral member in 1973, far from the EU's economic centre.
The European Regional Development Fund (ERDF) was set up in 1975 to fund infrastructure, enterprise, research and innovation in poorer regions.
The Structural Funds (ERDF, the European Social Fund and the farm guidance fund) doubled after the 1988-89 reform, to prepare poorer regions for the single market.
Poorer regions got the strongest support. Ireland qualified for two major schemes, one for its regions and one for the state as a whole.

Ireland was a single Objective 1 region (the EU's poorest category) from 1989 to 1999, because its income per head was below 75% of the EU average. National Development Plans were co-financed by the EU.

The Cohesion Fund began in 1993-94 under the Maastricht Treaty. It serves states with income below 90% of the EU average, namely Ireland, Spain, Portugal and Greece, and funds transport and environmental projects.
Ireland stopped qualifying for the Cohesion Fund as its income rose in the 2000s.
By 2000 parts of Ireland had grown richer, so the country was split in two to keep some EU funding for the poorer part.
Ireland was split into two regions. The Border, Midland and Western (BMW) region kept Objective 1 status.
The Southern and Eastern region was in transition (being phased out of top-level support), not Objective 1.
Regional funds paid for infrastructure and enterprise, the things poorer regions lacked.
Roads, such as inter-urban motorways and bypasses, and public transport.
Water and wastewater treatment, ports, airports and broadband.
Research centres and enterprise support, such as help for new firms, which builds jobs in poorer regions.

Better access for peripheral regions, because new roads and ports link them to markets, attraction of foreign direct investment, and a contribution to the Celtic Tiger (Ireland's rapid economic boom).
In the current period, the money is allocated by region and each region's classification depends on its income relative to the EU average.
ERDF regional programmes are run by the regional assemblies. Two regional programmes are worth about €853 million in total, of which about €396 million comes from the EU.
The Northern and Western Region was reclassified from a more developed to a transition region, because its income relative to the EU average fell.
The Southern and Eastern and Midland regions remain more developed regions.
Three regional assemblies have operated since 2015, so each region has its own body to run its programme.
Besides the ERDF, other EU funds target particular parts of Ireland.
PEACE PLUS (2021-27) and INTERREG support the border region. There is more on this in The complexity of regions (i).
The Just Transition Fund (2021-27) targets the Midlands peat region after Bord na Móna ended peat harvesting for electricity, because jobs there depended on peat.
The funds achieved a lot, but not everything. A balanced answer gives both sides.
The funds helped Ireland converge with EU incomes and modernised its infrastructure.
The gap between the Dublin-centred east and the Northern and Western region has persisted.
As a wealthy member, Ireland now receives far less, and EU regional funds go mainly to eastern Europe, an effect of enlargement.
Where regional funds target places, social funding targets people: their jobs, skills and inclusion.
The ESF was set up by the Treaty of Rome in 1957 and is the oldest structural fund.
It improves employment, skills and social inclusion (making sure disadvantaged groups are not left out of work and education).
In Ireland ESF money has paid for training and education, particularly for people who found it hard to get work.
The ESF co-financed training through FÁS (1988-2013), replaced in 2013 by SOLAS and 16 Education and Training Boards.
Youthreach, begun in 1989, helps early school-leavers. Post-Leaving Cert courses, apprenticeships and back-to-education schemes are also co-financed.
Programmes target the long-term unemployed, people with disabilities, Travellers and women returning to work.
The skilled workforce created this way helped attract foreign direct investment.
The ESF is now called ESF+ and in Ireland it is delivered through one programme, paid for by both the EU and the Irish state.
The Employment, Inclusion, Skills and Training (EIST) programme for 2021-2027 is worth about €1.08 billion: about €508 million from the EU and about €573 million national.
It was launched in March 2023, so the 2021-2027 period began delivery only partway through.

Priorities: about €500 million for social inclusion, about €280 million for upskilling and lifelong learning, and over €180 million for employment, mainly of young people and the long-term unemployed.
Global trade can move jobs abroad. The EGF helps workers who lose their jobs this way to retrain.
The EGF was set up in 2007 to retrain workers made redundant by shifts in global trade.

In 2009 the EU approved about €14.8 million to help about 2,400 former Dell and supplier workers in the Limerick area. Dell had announced in January 2009 that it was moving manufacturing from Limerick to Łódź in Poland.
Waterford Crystal workers also received EGF support, as another example of jobs lost to global trade.
The EU also shapes Irish society through laws. Irish equality and workplace rights follow EEC and EU directives (laws that member states must put into their own law).

The civil service marriage bar (the rule forcing women to leave their jobs on marrying) ended in 1973. Irish equality laws followed EEC directives: the Anti-Discrimination (Pay) Act 1974 and the Employment Equality Act 1977.
The Organisation of Working Time Act 1997, which applied the EU Working Time Directive, set an average maximum working week of 48 hours.
EU directives also set rules on health and safety, maternity and parental leave, and the rights of part-time workers.
EU membership also gives citizens freedom to move and study across member states.
Irish people can live and work anywhere in the EU.
The Erasmus student exchange programme, from 1987, lets students study abroad.
EU workers came to Ireland after 2004; there is more on this in The complexity of regions (ii).
As with regional funds, social funding has both strengths and weaknesses that you can use in an evaluation.
The ESF raised skills and employment, especially in the 1990s.
Some training schemes were criticised as poorly targeted, so money did not always reach those who needed it.
Social funding is now much smaller relative to the size of the Irish economy, because Ireland is a wealthy member.

A multinational company (MNC) is a company based in one home country that runs production or service branches in several other countries. The syllabus asks you to study one MNC to understand how it is structured and organised, so the general pattern comes first.

Definition: a company with its headquarters (the main control centre) in its home country and production or service branches in several host countries (the countries that receive the branches). It is also called a transnational corporation (TNC).

Typical structure: headquarters, research and development (R&D, the work of inventing and designing new products) and top management stay in the home country as the core. Branch plants, regional headquarters, and sales and service offices are placed abroad.
Decisions are made at headquarters, and branch plants compete with each other inside the company for investment, so a plant that is less efficient or more costly risks losing out to another.

Production is split into stages: design and R&D; basic processing of raw materials and components; assembly and testing; distribution and sales. Each stage is placed where it is cheapest or most efficient, which spreads sourcing, basic processing and markets across the world.

The largest MNCs have sales or market values (the total worth of the company's shares) greater than the gross domestic product (GDP, the value of all goods and services a country produces in a year) of many countries, and they control much of world trade and investment.
The largest companies by market value in the mid-2020s are American technology companies: Apple, Microsoft, Nvidia, Alphabet (Google's parent) and Amazon.
Foreign direct investment (FDI) is investment by a company in another country, made by building or buying a plant there. Ireland has a State agency whose job is to win this investment.

IDA Ireland (Industrial Development Authority), set up in 1949, is the State agency responsible for attracting and keeping FDI, so it is the body that supports foreign companies both before and after they arrive.

IDA client companies employ about 300,000 people in about 1,800 companies (2023-24), concentrated in the Dublin region, which has the largest labour pool, universities, Dublin Port and Airport, services and existing clusters of firms.

Other Irish-based MNCs: Pfizer (Ringaskiddy, Co. Cork, and Grange Castle, Dublin), Google (European headquarters, Barrow Street, Dublin), Meta (international headquarters, Dublin), Microsoft (in Ireland since 1985) and Dell (Limerick).

Ireland has no shortage of competition for foreign investment, so a company needs reasons to build here. These are the MNC-specific advantages of Ireland, and each one can be developed into an explained point.

Low corporation tax (the tax a company pays on its profits) of 12.5%, rising to 15% for very large multinational groups (turnover over 750 million euro) from 2024 under the OECD global minimum tax agreement.
A young, educated, English-speaking workforce, which suits high-skill and customer-facing work.
EU membership, which Ireland joined in 1973 as the EEC (now the EU), gives access to the single market (one trading area with no tariffs between members).
Since the UK left the EU on 31 January 2020, Ireland is the only euro-area country where English is the main language (Malta also has English as an official language).
IDA grants and support for companies that invest here, which lower the cost of setting up.
Good international links, including ports, airports and broadband, so goods, staff and data can move easily.
Clusters of similar firms and suppliers already in the country, so a new plant can find skilled workers and local suppliers.
Universities and research links with industry, which supply graduates and shared research.
A stable democracy with a pro-business government, which gives a company confidence its investment is safe.

Intel is the main case study. It is a clear example of an MNC whose headquarters and design work stay in the home country while manufacturing is spread across several continents. Intel was founded in 1968, which is earlier than Apple (1976).

Intel Corporation was founded in 1968 in California by Robert Noyce and Gordon Moore. Its headquarters are in Santa Clara, California, in Silicon Valley (the area of California where many technology companies are based).
Intel made the first commercial microprocessor (a computer's processing chip), the Intel 4004, in 1971.
Intel is best known for the processors inside most personal computers: the x86 family, sold as Pentium and Core, and Xeon for servers (powerful computers that serve other computers).

Wafer fabrication plants ('fabs', factories that make chips on silicon wafers) are at Hillsboro, Oregon (Intel's main research and development fabs); Chandler, Arizona; Rio Rancho, New Mexico; Leixlip, Ireland; and Kiryat Gat, Israel.
Assembly and test plants are at Penang and Kulim in Malaysia, Ho Chi Minh City in Vietnam, and Chengdu in China.
Sales offices are located around the world, close to the customers they serve.
Ireland's part of Intel is a manufacturing branch plant at Leixlip, Co. Kildare. It is the country's largest private-sector investment.
Intel came to Leixlip, Co. Kildare, in 1989.
Its campus is Ireland's largest private-sector investment, with over 30 billion euro invested by 2023. It has several fabs and employs several thousand people.

Fab 34 opened in 2023 and was the first fab in Europe to make chips in high volume using extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography (printing the tiny circuit patterns onto the wafer with a very short wavelength of light).
Fab 34 makes the Intel 4 and Intel 3 generations, such as Core Ultra processors.

In 2024 Intel sold a 49% share of the Fab 34 joint venture (a business owned jointly by two companies) to Apollo Global Management, an American investment firm, for about 11 billion US dollars, to raise money for its other projects.

A fab has very particular needs: easy transport, a big site, skilled people and huge supplies of water and electricity. Leixlip met them, which is the answer to the Ordinary question on the advantages of Ireland for Intel.
Leixlip is on the M4 motorway west of Dublin, giving road access to the capital, so staff and goods can travel easily.
A large, flat greenfield site, which is undeveloped land, so there was room to build very large plants.
Maynooth University is nearby in Co. Kildare, and Trinity College Dublin and University College Dublin are in the city, giving access to graduates and research links.
A large labour pool in the Dublin area, so Intel can recruit many workers.
A water and electricity supply; fabs use huge amounts of both, so a plant cannot work without a dependable supply.
For the syllabus you must study one product of the MNC. Intel's product is the microprocessor, and knowing how it is made explains why Intel needs the inputs and locations described next.
A microprocessor, or chip, is the 'brain' of a computer, because it carries out the computer's instructions.
It is made by building billions of tiny transistors (tiny electronic switches) in layers on a thin disc of pure silicon called a wafer.
Wafers are processed in a dust-free clean room, because dust would ruin the tiny circuits.
Sourcing means where a company gets the materials and parts it needs. A fab depends on a few specialist inputs, and some come from a single supplier.
Silicon, refined from quartz sand, is bought as silicon wafers from specialist wafer makers.
Chemicals, specialty gases and metals, which are used up in processing the wafers.
Huge volumes of ultra-pure water and electricity, because the fab uses them continuously.

Manufacturing machines, especially lithography machines (which print the circuit patterns onto wafers) from ASML, based at Veldhoven in the Netherlands. ASML is the only maker of EUV lithography machines, which cost hundreds of millions of euro each.
Intel splits chip making into stages and puts each where it suits best. Following the chain from wafer to computer shows how the stages are spread across several continents.
1. Stage 1: wafers are processed in fabs at Leixlip, Hillsboro, Chandler and Kiryat Gat.

2. Stage 2: finished wafers are flown to assembly and test plants in Penang and Kulim (Malaysia), Ho Chi Minh City (Vietnam) and Chengdu (China), where they are cut into individual chips, packaged and tested.
3. Stage 3: the chips go to computer makers' assembly plants, mostly in Asia.
Chips are small, light and very valuable, so they are moved by air.
The Leixlip plant makes processed wafers only. Cutting, packaging and testing of the chips are not done in Ireland.
A market is where a product is sold, and a market can be a country, a region or a type of customer. Intel's main customers are computer makers, server makers, governments and businesses.
Computer manufacturers are the main customers: Lenovo (China), HP and Dell (USA).
Makers of servers for data centres and cloud computing (storing and running data and programs on remote computers).
Governments and businesses worldwide, because they also buy computers and servers.
Markets are in North America, Europe and Asia, with China one of the largest.
Two markets outside Ireland can be named as countries, for example the USA and China.
Intel faces pressures from rivals, costs and supply chains. The exam asks for one difficulty, so learn several to choose from and give each in one explained sentence.

Competition from AMD (USA); TSMC (Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company), the world's largest contract chip maker; Samsung (South Korea); and Nvidia (USA), the leader in chips for artificial intelligence.
Loss of Apple as a customer: Apple began replacing Intel chips in its Mac computers with its own M1 chip in November 2020.
Very high cost of building new fabs.
Falling profits: about 15,000 global job cuts were announced in August 2024, with further cuts in 2025 under the new chief executive, Lip-Bu Tan.
In 2025 the US government took a stake of about 10% in Intel.
Risk that production moves abroad if Ireland's tax advantage narrows (the 15% minimum rate for very large groups) or if costs rise.
High energy costs and pressure on Ireland's electricity grid, since fabs need large amounts of power.
Dependence on Asian supply chains: the global chip shortage of 2021, caused by COVID-19 disruption, halted car and electronics production worldwide.
Intel's presence helps Ireland in several ways. These benefits are described without numbers because no checked figures exist for them.
Direct jobs on the Leixlip campus, and indirect (spin-off) jobs with local suppliers and services, which grow because Intel buys goods and services locally.
Corporation tax paid to the State, and exports from the plant.
Skills development and research links with universities.

Apple is the alternative case study to Intel. Its product is the iPhone, and it is a good example of a company that designs in one country and has others make its products. Apple was founded in 1976, later than Intel (1968).
Apple was founded in 1976 by Steve Jobs and Steve Wozniak. Its headquarters are at the Apple Park campus in Cupertino, California, which opened in 2017.
Products: the iPhone (2007), iPad (2010), Mac computers and Apple Watch (2015), plus services such as the App Store, iCloud and Apple Music.
Design, software and management are based in California, which makes California the core of the company.
Apple's Irish base is in Cork. It is mainly a European headquarters and operations centre, not a phone factory.
Apple opened at Hollyhill, Cork, in 1980. It was Apple's first manufacturing plant in Europe.
It employs about 6,000 people in Cork and is Apple's European headquarters.
The Cork campus runs operations and supply chain, finance, and customer support (AppleCare) in many European languages. It also assembles some built-to-order iMac computers.
The Cork campus does not make iPhones.
Unlike a company that builds everything itself, Apple concentrates on design and management and pays other firms to make its products.
Apple owns very little manufacturing itself and outsources production (pays other firms to make its products) to contract manufacturers, which lets it focus on design, software and management.
The chief contract manufacturer is Foxconn (Hon Hai Precision Industry), a Taiwanese company.
Apple runs its own retail stores and an online store.
An iPhone is built from parts and materials gathered from several countries, so its sourcing is spread across Asia and beyond.
Processor chips are designed by Apple and made by TSMC in Taiwan.
Screens are supplied by Samsung and LG (South Korea). Memory and other parts come from other Asian suppliers.
Raw materials include aluminium, lithium and cobalt for batteries, rare earth metals and gold.
Most of the world's cobalt is mined in the Democratic Republic of the Congo.
Apple's design is done in California, but the phones are put together elsewhere. Final assembly is concentrated in a few huge plants.
Final assembly is done by Foxconn at very large plants in China: Zhengzhou in Henan province, called 'iPhone City', and Shenzhen.
A growing share is assembled in India, around Chennai and Bengaluru, by Foxconn and the Indian Tata group. This reduces dependence on China.
Apple sells its iPhones in almost every region, through its own outlets and through phone companies.
iPhones are sold worldwide. The Americas, Europe and China are the largest regions.
Sales are made through Apple Stores, Apple's online store and mobile phone networks.
Apple has faced legal, supply and reputation problems. As with Intel, one difficulty explained well is what the exam asks for.
EU state aid tax case: in 2016 the European Commission ruled that Ireland had given Apple illegal tax benefits worth 13 billion euro, which must be recovered.
The EU General Court overturned the ruling in 2020. In September 2024 the EU Court of Justice reinstated it, and Ireland received about 14 billion euro, including interest.
This was recovery of illegal State aid (help from a government that gives a company an unfair advantage), which is unpaid tax, not a fine. Ireland had argued against collecting it.
Dependence on China for assembly, and trade tensions between the USA and China.
Competition from Samsung and from Chinese phone makers, which can take customers from Apple.
Criticism of working conditions in supplier factories, which can harm Apple's reputation.
Athenry, Co. Galway: Apple announced a data centre (about 850 million euro) in 2015 and abandoned it in 2018 after planning and appeal delays.
Use map evidence to justify a location, and give one reason against a location. The map question asks for two reasons an MNC might locate in a mapped area, with map evidence, and one reason against.
Look for transport: a motorway, national primary road, railway, port or airport, because an MNC needs to move goods and staff.
Look for a large, flat site, shown by widely spaced contours (the lines joining points of equal height; wide spacing means gentle slopes).
Look for a nearby town for labour and services, and for an industrial estate symbol, which shows land already set aside for industry.
Look for a water supply, such as a river or lake, because industry needs water.
Reasons against a site: steep or flood-prone land (closely spaced contours or marsh), poor roads, a remote location, or protected scenery.

Invented illustration, not a real map: a flat site beside a motorway junction, a market town nearby and a river for water. Each point should give the feature, the location and the reason it suits an MNC.
A data response may give a chart or table of the largest MNCs by value. You are then asked to draw a bar chart and calculate differences.
Draw a bar chart with one bar per company, a labelled value axis starting at zero, and units in the title, so the bars can be compared fairly.
Calculate a difference by subtracting the smaller value from the larger, and state the answer with its units.
The method is set out in the note Tables, Graphs and Data Skills.

Modern manufacturing and services can move between regions and countries far more easily than older heavy industry. They are described as footloose, which means they are not tied to a raw material, a coalfield or a port. A multinational company (MNC, a firm that operates in several countries) can therefore choose where to locate.
Light, high-value products such as chips, medicines and software are cheap to move by air, so the factory does not need to be near its customers.
Containerisation (shipping goods in standard sealed boxes) and cheaper transport lower the cost of moving goods between plants.
Information and communications technology lets headquarters, the central office that controls the company, direct branches on any continent.
Free movement of capital (money for investment) and lower trade barriers, through the World Trade Organization (WTO) and the EU single market, let companies serve markets across borders.
Governments compete with grants and low taxes to attract investment, which gives companies a choice of locations.
MNCs can switch production between their own plants, so a plant that becomes less attractive can lose work to another.
Companies move production when another location offers a better return. The reasons are mostly about cost, markets and risk, and the moves go in both directions.
Lower labour and land costs, because wages and rents are a large part of what it costs to make a product.
Tax advantages and grants, which lower the cost of setting up and running a plant.
Being inside a trade bloc (a group of countries with shared trade rules), which avoids tariffs (taxes on imported goods).
Being close to growing markets, so goods reach customers more cheaply.
Access to skills, and political and economic stability, which make an investment safer.
Investment moved into Ireland, for example Intel in Leixlip in 1989 and Dell in Limerick in 1990, from the 1970s to the 1990s.
Investment also moved out of Ireland when costs rose, for example Dell's manufacturing in 2009.
Mobility is not limited to the case study. These examples show the same forces at work for other companies and places, and they can support an answer on mobility.
Nissan opened a car plant at Sunderland, north-east England, in 1986. It is a Japanese company locating inside the EU (then EEC) market, so its cars avoid tariffs.

Bengaluru (Bangalore), India, is an IT and business-process outsourcing hub (a centre for work contracted out to another firm). Tata Consultancy Services, Infosys and Wipro are Indian IT firms, and call centres and IT services have moved there.
Apple is growing its iPhone assembly in India, with Foxconn and Tata near Chennai and Bengaluru, to reduce dependence on China.
Intel opened Fab 34 (a fab is a chip-making factory) at Leixlip in 2023. It cancelled a planned fab at Magdeburg, Germany, which had been announced in 2022 and was cancelled in 2025.
When a plant moves, one region gains what another loses. The effects on the region matter because many plants are controlled from outside it.
The receiving region gains jobs, skills and exports.
The losing region suffers unemployment, the loss of spin-off jobs (jobs in local suppliers and services that depended on the plant) and emigration of workers.
Branch-plant economies (regions whose factories are owned by companies based elsewhere) are vulnerable because the decisions about their plants are taken abroad.

A branch plant is a factory or office owned and controlled by a company headquartered elsewhere. Headquarters decides whether it opens or closes, to suit the whole company rather than the host region.

Strategies that open branch plants: expansion into new markets; locating inside a trade bloc; following tax incentives and grants; acquiring other companies through mergers and takeovers; joint ventures that share the cost of huge investments; and government subsidy schemes.
The US CHIPS and Science Act of 2022 is a subsidy scheme: it provided about 50 billion US dollars of US government support for chip making and research in the USA. The EU Chips Act followed in 2023.
Strategies that close branch plants: cost-cutting and rationalisation, which means concentrating production in fewer, larger plants; relocation to cheaper countries.
Other closing strategies: outsourcing to contract manufacturers (other firms paid to make the product); falling demand for a mature product; and mergers that leave duplicate plants.
Reshoring, which means bringing production back home for security of supply, so that the company is not dependent on distant plants.
Dell is the clearest Irish example of an MNC moving production. Its story begins with a company built on a new way of selling computers.
Dell was founded in 1984 by Michael Dell in Austin, Texas. Its headquarters are in Round Rock, Texas.
Dell sold direct: it built computers to order and sold them by phone and, from the mid-1990s, online, with no shops in between.
Dell set up in Limerick (Raheen) in 1990. Limerick became its European manufacturing base, and Dell was one of Ireland's largest exporters.
Dell went private in 2013 and bought EMC in 2016, which gave it EMC's large operation at Ovens, Co. Cork.
In 2009 Dell closed its Limerick manufacturing and moved it to Poland. The move shows headquarters choosing what suits the whole company, with serious effects on the host region.
In January 2009 Dell announced that it would move its Limerick manufacturing to Łódź, Poland, with the loss of about 1,900 jobs, plus job losses at local suppliers.
Reasons: lower wages and costs in Poland; Polish government aid, which the EU approved; nearness to growing markets in Central and Eastern Europe.
More reasons: falling PC prices, which squeezed profits, and the 2008-09 recession, which cut demand and made cost savings urgent.
Effects on Limerick: the loss of about 1,900 direct jobs and of jobs at local suppliers, and the loss of one of Ireland's largest exporters.
The EU Globalisation Adjustment Fund paid for retraining and support for the former Dell workers.
Dell kept its sales, support and other offices in Ireland. Manufacturing closed; the company did not leave Ireland.

Intel, the chip maker studied in the multinational company note, shows corporate strategy at work: heavy investment, raising money by selling a share, cutting jobs when profits fall, and relying on government support.
Intel invested billions of euro in its Leixlip campus, with over €30 billion invested by 2023.
In 2024 Intel sold 49% of the Fab 34 joint venture to Apollo Global Management, an American investment firm, for about 11 billion US dollars, to raise money for its other projects.
Intel announced about 15,000 global job cuts in August 2024, when its profits fell, with further cuts in 2025.
Government support includes the US CHIPS and Science Act and a US government stake of about 10% in Intel in 2025.

Product life cycle (PLC) theory, put forward by Raymond Vernon in 1966, says a product passes through introduction, growth, maturity and decline. Its best location changes at each stage, which is why MNCs move production over time.
Stages: introduction (development), growth, maturity and decline. Sales are drawn as a curve against time.
Introduction and growth happen in the core (the rich, developed countries), close to headquarters, research and development, skilled workers and wealthy early customers.

At maturity the product is standardised and competition cuts prices, so production moves to cheaper locations to keep costs down: first semi-peripheral countries (middle-income countries) such as Ireland in the past, then Eastern Europe and Asia.
In decline the plant closes, or it is upgraded to make a new product.
Dell's move to Poland is a textbook mature-stage relocation.
The personal computer became a mature, standardised product with falling prices, so competing on cost became essential.
Dell therefore moved its assembly from Limerick to Łódź in Poland, a cheaper location, in 2009.
The Dell case shows the mature-stage pattern: production is moved to cut costs while the company keeps sales and support in Ireland.
Intel's products have short lives, so its fabs are always being renewed. The cycle shapes where new technology is made and which plants survive.
Each chip generation has a short life of a few years.

New processes are developed at Hillsboro, Oregon, then copied exactly into fabs such as Leixlip. This is Intel's 'Copy Exactly!' policy, which copies equipment and procedures exactly from the development fab to the others.
Older fabs are upgraded or closed as the cycle moves on.
Ireland keeps its place by winning each new generation, as Fab 34 does for the Intel 4 and Intel 3 generations.
Intel missed the start of the smartphone and AI chip cycles, which helped rivals. Nvidia leads in chips for artificial intelligence, and Apple dropped Intel chips from its Macs from 2020.
Information technology (IT) changes how an MNC makes, controls and sells its products, and it changes what customers want. Exams pair this with the product life cycle.
Computer-aided design (designing on computer) and automation (machines doing tasks) are used in the fab.
Global communication lets one headquarters run plants on several continents.
Real-time stock control and just-in-time supply (parts arrive just when needed) reduce stock held at each plant.
Online sales: Dell's direct model moved online from the mid-1990s.
New technology changes demand, moving from PCs to smartphones and then to cloud computing (using remote servers to store and process data) and AI. This creates new markets and destroys older ones.
Moore's Law, from Gordon Moore in 1965, states that the number of transistors (tiny switches that make up a chip) on a chip doubles about every two years.

Teleservices are services delivered at a distance using telecommunications, such as call centres, customer support, technical help desks, and shared services such as payroll and accounts. They can be located almost anywhere, so countries compete for them.

Why Ireland attracted them: an English-speaking and multilingual workforce, a time zone between the USA and Europe, good broadband, and IDA support (help from the State agency that attracts foreign investment).
Apple's Cork campus provides AppleCare customer support in many European languages.
Microsoft has been in Ireland since 1985.
Threat: routine teleservices are moving to cheaper destinations such as India (Bengaluru) and the Philippines (Manila), and automation and AI chatbots are reducing routine jobs.
Ireland hosts the European or international headquarters of major internet companies, which makes the IT sector an important part of the economy.
Google's European headquarters are at Barrow Street, Grand Canal Dock, Dublin, in the area known as Silicon Docks.
Meta (Facebook) has its international headquarters in Dublin.
Ireland is one of the world's largest exporters of computer services.
Data centres are large buildings filled with servers (powerful computers) that run cloud computing. Ireland has attracted many, but they bring a pressure on the electricity grid.
Ireland attracts them because of its cool climate, which reduces cooling costs, its connectivity, and the technology companies already here.
Data centres used about 21% of Ireland's metered electricity in 2023 (CSO), up from 5% in 2015. Most are in the Dublin region.
Operators include Amazon Web Services, Microsoft and Google.
EirGrid (the company that runs the electricity grid) restricted new data-centre connections in the Dublin area from 2022, because they use such a large share of the electricity.
E-commerce is buying and selling goods and services online. It changes where goods are stored, how they are delivered and which shops survive.
Amazon was founded in 1994 by Jeff Bezos in Seattle, USA. Alibaba was founded in 1999 in Hangzhou, China.
Effects: online-only companies appear, some high-street shops decline, and warehouses and delivery services grow.
Dell was an early large online seller.
COVID-19 lockdowns, which began in Ireland in March 2020, accelerated online buying.
The future of economic activity is being shaped by new ways of working, new technology and changing politics. Each trend brings opportunities and risks.
Remote and hybrid working (partly at home, partly in the office) has continued after COVID-19.
Artificial intelligence and automation are reducing routine jobs.
Reshoring and friend-shoring (producing in allied countries): a move to secure supply of strategic industries such as chips.
Risks for Ireland come from the global minimum tax, under which the rate is 15% for groups with turnover over €750 million, which reduces the tax advantage, and from US tariffs.
Trade is the buying and selling of goods and services between countries. Exports leave a country and imports arrive in it, and data questions use these words constantly.
Visible trade is goods that can be seen and counted, such as cars, food and computer chips.
Invisible trade is services, which cannot be held or counted in the same way, such as software, financial services, tourism and aircraft leasing.
Balance of trade: the value of exports minus the value of imports, which gives one number that shows whether a country sells more than it buys.
A trade surplus means exports are greater than imports; a trade deficit means imports are greater than exports.
The balance of trade is only part of the picture of a country's dealings with the world. The balance of payments is the wider record.
Balance of payments: the record of all money flows between a country and the rest of the world.
It includes trade in goods and services, plus investment flows (money put into businesses abroad), profits sent home, borrowing and transfers.
It is a wider measure than the balance of trade, which records only exports and imports, so the two are not the same thing.
A country that keeps buying more from abroad than it sells pays a price at home, while exports bring benefits. Each effect follows from where the money goes.
A persistent trade deficit (imports greater than exports year after year) means money flows out of the country to pay for the extra imports.
The country may have to borrow or sell assets (things it owns, such as businesses or property) to pay for those imports.
Home industries and jobs can be lost as cheaper imports replace domestic production.
The currency (the country's money) may weaken when a country persistently imports more than it exports.
Exports bring jobs, tax revenue, foreign earnings and economic growth, because foreign buyers pay money into the country.
A country that sells to many different countries is safer than one that sells mainly to one. This is the advantage of many export partners.
A country with many export partners is less dependent on any one market.
A recession (a fall in economic activity), tariff or crisis in one country, such as the US tariffs imposed in 2025, then does less damage to its overall trade, because the other markets keep buying.
Governments can open their markets to imports or restrict them. Protectionism is the restricting approach, and international bodies try to set common rules.
Protectionism restricts imports to protect home industries from foreign competition, so home producers face less pressure from cheaper foreign goods.
Barriers to trade include tariffs (taxes on imports), quotas (limits on the quantity imported), subsidies (payments that help home producers compete with imports), and regulations.
Trade blocs (groups of countries that agree trade rules among themselves) remove barriers between their own members, so members trade with each other more easily than with outsiders.
GATT (General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade) was signed in 1947 to reduce tariffs between countries, so goods cost less to trade.
The World Trade Organisation (WTO) was set up on 1 January 1995, with headquarters in Geneva, Switzerland; it has over 160 member countries.
The WTO sets the rules of world trade and settles disputes between members, so countries have a common referee.
Fair trade gives producers in developing countries a guaranteed minimum price and a premium (an extra payment), shown by the Fairtrade mark.
World trade has grown much faster than world output since 1950, and most countries now depend on imports and exports. Several changes made this possible.
Falling trade barriers, through GATT and the WTO, made it cheaper to trade across borders.

Containerisation (shipping goods in standard-sized steel boxes) began with the first container ship voyage, the Ideal X of Malcolm McLean, USA, in 1956; containers made loading and shipping faster and cheaper.
Shanghai, China, has been the world's busiest container port since 2010.
Air freight and information and communication technology (ICT) speed up trade in high-value goods and services, for example by moving them quickly and sharing information instantly.
Multinational companies (MNCs, firms that operate in many countries) trade components between their own plants in different countries.
The entry of China and Eastern Europe into world trade added large new producers and markets, so there were more goods to sell and more buyers.

The three triad areas and the rest of the world are linked by shipping routes and by products whose parts come from many countries. Because they are so linked, a disruption in one place spreads worldwide.

One product links many countries: the iPhone and Intel chip supply chains (the series of countries and firms that make a product's parts and assemble it) each pass through several countries. There is more on this in One multinational company (MNC).
The Suez Canal, opened in 1869, and the Panama Canal, opened in 1914, are chokepoints (narrow passages that much shipping must use) on the shipping routes linking the triad.
In March 2021 the container ship Ever Given blocked the Suez Canal for about six days, holding up hundreds of ships.
From late 2023 attacks on shipping in the Red Sea forced many ships to sail around the Cape of Good Hope, Africa.
The 2008-09 global financial crisis caused world trade to fall sharply in 2009.
COVID-19 (2020-21) disrupted supply chains, for example in the 2021 chip shortage.
Most of the world's trade and production is concentrated in three areas. The trading triad is North America, Europe and the Pacific Rim, the three core economic areas of the world.
The triad produces most of the world's manufactured goods, such as cars and electronics.
It holds the headquarters of most multinational companies (MNCs), so company decisions are made there.
Most world trade takes place among the three areas, and most foreign direct investment (money that firms invest in businesses and factories in other countries) flows between them.
The USA is the triad's North American member and the dominant economy within it. Its trade is shaped by its size, its trade bloc and its use of tariffs.
The USA is the world's largest economy and its largest importer, so its demand matters to exporters everywhere.
It has had a trade deficit in goods every year since the mid-1970s, which means it imports more goods than it exports.
NAFTA (North American Free Trade Agreement: USA, Canada, Mexico) took effect on 1 January 1994.
USMCA (United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement) replaced NAFTA on 1 July 2020, so the three countries kept a trade bloc.
Mexico overtook China in 2023 as the largest source of US imports.
From 2018 the USA put tariffs (taxes on imports) on many Chinese goods in the US-China trade war.
In 2025 the USA raised tariffs on imports from most countries, which raised the price of goods entering the USA.
Europe is one of the three triad areas, and it trades as a bloc. The EU is a union of countries that trade freely with one another.
The EU is a single market (members trade as if in one market) of 27 member states, since the UK left the EU.
The single market began on 1 January 1993, removing barriers to trade between members, so goods move freely between them.
The EU is the largest trading bloc by value, with strong trade with the USA and China, for example in goods sold between the blocs.
The euro, the shared currency, was introduced in 1999; euro notes and coins followed in 2002.
In July 2025 the EU and USA agreed a 15% US tariff on most EU goods.
In the triad, the Pacific Rim means mainly East and South-East Asia, together with Australia. India is not part of it.
Members include, for example, Japan, China, South Korea, Taiwan, Hong Kong, Singapore, the ASEAN countries and Australia.
ASEAN (Association of Southeast Asian Nations) was founded in 1967 as a group of South-East Asian countries.
APEC (Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation) was founded in 1989.
RCEP (Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership) has 15 Asia-Pacific members, including China, Japan, South Korea, Australia and the ASEAN members.
RCEP was signed in November 2020 and came into force from 2022; its members hold about 30% of the world's population and GDP (the total value of goods and services a country produces in a year).
The Asian Tigers are South Korea, Taiwan, Hong Kong and Singapore, fast-growing Asian economies. China and Japan are not Tigers.
Japan is a Pacific Rim economy that grew after the Second World War by exporting manufactured goods. Its story shows how a country with few raw materials can grow by selling manufactured goods.
After the Second World War Japan's growth was based on exporting manufactured goods, mainly cars and electronics.
Japan has few raw materials, so it must import most of its oil, coal and iron ore.
Japan was the world's second-largest economy from the late 1960s until China overtook it in 2010; Germany overtook Japan in 2023.
Toyota, based in Toyota City, uses just-in-time production, which delivers parts as they are needed rather than storing them.
Other major Japanese companies are, for example, Honda, Sony and Nissan.

To avoid trade barriers, Japanese firms opened factories inside the EU and USA; Nissan's car plant at Sunderland, north-east England, opened in 1986, inside the European Economic Community (EEC, the EU's earlier name).
Japan's growth has been slower since the 1990s, so it is no longer expanding as quickly as it did after the war.
China moved from a closed economy to the world's largest exporter of goods, which is why it is called the workshop of the world. Government reforms opened it to trade and investment.
Deng Xiaoping's economic reforms, from 1978, opened China's closed economy to foreign trade and investment.
The first Special Economic Zones (SEZs, areas with special rules to attract foreign firms) were set up in 1980, including Shenzhen beside Hong Kong.
Shenzhen is in mainland China and is not part of Hong Kong; it grew from a small town to over 17 million people (2020 census).
China joined the WTO on 11 December 2001, which gave it a place under world trade rules.
China has been the world's largest exporter of goods since 2009, and it overtook Japan as the second-largest economy in 2010.
China runs a huge trade surplus, because it sells so much abroad; meaning its exports greatly exceed its imports.
The Belt and Road Initiative, launched in 2013, links China to Asia, Africa and Europe through ports, railways and roads.
The trade war with the USA, begun in 2018, also affects China; the US side is in the North America notes.

South Korea is the standard example of a newly industrialised country (NIC, a country that has recently built a large manufacturing economy). It went from poverty to high income by selling manufactured goods abroad.
South Korea was war-damaged by the Korean War (1950-53) and was one of the world's poorest countries in the early 1960s.
Under President Park Chung-hee (1961-79) it industrialised through exports and rose from poverty to high income.
Its economy is dominated by chaebol, family-controlled business groups such as Samsung (founded 1938), Hyundai, LG and SK.
Ulsan is home to Hyundai's shipyards, among the world's largest, and to a Hyundai car plant, as an example of an industrial city built on exports.
South Korea is a world leader in shipbuilding, cars, electronics and memory chips, and Samsung makes smartphones.
South Korea is one of the Asian Tigers and joined the OECD (the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development) in 1996.
Not every region shares in the triad's trade. Some areas are left on the edges of world trade.
Africa, much of Latin America and South Asia hold only a small share of world trade, mostly in raw materials. There is more on this in How the global economy is organised.
An international division of labour means that countries and regions specialise in different stages of production and different types of work. The first pattern grew out of colonial rule.
In the old, colonial pattern, colonies and developing countries exported raw materials and food, while Europe and later the USA manufactured goods and sold them back.
Sudan's Gezira Scheme, from 1925, grew irrigated cotton for the British (Lancashire) textile mills.
India exported raw cotton and tea to Britain under colonial rule, as an example of raw materials and food leaving a colony.
Ghana (then the Gold Coast) exported cocoa; Cote d'Ivoire and Ghana together grow over half of the world's cocoa today, still mostly exported unprocessed.
From the 1960s-70s the pattern changed. Multinational companies began to split production, placing each stage where it suited them best.
Multinational companies moved assembly and routine manufacturing to newly industrialised countries (NICs) and low-wage countries.
The core (the rich, powerful economies) kept headquarters, research and development (R&D, work on new products and technology), design, finance and marketing.
The periphery (the poorer countries on the edge of the world economy) still supplies raw materials.
As an example, Apple's packaging carried the line 'Designed by Apple in California. Assembled in China.'

Intel's R&D is at Hillsboro, Oregon; its fabs (chip factories) include Leixlip in Ireland; assembly and test take place in Malaysia and Vietnam. There is more on this in One multinational company (MNC).
The pattern is not fixed. Services are now divided between countries, and countries move up or spread to new places.
Services are now divided too: Bengaluru (Bangalore), India, is an IT services hub for firms such as Infosys, Wipro and Tata Consultancy Services, and IT and call centres are located in India.
China is moving into high-value products instead of only low-cost assembly.
Low-cost assembly is spreading to Vietnam, Bangladesh and India, because firms look for cheaper places to assemble.
Ireland is a very open economy: its exports are larger than its GDP. It has moved from supplying food to the UK to hosting high-value manufacturing and services by multinational companies (MNCs).
Goods exports passed 200 billion euro in 2024 (CSO, the Central Statistics Office), a record.
Most of this export value is produced by MNC plants, not by Irish-owned firms, so large exports reflect MNC production.

Main goods exports: pharmaceuticals and chemicals (the largest category), medical devices (a cluster at Galway, with firms such as Medtronic and Boston Scientific), computer chips and electronics, and food and drink (beef, dairy and whiskey).
Main services exports: computer services (Ireland is one of the world's largest exporters of them), financial services, aircraft leasing and tourism.
Irish-based lessors (companies that own aircraft and lease them to airlines) manage over half of the world's leased commercial aircraft, from Dublin and Shannon.
Ireland has a large goods trade surplus, because it exports far more goods than it imports, the largest of it with the USA.
Where Irish goods go reflects who makes them. The main market is the USA.
The USA is the largest single market for Irish goods, taking about a third of them, which makes it Ireland's biggest buyer.
Other main markets, such as EU partners Belgium, Germany and the Netherlands, then the UK and China.
US pharmaceutical and technology MNCs export from their Irish plants back to the USA and worldwide, which is why the USA dominates.
In early 2025 Irish exports to the USA rose sharply as US buyers stockpiled medicines (bought extra in advance) before new tariffs.
Ireland's trade with the UK changed after the UK left the EU. Brexit is the usual reason to give.
The UK left the EU on 31 January 2020; the transition period (when the old trade rules still applied) ended on 31 December 2020.
Brexit brought customs checks (inspections of goods at the border) on trade with the UK and took the UK out of the EU single market.
A weaker pound makes Irish goods dearer for UK buyers.
Irish firms have diversified into other markets, so they depend less on the UK.
Ireland's export success depends on a narrow base, which brings risk.
Ireland depends on a few US MNCs and on the US market, so a problem for those firms or that market hits Irish exports.
US tariffs from 2025 expose Irish exports to the USA to new barriers.
Data-response questions give charts and tables of trade and ask you to calculate. The method is the same every time.
Read values from the chart or table and state their units before calculating.
Balance of trade for one country: subtract imports from exports; a negative result is a trade deficit.
Difference between two countries: subtract the smaller value from the larger, so the answer is positive.
Total exports: add the values for every partner, so none is missed.
Use a bar chart to compare values between countries and a line graph to show change over time, because each suits that kind of data.

A basic processing unit is a factory carrying out one stage of production: processing a raw material, making a component (a part that goes into a finished product) or assembling a product. Multinational companies (MNCs, firms operating in many countries) place each stage in whichever country suits it best, which is why production is so widely spread.
The Intel and Apple chains, such as those in 'One multinational company (MNC)', are examples of stages spread across several countries.
Cheap labour suits labour-intensive assembly (work that needs many workers rather than machines), so firms put assembly where wages are low.
Units are placed close to raw materials or to markets, which cuts the distance inputs or finished goods must travel.
A factory inside a trade bloc (a group of countries with shared trade rules) sells to the bloc's members without the barriers that apply to imports from outside.
Tax breaks (reduced tax bills) and grants (money from government) lower the cost of operating in a country, so they attract factories.
Falling transport and communication costs make distant factories practical, because a plant far away can still be supplied and managed.
Spreading production across many countries means that one disaster or strike does not stop all production, so the firm spreads its risk.
Nike shows how far a firm can spread production: it designs and sells shoes but owns almost none of the factories that make them. Do not say Nike owns its Asian factories.
Founded as Blue Ribbon Sports in 1964 by Phil Knight and Bill Bowerman; renamed Nike in 1971.
Headquarters, design and marketing are in Beaverton, Oregon, USA, so the high-skill, high-value work stays at home.
