Footwear is made by independent contract factories (outside firms paid to make the product), mainly in Vietnam (the largest), China and Indonesia.

Sweatshop criticism in the 1990s (attacks on factories with very low pay and poor conditions), including of factories in Indonesia, led to factory monitoring and published supplier lists (lists of the factories Nike uses).

Governments attract factories by creating special areas with easy trade rules. In an export processing zone, firms import components and export finished goods free of customs duty (a tax on goods crossing a border), and they receive tax breaks.
Shannon Free Zone, Co. Clare, set up in 1959, was one of the world's first export processing zones and Ireland's pioneer. The duty-free shop at Shannon Airport was 1947, so do not swap the dates.
Shenzhen, China, became a Special Economic Zone (a region with special business rules to attract foreign firms) in 1980.
Maquiladoras are assembly plants along Mexico's border with the USA, such as those at Tijuana and Ciudad Juárez, set up from 1965.
A maquiladora imports components duty-free and exports finished goods to the USA, so it is an example of an export processing zone at work.
Spreading production across many countries brings risks as well as savings. The costs fall on supply chains, workers and the environment.

Long supply chains (the linked stages from raw material to finished product) are vulnerable to disruption, as the 2021 chip shortage, the Ever Given blockage and the Red Sea diversions showed. There is more on this in 'Patterns in world trade'.
Branch plants (factories owned by a firm whose headquarters is elsewhere) close when costs change, and their workers lose jobs.
Some plants pay low wages and have poor conditions.
Moving components and goods over long distances has an environmental cost.
Responses include reshoring (moving production back to the home country) and friend-shoring (moving it to politically allied countries).
At world scale, regions play different roles in the global economy. The core is the wealthy, powerful centre; the periphery is the poorer edge that supplies it.
Core regions have capital (money to invest), MNC headquarters, research and development, skilled labour, good infrastructure and political power.
The core's examples are the USA, western Europe's Blue Banana (Europe's core belt of dense development) and Japan.
The periphery supplies raw materials, food and cheap labour, with weak infrastructure and out-migration of people (people leaving to find work elsewhere).
Most of sub-Saharan Africa, parts of Latin America and parts of South Asia are periphery.
Some countries sit between the core and the periphery. They are changing their role in the global economy.
The semi-periphery is made up of newly industrialised countries (NICs, countries that have recently built large manufacturing industries) moving towards the core.
South Korea did so earlier; China, India, Brazil and Mexico are doing so now.
The core did not become rich by accident. An early start, overseas empires and a self-reinforcing cycle of growth built its lead.
Britain industrialised first, from the late 18th century (the Industrial Revolution), followed by western Europe and the USA.
Colonial empires supplied the core with raw materials and markets, and profits were reinvested in the core, which strengthened it further.
Cumulative causation, a model by Gunnar Myrdal (1957), says success attracts more investment, people and services, which increases success.
Backwash effects drain capital and skilled people from the periphery to the core, so the core grows at the periphery's expense.
The Blue Banana runs from south-east England and London through the Benelux countries and the Rhine valley to northern Italy. There is more on this in 'Socio-economic regions'.
The periphery's economy was shaped by outside rulers for their benefit, which left it badly placed after independence.
Colonial economies were built around exporting one or two raw materials, so they had little other industry.
Railways ran from mines and plantations to ports, rather than linking regions to each other, because their purpose was export.
Borders were drawn by the colonisers, not by the people who lived there.
After independence these economies depended on falling commodity prices (the prices of raw materials), were burdened by debt and suffered conflict.
Core and periphery are not fixed. Some places have moved up the ladder, and the North-South model is a simple picture of the pattern.
Spread effects (the benefits of growth passing outwards from the core) and investment can raise peripheral regions.
The Asian Tigers and China moved from periphery to semi-periphery or core in about two generations.
Ireland moved from the European periphery to a core-like economy through MNC investment. There is more on this in 'Irish Regions - Core and Peripheral'.
The Brandt Line, from the Brandt Report of 1980, is a simple North-South model (a line dividing richer northern from poorer southern countries) of the same pattern.
Sub-Saharan Africa is the main region excluded from world manufacturing. It has a very small share of world manufacturing and exports mostly unprocessed raw materials.
Nigeria: crude oil is most of its exports.
Zambia: copper is most of its exports.
The Democratic Republic of the Congo produces most of the world's cobalt and exports it raw despite its huge reserves, amid conflict.
Sudan: civil war between the Sudanese Armed Forces and the Rapid Support Forces since April 2023 has caused one of the world's largest displacement crises, with people forced to flee their homes.
South Sudan became independent from Sudan in 2011, taking most of the oil fields.
The 2023 war is within Sudan, not a war with South Sudan, because they have been separate countries since 2011.
Many linked problems keep sub-Saharan Africa out of manufacturing. Each one raises costs or risks for firms, or limits what the countries can do for themselves.
Poor infrastructure: roads and ports are inadequate and electricity is unreliable, which makes running a factory costly.
Landlocked countries (with no coast): Africa has 16, such as Chad, Niger, Mali and South Sudan, and they face high transport costs to reach ports.
Political instability, conflict and corruption scare off investment.
Low levels of education and skills, and poor health, limit the workforce.
Small, poor home markets give firms little reason to produce locally.
Heavy debt absorbs money that could fund development.
The colonial legacy: economies were set up to export raw materials, and that pattern persists.

Tariff escalation: rich countries charge higher tariffs (taxes on imports) on processed goods than on raw materials, so processing at home does not pay; coffee beans enter rich markets with low tariffs, while roasted coffee faces higher ones.
Several measures try to help excluded regions join world trade and industry. They target debt, trade barriers and infrastructure.
The Heavily Indebted Poor Countries (HIPC) initiative, begun in 1996, gives debt relief (cancelling or reducing debts) through the World Bank and IMF.
The African Continental Free Trade Area, which removes trade barriers between African countries, began trading on 1 January 2021.
Chinese and other foreign investment is building infrastructure.
Fair trade (a system that pays producers a fairer price). There is more on this in 'Patterns in world trade'.

Globalisation is the growing integration of the world's economies through trade, investment, MNCs, technology and the movement of people and ideas. It has changed what is traded, who trades and how goods move.
About 80% of world trade is linked to the international production networks of MNCs (UNCTAD, 2013).
Much of it is intra-firm trade, between parts of the same company or with its suppliers in global value chains (production split into stages across countries).
Trade is increasingly in components rather than finished goods, because each stage of production crosses borders.
Trade in services and digital trade has grown rapidly.
New trading powers, led by China, have entered world trade.
The WTO (World Trade Organization) and trade blocs have lowered barriers, so goods cross borders more easily.
Containerisation (shipping goods in standard steel boxes) and huge ports have cut the cost of shipping, so distant trade pays.
E-commerce (online selling) brings small sellers into world markets, so they can reach buyers abroad.
Globalisation does not benefit everyone equally. Some groups and regions gain, others lose.
Consumers gain cheaper goods, because production moves to low-cost countries.
NICs and China gain jobs and growth, because factories locate there.
Manufacturing regions in the core lose jobs, because production moves abroad.
Excluded regions fall further behind, because they get little of the new investment.
Workers in low-wage assembly can face poor and unsafe conditions, as the Rana Plaza collapse showed.
Transporting goods over long distances has environmental costs.
Since 2018 some governments have pushed back against open trade, raising barriers between major economies.
The US-China trade war from 2018, the US tariffs of 2025 and Brexit have raised barriers between major economies.
Governments are reshoring strategic industries such as chips (the microchips in electronics), bringing production back home so they do not depend on distant suppliers.
India's economy was tightly controlled before 1991, and it opened to globalisation only after a crisis.
Five-year plans from 1951 directed investment and production, so the state, not the market, decided what was made.
Protection (tariffs and rules that shut out imports) shielded Indian industries from foreign competition.
The Licence Raj: firms needed government licences to produce and expand, which limited competition and growth.
A balance-of-payments crisis (when a country cannot pay for its imports and debts) in 1991 forced change.
Prime Minister P. V. Narasimha Rao and Finance Minister Manmohan Singh removed most licences, cut tariffs and opened India to foreign investment.
Globalisation brought rapid growth, new industries and foreign investment.
Bengaluru became known as the 'Silicon Valley of India'.

IT and business-process outsourcing (hiring firms abroad to run tasks such as customer service) grew rapidly; Tata Consultancy Services (founded 1968), Infosys (founded 1981) and Wipro grew, with Bengaluru as a major hub.
Texas Instruments opened a design centre in Bengaluru in 1985.
Maruti Suzuki, a joint venture (a company shared between partners) with Suzuki of Japan, made its first car in 1983.
India is a leading maker of generic medicines (cheaper copies of branded drugs), earning it the name 'pharmacy of the world'.
Make in India, launched in 2014, aimed to attract manufacturing; iPhones are assembled near Chennai and Bengaluru.
Services produce over half of India's GDP (the value of everything it produces), and India is among the world's five largest economies (early 2020s). A growing middle class has emerged.
Hundreds of millions of people have been moved out of extreme poverty, as growth created jobs and income.
The gains from globalisation have been uneven, and it has brought costs for some people and places.
Inequality exists between cities and rural areas, and between states.
Small farmers are exposed to world prices, so they can lose when prices fall.
Farmers' protests in 2020-21 were against three farm laws, which were repealed in November 2021.
Most workers are still in the informal sector (jobs without contracts, regular pay or legal protection).
Pollution and accidents at MNC plants: the Bhopal gas leak at the Union Carbide pesticide plant in December 1984 killed thousands; Union Carbide was a US MNC.
China is a second developing economy, which opened to the world after 1978. It gained enormous growth but also costs.
Reforms under Deng Xiaoping from 1978 opened China to foreign trade and investment.
Special Economic Zones from 1980 attracted foreign investment, such as Shenzhen.
China joined the WTO on 11 December 2001, which gave it easier access to world markets.
China has been the largest goods exporter since 2009.
About 800 million people have been lifted out of extreme poverty since 1978 (World Bank).
Inequality exists between the coast and the interior, because growth centred on coastal zones.
Pollution from rapid industrial growth and dependence on exports are costs of this model, because a fall in world demand would hit China's economy.
Bangladesh shows both sides of globalisation: jobs from the garment industry, and the dangers of low-cost production.
Ready-made garments are most of Bangladesh's exports; it is the world's second-largest garment exporter after China.
The garment industry provides jobs, especially for women.
Rana Plaza, Savar, near Dhaka, collapsed on 24 April 2013, killing over 1,100 garment workers. It was a building collapse, not a fire.
The Accord on Fire and Building Safety in Bangladesh, signed in 2013 by clothing brands and unions, introduced factory inspections.
Geographers describe a population with a small set of measures. Learn each definition exactly, because every later block uses them.
Crude birth rate: live births per 1,000 people per year. It is 'crude' because it counts the whole population, not just women of childbearing age.
Crude death rate: deaths per 1,000 people per year.
Natural change: birth rate minus death rate. A positive result is natural increase (more births than deaths); a negative result is natural decrease (more deaths than births).
Net migration: immigrants (people moving in) minus emigrants (people moving out). It is positive when more people arrive than leave.
Total fertility rate: the average number of children per woman, which shows family size better than the crude birth rate.
Replacement level: a total fertility rate of about 2.1 children per woman in developed countries, the level at which a population replaces itself without migration.
Infant mortality rate: deaths of children under one year old per 1,000 live births.
Life expectancy: the average number of years a newborn is expected to live.
A population can only change in two ways: people are born or die, and people move in or out. The census, a regular count of everyone, shows which of the two drove the change.
Population change equals natural change plus net migration. In any period between two censuses (an inter-censal period), the larger of the two components explains the growth or decline.
The census is a count of every person on one night. In Ireland it is held every five years and run by the Central Statistics Office (CSO).
The Irish census records age, sex, place of residence, birthplace, nationality, religion, ethnicity, Irish language, housing, work and commuting.

Census 2016 to Census 2022: the population grew by about 360,000 (about 7.6%). Natural increase contributed about 170,000 and net migration about 190,000, so net migration was the slightly larger component.
The five-year rhythm of the Irish census has been broken a few times. Each break had a specific cause.
The 1926 census was the first held by the Irish Free State (the Irish State of that time).
The 1976 census was cancelled; a special census was held in 1979 instead.
The 2001 census was postponed to 2002 by foot-and-mouth disease (an animal disease outbreak).
The 2021 census was postponed to 2022 by COVID-19 and held on 3 April 2022.
Governments collect census data because it tells them how many people there are, how old they are and where they live. That information shapes decisions on money and services.
Planning schools, hospitals and housing: counts of children, patients and households show where services are needed.
Pensions: the age structure (how many people are in each age group) sets the cost of pensions; the State pension age has been 66 since 2014.
Transport and infrastructure: population size and location show where roads, rail and water services are needed, so money goes where demand is.
Constituency boundaries: the population of each constituency (the area that elects TDs, members of the Dail) determines the number of TDs it elects.
Funding and workforce planning: funding is allocated to regions by population, and population forecasts show future labour supply and the need for workers from abroad.
Two ideas describe where people live. They are different, so keep them apart: distribution is where people live. Density is the number of people per square kilometre of land.
Distribution is the spread of people across an area, so a map can show crowded and empty places. Density turns that into a number you can compare.
Illustrative example (invented figures): a region of 400 km² with 120,000 people has a density of 120,000 ÷ 400 = 300 people per km².
Physical factors are features of the natural environment. They decide how easy it is to farm, build and live in a place.
Relief (the shape and height of the land): lowlands attract more people than high mountains, which are costly to farm and build on.
Climate: temperate climates (mild, without extremes) support dense settlement; places that are too hot, too cold or too dry have fewer people.
Soils and water supply: fertile soils and reliable water support farming and settlement.
Natural resources: coalfields drew industrial populations in the 19th century, because mines and factories needed workers close by.
Human factors are choices and developments made by people. They work alongside the physical factors to decide where populations cluster.
Economic opportunity: jobs attract people, and regions with few jobs lose their young people.
Transport routes: roads, rail lines and navigable water (rivers deep enough for boats) attract settlement along them.
Cities and ports: cities and ports offer jobs and services, so they draw large populations.
History: colonial ports and plantations (large farms for cash crops, set up by colonial powers) shaped where people settled.
Government policy: policy can direct population into or out of particular areas.
Low-density areas have few people per square kilometre. The reasons are mostly the opposite of the factors that attract people.
High, steep or cold land is difficult to farm, build on and reach.
Deserts and dense forest offer little water, farmland or access.
Poor soils and remoteness limit farming, and remote areas lack markets and services.
Few jobs cause young people to leave, so the population falls and density drops.
World population is very uneven. Most people crowd into a few regions, while large areas are almost empty.
Dense: East Asia, South Asia, Europe, the north-eastern USA and the Nile valley, where farming, trade or industry support many people.
Sparse: the Sahara (a hot desert), the Amazon Basin (a vast rainforest), Siberia, northern Canada, Greenland and Antarctica.
About 90% of the world's people live in the northern hemisphere.
Most people live near coasts and rivers, where water and transport are easy to reach.
Europe has the same unevenness on a smaller scale: a crowded core and a thinly settled edge.

Dense core: the Benelux countries (Belgium, the Netherlands and Luxembourg), the Rhine-Ruhr (an industrial region of western Germany), south-east England, the Po valley (northern Italy) and the Paris region.
Sparse periphery (the outer edge): northern Scandinavia, the Scottish Highlands and interior Spain.
The Netherlands has over 500 people per km² (2020s), one of Europe's most densely populated countries.
The EU average is about 110 people per km² (2020s), so the Netherlands is more than four times as dense.
Ireland's people are not spread evenly. They gather around Dublin and the east coast, and thin out towards the west.
The Greater Dublin Area (Dublin, Meath, Kildare and Wicklow) has about 2.1 million people, about 40% of the State's population (Census 2022).
Co. Dublin has about 1.46 million people at about 1,600 people per km².
The population is concentrated in the east and in the five cities, where jobs and services are found.
Low density in the west and north-west, notably Mayo (about 25 people per km²), Leitrim and Roscommon, and in the uplands (high ground).
Today's eastern, urban pattern is not how Ireland always looked.
Before the Famine (the Great Famine of 1845-49) the population was rural and weighted to the west.
Since then the population has shifted to an eastern, urban pattern.
Dublin's commuter counties of Meath, Kildare and Wicklow (counties whose people travel into Dublin to work) have grown rapidly.
Every county's population grew between 2016 and 2022.
Density is population divided by area, so it rises when people are added to an area that does not grow.
The State's average density is about 73 people per km² (Census 2022).
Density is rising because the population has grown from natural increase (more births than deaths) and net immigration since the 1990s, while the land area is fixed.
For most of history the world's population grew very slowly. Then growth took off, and it is only now easing.

World population grew slowly until about 1800, then rapidly, producing an exponential J-curve (a graph line that climbs ever more steeply, shaped like a J) driven by falling death rates. The growth rate is now slowing.
Milestones: about 1 billion around 1800, 2 billion in 1927, 3 billion in 1960 and 4 billion in 1974.
Milestones continued: 5 billion in 1987, 6 billion in 1999, 7 billion in 2011 and 8 billion on 15 November 2022 (UN).
Global fertility is about 2.3 children per woman (early 2020s), down from about 5 in the 1950s.
China and India each have over 1.4 billion people (2023); India overtook China as the most populous country in 2023 (UN estimate).
Growth is not even across the world. Some regions are growing fast while others have stopped growing.
Rapid growth: sub-Saharan Africa (the part of Africa south of the Sahara), where fertility is high.
Slow growth, stagnation (no growth) or decline: Europe and East Asia, where fertility is low.
The Demographic Transition Model (DTM) shows how birth and death rates, and so population growth, change as a country develops. It has five stages, and stage 1 is where every society starts.
Birth rate high, death rate high, and little growth. 'Stationary' means the population stays roughly the same size because births and deaths nearly cancel out.
Example: no country is in stage 1 today; the best examples are pre-industrial societies (societies before factories and modern medicine).
In stage 2 the death rate drops quickly while births stay high, so the population expands fast. This stage is where the death rate falls most.
Birth rate high; death rate falling rapidly, and the death rate falls most in this stage; growth is rapid because many more people are born than die.
The death rate falls because of clean water and sanitation (safe disposal of sewage), vaccination, a better food supply and medical care.
Example: Niger, because its death rate has fallen while its birth rate stays very high.
In stage 3 the birth rate begins to fall too, so the gap between births and deaths narrows and growth slows.
Birth rate falling; death rate low; growth slows because births are no longer far above deaths.
Example: India, with a total fertility rate of about 2.0 (2019-21).
By stage 4 both rates are low. The population is large but steady, because births and deaths nearly balance.
Birth rate low, death rate low, and little growth.
Examples: Ireland and the USA. Ireland is in stage 4.
Stage 5 goes beyond the original steady state: the birth rate drops below the death rate, so the population begins to shrink.
Birth rate below death rate, so natural change is negative (natural decrease) and the population falls.
Niger is the example of stage 2: very high fertility and a population dominated by children and teenagers.
Niger is a West African, landlocked (no coastline) country, largely in the Sahel (the dry belt south of the Sahara) and Sahara.
Population is about 27 million (2023), growing by over 3% a year (early 2020s).
Total fertility rate is about 6 children per woman (early 2020s), among the highest in the world.
Median age (the age that splits the population into a younger half and an older half) is about 15, among the lowest in the world.
Its population pyramid (a graph of the population by age and sex) has a very wide base, because so many children are born.
Most people live in the south, where rainfall allows farming; the north is Sahara desert.
Japan is the opposite of Niger. It has very few births and many older people, so its population is falling.
Japan has the world's oldest population: about 29% of people are aged 65 or over (2023), the highest share in the world.
Population peaked at about 128 million around 2008-2010, was about 124 million in 2024, and is falling.
Total fertility rate is about 1.2 (2023), well below the replacement level of about 2.1.
Few immigrants by European standards, so immigration does little to offset the fall.
Its population pyramid is top-heavy, with a narrow base (few children) and a wide top (many older people).
Moving from stage 2 to stage 3 means families choose to have fewer children. Several changes in society make smaller families sensible.
Female education and paid work: women have later and fewer children.
Contraception (methods of preventing pregnancy) is widely available, so couples can choose family size.
Falling infant mortality removes the need for 'insurance' births (having extra children in case some die), as parents can expect their children to survive.
Urbanisation (growth of towns and cities): children cost more and earn less in towns and cities, unlike on farms where they can work.
Pensions replace children as old-age security, so parents no longer need many children to support them.
Later marriage, and weaker religious influence on family size.
A country with falling numbers and a rising share of older people faces economic strain. Governments have a few ways to respond.
Challenges: a shrinking workforce, labour shortages, rising pension and health costs, closing schools and rural depopulation (the loss of people from the countryside).
Responses: immigration, pro-natalist incentives (rewards that encourage couples to have more children) to raise birth rates, and later retirement.
The DTM is a useful simplification, but it does not fit every country. Know why.
The model is based on European experience, so it may not describe other regions.
It ignores migration, although moving people can change a country's population sharply.
Developing countries' death rates fell much faster than Europe's, because medicine was imported, so their growth has been faster.
Some countries may not complete the transition, and it has no fixed time scale.
A population pyramid is a graph that shows how a population is made up by age and sex. Planners and geographers read it to understand a country at a glance.
A population pyramid shows age cohorts (groups of people of similar age) in five-year bands, with males on the left and females on the right, as percentages or numbers.
Uses: planning services, forecasting future needs, comparing countries, and showing past events such as baby booms, wars and emigration.
The overall shape of a pyramid tells you the stage a country has reached: how many children are born and how long people live.
Wide base and narrow top: high fertility and short life expectancy, as in Niger.
Straight sides: a stable population with low birth and death rates.
Narrow base and wide top (top-heavy): an ageing population, as in Japan.
A developed country's pyramid is typically straight-sided or top-heavy, while a developing country's is wide-based.
Beyond the overall shape, bulges and notches in the sides record events in a country's past.
Bulges (a band wider than those around it) show baby booms or immigration of young adults.
Notches (a band narrower than those around it) show emigration, low birth years or war.
More women than men at the oldest ages, because women live longer.
Children and older people usually do not earn a wage, so they depend on the working-age population. The dependency ratio measures how heavy that load is.
Dependency ratio = (people aged 0-14 + people aged 65 and over) ÷ people aged 15-64 × 100.
Young dependency ratio = people aged 0-14 ÷ people aged 15-64 × 100. Old-age dependency ratio = people aged 65 and over ÷ people aged 15-64 × 100.
Illustrative example (invented figures): 30,000 aged 0-14, 10,000 aged 65 and over and 80,000 aged 15-64 give (30,000 + 10,000) ÷ 80,000 × 100 = 50.
The ratio is not the same everywhere inside a country. Migration within a country changes who lives in towns and who lives in the countryside.
Urban dependency ratios are usually lower than rural ones.
Young working adults migrate to cities for jobs and college, leaving older people, and sometimes children, in rural areas, which raises the share of dependants there.
When the old-age dependency ratio (the number of people aged 65 and over for every 100 people aged 15-64) rises, there are more people to support and fewer workers to pay for it.
Higher pension costs, because more people claim pensions for longer.
More demand for health care, nursing homes and carers, because older people need more care.
A smaller tax base (the pool of workers paying tax) from fewer workers.
Pressure to raise the pension age, so that people work and pay tax for longer.
Changing housing and transport needs, for example more homes suited to older people.
Planning responses in Ireland: home-care supports, pension reform, more geriatric services (health care for older people), encouraging immigration of workers, and age-friendly towns.
A country with many children has the opposite pressure: it must provide for the young now, but it gains workers later.
Demand for schools, maternity and child health care, and for future jobs and housing.

A future workforce, which is the basis of the demographic dividend (the economic boost a country can get when many young people grow up and start working). There is more on this in the overpopulation notes.
Birth rates differ between countries because of economic and social conditions. These factors link income, culture and society.
Income and economic development: birth rates fall as income rises.
Status and education of women: educated women with status tend to have fewer children.
Religion and culture, because beliefs and traditions shape ideas of a normal family size.
Access to contraception, because it lets couples plan how many children to have.
Government policy, for example rules or incentives that encourage or discourage births.
Infant mortality: high infant mortality encourages larger families, because parents have more children to be sure some survive.
Urban or rural living: rural families tend to have more children.
Death rates depend on how healthy and safe people's lives are. The main causes of death differ between rich and poor countries.
Medical technology: vaccines and antibiotics (medicines that kill bacteria), which prevent or cure diseases that once killed many people.
Sanitation, diet, income and health services, because clean water, enough food and access to care all help people survive.
Lifestyle diseases such as heart disease and cancer are the main causes of death in rich countries.
Conflict, famine and disease, such as malaria and HIV/AIDS, are the main causes of death in poor countries.
Fertility and mortality shape the pyramid directly: births fill the base and survival fills the top.
Falling fertility narrows the base of the pyramid, because fewer children are born.
Rising life expectancy widens the top of the pyramid, because more people survive into old age.
The result is an older population with a higher median age.
Life expectancy is low where disease, poor water and poor nutrition kill people young. Each measure below tackles one of those causes.
Clean water and sanitation, which stop water-borne disease.
Mosquito nets and malaria treatment, because mosquitoes spread malaria.
More doctors and clinics, so illness is treated sooner.
Better nutrition, so people are stronger against disease.
Irish life expectancy is high because the causes of early death in poorer countries have been largely dealt with.
A good diet and housing, which keep people healthy.
Effective health services and vaccination, which treat and prevent illness.
Clean water, so water-borne disease is rare.
Fewer smokers, so fewer deaths from smoking-related disease.
Safer work, so fewer deaths from accidents.
All Irish census figures here are for the State (the 26-county area). Do not mix them with whole-island figures. For more than a century the population fell.
Census 1841: about 6.5 million, the starting point before the Famine.
Census 1851, after the Great Famine (1845-49): about 5.1 million, so the Famine's deaths and emigration cut the population sharply.
Census 1926: about 3.0 million, so the fall continued long after the Famine.
Census 1961: about 2.8 million, the lowest census population ever recorded.
The population fell at almost every census from 1841 to 1961; the only break was a very slight rise between Census 1946 and Census 1951.
From 1961 the trend reversed, and the population has grown with only one short pause.
Census 1971: about 3.0 million. Census 1981: about 3.4 million, so growth had clearly resumed.
Census 1986 and Census 1991: both about 3.5 million, a small fall between them.
Census 2002: about 3.9 million. Census 2006: about 4.2 million. Census 2011: about 4.6 million. Census 2016: about 4.76 million.
Census 2022: about 5.15 million, above 5 million for the first time since 1851.
Irish births stayed high for decades, then fell sharply. Even so, births still exceed deaths.
Fertility was high into the 1970s, with Catholic culture, large families and little access to contraception.
The total fertility rate was about 4 in the early 1970s, fell below replacement level around 1990, and was about 1.5 in 2023.
Births were about 55,000 in 2023 against about 35,000 deaths, giving natural increase of about 20,000 (55,000 minus 35,000).
Irish fertility fell because law, education, work and attitudes all changed. This is the core of the 30-mark question on how Ireland's population has changed since the 1950s.
Free secondary education, introduced in 1967 by Donogh O'Malley, and more women in third-level education.
The marriage bar, which forced women in the public service to resign on marriage, was removed in 1973.
Contraception was legalised by the Health (Family Planning) Act 1979, on prescription; access was widened in 1985 and the early 1990s.
More women in paid employment, later marriage and later first births.
Secularisation (religion having less influence on daily life and choices), and the cost of housing and childcare.
Life expectancy rose and infant mortality fell to very low levels.
Life expectancy at birth is about 82-83 years (early 2020s).
Women live about 4 years longer than men, which is why they outnumber men at the oldest ages.
Infant mortality is about 3 per 1,000 live births (2020s).
Migration is the second component of population change. Irish migration switched direction several times, and the next points give only the outline.

Heavy net emigration (more people leaving than arriving) in the 1950s and 1980s; net emigration of about 400,000 between 1951 and 1961, which the 1954 Report of the Commission on Emigration and Other Population Problems examined.
Net immigration in the 1970s, from the mid-1990s to 2008, and again from the mid-2010s. There is more on this in Changing migration patterns in Ireland.
As fertility fell and people lived longer, Ireland's population got older. It also became more diverse.
Census 2022: about 776,000 people aged 65 and over (about 15% of the population), up about 22% since 2016.
Average age rose from 37.4 in 2016 to 38.8 in 2022.
About one-fifth of the population is under 15.
The pyramid has moved from a young, wide-based shape to an ageing one.
About one in five people (just over 1 million) was born outside Ireland.
Where and how Irish people live has changed as well as how many they are.
Census 1971 was the first census in which more people lived in towns than in rural areas.
By Census 2016 about 63% of the population was urban.
The population has shifted to the east. There is more on this in Rural-to-urban migration in developed and developing regions.
Households are smaller, and more people live alone, for example because families are smaller and people live longer.
The EU shows the ageing pattern across a whole group of countries: few births, long lives and growth that comes from outside.
The EU has 27 member states and about 450 million people (2024).
Fertility is below replacement: the EU total fertility rate is about 1.4 (2023), well under 2.1, so each generation is smaller.
Natural decrease occurs in many member states; immigration supplies most of the EU's growth.
The EU median age is about 44.5 (2023), and about 21% of its population is aged 65 or over (2023).
Germany is a stage 5 example in the EU, where the population would shrink without incoming people.
Deaths have exceeded births every year since 1972, so Germany has natural decrease.
Population is about 84 million (2020s), and growth comes from immigration.
Italy is another stage 5 country, with one of the EU's weakest birth rates and oldest populations.
Italy has among the EU's lowest fertility rates and oldest populations: its total fertility rate is about 1.2 (2023).
Population is about 59 million (2024), so Italy is a large country with an ageing base.
There is more on Italy's regional pattern in A Peripheral European Region: the Mezzogiorno.
Bulgaria shows a population that shrinks for two reasons at once: few births and people leaving.
Population was about 9 million in 1989 and about 6.5 million at Census 2021.
Causes: emigration to western Europe after the fall of communism (1989) and EU entry (2007), together with low fertility.
Fertility can fall far below replacement level, and the contrast with the highest rates is stark.
South Korea's total fertility rate is about 0.7 (2023), the lowest in the world.
Compare Niger's total fertility rate of about 6 children per woman, which shows how far apart countries can be.
Overpopulation is about the balance between people and what they have to live on, not about how crowded a place looks. Two places with the same number of people can be very differently placed.
Overpopulation: the population of an area is too large for its resources, technology and economy to support an acceptable standard of living.
It is a balance between people and resources, not a matter of numbers or density (people per square kilometre) alone.
Underpopulation: too few people to develop the resources fully, so some resources go unused.
Optimum population: the number that gives the highest standard of living with existing resources and technology.
The Netherlands has over 500 people per km² (2020s) and is densely populated but not overpopulated, because its wealth, technology and trade let it support them well.
The Sahel (the dry belt south of the Sahara) is thinly populated but overpopulated, because its fragile resources, drought and poverty cannot support its people.
Niger, a Sahel country, has about 27 million people (2023) in a very large, mostly desert country, so little of the land can feed anyone.
Thinkers have long argued about whether population or resources win out. Three views are worth knowing, each with a date and a title.

Malthus, 'An Essay on the Principle of Population' (1798): population grows geometrically (doubling again and again) while food grows arithmetically (by a fixed amount each time), so famine, disease and war act as positive checks that cut numbers back.
Ireland's Great Famine is often cited in support of Malthus.
Boserup, 'The Conditions of Agricultural Growth' (1965): population pressure drives farming innovation, so food supply can rise to meet demand.
The Green Revolution (the spread of high-yield crops and modern farming from the mid-1960s) is often cited in support of Boserup.
Club of Rome, 'The Limits to Growth' (1972): argues that growth is limited by finite resources.
Resources are what a population lives on. Where they are not developed, are degraded or shrink, the same population becomes too many.
Sahel: desertification (fertile land turning to desert), drought, overgrazing, fuelwood cutting and the shrinking of Lake Chad all cut what the land can support.
Lake Chad has shrunk by about 90% since the 1960s, because of irrigation demand and drought, which is a resource shrinking under the same population.
Pre-Famine Ireland: over-reliance on one resource, the potato, and subdivision of holdings (farms split among sons) into ever-smaller plots, so many families had too little land.
Developing resources raises carrying capacity (the number of people an area can support): India's Green Revolution and Ireland's industrial growth since the 1960s.
Ireland shows how one fragile resource can leave a large population exposed. Here the checked facts are the whole-island figures and the blight.
The population of the whole island was about 8.2 million in 1841; use this whole-island figure, not the 26-county one.
The rural poor depended heavily on the potato, so they had no other food when it failed.
Holdings were subdivided among sons into ever-smaller plots, and landlords were often absentee (living elsewhere).
Conacre meant renting a small plot for one season.
Potato blight (Phytophthora infestans, a disease of potato plants) struck in 1845, and the Great Famine ran from 1845 to 1849.
About 1 million people died and about 1 million emigrated, leaving a whole-island population of about 6.6 million by 1851.
Desertification (fertile land turning to desert) is the clearest case of resources shrinking under pressure. It happens because a poor, fast-growing population overuses a dry land.
The Sahel is a semi-arid belt along the southern edge of the Sahara, from Senegal and Mauritania through Mali, Burkina Faso, Niger and Chad to Sudan.
Rainfall is about 200–600 mm a year, falls in a short summer rainy season and is very unreliable, so crops and grass can fail.

Causes of desertification: overgrazing (too many animals for the grass), overcultivation with fallow periods (rests that let soil recover) abandoned, cutting trees and shrubs for fuelwood, and drought.
Wind and rain then erode the bare soil, because nothing is left to hold it in place.
People and governments have tried to reverse desertification by holding water and soil in place and by bringing back trees.
The Great Green Wall, an African Union initiative launched in 2007, aims to restore a belt of land across the Sahel.
Stone lines (diguettes) along contours (lines of equal height) and zaï planting pits in Burkina Faso trap water and soil, so crops can grow on degraded ground.
Farmer-managed natural regeneration of trees in Niger lets farmers protect and regrow trees that spring from existing roots and stumps.
Attitudes and customs affect how many children people have, and so how fast a population grows against its resources.

Factors include religion and attitudes to contraception (methods of avoiding pregnancy), the status and education of women, early marriage, preference for sons, children as farm labour and old-age security, and the prestige of large families.
Niger shows what happens when several of these cultural factors act together.
Early marriage of girls is common, so women start having children young and have more of them over their lives.
Female literacy is low, which limits women's choices and their use of family planning.
Large families carry prestige, so having many children raises a family's standing.
Total fertility rate (the average number of children a woman has in her lifetime) is about 6 (early 2020s), among the highest in the world, with population growth over 3% a year.

Median age (the age that splits the population in half) is about 15, so the population is very young, and Niger is among the lowest-ranked countries in the UN Human Development Index (a ranking of countries by health, education and income) (2020s).
Within India, two states show how education and the status of women change family size.
Son preference and the low status of women in some Indian states keep families having children until they have sons.
Kerala: total fertility rate about 1.8 (National Family Health Survey 2019–21), literacy about 94% (Census 2011), the highest of any state, with high female literacy and good health care.
Bihar: total fertility rate about 3.0 (National Family Health Survey 2019–21), literacy about 62% (Census 2011), the lowest of any state.
India's total fertility rate is about 2.0 (2019–21), down from about 6 in the 1950s.
Ireland shows culture changing fertility within living memory, as law and attitudes shifted.
Before the 1970s, Catholic teaching, large families and illegal contraception kept fertility high.
Contraception was legalised by the Health (Family Planning) Act 1979, on prescription, so couples could plan family size legally.

The total fertility rate (average children per woman) was about 4 in the early 1970s, fell below replacement (the level at which each generation just replaces itself) around 1990 and was about 1.5 in 2023.
Income and family size are linked in both directions. Poor families tend to have more children, and large families make it harder to escape poverty.

Low-income countries have high birth rates: children are economic assets (they work and earn), infant mortality is high so parents have extra children, and there are no pensions, so children support parents in old age.
Rising incomes bring falling fertility, through the cost of raising children, women's paid work and education.
Poverty also limits the ability to develop resources or import food, so a poor country cannot easily make up for a shortage.
Contrast low-income Niger with high-income Ireland, the EU and Japan.
High-income countries show where rising incomes lead: low fertility, long lives and, in Japan, an ageing and shrinking population.
Ireland: total fertility rate about 1.5 (2023); life expectancy (average years a person lives) about 82–83 years.
Japan: about 29% aged 65 or over (2023); population falling from a peak of about 128 million around 2008–2010.
Bangladesh is an exception: its fertility fell sharply while it was still poor.
Bangladesh shows that fertility can fall without wealth when policy, education and women's work change.
Independent since 1971, so its fertility fall happened within a few decades of nationhood.
Total fertility rate fell, for example, from about 6–7 in the early 1970s to about 2 in the 2020s.

Reasons: a national family planning programme with community health workers visiting homes, NGOs (non-governmental organisations, such as charities), girls' education and millions of women employed in the garment industry.
Population density is over 1,100 people per km² (2020s), one of the highest of any large country; it is used here for its fertility fall, not as overpopulation.
Technology changes both sides of the balance. It lowers deaths, raises food output and lowers births, and where it is missing, it keeps carrying capacity low.

Medical technology (vaccines, antibiotics, clean water) cut death rates far faster than birth rates fell, causing the population explosion of the 20th century; this is DTM (demographic transition model) stage 2 in Changing population characteristics.
Penicillin (an antibiotic) was discovered by Alexander Fleming in 1928.
Smallpox was declared eradicated by the World Health Organization in 1980.
Agricultural technology: the Green Revolution, with high-yield seeds, irrigation and fertilisers, increased carrying capacity.
Contraceptive technology lowered birth rates, because couples could choose family size.
Lack of technology: subsistence farming (growing food mainly for the family's own use) keeps carrying capacity low in the Sahel.
India shows technology raising carrying capacity, but with costs that you must also give.
Green Revolution from the mid-1960s: high-yield wheat bred in Mexico by Norman Borlaug, introduced in India under M. S. Swaminathan.
Food-grain output rose, for example, from about 51 million tonnes (1950–51) to about 330 million tonnes (2022–23).
Core areas: Punjab, Haryana and western Uttar Pradesh.
Side effects: falling water tables (the underground water level, which drops when too much is pumped for irrigation), soil degradation and debt among small farmers.
Governments can try to change birth rates directly. Policies that aim to cut births are called anti-natalist, and they can succeed but carry a human cost.
India launched the world's first national family planning programme in 1952.
Forced sterilisations (operations that end a person's ability to have children) during the Emergency, 1975–77, caused a backlash against family planning.
China's one-child policy was introduced in 1979–80.
China's policy cut fertility sharply, but its enforcement and its effects on the population show the human cost.
Enforced through fines, loss of jobs and benefits, and in places forced abortions and sterilisations.
Exceptions existed for many rural families whose first child was a girl and for ethnic minorities, so it did not apply to every family.

Effects: fertility fell well below replacement; the sex ratio at birth (boys born per 100 girls) rose above 115 in the 2000s, through son preference and sex-selective abortion, leaving millions more men than women.
The '4-2-1' problem: four grandparents, two parents and one child per family, so one child may support six older people.
Rapid ageing followed, because fewer young people replaced older ones.
Replaced by a two-child policy from 2016 and a three-child policy in 2021.
China's population fell in 2022, the first fall since 1961.
When there are too many people for the land, the first effects are on food and on the land itself.
Food shortages, malnutrition (not enough food or the wrong nutrients) and famine.
Environmental damage: soil erosion, desertification, deforestation, overgrazing and water shortages, because people strip the land to get food and fuel.
The Sahel shows both: famines in the late 1960s–1970s and the early-to-mid 1980s, and desertification.
Too many people for the jobs and services available means poverty and strain on public provision.
Unemployment (no work) and underemployment (part-time or low-productivity work, below what a person could do), poverty and low incomes.
Pressure on schools, hospitals, housing, water and sanitation, because these cannot expand as fast as the population.
A high young dependency ratio: many children per worker, so each worker supports more people who do not earn.
When an area cannot support its people, some leave and others compete for what remains.
Rural-to-urban migration to shanty towns (areas of poor, self-built housing on the edge of cities). There is more on this in Rural-to-urban migration in developed and developing regions.
Emigration, as people leave the country in search of work or food.
Conflict over land and water, because shrinking resources are fought over.
The speed of population growth affects how fast a country can develop. Rapid growth tends to hold development back.
Savings go on feeding and educating more people rather than investment, so there is less money for factories and infrastructure.
Per-capita income (income per person) gains are cancelled out, because the extra output is shared among more people.
Jobs cannot keep up with population growth, and the environment is degraded.
The 'poverty trap' of high fertility keeps families and countries poor.
When growth slows, development can speed up. Fewer children means a bigger share of the population is of working age.
The demographic dividend is a large working-age population with fewer dependants (children and older people who rely on others).
East Asian economies such as South Korea and China, and Ireland from the 1990s, benefited.
Ireland's dividend: the large generation born around 1980 (births peaked at about 74,000 that year) entered the workforce in the late 1990s and 2000s, helping the Celtic Tiger economy.
Very slow growth or falling population also harms development, because the population ages.
Ageing, labour shortages, a shrinking tax base (fewer workers paying tax) and high pension and health costs.
Examples: Japan, Italy and South Korea, all countries with very low fertility.
South Korea: total fertility rate about 0.7 (2023), the lowest in the world.
Migration has its own vocabulary, and examiners expect you to use it precisely. These terms let you describe who moves, where, and why.
Migration is a permanent or long-term change of residence, so a holiday or a short work trip does not count.

Emigration is leaving a country; immigration is arriving in one. Net migration is immigrants minus emigrants, so it is positive when more people arrive than leave and negative when more leave than arrive.
Internal migration moves people within a country; international migration crosses borders, so it is the kind that meets immigration laws.

Voluntary migration is a free choice; forced migration is driven by conflict or persecution (being treated badly or harmed because of who you are or what you believe), so people have little or no choice.
Economic migrants move for work; refugees and asylum seekers (people who ask another country for protection) flee persecution. Asylum policy is in Migration policy in Ireland and the EU.
Return migration is emigrants coming back to their home country, such as Irish emigrants returning in the 1970s.
Chain migration is when migrants follow family or friends who have already moved, because those contacts offer information, a place to stay and help finding work.
People move because something drives them away from home (a push factor) or something attracts them to another place (a pull factor). Ireland has examples of both.

Push factors in Ireland: unemployment, low wages, emigration of young people in recession (a period when the economy shrinks and jobs are lost) and the decline of farm labouring (paid work on other people's farms), which left rural workers without jobs.

Pull factors in Ireland: jobs in the Celtic Tiger economy (the period of rapid growth from the mid-1990s), high wages in the UK, the USA and Australia, and the availability of work permits (official permission to take a job in a country).
Even when push and pull factors favour a move, obstacles can stop or reduce it. These barriers are also called intervening obstacles.
Distance and the cost of travel, because a longer journey costs more money and time.
Immigration laws, visas (permits to enter or stay) and quotas (limits on how many people may enter).
Language, because it is hard to work or settle where you cannot communicate.
Family ties and age: people with family at home, or older people, are less willing or able to move.
Lack of information, because people will not move to a place they know little about.
Cultural difference, such as unfamiliar customs, which makes settling in harder.
Geographers have turned patterns in migration into simple models. Each gives a short rule you can use to explain why and how people move.
Ravenstein's laws of migration say that most migrants move short distances, in steps (for example from a village to a town and then to a city).
Ravenstein also said that each migration stream has a counter-stream (people moving the opposite way), that young adults are most likely to migrate, and that cities attract migrants.
Lee's push-pull model says migration is driven by push and pull factors and reduced by intervening obstacles (the barriers to migration listed above).
Migrants are not a random sample of the population. Certain groups move far more than others, which shapes both the place they leave and the place they reach.
Migration is age-selective: mostly young adults move, because they are free to take jobs and have fewest ties.
In the 1950s more women than men left some rural areas.
Emigration has shaped Irish population for well over a century. The Great Famine (a disaster in the 1840s when the potato crop failed and many starved) began a long decline in numbers.
The Great Famine (1845-49) and continuous emigration from the 1840s: about 1 million died and about 1 million emigrated across the whole island.
The State's population fell at almost every census (the official count of the population, taken regularly) from 1841 to 1961.
State population was about 6.5 million (Census 1841), about 3.0 million (Census 1926) and about 2.8 million (Census 1961), the lowest ever recorded.
The only break in the decline was a very slight rise between Census 1946 and Census 1951.
Over 30 million Americans report Irish ancestry (US Census Bureau surveys, 2020s), a sign of how many people left.
The 1950s saw the highest emigration since the 1880s. Ireland was a donor region (a place people leave), and most emigrants went to Britain.

Causes at home: economic stagnation (no growth) and protectionism (taxing imports to shield home industry), unemployment, and the decline of small farms and farm labouring as farming mechanised and needed fewer workers.
Britain pulled workers because its post-war economy needed labour in building, factories, nursing and transport.
Low fares and the Common Travel Area made the move easy. The Common Travel Area dates from the 1920s and lets Irish citizens live and work in the UK without permits.
Chain migration also helped, as people followed relatives who had already gone.
Net emigration (people leaving minus people arriving) was about 400,000 between 1951 and 1961.
Most went to Britain: London, Birmingham, Manchester, Coventry and Liverpool.
The Commission on Emigration and Other Population Problems reported in 1954.
Impact: Ireland, as donor region, lost young workers and its rural population declined.

Government policy changed direction around 1958, turning towards economic growth and foreign investment. As jobs appeared, emigration fell and, for the first time since the Famine, more people arrived than left.
Economic Development by T. K. Whitaker and the First Programme for Economic Expansion, 1958, cut emigration.
The IDA (Industrial Development Authority), set up in 1949, was given a central role in attracting foreign investment from 1969.
The 1970s were the first decade of net immigration since the Famine: returning emigrants and their children came back, and jobs were available in new factories.
Ireland joined the EEC (the European Economic Community, forerunner of the EU) on 1 January 1973.
State population rose from about 3.0 million (Census 1971) to about 3.4 million (Census 1981).
The gains of the 1970s did not last. A weak economy in the 1980s sent many people abroad again.
Causes: recession, high unemployment and high taxes.
Net emigration of over 200,000 between 1981 and 1991, including many graduates. This loss of educated people is the so-called brain drain.
Destinations: Britain and the USA, where many emigrants were undocumented (living and working without legal permission).
US visa programmes in the late 1980s and early 1990s (the Donnelly and Morrison visas) regularised many Irish emigrants, meaning they gained legal status.
The State's population fell slightly between Census 1986 and Census 1991; both were about 3.5 million.
From the mid-1990s a booming economy, nicknamed the Celtic Tiger, reversed the old pattern. Ireland now attracted workers from many countries.
Net immigration from 1996, as returning Irish, EU migrants, non-EU workers on work permits and asylum seekers (people seeking protection from persecution) arrived.
EU enlargement on 1 May 2004 added 10 new members, including Poland, Lithuania, Latvia, Slovakia and the Czech Republic.
Ireland, the UK and Sweden were the only existing members to open their labour markets immediately, so citizens of the new members could work here without delay.
Census 2006: about 420,000 non-Irish nationals (about 10% of the population); Polish about 63,000, the largest group after UK nationals.
Census 2006 State population was about 4.2 million.
Ireland became a country of immigration, meaning it now received more people than it sent abroad.
The Celtic Tiger ended abruptly in 2008, and emigration returned. Many of those leaving were the young and skilled.
Causes: the property crash, the banking crisis, which began in 2008, unemployment, and the EU-IMF bailout (emergency loans from the EU and International Monetary Fund) agreed in November 2010.
Net emigration from about 2009 to the mid-2010s; many leavers were skilled young graduates, and many recent immigrants also left.
Emigration peaked at about 89,000 in the year to April 2013 (CSO estimate), the highest since the 1980s; about half were Irish nationals.
Main destinations: Australia, the UK, Canada and the USA. Australia's working holiday visa (a visa letting young people live and work there for a limited time) was widely used.
As the economy recovered, the flow reversed once more. Net immigration returned in the mid-2010s and continued.
Causes: economic recovery, job growth in multinationals and services, returning Irish emigrants, and non-EU skilled workers.
Ukrainians came under EU temporary protection after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine on 24 February 2022; over 100,000 people from Ukraine came to Ireland by 2024.
International protection applicants (people applying for asylum) also arrived.
Housing pressure, because more people needing homes added to demand for housing.
Population change has two parts: natural increase (births minus deaths) and net migration. Comparing them shows which one drove growth.
Net migration of about 190,000 between 2016 and 2022 was larger than natural increase (about 170,000), so migration was the bigger source of population growth.
Decades of immigration have made Ireland's population much more varied. The 2022 census gives the size of the immigrant population and its main nationalities.
About 630,000 non-Irish nationals (about 12% of the population), plus about 170,000 dual Irish citizens (people who hold Irish and another citizenship).
Just over 1 million people (about one in five) were born outside Ireland.
Largest non-Irish groups: Polish about 94,000; UK about 83,000; Indian about 45,000; Romanian about 43,000; Lithuanian about 31,000; Brazilian about 27,000.
Polish is the most common language other than English and Irish spoken at home (Census 2016 and 2022).
Centuries of emigration have left Irish people spread around the world. This scattered population is called the diaspora.
Irish communities and people of Irish descent live in Britain, the USA and Australia.
A donor region is a place that loses people through emigration. Losing so many people, mostly young, damaged Irish communities.
Loss of young workers and skills (brain drain), and of the State's investment in their education, because the country paid to train people who then worked abroad.
Ageing rural population and an imbalanced age structure, because the young left and the old stayed.
Rural decline: closed schools, fewer marriages and depopulated parishes.
Lower birth rates, because fewer young adults remained to have children, and family separation.
Emigration was not all loss. It also brought some benefits to Ireland.
Emigrant remittances (money sent home by emigrants to their families).
Less pressure on jobs and welfare, because fewer people were looking for work or needing support.
Emigrants returned with skills, capital (money to invest) and experience in the 1970s and 1990s.
Diaspora links support trade, tourism and investment.
A receiver region is a place that gains people through immigration. Immigration since the 1990s has brought Ireland a range of benefits.
Fills labour shortages in construction, health care, hospitality and technology.
Young workers pay taxes and offset ageing, because they balance a population with many older people.
New skills and enterprise (business start-ups), because migrants bring training and ideas from abroad.
Cultural diversity, such as food, sport, languages and religions.
Keeps rural schools and parishes open, because newcomers add children and residents.
Boosts population growth, as net migration was the larger component of growth in 2016-2022.
Rapid immigration also creates problems. Services and communities have to adjust to more people.
Pressure on housing, schools and health services, because more people share the same supply.
Exploitation of some migrant workers, such as being badly treated or underpaid.
Language barriers in schools, where children may not speak English or Irish.
Integration challenges (helping newcomers to take part fully in society) and racism, detailed in Ethnic, racial and religious issues arising from migration.
Remittances leave Ireland, because migrants send money to families abroad.
Data questions ask why immigration to Ireland increased once the recession ended. These reasons explain the rise.
Economic recovery and job creation, which drew workers.
Multinational investment, as large foreign-owned companies created jobs.
EU free movement, which lets citizens of EU countries live and work in Ireland.
Ireland is English-speaking and in the EU.
Immigration dropped sharply in these years because the Celtic Tiger economy collapsed. Data questions ask for a reason.
The recession, the collapse of construction and rising unemployment, which removed the jobs that had attracted migrants.
Many EU accession migrants (those from the countries that joined in 2004) returned home.

Every government has to decide who may enter, work and stay. Governments balance the economic need for migrants against public opinion and their legal duties to refugees, and the key terms below show why different migrants are treated differently.

Aims of policy: to control the numbers admitted, fill labour and skills shortages, meet humanitarian and legal duties to refugees, protect security and support integration (helping newcomers take part in society).
EU citizens hold free movement rights within the EU, meaning they can live and work in any member state. Non-EU citizens are third-country nationals, so national policy controls their entry and stay.
An economic migrant moves mainly to work or to improve living standards, so the state can decide whether it needs that worker.

A refugee meets the 1951 Refugee Convention definition: a well-founded fear of persecution (serious harm or mistreatment) for reasons of race, religion, nationality, membership of a particular social group or political opinion.
An asylum seeker is a person who has applied for protection and is awaiting a decision, so not every asylum seeker is recognised as a refugee.
The Refugee Convention was signed in Geneva in 1951; its 1967 Protocol removed its geographic and time limits, so it applies to refugees anywhere and at any time.
UNHCR is the UN refugee agency.
People seek asylum (protection in another country) when staying at home is unsafe. Exams ask for one reason, so learn all three.
War and conflict force people to flee their country because their lives are in danger, for example the war in Syria.
Persecution for religion, ethnicity, political opinion or sexuality means people are targeted for who they are or what they believe.
Human rights abuses by the state against its own people leave citizens with no protection at home.
These are the pull factors (features of a destination that attract people) drawing migrants to Europe. They combine the quality of life in EU states with their position on the map.
Safety, the rule of law (everyone is subject to the same fair laws) and respect for human rights give people protection they lack at home.
High living standards, jobs and welfare provision (state support such as benefits) offer a better life and income.
Existing family and diaspora communities (people from the same homeland already settled abroad) already live in EU states, so newcomers have support and contacts.
Nearness to conflict zones in the Middle East and Africa makes Europe the closest destination for many.
Ireland's borders with the UK and the EU are governed by different arrangements, and Ireland is outside Schengen (the EU area without internal border checks).
The Common Travel Area lets Irish and British citizens move, live and work freely between Ireland and the UK. It dates from the 1920s and was kept after the UK left the EU on 31 January 2020.
Ireland is outside Schengen because of the Common Travel Area; Brexit (the UK leaving the EU) did not end it.
EU, EEA (the EU plus Norway, Iceland and Liechtenstein) and Swiss citizens may live and work in Ireland without permits.
On 1 May 2004 Ireland, the UK and Sweden were the only existing members to give citizens of the new member states immediate access to their labour markets.
Ireland's labour market was later opened to Bulgaria and Romania, after a delay.
Polish nationals were the largest non-Irish group in Census 2022, at about 94,000, which shows the effect of the open labour market.
Non-EU workers need a permit before they can work in Ireland, and the system is skills-based: it favours the jobs the economy lacks workers for.
Employment permits are issued by the Department of Enterprise.
The Critical Skills Employment Permit covers occupations in short supply, such as ICT, engineering and medicine, and can lead to family reunification (the worker's family joining them in Ireland).
The General Employment Permit is the second main type, and a list of ineligible occupations restricts which jobs qualify.
A labour-market test checks that no suitable Irish or EU worker is available, so a non-EU worker is only hired when the job cannot be filled locally.
Purpose: to fill gaps in the labour market without displacing Irish or EU workers.
International protection is the Irish name for the asylum system, the legal process by which a person asks Ireland for refuge. Two laws set it up, and applications rose sharply in 2022 and 2023.
The Refugee Act 1996 established the original asylum system.
The International Protection Act 2015 introduced a single application procedure, in which all protection claims are considered together rather than one after another.
The International Protection Office decides first-instance claims (the first decision on each application, before any appeal).
Over 13,000 international protection applications were made in 2022, a record at the time; numbers in 2023 were comparable.
Recent countries of origin include Algeria, Georgia, Nigeria, Somalia and Afghanistan.
Direct provision is the accommodation system for international protection applicants while their claims are decided. It was heavily criticised, and reform has been slow.
Applicants receive accommodation and meals in centres, plus a small weekly allowance; the system was introduced in 2000.
Accommodation is now run by IPAS (International Protection Accommodation Services).
Criticisms: long stays, lack of privacy, unsuitability for children, isolation in rural centres and poor mental health.
The McMahon Report (2015) criticised direct provision, which added to pressure for reform.
A 2017 Supreme Court ruling found an absolute ban on work for applicants unconstitutional, so applicants gained a right to work after a waiting period from 2018.
The White Paper (a government policy plan) of February 2021 planned to end direct provision by the end of 2024; the plan was abandoned as numbers rose.
Shortages of accommodation, as numbers rose, left some applicants without accommodation.
Citizenship is full legal membership of the state. Ireland changed who gets it automatically in 2004, and others can still earn it.
The citizenship referendum (a public vote) of June 2004 (27th Amendment) ended the automatic right to citizenship for children born in Ireland to non-national parents.
About 79% of voters said yes to the 2004 amendment.
Non-nationals may apply for naturalisation (becoming a citizen by application) after a period of residence, and successful applicants take part in a citizenship ceremony.
Ireland also takes refugees through planned programmes and, since 2022, through a temporary route for people fleeing the war in Ukraine. The two routes work very differently.

The Irish Refugee Protection Programme, established in September 2015, committed to taking up to 4,000 people, including refugees from Syria, through EU relocation (moving asylum seekers between member states) and UNHCR resettlement.

The EU Temporary Protection Directive, from 4 March 2022, gave people fleeing Russia's invasion of Ukraine (which began on 24 February 2022) the immediate right to live, work and access services without making an asylum claim.
Temporary protection is not international protection, and Ukrainians are not counted in asylum applications.
Housing pressure from Ukrainian arrivals contrasts with the accommodation-based system for international protection applicants.
Weighing Irish policy up means setting its strengths against its weaknesses. The result is an uneven system that favours some migrants and strains housing.
Policy is open to EU citizens and skilled workers, but restrictive for low-skilled non-EU workers.
The asylum system is slow and accommodation-based, relying on direct provision.
Labour needs pull in one direction (towards admitting more workers) and housing pressure in the other (towards limiting numbers).
Anti-immigration protests show public opposition. There is more on this in the notes on Ethnic, racial and religious issues arising from migration.
The EU removed barriers for its own citizens in two steps: the right to live and work anywhere in the Union, then the removal of border checks.
Free movement of workers, from the Treaty of Rome (1957), and EU citizenship, from the Maastricht Treaty (1992), let EU citizens live and work in any member state.
The Schengen Agreement was signed in 1985 at Schengen, Luxembourg, and came into effect in 1995; it removed internal border checks between members.
A common external border and common visa rules apply across the Schengen area, so a visa for one member lets a visitor cross the others.
The Schengen area had 29 countries from 2025, when Bulgaria and Romania became full members in January 2025; it includes non-EU Norway, Iceland, Switzerland and Liechtenstein.
Ireland and Cyprus are EU members outside Schengen; Ireland's reason is the Common Travel Area with the UK.
After 2015 some states temporarily reintroduced internal border checks, because of the large numbers of arrivals.
The Dublin system decides which EU state must handle an asylum claim. It is an EU rule, not an Irish law, and it was named after the city where the 1990 Convention was signed.
The member state where an asylum seeker first enters the EU is responsible for the claim.
The system is named after the city where the 1990 Dublin Convention was signed; it was replaced by the Dublin II Regulation (2003) and Dublin III (2013).
It is an EU asylum rule, not an Irish law.
It is meant to prevent asylum shopping, where applicants choose the state in which they claim.
It places most pressure on frontier states (those at the EU's edge, where migrants arrive first) such as Italy, Greece, Spain and Malta.
The rule broke down in 2015, when arrivals were too many for frontier states to handle.
The EU controls its outer border through Frontex and also opens legal routes for workers it needs.
Frontex, established in 2004 with its headquarters in Warsaw, is the EU border and coast guard agency.
Frontex runs patrols and returns (sending migrants back to their country of origin), and its search-and-rescue role is debated.
The EU Blue Card directive, adopted in 2009, admits highly skilled non-EU workers; seasonal worker rules also apply.

Labour shortages and ageing populations are reasons for admitting workers, because there are too few young workers to fill jobs. There is more on this in the notes on Changing population characteristics.
The main trends behind recent EU policy are the 2015 to 2016 crisis, Mediterranean routes and the Ukrainian movement. Each trend forced governments to change policy.
The war in Syria from 2011, along with conflict in Afghanistan, Iraq and Eritrea, drove large movements of people.
About 1.3 million asylum applications were made in the EU in 2015, and a similar number in 2016.
Over 1 million people crossed the Mediterranean to Europe in 2015, most reaching the Greek islands from Turkey, with Lesbos the main landing point.
The Eastern Mediterranean route runs from Turkey to Greece, and the Balkan route carries migrants onwards from Greece through the Balkans.
The Central Mediterranean route runs from Libya to Italy; Lampedusa, south of Sicily, is a main landing point.
The Lampedusa shipwreck of October 2013 killed over 360 people and led to Italy's Mare Nostrum search-and-rescue operation (2013 to 2014).
Deaths at sea and smuggling gangs accompanied these routes, and irregular arrivals (entry outside legal channels) continued.
The Ukrainian refugee movement from 2022 added to these pressures, because so many people arrived in a short time.
EU states reacted to the crisis in very different ways, from welcome to fences. The responses show how divided the EU was.
In August 2015 German Chancellor Angela Merkel said 'Wir schaffen das' ('We can do this'); Germany received the largest number of asylum seekers in the EU in 2015 to 2016.
In September 2015 the EU agreed to relocate 160,000 asylum seekers from Italy and Greece, to ease pressure on those frontier states.
Hungary, Poland and the Czech Republic refused to take part, and in 2020 the EU Court of Justice ruled that they had broken EU law.
Hungary, under Viktor Orbán, built a fence on its border with Serbia in 2015, so that migrants could not cross on foot.

The EU-Turkey statement of March 2016 required irregular migrants reaching the Greek islands to be returned to Turkey; the EU was to provide €6 billion for refugees in Turkey, and arrivals in Greece fell sharply.
Externalisation (moving border control outside EU territory): deals with Turkey and with Libya and other North African states aimed to control departures before migrants reached EU borders.
Frontex was strengthened and internal border checks were reintroduced, for example by states wanting to control arrivals.
After 2022 the EU used a protection tool created in 2001 for the first time, and in 2024 it adopted a new Pact on Migration and Asylum.
The Temporary Protection Directive (2001) was activated for the first time on 4 March 2022, because of the Ukraine war.
Over 4 million people held temporary protection in the EU in 2024.
The Pact on Migration and Asylum was adopted in May 2024 and applies from mid-2026.
The Pact's main ideas are faster border procedures and mandatory solidarity, under which each state either accepts relocated asylum seekers or pays into a fund.
Ireland chose to opt in to the Pact in 2024, so it takes part in the new system.
Large numbers of arrivals put pressure on public services and politics. Exams ask for two challenges, so know several.
Cost of reception and housing, because states must provide shelter and support for each arrival.
Slow processing and backlogs, because decisions take time and applications build up.
Integration, including language, jobs and schooling.
An unequal burden on frontier states, because under the Dublin rule they handle the claims of those who arrive first.
Political division and the rise of anti-immigration parties, because public opinion is split on admitting migrants.
