Security screening of new arrivals, so that states can check who is entering.
Deaths at sea and smuggling gangs, because migrants take dangerous routes when there is no legal way to travel.
Evaluating EU policy means naming the tensions it cannot resolve. These tensions explain why agreement has been so hard.
Tension between humanitarian duty (protecting people in need) and border control.
Tension between solidarity between member states and national sovereignty (each state's right to make its own decisions), as the relocation dispute shows.
Europe needs workers but faces public opposition to immigration.
When people move, they carry their culture, appearance and beliefs with them. These three categories overlap but are not the same, and migration can bring all three into contact in one place.
An ethnic group is a group of people who share culture, language, ancestry, traditions or religion, which is why members often feel they belong to the same community.
A race is a group classed by physical traits such as skin colour. Race is a social idea with no biological basis for ranking people, so no race is naturally better than another.
Religion is a shared system of belief and practice. It can cut across ethnic and racial groups, so people of different ethnic groups or races may share one religion.
A multi-ethnic society contains several ethnic groups living together. A multicultural society goes further: it is one in which those groups keep distinct cultural practices.
When migrants and the host population meet, the result can be hostility or acceptance. These terms name the attitudes, the settlement patterns and the policies that governments use in response.
Racism is prejudice (an unfair opinion formed in advance) or discrimination (unfair treatment) based on race or ethnicity.
Xenophobia is fear or hostility towards foreigners. Islamophobia is prejudice against Muslims, so it targets people because of their religion.

Segregation is the clustering of migrants in particular areas. It happens either by choice, for support, cheap housing and chain migration (earlier migrants helping relatives and neighbours to follow them), or because discrimination forces migrants there.
Assimilation is the adoption of the majority culture by migrants, so their own culture is gradually given up.
Integration is the joining of migrants to society while they keep some of their own culture.
Multiculturalism is the acceptance of several cultures as equal within one society, so no single culture is treated as the norm.
Tensions rarely come from difference alone. They arise from circumstances, discrimination and politics, and the same general mechanisms appear in each of the case studies below.
Competition for jobs, housing and services, especially in recessions (periods when the economy shrinks and jobs are scarce), and fear that migrants will undercut wages by working for less.
Visible difference, such as skin colour or dress like the hijab (the headscarf worn by some Muslim women), makes minorities easy targets of prejudice.

Religious practice in public space can clash with secular (non-religious) or majority-religion norms. Examples are places of worship, dress, halal food (food prepared according to Islamic rules), holy days and faith schools.
Residential segregation and concentration in deprived areas reinforce poverty and separation, because people who live apart have fewer chances to mix at school or work.
Language barriers in schools, work and services make it harder for migrants to take part fully.
Political exploitation: far-right and anti-immigration parties and movements, and misinformation on social media, turn worries into hostility.
Second-generation issues: children born in the host country may face discrimination and conflict over identity, since they belong to two cultures.
Positive outcomes include cultural enrichment through food, music, sport and festivals, new places of worship, intercultural schools and mixed marriages.
Ireland moved from a mostly white, Catholic society to a diverse one from the 1990s. The census shows both the new nationalities and the shift in religion.
Census 2022: about one in five people (just over 1 million) were born outside Ireland, and about 630,000 were non-Irish nationals (about 12%).
The largest non-Irish groups are Polish, UK, Indian, Romanian, Lithuanian and Brazilian.
Census 2022: about 69% of people were Roman Catholic, down from about 78% in 2016, so the majority religion is shrinking in share.
Census 2022: about 14% had no religion, up from about 10% in 2016.
Census 2022 counted about 82,000 Muslims, about 100,000 Orthodox Christians and about 33,000 Hindus, showing growth in religions that were once rare in Ireland.
The Islamic Cultural Centre of Ireland is in Clonskeagh, Dublin, an example of a new place of worship and community centre.
About 9 in 10 primary schools are under Catholic patronage (the Catholic Church runs them), so religion once decided many school admissions.
Rapid change brought hostility as well as welcome. Several incidents show how housing pressure and anti-immigration feeling can turn to protest and violence.
East Wall, Dublin: protests from November 2022 against housing international protection applicants (people seeking asylum) in a former office building.
Dublin riot, 23 November 2023: after a knife attack on children outside a school on Parnell Square, buses, a Luas tram (Dublin's light-rail line) and shops were burned and looted.
Arson attacks (deliberate fires) on several buildings proposed for asylum accommodation (2023 to 2024).
Racism and hate crime (crime motivated by hatred of a group) accompany these tensions, and the protests show how hostility can turn to violence.

Irish policy combines equality law, an integration strategy and anti-racism measures, with specific reforms to schools and recognition of Travellers. Each tackles an issue raised in the earlier blocks.
The Employment Equality Act 1998 and the Equal Status Act 2000 prohibit discrimination on nine grounds, including race, religion and membership of the Traveller community.
The Prohibition of Incitement to Hatred Act 1989 is an earlier law against hatred, so Ireland had some protection before the recent migration.
The Irish Human Rights and Equality Commission was established in 2014 to promote and protect human rights and equality.
The Migrant Integration Strategy ran from 2017 to 2020, aiming to help migrants join Irish society.
The National Action Plan Against Racism was published in March 2023.
The Criminal Justice (Hate Offences) Act 2024 gives tougher sentences for crimes motivated by hatred of a protected characteristic (such as race or religion).

The Education (Admission to Schools) Act 2018 removed the baptism barrier, so most Catholic primary schools can no longer use religion to decide admissions. Educate Together, a multi-denominational school body founded in 1984, runs schools open to all faiths and none.
Irish Travellers were formally recognised by the State as an ethnic minority on 1 March 2017.
Judging Irish policy means asking whether the laws have worked in practice. The Traveller community also belongs in this discussion, but not as migrants.
The legal framework is strong, but the 2022 to 2023 protests show that hostility persists.

Direct provision (the system of housing asylum applicants in centres while their claims are processed) isolates applicants in rural centres, and this works against integration. There is more on this in Migration policy in Ireland and the EU.
The Traveller community is an indigenous Irish ethnic minority, not a migrant group, so it is included here only as part of Irish ethnic policy.
About 33,000 Travellers were counted in Census 2022.
France has a large Muslim population and a strict model of secularism, and it follows an assimilation approach. Its laws on religious dress show how the model works in practice.
Post-war immigrant labour came from Algeria, Morocco, Tunisia and Portugal. Large-scale Algerian migration followed the Algerian War of Independence (1954 to 1962) and Algeria's independence in 1962.
France has the largest Muslim population in western Europe.
Laïcité, the principle of strict separation of religion and state, dates from the 1905 law. This is why the state treats religion as a private matter.
A 2004 law banned conspicuous religious symbols, including the Islamic headscarf, in state schools.
A 2010 law banned face coverings, such as the burqa and niqab (veils covering the face), in public places, in force from 2011.
Banlieues are segregated high-rise estates on the edge of cities, with high unemployment, so residents are concentrated in deprived areas apart from the city centre.
In the banlieues, segregation and unemployment have fed unrest. Terrorist attacks and politics have then added to tension with the Muslim community.

The October to November 2005 riots began in Clichy-sous-Bois, a Paris banlieue, after two teenagers died fleeing police. They spread across France and a state of emergency (special powers for the government) was declared.
June 2023 riots followed the police shooting of a 17-year-old in Nanterre.
The Charlie Hebdo attack in January 2015 and the Paris attacks of 13 November 2015 (130 killed) were followed by rising Islamophobia.
The National Front, a far-right party founded in 1972 by Jean-Marie Le Pen, was renamed the National Rally (Rassemblement National) in 2018 under Marine Le Pen.
Germany recruited workers to rebuild its economy, expecting them to leave. Many stayed, and the question of their citizenship shaped integration for decades.
A recruitment agreement with Turkey was signed in 1961, and recruitment of guest workers (Gastarbeiter, workers invited for a limited time) stopped in 1973.
Guest workers were expected to return home, but many stayed and brought their families.
Germany long denied them citizenship, and segregated districts formed, such as Kreuzberg in Berlin, which has a large Turkish community.
The 2000 citizenship law gave citizenship to children born in Germany to long-resident foreign parents.
The 2024 reform allowed dual citizenship (holding two nationalities) generally and shortened the residence requirement.
About 3 million people of Turkish origin live in Germany (2020s).
The Alternative für Deutschland (AfD), founded in 2013, grew after the 2015 refugee arrivals on an anti-immigration platform, so it is an example of political exploitation of migration.
Caribbean migrants arrived in Britain from 1948. Their arrival shows racism in housing and work, and how policy later had to respond.
The Empire Windrush, a ship, arrived at Tilbury (a port on the Thames) in June 1948 with passengers from the Caribbean.
Caribbean migrants faced racism in housing and work, which made it harder for them to settle, for example in finding a home to rent or a job.
The Notting Hill riots in London in 1958 showed racial tension turning violent.
The Race Relations Act 1965 was the first UK law against racial discrimination.
The Windrush scandal of 2018: long-settled Caribbean-born residents were wrongly detained, denied services or deported because they lacked documents.
The Plantation was a historic migration whose religious legacy still divides Northern Ireland. Here it is studied only as a migration and its religious legacy.
The Plantation of Ulster began in 1609, after the Flight of the Earls (1607). Land taken from Catholic Irish was settled by Protestant colonists from Scotland and England.
Centuries of religious and political division followed, leading to the Troubles (the conflict) from the late 1960s to 1998, in which about 3,500 people were killed.
The Good Friday (Belfast) Agreement was signed on 10 April 1998.
Census 2021 (Northern Ireland): about 46% Catholic and about 43% Protestant and other Christian.
Most children attend schools of their own community, and peace walls (barriers) still divide some Belfast neighbourhoods, so the division is still visible in housing and schooling.
The Roma are an example of an ethnic minority that has been on the move for centuries and has often been excluded wherever it settles.
The Roma are about 10 to 12 million people in Europe (Council of Europe estimate) and Europe's largest ethnic minority.
The Roma originated in northern India and migrated to Europe about 1,000 years ago.
The Roma have faced discrimination in housing, education and employment, and segregated schooling in parts of central and eastern Europe.
France expelled Roma to Romania and Bulgaria in 2010, which drew EU criticism, so exclusion has come from governments as well as individuals.
The case studies show three different responses to migrant minorities. Comparing them is a good way to finish an answer on government policy.
France's assimilation model treats all citizens alike and collects no official ethnic statistics.
Ireland's approach rests on equality law and an integration strategy.
Germany moved from excluding guest workers from citizenship to citizenship reform in 2000 and 2024.

Rural-to-urban migration means people leaving the countryside (the donor region, which gives up people) for cities (the receiver region, which takes them in). It is one of the biggest forces reshaping where the world's people live.
Urbanisation is the growing share of people living in towns, while urban growth is the rise in the number of people living in towns. The two are different measures, so keep them apart.

Rural-to-urban migration is the main driver of urbanisation in developing countries (poorer countries with fast-growing populations). Natural increase in the cities, meaning births outnumbering deaths, is the other driver.
Over half the world's people have lived in urban areas since about 2007 (UN), so the world passed the point where towns held more people than the countryside.
About 68% of the world's people are expected to be urban by 2050 (UN, 2018 projection), which shows the trend is still rising.
The fastest urban growth is now in Asia and Africa, where megacities (cities with very large populations) are forming.
Push factors are the conditions that make people want to leave the countryside. Most come down to too little work, income or service in the place they live.
Lack of jobs and low farm incomes leave rural people with too little money to live on, so they look for work elsewhere.
Mechanisation of farming (using machines instead of workers) reduces the labour needed on the land, so fewer people are employed in farming.
Small, subdivided holdings (farms split into ever smaller pieces) cannot support a family, so family members move away.
Poor services, including schools, hospitals, broadband and transport, make rural life harder and push people toward places that have them.
Drought, famine and land degradation (the land losing its ability to grow crops) push people out in the developing world.
Isolation and lack of social life push people out, because rural life offers little to do and few people to meet.
Pull factors are the attractions that draw people to cities. They are largely the opposite of the push factors, which is why movement from the countryside is so steady.
Jobs in industry and services (work such as shops, offices and banks) give people a way to earn a living.
Higher wages in the city make the move worth the cost.
Third-level education (university and college) is found in cities, so young people go there to study.
Better health care and services are available in cities, where there are more hospitals and facilities.
Entertainment and the 'bright lights' of the city attract young people looking for a more exciting social life.
Existing family networks create chain migration, which means one person moves and relatives and neighbours follow because someone is already there to help them settle.
Not all movement is toward cities. In developed countries some people now move the other way.
Counter-urbanisation is people moving out of cities to towns and the countryside, and it is found in developed countries (richer countries).
Remote working since COVID-19 lets people live outside cities while working in them, because they no longer need to be near the office every day.
Ireland was a rural country until the later 20th century, and its population then concentrated in cities. This is the main developed-world case study.
Census 1971 was the first census in which more people lived in towns than in rural areas, so the urban share crossed half in that year.
Census 2016: about 63% of the population was urban.
Flight from the land happened because farming mechanised and small farms became unviable (could no longer earn enough to survive), so people moved to cities.
Industrial and service jobs concentrated in Dublin and the cities, which pulled the people who left farming toward them.

Growth is concentrated in Dublin, with the commuter counties (counties near Dublin where people live and travel to work) and the regional cities also growing. Be careful with which Dublin figure you use.
Census 2022: the State had about 5.15 million people.

Co. Dublin had about 1.46 million; Dublin city and suburbs had about 1.26 million; the Greater Dublin Area (Dublin, Meath, Kildare and Wicklow) had about 2.1 million, about 40% of the State's population.
Dublin is the primate city, a city much larger than any other in its country, so it dominates Irish life.
Commuter towns, where many residents travel daily to work in Dublin, include Navan, Drogheda, Naas and Newbridge.
Regional cities (city and suburbs): Cork about 220,000; Limerick about 100,000; Galway city about 85,000; Waterford about 60,000.
Dublin's earlier planned growth created the new towns of Tallaght, Clondalkin, Lucan and Blanchardstown under the Myles Wright plan of 1967.
Receiving large numbers of migrants brings Dublin both benefits and strains. The positives come from having many people in one place, and the negatives from fitting them all in.
A large labour pool (many workers available to hire) attracts multinationals and service firms.
Economies of scale support transport, universities and hospitals, because a large population makes these services cheaper per person to provide.
A rich cultural life develops where so many people live.
Housing shortages, high rents and prices, and homelessness occur because homes cannot be built as fast as people arrive.
Urban sprawl (the city spreading outward over farmland) reaches into Meath, Kildare and Wicklow.
Long commutes and traffic congestion result when workers live far out and travel in.
Pressure on water supply and other services builds as the population grows.
High-rise and infill development pressure (building taller, and building on gaps within the city) grows because land is scarce.

Rural decline in Ireland is now local, in remote parishes and townlands (the smallest rural land divisions), rather than county-wide. The figures below show how uneven population is across the country.
Census 2022: the population of every county grew between 2016 and 2022, so decline is within counties rather than whole counties.
Leitrim had about 155,000 people in 1841 and about 35,000 in Census 2022, the least populous county.
Mayo had about 138,000 people and about 25 people per km² in Census 2022; Co. Dublin had about 1,600 per km², so the contrast in density is very large.
An ageing population and higher dependency ratios (more people too old or too young to work for each worker) follow because young adults leave.
Fewer young adults and lower birth rates follow, since the people most likely to have children are the ones who move away.
When young people leave, the services and community life that depended on them go too. Migration is not all loss for the donor region, though.
Closure of schools, post offices, Garda stations, shops and pubs, and derelict houses, happen because too few customers and users remain to keep them open.
Loss of community and sporting clubs, with GAA teams amalgamating (joining with neighbouring clubs to field a team), and farms with no successor, follow as young people leave.
Cultural loss, including the decline of the Gaeltacht (the Irish-speaking regions), occurs as Irish speakers move away.
Positive effects: less pressure on land, remittances (money sent home by migrants) and returning migrants, and some farm consolidation (neighbouring farms joined into larger, more viable ones).
The State has tried to slow decline in the regions and to spread growth more evenly, with plans and agencies set up between 1980 and 2018.
The National Spatial Strategy (2002) set out gateways and hubs (larger and smaller centres chosen to attract growth) to spread growth.
The decentralisation programme, announced in 2003, moves public service jobs out of Dublin.
The Western Development Commission has been a statutory body (set up by law) since 1999.
CLÁR, a programme of investment in depopulated rural areas, was launched in 2001.
Údarás na Gaeltachta, founded in 1980, creates jobs in the Gaeltacht.

The National Planning Framework (Project Ireland 2040), published in February 2018, plans for about 1 million more people by 2040, with about half of growth in the five cities (Dublin, Cork, Limerick, Galway and Waterford) and their suburbs, and with the four cities other than Dublin growing faster than Dublin.
The Town and Village Renewal Scheme and rural broadband with remote working hubs support rural areas, since remote work lets people stay in the countryside.
Limitation: rural areas and regional cities still depend on the jobs and services that drew people to Dublin, so the pull of Dublin remains.
Two European countries show the same donor and receiver pattern: a poorer region loses people to richer cities, and one capital dominates its country.
Italy: after the Second World War, people moved from the Mezzogiorno (southern Italy) to the industrial cities of the north, Turin and Milan, and abroad to Germany, Switzerland and Belgium.
The Mezzogiorno has about 20 million people (2020s), about one-third of Italy's population.
Depopulating southern villages responded with €1 house schemes (selling empty houses very cheaply to attract new residents), such as Sambuca di Sicilia.
France: Paris dominates the country; Jean-François Gravier's Paris et le désert français (1947) described the regions outside Paris as a French desert.
Île-de-France (the region around Paris) has about 12 million people (2020s), about 18% of France's population.
Migration from poor rural states to the big cities fills slums and sends remittances back to the villages.
Migrants come from poorer rural states, Bihar and Uttar Pradesh, to Mumbai, Delhi and Kolkata.
Push factors: small holdings, debt, landlessness (owning no land to farm) and drought.
Pull factors: jobs in construction, factories and the informal sector (work without contracts or regular pay, such as street trading).
Census 2011: about 31% of Indians were urban, up from about 17% in 1951; about 833 million people (about 69%) were rural.
Census 2011 urban agglomerations (a city with its built-up surroundings): Greater Mumbai about 18.4 million; Delhi about 16.3 million; Kolkata about 14.1 million.
Bihar is India's densest state, at about 1,100 per km², which adds to the pressure to leave.
The cities cannot house everyone who arrives, so slums grow. Villages left behind lose workers but gain money sent home.
About 65 million people lived in slums (crowded areas of poor housing).

Dharavi, Mumbai, is one of Asia's largest slums, about 2 km² near the city centre, with hundreds of thousands of residents and many small industries such as recycling, leather, pottery and garments. Kolkata's slums are called bustees.
Receiver impacts: pressure on water, sanitation and transport; informal work; and a large supply of cheap labour.
Donor impacts: male out-migration leaves women, children and the old to farm, and working-age labour is lost.
Remittances (money sent home) fund houses, education and farm inputs in donor villages.
India is the world's largest recipient of remittances, mostly from international migrants, so the figure does not measure rural-to-urban flows directly.
In the March 2020 COVID-19 lockdown, millions of migrant workers walked or travelled home from the cities.
Brazil's migration runs from the drought-prone North-East to the south-east, and Brazil is now highly urbanised.
Migrants from the sertão, the drought-prone semi-arid interior of the North-East (nordestinos), moved to São Paulo and Rio de Janeiro; some also helped build Brasília, the capital from 1960.
Census 2022: Brazil had about 203 million people, about 87% of them urban (2020s).
São Paulo city had about 11.5 million people (Census 2022), and over 20 million in its metropolitan region; it is Brazil's largest city and industrial centre.
Favelas (shanty towns) grow on hillsides and at the urban edge; Rocinha in Rio de Janeiro is one of Brazil's largest.
Informal work is common in the favelas, and some favelas have crime and gang violence.
The North-East, the donor region, loses young people.
In China the government's household registration rules shape who can settle in a city, so migrants often work in cities without the rights of residents.
The hukou (household registration) system, introduced in 1958, ties public services to a person's registered home, so a migrant is not fully entitled to services in the city.
Nearly 300 million rural migrant workers (2023), many of them in coastal cities such as Shenzhen, Guangzhou and Shanghai.
Shenzhen grew from a small town to a city of over 17 million after becoming China's first Special Economic Zone (an area with special rules to attract business) in 1980.
Rural villages are left with 'left-behind' children and elderly people, because working-age adults have gone to the cities.
Migrants lack full access to urban schools, health care and housing, because their services are tied to their registered home.
The scale, speed and capacity of cities differ between the two kinds of region, so the impacts differ.
In developed regions migration is slower, and cities can largely absorb it with planned housing and services.
In developed regions the donor problem is ageing rural decline.
In developing regions migration is fast and very large; cities cannot provide housing, jobs or services, so slums and the informal sector grow.
In developing regions donor villages depend on remittances and lose working-age men.
Urban growth in developing cities comes from both migration and high natural increase among young migrants, because young adults have many children.
Geographers describe where and why a settlement exists with three terms: site, situation and function. Keeping them apart lets you explain a settlement's location precisely.

Site is the exact ground a settlement is built on, such as a dry point (a patch of dry ground in wet land), a wet point (a water source), a defensive hill, a river loop, a bridging point (where a river can be crossed) or a sheltered harbour.
Example of site: Mount Sandel, near Coleraine, Co. Derry, on a bluff (a steep bank) above the River Bann.

Situation is where the settlement lies relative to the land around it, including its routes, resources and hinterland (the surrounding area it serves). Example: Clonmacnoise, Co. Offaly, beside the River Shannon where the Esker Riada routeway (a ridge of glacial gravel used as a road) crosses it.
Function is the economic and social purpose of a settlement, what people there do. Example: Glendalough, Co. Wicklow, where a monastery (a community of monks) served a religious function.

People in every period chose where to settle using the same practical factors. Later blocks apply these factors to each period in turn, and they are the reasons an exam answer on why a town developed at its location should give.
Water supply: a river, lake or spring gave drinking water, fishing and a means of transport.
Defence: high ground, cliffs, river loops, islands and marsh edges made a site harder to attack.
Fertile, well-drained land: soil that supported crops and grazing without flooding.
Shelter: sheltered valleys, bays and estuaries (wide river mouths where the river meets the sea) protected people and boats from the weather.
Routeways and fords or bridging points: places where roads, valleys or rivers could be crossed easily, so people and trade passed through.
Resources: fish, timber and stone, which were needed for food, fuel and building.
Religious or political importance: a holy site or a seat of power attracted people and the services they needed.
Finding and naming historic settlements on an OS map is a separate skill. There is more on this in Map interpretation.

The Mesolithic (Middle Stone Age) people were the first to live in Ireland. They were hunter-gatherers, meaning they lived by hunting, fishing and collecting wild food rather than farming, so they had no reason to stay in one place.
They made temporary camps on coasts, lakeshores and river banks, where they could fish and gather food. This is why their sites are camps, not farms.
Mount Sandel, near Coleraine, Co. Derry, is the earliest known house site in Ireland. It is Mesolithic and over 9,000 years old, such as a camp beside a river.
The people of Mount Sandel fished for salmon and eels and gathered hazelnuts, which shows how they lived off wild food.
Neolithic (New Stone Age) farmers cleared forest for fields and lived in permanent farmsteads, so settlement became fixed in place. They left large stone tombs and field walls that still survive.
Megalithic tombs (tombs built of huge stones) were built on high, visible ground, so they could be seen across the landscape. The main types are court, portal (dolmen), passage and wedge tombs.
Poulnabrone, in the Burren, Co. Clare, is a portal tomb (dolmen), such as the Neolithic tombs built on high, visible ground.
Brú na Bóinne, Co. Meath, lies in a bend of the River Boyne and holds the passage tombs of Newgrange, Knowth and Dowth.
Newgrange is about 5,000 years old (about 3200 BC). Brú na Bóinne has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site (a place protected as important to all humanity) since 1993.
Céide Fields, near Ballycastle, north Co. Mayo, is a Neolithic field system of stone walls preserved under blanket bog (a thick layer of peat that grew over the land). It is over 5,000 years old.
The walls of the Céide Fields show organised farming in the Neolithic period, because the fields were planned and divided by walls.
In the Bronze Age and Iron Age people learned to work metal, and defence and royal power began to shape where they settled. Some sites were for ceremony or kingship rather than everyday living.
Metalworking developed in the Bronze Age and Iron Age, so tools and weapons improved. Standing stones and stone circles survive from this period.
Fulachta fia were Bronze Age cooking sites beside streams, so water was close at hand.
Hillforts and promontory forts (forts on headlands jutting into the sea) gave defence on high ground and headlands.
Dún Aonghasa, on Inis Mór in the Aran Islands, Co. Galway, is a stone fort on the edge of a sheer sea cliff, so the cliff itself defends one side.
Crannógs were artificial islands in lakes, used over a long period. The water around them made them hard to attack.
The Hill of Tara, Co. Meath, was the traditional seat of the High Kings of Ireland. This is why it was a ceremonial site, not a town.
Navan Fort (Emain Macha), Co. Armagh, was the royal site of Ulster.
The Hill of Tara and Navan Fort were royal and ceremonial sites, not towns.
From the 5th century, in the early Christian (early medieval) period, many farmers lived in defended farmsteads called ringforts. Unlike the later towns, these were spread across the countryside.
Ringforts (raths and lios; stone versions are cashels, cahers and dúns) were dispersed (spread out, not clustered), defended farmsteads, enclosed by a bank and ditch or a stone wall.
Ringforts were built on well-drained hillsides, which kept the farmstead dry and gave a view of approaching danger.
Souterrains were underground stone passages built alongside ringforts, so they are found at ringfort sites.
Place-name evidence: kil or cill (church), rath or lios (ringfort) and dun (fort) mark early Christian sites, so a townland name can show an old settlement.
Ringforts are early medieval. They are not prehistoric, Viking or Norman.

Monasteries were the first centres of people and trade in the early Christian period. They were proto-towns (early forms of town), not true towns, because they lacked the full range of town functions.
Monasteries were sited on routeways, rivers, eskers (long ridges of glacial gravel that made dry routes) or remote islands, so they were either easy to reach or secluded.
Glendalough, Co. Wicklow, was founded by St Kevin in the 6th century in a glaciated valley (a valley shaped by ice).
Clonmacnoise, Co. Offaly, was founded by St Ciarán in the mid-6th century beside the River Shannon.
Skellig Michael, Co. Kerry, is an island monastery and a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1996.
Kells, Co. Meath, and Armagh are towns that grew from early monasteries.
Round towers served as bell towers and refuges, places to shelter from attack.
High crosses (tall carved stone crosses) and holy wells also mark early Christian sites.
The Vikings founded Ireland's first true towns, which began as fortified bases for their ships. They chose sites for trade and access by sea.
From the 9th century, Viking raids were followed by longphorts, fortified ship bases.
The Vikings sited their settlements on sheltered estuaries and harbours at river mouths, for trade and access by sea.
Dublin was founded as a longphort in 841, on the Liffey near its mouth, so ships could come and go by sea.
Waterford was founded by Vikings in 914, on the Suir estuary, so ships could reach the sea.
Limerick was a Viking settlement from about 922, on an island in the Shannon, which made it easy to defend.
Wexford and Cork were also Viking towns. Like Dublin, they were coastal or estuary sites suited to trade by sea.
Norse (Viking) place names include Wexford, Waterford, Wicklow and Arklow. Leixlip, Co. Kildare, comes from Old Norse for salmon leap.
Wood Quay, Dublin: excavations in the 1970s uncovered a large Viking town site. There is more on this in Urban problems in developed-world cities.
The Normans (Anglo-Normans) took over and extended existing Viking towns rather than founding them. They also built castles to hold the land they conquered.
The Normans landed at Bannow Bay, Co. Wexford, in 1169.
Strongbow (Richard de Clare) took Waterford in 1170, a Viking town, which shows the Normans captured towns rather than founding them.
Motte and bailey castles came first. A motte was an earth mound topped by a wooden tower, with a fortified enclosure (the bailey) beside it. Stone castles followed.
Trim Castle, Co. Meath, on the River Boyne, is the largest Anglo-Norman castle in Ireland, a stone castle of the kind that followed the mottes. Hugh de Lacy began it in the 1170s.
Carrickfergus Castle, Co. Antrim, was built by John de Courcy from 1177.
Norman towns were sited at bridging points and on navigable rivers in fertile lowlands, for defence and control of land and trade. They were planned places with a set of recognisable features.

Walled towns had gates, market squares, charters (documents granting the town rights), burgage plots (long narrow strips of land rented by townspeople), parish churches and abbeys. The walls gave defence and the market square supported trade.
Manor villages grew up around a lord's manor (his estate and house), with tenants farming the surrounding land.
Athenry, Co. Galway, and Fethard, Co. Tipperary, have among the most complete medieval town walls in Ireland, which survive as evidence of Norman defence.
Kilkenny shows how a Norman town became a centre of power. Its castle, and later laws and assemblies, tie it to the history of Norman Ireland.
Kilkenny is a Norman town on the River Nore. A stone castle was built there by William Marshal around 1200.
The Statutes of Kilkenny, 1366, tried to stop the Normans adopting Irish language and customs.
The Confederation of Kilkenny was formed in 1642.
After the first Norman phase, lords built fortified homes of their own. Outside the Norman towns, much of the country was run on a different pattern.
Tower houses were fortified homes of local lords, built in the 15th and 16th centuries, so lords could defend themselves.
Gaelic Ireland (the parts ruled by Irish lords, not the Normans) was largely without towns.
A plantation was the official settling of land with new settlers loyal to the Crown. The Laois and Offaly, Munster and Ulster plantations each produced planned towns.
Plantation of Laois and Offaly, 1556: Maryborough (now Portlaoise) and Philipstown (now Daingean) were planned as plantation towns.
Munster Plantation, from the 1580s: Bandon, Co. Cork, is a plantation town.
Plantation towns had a central square or diamond, a wide main street, a market house and an Established (Protestant) church. Donegal town is an Ulster example.
Ulster Plantation, from 1609: Derry was renamed Londonderry in 1613.
Derry's city walls were built 1613–1618. They are the only complete city walls in Ireland.

Improving landlords (estate owners who invested in their land) laid out planned towns beside their estates, with wide streets, squares, malls (tree-lined walks) and market houses. Georgian (18th-century) towns followed the same orderly pattern.
Westport, Co. Mayo, was laid out in the 18th century by the Browne family of Westport House. It has the Octagon and a tree-lined Mall along the Carrowbeg River.
Birr, Co. Offaly, is a Georgian planned town of the Parsons family (Earls of Rosse), built beside Birr Castle, so the landlord's home and his town sit together.
The Leviathan telescope at Birr, built in 1845, was the largest telescope in the world for decades.
Kenmare, Co. Kerry, was laid out in 1775 by the first Marquess of Lansdowne.
Adare, Co. Limerick, is an estate village of the Dunraven estate, with thatched cottages.
The Wide Streets Commissioners were set up in Dublin in 1757. Georgian Dublin has wide streets, squares such as Merrion Square and Fitzwilliam Square, and red-brick terraces (rows of joined houses).
Limerick's Georgian Newtown Pery was laid out in the late 18th century on land of Edmund Sexton Pery.
The full development of Georgian Dublin is a larger story. There is more on this in A Core Irish Region.
In the 19th century transport and industry created new towns, while poverty and famine emptied parts of the countryside.
Canals and railways created railway junction towns, where lines met and traffic changed, and seaside resorts, which people could now reach.
Mills and industrial villages were a feature of the 19th century.
The first railway in Ireland, Dublin–Kingstown (Dún Laoghaire), opened in 1834.
The Irish Poor Law Act of 1838 built a workhouse (an institution housing the poor) in each Poor Law union (a district grouped for poor relief).
The Great Famine (1845–49) and emigration emptied much of the rural west. This is why the west had fewer people afterwards.
Clonmel, Co. Tipperary: Charles Bianconi began Ireland's first public horse-drawn passenger car service there in 1815, so people could travel between towns.
Belfast grew on linen and shipbuilding, such as Harland and Wolff, who built the Titanic, launched in 1911.
In the modern period the State began to plan new towns, and cities spread outward.
Shannon, Co. Clare, was Ireland's first planned new town. It was built from the 1960s for workers at the Shannon Free Zone (an area set up in 1959 to attract industry) beside Shannon Airport.
The Wright Report of 1967 set out new towns for Dublin at Tallaght, Clondalkin, Lucan and Blanchardstown.
Suburban expansion and commuter towns (towns whose residents travel out to work) grew outward from cities.
A modern Irish town keeps the features of each historic phase in its street pattern and buildings. Kilkenny is the worked example.
The street plan links Kilkenny Castle and the cathedral. It is promoted as the Medieval Mile. This is why the old castle and church still shape the town.
St Canice's Cathedral, with its round tower beside it, marks the early Christian monastery that gave the city its name, Cill Chainnigh, meaning church of Canice.

In an Irish town, walls and gates date from the Norman period, the market square and market house from the plantation and landlord towns, Georgian terraces from the 18th century, and mills and the railway station from the 19th century.

Rural settlement is the farmhouses, hamlets (very small groups of houses) and villages in the countryside. Its pattern is the way the buildings are spread over the land, and geographers sort patterns into three types.
Dispersed: individual farmhouses scattered across the land, each on its own farm.
Clustered (also called nucleated): buildings grouped together in one place, usually for a shared reason such as a crossroads or a water supply.
Linear (also called ribbon): houses strung along a line such as a road, a coast road, a valley or a ridge.
Clustered and nucleated mean the same pattern, and linear is the same as ribbon when it extends out of a town along approach roads, so there are three patterns, not four.
In Census 2016 (the national count of the population), about 63% of Ireland's population lived in urban areas and about 37% in rural areas.
Dispersed settlement is the dominant rural pattern in Ireland. It exists for farming, historical and physical reasons.
Irish farms are family-owned, and each family lives on its own holding (its own farm), so the houses end up spread out across the countryside.

The Land Commission was set up in 1881 under the Land Law (Ireland) Act 1881. After the Land Acts, consolidation of holdings (joining scattered plots into one compact farm) moved houses out of clusters onto individual farms.
The Wyndham Land Act of 1903 helped tenants to buy their holdings, which strengthened the pattern of families owning and living on their own land.
Fertile, well-drained lowland with plentiful water lets houses be built almost anywhere, because no site is much better than another.
Pastoral farming (rearing animals, especially cattle and sheep) keeps the farmer close to the animals, so the house sits on the farm.
Buildings are grouped together where a shared reason made the site worth using. Each reason below explains why people chose to build close together instead of apart.
Route focus: a crossroads where roads meet brings travellers and trade, so buildings gather there.
A bridging point or ford (a shallow place where a river can be crossed) draws settlement because routes must pass through it.
A church, a castle or estate gates act as a focus, and people settle beside them for work, worship or protection.
Defence: a hill or other defensible site was chosen so the settlement could be defended.
Water supply at a spring or well gives a wet-point site, where people settle because they need water.
A dry-point site is a patch of dry ground above flood land, chosen so houses stay dry.
A harbour is the reason for a fishing village, because the boats and the catch are landed there.
Services such as a shop, pub, school and Garda station (police station) gather in the cluster, which then attracts further settlement.
Estate village: Enniskerry, Co. Wicklow, lies at the gates of the Powerscourt estate (a large landowner's property), and Adare, Co. Limerick, grew by the Dunraven estate, with thatched cottages.
Before the Famine many farmers in the west lived in clachans instead of on separate farms. The way land was held in common explains why.
A clachan is a cluster of farmhouses of related families, with no church, shop or other services. It is not a village, because a village has services.

Rundale was a landholding system in which families worked land in common, in scattered strips of infield (the better land near the houses) and outfield (poorer land further out). It explains the clachan; it is not a settlement pattern.
Clachans and rundale were common in the west before the Famine.
The Great Famine (1845-49), when the potato crop failed and many people died or emigrated, hit the clachan districts of the west hardest.

Clachans broke up as the population fell and holdings were consolidated. The Congested Districts Board, set up in 1891 for the poor western districts, consolidated holdings, built roads and piers, and rehoused families on separate farms.
The Land Commission also moved houses onto individual farms, which is how dispersed settlement replaced the clachans.
A few clachans survive in the west.
Linear settlement is the third pattern. Houses line up along a feature that offers a route or dry, firm ground.

Houses are strung along a line: a road, a coast road, a valley floor, a river or a raised ridge such as an esker (a long ridge of gravel left by a glacier) or the edge of a drumlin (an oval hill of glacial deposit).
Linear settlement avoids marshy or steep land, because it is hard and costly to build on.
Some land on a map has no settlement at all, and exams ask you to explain why. There is more on reading this from OS maps in Map interpretation.
Uplands are steep, exposed and have poor soils, so they are hard to build on and farm.
Bogs are wet, poorly drained land, so houses cannot be built safely on them.
Flood plains (flat land beside a river that floods) are unsuitable for houses because of the risk of flooding.
Lakes take up land that could hold houses.
Forestry plantations are large areas of planted trees with no houses.
Two European examples show how planning and history shape rural settlement very differently from the Irish pattern.

Noordoostpolder, Netherlands, a polder (land drained from water) drained in 1942, is a planned rural landscape with a central town, Emmeloord, ringed by ten planned villages. There is more on this in Urban settlement: site, hierarchy, hinterland and central place theory.

In southern Italy, the Mezzogiorno's rural population lived in hilltop villages. The 1950 land reform scattered new farmhouses on reclaimed lowlands, so settlement moved from clustered to dispersed. There is more on this in A Peripheral European Region: the Mezzogiorno.
Ribbon development is houses built one plot deep along the roads leading out of towns and villages, and along rural roads generally. Several pressures made roadsides the favoured building sites.
Sites are cheaper than in towns, so buyers get more for their money.
Road frontage gives access to services such as electricity, water mains and phone or broadband lines, which already run along the road.
Farmers sold roadside sites, because these were the easiest plots to sell.
People wanted rural living near a town, with the countryside around them and work or schools close by.
Car ownership made commuting (travelling daily to work) and rural living practical.
Planning control was historically weak, so few limits stopped houses going up along roads.
Tax incentives and the property boom of the Celtic Tiger (the period of rapid economic growth in Ireland) encouraged building.
Ribbon housing suits the people who live in it, but it causes problems for roads, services, the environment and towns.
Traffic hazards: many entrances onto fast roads, because every house needs its own access and drivers have to slow or turn.
It is costly to service. School buses, post, waste collection, water and sewers must all reach scattered houses, which are far apart.
Septic tanks (private tanks that treat a house's own sewage) can pollute groundwater and private wells.
Loss of scenic landscape, because the roadsides fill with houses.
Car dependence: residents need a car for almost every journey, as shops and services are far away.
Town centres decline as people live outside them and spend less in them.
The boundary between town and country becomes blurred, because houses line the roads where the town should end.
Rural people often see ribbon housing differently, because it helps keep their communities going.
Ribbon development keeps rural populations, schools, GAA clubs and shops alive, because they need people living nearby to survive.
It lets families live near relatives and farms.
Housing is cheaper than in towns.
Planning is how the State controls where building takes place. It works through the local authority (the county or city council), with plans made at county and local level.
Planning permission is granted by the local authority.
Decisions can be appealed to An Bord Pleanála, the national planning appeals board, set up in 1977. It was renamed An Coimisiún Pleanála in 2025.
The Planning and Development Act 2000 requires each planning authority to make a County Development Plan every six years.
The County Development Plan sets zoning (deciding which land may be used for housing, industry or farming), rural housing policy, design rules and protected areas.
Local Area Plans cover towns and villages.
National policy sets the aims that county plans must follow. Rural housing is treated differently depending on how much pressure an area is under.
The National Spatial Strategy (2002) and the National Planning Framework (2018, also called Project Ireland 2040) set rural housing aims. There is more on both in Urban planning and renewal.
Sustainable Rural Housing Guidelines for Planning Authorities, 2005, tell councils how to treat different types of rural area.
In areas under strong urban influence (close to a city or large town), rural houses are limited to people with a local economic or social need, to prevent commuter housing spreading.
In structurally weak areas (areas losing people and jobs), rural housing is encouraged to keep the population.
County Development Plans turn national aims into rules for each county. These are the typical rural policies.
Local-needs criteria restrict who may build a house in some rural areas, for example to those with a local economic or social need.
New entrances onto national and regional roads are restricted, because many entrances onto fast roads are a traffic hazard.
New housing is directed into villages and serviced sites (sites with water and sewers), which avoids scattered one-off houses.
Design guidelines cover siting, materials and hedgerows.
Minimum site sizes apply to septic tanks, so that there is enough land to treat the waste safely.
Scenic areas and views are protected from development.
Land is zoned around towns, so that building is guided to where it is planned.
Septic tanks serve houses with no connection to a public sewer, so poorly maintained ones can pollute the water that rural households drink.
Water Services (Amendment) Act 2012: domestic septic tanks must be registered, and they are inspected under an EPA (Environmental Protection Agency) plan.
Ireland has about half a million domestic wastewater treatment systems, mostly septic tanks (EPA estimate).
These programmes respond to rural depopulation (people leaving rural areas) and the decline of services such as post offices, Garda stations and pubs. They aim to sustain rural communities.
LEADER, an EU rural development programme, from 1991.
CLÁR, a State programme for rural areas suffering depopulation, from 2001.
The Town and Village Renewal Scheme, from 2016.
Our Rural Future, the Government's rural development policy for 2021-2025, published in 2021, supports remote working hubs (shared workplaces where people can work remotely from home areas).
To judge how well rural planning works, weigh the aims against each other and against what has happened.
The central tension is keeping rural communities alive while preventing sprawl (unplanned spread of housing).

Local-needs conditions have been criticised as unfair. In 2013 the EU Court of Justice ruled against a Flemish (Belgian) rule restricting who could buy land in some communes, which raised doubts about Irish local-needs conditions.
Planning has reduced ribbon development but has not stopped it.
Villages need sewage treatment before they can take more housing, which limits the policy of directing housing into villages.
A town's site is the exact ground it is built on. Towns grew where the land gave an advantage for crossing rivers, trading, defence or getting resources, and Irish towns show each type.
Bridging point or ford (a shallow place where a river can be crossed): Dublin, on the Liffey, is the lowest bridging point on the river, so traffic had to cross there.
Route focus, where several roads meet: Athlone, at a crossing of the River Shannon in the centre of Ireland, gathers traffic from many directions.
Island site: Limerick, on King's Island in the Shannon, which gave natural protection from water on all sides.
Sheltered harbour or estuary head (the inner end of a river mouth where it widens to the sea): Waterford, on the Suir estuary, and Galway, at the mouth of the River Corrib, both suit ships.
Defensive sites on a hill, river loop or island, because attackers find them hard to approach, and dry points above wet ground, which are safe to build on.
Resources close to the site, such as water, fish, timber and stone, which settlers need for living and building.
A river confluence (where two rivers join) is another site characteristic.
Site is the spot itself. Situation is the wider picture: where the town lies in relation to the land and trade around it.
Centre of a fertile farming area, so the town can supply goods to farmers and take in their produce.
On a coast facing trade partners, which gives access to sea routes.
At a gap through the uplands (high ground), where routes crossing the high ground are forced to pass through the town.
A function is the job a town does for its own people and for the area around it. Knowing the functions lets you describe what a town is for and, later, how that has changed.
Residential (people live there), market and retail (buying and selling), and services such as health, education and administration.
Industrial (making goods), port (handling ships and cargo) and transport (road and rail links).
Tourism and recreation, ecclesiastical (to do with the Church) and defence or garrison (soldiers and fortifications).
Commuter (dormitory) towns, where most residents work elsewhere and the town is mainly a place to sleep.
Most towns are multi-functional, which means they carry out several of these functions at once.
Settlements are not all alike. A hierarchy ranks them by size and by the number and range of their functions and services.
The ranking runs from hamlet to village, small town, large town, city and capital (primate) city.
There are few large centres and many small ones, so the hierarchy takes the shape of a pyramid.
A place higher in the hierarchy has more functions and services, so it draws people from a wider area.
Ireland's settlements fit this ranking from one very large capital down to many small villages. These are Census 2022 figures for cities and suburbs, and for towns.
Dublin: about 1.26 million people, far above any other city, so it tops the hierarchy.
Regional cities: Cork, about 222,000; Limerick, about 102,000; Galway, about 86,000; Waterford, about 60,000.
Largest towns: Drogheda, about 44,000, which is Ireland's largest town; Dundalk, about 43,000; Swords, about 41,000. Swords is a town in Fingal, not a separate city.
Many smaller county and market towns, and villages. The State's population is about 5.1 million.
In some countries one city dwarfs all the others. A primate city is much larger than the second city in the country and dominates its functions.
Dublin is a primate city: about six times the size of Cork, the second city.
Causes of Dublin's primacy: its role as capital, its port, its routeway focus (where routes meet), colonial administration (rule by Britain), multinational firms and services.
The rank-size rule, in which the nth city is one nth the size of the largest, does not fit Ireland, because Dublin is far bigger than that rule predicts.
The National Spatial Strategy and the National Planning Framework (government plans) try to balance Dublin's growth with other centres. There is more on this in Urban planning and renewal.
Goods and services differ in how often people buy them and how far they will travel for them. This explains why some are in every village and others only in cities.
Low-order goods are for convenience, such as bread and newspapers. They are found in every village, are bought often and have a low threshold (few customers are needed to keep the shop open).

High-order goods are comparison goods (shoppers compare before buying) and specialised services, such as jewellers, department stores, hospitals and universities. They have a high threshold, needing many customers, so they are found only in large centres.
No town serves only its own residents. The hinterland, also called the sphere of influence, catchment area or umland, is the surrounding area a town serves and draws people from.
The size of a hinterland depends on the town's size and functions, on transport, and on competition from nearby centres.
A hinterland has no fixed edge, so geographers find it by collecting evidence of where people come from to use a town.
Newspaper circulation areas (where the town's paper is sold).
Bus routes and timetables, which show where services run to and from the town.
Catchments of schools and hospitals, meaning the areas they draw pupils and patients from.
Shop customer surveys and delivery areas.
Commuter flows, the movements of people travelling to work in the town.
Sports club catchments, such as the areas their members come from.
Hinterlands are not fixed. They shift as travel and shopping habits change.
Hinterlands overlap, because nearby towns compete for the same customers, and they change over time.
Cars, motorways and online shopping widen hinterlands, because people can reach a town from further away.
Bypasses (roads taking traffic around a town) and out-of-town centres change them.
Example: the large hinterland of Galway city across the West.

Central place theory tries to explain why settlements of different sizes are spaced the way they are. Walter Christaller, a German geographer, published it in 1933, based on a study of southern Germany.
A central place is a settlement providing goods and services to people in its surrounding area.
Threshold is the minimum number of customers needed to keep a service in business. It is a number of people.
Range is the maximum distance people will travel to obtain a service. It is a distance.
A service locates where its threshold falls within its range, so it has enough customers and they are prepared to travel to it.
To make the theory work, Christaller imagined an ideal landscape with no differences between places.
A flat, uniform (isotropic, the same in every direction) plain, so nothing blocks movement.
An evenly spread population with equal purchasing power, so demand is the same everywhere.
Equal ease of transport in all directions.
Consumers buy at the nearest centre.
No excess profits, so no centre earns more than the others.
On such an ideal plain, the theory predicts a regular pattern of centres and market areas.
Market areas are hexagonal, because circles overlap or leave gaps and hexagons fit together.
A hierarchy of centres forms: many small, closely spaced low-order centres, and fewer, more widely spaced high-order centres.
Each higher-order centre also supplies all the lower-order goods, so a city has everything a village has.
Nesting (smaller areas fitting inside larger ones): k = 3 is the marketing principle, k = 4 the transport principle and k = 7 the administrative principle.
Some real places roughly match the theory, especially where farming land is fairly even and settlements were planned.
In parts of the Irish Midlands, market towns serving farming areas are regularly spaced.

The Dutch polder (land reclaimed from water) Noordoostpolder, in the Netherlands, was drained in 1942. Emmeloord was planned as the central town, with ten villages around it, including Marknesse, Ens, Kraggenburg and Bant.
The villages were spaced so that farmers could reach one by bicycle. This gives a planned two-level hierarchy, an almost perfect example of the theory.
Real landscapes are not the ideal plain, so the theory has many weaknesses. Each criticism below breaks one of the assumptions or ignores something real.
Relief (the shape of the land), rivers and coasts are not uniform, and population is unevenly spread.
Transport routes are linear, not equal in all directions, so some places are easier to reach.
People shop on the way to work or on multi-purpose trips, not always at the nearest centre.
Car ownership, motorways, out-of-town shopping centres and online shopping change ranges and thresholds.
Government decisions, such as county towns and new towns, and history, such as Viking and Norman towns, fix locations.
Dublin's primacy breaks the regular hierarchy.
The theory was designed for market (service) towns, not for industrial, port or tourist towns.
Irish settlements can be set against the theory to see how well it fits.
Dublin is at the top, the regional cities come next, then county and market towns, then villages.
The Irish hierarchy is broadly hierarchical but distorted by Dublin's primacy and by the coastline.
Towns do not keep the same jobs forever. Across Ireland, some functions have faded and others have grown.
Defence functions were lost, so walls and garrisons no longer shape towns.
Market and fair functions declined, as marts (livestock markets) and supermarkets took over.
Industrial functions moved from the inner city to the suburbs or closed, so those areas lost jobs.
Services grew, such as offices, tourism, education and health.
Many towns near cities became commuter towns, for example Navan and Naas.
Village services such as the post office, Garda station, pub, shop and school have closed.
Galway is the main case study for changing functions. It began as a walled trading port and grew rich on merchant trade before decline set in.
Galway was a Norman town founded by the de Burgo family in the 13th century.
It was governed by 14 merchant families, the Tribes of Galway. A royal charter (a grant of rights from the Crown) of 1484 was granted.
Galway traded wine with Spain and France, which made it a merchant town and port.
The Spanish Arch, built in 1584, is a surviving part of the town walls.
Galway surrendered to Cromwellian forces in 1652, and a long decline followed.
After its decline, Galway gained new functions in education, high-tech industry, culture and tourism, and became the regional capital of the West.
Queen's College Galway was founded in 1845. It is now the University of Galway, renamed in 2022.
Digital Equipment Corporation opened a plant in Galway in 1971 and closed its manufacturing there in 1993.
Galway is now a centre of the medical devices industry, with multinationals such as Medtronic and Boston Scientific.
The National Spatial Strategy of 2002 named Galway a gateway (a centre chosen for growth). The National Planning Framework of 2018 aims for at least 50% growth in Galway by 2040.
Galway was European Capital of Culture in 2020, jointly with Rijeka, Croatia.
The Galway Arts Festival and the Galway Races at Ballybrit attract visitors, which supports its tourism function.
Galway is the regional capital of the West.
Limerick shows a different path: a river-island settlement that became a fortified city and then a trading port.
Limerick began as a Viking settlement, from about 922.
King John's Castle was built in the early 13th century on King's Island, the island site in the Shannon.
The Treaty of Limerick was signed in 1691.
Limerick developed as a Georgian commercial port (Georgian means the 18th-century style of planning and building). Its Georgian Newtown Pery dates from the late 18th century.
Limerick moved from port and milling to multinational manufacturing, then lost some of that industry and has rebuilt through education, culture and new governance.
Limerick became an industrial city based on its port and flour milling.
Later industry linked to the Shannon area brought multinational investment, including the Shannon Free Zone of 1959 and Shannon Airport nearby.
Dell opened in Limerick in 1990. In January 2009 it announced that it would move manufacturing to Łódź, Poland, with the loss of about 1,900 jobs.
The University of Limerick was founded in 1972 as the National Institute for Higher Education and became a university in 1989.
Limerick was Ireland's first National City of Culture, in 2014.
Limerick City and County Councils merged in 2014.
In 2024 Limerick elected Ireland's first directly elected mayor.
Dublin's functions changed in stages as new roles were added to the old ones.
Georgian city, with the Wide Streets Commissioners of 1757 (the body that planned wide new streets).
Services and technology in the Docklands: the International Financial Services Centre (1987), and Google at Grand Canal Dock.
Smaller towns change too. A market town near a big city can lose its old role and take on a new one as a home for people who work elsewhere.
Market functions, such as the mart and shops serving farmers, decline as the town's population changes.
Services, housing and shops shift to serve commuters who travel to work in a larger city.
Commuter towns of the Greater Dublin Area include Navan, Ashbourne, Naas, Newbridge, Maynooth, Bray and Greystones.
When asked why an urban area grew, use this checklist and back each reason with a case study such as Galway or Limerick.
Site and situation: a bridging point, island, estuary or harbour.
Route focus and port: the town gathers traffic from roads, rivers or the sea.
Administrative role: a national capital, a regional capital or a merged council.
Industry and multinationals: manufacturing and foreign investment.
Services and education: universities and hospitals.
Government policy: national gateways and growth targets, as in the National Spatial Strategy and National Planning Framework.
In-migration: people moving in for work and study.

A large city is divided into zones of land use (areas where one kind of activity dominates). Each zone has its own pattern of buildings and activity, and its own land value. The zones below are typical of a large European city and can all be identified in Dublin.
CBD (central business district): the commercial heart of the city, with the highest land values, tall buildings and the most intensive use of land, meaning the most activity packed onto each site.

Zone in transition: the inner-city area of mixed old housing, warehouses and small industry, where decay and renewal exist side by side. It is called a zone of transition because it is changing from one use to another.
Inner residential zone: older terraced housing (houses joined in rows) close to the centre, so it lies near the CBD and jobs.
Suburbs: lower-density housing, mainly semi-detached houses (pairs of houses sharing one wall), built later and further from the centre, so there is more space for each house.
Industrial zones: the port, inner-city industry, suburban industrial estates and business parks (landscaped sites of modern offices and light industry).
Open space and recreation: parks, playing fields and other green areas within the built-up city, such as Phoenix Park in Dublin.
Transport land: roads, railway lines, the port and the airport, such as Dublin Port and Dublin Airport.
Rural-urban fringe: the transitional land at the edge of the built-up area, where urban and rural land uses meet and compete for the same sites.
The CBD is the most intensively used part of any city. Almost everything about it follows from one fact: it is the most accessible place, so everyone wants a site there.
Land values are highest here because accessibility is greatest, so the most valuable sites are used for the most profitable activities.
Tall buildings maximise the use of expensive land, with several floors of offices or shops on a small site.
Vertical zoning: shops occupy the ground floor, with offices or other uses above, so each floor of a costly site earns money.
Department stores, chain stores and specialist shops occupy the main shopping streets, because these sites bring the most customers.
Offices, banks and the head offices of companies cluster together in the centre, because they can pay the high land values and need to be close to each other and to clients.
Government and cultural buildings are located in the centre, where they are most accessible to the whole population.
Few people live in the CBD, so it is crowded during the working day and quiet at night, when workers and shoppers go home.
Pedestrian streets are used in the busiest shopping areas, where traffic and crowds would otherwise congest the streets.
Dublin's CBD shows these features on a real map, and it is the Irish example to use for the CBD.
Dublin's CBD lies on both sides of the River Liffey.
Its main shopping streets are Grafton Street, south of the Liffey, and Henry Street, north of it. Both are pedestrianised, meaning closed to traffic.
O'Connell Street is the city's main street.

Three models describe how land uses arrange themselves around a city centre. Each is a simplified generalisation, so it is judged by how well it fits the real city. The first is the oldest, and it draws the city as a set of rings.

Ernest Burgess proposed the concentric zone model in 1925, based on Chicago. Land uses form rings around the CBD, with land values and densities (the number of people per area) falling with distance from the centre.
Strength: it shows the regular fall in land value and density outwards from the CBD. Limitation: it ignores transport routes, so it does not fit cities whose growth follows roads and rail lines.
Diagram: concentric rings drawn around a central point labelled CBD, with the zones of transition, residential and commuter land shown in turn.
The second model answers the weakness of the rings: cities do not grow evenly in all directions. Roads, railways and rivers pull growth outwards in lines.
Homer Hoyt proposed the sector model in 1939. Land uses extend outwards in wedge-shaped sectors along transport routes, and a high-class residential sector lies away from industry.

Strength: it explains why sectors of the city are elongated along roads, rail lines and rivers, because transport routes make the land beside them more accessible. Limitation: it does not show the separate suburban centres that grow in large cities.

Diagram: a circle divided into wedge-shaped sectors, with radial transport routes (routes running out from the centre) marked and the high-class residential sector shown away from the industrial sector.
The third model drops the idea of a single centre. In a large modern city, activities gather around several centres (nuclei) at once.
Chauncy Harris and Edward Ullman proposed the multiple nuclei model in 1945. A city grows around several separate centres, such as the CBD, suburban shopping centres, an airport and business parks.
Strength: it explains the growth of suburban centres. Limitation: it gives no simple pattern of rings or sectors, so it is less clear as a general description.
Diagram: a city outline with several separate centres marked, each surrounded by its own cluster of land use.

Dublin fits the multiple nuclei and sector models better than the concentric model: the CBD is one nucleus, while suburban shopping centres and business parks are other nuclei, and growth follows the main roads out of the city.
Dublin shows the zones of a modern European city, with the inner city in transition and the outer city growing along the M50 (the orbital motorway circling the city) and the western new towns.
Georgian core: the Georgian squares (planned 18th-century squares), such as Merrion Square and Fitzwilliam Square, are now largely offices.
The Wide Streets Commissioners, set up in 1757, widened and improved the city's streets, shaping the centre's wide thoroughfares.
Inner-city docklands and the north inner city are in transition, with older industrial and port land being renewed.
Older inner suburbs lie between the centre and the outer suburbs, so their older housing forms an inner residential zone.
Outer suburbs and the western new towns: Tallaght, Clondalkin, Lucan and Blanchardstown, planned in the Wright Report of 1967 (a planning report for the growth of the city).

Business and industrial parks lie near the M50 and the N7 (the national road running south-west from Dublin): Grange Castle, Citywest, Park West and Sandyford. Roads give them access for lorries and workers.
The port and airport are major transport and industrial land uses: Dublin Port and Dublin Airport.

Open space includes Phoenix Park, about 700 hectares and one of Europe's largest enclosed city parks, established in 1662; the Dublin Mountains and Dublin Bay are further open spaces at the edge of the city.
Paris is the world city studied for comparison with Dublin. Its land uses are concentrated in the inner city and organised around a ring road and a set of outer business and housing areas.
The City of Paris has about 2.1 million people on about 105 km2, divided into 20 arrondissements (administrative districts). The wider Ile-de-France region has about 12 million people.
The CBD and government quarter lie in the inner arrondissements, the most central districts.
Haussmann's boulevards: Haussmann rebuilt central Paris between 1853 and 1870, creating wide boulevards that give the inner city its formal street pattern.
La Défense, west of the city, is one of Europe's largest purpose-built business districts, an office district outside the historic inner city.
The Boulevard Périphérique, completed in 1973, is the ring road that forms the boundary of the inner city.
The banlieues are the suburbs beyond the Périphérique, where grands ensembles (large public housing estates built in the 1950s to 1970s) are found, for example Sarcelles.
The 1965 regional plan created five new towns (planned towns built to take growth away from the city): Cergy-Pontoise, Évry, Marne-la-Vallée, Melun-Sénart and Saint-Quentin-en-Yvelines.

Industry has moved out of the inner city to the edge, where land is cheaper and road access is better. This is the first of three movements (industrial, residential, commercial) that change a city's land-use pattern.
Old inner-city industry beside the port, canals and railways (the transport of the time) included brewing, biscuit-making and distilling.
Many of these sites closed or moved to suburban industrial estates and business parks near motorways, so that lorries can reach them easily.

Reasons for the move: lack of space for expansion in the inner city, cheaper land on the edge, road access for lorries, less congestion, planning policy, and new industries needing clean, modern sites.
The vacated inner-city sites are brownfield land (land previously developed, now available for reuse), which can then be redeveloped for other uses.
The Guinness brewery is an exception, having stayed at St James's Gate since Arthur Guinness's lease of 1759.
Jacob's biscuit factory moved from Bishop Street in the inner city to Tallaght in the 1970s. The old factory now houses the National Archives, an example of a brownfield site reused.
Paris: Renault's Boulogne-Billancourt plant closed in 1992, an example of industry leaving the inner city.
Housing has also moved outwards, but in recent years some people have moved back in. Each change raises planning issues.
Inner-city tenements (old multi-occupied houses) were cleared in the 20th century, and their residents were moved to new suburbs and new towns.
Growth of suburban housing spread the city outwards, with sprawl (uncontrolled spread of building) into commuter counties, the counties around the city whose residents travel in to work.
The trend has been reversed in places, with a return to inner-city apartment living in areas such as the Docklands, through regeneration (investment to renew a run-down area).
Issues raised by residential change: the density of housing, the height of buildings and the social mix of the area.
Shops and offices have followed the roads and the car-owning population to the edge of the city. This takes trade and activity away from the centre.
Suburban shopping centres and retail parks have been built beside motorway junctions, where there is car access, free parking and cheaper land.
The Square, Tallaght, opened in 1990; Blanchardstown Centre in 1996; Liffey Valley in 1998; and Dundrum Town Centre in 2005. All are beside major roads or the M50.
Out-of-town office parks have been built in the same way, on sites with good road access, so that workers can drive to them.
Effects on the city centre: vacant units and lost trade, because shoppers move to the edge.
Responses: pedestrianisation of the centre, regeneration of central streets and limits on the size of retail parks, so that the centre can keep its shoppers.
Paris: La Défense takes offices out of the inner city, while the suburban business districts of the region take other commercial uses.
Industry, housing and shops all moving at once creates problems that planners have to manage. These are the main issues.
Zoning: planning authorities divide land into use zones through development plans (official plans for an area) to control where each use may be located.
Brownfield and greenfield development: reuse of old urban land must be balanced against building on undeveloped edge land.
Height and density: taller and denser buildings in the centre raise questions of design, light and services.
Transport: new zones must be linked to public transport, or they generate car journeys and congestion.
Mixed land use: combining housing, offices and shops in one area reduces travel but can cause conflict between uses.
Conflict between business, residents and heritage: new offices or roads can threaten housing or historic buildings.
Bid-rent theory, put forward by William Alonso in 1964, explains why land values and land uses change with distance from the centre. Bid-rent is the most a user can afford to pay for a plot of land.

Accessibility (how easily a site can be reached by people) is greatest at the centre, so competition for sites is fiercest there and land is dearest at the peak land value intersection (PLVI), the point of highest value.
Land values fall with distance from the centre, because each step outwards means less accessibility.
Commerce outbids industry for central sites, and industry outbids housing, because each use can pay a different amount for the same land.
Secondary peaks of land value form at suburban centres, ring-road junctions and along main roads, where accessibility is also high.
Effect on building: tall buildings and intensive use occur at the centre, while large, low-density uses such as warehouses and car parks occur at the edge.
Social stratification is the division of a city's population into groups by income, class, ethnicity, age and family stage, and segregation is the separation of these groups into different areas.

Causes: land and house prices, the allocation of social housing (housing provided by the State for those who cannot afford to buy or rent privately), planning decisions, transport access, household choice and discrimination.
Results: affluent areas are set against areas of concentrated disadvantage, and gated developments (housing estates closed off by gates) create closed residential areas.

Gentrification: better-off people move into and renovate a poorer inner-city area, raising prices and displacing lower-income residents. It is a different process from urban renewal and redevelopment. There is more on this in Urban planning and renewal.
