Both of the case-study cities show segregation on the map. Use these named examples, and keep descriptions of places factual.
Dublin: affluent south-east suburbs, including Ballsbridge, Donnybrook, Dalkey and Foxrock, contrast with lower-income areas in parts of the north inner city and in some outer social-housing estates.
Ballymun is the case of concentrated social housing in Dublin, with seven 15-storey tower blocks built between 1966 and 1969.
Gentrification around the Docklands: the inner-city area has attracted new residents and businesses, including Google's European headquarters at Grand Canal Dock, known as 'Silicon Docks'.
Paris: the wealthy western districts contrast with the poorer north-eastern banlieues of Seine-Saint-Denis, the poorest département (administrative area) in mainland France.
Immigrant residents are concentrated in grands ensembles, and the riots that began in Clichy-sous-Bois in October 2005 showed the tensions in these areas.
As cities grow, they take in rural land at the rural-urban fringe. The pressures on rural land are caused by population growth and by the choices made by households and firms.

Causes: population growth and in-migration (people moving in from elsewhere); demand for cheaper, larger houses; car ownership and motorways; high house prices in the city; and jobs moving to the suburbs.
Loss of farmland: housing, roads and business parks replace fields, and rising land prices encourage farmers to sell, because the land is worth more built on than farmed.
Hobby farms and horse paddocks spread across the fringe, which takes land out of commercial farming.
Commuter villages gain new estates, and their character and community can be lost as their population changes.
Other uses on the fringe: retail parks, business parks, data centres (buildings full of computer servers), landfill sites, quarries and golf courses.
Environmental effects: loss of habitats and hedgerows, and flooding as paved surfaces replace soil that would absorb rainwater.
Conflicts between farmers, residents and developers over the future of the fringe.
Dublin's growth shows these pressures at work in the counties around it.
Sprawl into Meath, Kildare and Wicklow. The Greater Dublin Area had about 2.1 million people at the Census of 2022, about 40% of the State.
Commuter towns: Navan, Ashbourne, Naas, Newbridge, Maynooth, Bray and Greystones, with one-off housing (single houses built in the countryside) across the commuter belt.
Data centres on the city edge used about a fifth of Ireland's metered electricity in 2023 (CSO), most of them in the Dublin region.
Planners have tried to control expansion by protecting land, by building new settlements and by deciding in advance where growth may go.
Green belts (protected rings of open land around a city): London's Metropolitan Green Belt was protected from the 1940s and 1950s to stop the outward sprawl of London.
New towns (planned towns built to take growth away from a city): Britain's New Towns Act 1946 led to Stevenage, the first new town designated, in 1946, and Milton Keynes, designated in 1967.
Paris's five new towns, from the 1965 plan, took population growth away from the city, so that it did not all go into the existing built-up area.
Dublin's western new towns of Tallaght, Clondalkin, Lucan and Blanchardstown were planned after the Wright Report of 1967, so that growth went into planned towns.
Compact growth and brownfield targets, set out in the National Planning Framework, aim to build on land within existing settlements. There is more on this in Urban planning and renewal.
Development plans zone land for particular uses, so that the authorities decide where expansion may take place.

Congestion occurs when the volume of traffic on a road network exceeds the space and capacity available, so vehicles move slowly or stop. Most causes come from how cities grew and how people travel in them.
Rising car ownership puts more vehicles onto streets that were laid out for far fewer, so the same road space has to carry more traffic.

Low-density suburbs (spread-out housing with few homes per hectare) and commuter towns (towns whose residents travel to work elsewhere) are poorly served by public transport, so most journeys are made by car.
Radial roads (roads that run out from the centre like spokes) converge on a historic centre with narrow streets and few river crossings, funnelling traffic into one place.
Journeys to work and school peak at the same times of day, so the network is filled all at once.
Delivery vehicles and heavy goods vehicles (HGVs, large lorries) share the same streets as commuters and shoppers.
Jobs and shopping have dispersed (spread out) to suburbs that can be reached only by car, so even short trips add to road traffic.
Historically weak investment in rail has left cities without a fast alternative to the car.
Congestion costs a city time, money and health. Several of its effects feed back into more congestion.
Workers lose time and productivity, and businesses face higher costs because deliveries and staff are delayed.
Commuters suffer stress and a reduced quality of life.
Stop-start traffic causes air and noise pollution, with carbon emissions from idling engines (engines left running while the vehicle is stationary).
Crowded routes lead to road accidents.
Buses are slowed by the same traffic, which makes public transport less attractive and so adds to car use.
Businesses and tourism are harmed by poor access to the centre.
There is less space for pedestrians and cyclists, because road space is given over to traffic.
Dublin is the Irish city the exams use for traffic congestion. Its congestion comes from the way it spread out and the late arrival of alternatives to the car.
Sprawl (the spread of low-density development at the city edge) and car dependence bring large numbers of commuters into the city every day by car.
Radial routes converge on the centre, and there are few crossings of the River Liffey, so traffic is squeezed onto a handful of bridges.
The light rail network (electric trams) arrived late: the Luas opened in 2004, after the city's roads had already become congested.
Port traffic formerly ran through the city centre until the Port Tunnel opened in 2006.
Cities tackle congestion in two ways: by giving people a better alternative to the car and by managing where and how vehicles travel. These measures are mostly drawn from Dublin.

Public transport: DART (the electric commuter rail along the coast, opened 1984), Luas (opened 2004), commuter rail and BusConnects (a redesign of the bus network), plus the planned MetroLink, which has no date or cost yet.
Luas Cross City linked the Red and Green lines through the city centre in December 2017, so passengers could travel between the two lines.
Bus lanes and quality bus corridors give buses priority over cars, so buses are not slowed by general traffic.
Park and ride: car parks at the edge of the city where drivers can switch to public transport, so fewer cars enter the centre.
Cycle lanes and Dublin Bikes, the public bicycle scheme launched in 2009.
Integrated ticketing: the Leap card, introduced in 2011, allows one card to be used across different transport services.
Orbital roads and bypasses: the M50 orbital motorway, built in stages from 1990, takes traffic around the city instead of through it.
The Port Tunnel, opened in 2006, took port traffic out of the city centre; a 2007 restriction banned most five-axle heavy goods vehicles from the centre.
The second group of measures aims to cut the number of car journeys, by making driving dearer or by making journeys unnecessary.
Pedestrianisation: the busiest shopping streets are closed to traffic.
Parking charges and limits discourage commuters from driving into the centre.
Congestion charging: the London Congestion Charge, introduced in February 2003, is a daily charge to drive into central London on weekdays, and traffic in the zone fell in its early years.
Car sharing, remote working (working from home) and staggered working hours (different start times) spread traffic over time.
Land-use planning that puts homes close to jobs and transport reduces the need to travel by car.

Urban decay is the physical, economic and social decline of part of a city, usually the inner city (the older area close to the centre). It is decline inside the built-up area, not growth at the edge.
Old industries and port jobs close, removing the economic base of the inner city.
Better-off residents move to the suburbs, leaving a smaller and poorer population behind.
Buildings are left derelict (empty and falling into disrepair) and are poorly maintained, particularly social housing (homes provided by the local authority).
Reduced rates income (the local tax paid by businesses and property) means the local authority has less money to maintain buildings and services.
Dereliction attracts crime and vandalism, which deter investment and residents.
Road schemes and planning blight: the threat of future road building leaves property uncertain, so owners stop investing in repairs.
Once decay begins, its effects reinforce each other, so a run-down area is hard to recover without outside help.
Unemployment and poverty among residents of the affected area, because local jobs have gone.
Derelict sites stand empty for long periods, because owners and investors see little reason to rebuild.
Population decline as families leave, so fewer people remain to support local shops and services.
Drug and crime problems, which grow where there are empty buildings and few jobs.
Poor services, because fewer people and less money remain to support them.
Stigma: the reputation of the area discourages investment and visitors.
A cycle of decline, in which each problem makes the others worse.
Dublin's inner city shows how the loss of port jobs and the clearing of old housing left an area empty and run down.
Dublin's docks lost most of their jobs with containerisation (the shift to shipping goods in standard metal containers handled by machinery, needing far fewer workers) from the 1960s and 1970s.
Inner-city tenements (old, overcrowded rented housing) were cleared, and their residents moved to the suburbs.
Dereliction of inner-city streets and buildings followed through the 1970s and 1980s. There is more on this in Urban planning and renewal, which covers the renewal of these areas.
Limerick is an Irish example of decay concentrated in social-housing estates rather than in the old centre.
Disadvantage (poverty and lack of opportunity) was concentrated in social-housing estates: Moyross, Southill, St Mary's Park and Ballinacurra Weston.
After an arson attack on two children in Moyross in 2006, the Government commissioned John Fitzgerald's report, published in 2007.
The report led to the Limerick Regeneration programme for Moyross, Southill, St Mary's Park and Ballinacurra Weston. There is more on its results in Urban planning and renewal.
Detroit, Michigan, USA, is known as 'Motor City', the home of Ford, General Motors and Chrysler. Its decline shows decay on a city-wide scale.
Population peaked at about 1.85 million at the 1950 US census and fell to about 640,000 at the 2020 US census.
Middle-class, largely white families moved to the suburbs from the 1950s, helped by freeways (high-speed urban motorways), which left the city with fewer taxpayers.
Car-industry jobs moved out of the city or were automated (done by machines), so the city lost its main employer base.
Tens of thousands of houses were abandoned, because families had left and there was no demand for them.
Detroit filed for bankruptcy in July 2013, the largest municipal bankruptcy in US history, and exited it in December 2014.
Downtown and Midtown have since seen new investment, although many areas remain derelict.

Urban sprawl is the uncontrolled outward spread of low-density housing and other development over rural land at the edge of a city. It is growth at the edge, unlike urban decay, which is decline inside the city.
Population growth, high prices in the inner city, and demand for houses with gardens push development outwards.
Car ownership and motorways make distant sites accessible, so people can live far from where they work.
Planning that zoned greenfield land (land never built on before) for development, and developers' preference for cheaper greenfield sites, drive building at the edge.
Tax incentives during the Celtic Tiger boom (the period of rapid Irish economic growth in the late 1990s and 2000s) encouraged building.
Sprawl spreads people thinly over a large area, which is costly for the people who live there and for the city they left behind.
Long commutes and congestion, and car dependence, because distances are too long to walk or cycle and public transport is poor.
Loss of farmland and habitats, because rural land is built on. There is more on this in Urban land use and planning.
Costly services, such as roads, water and schools, spread thinly over a large area, so each household costs more to serve.
Dormitory towns, whose residents sleep there and work elsewhere, leaving little local activity.
Decline of the city centre as people and spending move out, and higher carbon emissions from longer car journeys.
Dublin is the Irish example of sprawl, and its sprawl left a visible legacy when the property market collapsed.
Dublin's sprawl has extended into the commuter counties beyond the city boundary.
A Government survey in 2010 found almost 3,000 unfinished housing estates, known as ghost estates, after the 2008 property crash (the sudden collapse in house prices and building).
Solutions either stop the city spreading outwards or make better use of land already built on.
Green belts: a protected ring of open land around the city to stop its spread.
Compact growth and brownfield development (reusing land that was built on before), set out in the National Planning Framework, to build on land within the city.
Higher densities of housing near public transport, so that fewer people need cars.
New towns planned as self-contained settlements with their own services, so residents do not have to travel far.
Regeneration of inner-city sites that are vacant or derelict, so growth is directed inwards.
A community is a group of neighbours who know each other and share local life. In some urban areas the way housing was planned or built stops this from forming.
New estates are built quickly without schools, shops, community centres or public transport, so residents have nowhere to meet.
High-rise flats have no shared space where neighbours can meet.
Long commutes leave little time for local life.
Transient renting populations (tenants who move often) do not put down roots.
Old inner-city communities were demolished when tenements were cleared, breaking up established networks of family and neighbours.
Social segregation separates people by income and class into different areas.
When a place has no shared life, the people in it feel the lack, and the area itself suffers.
Isolation and loneliness among residents who do not know their neighbours.
Anti-social behaviour, which is harder to deal with where neighbours do not know each other.
Little sense of belonging or local organisation, so there are few residents' groups or clubs to take action on local problems.
Examples come from Dublin and from Paris. The responses aim to build the facilities and involvement that were missing.
Ballymun's tower blocks in Dublin: seven 15-storey towers built 1966 to 1969, demolished 2004 to 2015.
Commuter estates and the ghost estates of Dublin's commuter counties.

Paris banlieues (the suburbs on the edge of Paris): large grands ensembles (estates built in the 1950s to 1970s) such as Sarcelles, with high unemployment and the riots that began in Clichy-sous-Bois in October 2005.
Responses: community facilities built alongside housing, with phasing conditions (planning rules) so that schools and shops come before the homes are occupied.
Responses: regeneration with resident participation, mixed tenure (a mix of owned, rented and social homes in one area), and sports clubs and family resource centres.
Urban heritage includes historic buildings, streetscapes (the look of a street as a whole), archaeological sites and monuments, together with their setting. It is valuable in three ways.
Identity: heritage gives a city and its residents a sense of their history and place.
Tourism: historic buildings and monuments attract visitors and the income they bring.
Economic value: restored heritage buildings can support shops, hotels and cultural venues.
Heritage is easily lost because the pressures of a growing city work against old buildings.
Demolition for offices and roads, as when historic buildings are cleared for new development.
Neglect and dereliction of old buildings, so that without repair they decay and may have to be demolished.
Inappropriate new buildings, with heights that are out of scale with the historic streetscape.
Traffic vibration and pollution, which damage old buildings and monuments.
Tourist pressure, which can wear down historic sites and crowd out local residents.
Dublin has both losses and successes. The losses show the threats above, and the reuse examples show heritage put to work.

Lower Fitzwilliam Street: the ESB (Ireland's electricity company) demolished a row of 16 Georgian houses in 1965 to build its head office. That office block has itself since been demolished and replaced.
Wood Quay: one of the largest Viking-age sites in Europe. Despite protests and court cases in the late 1970s, Dublin Corporation (the city council) built its civic offices on the site.
14 to 17 Moore Street, where the 1916 leaders spent their last hours before surrender, was declared a national monument in 2007.
Positive reuse: Temple Bar was regenerated in the 1990s, and Docklands warehouses have been reused for new purposes.
Heritage is protected by law, by voluntary groups and by international listing.

The Planning and Development Act 2000 created the Record of Protected Structures (a list of buildings the law protects) and Architectural Conservation Areas (whole areas protected for their character).
National monuments are protected by the State.
An Taisce (the National Trust for Ireland), founded in 1948, campaigns for the protection of heritage.

UNESCO World Heritage listing (international recognition of sites of outstanding value): Ireland's two World Heritage Sites are Brú na Bóinne, listed in 1993, and Skellig Michael, listed in 1996. Neither is urban.
International urban examples: the Old and New Towns of Edinburgh, listed by UNESCO in 1995, and the Historic Centre of Rome, listed in 1980.
Heritage attracts visitors in smaller cities as well as in Dublin.
Kilkenny's Medieval Mile attracts heritage tourism to a smaller Irish city. There is more on its medieval history in Pre-historic and historic settlement.
Environmental quality is how clean, quiet and pleasant an urban area is. Air quality is the first aspect, and Dublin's ban on smoky coal is the Irish example of a response to air pollution.
Sources of urban air pollution: smoke from coal fires, and traffic emissions of nitrogen dioxide and particulates (tiny solid particles in the air).
Dublin's severe winter smog (smoke and fog mixed) in the 1980s led to the ban on smoky coal in Dublin from 1 September 1990.
Research after the ban found that black smoke levels and winter death rates fell.
The ban on smoky coal was extended nationwide in October 2022.
Cities produce large amounts of sewage and polluted runoff, which must be treated before it reaches rivers and the sea.
The Ringsend wastewater treatment plant treats most of Dublin's sewage and discharges into Dublin Bay.
The Ringsend plant is being upgraded, so that it can keep treating the sewage of a growing city.
Storm overflows: heavy rain can send mixed sewage and surface water into urban rivers and the bay, because the drains cannot carry the extra volume.
Urban rivers carry pollution from paved surfaces, roads and drains.
Waste that is not recycled or treated becomes litter or goes to landfill, which harms the look and quality of an urban area. Ireland has used charges, recycling and energy recovery to cut it.
Litter and landfill: waste that is not recycled or treated goes to landfill (buried in the ground).
Plastic bag levy: introduced in March 2002 at 15 cent, after which plastic bag use fell sharply, showing a charge can change behaviour.
Recycling schemes reduce the amount of waste sent to landfill, because materials are reused instead of buried.
Poolbeg (Dublin Waste-to-Energy) incinerator, operating since 2017, burns residual waste (what is left after recycling) to generate energy.
Not all pollution is chemical. Noise and an ugly environment also lower the quality of life in a city.
Noise from traffic, construction and night-time activity affects residents, for example by disturbing sleep.
Visual pollution: graffiti, poor signage and unsightly derelict buildings reduce the quality of the streetscape.
Derelict sites: the Derelict Sites levy is a charge on owners of derelict property to encourage its reuse.
Green space gives wildlife a home and gives residents somewhere to relax. Dublin has several examples.
Parks provide habitats and recreation: Phoenix Park, about 700 hectares, established 1662.
Canals provide green corridors (strips of greenery that wildlife can move along) through the city: the Royal Canal and the Grand Canal.
North Bull Island, in Dublin Bay, is a green space beside the city.
Loss of green space to infill: small gaps between buildings are built on, reducing open space for wildlife and residents.
Building over land changes how water and heat behave in a city, which causes two problems.
Urban flooding: paved surfaces stop rain soaking into the ground, so runoff (water flowing over the surface) rises quickly into rivers and drains.
Hurricane Charley, in August 1986, caused severe flooding of the River Dodder in Dublin.
Urban heat island: built-up areas are warmer than the surrounding countryside because buildings and paving absorb and hold heat.
Cities try to solve their problems by controlling how land is used and by fixing areas that have decayed. Three terms describe the different approaches, and examiners expect you to keep them apart.

Urban planning is controlling the use and development of land through development plans (official documents setting out what may be built where), zoning (assigning each area a permitted use), planning permission and public investment.
Urban renewal is improving and rehabilitating existing run-down areas, keeping the community in place, so the buildings are upgraded but the people stay.
Urban redevelopment is clearing an area completely and rebuilding it, often with new uses and new people, so the old community is usually not the one that returns.
Renewal improves what is already there, while redevelopment clears and rebuilds. Ballymun and Limerick combined both, while the Docklands was mainly redevelopment because it was cleared and rebuilt.

Gentrification can be a side-effect of renewal or redevelopment: better-off people move in, prices rise and original residents are displaced, meaning they are forced out because they can no longer afford to live there.
Planners have a toolkit of legal controls, financial incentives and special bodies. Each one is used to steer where and how a city grows or is renewed.
Development plans and zoning decide the uses permitted in each area, such as housing, industry or open space, so that incompatible uses are kept apart.
Tax incentives in designated areas (areas officially chosen for support) reduce the cost of restoring or building there, which makes private developers willing to invest in run-down places.

Special development agencies with planning powers, such as the Dublin Docklands Development Authority (DDDA) and the London Docklands Development Corporation (LDDC), take charge of one area and drive its renewal.
Strategic Development Zones are fast-track planning for areas of national importance, so large projects avoid the usual delays.

Part V of the Planning and Development Act 2000 requires that part of new housing development be social (State-provided for low-income households) and affordable housing. Up to 20% of land zoned for housing could be required for this purpose.
The Part V share was reduced to 10% in 2015 and restored to 20% by the Affordable Housing Act 2021. Strategic Development Zones are created under the same Act.
Other tools aim at reusing unused land, connecting areas and involving the people who live there.
Derelict and vacant sites levies charge owners of unused property, to encourage its reuse instead of leaving it empty.
Public transport investment links new and renewed areas to the rest of the city, so residents can reach jobs and services.
New towns are planned as new settlements away from the existing city, taking growth from the older built-up area.
Regeneration companies with community participation bring residents into decisions about their area, so renewal is done with local people and not just to them.

The Advisory Regional Plan for Dublin, by Myles Wright in 1967, proposed the western new towns of Tallaght, Clondalkin, Lucan and Blanchardstown. It is the first national-scale plan to judge for effectiveness.
What it did: it housed rapid growth in new towns on the western edge of Dublin, rather than letting the existing city spread unplanned.
Effectiveness: the towns were built before services, jobs and transport, so their residents depended on distant jobs and facilities.
Tallaght's shopping centre, The Square, opened only in 1990, and the Luas Red Line (Dublin's light rail tram line) to Tallaght opened in 2004, decades after the first homes.

Criticism: the plan produced sprawl (unplanned spreading of the built-up area into the countryside) and the absence of community, because the towns lacked the facilities that would have made them places in their own right.
The National Spatial Strategy tried to balance growth across the country so that Dublin did not take everything. It did this by building up other centres.

What it did: it named nine gateways (large centres to drive regional growth: Dublin, Cork, Limerick/Shannon, Galway, Waterford, Dundalk, Sligo, Letterkenny with Derry, and Athlone-Tullamore-Mullingar) and nine hubs (smaller supporting centres), to balance growth away from Dublin.
The 2003 Budget announced a decentralisation programme (moving government jobs out of Dublin) that moved civil servants to dozens of towns.
Effectiveness: the plan was weakened by too many designated centres, which spread investment thinly, by decentralisation to towns not named in the plan, and by the property boom.
Dublin continued to sprawl, so the plan did not achieve its aim of balancing growth.
The strategy was replaced in 2018 by the National Planning Framework.
The National Planning Framework, known as Project Ireland 2040, was published in 2018 to replace the National Spatial Strategy. It plans where a growing population will live.
It plans for about 1 million more people in Ireland by 2040.
Half of future population growth is to be in Dublin, Cork, Limerick, Galway and Waterford, the five cities.
Galway, Cork, Limerick and Waterford are each to grow by at least 50%, so that the regional cities act as a counterweight to Dublin.

Compact growth: 40% of new homes nationally are to be within the built-up footprint of existing settlements, on brownfield (previously used) and infill (gaps between existing buildings) land. This limits sprawl.
Regional Spatial and Economic Strategies are prepared by the three regional assemblies (regional bodies of local councillors), to apply the national plan at regional level.
The Urban Regeneration and Development Fund was set up in 2018 so as to fund renewal projects.
Effectiveness: too early to judge fully, but housing supply has lagged behind the targets.

Housing is one of three urban problems (with transport and pollution) on which planning effectiveness is judged. The strategies are the Part V requirement, Rent Pressure Zones and national housing targets.
Housing for All (2021) set a target of an average of about 33,000 new homes a year to 2030.
Rent Pressure Zones (areas where rent rises are capped) were introduced in December 2016, first in Dublin and Cork, to limit rent increases.
Part V social and affordable housing, described under Tools available to planners, adds homes within private developments, so new estates are not only for those who can pay market prices.
Effectiveness: completions (finished new homes) have risen, but they have stayed below the level of need, so shortages continue.
Over 15,000 people were in State-funded emergency accommodation in 2025, a record level of homelessness.
High rents remain a problem, which shows that the strategies have not yet matched demand.
The transport strategy covers public transport investment and cycling, with the aim of reducing congestion (traffic jams caused by too many vehicles on the roads).
DART (the electric coastal rail line) opened in 1984, and the Luas Cross City linked the Red and Green lines through the city centre in December 2017.
The Port Tunnel opened in 2006, and the 2007 restriction on heavy goods vehicles kept most five-axle lorries out of the city centre.
Dublin Bikes (a public bike-hire scheme) was launched in 2009 to encourage cycling, and BusConnects is the bus network redesign.
The NTA (National Transport Authority) Greater Dublin Area Transport Strategy 2022 to 2042 sets out the long-term plan.
Effectiveness: the Luas and the Port Tunnel succeeded in their aims, because they added rail capacity and took heavy lorries out of the centre.

Metro North, a planned rail line to Dublin Airport and Swords, was shelved by the Government in 2011. Its successor, MetroLink, is planned but has been repeatedly delayed, and no date or cost is yet set.
Congestion persists because land use remains dispersed (spread out), so people still need cars to reach jobs and shops.
Pollution policy mixes bans, charges and infrastructure upgrades. Some measures have clearly worked, while others have left problems behind.
Smoky coal ban: introduced in Dublin on 1 September 1990 and extended nationwide in October 2022.
Plastic bag levy, introduced in 2002 to make bags cost money, which cut plastic bag use sharply.
Ringsend wastewater treatment plant upgrade, so as to reduce discharges into Dublin Bay.
Clean Air Strategy, published in 2023 to tackle air pollution from traffic and solid fuel.
Effectiveness: smoke and smog were largely removed after the coal ban, because the main source of the smoke was banned.
Limits: traffic nitrogen dioxide (a gas from vehicle exhausts) and particulates (tiny airborne particles) from solid fuel remain problems.

The Docklands were derelict after the docks lost their trade to containerisation (goods moving in standard steel containers, which needed deep-water ports with more space). Renewal there was mainly redevelopment, clearing and rebuilding the area.
Actions: the Urban Renewal Act 1986 gave tax incentives in the designated area.

The Custom House Docks Development Authority was set up in 1986 to lead the renewal, and the International Financial Services Centre (IFSC) was set up in 1987. These are two different dates from the DDDA.
The Dublin Docklands Development Authority was set up in 1997, and was wound up in 2016 with its functions passing to Dublin City Council.

Flagship projects (high-profile showpiece developments): the Samuel Beckett Bridge (2009), the Convention Centre Dublin (2010), the Bord Gais Energy Theatre (2010) and the Luas Red Line extension to The Point (2009).
A Strategic Development Zone covering North Lotts and Grand Canal Dock was designated in 2014.
Results: new offices, homes and culture venues, and the Docklands became a centre for tech firms, including Google's European headquarters at Grand Canal Dock, known as 'Silicon Docks'.

Criticism: early schemes favoured offices and expensive apartments, while local residents got few of the jobs created. Social housing was slow to be built, and gentrification pushed up prices, so locals could not afford the area.
The DDDA was damaged by its role in the purchase of the Irish Glass Bottle site, Ringsend, in 2006 for about €412 million, at the peak of the property bubble. The land value collapsed after 2008.
Temple Bar is a renewal case: an existing run-down area was improved and turned into a cultural quarter rather than cleared.
Problem: the CIÉ (the State transport company) planned a central bus station in Temple Bar in the 1980s, and bought up property in the area.
Artists and small businesses moved in on short leases because rents were cheap in the run-down area, bringing new life to the area.
The bus station plan was dropped, and Temple Bar Properties was set up in 1991 under the Temple Bar Area Renewal and Development Act 1991.
Dublin was European City of Culture in 1991, which gave the area national attention.
Results: cultural venues, including the Irish Film Institute and the Project Arts Centre; restored buildings; and tourism.
Criticism: the area became dominated by pubs and night-time tourism, and few people live there permanently.
Ballymun combined renewal and redevelopment. Its 1960s high-rise flats were replaced by new low-rise housing and a new town centre.
Problems: seven 15-storey towers built in 1966 to 1969 suffered isolation, poor maintenance, unemployment and drugs.
Ballymun Regeneration Ltd was set up by Dublin Corporation in 1997.
The towers were demolished between 2004 and 2015, and new low-rise homes were built.
New facilities included Main Street, the Axis arts and community centre, and an IKEA store, which opened in 2009 as IKEA's first store in the Republic of Ireland.
Effectiveness: housing quality improved, and residents were involved in the regeneration, so people had a say.
Limits: the recession stalled the town centre, so it stayed unfinished; the promised Metro North rail link was never built (it was shelved in 2011), and unemployment stayed high.

Limerick Regeneration addresses estates of concentrated disadvantage (where poverty and social problems are clustered together), after the 2006 arson attack in Moyross and the 2007 report by John Fitzgerald.
Limerick Regeneration agencies were set up in 2007, and were later integrated into Limerick City and County Council, formed in 2014.
The programme covered Moyross, Southill, St Mary's Park and Ballinacurra Weston.
Actions: demolition of the worst estates, building of new homes, and social and economic programmes.
Criticism: the regeneration was slow, and demolition outpaced rebuilding, so families were left waiting for new homes.
Criticism: the populations of the estates fell during the process, because residents moved away.
Adamstown, near Lucan in South Dublin, is a planned new suburb built as a Strategic Development Zone. It tests whether planners can deliver services alongside homes, the failing of earlier new towns.
Designated a Strategic Development Zone in 2001, with fast-track planning.
Planned as a new suburb with its own railway station on the Kildare line, and with schools and services built in phases alongside the housing.
Effectiveness: a model of planned phasing, in which services arrive with the homes, so residents are not left without schools or transport.
Development stalled after the 2008 property crash and resumed in the late 2010s, showing how much the scheme depended on the market.
Renewal is not only a Dublin matter. Tax relief and strategic plans were also used in the smaller cities, with Cork the main example.
Living City Initiative, introduced in 2015: tax relief for refurbishing older buildings in special regeneration areas of Dublin, Cork, Limerick, Galway, Waterford and Kilkenny, later extended.
Cork Area Strategic Plan, 2001, a plan for the city and its surroundings, guided planning in the city.
The Cork city boundary was extended in 2019, so the city could plan for its growing suburbs.
Luas Cork: a light rail line proposed in the Cork Metropolitan Area Transport Strategy of 2020. It is proposed only, and no cost, route length or opening date has been set.
Cork Docklands is the next large regeneration project in the city.

The London Docklands were redeveloped after the docks closed in the 1960s to 1980s. The scheme was top-down (decided and run from above rather than by local people), led by an agency with its own planning powers.
London Docklands Development Corporation, 1981 to 1998, was an unelected body with planning powers.
An Enterprise Zone on the Isle of Dogs gave tax breaks and simplified planning, to attract investors.
Canary Wharf was developed, with One Canada Square completed in 1991.
The Docklands Light Railway opened in 1987, and London City Airport opened in 1987.
The Jubilee Line extension opened in 1999, which is why critics say transport came late.
Results: a second financial centre (after the City of London), so jobs and housing followed.
Criticism: the corporation was top-down and bypassed local councils, because it was unelected and held the planning powers.
Criticism: jobs went to commuters from outside the area, while local residents were priced out, and transport came late.
Paris gives a second developed-world example of planning by new towns and large estates.
The five new towns from the 1965 regional plan, so as to relieve pressure, took growth away from the city of Paris.
The grands ensembles, large housing estates in the banlieues (the suburbs around the city), became problem estates.
The Grand Paris Express, about 200 km of new automatic metro lines with 68 stations, aims to link the banlieues to the rest of the region.
Putting the strategies and case studies together gives three conclusions that you can use to finish a long answer.
Planning works best, for example in Adamstown, when housing, jobs, services and transport are delivered together, and when residents are involved in decisions.
Flagship property-led schemes create jobs and buildings, but do not always bring benefits to local people, as in the Docklands.
National plans are undermined when other policies pull in the opposite direction, such as tax incentives for development and decentralisation to towns outside the plan.
Cities in the developing world (poorer countries, mostly in Asia, Africa and Latin America) now account for most of the world's urban growth. The UN figures below show how big the shift is.
Most of the world's urban growth now takes place in developing countries in Asia, Africa and Latin America, so the fastest-growing cities are no longer in Europe or North America.
About 30% of the world's population was urban (living in towns and cities) in 1950 and about 55% in 2018 (UN, World Urbanization Prospects 2018).
Over half of the world's population has been urban since about 2007, so the world passed the point where city dwellers outnumber rural dwellers.
The UN projects that about 68% of the world's population will be urban by 2050.
Close to 90% of the increase to 2050 is expected in Asia and Africa; India, China and Nigeria together account for over a third of it.
Megacities, with over 10 million people, are a growing feature of urbanisation in the developing world.
UN-Habitat (the UN agency for human settlements) estimates that over 1 billion people live in slums or informal settlements, meaning crowded housing built without legal permission or services.

Cities grow in two ways: more babies than deaths, and more people arriving than leaving. In developing countries both are strong at once. There is more on migration theory in the Rural-to-urban migration in developed and developing regions note.
Natural increase (births minus deaths): the urban population is young, birth rates are high and death rates have fallen, so the city grows even without newcomers.

Push factors (things that drive people out of the countryside): rural poverty, landlessness, small farms, mechanisation (machines replacing farm workers), drought and crop failure, lack of services, conflict and natural disasters.
Pull factors (things that draw people to the city): jobs in the formal and informal sectors, higher wages, schools and hospitals, perceived opportunities, and family already living in the city.
Primate cities (a country's largest city, far bigger than any other) attract investment and government spending, which reinforces their pull on migrants.
Migrants arrive faster than the city can build homes, and most have little money. They build their own shelter wherever they can, which creates the first and most visible problem of rapid growth.
Migrants with little money and no legal land settle in shanty towns, slums and informal settlements, called bustees, favelas, chawls or jhopadpattis depending on the country.
These settlements are built on marginal land (land nobody else wants because it is unsafe or unsuitable): river banks, steep slopes, beside railways, rubbish dumps and floodplains.
Tenure (the legal right to occupy land) is insecure, so residents can be evicted and have no legal right to the land they occupy.
Overcrowding is severe, and some people have no shelter at all, living as homeless pavement dwellers.
Informal settlements are built without services, and this directly harms health. Sanitation means the safe disposal of human waste and dirty water.
Without piped water or sewers, settlements rely on open drains and shared toilets, so waste stays close to where people live and cook.
Contaminated water and waste spread water-borne disease (illness carried in dirty water): cholera, typhoid and dysentery.
There are not enough regular jobs for all the migrants, so many make a living outside the formal economy. The informal sector means work that is unregistered, untaxed and unprotected.
Many residents work in the informal sector as street vendors, rickshaw pullers, waste pickers and home workers.
Informal work offers no job security and low pay; child labour is part of informal employment.
Underemployment means that people have work but not enough of it to earn a living, so they are counted as working yet remain poor.
Road and rail systems were built for much smaller populations. When the city expands faster than its transport, movement slows for everyone.
Road networks cannot cope with the growth in traffic, so journeys take longer and congestion (traffic jams) becomes permanent.
Trains and buses are overcrowded at peak times, when most people travel to and from work.
Road deaths are a serious problem in the city, because crowded roads mix heavy traffic with pedestrians.
Crowded cities with weak services release waste into the air, rivers and streets faster than it can be removed.
Air pollution comes from traffic, industry and cooking fuels burned in crowded homes.
Untreated sewage and industrial waste are discharged into rivers, because there are no treatment plants to clean them first.
Rubbish is not collected in many areas, so it builds up in streets and drains.
Poor people settle on the land most exposed to danger, so natural hazards hit informal settlements hardest.

Monsoon (seasonal heavy rain) or tropical downpours flood low-lying, paved and badly drained land, where settlements are often built; paving stops rain soaking into the ground and poor drains cannot carry it away.
Hillside slums are at risk of landslides, and crowded, poorly built homes are at risk of fire.
Rapid growth also produces social strains, which weak city government is too stretched to manage.
Crime and drugs are social problems, and street children live and work on the streets.
Rich and poor districts sit side by side, so inequality is visible within the city.
Local government is weak, so it struggles to provide services.
The first response to slums is often to remove them. This is the least successful of the solutions.
Slum clearance removes informal settlements by demolition and eviction (forcing residents out).
It usually fails, because residents are moved further out or into new slums and the underlying problems (poverty and lack of housing) remain.
Instead of building homes for people, the authorities prepare land and let residents do the building. No named scheme is needed for this general solution.
In a site-and-service scheme the authorities provide serviced plots with water, drains and power.
Residents build their own homes on these plots, which is known as aided self-help (the authorities help with the services, the residents do the building).
Upgrading improves a slum where it stands rather than removing it, so nobody has to move.
Lanes are paved, water taps, toilets, drains and electricity are installed, and residents are given secure tenure (a legal right to stay).
Because the community stays in place, people can improve their own homes over time, as they no longer fear eviction.
Another approach is to build new towns beside the city so that growth goes there instead of into the crowded centre.
Planned satellite towns and new towns (towns built beside a large city, with planned housing, jobs and services) divert growth away from the overcrowded core.
Examples are given in the Mumbai case study (Navi Mumbai) and the Kolkata case study (Salt Lake and New Town).
Cities cannot solve congestion just by building more roads, so they invest in public transport that carries many people at once.

Metros (underground or elevated urban railways), suburban rail and bus rapid transit (buses with their own lanes and fast boarding, working like a train system) move large numbers of people without adding more cars to the roads.
Curitiba in Brazil is the leading example of bus rapid transit, described below.
Curitiba, in southern Brazil, shows how a cheap, well-planned bus system can ease traffic in a developing-world city.
Bus rapid transit began in Curitiba in 1974 under architect-mayor Jaime Lerner.
Dedicated bus lanes and raised tube stations allow fast boarding, which reduces car use because the bus is quicker than sitting in traffic.
Recyclable waste could be exchanged for food or bus tokens, which tackled rubbish and helped poorer residents at the same time.
The model has been copied worldwide, for example in Bogotá's TransMilenio (2000).
Some solutions act on the push factors in the countryside, so fewer people leave for the city in the first place.
Rural development, land reform (giving landless farmers land) and jobs in smaller cities give people reasons to stay in rural areas.
NGOs (non-governmental organisations, i.e. charities) and community groups also act on these problems, as the Missionaries of Charity do in Kolkata.
Kolkata (called Calcutta until 2001) is the main developing-world case study. Its site and history explain why it became one of India's largest cities.
Kolkata lies on the Hooghly river near the Bay of Bengal, on low-lying delta land (flat land built up by river deposits), which is why it floods easily.
It was founded in 1690 by the British East India Company (Job Charnock).
It developed as a port on the Hooghly, with jute mills (factories making cloth and sacks from the jute plant); Howrah Bridge across the river opened in 1943.
It was the capital of British India until 1911, so government jobs and trade drew people to it.
The city was renamed from Calcutta to Kolkata in 2001.
Kolkata grew because colonial rule built an economy that drew people in, and because disasters and wars then pushed more people towards it.
It was a colonial port and administrative capital, and its jute and engineering industries attracted migrants from Bihar, Odisha and rural Bengal.
The Bengal famine of 1943 drove millions of rural people towards the city.
Partition in 1947 (the division of British India into India and Pakistan) brought refugees, and the 1971 Bangladesh Liberation War brought a further wave.
Natural increase adds to the population, and the city has regional primacy in eastern India, meaning it dominates the region's economy and services.
Census 2011 gave an urban agglomeration (the built-up city and its suburbs) of about 14.1 million people.
Migrants arriving faster than housing could be built ended up in slums or on the streets.
Bustees (slums) house many of the city's poorest people, in overcrowded conditions, because they cannot afford other housing.
Pavement dwellers have no shelter and live on the streets.
Census 2011 counted about 65 million people in slums across India; this is an India-wide figure, not a Kolkata figure.
Kolkata's economy weakened just as migrants kept arriving, so there were too few jobs.
Partition cut the city off from the jute-growing lands that became East Pakistan, so the economy declined because the jute mills lost their raw material.
Jobs did not keep pace with migrants, so many people depend on informal work.
Informal work includes hand-pulled rickshaws; Kolkata is one of the few cities in the world where these still operate.
Services and infrastructure (the basic systems a city runs on) were never built for so many people, and the city's low-lying site adds to the problems.
Water supply and sewerage (the system of pipes carrying away waste water) are poor, so many residents lack safe water and proper sanitation.
Monsoon rain floods the low-lying streets of the city.
Air pollution and traffic congestion add to the city's environmental problems.
Kolkata's planners, governments and charities have tried housing, transport, new towns and environmental solutions. Together these form the solutions part of the case study.
The Calcutta Metropolitan Development Authority, the city's planning body, was set up in 1970.
From the 1970s its bustee improvement programme provided water taps, toilets, paved lanes and drains.
Kolkata Metro, India's first, opened in 1984, which eases congestion by moving people underground.
Salt Lake City (Bidhannagar) is a planned township built from the 1960s on reclaimed wetland (wetland drained and filled to make building land) east of the city; its Sector V is an IT hub.
New Town (Rajarhat) was planned from the late 1990s, with IT parks (business parks for information technology firms).
The East Kolkata Wetlands were designated a Ramsar wetland of international importance in 2002; their fish ponds and fields use and naturally treat much of the city's sewage.
Mother Teresa founded the Missionaries of Charity in the city in 1950 and received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1979.
To judge the responses, ask who benefited and what is left unsolved.
Bustee upgrading improved conditions for many residents, but slums remain.
The new towns serve the middle classes more than the poor.
Mumbai (called Bombay until 1995) is the second Indian case study. Its natural harbour and its role as a trading centre made it a magnet for migrants.
Mumbai was originally seven islands, joined together by land reclamation (building up land from the sea), with a deep, sheltered natural harbour.
It was a British East India Company port, and cotton mills were built there from the 19th century.
Mumbai is India's financial capital, not its political capital; it houses the Reserve Bank of India headquarters and the Bombay Stock Exchange, founded in 1875, Asia's oldest.
It is the centre of the Bollywood film industry, which is another source of jobs that attracts migrants.
The city was renamed from Bombay in 1995.
Migrants come from across India, including Bihar and Uttar Pradesh, drawn by industry and jobs.
Census 2011 gave a Greater Mumbai urban agglomeration (the city plus its built-up suburbs) of about 18.4 million people.
Mumbai is built on a narrow strip of land, so space is short and housing is expensive. Many people end up in slums.
Dharavi is one of Asia's largest slums, in central Mumbai, with many small home-based industries such as recycling, leather and pottery.
Land and housing costs are very high on the narrow peninsula (a strip of land almost surrounded by water), which limits the space available for housing.
Dense population puts pressure on transport and services, and heavy monsoon rain can overwhelm the city.
The suburban railway carries several million passengers a day, and its trains are overcrowded.
Road congestion adds to the pressure on the transport network.
On 26 July 2005 about 944 mm of rain fell in one day at Santacruz, flooding the city.
Water supply and sanitation cannot keep pace with the dense population.
Mumbai's old industrial base collapsed in the 1980s, which changed where people worked.
The Great Bombay textile strike of 1982 led to the closure of most cotton mills.
Mill land was later redeveloped, so the city's industrial base changed, for example away from cotton.
Mumbai's planners tried to relieve the crowded island city by building a second city across the water.
Navi Mumbai is a planned twin city across the harbour, begun in the 1970s by CIDCO (City and Industrial Development Corporation of Maharashtra, set up 1970).
It is designed to take population and industry away from the crowded core of Mumbai.
Rehabilitation means rehousing slum dwellers in new buildings, with private developers paying for it.
The Slum Rehabilitation Authority, set up in 1995, lets developers rehouse slum dwellers free in new blocks and sell the remaining flats, so the developers pay for it from those sales.
The Dharavi Redevelopment Project was awarded to the Adani Group in 2022, as a plan to rebuild the slum, for example with new housing.
New rail and road links ease pressure on Mumbai's transport and tie it to Navi Mumbai.
Mumbai Metro Line 1 opened in 2014, so some commuters have an alternative to the overcrowded roads and trains.
The Bandra–Worli Sea Link opened in 2009, a road bridge over the sea that shortens journeys across the city.
The Mumbai Trans Harbour Link (Atal Setu), opened in January 2024, is India's longest sea bridge and links Mumbai to Navi Mumbai.
Rehousing gave people new homes but has drawbacks.
Rehousing flats under the Slum Rehabilitation Authority are criticised for poor design.
Rehousing is also criticised for breaking up Dharavi's home-based industries, which depended on the slum's layout and community for their work.
São Paulo is the Latin American case study. It is not Brazil's capital (that is Brasília) and it is not on the coast.
São Paulo lies on a plateau inland from the port of Santos, not on the coast.
It was founded on 25 January 1554 by Jesuit missionaries, long before its coffee and industrial growth.
Santos is now Latin America's busiest container port, which is why trade and growth gathered inland at São Paulo.
Coffee, immigration and industry each brought a new wave of people to São Paulo.
Coffee wealth in the 19th century was exported through Santos and carried by the Santos–Jundiaí railway, opened in 1867.
Immigration from Europe, especially Italy, in the late 19th and early 20th centuries.
Japanese immigration began in 1908 with the ship Kasato Maru; the city has the largest Japanese community outside Japan, centred on the Liberdade district.
From the 1950s São Paulo became Brazil's industrial heartland; car plants, including Volkswagen, opened in the ABC region (Santo André, São Bernardo do Campo and São Caetano do Sul).
Migrants from the drought-prone North-East of Brazil, known as nordestinos, moved to the city to work in its industries.
Be clear whether a figure refers to the city or the wider metropolitan region, because the two are very different.
IBGE (the Brazilian statistics agency) Census 2022 gave the city of São Paulo about 11.5 million people and the metropolitan region about 21 million.
São Paulo is the largest city in South America and in the Southern Hemisphere.
Brazil is over 80% urban, so São Paulo's growth is part of a country-wide shift.
São Paulo's wealth sits right beside poverty, and informal housing (favelas) is the clearest sign of this.
Paraisópolis favela borders the wealthy district of Morumbi, so extreme inequality is visible from one street to the next.
Heliópolis is São Paulo's largest favela.
Crime is a problem in the city, including in its favelas, so inequality has social effects as well as housing ones.
A very large metropolitan region puts heavy pressure on its roads, air and rivers.
Traffic congestion is severe across the metropolitan region.
Air pollution from vehicles and industry adds to the city's environmental problems.
The Tietê river flows through the city and floods in heavy summer rain.
Unusually, São Paulo's problem was too little water, not too much.
The Cantareira reservoir system (a group of reservoirs) is the main source of the city's water.
During the 2014–2015 drought the Cantareira fell to very low levels, and water rationing (limiting how much water people receive) was introduced.
The authorities have tried traffic limits, new transport and new housing.
Rodízio, from 1997: cars are banned from central São Paulo at rush hours on one weekday, according to the last digit of the number plate, which cuts the number of cars on the road each day.
The São Paulo Metro opened its first line in 1974, so that people can travel without using the congested roads.
The Rodoanel Mário Covas ring road encircles the metropolitan region, so traffic can bypass the centre; its first section opened in 2002.
Projeto Cingapura (1990s) replaced some favela shacks with apartment blocks on the same sites.
Minha Casa, Minha Vida, a national subsidised housing programme (the state pays part of the cost), was launched in 2009.
The measures have made a difference, but not enough.
Favela upgrading and transport improvements have helped.
Favelas and traffic congestion persist, because growth has outpaced the measures taken.

The world keeps urbanising, which means a growing share of people live in towns and cities rather than the countryside. All the issues facing cities of the future follow from this trend. The UN figures below are projections for the future, not facts.
About 30% of the world's population was urban in 1950 and about 55% in 2018 (UN, World Urbanization Prospects 2018).
The UN projects about 68% of the world's population to be urban by 2050. Write it as a projection, not as a fact.
Close to 90% of the increase in urban population is expected in Asia and Africa. India, China and Nigeria together account for over a third of it.
In 2018 there were 33 megacities (cities with over 10 million people).
Tokyo was the largest urban agglomeration (a city together with its built-up surrounding area) in 2018, with about 37 million people. The UN projected that Delhi would overtake it around 2028.
Ireland is urbanising too: Census 2016 counted about 63% of Ireland's population as urban.
Demand for homes rises with population growth, smaller households and migration, and supply has not kept pace in successful cities. The result is that housing costs more than many people can pay.
High rents and house prices in Dublin and other successful cities put homes beyond the reach of many households, because so many people want to live where the jobs are.
Homelessness is a visible result: over 15,000 people were in emergency accommodation in 2025.
Housing for All (2021), the Irish government's housing plan, aims for about 33,000 new homes a year on average to 2030.
Rent Pressure Zones, introduced from 2016, limit rent increases in the areas where they apply, so tenants in high-demand areas face smaller rises.
Higher-density apartments near transport use land and transport more efficiently, because many people live on a small site close to public transport.
Public and cost-rental housing provide homes at below-market rents, helping households who cannot afford private rents.
The developing-world form of this issue is slum growth (crowded informal housing), because new arrivals cannot afford formal homes. There is more on this in Developing-world cities.

Car dependence causes congestion and emissions, and cities are responding with mass transit, restrictions on cars and new neighbourhood designs. Sustainable mobility means getting people around in ways that cause less pollution.
Car dependence produces congestion (traffic jams) and vehicle emissions in growing cities, because more people mean more cars on the same roads.
Dublin plans MetroLink (a planned metro rail line, with no date or cost yet) and BusConnects (a redesign of the bus network).
The NTA's Greater Dublin Area Transport Strategy 2022–2042 is the long-term transport plan for the region. The NTA is the National Transport Authority.
The Grand Paris Express will add about 200 km of new automatic (driverless) metro lines and 68 stations in the Paris region.
Copenhagen is a cycling city: cycling is the most common way of commuting to work or study.
London's Ultra Low Emission Zone (ULEZ), an area where the most polluting vehicles must pay a charge, began in 2019 and was extended London-wide in August 2023.

Paris is promoting the 15-minute city, where everyday needs can be met within 15 minutes on foot or by bike. The idea is associated with Carlos Moreno and was promoted by Mayor Anne Hidalgo in her 2020 re-election campaign; it is not yet fully built.

Vauban in Freiburg, Germany, is a low-car eco-district built from the late 1990s on a former military barracks. Homes are built to high energy standards and residents are encouraged to live without a car. Electric vehicles reduce emissions from the cars that remain on the roads.

Cities produce most of the world's emissions and are exposed to sea-level rise, flooding and heat waves, so climate action and adaptation are needed together. Mitigation means cutting emissions; adaptation means coping with changes already under way.
Heat waves are intensified in cities by the urban heat island effect, where buildings and paved surfaces make the city warmer than its surroundings.
Cork city's low-lying centre suffers repeated tidal flooding; a flood-relief scheme for the River Lee is planned and disputed.

The Climate Action and Low Carbon Development (Amendment) Act 2021 sets a legally binding target to cut Ireland's greenhouse gas emissions by 51% by 2030 from 2018 levels, and net zero (no net emissions) by 2050.
Adaptation responses include flood defences, green roofs (roofs planted with vegetation) and green infrastructure (parks, trees and other planted space that soak up water and cool the city).
Mitigation responses include energy-efficient buildings, district heating (one central plant heating many buildings) and renewable energy.
Masdar City in Abu Dhabi, UAE, was begun in 2006 as a planned low-carbon city; its original zero-carbon target has been scaled back.
Sprawl is low-density outward spread of a city onto surrounding land. It wastes land and energy, so planners promote compact growth instead.
Compact growth policy directs new housing into existing towns and cities rather than onto greenfield land (land not built on before), which saves countryside.
The National Planning Framework (NPF, 2018) sets a target of 40% of new homes within the built-up footprint of existing settlements.
The NPF expects half of growth to be in the five cities.
Brownfield regeneration reuses old industrial and urban land for new housing, so new homes do not need new land.
Height and density are debated: taller buildings save land but can change the character of a neighbourhood.
Green belts are planned areas of open land around cities that limit sprawl, because building on them is restricted.
Developed-world cities have more older residents, while fewer workers pay taxes to support services. Cities must therefore be redesigned for an older population.
Older people need accessible housing, accessible transport and health care close to home, because mobility often becomes harder with age.
Age-friendly design makes streets, buildings and services usable by older people, so they can stay independent.
Fewer workers paying taxes place pressure on the funding of services, since a smaller working population supports a larger older one.
Smart cities use sensors and data to manage traffic, energy and waste, but raise risks of cost, privacy and inequality.
Sensors and data are used to manage traffic, energy use and waste collection, so services respond to what is actually happening in the city.
Songdo in South Korea is a smart city built from the 2000s on land reclaimed from the Yellow Sea near Incheon.
Smart Dublin is a programme of the four Dublin local authorities to trial smart-city technology.
Risks include high cost, threats to privacy because so much data is collected, and a digital divide between those who can and cannot use digital services.
The COVID-19 pandemic from 2020 made remote and hybrid working (part at home, part in the office) common, which changed how city centres are used.
Remote and hybrid working reduce commuting, leaving offices and shops empty in city centres because fewer workers travel in.
City centres are converting offices to homes and leisure uses, so empty buildings find a new purpose.
Remote-working hubs in towns allow people to work close to home; Our Rural Future (2021–2025), the government's rural development policy, supports them.
Deindustrialised cities, where factories have closed, lose population and jobs, leaving vacant land and buildings. Not every future city grows.
Detroit fell from about 1.85 million people in 1950 to about 640,000 in 2020, and filed for bankruptcy in 2013. There is more on this in Urban problems in developed-world cities.
Vacant land is reused for parks and urban farming, so empty plots become useful instead of derelict.
Managed decline accepts a smaller population and plans services and land use for it, rather than trying to bring back the old population.
Rich and poor areas drift apart, which can lead to segregation (different groups living separately) and conflict.
Gentrification, where wealthier people move into and renovate a district, pushes lower-income residents out.
Gated communities (housing estates with controlled entry) separate wealthy households from the rest of the city.
Immigrants concentrate in some districts, such as the banlieues (suburbs) of Paris; Seine-Saint-Denis saw riots in 2005.
Social mix and inclusive planning spread housing for different incomes across the city, so no area is only rich or only poor.
Cities grow beyond their administrative boundaries, so governance (who runs the city region) is fragmented.
Dublin is divided between four councils: Dublin City, Fingal, South Dublin and Dún Laoghaire–Rathdown, so no single body runs the whole city region.
A Citizens' Assembly (a group of ordinary citizens asked to consider an issue) reported in 2023 recommending a directly elected mayor for Dublin; Dublin does not yet have one.
Limerick elected its first directly elected mayor in June 2024, unlike Dublin, which does not yet have one.
The Métropole du Grand Paris, created in 2016, is a metropolitan governance body for the Paris region.
Growing cities need water, energy and waste services that must keep pace with demand.
Uisce Éireann (Irish Water) has proposed a pipeline to bring water from the River Shannon to the Dublin region; no date or cost is set.
Data centres (buildings full of computer servers) used about a fifth of Ireland's metered electricity in 2023 (CSO), so they add large demand to the energy supply.
São Paulo's 2014–2015 Cantareira drought showed how a large city can run short of water. There is more on this in Developing-world cities.
Waste collection and disposal must keep pace with growing populations, because more people produce more waste.
Most urban growth to 2050 falls in Asia and Africa, in cities with slums, poor water and sanitation, and high climate vulnerability.
Megacities are growing fastest in Asia and Africa, because that is where close to 90% of the world's urban increase is expected.
Kolkata and Mumbai sit on low-lying land, so this makes them vulnerable to flooding: Kolkata on the Hooghly delta, and Mumbai's 2005 flood brought about 944 mm of rain in one day.
Informal work (jobs outside regular employment), slums and inadequate water and sanitation remain the core challenges of these cities.
Innovative low-cost solutions exist, such as Curitiba's bus rapid transit (a bus system that works like a metro), begun in 1974.
The National Planning Framework (NPF) plans for Ireland's growth, and many of the issues above come together in Irish cities.
The NPF (2018) projects about 1 million more people in Ireland by 2040.
Galway, Cork, Limerick and Waterford, the regional cities, are each to grow by at least 50% by 2040.
Dublin's MetroLink is planned, with no date or cost yet.
Cork's light rail (a tram-style system) is proposed in the Cork Metropolitan Area Transport Strategy (2020).
Housing for All targets are covered under issue 1, and the emissions targets under issue 3.
Data centres and electricity demand are covered under issue 11.
The atmosphere (the envelope of gases around the earth) and the oceans are not separate. They swap heat, water, gases and momentum (movement), so a change in one alters the other.
Heat: the ocean warms or cools the air above it, depending on whether the sea surface is warmer or colder than the air.
Water: evaporation (liquid water turning to vapour) from the sea supplies the moisture for precipitation (rain, snow and so on) over both sea and land.
Gases: the ocean absorbs and releases carbon dioxide and oxygen, so it takes part in the air's chemistry as well as its weather.
Momentum: wind drives surface ocean currents, and the currents in turn shift the pressure and wind patterns above them, so the push goes both ways.

El Niño shows the link at work: a change in sea surface temperature across the Pacific alters atmospheric circulation (the large-scale pattern of air movement) there. There is more on this in Climatic environments and climate change.
The ocean's effect on climate depends on how water handles heat. Specific heat capacity is the amount of heat needed to raise the temperature of a material, and water's is high.
Water has a high specific heat capacity, so the ocean heats and cools far more slowly than land and stores very large amounts of heat.
Because the ocean responds slowly, maritime climates (those near the sea) have small temperature ranges, the gap between the warmest and coldest readings.

The ocean has absorbed over 90% of the extra heat trapped by global warming, according to the IPCC (the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, the international body that assesses climate science). This shows how large its heat store is.
Air is a mixture of gases. The permanent gases are those whose share stays the same everywhere, and these figures are percentages by volume of dry air (air with the water vapour left out).
By volume, dry air is about 78% nitrogen and about 21% oxygen, so these two gases make up nearly all of it.
Argon makes up about 0.9% and carbon dioxide about 0.04%, so even the fourth gas is a tiny fraction.
Traces of neon, helium, methane, ozone and other gases make up the rest.
Some parts of the air change from place to place and time to time, unlike the permanent gases. These variable components matter far more than their small amounts suggest.
Water vapour (water as an invisible gas) ranges from almost 0% of the air over deserts and the poles to about 4% in hot, humid tropical air, because warm air can hold more of it.

Aerosols (tiny solid or liquid particles floating in the air), including dust, sea salt, smoke, volcanic ash and pollen, act as condensation nuclei, the surfaces on which water vapour condenses into droplets, and they scatter sunlight.
Ozone, a form of oxygen with three atoms per molecule, is concentrated in the stratosphere, the layer of the atmosphere above the weather layer.
Gases that make up only a tiny share of the air still control how much heat the earth keeps and how much harmful radiation reaches the ground.

Water vapour, carbon dioxide, methane and nitrous oxide are greenhouse gases: they absorb long-wave radiation (heat given off by the warm earth), which keeps the lower atmosphere warmer. There is more on this in Solar energy and its redistribution.
Ozone absorbs harmful ultraviolet radiation, the high-energy part of sunlight that damages living tissue.
Atmospheric carbon dioxide was about 280 ppm (parts per million) before the Industrial Revolution and was over 420 ppm by the mid-2020s, because of human activity.
Carbon dioxide has been measured continuously at Mauna Loa, Hawaii, since 1958. The record, known as the Keeling Curve, was begun by Charles David Keeling.
The air has weight, and gravity (the pull of the earth) keeps it from drifting off into space. This explains why the air gets thinner as you go up.
Gravity holds the atmosphere, so it is densest (most mass packed into a given space) at the surface and thins rapidly with height.
Pressure (the weight of the air pressing down) therefore falls with altitude, because less air lies above; about half the mass of the atmosphere lies below about 5.5 km.
The atmosphere has four layers, separated by three pauses (boundaries between layers). Each layer is defined by how its temperature changes with height.
Diagram: draw a vertical profile with height in km on the vertical axis, label the four layers and the three pauses, and add the temperature line, which falls, rises, falls and rises again.
The troposphere is the lowest layer and the one we live in. It is where weather happens.
It extends from the surface to about 8 km over the poles and about 16-18 km over the equator, being thicker where warm air expands and convection (warm air rising) is strongest.
Temperature falls with height at an average of about 6.5 °C per 1,000 m (the environmental lapse rate), because the air is heated from below by the ground.
It contains most of the atmosphere's mass and nearly all its water vapour, so nearly all weather and clouds occur here.
Its top is the tropopause, where the temperature stops falling; jet streams (fast, narrow bands of high-altitude wind) blow near it.
Above the tropopause the temperature trend reverses, because of the ozone layer, the stratosphere's special feature.
It extends from the tropopause to about 50 km.
Temperature rises with height because ozone absorbs ultraviolet radiation and the absorbed energy warms the air; the ozone layer is concentrated at about 15-35 km.
It is very dry and stable, so few clouds form, but the anvils (flat, spread-out tops) of cumulonimbus clouds (tall storm clouds) spread out at its base.
Long-haul jets cruise near the tropopause to avoid turbulence (rough, bumpy air).
In the mesosphere, above the ozone layer's warming effect, temperature falls with height again.
It extends from about 50 km to about 80-85 km.
Temperature falls again with height, reaching about -90 °C at its top, the coldest point in the atmosphere.
Most meteors (rock fragments from space) burn up here. Its top is the mesopause.
The outer layers are so thin that they behave very differently from the air near the ground.
Above about 85 km the air is very thin and its temperature rises sharply, because the few molecules absorb high-energy solar radiation; there are too few molecules for it to feel hot.
Auroras (northern lights, glowing displays in the sky) occur here, and the International Space Station orbits within it at about 400 km.
The exosphere is the outermost fringe, merging into space.
Oceans dominate the planet's surface and its water, so they are the other half of the linked system.
The oceans cover about 71% of the earth's surface and hold about 97% of its water.
The five oceans are the Pacific (the largest and deepest), Atlantic, Indian, Southern and Arctic; the Pacific covers about a third of the earth's surface.
Average ocean depth is about 3.7 km. The deepest point is the Challenger Deep in the Mariana Trench (a very deep, narrow trough in the sea floor), in the western Pacific, at about 11,000 m.
Seawater is salty, and salinity is the measure of how salty. It is one of the main physical and chemical characteristics of the oceans.
Salinity is the dissolved salt content of seawater: about 35 parts per thousand on average, or 35 g of salt per kg.
Sodium chloride is the main salt, with magnesium, sulphate, calcium and potassium also present.
The salts come from rocks weathered (broken down) and carried by rivers and from volcanic gases and vents.
Salinity is not the same everywhere. It rises where water is lost to the air and falls where fresh water is added.
Salinity is higher where evaporation exceeds precipitation, because water leaves but the salt stays behind, as in the subtropical oceans and in nearly enclosed seas in hot, dry areas.
The Red Sea, at about 40 parts per thousand, is among the saltiest open seas, and the Mediterranean is saltier than the Atlantic.
Salinity is lower where rainfall is heavy (the equatorial belt), where large rivers enter the sea and where ice melts (polar seas), because fresh water dilutes the salt.
The Baltic Sea is brackish (slightly salty), well under 10 parts per thousand in much of it, because of heavy river inflow and little evaporation.

When sea ice forms it leaves its salt behind, so the water beneath becomes saltier and denser; this feeds the thermohaline circulation (the deep ocean circulation driven by differences in temperature and salt). There is more on this in Atmospheric and oceanic circulation.
The ocean is layered by temperature, just as the atmosphere is. The sun heats only the top, so the layers run from warm at the surface to cold below.
A warm, well-mixed surface layer, heated by the sun and stirred by wind, lies at the top of the tropical ocean, about the top 100-200 m.
The thermocline is the layer where temperature falls rapidly with depth.
The deep ocean is cold (about 0-4 °C) and dark, and is the largest part of the ocean by volume.
In polar waters there is little difference between the surface and the deep, so there is no strong thermocline.
Diagram: temperature against depth for a tropical ocean, showing the three layers.
How dense seawater is decides whether it sinks or floats, and density depends on temperature and salinity.
Seawater is denser when it is colder and saltier; differences in density make water sink or rise and drive deep ocean circulation. There is more on this in Atmospheric and oceanic circulation.
Surface temperature varies with latitude, from about 28-30 °C in the tropics to about -2 °C at the poles, which is the freezing point of seawater; ocean currents shift these patterns.
The ocean also holds dissolved gases. Its uptake of carbon dioxide has a useful and a harmful effect.
The ocean dissolves oxygen, from the air and from phytoplankton (tiny floating plant-like organisms that give off oxygen), and carbon dioxide.
It has absorbed roughly a quarter of the carbon dioxide released by human activity. This slows global warming but makes the water more acidic (ocean acidification), which harms corals and shellfish.
Average surface ocean pH (a scale measuring acidity, where lower means more acidic) has fallen from about 8.2 to about 8.1 since pre-industrial times.
To observe the atmosphere and oceans you need readings from many places at the same moment. Observing networks provide them.

Synoptic weather stations (stations that record the weather at the same moment as others), staffed or automatic, record at fixed times in UTC (a single world time standard) to World Meteorological Organization (WMO) standards, so that readings can be compared worldwide.
Other sources include ships, buoys, aircraft, weather balloons, radar and satellites.
Met Éireann (the Irish national weather service) collects the Irish data. There is more on this in Weather maps and weather data.
