Temperature is measured by several instruments, each suited to a different job, and a screen keeps the readings honest.
A liquid-in-glass thermometer uses mercury or alcohol, which expands and rises up a narrow tube as it warms.

A maximum-minimum thermometer, Six's thermometer, uses small metal indexes (markers) that are pushed up to the highest and lowest points reached and stay there until reset with a magnet; it is read once a day and then reset. James Six invented it in 1782.
Electronic thermometers in automatic stations use sensors whose electrical resistance changes with temperature; a thermograph gives a continuous trace.

Thermometers sit in a Stevenson screen (a ventilated white box) about 1.25 m above the ground. It is white to reflect sunlight, louvred (slatted) to let air circulate, and mounted on legs above grass.
The Stevenson screen's door faces away from direct sun (north in Ireland), so readings are true shade air temperatures.
A grass minimum thermometer, laid just above short grass, measures ground frost.
Daily mean, daily range and annual range are derived from these readings. There is more on the calculation method in Weather maps and weather data.
Air pressure is the weight of the air above, and two types of barometer measure it in different ways.
A mercury barometer: the weight of the atmosphere supports a column of mercury in a glass tube, and the column rises as pressure rises. Evangelista Torricelli invented it in 1643.

An aneroid barometer (aneroid means without liquid) uses a sealed, partly emptied metal capsule that is squeezed in as pressure rises and expands as it falls; levers move a needle on a dial. It is portable, so it is used in homes and on ships.
A barograph links an aneroid to a pen that draws a continuous record on a rotating drum; the trend of rising or falling pressure matters most in forecasting.
Electronic pressure sensors are used in automatic stations.

Readings are corrected to mean sea level so that stations at different heights can be compared and isobars (lines joining places of equal pressure) drawn. Pressure is measured in hPa (hectopascals, equal to mb), with an average of about 1013 hPa.
Wind speed is measured by an anemometer, standing at a standard height so that readings can be compared.
A cup anemometer has three or four cups on arms that spin faster as wind speed rises; the turns are counted electrically and converted to speed.
Sonic anemometers, which have no moving parts, are used on some modern stations.
The WMO standard height for surface wind is 10 m above open ground, away from buildings and trees, which would shelter the instrument and lower its readings.
Speed is given in km/h, knots or m/s, and gusts (short bursts of stronger wind) are recorded separately from mean speed. Without instruments, speed is estimated using the Beaufort scale.
Wind direction is the way the wind blows from, and it is shown by a vane or a windsock.
A wind vane has a large tail that is pushed downwind, so its pointer faces the direction the wind blows from; direction is read against compass points or degrees.
Windsocks show wind direction and strength at airports.
Wind is always named from the direction it comes from, so a westerly wind blows from the west.
Humidity is the amount of water vapour in the air. The wet-and-dry bulb hygrometer measures it by using evaporative cooling.

A wet-and-dry bulb hygrometer (psychrometer) has two thermometers side by side. The wet bulb is wrapped in muslin (thin cloth) kept wet from a water reservoir; evaporation from the muslin cools it, so it reads lower than the dry bulb.
The drier the air, the faster the evaporation and the bigger the difference, called the wet bulb depression. If both thermometers read the same, the air is saturated (holding all the vapour it can).
Relative humidity, given as a percentage, is read from tables using the dry bulb reading and the difference between the two readings.
A hair hygrometer uses human hair, which lengthens in humid air and shortens in dry air, to move a pointer.
Rain, sunshine, evaporation and cloud each have their own instrument.

Rain gauge: a funnel of standard size, set in open ground with its rim raised above the surface to avoid splash, collects rain into a measuring cylinder that is read in mm each day; tipping-bucket gauges record automatically.
Campbell-Stokes sunshine recorder: a glass sphere focuses the sun's rays and burns a trace on a card; the length of the burn gives hours of bright sunshine.
Evaporation pan: measures the water lost from an open water surface by evaporation.
Cloud cover is estimated in oktas (eighths of the sky covered) by observers or measured by ceilometers (instruments that find the height of cloud bases).
Weather also has to be measured high above the ground, where ground instruments cannot reach.
Weather balloons carry radiosondes, small instrument packs that measure temperature, humidity and pressure and radio them back; tracking the balloon gives the upper winds.

Balloons are launched twice a day, at fixed times, from stations worldwide, including Valentia Observatory, Co. Kerry, which has one of the longest weather records in Ireland, dating from the 19th century.
Aircraft also report temperature and wind automatically.
Remote sensing means measuring from a distance, without touching the thing measured.

Geostationary (fixed over one spot) and polar-orbiting (passing over the poles) weather satellites measure cloud, sea-surface temperature, water vapour and ice. There is more on this in Satellite imagery.
Rainfall radar detects precipitation from the echo returned by raindrops.
Ocean measurements come from instruments floating on, drifting in and orbiting above the sea. Together they supply the data on the ocean side of the linked system.

Moored weather buoys (anchored floating stations) record air pressure, air and sea temperature, wind, wave height and humidity, and transmit the readings, hourly. The Irish Marine Data Buoy Observation Network, run by the Marine Institute with Met Éireann, moors such buoys off the Irish coast.
Drifting buoys follow ocean currents, and voluntary observing ships report weather at sea.

Argo floats drift at depth, rise to the surface every 10 days or so, and measure temperature and salinity down to about 2,000 m before transmitting by satellite. The Argo programme began in 2000, and about 4,000 floats now drift in the world's oceans.
Tide gauges and satellite altimeters (instruments that measure height from space) measure sea level; satellites also measure sea-surface temperature and sea ice.
Research ships lower CTD instruments (conductivity, temperature, depth) to sample salinity and temperature at depth.
The TAO array, a line of moored buoys across the equatorial Pacific, monitors the ocean to give warning of El Niño.
A reading is only useful if it is trustworthy, so how and where instruments are set up matters as much as the instrument.
Instruments must be correctly sited: in an open place, at the standard height, shaded for thermometers and away from buildings and heated surfaces, which would distort the readings.
Instruments must be regularly calibrated (checked against a standard), read at the same times each day, and long records kept at the same site, so the record stays consistent.
Urban growth around a station (the urban heat island, the extra warmth of built-up areas) can bias its records upward.
Measurements are collected because they are used. Each use below is a separate reason, from forecasting and safety to farming, energy and climate science.
Forecasting: observations are the starting point (initial conditions) for computer forecast models, and more and better observations give better forecasts.
Warnings: storm, rain, snow and heat warnings, including Met Éireann's colour codes, save lives and property. There is more on this in Weather maps and weather data.

Storm surge (sea level raised by a storm) and flood warnings are issued, and tropical cyclones are tracked; a falling barograph trace warns of an approaching depression (a low-pressure weather system).

Aviation needs wind, visibility, icing and pressure for altimeter settings (so a plane's height reading is correct); shipping and fishing need sea area forecasts and wave heights from buoys; offshore work depends on the same data.

Farming: the timing of silage and hay making, spraying, sowing and harvesting depends on forecasts; frost warnings protect crops; soil temperature and moisture show when grass starts to grow; drought monitoring is also part of this use. There is more on drought in Climate and economic development.

Energy and the economy: wind measurements are used to site wind farms and predict their output; temperature forecasts predict electricity and gas demand; construction, retail, insurance, sport and tourism planning all use weather data.

Climate records: long, consistent records, such as the Mauna Loa carbon dioxide record and Valentia's long weather record, show trends including global warming, sea-level rise and ocean warming; they are the evidence used by the IPCC and by governments.
The IPCC was set up in 1988 by the WMO and the UN Environment Programme.
Ocean-atmosphere link: buoy and Argo data on sea temperature and salinity track El Niño, ocean heat content and the Atlantic circulation, and they improve seasonal forecasts.

Everything in the atmosphere and oceans is driven by energy from the sun. The kind of radiation (energy travelling as waves) that arrives is different from the kind the earth sends back out, and that difference matters for the greenhouse effect.
Solar energy arrives as short-wave radiation, mostly visible light with some ultraviolet and near-infrared. The sun is extremely hot, so it gives off short waves.
The much cooler earth gives off long-wave (infrared, heat) radiation. This difference between short-wave in and long-wave out is the basis of the greenhouse effect.

Insolation (short for incoming solar radiation) is the solar energy that reaches the earth. The solar constant, about 1,361 W/m², is the energy reaching the top of the atmosphere, and far less reaches the surface.
The syllabus says solar energy is transformed, meaning it changes form on its way through the system. Each change below is a separate step that an essay can name.
Radiant energy (energy carried by radiation) absorbed by surfaces becomes heat, called sensible heat because you can feel it and measure it with a thermometer.
Energy used to evaporate water is stored as latent heat (hidden heat) in water vapour, which later powers storms when the vapour condenses. There is more on this in Latent heat and tropical cyclones.
Heat differences create pressure differences, because warm air rises and cool air sinks. These become the kinetic energy (energy of movement) of wind and, through wind drag, of waves and currents.
Plants convert a small fraction of absorbed energy into chemical energy by photosynthesis, the process that makes food from light.
Not all the sunlight arriving at the top of the atmosphere warms the ground. The heat budget below uses a rounded model of 100 units of incoming solar radiation, so the figures are approximate.
About 30 units are reflected back to space, mainly by clouds and also by the surface and by scattering; the earth's overall albedo (the share of radiation reflected) is therefore about 30% (0.3).
About 20 units are absorbed by the atmosphere and clouds, by ozone, water vapour, dust and clouds, so this energy warms the air directly.
About 50 units are absorbed by the land and ocean surface, which is why the ground, not the air, is the main heat source.
Scattering (radiation bounced in all directions) by gas molecules and dust makes the sky blue, as blue light is scattered most.
Diagram: a labelled flow diagram with incoming short-wave arrows split into reflected, absorbed by atmosphere and absorbed by surface, and outgoing long-wave, latent and sensible heat arrows.
Albedo is how shiny a surface is to sunlight. Light surfaces send most radiation back to space, while dark ones absorb it as heat.
Albedo is the proportion of radiation a surface reflects.
Fresh snow reflects about 80–90%, sea ice about 50–70% and thick cloud up to about 80%, so these are high-albedo surfaces that stay cool.
Desert sand reflects about 30–40%, grassland about 25% and forest about 10–20%; open ocean reflects under 10% when the sun is high, so dark surfaces absorb most of what reaches them.
Changing the surface changes the heat it absorbs, because albedo changes with it: deforestation (clearing forest) and urban surfaces alter albedo.
The surface does not keep all the 50 units it absorbs. It gets rid of energy in three ways, which together balance the input.
Long-wave radiation is emitted by the surface, as heat radiating out to the atmosphere and space.

Latent heat transfer (evaporation, which stores heat in water vapour) is the largest non-radiative loss, especially from oceans, because they cover so much of the earth and supply so much water to evaporate.
Sensible heat transfer moves heat by conduction (direct contact) to the air touching the ground, which then rises by convection (warm air rising in currents).
Some gases in the air act like the glass of a greenhouse: they let sunlight in but slow the escape of heat. This natural effect is what makes the earth habitable.
Water vapour, carbon dioxide, methane and other gases are largely transparent to incoming short-wave radiation, but they absorb outgoing long-wave radiation and re-radiate much of it back down.
This keeps the earth's average surface temperature at about 15 °C; without the natural greenhouse effect it would be about −18 °C.
The enhanced greenhouse effect, caused by added gases, is examined in Climatic environments and climate change and in Environmental pollution.
The heat budget is the balance between energy gained and energy lost. It balances for the whole earth, but not in each place, and that imbalance is why energy has to be moved around.
Over a year the heat budget of the earth as a whole balances: energy in equals energy out, so the average temperature stays stable.
If more energy is retained than lost, as when greenhouse gases increase, the earth warms until a new balance is reached.
The budget does not balance at each latitude. Between the equator and about 35–40° north and south more energy is received than is radiated away: this is the surplus.
Poleward of about 35–40° (towards the poles) more energy is lost than received: this is the deficit.
Without a poleward transfer the tropics would keep heating and the poles would keep cooling. Because they do not, energy must be moved.
Diagram: a graph of incoming and outgoing radiation against latitude, with the surplus and deficit areas shaded.
The first reason the sun's energy is spread unevenly is the angle at which its rays hit the curved earth.
At the equator the sun's rays strike nearly vertically, concentrating energy on a small area, so that area heats strongly.
Towards the poles the same beam strikes at a low angle and is spread over a larger area, so each square metre gets less energy.
Diagram: two equal beams hitting the curved earth.
A low sun angle has a second effect, because of the distance the rays travel through the air.
Low-angle rays pass through more atmosphere, so more energy is absorbed, scattered and reflected before it reaches the ground.
The earth's tilt moves the zone of strongest sunlight north and south through the year. This causes the seasons and changes how long the day lasts.

The axis is tilted about 23.5°, so the overhead sun migrates between the Tropic of Cancer (about 23.5° N) and the Tropic of Capricorn (about 23.5° S) through the year, giving seasons and changing day length.

The sun is overhead at the equator at the equinoxes (about 21 March and 23 September), at the Tropic of Cancer at the June solstice (about 21 June) and at the Tropic of Capricorn at the December solstice (about 21 December).
The poles have months of continuous daylight in summer and continuous darkness in winter, because of the tilt.
Three more factors change how much insolation a place actually receives: how long the sun is up, how cloudy it is and how reflective the ground is.
Long summer days at high latitudes partly offset the low sun angle; the equator has almost the same length of day and night all year (about 12 hours of daylight).
Cloudy regions, such as the equatorial belt and mid-latitude west coasts, reflect much insolation, while clear-skied subtropical deserts receive the most at the surface.
Clouds keep nights warmer by trapping long-wave radiation, so heat escapes more slowly.
Snow-covered polar regions reflect most of the little radiation they receive, because snow has a high albedo.

Because insolation falls from the equator to the poles, latitude is the first thing to name when explaining the pattern of temperature. Isotherms are lines on a map joining places with the same temperature.
Latitude is the main control: temperatures generally fall from the equator to the poles, so isotherms run broadly east–west.

Land and sea respond very differently to the same sunshine. Continentality means the effect of being far from the sea, and it explains why places at the same latitude can have very different temperatures.
Land heats and cools quickly, while the sea heats and cools slowly, because water has a high specific heat (it takes a lot of energy to warm it), mixes, is transparent and evaporates.
Continental interiors have hot summers, cold winters and a large annual range (the gap between the warmest and coldest months); coasts and islands have a small range.
Ireland's annual range is only about 10 °C, with a mean January of about 4–7 °C and a mean July of about 14–16 °C.
Verkhoyansk, in north-east Siberia (Russia), has a mean January temperature of about −45 °C and a mean July of about +15 °C, an annual range of over 60 °C and one of the largest on earth.
Isotherms bend where they cross coasts, because temperatures change at the land–sea edge.
Ocean currents carry warm or cold water to coasts and change the temperature there, so isotherms bend where currents flow.

Warm currents raise coastal temperatures: the North Atlantic Drift, the extension of the Gulf Stream, keeps Ireland and Britain mild, so January isotherms bend sharply northward over the north-east Atlantic.
Cold currents lower coastal temperatures, as on the coasts of Peru and south-west Africa, where the Humboldt and Benguela currents flow.
Height above sea level also controls temperature, independently of latitude.
Temperature falls by about 6.5 °C per 1,000 m, so mountains and plateaus are cooler than lowlands at the same latitude.
Mount Kilimanjaro, Tanzania, about 5,900 m high and only about 3° south of the equator, is snow-capped, which shows that height can outweigh latitude.
Winds carry the temperature of the area they blow from, so the direction of the prevailing (most usual) wind affects a coast's climate.
Onshore westerlies (westerly winds blowing from sea to land) carry ocean warmth in winter and ocean coolness in summer over the west coasts of the mid-latitudes.
Winds from cold continental interiors bring cold spells, such as polar continental air reaching Ireland. There is more on this in Atmospheric and oceanic circulation.
Aspect is the direction a slope faces. Small-scale factors can change temperature even where latitude and altitude are the same.
South-facing slopes in the northern hemisphere receive more sun and are warmer, which is why vineyards are often planted on them.
Urban heat islands (built-up areas) are warmer than the surrounding countryside.
Snow cover keeps the ground cold.
The hottest zone does not follow the geographical equator exactly. It is a line drawn from temperature, not from latitude.
The thermal equator is the line of highest mean temperature.
It lies mostly north of the geographical equator because the northern hemisphere has more land, and it moves north and south with the seasons, further over land than over sea.
The record temperatures show the pattern of the controls above: dry, clear subtropical deserts are hottest, while high-latitude interiors are coldest.

The hottest places are subtropical deserts, not the equator, where cloud and rain limit heating. Furnace Creek, Death Valley, California, recorded 56.7 °C on 10 July 1913, the highest temperature officially recognised by the WMO (World Meteorological Organization).
The coldest places are the interior of Antarctica and, in winter, north-east Siberia. Vostok Station, Antarctica, recorded −89.2 °C on 21 July 1983, the lowest temperature on earth.
Verkhoyansk and Oymyakon share the northern hemisphere's lowest recorded temperature, about −68 °C.
On 20 June 2020 Verkhoyansk recorded 38 °C, accepted by the WMO as the highest temperature recorded in the Arctic.
The annual range is smallest at the equator and over oceans, and largest in high-latitude continental interiors.
The surplus at the equator and deficit at the poles are evened out because the atmosphere and the oceans carry heat poleward. This is the redistribution part of the syllabus statement.

Heat is transferred by the atmosphere (winds, depressions, which are areas of low pressure, and tropical cyclones) and by the oceans (surface currents and the deep thermohaline circulation, driven by differences in water temperature and salt).
Together they move heat from the surplus belt to the deficit belt. The atmosphere carries most of it at mid and high latitudes, and the oceans carry a large share in the tropics.
A cell is a closed loop of moving air. The three-cell model has one loop in each band of latitude, and the Hadley cell, nearest the equator, is the first.

Intense heating at the equator makes air rise, creating low pressure and the ITCZ (the Inter-Tropical Convergence Zone, where the winds meet); the air cools and releases latent heat as convectional rain.
At height the air flows poleward, sinks at about 30° to form the subtropical high pressure and deserts, and returns to the equator as the trade winds, carrying heat poleward at height.
The cell is named after George Hadley, who proposed in 1735 that the trade winds came from heated air rising at the equator.
Diagram: the three-cell model, shown in both hemispheres.
Further from the equator, two more cells continue the transfer of heat towards the poles.
The Ferrel cell (30–60°): surface westerlies carry warm air poleward to meet cold polar air at the polar front, at about 60°.
The polar cell (60–90°): polar air sinks at the poles, forming the polar high, and flows out as polar easterlies.

Most mid-latitude heat transfer is done by depressions and anticyclones (areas of high pressure) forming along the polar front and by the meandering jet stream (a fast, high-altitude wind). There is more on this in Atmospheric and oceanic circulation.
Water vapour is a heat carrier. Energy taken up when water evaporates in the tropics is delivered far away when the vapour turns back into water.
Water evaporated over warm tropical oceans carries latent heat poleward; the heat is released where the vapour condenses, for example in a depression over Ireland.
Tropical cyclones (hurricanes) draw large quantities of heat and moisture from tropical oceans and carry them poleward.
Ex-hurricane Ophelia began as a hurricane in the tropical Atlantic and reached Ireland on 16 October 2017. There is more on this in Weather maps and weather data.

Ocean currents are large streams of water moving in set paths. Warm currents move heat poleward and cold currents move cooled water back towards the equator, in a pattern that follows the sides of the ocean basins.
Warm currents carry heat poleward along the western sides of ocean basins: the Gulf Stream, Kuroshio, Brazil Current, East Australian Current and Agulhas Current.
Cold currents return cooled water towards the equator along the eastern sides of ocean basins: the Canary, Benguela, Humboldt (Peru) and California currents, and the Labrador Current.
The Gulf Stream flows from the Gulf of Mexico and the Straits of Florida north-east along the US east coast and across the Atlantic; it carries more water than all the world's rivers combined.

Off Europe the Gulf Stream is called the North Atlantic Drift. It reaches the eastern side of the Atlantic at high latitude, so it is the exception to the rule that warm currents lie on western sides.
Below the surface currents there is a slow, deep flow of water driven by differences in temperature (thermo) and salt (haline).
The thermohaline circulation, the global conveyor belt, is driven by cold, salty, dense water that sinks in the North Atlantic and around Antarctica and spreads through the deep ocean.
Warm surface water flows in to replace the sinking water, so heat is carried slowly round the globe over centuries. Detail is in Atmospheric and oceanic circulation.
If heat were not moved, the equator would keep heating and the poles cooling. Two contrasting coasts show currents at work.
Norway's coast stays ice-free in winter, even north of the Arctic Circle (Hammerfest), and Murmansk, Russia, is an ice-free Arctic port, because of the warm water of the North Atlantic Drift.
The coast of Labrador, Canada, at about the same latitude as Ireland, has long, freezing winters and sea ice, because the cold Labrador Current flows south past it.
The pattern of heat transfer is not fixed, and changes in one part can affect the others.
Melting Arctic ice lowers albedo, so more heat is absorbed.
A weaker Atlantic circulation could change Europe's climate.
El Niño shifts heat across the Pacific.

Water is constantly moving between the oceans, the air and the land. This continuous circulation is the hydrological (water) cycle, and it is the starting point for understanding how the oceans and atmosphere exchange water.
The cycle is a closed system, meaning nothing enters or leaves: the total amount of water on earth stays the same, and water only moves between stores (the places where it is held).

Two forces drive the movement: solar energy, which powers evaporation (liquid water turning to vapour), and gravity, which pulls water down as precipitation (rain, snow and so on) and runoff (water flowing over the land).
Diagram: draw a labelled cycle from ocean to atmosphere to land and back, with the stores drawn as boxes and the flows as arrows.
A store is a place where water is held for a time. The oceans dwarf all the others, and only a tiny part of the earth's water is fresh liquid water at the surface.
Oceans hold about 97% of the earth's water; ice sheets and glaciers hold about 2%, most of it in Antarctica; groundwater (water stored underground in soil and rock) holds under 1%.
Lakes, rivers, soil moisture, the atmosphere and living things together hold only a tiny fraction. The atmosphere holds about 0.001% of the earth's water.
About 2.5-3% of all water is fresh (not salty), and most of that is frozen, so liquid fresh surface water is a very small part of the total.
Flows are the processes that move water from one store to another. Each has its own name, and the ocean-atmosphere exchange depends on the first few.
Evaporation: liquid water turns to vapour (water as an invisible gas), mainly from the ocean because the oceans are by far the biggest store.
Transpiration: vapour is released from plant leaves; evapotranspiration is transpiration and evaporation combined over land.
Sublimation: ice turns directly into vapour without first melting.
Advection: wind carries water vapour horizontally from sea to land, so rain can fall far from where the water evaporated.
Condensation: vapour turns to liquid droplets, forming cloud, fog or dew, for example when air cools.

Precipitation, interception (rain caught by leaves), infiltration (soaking into the soil), surface runoff, throughflow (water moving sideways through soil) and groundwater flow return water to the sea. There is more on these drainage-basin flows in the chapter Rivers - Fluvial Processes and Landforms.
The oceans are both the main source and the main destination of the water that moves through the air. This shows how much of the cycle happens over the sea.
Roughly 85-90% of global evaporation comes from the oceans, and roughly three-quarters of global precipitation falls on them.
Evaporation over the oceans exceeds the rain falling back on them, so the surplus is carried over the land by wind, and returns to the sea through rivers and groundwater.
Residence time is how long a water molecule stays in a store before moving on. It differs enormously between stores.
Water stays in the atmosphere for only about 9 days on average, but in the ocean for thousands of years and in the Antarctic ice sheet for far longer.
The atmosphere's water is therefore recycled quickly, while ocean water changes slowly.
The exchange is not the same everywhere. Where evaporation and precipitation differ, distinctive climates result, and human activity can change the balance.

Evaporation exceeds precipitation over the subtropical oceans, which helps explain their high salinity (saltiness), because water leaves but the salt stays. There is more on this in The atmosphere and oceans as linked systems.
Precipitation exceeds evaporation in the equatorial belt and in the mid-latitude westerly belt (the zone of prevailing westerly winds).
Deforestation reduces evapotranspiration and so the recycling of rainfall; a large share of the Amazon's rain is water recycled from the forest by evapotranspiration.
Global warming intensifies the water cycle. There is more on this in Climatic environments and climate change.
Humidity describes how much water vapour the air holds. It matters because it decides whether air can form cloud, fog or dew.
Humidity is the amount of water vapour in the air. Absolute humidity is the mass of water vapour in a volume of air, in g/m³.
Relative humidity is the amount of water vapour present as a percentage of the most the air could hold at that temperature. Saturated air (air holding all it can) has a relative humidity of 100%.
Warm air can hold about 7% more water vapour for each 1 °C rise in temperature, so warm air holds much more than cold air.

Cooling air raises its relative humidity without adding any water, because the most it can hold falls; warming lowers it. This is why relative humidity is usually highest at dawn and lowest in mid-afternoon.
Dew point is the temperature at which air becomes saturated as it cools; further cooling causes condensation. There is more on measuring humidity in The atmosphere and oceans as linked systems.
The amount of vapour in the air affects how evaporation works, and so how the climate feels and how temperatures behave.
High humidity in the tropics makes heat oppressive, because sweat evaporates slowly into air that is already full of vapour.
Low humidity in deserts allows rapid evaporation and large daily temperature ranges (the difference between day and night temperature).
Evaporation is the step that puts water into the atmosphere. Its rate depends on energy, on the state of the air and on whether there is water to evaporate.

Evaporation is water molecules gaining enough energy to escape as vapour. It takes latent heat (hidden heat energy) from the surface, cooling it, and that energy is released again on condensation. There is more on this in Solar energy and its redistribution.
Higher temperature increases evaporation because it gives more energy; strong sunshine and low air pressure also increase it.
Drier air, with low relative humidity, increases evaporation because it can take up more vapour.
Wind increases evaporation by removing moist air and replacing it with drier air.
A large supply of water, such as oceans, lakes or wet ground, allows evaporation to continue.
Because evaporation needs heat, wind and water together, it is strongest in some parts of the world and weak in others.

Evaporation is greatest over the subtropical oceans under clear skies and steady trade winds (the regular winds blowing towards the equator), and along warm currents such as the Gulf Stream; it is least over cold polar seas.

Potential evapotranspiration (the water that could evaporate if supply were unlimited) far exceeds rainfall in hot deserts, which is the cause of drought. There is more on this in Climate and economic development.
Condensation is the reverse of evaporation and is how clouds begin. Vapour will not simply turn to droplets in clean air, so it needs something to form on.
Condensation is water vapour turning into liquid droplets when air cools to its dew point (the temperature at which it is saturated).
Condensation needs condensation nuclei: tiny particles of dust, sea salt, smoke or pollen around which droplets form.
Air only condenses when it is cooled to dew point, so the question is what cools it. There are four ways.
Adiabatic cooling (cooling caused by expansion, with no heat lost) of rising air is the main cause of cloud.
Contact cooling by radiation occurs when air touches ground that has lost heat at night.
Advection cooling occurs when warm, moist air moves over a cold surface.
Mixing of air masses of different temperatures can bring air to dew point, because the blend is cooler than the warm air alone.
Rising air cools even though no heat is taken from it. Understanding why explains cloud height and the rates at which air cools.
Rising air expands because pressure falls with height, and it cools without losing heat to its surroundings; sinking air is compressed and warms.
Unsaturated air cools at the dry adiabatic lapse rate (the rate of cooling with height), about 10 °C per 1,000 m.
Once condensation begins, the latent heat released slows the cooling to the saturated adiabatic lapse rate, about 5-7 °C per 1,000 m, which varies with temperature.
The height at which condensation begins is the condensation level, or cloud base.
Whether rising air keeps rising depends on how its temperature compares with the air around it. This decides whether the sky gives towering storm cloud or flat layer cloud.

Unstable air: if rising air stays warmer than its surroundings, because the environment cools faster than the rising air does, it keeps rising and forms towering cumulus, showers and thunderstorms. The environmental lapse rate (the cooling of the surrounding air with height) averages about 6.5 °C per 1,000 m.
Stable air: if rising air becomes cooler than its surroundings, it sinks back, giving layer cloud or clear skies.
A temperature inversion, with warmer air above cooler air, is very stable because the cooler air below cannot rise, and it traps fog and pollution.
Diagram: a temperature-height graph comparing the environmental and adiabatic lapse rates.
Condensation also happens at ground level, where it gives dew, frost and fog. The type depends on how the air is cooled.
Dew forms on surfaces cooled below dew point on clear, calm nights.
Hoar frost forms when the dew point is below 0 °C, as vapour turns straight to ice crystals.
Radiation fog forms on clear, calm nights, usually under anticyclones (areas of high pressure) in autumn and winter, in valleys and hollows; it burns off in the morning sun.

Advection fog forms when warm, moist air moves over a cold sea or land. The Grand Banks off Newfoundland, Canada, are among the foggiest places on earth, where warm moist air from over the Gulf Stream crosses the cold Labrador Current.
San Francisco's summer fogs are also advection fog: they form where moist Pacific air crosses the cold California Current.
Hill fog is cloud on high ground, where air is forced up and cools; smog is fog mixed with smoke.
Clouds form wherever air is lifted and cooled below its dew point. The ways air is forced upward give five causes of cloud.
Clouds are visible masses of tiny water droplets or ice crystals, formed when rising air cools below its dew point.
Convection: uplift from surface heating, which warms the air so that it rises.
Orographic (relief) uplift: air is forced up over high ground.
Frontal uplift: warm air rises over cold air at a front (the boundary between two air masses).
Convergence: air streams meet and, with nowhere else to go, are forced upward, as at the ITCZ (the Intertropical Convergence Zone, where the trade winds meet).
Turbulence: mixing of air that lifts it.
Cloud names are built from a few Latin words that describe shape, height and rain. Once you know them, a name tells you what the cloud looks like and what weather it brings.
Luke Howard, an English pharmacist and amateur meteorologist, proposed the Latin cloud names cirrus, cumulus, stratus and nimbus in 1803.
Cirrus means wispy and fibrous, a curl of hair; cumulus means heaped and puffy, a heap; stratus means a layered sheet.
Nimbus or nimbo- means rain-bearing; alto- means middle level.
The WMO's International Cloud Atlas sets out the ten main cloud types (the WMO is the World Meteorological Organization).
High clouds sit above about 6,000 m and are made of ice crystals. All three types here are thin, wispy or veil-like clouds.
Cirrus: thin wisps, often called mares' tails; fair weather, but often the first sign of an approaching warm front.
Cirrostratus: a thin milky veil that produces a halo round the sun or moon; rain is likely within hours.
Cirrocumulus: small ripples, known as a mackerel sky because the pattern looks like fish scales.
Middle clouds sit between about 2,000 m and 6,000 m, which is why their names begin with alto-, meaning middle level.
Altocumulus: grey or white patches in rolls.
Altostratus: a grey sheet through which the sun shows as if through frosted glass; it thickens ahead of a warm front.
Low clouds are the ones that most often sit over Ireland and bring its drizzle and steady rain.
Stratus: a grey, featureless layer, so it has no towering shape, that produces drizzle and hill fog.
Stratocumulus: a lumpy grey layer, the commonest cloud over Ireland, usually dry or giving light drizzle.
Nimbostratus: a thick, dark rain cloud giving long periods of steady rain or snow at warm fronts.
Some clouds do not stay in one layer. Their base is low but their tops reach high, because strong rising air builds them upward.
Cumulus: fair-weather heaps with flat bases on sunny days, which can grow into showers if the air keeps rising.

Cumulonimbus: a towering cloud with an anvil-shaped top spreading at the tropopause (the top of the lowest layer of the atmosphere), bringing heavy showers, hail, thunder and lightning, and squalls (sudden strong gusts).
Clouds appear in a predictable order as a front approaches, so they can be used to forecast weather.
Ahead of a warm front, cirrus is followed by cirrostratus, altostratus and nimbostratus in turn. There is more on this in Atmospheric and oceanic circulation.
Diagram: a chart of the ten cloud types arranged by height.
Clouds affect temperature on the ground as well as producing rain, and the effect depends on the type of cloud.
Low thick clouds cool the surface by reflecting sunlight; high thin clouds warm it by trapping long-wave radiation (heat given off by the earth); cloudy nights are milder.
Cloud is not the same as rain. Droplets must first grow, by one of two processes, before they can fall.
Cloud droplets are far too small to fall; they must grow about a million times in volume to form a raindrop heavy enough to reach the ground.
In cold clouds, ice crystals grow at the expense of water droplets. This is the main way rain forms in Ireland.

In clouds colder than 0 °C, supercooled droplets (liquid droplets still unfrozen below 0 °C) and ice crystals exist together. Vapour is deposited on the ice crystals, which grow at the droplets' expense, become heavy and fall as snow, melting into rain below the freezing level.
This Bergeron-Findeisen process is the main one in mid-latitude clouds, including Ireland's.
In clouds that are never cold enough for ice, droplets grow by colliding with each other instead.
In warm clouds, which are above 0 °C throughout and are common in the tropics, larger droplets fall faster, collide with and absorb smaller ones (coalesce) until they are heavy enough to fall.
Precipitation can fall as liquid or ice. The form depends on the size of the drops and on the temperature of the air they fall through.
Rain: liquid drops, such as the steady rain from nimbostratus.
Drizzle: very small drops falling from stratus.
Snow: ice crystals clumped as flakes, falling when the air is near or below freezing to the ground.
Sleet: melting snow, or rain and snow mixed.
Hail: layered ice balls formed when strong updrafts in cumulonimbus carry frozen drops up and down repeatedly, adding layers until they are too heavy; hail is mostly a warm-season phenomenon.
Freezing rain and glaze: rain that freezes on contact with cold surfaces.
Convectional rain comes from air that is heated from below and rises. It is the daily rain of the equator.
1. The ground is heated strongly, warming the air above it.
2. The warm air expands, rises and cools adiabatically.
3. When it reaches dew point, cumulus and then cumulonimbus clouds form.
4. Heavy showers, often with thunder, follow, usually in the afternoon, because that is when the ground is hottest.
This type is typical of the equatorial belt every day, and of Irish summer afternoons occasionally, especially inland.
Diagram: a column of rising air above heated ground, topped by cumulonimbus.
Relief rain forms when moist air is forced up over mountains. It leaves a wet windward side and a dry leeward side.
1. Moist air from the sea is forced to rise over a mountain barrier.
2. It cools, condenses and gives heavy rain on the windward slope (the side facing the wind).
3. On the leeward side (the sheltered side) the air descends, is compressed and warms, so clouds evaporate and a rain shadow (a dry area) results.
4. A warm, dry föhn-type wind may blow down the lee side. There is more on this in Atmospheric and oceanic circulation.
Ireland's west coast mountains receive this rain.

In India, the Western Ghats force the Arabian Sea branch of the monsoon to rise, giving heavy rain on the Konkan and Malabar coasts, with the Deccan in rain shadow; Mawsynram and Cherrapunji in the Khasi Hills, Meghalaya, are among the wettest places on earth.
Diagram: a cross-section of a mountain barrier showing the windward wet slope and the leeward rain shadow.
Frontal rain falls where warm air meets cold air in a depression (a low-pressure weather system). It is Ireland's main source of rain.
1. In a depression, warm, moist tropical air is forced to rise over cold polar air at the warm front, giving gentle ascent and long, steady rain.
2. At the cold front the warm air is undercut, causing sharp ascent and short, heavy showers.
Frontal rain is Ireland's main source of rain. There is more on depressions in Atmospheric and oceanic circulation.
Rain also falls where winds meet, because air that cannot go sideways is forced upward.
Where air streams meet they are forced to rise, as where the trade winds converge at the ITCZ, giving heavy rain.
World rainfall follows the pressure belts, which are bands of rising or sinking air arranged by latitude. Rising air gives rain and sinking air gives dry conditions.

Equatorial belt (about 0-10°): heavy rain all year, over 2,000 mm a year, from low pressure, rising air, convergence at the ITCZ, convection and high evaporation from warm seas and forests. Manaus, central Amazon, Brazil, receives about 2,300 mm a year.
Tropics with a wet and dry season (about 10-20°, savanna and monsoon lands): rain falls in summer when the ITCZ moves over them, and the winter is dry.
Subtropical high-pressure belts (about 20-30°): very low rainfall and the world's great hot deserts, from sinking, warming, stable air and clear skies.
The Atacama, Chile, is the driest non-polar desert on earth, and the Namib receives much of its moisture as fog from the cold Benguela Current.
Mid-latitudes (about 40-60°): moderate to heavy rain from depressions in the westerlies, wettest on west coasts facing onshore winds (Ireland), decreasing into continental interiors.
Polar regions: very low precipitation, since cold air holds little vapour and sinking air lies under the polar high pressure. Antarctica is the driest continent, a cold desert.
Diagram: a pole-to-pole profile of rainfall under the three-cell model (the pattern of three circulation cells in each hemisphere).
The latitude pattern is changed locally by five factors, each of which can make a place wetter or drier than its latitude suggests.
Relief and rain shadow: the leeward side of a mountain barrier receives much less rain. There is more on this in the block on relief (orographic) rainfall.
Distance from the sea: continental interiors are dry because they lie far from the moisture of the oceans.
Prevailing winds: onshore winds bring rain, while offshore winds bring dry air.
Ocean currents: warm currents add moisture and instability; cold currents chill the air and make it stable, so rain is rare though fog is common on the coasts named above.
Seasonal migration: the pressure belts move north and south with the overhead sun, shifting the rain belts with them.
A rainfall regime is the pattern of rain through the year. Five regimes are worth knowing.
Equatorial: rain all year because the air is warm and rising every day, often peaking after the equinoxes.
Monsoon: a very wet summer and a dry winter, as in India.
Mediterranean: a wet winter and a dry summer.
Continental interiors: a summer maximum, because summer heating drives convection.
Irish (oceanic): rain all year, with a maximum in autumn and winter.
Ireland shows how wind, depressions and relief combine to make the west wet and the east drier.
The west is wetter than the east, the mountains are wettest, and the west has more wet days, because moist Atlantic air arrives there first.
Annual rainfall is about 750 mm in the driest parts of the east, around Dublin, about 1,000-1,250 mm across much of the west, and over 2,000 mm on many western mountains.
Wet days number about 150 a year on the east and south-east coasts, and up to about 225 a year in parts of the west.
Causes: prevailing south-westerly winds, Atlantic depressions reaching the west first, relief uplift on the western mountains, and the rain shadow in the east.
Variability is how much rainfall changes from year to year. It is a problem for farming and water supply.
Rainfall is least reliable where totals are lowest. In the Sahel, annual rainfall is roughly 200-600 mm, falling in one short summer wet season when the ITCZ moves north.
It varies greatly from year to year, so drought risk is greatest there. There is more on this in One major biome in detail.
The exchanges of water between ocean and atmosphere give rise to distinctive weather and climate regimes in different parts of the world. Each is a one-line summary here.
Equatorial regime: morning heating gives way to afternoon storms every day.
Monsoon regime: moist sea air brings a wet summer and dry land air a dry winter over India, as the monsoon (a seasonal wind) reverses.
Fog deserts: cold-current coasts, such as the Atacama and Namib, have fog rather than rain.
Irish maritime regime: a cool, cloudy, wet climate fed by moisture from the Atlantic and warmed by the North Atlantic Drift.
Snowy continental and lake-effect winters: cold, snowy winters with heavy snowfall downwind of large lakes and in continental interiors.
Intensified water cycle: warming increases evaporation and brings heavier downpours. There is more on this in Climatic environments and climate change.
Air moves because pressure differences push it. The Earth's rotation then bends its path, so winds away from the equator do not blow straight from high to low pressure.

Pressure gradient force: air moves from high to low pressure. The closer the isobars (lines on a weather map joining places of equal pressure), the steeper the gradient and the stronger the force and wind.
Pressure differences arise from unequal heating (thermal causes) and from air converging or diverging aloft (dynamic causes), which means air piles up or is drawn away high in the atmosphere.
Coriolis force: because the Earth rotates, moving air is deflected to the right in the northern hemisphere and to the left in the southern hemisphere.

The Coriolis effect is zero at the equator and strongest at the poles, and it is greater for faster-moving air. It changes the direction of the wind, not its speed, because it acts sideways on moving air.
Gaspard-Gustave de Coriolis, a French scientist, described the effect mathematically in 1835.
Geostrophic wind: above about 1 km, where there is little friction, the pressure gradient force and the Coriolis force balance, so the wind blows parallel to the isobars.
Diagram: a globe with arrows showing the Coriolis deflection to the right in the northern hemisphere and to the left in the southern hemisphere.
Near the ground, friction changes the balance of forces. Together with the Coriolis force it makes surface air spiral round pressure systems instead of blowing straight into or out of them.
Friction: near the surface, friction with the ground slows the wind and weakens the Coriolis effect, so surface winds cross the isobars at an angle, blowing into lows and out of highs.
Friction is greater over land (rough) than over sea (smooth), so surface winds are stronger over the sea and on coasts.

Result: in the northern hemisphere air spirals anticlockwise into a depression (a low-pressure system) and clockwise out of an anticyclone (a high-pressure system). The directions reverse in the southern hemisphere.
Buys Ballot's law, from Weather and Climate — Weather Maps and Satellite Imagery, links the direction of the wind to the position of low pressure.
Ocean currents are driven mainly by wind. The Coriolis effect, the continents and density then shape them.

Wind drag: prevailing winds (the winds that blow most often from one direction) blowing over the sea surface drive the surface currents. The trade winds push the equatorial currents westward, and the westerlies push the mid-latitude currents eastward.
The surface current is deflected about 45° from the wind direction, because the Coriolis effect acts on moving water as it does on air.
The net movement of the whole wind-driven layer is about 90° to the right of the wind in the northern hemisphere. This is Ekman transport.
Vagn Walfrid Ekman, a Swedish oceanographer, described the Ekman spiral and Ekman transport in the early 20th century.

Density differences: colder and saltier water is denser and sinks, while warmer and fresher water rises or spreads at the surface. This drives the deep thermohaline circulation (the slow ocean circulation driven by temperature and salt differences).
Continents and the shape of the ocean floor: land masses block and deflect currents north or south, turning them into closed gyres (circular current systems).
Gravity and tides also move water.
Air rises near the equator and sinks at around 30° and at the poles. This creates a regular pattern of pressure belts in each hemisphere, and each belt has its own weather.
Equatorial low, also called the ITCZ (the Inter-Tropical Convergence Zone, where the trade winds meet) or doldrums: calm, rising air and heavy rain, because strong heating makes moist air rise.
Subtropical highs at about 30° north and south, also called the horse latitudes: sinking, dry air, which is why deserts lie in these belts.
Subpolar lows at about 60° north and south: the polar front (where cold polar air meets warm tropical air), where depressions form.
Polar highs: cold, sinking air, because cold air is dense.
Diagram: a tri-cellular model (a model with three circulation cells in each hemisphere) showing the pressure belts, cells and surface winds for both hemispheres.
Surface air flows from the high-pressure belts towards the low-pressure belts. The Coriolis force bends each flow, which gives the three great wind systems.
North-east and south-east trade winds blow from the subtropical highs towards the ITCZ.
Westerlies blow from the subtropical highs towards the subpolar lows: south-westerly in the northern hemisphere and north-westerly in the southern hemisphere.
Polar easterlies blow from the polar highs towards the subpolar lows, because air always flows from high to low pressure.
Each of these winds is deflected by the Coriolis force, which is why none blows due north or south.
The pressure belts and winds belong to three circulation cells (closed loops of rising and sinking air) in each hemisphere.
Hadley cell: a thermal cell (driven by heating) powered by equatorial heating. George Hadley described it in 1735.

Ferrel cell: an indirect cell, which means it is driven by the Hadley and polar cells on either side rather than by heating of its own. William Ferrel, an American meteorologist of the 19th century, is associated with it.
Polar cell: a thermal cell in which cold, dense air sinks at the poles.
The pressure belts follow the overhead sun, so the whole system shifts with the seasons. This explains why some climates have a dry season and a wet season.
The pressure belts and the ITCZ move north in the northern summer and south in the northern winter.
The shift is greater over continents than over oceans, because land heats and cools faster than sea.
This shift produces the dry summer of the Mediterranean, which lies under the subtropical high in summer.

It also brings the summer rain of the monsoon (a seasonal wind reversal that brings heavy rain) and the single wet season of the Sahel (the semi-arid belt south of the Sahara). There is more on this in A Continental / Subcontinental Region.
High above the surface, narrow rivers of fast air steer weather systems. Their path decides what kind of weather Ireland gets.
Jet streams are narrow, fast bands of westerly wind in the upper troposphere (the lowest layer of the atmosphere, where weather happens), near the tropopause (its upper limit), at about 9–12 km up.
They form where temperature contrasts are sharpest, because big contrasts mean steep pressure gradients, and often blow at over 150 km/h. They are faster in winter.
The polar front jet stream meanders in large waves, called Rossby waves, and steers depressions.
A strong, straight jet over the Atlantic brings stormy winters to Ireland. Its position decides whether Ireland gets a run of wet, windy depressions or settled weather.
A slow, looping jet can block weather systems in place for weeks, so one kind of weather persists.
The subtropical jet also has a role in the Indian monsoon. There is more on this in A Continental / Subcontinental Region.
The North Atlantic pressure systems that dominate Ireland's weather are linked by a seesaw of pressure. When one is strong the other changes with it, and this decides the winter.
The Icelandic Low and the Azores High are semi-permanent pressure systems (always present, though they shift in strength) that dominate Ireland's weather.
The North Atlantic Oscillation (NAO) is the seesaw of pressure between these two systems. It controls the strength of the westerlies.
In the positive phase, with a large pressure difference, the westerlies are strong and Irish winters are mild, wet and stormy.

In the negative phase, with a small pressure difference, the westerlies are weaker, blocking highs (highs that stay in place and block the westerly flow) are more common, and Irish winters are colder and drier.
An air mass is a large body of air that takes on the temperature and moisture of the region it comes from. Ireland receives five, and each brings its own weather.
Tropical maritime: comes from the Atlantic near the Azores. It is warm, moist and mild, with cloud and drizzle.
Polar maritime: comes from the North Atlantic near Greenland and Iceland. It is cool, moist and showery, because it crosses the sea, and is Ireland's most frequent air mass.
Arctic maritime: comes from the Arctic. It is cold, with snow showers in the north and west in winter.

Polar continental: comes from Russia and Scandinavia in winter. It is very cold and dry, and it brings snow to east coasts after crossing the Irish Sea. The 2018 case is described under Blocking anticyclones.
Tropical continental: comes from North Africa and southern Europe in summer. It is hot, dry and hazy because it has crossed warm land, and it brings heatwaves.
Surface currents do not run in straight lines across an ocean. Wind, the Coriolis effect and the continents bend them into great circles.
Gyres are large, circular systems of surface currents, driven by wind, the Coriolis effect and the continents.
Gyres turn clockwise in northern hemisphere oceans and anticlockwise in southern hemisphere oceans, because the Coriolis effect deflects water right in the north and left in the south.
The five main gyres are the North Atlantic, South Atlantic, North Pacific, South Pacific and Indian Ocean gyres.
Diagram: a world map of the main surface currents, with warm currents in red, cold currents in blue, and the five gyres marked.
The North Atlantic gyre carries warm water to Ireland and returns cold water to the tropics. It is the circulation pattern the syllabus names as its setting.
The North Equatorial Current flows west with the trade winds.
The current turns north as the Gulf Stream along the North American coast, because the land blocks its westward path.
The Gulf Stream starts in the Gulf of Mexico and the Straits of Florida, and it carries more water than all the world's rivers combined.
The westerlies carry the Gulf Stream north-east across the Atlantic as the North Atlantic Drift, towards Ireland, Britain and Norway.
Part of the current turns south as the cold Canary Current along north-west Africa and rejoins the North Equatorial Current.
The calm Sargasso Sea sits in the centre of the gyre, inside the circling currents. It is named after its floating sargassum seaweed.
The cold Labrador Current flows south from the Arctic between Greenland and Canada.
Where a current goes decides the climate of the coast it passes. Warm and cold currents in the North Atlantic give very different results.
The North Atlantic Drift gives Ireland mild winters. It also keeps ports ice-free, and the Norwegian coast stays ice-free at Hammerfest and Murmansk, while Labrador's coast is frozen.
Warm sea adds moisture and energy to Atlantic depressions (low-pressure systems that bring rain and wind).
Fog forms where the Gulf Stream meets the Labrador Current, and advection fog (fog formed when warm, moist air moves over a cold surface) forms on the Grand Banks off Newfoundland.
Icebergs are carried south in the Labrador Current. The Titanic sank on 15 April 1912 after hitting an iceberg south of Newfoundland.
The Saharan coast of north-west Africa is arid, because it lies beside the cold Canary Current.
The same pattern repeats round the world. Warm currents flow along the western edges of oceans and cold currents along the eastern edges.
Warm western-boundary currents carry warm water away from the tropics along the western sides of ocean basins, such as the Kuroshio, Brazil, East Australian and Agulhas currents.
Cold eastern-boundary currents bring cold water towards the equator along the eastern sides of ocean basins, such as the California, Humboldt and Benguela currents.
The Antarctic Circumpolar Current flows west to east round Antarctica. It is the largest ocean current by volume, because no land blocks it.
The strong westerlies of the Southern Ocean (the ocean around Antarctica) are called the Roaring Forties and the Furious Fifties.
Where winds move surface water away from a coast, deep water must rise to fill the gap. This brings food and cold to the surface.
Winds push surface water away from a coast (Ekman transport), and cold, nutrient-rich deep water rises to replace it.
Plankton (tiny floating organisms) thrive in the nutrient-rich water, supporting rich fisheries off Peru, south-west Africa, California and north-west Africa.
The Peruvian anchoveta fishery, fed by upwelling off Peru in the Humboldt Current, is the largest single-species fishery in the world.
The cold upwelled water chills the air above it, which gives the coast fog and aridity.

The thermohaline circulation (thermo means temperature, haline means salt) is the global ocean conveyor belt. It is driven by differences in temperature and salinity, and it moves water through the deep ocean.
Surface water is cooled and made saltier by evaporation and sea-ice formation in the Greenland, Norwegian and Labrador Seas and around Antarctica. It becomes dense and sinks to the ocean floor.
The deep water flows slowly south through the Atlantic, round Antarctica and into the Indian and Pacific Oceans.
There the water gradually rises and returns to the surface as warm currents, so the loop is complete.
One circuit of the conveyor belt takes about 1,000 years, because the deep water moves so slowly.

The Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC) is the Atlantic part of this system. It pulls the Gulf Stream's warm water north, because sinking water in the north draws surface water towards it.
Diagram: a world map showing the conveyor belt of deep and surface currents.
The AMOC depends on cold, salty water sinking in the North Atlantic. Anything that changes that water could slow the whole system.
Melting Greenland ice and more rain make North Atlantic water fresher and less dense. It may then sink less, and the AMOC may weaken.
The IPCC (AR6, 2021) judged that the AMOC is very likely to weaken over the 21st century, because of the fresher water.
A weaker AMOC could cool north-west Europe relative to the rest of the world and change rainfall patterns.
A depression is a low-pressure system in the mid-latitudes (the zones between the tropics and the poles). It is the main source of Ireland's rain and wind.

A depression is roughly 1,000–3,000 km across, with closed isobars, winds blowing anticlockwise inwards in the northern hemisphere, and warm and cold fronts (the boundaries between warm and cold air).
Depressions move from west to east, steered by the jet stream, so they reach Ireland first from the Atlantic, and bring most of Ireland's rain and wind.

Polar front theory, which explains how depressions form along the polar front, was developed by the Bergen School of Norwegian meteorologists, led by Vilhelm Bjerknes and his son Jacob, around the end of the First World War.
Diagram: a plan view of a mature depression with isobars, fronts and the warm sector.
A depression grows in stages along the polar front, where two air masses meet and move in opposite directions. Learn the stages in order.
1. At the polar front, cold polar maritime air from the north meets warm, moist tropical maritime air from the south-west, and the two move in opposite directions.
2. A small wave or kink develops on the front, which starts the depression, often where the jet stream above is diverging and removing air aloft.
3. Warm air pushes into the cold air and begins to rise over it. Surface pressure falls because air is rising, so air is drawn in, and it turns anticlockwise under the Coriolis force.

4. A warm front forms ahead of the warm air and a cold front forms behind it, with the warm sector between them. The system deepens (pressure falls) as more warm air rises and latent heat (heat released when water vapour condenses) is released.
5. The cold front moves faster than the warm front and catches up with it, lifting the warm sector off the ground to form an occluded front. This is occlusion.

6. Once the warm air is cut off from the surface, the depression fills as pressure rises, and it dies. This usually takes a few days to about a week, because the fronts have lost their supply of warm air.
Diagram: a cross-section along a line through both fronts, showing cloud types and rain belts.
As a depression moves from west to east, the front, the warm sector and the cold front pass over a place one after another. Each brings its own cloud, rain, wind and pressure.

Approach: pressure starts to fall. High cirrus (wispy ice cloud) is followed by cirrostratus (a thin high sheet), which gives a halo round the sun. The wind backs (changes anticlockwise), for example from westerly to southerly or south-easterly, and strengthens.

Warm front: cloud thickens and lowers, first to altostratus (a mid-level grey sheet) and then to nimbostratus (thick rain cloud). A long period of steady, moderate rain follows, sometimes for several hours. Pressure falls steadily and temperature rises slightly.

Warm sector: rain eases to drizzle or stops. Low stratus (a low grey layer of cloud) and mist form on hills. The air is mild and humid, the wind veers (changes clockwise) to south-westerly, and pressure is steady.

Cold front: cumulonimbus clouds (towering storm clouds) form and bring short, heavy showers, sometimes with hail, thunder and gusty squalls. Temperature falls sharply, the wind veers to westerly or north-westerly, and pressure begins to rise.
Behind the cold front: the air is clearer, colder and brighter, with scattered cumulus (heaped clouds) and showers and good visibility. Pressure rises.
Occluded front: the cloud and rain of both fronts combine, often with lighter rain as the system ages.
Because Ireland lies in the path of the depressions that cross the Atlantic, their passing shapes the whole climate.
Ireland's weather is changeable, with rain in every month, because depressions cross the country regularly.
The west is wetter than the east, because depressions arrive there first.
Strong winds and storms are most common in autumn and winter, when the temperature contrast between warm and cold air and the jet stream are strongest.
Coastal storm surges, which flood low coasts (a rise in sea level driven by wind and low pressure) accompany the strongest depressions.
Flooding happens when depressions follow each other in quick succession, because the ground has no time to drain.
Storms named by Met Éireann include ex-hurricane Ophelia (16 October 2017) and Storm Éowyn (24 January 2025, when Red wind warnings were issued).
An anticyclone is the opposite of a depression: a large area of sinking air and high pressure. Its sinking air explains its settled weather.
An anticyclone is an area of high pressure with widely spaced, closed isobars. It has light winds blowing clockwise outwards in the northern hemisphere, and no fronts.
Anticyclones are large and slow-moving, so they can last for days or weeks.

Air converging high in the atmosphere sinks, a process called subsidence. As it sinks it is compressed and warms adiabatically (by compression alone, without taking in heat), so its relative humidity falls and clouds evaporate.
Dynamic (warm) highs form from sinking air in the general circulation. The Azores High is an example, and it often extends a ridge (a long narrow extension of high pressure) over Ireland in summer.
Thermal (cold) highs form when the ground cools intensely in winter. The Siberian High, a cold anticyclone over Central Asia, is an example.
A temperature inversion (a layer where temperature rises with height instead of falling) often forms in the sinking air, trapping moisture and pollution beneath it.
Sinking, drying air means few clouds. In summer this gives hot, bright weather.
Clear skies, strong sunshine, high daytime temperatures and light winds.
Cool nights with dew and sometimes morning mist, because clear skies let heat escape.
Occasional thunderstorms, triggered by the heat, at the edges of the high.
Sea breezes on coasts by day, because the land heats faster than the sea.
Prolonged summer highs cause heatwaves and drought, because there is little cloud or rain for days.
In winter the same clear skies let the ground lose heat, so an anticyclone can bring cold rather than warmth.
Clear nights let the ground lose heat rapidly. This causes hard frost and freezing fog in valleys (radiation fog, fog formed when the ground cools the air above it), which may persist all day.
Cold, crisp, sunny days are common, because the sky is clear.
Anticyclonic gloom: a layer of stratocumulus (low, lumpy layered cloud) is trapped under the inversion, keeping the sky grey and dull.
Smog (smoke and fog) forms in towns where pollution is trapped beneath the inversion. There is more on this in Economic Activity and Environmental Impact.
A high that stays put can steer weather away from a region for weeks. The 2018 cold spell in Ireland is the example.
A high that stays in place, often over Scandinavia or west of Ireland, blocks the westerly flow and diverts depressions north or south.
The result is a long spell of dry weather, with a heatwave in summer or a cold spell in winter, while other regions get prolonged rain.
A block to the east can draw very cold polar continental air to Ireland.
In late February and early March 2018, a block of high pressure over Scandinavia drew bitterly cold polar continental air from Russia over Ireland. This was the Beast from the East.
Storm Emma then arrived from the south on 1–2 March 2018, bringing heavy snow.
Met Éireann issued a Red snow warning for the whole country. It was the first nationwide Red warning.
The two systems are opposites in almost every respect. Set them side by side, point for point.
Pressure: a depression has low pressure at its centre and an anticyclone has high pressure.
Isobars: closely spaced in a depression, widely spaced in an anticyclone.
Wind: strong in a depression and light in an anticyclone.
Air movement: air rises in a depression and sinks in an anticyclone.
Cloud and rain: cloud and rain in a depression, clear skies in an anticyclone.
Typical weather: changeable, windy and wet in a depression, and settled, dry and calm in an anticyclone.
Movement: depressions travel from west to east, while anticyclones are slow-moving.
Land and sea heat up at different rates. By day this difference sets up a small circulation that blows from the sea onto the land.
Land heats faster than the sea under sunshine. Air over the land warms, expands and rises, creating lower pressure over the land, while the cooler sea has relatively higher pressure.
Cool air flows onshore from the sea to the land, because air moves towards the lower pressure.
The air that rose returns seaward at height and sinks over the sea, completing a circulation cell.
Sea breezes are strongest on hot, calm, sunny summer afternoons, often under an anticyclone, and in the tropics they may blow most days.
After dark the heating difference reverses, so the breeze reverses with it.
After sunset, land loses heat faster than the sea. Air over the land cools and becomes denser, creating higher pressure over the land and lower pressure over the warmer sea.
Air flows offshore, from the land to the sea, because air moves towards the lower pressure over the sea.
The land breeze is weaker than the sea breeze, because the night-time temperature difference is smaller.
Diagram: two cross-sections, one for day and one for night, with arrows showing the direction of the air and the relative pressure.
These local winds change the temperature, humidity and cloud along a coast, and people have used them for centuries.
Sea breezes lower coastal temperatures in the afternoon and raise humidity.
A sea-breeze front (the line where the cool sea air meets the warmer land air) can trigger a line of cumulus or showers inland.
Sea breezes can carry sea fog onshore and trap urban pollution.
Land breezes help clear coastal fog, because they blow the fog out to sea.
Sailing fishermen traditionally went out at dawn with the land breeze and came back in the afternoon with the sea breeze.
Lake breezes form in the same way on large lakes.
Slopes in the mountains heat and cool faster than the air above the valley. By day this makes air flow up the slopes.
Sunshine heats the valley sides. Air in contact with them warms and rises upslope.
Cumulus may form over the peaks in the afternoon, because the rising air cools and its moisture condenses.
At night the slopes cool and the process runs in reverse. Cold air drains downhill and collects in the valley.
Slopes lose heat by radiation. Air in contact with them cools, becomes denser and drains downslope under gravity, collecting on the valley floor.
Cold air pooling on the valley floor creates frost hollows and temperature inversions, so valley floors are colder than the slopes above.
Orchards and vineyards are planted on slopes above the frost line to avoid frost hollows.
Radiation fog forms in the valleys, because the cold pooled air chills moisture to saturation.
In Antarctica and Greenland, where the ice sheets are very cold, katabatic winds flowing off the ice sheets can reach gale force.
Diagram: a day and night cross-section of a valley showing the anabatic and katabatic flows.

A föhn is a warm, dry wind on the lee side of a mountain range (the side sheltered from the prevailing wind). Its temperature change comes from the difference between saturated and dry cooling and warming.
The name föhn comes from the Alps, the original area where the wind was described, in the German-speaking Alpine valleys.
Air rising on the windward side cools at the saturated rate (the slower rate) after condensation begins, because condensation releases latent heat.
Air descending on the lee side warms at the faster dry rate, so it arrives warmer and drier than it started.
The föhn is warm because of this difference in rates, not because the air comes from a warm place.
Effects: rapid snowmelt, avalanche and fire risk, and sudden temperature rises.
The Chinook is a föhn on the eastern (lee) side of the Rocky Mountains in Canada and the USA. It is called the snow eater because it melts snow rapidly.
Where high ground meets the Mediterranean coast, cold air can pour through gaps in the mountains. Two such winds have local names.
The mistral is a cold, dry northerly wind funnelled down the Rhône valley in southern France to the Mediterranean.
The bora is a cold, dry north-easterly wind descending to the Adriatic coast, in Croatia and at Trieste in Italy.
Both winds pour from high ground towards the sea, usually when high pressure lies inland and low pressure lies over the sea, because air flows from high to low pressure.
A thunderstorm is a violent storm of heavy rain, lightning and thunder, which grows in a tall cumulonimbus cloud. It needs three things to start.
Thunderstorms need plentiful moisture, which fuels the cloud, and unstable air (air that keeps rising once it is lifted).
They also need a trigger to lift the air: strong surface heating (convection), a cold front, mountains, or converging air.
A thunderstorm cell (one storm unit of the cloud) passes through three stages. Rising air builds it and falling air destroys it.

1. Cumulus (developing) stage: warm, moist air rises in strong updrafts. Condensation releases latent heat, which keeps the air warmer than its surroundings so that it rises faster. Cloud grows above the freezing level, but there is no rain yet.

2. Mature stage: water drops and ice grow large enough to fall. They drag air down and create downdrafts beside the updrafts. Heavy rain, hail, lightning, thunder and gusty winds reach the surface, and the cloud top spreads into an anvil at the tropopause. This is the most violent stage.
3. Dissipating stage: downdrafts spread through the cloud and cut off the supply of warm, moist air. The rain becomes lighter and the cloud breaks up. A single cell lasts about an hour.
Diagram: a cumulonimbus cell in its three stages, with updraft and downdraft arrows, the freezing level and the anvil at the tropopause.
Lightning is a giant electric spark inside a storm cloud, and thunder is the sound it makes. Both come from the ice and water in the cloud.

Collisions between ice crystals, hailstones and supercooled droplets (water that is still liquid below freezing) separate electrical charges. The top of the cloud is usually positive and the base negative.
A lightning discharge occurs within the cloud, between clouds, or to the ground.
A lightning bolt heats the air along its path to around 30,000 °C, several times hotter than the surface of the sun.
The heated air expands explosively. This expansion, not collisions between clouds, is the thunder.
Light travels faster than sound, so the flash arrives first. Counting the seconds to the thunder gives the distance, at about 3 seconds per km.
Thunderstorms are grouped by what lifts the air to start them, plus one especially violent type.
Air-mass (convectional) thunderstorms form in hot, humid air.
Frontal thunderstorms form along vigorous cold fronts.
Orographic thunderstorms form over mountains, where the ground forces air upward.
Supercells, such as those on the US Great Plains, are long-lived, rotating storms that can produce tornadoes and very large hail. They are common on the US Great Plains.
Thunderstorms need heat and moisture, so they cluster in the warm, wet tropics and thin out towards the poles.

Thunderstorms are most frequent over tropical land, because heat and moisture are plentiful, where they occur daily in the equatorial belt. They are less frequent in the mid-latitudes and rare at the poles.
Lake Maracaibo, Venezuela, has the highest density of lightning on Earth. This is the Catatumbo lightning, measured by NASA satellites.
The Congo Basin in Central Africa also has very frequent thunderstorms.
Ireland has relatively few thunderstorms, because the air is rarely hot and unstable, mainly in summer inland and with active cold fronts.
Impacts: flash flooding, hail damage to crops, lightning strikes that cause fires, power cuts and deaths, and downbursts (violent downdrafts) that are dangerous to aircraft.
A tropical cyclone is a huge rotating storm that feeds on warm ocean water. It can only form where several conditions are met together.
They form over sea-surface temperatures of at least about 26–27 °C, over a deep layer of ocean.
They form at least about 5° from the equator, because the Coriolis force is needed to start the rotation and it is zero at the equator.
Light winds aloft (low wind shear) and warm, moist, unstable air are also needed.
The North Atlantic hurricane season runs from 1 June to 30 November.
Warm sea feeds a tropical cyclone with moisture and heat. The result is a ring of violent storms round a calm centre.
Clusters of thunderstorms form over warm ocean. Rising air and released latent heat lower the pressure at the centre.
Inflowing air spirals in and rises in the eyewall (the ring of storm cloud round the centre). The calm, clear eye at the centre has sinking air, and spiral rain bands surround the eye.
Cyclones weaken over land or cold water, because the evaporation from warm sea that fuels them is cut off.
Diagram: a cross-section of a tropical cyclone showing the eye and the eyewall.
The same type of storm has different names in different oceans, and a scale rates its strength by wind speed.
For example, a hurricane forms in the Atlantic and north-east Pacific.
A typhoon forms in the north-west Pacific.
A cyclone forms in the Indian Ocean and the South Pacific.
The Saffir–Simpson scale has categories 1 to 5. Category 1 begins at sustained winds of 119 km/h (74 mph), and category 5 at 252 km/h (157 mph) or more.
Tropical cyclones kill through wind, rain and, above all, the sea. Four events show the scale of the loss.
Tropical cyclones bring destructive winds, torrential rain and flooding. Storm surge (a wall of sea water driven ashore by the storm) is usually the biggest killer.
Hurricane Katrina, August 2005: levee and floodwall failures flooded about 80% of New Orleans, and about 1,800 people died.
