Typhoon Haiyan, called Yolanda in the Philippines, November 2013: one of the strongest tropical cyclones ever recorded at landfall. Its storm surge devastated Tacloban on Leyte, and over 6,000 people died in the Philippines.
Odisha super cyclone, October 1999: about 10,000 deaths.
Hurricane Mitch, October 1998: about 11,000 people were killed in Central America, mainly in Honduras and Nicaragua, by floods and landslides.

A climatic environment (or climate region) is a large area with a similar pattern of temperature, precipitation and seasons, usually matched by similar vegetation and soils. Weather is the short-term state of the atmosphere, while climate is the average pattern over many years, so a climate region is defined by long-term averages, not by one day's weather.

The Köppen system, devised by Wladimir Köppen, a German-Russian climatologist, divides the world mainly by temperature and precipitation thresholds (cut-off values) that match vegetation, so each climate type has a typical plant cover.
Its broad groups are tropical, dry, warm temperate, cool temperate (continental) and polar, so a place is placed in a group by its temperature and rainfall.

Climates are arranged in belts by latitude (distance north or south of the equator), then modified by distance from the sea, ocean currents, relief (the height and shape of the land), and whether a place lies on the east or the west side of a continent.

Controls on climate: latitude and insolation (incoming solar energy); pressure belts and planetary winds with their seasonal shift; air masses (large bodies of air with uniform temperature and moisture); ocean currents; continentality (distance from the sea); altitude and relief.
Diagram: a world map of the main climate regions.

The equatorial (tropical rainforest) climate lies close to the equator, about 0-10 degrees N and S. It is found mainly in the Amazon Basin, the Congo Basin and South-East Asia (Indonesia and Malaysia). Its temperature is the steadiest on earth, and the reasons come from the sun's position.
Temperatures are high all year, with monthly means of about 26–28 °C.

The annual range (the difference between the warmest and coolest month) is tiny, about 2–3 °C, but the daily range is larger than the annual range: afternoon highs of about 30–32 °C and night lows of about 22–24 °C.

The sun is always high in the sky and is overhead at the equator at the equinoxes (March and September), so there is little change in heat input through the year. Day length is also about 12 hours all year.
Cloud cover reflects sunlight and stops temperatures rising much above the low 30s °C, which is why maximum temperatures here are lower than in deserts.
Pressure is permanently low in the equatorial trough (the ITCZ, or doldrums, the belt where the trade winds from north and south meet), so winds are light and variable.

Rain falls here every month, and nearly all of it comes from one process, convection (warm air rising, cooling and condensing into cloud). That process also produces a predictable daily pattern of weather.
Rainfall is over 2,000 mm a year (Manaus, Brazil, about 2,300 mm) and falls in every month.
There are often two wetter peaks after the equinoxes, when the overhead sun and the ITCZ pass over.

The rain is convectional: intense heating and very moist air from warm seas and forest transpiration (water given off by plant leaves) build towering clouds that produce heavy afternoon thunderstorms.
Trade winds converge at the ITCZ, which lifts and reinforces the moist air, so rising air is supplied from two directions.
Relative humidity (how much water vapour the air holds compared with the most it could hold) is often over 80%, and the air is humid at night too.

Daily cycle: a clear, calm, humid morning; cumulus (heaped, fluffy cloud) building by late morning; cumulonimbus (towering storm cloud) and torrential rain with thunder in the afternoon; clearing in the evening.
The climate has no temperate-style seasons, because temperature and rainfall barely change through the year.
The constant heat and rain support the richest plant cover on land, and that in turn shapes how people use the region.
Tropical rainforest grows on latosols (deep, reddish tropical soils). There is more on this in One major biome in detail.
Forest clearance for farming and timber is the main human pressure on the rainforest.

A monsoon climate has a seasonal reversal of wind direction, bringing a very wet summer and a dry winter. The word monsoon comes from the Arabic word for season. The classic monsoon climate is in South and South-East Asia, especially India, Bangladesh and Myanmar; weaker monsoon climates occur in northern Australia and West Africa.
The hot season before the rains (March–May): temperatures often exceed 40 °C on the northern plains.
The wet south-west monsoon, from June to September: slightly cooler than the hot season because of cloud and rain.
The cool dry season (October–February): pleasant, with cool nights in the north.
The south-west monsoon normally reaches Kerala around 1 June and covers all of India by mid-July. It brings about three-quarters of India's annual rainfall.
The summer monsoon starts with the land heating faster than the sea. Four linked steps then pull moist air onto India.
1. Intense heating of the land and of the high land to the north (the Tibetan Plateau) creates low pressure over north-west India.
2. The ITCZ (the belt of low pressure where trade winds meet) moves north.

3. The south-east trade winds cross the equator and are deflected by the Coriolis force (the turning effect of the earth's rotation on moving air) into south-west winds, which gather moisture over the Indian Ocean to the south.
4. The subtropical jet stream (a fast, high-altitude river of air) shifts north of the Himalayas, the mountains to the north, allowing the monsoon to burst suddenly. There is more on this in India.
Rain is not spread evenly across India: relief and distance from the moisture source decide who gets most. In winter the wind reverses and blows from the land, which is why the dry season follows.

Relief rain (rain from moist air forced up high ground) falls on the Western Ghats and on the north-east hills, the Khasi Hills of Meghalaya; Mawsynram and Cherrapunji, in the Khasi Hills, are among the wettest places on earth.

The Deccan lies in a rain shadow (the dry area on the sheltered side of high ground), and rainfall decreases north-westwards along the Ganges plain, with the Thar Desert in Rajasthan the driest region.
Kolkata is wetter than Delhi, which shows how rainfall falls away from the moisture source.
In winter the land cools and high pressure builds over the interior of Asia; dry north-east winds blow off the land.
The Himalayas, the mountains to the north, block cold air from the interior of Asia from reaching India.
The east coast of southern India (the Tamil Nadu coast) gets winter rain from the north-east monsoon after it has crossed the Bay of Bengal, because the wind picks up moisture over the sea.
Farmers depend on the monsoon arriving on time and in the right amount, so any variation has serious effects.
Late, weak or broken monsoons bring drought; very heavy ones bring floods.
Cyclones (intense tropical storms) in the Bay of Bengal are also a hazard: the Odisha super cyclone of October 1999 killed about 10,000 people.
El Niño years (when the central and eastern Pacific warms) often bring a weaker Indian monsoon.
Kharif crops such as rice are sown with the monsoon rains; rabi crops such as wheat rely on stored water and irrigation, because they grow in the dry season.

This climate lies on west coasts between about 40° and 60° in the path of the westerlies (the prevailing winds that blow from the west). Because the sea warms and cools slowly, it gives mild winters and cool summers.

Locations: north-west Europe, including Ireland, Britain, north-west France (Brittany), Belgium, the Netherlands, Denmark and coastal Norway; also British Columbia and the Pacific north-west of the USA, southern Chile, New Zealand and Tasmania.
Winters are mild and summers are cool, with a small annual range: Ireland's mean January is about 4–7 °C and its mean July about 14–16 °C, an annual range of about 10 °C.
Frost and snow are infrequent on low ground, because the sea keeps winters mild.
The climate of Ireland is also described at Core level in the note Physical regions.
Rain falls in every month, and the pattern is wet, mild and changeable. Most of it comes from fronts (the boundaries between warm and cold air) and from hills in the way of the wind.
Rain falls in all months, with a maximum in autumn and winter and many wet days: about 150 a year in the east and south-east of Ireland and up to about 225 in parts of the west.
Annual rainfall is about 750 mm in the driest east (around Dublin), about 1,000–1,250 mm across much of the west, and over 2,000 mm on many western mountains.

Most rain is frontal (cyclonic, produced where warm air rises over cold air in a depression), with relief rain on west-facing mountains; amounts fall from west to east because the air has already lost moisture.
The weather is changeable because depressions (low-pressure systems) and ridges of high pressure alternate.
Occasional anticyclones (high-pressure systems with sinking air) bring dry spells, most often in summer.
Vegetation is deciduous woodland (trees that shed leaves in winter) and grass on brown earths (fertile, mid-brown soils).
Each feature of the climate has a cause in the atmosphere or ocean. Wind, sea, pressure systems and air masses work together.
Prevailing south-westerly winds bring maritime air (air that has crossed the sea, so it is mild and moist) off the Atlantic.
The North Atlantic Drift, the extension of the Gulf Stream (a warm ocean current), warms winter air and seas.
The sea heats and cools slowly, moderating the seasons, so winters are not very cold and summers are not hot.

Depressions form frequently on the polar front (where warm tropical and cold polar air meet) and are steered by the jet stream (fast high-altitude winds), so they bring bursts of rain across the region.
Tropical and polar maritime air masses (the warm one from the south, the cold one from the north, both moist) are the most common.
Eastwards the oceanic influence weakens, because the sea is further away, and the climate grades into the continental climate of central and eastern Europe. There is more on this in Physical regions.
The Mediterranean climate lies on the west sides of continents between about 30° and 40° (some places to about 45°). It has hot summers and mild winters.

Locations: the lands around the Mediterranean Sea (for example southern Italy, southern Spain and Greece), central and southern California, central Chile, the Cape Town area of South Africa, and south-western and southern Australia (around Perth and Adelaide).
Summers are hot: lowland July means are about 25 °C or more, for example in southern Italy.
Winters are mild: coastal January means are about 9–12 °C, and frost is rare on the coasts.
Inland and upland areas have hotter summers and colder winters than the coast, because the sea has less moderating effect there.
Winter rain and summer drought both come from the seasonal shift of the pressure belts. The summer subtropical high (a belt of high pressure with sinking air) is the key to the explanation.
Rainfall is moderate (commonly about 400–900 mm), under 600 mm a year on parts of the Puglia lowlands and Sicily, and most of it falls from October to March.
Summers are dry, with drought for several months; rain often falls in intense downpours that cause flash floods and soil erosion.
In summer the subtropical high (the Azores High in the Mediterranean, the North Pacific High in California) moves poleward over the region, bringing sinking, warming air, clear skies and no rain.
In winter the pressure belts shift towards the equator, so the westerlies and their depressions bring rain; the warm Mediterranean Sea also spawns its own winter depressions.
On some of these coasts cold currents (the California, Humboldt, Benguela and Canary currents) keep summers cooler and drier.
The sirocco is a hot, dry, dusty wind from the Sahara; the mistral and the bora are cold winds.
Dry summers shape both the plants that survive and the dangers people face.
Drought-tolerant vegetation: olives, vines and cork oak, and maquis scrub (low, tough evergreen shrubs); citrus grows where it is irrigated.
Hazards: summer water shortage, and wildfires in hot, dry, windy summers.
The Mati wildfire near Athens, Greece, in July 2018 killed about 100 people, one of the deadliest wildfires in Europe.
Human response: water storage and irrigation, and tourism. There is more on this in Climate and economic development.

The continental climate lies in the interiors of large northern-hemisphere continents between about 40° and 60° N, far from the sea. With no ocean to moderate the temperature, it has the largest annual ranges on earth.
Locations: central and eastern Europe into Russia (Moscow) and Ukraine, the steppes of Ukraine and southern Russia, Central Asia, the Canadian Prairies, and the US Midwest and Great Plains.
There is no large equivalent in the southern hemisphere, which has too little land at these latitudes.
Winters are very cold, with monthly means well below 0 °C for several months: Moscow about −7 °C in January and Winnipeg about −16 °C in January.
Summers are warm to hot: Moscow about 19 °C and Winnipeg about 20 °C in July.
The annual range is large and increases with distance from the sea; Verkhoyansk has an annual range of over 60 °C.
Precipitation is lower than on oceanic coasts and peaks in summer, the opposite of Ireland. The reasons are the land itself, the distance from moisture and the pressure systems.
Precipitation is low to moderate (roughly 250–750 mm) and decreases into the interior: Moscow receives about 600–700 mm a year, with a summer maximum.
The summer maximum comes from convectional thunderstorms (rising currents of heated air) as the land heats up; winter precipitation falls as snow, which lies for months.
Continentality: the land heats and cools quickly, and there is no sea to moderate the temperature.
Distance from the oceans: the westerlies have lost most of their moisture crossing Europe, and in North America the Rockies block Pacific air from reaching the interior.
The winter Siberian High, a cold, dry, clear thermal anticyclone (high pressure caused by intense cooling of the land), sits over the continent; North America has an equivalent.
Summer low pressure over the heated land draws in some moist air.
Extreme temperatures and a short growing season create hazards, but the open grasslands also support large-scale farming.
Hazards: blizzards; cold waves of arctic air; summer heatwaves, drought and dust storms, as in the Dust Bowl of the 1930s on the Great Plains; floods when the spring snowmelt comes.
Vegetation is temperate grassland (steppe and prairie) on chernozems, the black, humus-rich soils of the steppes of Ukraine and southern Russia, the Prairies and the Pampas.
Human response: wheat and maize belts on the grassland; boreal forest (northern coniferous forest) further north.

Hot deserts lie about 15–30° N and S on the west sides of continents, for example the Sahara, Arabian, Namib, Atacama, Sonoran and Mojave, and Australian deserts. They have the highest temperatures on earth and very little rain.
Rainfall is very low (under about 250 mm) and unreliable because of sinking air in the subtropical high pressure belt, offshore trade winds (blowing from land to sea), cold currents and rain shadows.
The highest air temperatures on earth were recorded: 56.7 °C at Furnace Creek, Death Valley, on 10 July 1913, a WMO record, because of clear skies and high sun.
The daily range is very large, often 20–30 °C or more, because dry, cloudless air lets heat escape at night.
Fog forms on coasts with cold currents, because the cold water chills the air above it.
The Sahara covers about 9 million km², the world's largest hot desert; the Atacama is the driest non-polar desert.
Cold currents on desert coasts: the Canary (Sahara), Benguela (Namib), Humboldt (Atacama) and California (Sonoran coast).
Climate is not the same everywhere because the controls on it vary from place to place. Each kind of change across space has its own cause.
From equator to pole (latitude): temperature falls and seasonal contrasts grow with latitude.
From coast to interior: continentality increases the annual range; Ireland's annual range is about 10 °C, while Verkhoyansk's is over 60 °C.
From west to east coasts: cold currents cool and dry west coasts, while warm currents such as the North Atlantic Drift warm them.
With altitude: temperature falls with height, so high mountains have a vertical sequence of climates, and snow lies on high ground even near the equator.
Across a mountain range: the windward side gets relief rain, while the leeward side lies in a rain shadow, as the Deccan does in India.
Climate boundaries are transition zones that shift: the Sahel lies between the desert and wetter land and moves with the ITCZ from year to year, with rainfall of roughly 200–600 mm.
Climate changes over very different timescales, and each timescale has its own natural causes. Human activity has added a further cause in recent times.

Timescales: long-term change over millions of years (plate movement, mountain building); glacial cycles over tens to hundreds of thousands of years; centuries (the Little Ice Age); years (El Niño and volcanic eruptions); and recent human-caused warming.
Milankovitch orbital cycles (regular changes in the earth's orbit and tilt, described under Ice Ages causes below).
Changes in solar output (the energy the sun gives off), which means the earth receives more or less heat.

Volcanic eruptions: sulphate aerosols (tiny airborne particles) reflect sunlight and cool the earth for a year or two; after Mount Pinatubo, Philippines, erupted in June 1991, global average temperature fell by about 0.5 °C for about a year (1992).
Plate tectonics: moving continents and opening or closing seaways change ocean currents, so heat is redistributed around the world.
Changes in ocean circulation, because currents carry heat around the globe.

Feedbacks (effects that amplify a change): the ice–albedo feedback (albedo is how much sunlight a surface reflects), and CO2 and methane released or absorbed by oceans and permafrost (permanently frozen ground).
Since the Industrial Revolution people have become a cause of climate change.

The enhanced greenhouse effect (extra heat trapped by added greenhouse gases) comes from burning fossil fuels, deforestation and agriculture; land-use change and aerosols also alter the climate. There is more on this in Environmental pollution.
Nobody measured temperature in the distant past, so scientists use natural records that preserve clues, called proxies. Each source reaches back a different distance in time.

Ice cores: bubbles of ancient air record past CO2, and oxygen isotopes (forms of oxygen of different weight) record past temperature; Antarctic ice cores (EPICA Dome C) record about 800,000 years of climate and CO2.
Ocean-floor sediments, because layers of mud build up over time and keep a record of past conditions.
Tree rings, because trees grow a new ring each year and the rings record the conditions of that year.
Pollen preserved in peat bogs and lake muds; Irish bogs record changes in vegetation, and therefore climate, since the Ice Age.
Glacial landforms, the features left by ice, show where ice once lay.
Historical records such as harvest dates, frost fairs and ships' logs; instrument records since the 19th century.
The first of the three climate-change settings is the Ice Ages. The present era has swung repeatedly between very cold and warmer conditions.
The Quaternary glaciation began about 2.6 million years ago; since then the earth has swung between long glacial periods and shorter, warm interglacials.
Over the last 800,000 years the cycle has been about 100,000 years long; we now live in an interglacial.

At the Last Glacial Maximum (the coldest point of the last glacial period), about 20,000 years ago, ice sheets covered much of North America and northern Europe, including Scandinavia, Britain and Ireland.
Global sea level was about 120 m lower than today, because water was locked in ice, exposing land bridges between islands and continents (for example between Britain and continental Europe).
Global average temperature was several degrees colder, so the climate belts were pushed towards the equator.
Ireland was covered by ice, and the landscape still carries the evidence. The effects of the Ice Ages also reached well beyond the ice itself.
Ireland had two main cold stages, the Munsterian and the Midlandian. The Munsterian ice covered almost all of Ireland; the Midlandian ice had gone by about 10,000 years ago.
The evidence is in the landscape of drumlins, eskers, corries and U-shaped valleys, all landforms made by ice.
Isostatic rebound (land rising after the weight of ice is removed) and raised beaches are after-effects of the ice.
Beyond the ice, climates were drier and windier and deserts expanded, which is why loess was later blown about.
Loess (wind-blown dust) was blown from outwash plains (the gravel plains laid down by meltwater beyond the ice).
Sea level fell, and plants and animals migrated towards the equator to escape the cold and recolonised the land afterwards.
Small changes in the earth's orbit start an ice age, and feedbacks make the change much bigger. The orbital changes alter the distribution of sunlight, not the total amount.

Milankovitch cycles, named after Milutin Milanković, a Serbian scientist who calculated them in the early 20th century, change the distribution of sunlight by latitude and season more than its total amount.

Eccentricity (the shape of the orbit) varies over about 100,000 years; obliquity (the tilt, varying between about 22° and 24.5°) over about 41,000 years; precession (the wobble of the axis) over roughly 19,000–26,000 years.
When northern summers are cool, snow survives the winter and ice sheets grow.
Feedbacks amplify the small orbital change: more ice raises albedo (reflects more sunlight), and colder oceans absorb more CO2, lowering greenhouse gases.
Ice cores show CO2 near 180 ppm (parts per million) at glacial maxima and about 280 ppm in interglacials.
Changes in the Atlantic circulation, which means a change in how heat is carried to the north.
Land near the North Pole allows ice sheets to build, because snow can pile up on land but not on open sea.
Within the last thousand years there were warm and cold spells that are recorded in writing. Both are regional, mainly in the North Atlantic and Europe, and approximate in date.
Medieval Warm Period, roughly AD 950–1250: a regional warm phase mainly in the North Atlantic and Europe. Vines were grown further north in England than in the colder centuries that followed.
Norse settlers led by Erik the Red settled Greenland from about AD 985; the settlements were abandoned in the 15th century as the climate cooled.
Little Ice Age, roughly the 14th to the mid-19th century, coldest in the 17th century: a regional cold phase mainly in the North Atlantic and Europe, with Alpine glaciers advancing.
The River Thames in London froze in severe winters, and frost fairs were held on the ice, the last in 1814.
The Maunder Minimum (about 1645–1715), a period with very few sunspots, coincided with some of the coldest decades.
In Ireland the Great Frost of the winter of 1739–40 was followed by famine in 1740–41.
The eruption of Tambora, Indonesia, in April 1815 led to 1816 being the year without a summer, with harvest failures across Europe and north-eastern North America.
The second climate-change setting is the warming of the 20th century and the present. The evidence comes from many independent measurements.
CO2 was about 280 ppm before the Industrial Revolution and is over 420 ppm by the mid-2020s; it has been measured at Mauna Loa, Hawaii, since 1958.
Global average surface temperature has risen about 1.1–1.2 °C since the late 1800s (IPCC).
2024 was the warmest year on record and the first calendar year more than 1.5 °C above pre-industrial levels (Copernicus).
Arctic summer sea ice has shrunk by about 13% per decade since satellite records began in 1979.
Global sea level rose about 20 cm between 1901 and 2018 (IPCC).
Glaciers are retreating in most mountain regions, so this is further evidence of warming.
Ireland's average temperature has risen about 0.9 °C since 1900 (EPA and Met Éireann).
Warming happens because more greenhouse gases hold more heat in the climate system. Feedbacks then speed it up.

The enhanced greenhouse effect: more CO2, methane and nitrous oxide absorb more outgoing long-wave radiation (heat given off by the earth), so the heat budget is out of balance and the earth warms until a new balance is reached.
Most of the extra heat goes into the ocean, so the sea warms and expands.
Ice–albedo feedback: melting ice exposes dark ocean, which absorbs more heat; this is why the Arctic is warming fastest.
Water vapour feedback: warmer air holds more water vapour, itself a greenhouse gas, so warming leads to more warming.
Permafrost thaw releases methane and CO2, so warming leads to more greenhouse gases.
Reduced ocean CO2 uptake as the water warms, so more CO2 stays in the air.
A warmer atmosphere and ocean change how climate is spread across the world. The effects follow from more heat and more water vapour in the system.
A more intense hydrological cycle (the cycle of evaporation, rain and runoff): heavier downpours and more severe droughts.
More intense heatwaves: the European heatwave of summer 2003 caused an estimated 70,000 or so extra deaths.
A poleward shift of climate belts and storm tracks, and an expansion of the subtropical dry zones.
A possible weakening of the Atlantic circulation (AMOC, the ocean conveyor that carries warm water northwards).
Stronger tropical cyclones, because a warmer ocean supplies more heat to the storm.
Sea-level rise from the thermal expansion of warmer water and the melting of land ice.
Ireland is affected through temperature, rainfall and storms. The world has responded through scientific assessment and international agreement.
Ireland: warmer temperatures; wetter winters and more flooding; a risk of summer drought, as in the summer of 2018; stronger storms and coastal erosion.

The IPCC (the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change) was set up in 1988; its Sixth Assessment Report (2021) stated that it is unequivocal that human influence has warmed the atmosphere, ocean and land.
The Paris Agreement of 2015 aims to keep warming well below 2 °C and to pursue 1.5 °C. There is more on this in Environmental pollution.
The third climate-change setting is El Niño. To understand it you first need the normal pattern across the equatorial Pacific, known as the Walker circulation.
Strong south-east trade winds push warm surface water westward across the Pacific, piling up a warm pool near Indonesia and northern Australia, where sea level is higher.

Warm, moist air rises over the warm pool, producing low pressure and heavy rain. Air returns eastward at height and sinks over the cool eastern Pacific, giving high pressure and dry conditions on the coast of Peru and northern Chile.
Cold, nutrient-rich water upwells (rises from depth) off Peru (the Humboldt Current), supporting the Peruvian anchoveta fishery, the largest single-species fishery in the world.
The Walker circulation is named after Gilbert Walker, a British scientist who worked in India in the early 20th century.
In an El Niño year the normal pattern breaks down. The warm water, and with it the rain, moves east.
Every 2–7 years the trade winds weaken or even reverse, and the warm water flows back east towards South America.

The thermocline (the boundary between warm surface water and cold deep water) deepens in the east and upwelling stops; sea-surface temperatures in the central and eastern Pacific rise well above normal; the zone of rising air and rain shifts east.
It usually begins around the end of the year and lasts about 9–12 months, sometimes longer.
El Niño is a natural variation; scientists are still researching whether global warming changes it.

It was named by Peruvian fishermen after the Christ child because the warm water appeared around Christmas. Together with the Southern Oscillation, the see-saw of air pressure across the Pacific studied by Gilbert Walker, it is called ENSO.
Because the rain moves east, regions that are normally wet or dry swap roles. These distant effects are called teleconnections.
Heavy rain and floods in coastal Peru and Ecuador, which are normally dry, because the zone of rising air and rain has shifted east.
Collapse of the anchoveta catch and the fishmeal industry, with seabird deaths, because the cold, nutrient-rich water no longer upwells.
Drought in Indonesia, the Philippines and eastern Australia, with crop failure, bushfires, forest fires and haze.
Often a weaker Indian monsoon and drought in southern Africa, so these are El Niño effects far from the Pacific.
Fewer Atlantic hurricanes and more in the central and eastern Pacific, so the hurricane pattern shifts with the warm water.
Global average temperature rises temporarily, and strong El Niño years set temperature records.
Effects on Ireland and Europe are weak and uncertain.
Past El Niño events show how large the effects can be.
1972–73: an El Niño, combined with overfishing, caused the collapse of the Peruvian anchoveta fishery.
1982–83 and 1997–98: very strong El Niños. In 1997–98 coastal Peru and Ecuador had severe floods, and drought in Indonesia allowed huge forest fires whose smoke haze spread across South-East Asia.
2015–16: one of the three strongest El Niños on record.
2023–24: helped make 2023 and 2024 the warmest years on record.
La Niña is the reverse of El Niño: the normal Pacific pattern becomes stronger than usual, and the weather effects swap over.
Stronger trade winds, a cooler than normal eastern Pacific and stronger upwelling, so cold water reaches the surface off Peru.
Heavier rain in Indonesia and in Queensland, Australia, drought in Peru and the south-western USA, and more Atlantic hurricanes.
The strong La Niña of 2010–11 brought record rain and floods to Queensland, Australia, including the Brisbane flood of January 2011.
El Niño is on the syllabus because it shows two parts of the climate system acting as one.
It shows the atmosphere and ocean acting as one linked system, because a change in ocean temperature alters the winds and rain above it.
It shows how a change in ocean circulation changes weather around the world (teleconnections).
Monitoring by buoys and satellites in the equatorial Pacific gives months of warning, so countries can prepare for floods and drought.

Climate is both a resource and a limit. Temperature, the amount of rainfall, its seasonal timing and its reliability, sunshine and wind decide what can be grown, how much water is available, where tourists go and what it costs to adapt.

Rich economies can overcome climatic limits with technology: irrigation (supplying water to crops by channels or pipes), reservoirs, desalination (removing salt from seawater) and snow-making. They can afford to pay for these.
Poor economies that depend on rain-fed farming (crops watered only by rainfall) are the most exposed, because they have no stored or piped water to fall back on when the rain fails.
Climate change is shifting all of these. Its evidence and causes are taught in the notes on climatic environments and climate change.

Ireland's rainfall and mild temperatures give a long grass-growing season, so grass is the most important crop. Most farmland is grassland, used for dairy, beef and sheep (pastoral farming, meaning rearing animals). Rainfall and soils then split the country into farming regions.
Grass grows when soil temperature is above about 6 °C. In Ireland's mild climate that is for most of the year, and the season is longest in the south and south-west.

Annual rainfall is about 750 mm in the driest east, about 1,000–1,250 mm across much of the west and over 2,000 mm on many western mountains. This is why farming differs so much between east and west.
The south and east are drier and sunnier, and the south-east is the sunniest region. The 2020 Census of Agriculture counted about 135,000 farms.

Tillage (growing crops on ploughed land) is concentrated in the drier south and east, e.g. Co. Wexford, Co. Carlow and Co. Kildare. Barley, wheat, oats, potatoes and vegetables can be harvested there in dry conditions.

The Golden Vale (Co. Tipperary and Co. Limerick) has moderate rainfall and good soils on brown earths (well-drained fertile soils), which suit intensive dairying. EU milk quotas (limits on milk output) ended in 2015, after which dairying expanded.

Gley soils (waterlogged, poorly drained soils) of the drumlin belt (the lowland of low hills in Co. Cavan, Co. Monaghan and Co. Leitrim) and Co. Clare carry mainly grass for cattle, with a short grazing season.

The very wet west and north-west, with poorly drained gley and peat soils, suit mainly beef and sheep rearing on rough grazing, with small farms and low incomes. There is more on this in the notes on a peripheral Irish region.
Too much rain is as much a problem for Irish farming as too little. Wet weather raises costs, delays work and spreads disease.
Waterlogged soils are poached (trampled into mud) by cattle, and the grazing season is shortened. Animals must then be housed and fed silage (stored fermented grass) for longer, which raises costs.
Wet spells make it hard to make silage and hay and to harvest cereals, because the crops cannot be cut and dried in dry conditions.

Heavy rain leaches nutrients from the soil (washes them down out of reach of roots), and slurry (liquid animal manure) runs off when it rains after spreading. There is more on this in the notes on environmental pollution.
Damp weather favours diseases: potato blight, and liver fluke (a parasite) in sheep and cattle.
The summer of 2012 was exceptionally wet in Ireland. Poor silage and hay harvests, followed by a cold, late spring in 2013, caused a fodder (animal feed) crisis in spring 2013.
Farmers ran out of feed in spring 2013. Fodder was imported, including from Britain and France, and the Government funded a fodder transport subsidy.
The Great Famine (1845–49) followed potato blight, a disease favoured by mild, damp weather.
Ireland is a wet country, but dry spells also hurt farmers because grass is the crop that feeds the animals.
Grass stops growing in prolonged dry spells, so farmers have to feed winter fodder (stored feed) in summer.
Milk yields fall, and fodder runs short the following winter because the winter feed was used up in summer. Light soils (free-draining soils that dry out fast) of the south-east suffer most.

Summer 2018: a long anticyclonic spell (settled high-pressure weather) from late May to mid-July brought heat and drought to Ireland. Met Éireann, the national weather service, recorded absolute drought (a spell with almost no rain) at many stations.
Grass growth almost stopped that summer. Teagasc (the agriculture and food development authority) and the Government organised fodder imports and supports for the following winter.
Climate change brings both gains and risks to Irish farming, and farming is itself a source of the gases that cause it.
Warmer temperatures lengthen the growing season, and maize and other crops become more feasible. Wetter winters and more frequent summer droughts add risk.

Agriculture produces over a third of Ireland's greenhouse gas emissions (EPA, early 2020s). The EPA is the Environmental Protection Agency. There is more on this in the notes on environmental pollution.
In India, farming follows the monsoon, the seasonal wind that brings the summer rains. When the rains arrive, and how strong they are, set the farming year.
The south-west monsoon reaches Kerala around 1 June, covers India by mid-July and brings about three-quarters of the annual rainfall.

Kharif (summer) crops such as rice and cotton are sown with the monsoon rains. Rabi (winter) crops such as wheat rely on stored water, irrigation and western disturbances (winter rain-bearing weather systems).
A late or weak monsoon cuts harvests, farm incomes and GDP (the value of what the country produces), because so much of the year's water arrives in one season.

The Green Revolution (high-yielding crop varieties) from the mid-1960s, in Punjab, Haryana and western Uttar Pradesh, relied on irrigation. Canal irrigation in Punjab and Haryana brought salinisation (salt building up in the soil) and waterlogging.
The Indira Gandhi Canal in Rajasthan carries irrigation water into the dry north-west.
Egypt shows a country with almost no rain of its own, so farming depends entirely on one river. A dam turned an unpredictable flood into a controlled supply, but at a cost.
Egypt is almost rainless, so farming depends on irrigation from the Nile. The green strip of the Nile valley and delta shows through the desert.
The Nile's flood came from summer rain far upstream, and its uncertainty ended when the Aswan High Dam was completed in 1970.
The dam created Lake Nasser, one of the world's largest reservoirs. This allows year-round (perennial) irrigation, more than one crop a year and hydroelectricity (electricity from flowing water).
Costs: the fertile silt is trapped behind the dam, so farmers need artificial fertiliser. Salinisation and waterlogging have spread, and the delta is eroding.
California's Central Valley is a farming region where the summers are dry, so its high-value crops depend on irrigation. It shows what happens when drought cuts that supply.
California's Central Valley is one of the world's most productive farming regions. Its dry summers mean that high-value fruit, nuts and vegetables depend on irrigation.
Irrigation comes from large state and federal water projects, which carry snowmelt from the mountains, and from groundwater (water pumped from underground).
In the drought of about 2012–2016, farmers left land fallow (unplanted) and over-pumped groundwater. Heavy groundwater pumping caused land subsidence (the ground sinking) in the valley.
Governor Jerry Brown ordered a mandatory 25% cut in urban water use in April 2015, so cities as well as farms had to cut their water use.
In the Sahel, the dry belt south of the Sahara, crops rely on rain alone. This shows that how reliable rainfall is matters as much as how much falls.
The Sahel has one short wet season, in which millet and sorghum are grown alongside pastoral herding (keeping livestock).
Any shortfall in rain means crop failure, with losses of food and livestock, because farmers have no irrigation to fall back on.
Rainfall reliability matters as much as the total: the lower the average rainfall, the more variable it is from year to year. Dry regions therefore face both low and unpredictable harvests.
Water for homes comes from rain that has collected in rivers, lakes, reservoirs and underground. So rainfall shapes how secure a household supply is, even in a wet country.
Domestic water depends on rainfall refilling rivers, lakes, reservoirs and groundwater. Supply must be stored to cover dry periods.
Demand peaks in hot, dry weather, exactly when supply is lowest.
Group water schemes (community-run supplies) and private wells serve many rural homes. Wells can run dry in drought and be contaminated after heavy rain.
In arid and monsoon countries, water supply depends on seasonal rain, groundwater and long-distance transfers (carrying water from one region to another).
Rich, dry countries such as the Gulf states and Israel rely heavily on desalination for domestic water.
Women and children in poor rural areas spend hours a day collecting water, which keeps girls out of school.
Ireland has plenty of rain, yet water supply is still a problem. The cause is where the rain falls compared with where people live.
Ireland's paradox: there is plenty of rain overall, but most of it falls in the west while most people live in the east, where rainfall is lowest (about 750 mm a year around Dublin).
Census 2022 counted about 1.45 million people in Dublin county, out of about 5.1 million in Ireland.
Old, leaking pipes waste a large share of treated water, and treatment capacity (how much water can be cleaned for drinking) is tight.
Dublin's water comes mainly from the River Liffey, through the Poulaphouca reservoir (also called the Blessington lakes, Co. Wicklow), and from the Vartry reservoir at Roundwood, Co. Wicklow.
The Water Supply Project would take water from the River Shannon at Parteen Basin, just south of Lough Derg, by a pipeline of about 170 km to the Greater Dublin Area. It is planned, not built.
Uisce Éireann (Irish Water), which adopted its name in 2023, is responsible for public water supply.
The 2018 drought showed that a wet country can still run short of water for homes.
Irish Water imposed a hosepipe ban (a Water Conservation Order, a legal limit on using water outdoors), first in the Greater Dublin Area in early July 2018 and later extended to the whole country.
The ban shows a rainfall shortfall affecting domestic supply in a wet country.
Cape Town came close to running out of water. It shows how a rainfall failure becomes a supply crisis, and how a city can respond.
Cape Town, South Africa, has a Mediterranean climate (wet winters and dry summers). Three dry winters, about 2015–2017, left its reservoirs very low.
In early 2018 the city warned of 'Day Zero', when household taps would be shut off.
From 1 February 2018 residents were limited to 50 litres per person per day, with higher tariffs (prices), reduced water pressure and public campaigns.
Day Zero was avoided after usage was roughly halved and the winter rains of 2018 returned.
Lessons: diversify supply (groundwater, recycling and desalination), reduce leaks, and plan for longer droughts.

Drought is a long period with much less precipitation (rain, snow and other falling moisture) than normal for that place, so that water supply falls short of demand. It can be measured at three stages, from sky to soil to rivers.
Meteorological drought is a shortfall of rain, so it is measured by rainfall totals.
Agricultural drought is soil moisture too low for crops, so plants wilt even if some rain has fallen.
Hydrological drought is low rivers, reservoirs and groundwater, which means the water supply itself runs short.

Causes: blocking anticyclones (high-pressure systems that stay put and divert rain-bearing weather); failure or shift of the ITCZ (the belt of rising air and heavy rain near the equator) or monsoon; El Niño (a warming of the Pacific that disturbs rainfall worldwide); and climate change.
Drought hits the economy through farming first, then spreads to prices, jobs, energy and public spending.
Crop failure and loss of livestock, because grass and crops die without water.
Higher food prices, because less is produced, and loss of farm income and rural jobs.
Famine in poor countries, and migration to cities and abroad, because people leave when farming can no longer feed them.
Less hydroelectricity and less cooling water for power stations, and river transport disrupted because water levels fall.
Wildfires, because dry vegetation burns easily, and government spending on relief.
A rich economy can absorb drought, but not without losses. The Millennium Drought in Australia shows this.
The Millennium Drought in south-eastern Australia lasted roughly from the late 1990s to 2009, hitting farming in the Murray–Darling Basin, Australia's main irrigated farming region.
Losses were absorbed through insurance, government aid, water trading and technology, but farm output fell and towns faced water restrictions.
Australian cities, including Melbourne, built large desalination plants in response.

Rich and poor responses contrast: a developed economy absorbs drought through insurance, aid, water trading, technology and desalination, while a poor economy with few of these faces famine. The Horn of Africa case below shows this.
Where people have little saving, insurance or state support, drought turns into famine. The Horn of Africa in 2011 is the example.
Drought across the Horn of Africa in 2011 followed two failed rainy seasons, linked to La Niña (the cool counterpart of El Niño in the Pacific).
Crops failed, livestock died and food prices soared, because the failed rains cut food supply.
The UN declared famine in parts of southern Somalia in July 2011, where conflict (al-Shabaab) blocked aid.
A later UN-backed study estimated about 260,000 deaths in Somalia, about half of them children under five.
Large numbers fled to the Dadaab camps in Kenya and to camps in Ethiopia.
Ethiopia's famine of 1983–85 followed drought and was worsened by civil war. It led to Band Aid (1984) and the Live Aid concerts (July 1985) organised by Bob Geldof.
Responses either warn of drought early, store or save water, or help people once it hits.
Early warning systems using rainfall, satellite and market data, so that governments and aid agencies can act before famine sets in.
Water storage in dams, tanks and rainwater harvesting (collecting rain from roofs and surfaces).
Drought-tolerant crops and seed varieties, which can still yield with less water.
Irrigation efficiency, such as drip irrigation (water delivered slowly to plant roots, so less is wasted).
Food aid and cash transfers, so that people can buy food; insurance, which pays out when crops fail.
Restrictions such as hosepipe bans, which cut demand; desalination, which adds a supply that does not depend on rain.
Desertification is often misunderstood as the Sahara advancing. It is really damage to land, and climate and people together cause it.

Desertification is land degradation in arid, semi-arid and dry sub-humid areas caused by climatic variations and human activities (UNCCD definition, adopted 1994). The UNCCD is the UN Convention to Combat Desertification.
It is the spread of desert-like conditions, not the advance of sand dunes from the Sahara.
Drought is a climatic event; desertification is a process of land degradation that drought can trigger.
17 June is World Day to Combat Desertification.
The Sahel is a key example of desertification. Here the focus is on rainfall, drought and the economy: harvests, incomes, food, migration and conflict.

The Sahel runs from Senegal and Mauritania through Mali, Burkina Faso, Niger and Chad to Sudan. Rainfall is roughly 200–600 mm, falling in one short summer wet season when the ITCZ (the rain belt) moves north.
Droughts in the 1970s and 1980s caused failed harvests and livestock deaths.
Pastoralists (herding peoples) lost their livelihoods, and the region became dependent on food imports.
Migration to cities, including coastal cities, and abroad; conflict between herders and farmers over shrinking land and water.
Lake Chad has shrunk dramatically since the 1960s (about 90%, widely quoted), hitting fishing and farming around it.
There is more on the soil causes of Sahel degradation in the notes on human interference with soils.
Responses to desertification range from international agreements to local farming methods that restore the land.
The UNCCD, adopted in 1994, coordinates international action.
The Great Green Wall, launched by the African Union in 2007, aims to run about 8,000 km from Senegal to Djibouti. Progress has been slow and well short of target.
Zaï pits (planting holes that catch rain) and stone lines (lines of stones that slow runoff) in the Yatenga region of Burkina Faso, associated with the farmer Yacouba Sawadogo.
In Niger, farmer-managed natural regeneration (farmers letting trees regrow on their land) has regreened about 5 million hectares since the 1980s.
Desertification is not only a poor-country problem. The Dust Bowl in the United States shows drought and ploughing together wrecking farmland in a rich economy.
Drought on ploughed grassland in the 1930s, on the Great Plains of Oklahoma and Kansas, produced dust storms.
Farm failures and migration followed, because the dust storms stripped the land of its topsoil.

The US Soil Conservation Service, set up in 1935, promoted shelter belts (rows of trees that block wind), contour ploughing (ploughing along the slope's contours to slow runoff) and crop rotation (changing the crop each year).
The Dust Bowl shows desertification-type damage in a rich economy. There is more on its soil side in the notes on human interaction and mass movement.
Tourists choose places for their weather, so climate is a resource that tourism can sell.
Sunshine, warmth, low rainfall and a warm sea attract 'sun, sea and sand' tourism.
Reliable snow attracts winter sports, and a mild climate allows outdoor activities.
Climate decides the tourist season, because visitors come when the weather suits the activity.
The Mediterranean is the main case of climate creating a tourist economy. The same dry summers that attract visitors also create problems.
Hot, dry, sunny summers have made the Mediterranean one of the world's most visited regions. Mass package tourism grew from the 1960s with cheap jet flights.
Spain received about 85 million international tourists in 2023, a record, making it the world's second most visited country after France.
Spain is the most popular foreign holiday destination for Irish people.
Benefits: jobs, foreign earnings, infrastructure and regional development. There is more on this in the notes on a peripheral European region, the Mezzogiorno.
Climate problem: tourists arrive in the driest season, so water demand from hotels, pools and golf courses peaks when supply is lowest.
Other problems: jobs are seasonal, and coasts are overdeveloped.
Protests against mass tourism took place in 2024 in the Canary Islands and in Barcelona.
Some destinations sell warmth in winter, when northern Europe is cold. The Canary Islands do this.
The Canary Islands lie off north-west Africa at about 28° N.
Mild, dry winters and the cooling Canary Current (a cool ocean current) give them a year-round tourist season that attracts northern Europeans.
Ski resorts depend on snow, so they are very sensitive to a warming climate.
Ski tourism depends on reliable snow cover, and it supports mountain economies in several European countries.
Climate change is raising the snow line (the height above which snow lies) and shortening seasons, so lower-altitude resorts struggle or close.
Resorts invest in artificial snow-making, which needs water, energy and cold enough nights.
Resorts also diversify into summer walking and cycling, so they earn money when there is no snow.
Tropical islands sell warm weather and coral reefs, but the same climate brings hurricanes, bleaching and rising seas.

Tropical island destinations depend on warm weather and coral reefs. Their peak season is the dry season of the northern winter, and the Atlantic hurricane season (1 June to 30 November) is the low season.
Hurricane Irma, a Category 5 hurricane (the top category) in September 2017, damaged or destroyed almost every building on Barbuda. Its whole population was evacuated to Antigua.
Hurricane Maria, in September 2017, devastated Puerto Rico. An official study estimated about 3,000 deaths.
Mass bleaching of the Great Barrier Reef (corals losing their colour as stressed by warm water) has occurred repeatedly since the late 1990s, damaging reef tourism.
Sea-level rise threatens low-lying island nations such as the Maldives. There is more on this in the notes on environmental pollution.
Ireland's climate is poor for beach holidays, so its tourism has to sell something else.
Ireland's cool, cloudy, wet and unreliable summer climate limits beach tourism and pushes Irish holidaymakers abroad.
Irish tourism instead markets scenery (the green landscape produced by the rain), culture, heritage, golf, walking, surfing and other outdoor activities.
The Wild Atlantic Way, a touring route of about 2,500 km along the west coast from Inishowen, Co. Donegal, to Kinsale, Co. Cork, was launched by Fáilte Ireland in 2014.
Domestic holidays rise in warm, sunny summers because fewer people go abroad for the sun.
A warming climate changes where and when people take holidays, helping some places and hurting others.

Hotter Mediterranean summers bring heatwaves and wildfires that can deter or endanger tourists. In July 2023, wildfires on the Greek island of Rhodes forced thousands of tourists to be evacuated from resorts.
Visits may shift to spring and autumn, or to more northern destinations, possibly including Ireland.
Ski seasons shorten because there is less reliable snow.
Reefs bleach because seas warm, and islands face flooding because sea level rises.
Climate also affects energy, health and productivity, and a final judgement on how far it controls development.
Energy: wind supplied about a third of Ireland's electricity in the early 2020s. Solar power is strong in sunny deserts, and hydroelectricity depends on high rainfall.
Climate also drives energy demand, for example heating in cold climates and air-conditioning in hot ones.
Health and productivity: tropical climates favour diseases such as malaria; extreme heat lowers the capacity for outdoor work; heatwaves kill.

Assessment: climate influences development but does not decide it alone. Rich countries with harsh climates, such as Israel, the Gulf states and Australia, overcome limits through capital and technology, while poor, rain-fed economies are the most vulnerable. Climate change widens this gap.
Geographers can group a population by physical indicators (race) or by cultural indicators (ethnicity). The two ideas are easy to mix up, so keep them separate from the start.
Race: a grouping of people by inherited physical traits such as skin colour, hair type and facial features. It describes the body, not the way of life.
Ethnic group: a group that shares culture, ancestry, language, religion or history and is seen as distinct both by its members and by others. It describes shared culture, not appearance.

The syllabus treats race as one part of ethnicity, so race is one of several ethnic indicators. Language, religion and nationality (citizenship of a state) are the other cultural indicators, covered in the notes Language as a cultural indicator, Religion as a cultural indicator and Nationality and the nation state.
Modern science has changed how race is understood. Biologists now see it as a weak way of dividing people, yet it still shapes the human map because people have acted on it.
All humans belong to one species, and people share about 99.9% of their DNA (the genetic code in every cell), so the differences between groups are tiny.
There is more genetic variation within any so-called race than between races, which is why the groupings do not mark real biological divisions.

Physical traits such as skin colour change gradually across space (these gradual changes are called clines) and have no sharp boundaries, so there is no point where one group clearly stops and another starts.
Race is therefore largely a social classification (one made by societies, not by biology)

It still matters geographically because people, laws and states have acted on it through segregation (forcing groups to live apart), apartheid (South Africa's system of legal racial separation) and genocide (the deliberate killing of a whole group of people).
Older textbooks sorted humanity into four racial groupings. Biologists now reject this scheme, and it is presented here only as a historical, outdated classification.
Caucasoid: textbooks linked this grouping with lighter skin, straight or wavy hair and a narrow nose.
Mongoloid: textbooks linked this grouping with straight dark hair, an eyelid fold (epicanthic fold) and a broad face.
Negroid: textbooks linked this grouping with dark skin, tightly curled hair and a broad nose.
Australoid: textbooks linked this grouping with dark skin, wavy hair and a broad nose.
None of these traits makes one group superior to another, and the classification says nothing about ability or culture.
Differences in appearance are not random. They built up as human populations adapted to the places they lived in.
Physical traits developed through adaptation to environment over thousands of years.

Skin pigmentation (melanin, the dark pigment in skin) increases towards the tropics, where ultraviolet radiation (the harmful part of sunlight) is strongest, so darker skin gives more protection there.
Lighter skin at high latitudes (places far from the equator) allows the body to make vitamin D from less sunlight, because skin needs sunlight to produce it.

Before European colonisation (European powers taking over and settling other lands), and before about 1500, the main racial groupings were largely separated by oceans, deserts and mountains. This long isolation kept each grouping mostly in its own region.
Caucasoid peoples, such as Europeans, North Africans, Middle Eastern and South Asian peoples.
Mongoloid peoples: East Asians, Central Asians, the Inuit (the Arctic peoples) and the native peoples of the Americas.
Negroid peoples, such as the peoples of sub-Saharan Africa (Africa south of the Sahara Desert).
Australoid peoples: Aboriginal Australians and Melanesians (the peoples of the islands of Melanesia in the south-west Pacific).
Colonialism (rule over other lands by a foreign power) and migration since 1500 overturned the old pattern, so most large countries are now multi-racial. The Americas show this most clearly.
Columbus reached the Americas in 1492. Disease (e.g. smallpox), war and forced labour caused the native population to collapse in the following century.

Spanish and Portuguese settlers produced racially mixed populations. Mestizo means European and Native American ancestry; mulatto means European and African ancestry. Mexico's population is mainly mestizo, so it is an example of racial mixing.
About 12.5 million Africans were shipped across the Atlantic as slaves between the 16th and 19th centuries.
Most went to Brazil and the Caribbean; far fewer went to the American South. Brazil received about 4-5 million Africans, more than any other country.
Brazil abolished slavery on 13 May 1888, the last country in the Americas to do so. The USA abolished it by the 13th Amendment (1865), after the Civil War (1861-65).
The legacy is large Black populations and racial inequality across the Americas, which is why the slave trade still shapes the region.
In settler colonies, newcomers from Britain took over land where Indigenous peoples already lived. The result was lasting change to who lived there and how they were treated.
The First Fleet of British settlers and convicts arrived at Sydney Cove on 26 January 1788.
The Immigration Restriction Act 1901 began the White Australia Policy (a policy of keeping non-White immigrants out), which was dismantled between 1966 and 1973.
Stolen Generations: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children were removed from their families by governments, roughly from 1910 to the 1970s.
In the 1967 referendum (a national vote on one question) about 91% voted to count Aboriginal people in the census (the official population count) and let the federal government make laws for them.
Prime Minister Kevin Rudd made a national apology on 13 February 2008.
Census 2021 shows, for example, that about 3.2% of Australians identified as Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander, and over a quarter of Australians were born overseas.
The Indigenous Voice to Parliament referendum of 14 October 2023 was rejected, with about 60% voting No.
New Zealand: the Treaty of Waitangi between the British Crown and Māori chiefs was signed on 6 February 1840. Māori are about one in six of New Zealand's population.
The USA also moved its native peoples off their land. This changed where Native Americans live today.
The Indian Removal Act 1830 led to the forced removal of the Cherokee in 1838, known as the Trail of Tears.
Many Native Americans now live on reservations, a legacy of the removals (areas of land set aside for Native American peoples).
When slavery ended, colonial planters still needed workers. Britain moved people within its own empire instead, which created new Indian communities far from India.

After slavery was abolished, Britain shipped indentured Indian labourers (workers bound by contract to work for a set period) to sugar colonies: to the Caribbean (Trinidad, Guyana), to Fiji (1879-1916), to Mauritius, and to Natal in South Africa (from 1860).
People of Indian descent are a large share of the population in Trinidad, Guyana, Fiji and Mauritius.
These movements created Indian communities in each destination, which is why Indian descent is common there.
Colonial rulers did not only move people. They could also fix labels onto groups, and in Rwanda those labels later mattered terribly.
Belgium ruled Rwanda after the First World War.
From 1933 Belgian identity cards recorded each person as Hutu, Tutsi or Twa, so the labels became fixed and official.
The 1994 genocide, in which Hutu extremists killed mostly Tutsi, is set out in the racial conflict blocks below.
After empires ended, migration reversed direction. People from former colonies moved to the colonial power (the mother country), which made European cities multi-racial.
After 1945 people from former colonies moved to the mother country. Caribbean and South Asian migrants came to Britain.
The Empire Windrush brought several hundred Caribbean migrants to Tilbury, near London, on 22 June 1948; post-war Caribbean migrants are known as the Windrush generation.
Later migration from India, Pakistan and Bangladesh also brought South Asian communities to Britain.
Algerians and other North and West Africans moved to France, and Indonesians and Surinamese moved to the Netherlands.
This migration created multi-racial European cities, because settled communities stayed and grew.
Migration within a country can also change its racial pattern. In the USA, a huge movement of African Americans changed two regions at once.
About 6 million African Americans moved from the rural South to cities of the North and West, such as Chicago, Detroit and New York, between about 1910 and 1970.
Segregation and poverty pushed them out of the South, and industrial jobs pulled them to northern and western cities.
The movement changed the racial make-up of both regions and created segregated inner-city neighbourhoods.
Some European countries invited workers from abroad to fill jobs. Many of these workers stayed, which added new ethnic groups to the population.
West Germany signed a recruitment agreement with Turkey on 30 October 1961.
Guest workers (Gastarbeiter, the German word for them) were expected to return home, but many settled with their families, so Germany now has a large population of Turkish origin.
Belgium signed labour agreements with Morocco and Turkey in 1964.
North Africans also came to France and Belgium as labour migrants.
People who move are not all moving for the same reason, and the law treats the groups differently. Learn the four terms and how they differ.

Refugee: a person outside their own country who cannot return because of a well-founded fear of persecution (serious mistreatment) based on race, religion, nationality, political opinion or membership of a social group.
The 1951 UN Refugee Convention, with its 1967 Protocol, defines a refugee.
Asylum seeker: a person who has applied for refugee status and is waiting for a decision. An asylum seeker becomes a refugee only if the claim is accepted.
Economic migrant: a person who moves mainly for work or a better income.
Internally displaced person: a person forced from home who is still inside their own country.
UNHCR (the UN refugee agency) figures: over 120 million people were forcibly displaced worldwide in 2024.
The Syrian civil war is the main example of refugees changing the population of other countries, including in Europe.
The Syrian civil war from 2011 made over 6 million Syrians refugees, most of them in neighbouring countries.
Turkey hosted about 3.5 million of them, the largest number of any country.
In 2015 over 1 million refugees and migrants reached Europe across the Mediterranean, many travelling on to Germany.
Germany received about 1 million asylum seekers in 2015-16.
The Assad government (Syria's government during the war) fell on 8 December 2024, and some refugees began to return.
The Rohingya show how losing citizenship can lead to mass flight.
The Rohingya are a Muslim minority in Myanmar, made stateless (belonging to no country as a citizen) by Myanmar's 1982 citizenship law.
From August 2017 over 700,000 Rohingya fled to Bangladesh, mostly to camps near Cox's Bazar.

Ireland moved from a largely White, Irish, Catholic population to a multi-ethnic one. These are the figures to use for Ireland as the national example. The causes and patterns of Irish migration are covered in the note Changing migration patterns in Ireland.
Census 2022: about 5.15 million people lived in Ireland, and about 20% (over 1 million) were born outside Ireland.
About 12% were non-Irish citizens, the largest groups being Polish and UK citizens.
About three-quarters described their ethnicity as White Irish, so about a quarter did not.
Polish is the most common language spoken at home after English and Irish, reflecting the large Polish-citizen group (Census 2016 and 2022).
Irish Travellers: about 33,000 people (Census 2022), under 1% of the population. The State formally recognised them as an ethnic minority on 1 March 2017.
Citizenship referendum, June 2004 (about 79% Yes): ended the automatic right to Irish citizenship for every child born in Ireland.
Ukrainians came to Ireland under the EU Temporary Protection Directive (an EU rule giving people fleeing war the right to stay), activated in March 2022 after Russia's invasion. Over 100,000 arrived.
Ireland's system for people seeking protection is part of the syllabus's national setting. Direct Provision and the right to work are the main points.
Direct Provision, which gives asylum seekers State accommodation and a weekly allowance while their claims are decided, began in 2000 and was widely criticised for long stays in shared centres.
A 2017 Supreme Court ruling found the total ban on asylum seekers working unconstitutional; from 2018 they gained a limited right to work.
More than 13,000 people applied for international protection (the formal term for asking for refugee status) in Ireland in each of 2022 and 2023.
Irish and EU migration policy is covered in the note Migration policy in Ireland and the EU.
Migrants change the place they move to, in ways that can help and in ways that can cause conflict. Keep your answer to the racial and ethnic pattern.
The population becomes more diverse, for example with new places of worship, shops and food.
Ethnic neighbourhoods form as migrants cluster near others from their own group.
Migrants supply labour to the receiving economy, so they fill jobs.
Discrimination, segregation and tension can follow. On 23 November 2023 a riot broke out in Dublin city centre after a stabbing on Parnell Square, fuelled by anti-immigrant agitation online.
The place migrants leave is changed too, in two ways.
The source area loses young adults, who are the most likely to migrate, so fewer workers are left.
Migrants send remittances, money that supports families who stay behind.
A multi-racial society is one in which two or more racial groups make up significant shares of the population. Colonialism and migration have made this the normal pattern in large countries.
Examples include the USA, Brazil, South Africa, the UK and Ireland today.
Racial mixing, for example in Brazil: people of different racial backgrounds have children together, producing mixed-race populations.
The USA is a multi-racial society whose census shows growing Hispanic and mixed populations. Two images describe how its groups live together.
US Census 2020: White (alone) about 62%; Hispanic or Latino (of any race) about 19%; Black about 12%; Asian about 6%.
About 10% identified with two or more races, more than double the 2010 figure. Hispanics are the largest minority, so they make up about 19% of the population.
Melting pot: minority groups assimilate (adopt the majority's way of life) into one common national culture.
Salad bowl: groups keep distinct identities while sharing one nation.
Brazil is the main example of racial mixing in this option. Its population grew from three starting groups, then added later immigrants.
Brazil's population descends from Portuguese colonists, enslaved Africans and Indigenous peoples, with later Italian, German, Japanese and Arab immigrants.
Brazil has the largest Japanese-descended population outside Japan, mainly in São Paulo state, which shows the effect of later immigrants.
Census 2022: pardo (mixed race) about 45%, White (branco) about 44%, Black (preto) about 10%, Indigenous under 1%.
Census 2022 was the first census since 1991 in which pardo was the largest group, so mixed race is now the biggest category.
The ideal of racial democracy claims that mixing has removed racial division, but White Brazilians on average remain wealthier.
The UK became multi-racial mainly through post-war migration from Commonwealth countries (former British colonies). Its census and the Windrush scandal show the result.
Census 2021 (England and Wales): White about 82%; Asian or Asian British about 9%; Black about 4%; Mixed about 3%.
The Windrush scandal (2018): some long-settled Caribbean-born residents were wrongly detained, denied services or deported because they lacked documents.
Governments can respond to diversity in different ways. Multiculturalism and assimilation are the two policy approaches you should be able to compare.
Multiculturalism: a policy of accepting and supporting distinct cultures within one society, as in Canada, which adopted an official multiculturalism policy in 1971, and Australia.
Assimilation: minorities adopt the majority culture. France's model expects integration into one secular French identity and does not collect ethnic statistics in its census.
Arguments for multiculturalism: enrichment, labour supply and tolerance.
Arguments against multiculturalism: segregation, parallel societies and backlash, including far-right politics.
Racial conflict (violent or serious conflict between racial or ethnic groups) has several causes.
Segregation, which separates groups and limits contact between them, so suspicion can grow.
Unequal power inherited from colonialism and slavery.
Racist ideologies, and fear of newcomers.
South Africa is the main case study of racial conflict. Apartheid was a system of laws that separated people by race and gave power to the White minority.
Apartheid was introduced by the National Party after it won the 1948 election.
The Population Registration Act 1950 classified everyone as White, Black (African), Coloured (mixed race) or Indian/Asian.
The Group Areas Act 1950 assigned residential areas by race, so it enforced segregation.
Homelands, known as Bantustans, were set up for Black South Africans, so that Black South Africans were kept in separate areas.
District Six, Cape Town, was declared a White area in 1966. About 60,000 residents were forcibly removed and their homes bulldozed.
Resistance and protest grew against apartheid and eventually ended it, but its effects have not disappeared.
Sharpeville, 21 March 1960: police killed 69 protesters, which shows the violence used against resistance.
Soweto uprising, 16 June 1976: students protested against being taught through Afrikaans (the language of many White South Africans).
Nelson Mandela was released on 11 February 1990 after 27 years in prison. The first all-race election, on 27 April 1994, made him President.
The Truth and Reconciliation Commission began work in 1996, so that the wrongs of apartheid could be faced.
South Africa Census 2022: Black African about 81%, Coloured about 8%, White about 7%, Indian/Asian about 3%.
Wealth and land ownership remain highly unequal by race, so the legacy of apartheid continues.
After slavery ended, the American South kept racial separation in law. The civil rights movement challenged it and won new laws, but tension has continued.
Jim Crow laws enforced segregation in the southern states after the Civil War.
Brown v Board of Education (1954): the Supreme Court ruled school segregation unconstitutional, so separate schools by race were not allowed.
The Montgomery bus boycott (1955) began after Rosa Parks refused to give up her seat.
The Civil Rights Act 1964 and the Voting Rights Act 1965 followed, because of the movement's pressure.
Martin Luther King, a leader of the civil rights movement, was assassinated on 4 April 1968.
George Floyd was killed by a Minneapolis police officer on 25 May 2020, leading to worldwide Black Lives Matter protests. The movement itself began in 2013.
Nazi Germany shows racist ideology being turned into law and then into genocide.
The Nuremberg Laws (1935) stripped Jews of citizenship and banned marriage between Jews and other Germans.
Racist ideology was turned into law and then into genocide, so the Nuremberg Laws were a step towards the Holocaust.
About 6 million Jews were murdered in the Holocaust. Roma were also targeted for extermination.
Rwanda is a genocide linked to the colonial labels described earlier, when Belgian identity cards fixed Hutu and Tutsi identities.
From 7 April 1994, Hutu extremists killed about 800,000 people, mostly Tutsi, in about 100 days.
Racial tension in Europe has also shown itself in riots in cities, in Britain and France.
Notting Hill, London, 1958, for example: white mobs attacked Caribbean residents.
Brixton, London, April 1981: clashes between mainly Black youths and police.
France, October-November 2005: riots spread through the suburbs (banlieues) of Paris and other cities after two teenagers died fleeing police in Clichy-sous-Bois. A state of emergency was declared.
Similar riots followed the police shooting of a teenager, Nahel Merzouk, in Nanterre in June 2023.
A cultural indicator is a feature that helps you identify and map a cultural group. Language is one of the strongest, because it is both part of a group's identity and easy to measure.
Language carries a group's history, literature, songs, place names and ways of thinking, so losing a language means losing a store of the group's culture.
Language marks who belongs to a group, because sharing a language means sharing a way of speaking and thinking that outsiders do not have.

Language is easy to map from census questions on language (a census is the official population count, held at regular intervals), so it is used to define cultural regions (areas with a shared culture).

Nationalism (the belief that a people with a shared culture should govern themselves) has often rested on language. Governments have therefore either promoted a language to build a nation or suppressed one to weaken a group.
Many nation states (states whose people share one national identity) were built around a single language, because a common language helps unite the population.

The Gaelic League (Conradh na Gaeilge), founded in 1893 by Douglas Hyde and Eoin MacNeill, led a language revival that fed the Irish independence movement, though it was founded as a non-political body.
Suppressing a language has been used to weaken a group. Basque and Catalan were banned from public life and schools under Franco (1939–1975).
The Welsh Not was a wooden board hung round the neck of children caught speaking Welsh in some 19th-century schools, so children were punished for using their own language.
Kurdish was banned in public life and broadcasting in Turkey until the early 1990s, which is an example of a state weakening a group by silencing its language.
Languages carry power as well as culture. The language of the rulers or the wealthy tends to spread, and smaller languages lose ground.

Colonial languages (those of the empires that ruled a territory) became official languages of former colonies: English in India and Nigeria, French in Senegal and Côte d'Ivoire, Spanish across most of Latin America, and Portuguese in Brazil.
The language of the powerful brings jobs and status, so speakers of minority languages shift to it.
The Organisation internationale de la Francophonie, founded in 1970, links French-speaking states, which shows how a colonial language can keep a group of countries connected.
Place names preserve the language spoken in an area long after it has been replaced. Reading them is a way of tracing a region's linguistic history.

Irish place-name elements show the Irish-speaking past of areas that are now English-speaking: baile (townland or homestead; a townland is a small traditional land division), cill (church), dún (fort), inis (island) and cluain (meadow).

Examples: Clonmel (Cluain Meala), Kilkenny (Cill Chainnigh), Dundalk (Dún Dealgan) and Ennis (Inis). Each English name is a version of the older Irish one, which is why the Irish elements are still visible in them.
Language can bind people together or split them apart, and it pays no attention to state borders.
A shared national language can unite a state, but language borders can divide it, as Belgium's does. There is more on this in The complexity of regions (ii).
French is spoken in France, Belgium (Wallonia), Switzerland (west) and Quebec (Canada), so one language links four different places.
Languages cross borders: French is spoken in several states, and Basque is spoken in both Spain and France, so a language community can be split between two states.
Languages are grouped by descent, from the largest unit to the smallest. This lets us show how languages that look different are related.
A language family is a set of languages descended from a common ancestor. Each family divides into branches, and each branch contains languages.
A dialect is a regional variety of a single language, so it is smaller than a language.
About 7,000 languages are spoken in the world today, for example across the families below.
The world's languages fall into a small number of large families. Know each family's main languages and the regions where it is spoken.
Indo-European is the largest family, spoken by nearly half the world's people. It covers Europe, the Americas, Iran and South Asia.
Sino-Tibetan: Mandarin and other Chinese languages, Tibetan and Burmese.
Afro-Asiatic: Arabic, Hebrew, Amharic and Hausa.
Niger-Congo: most of sub-Saharan Africa (Africa south of the Sahara), e.g. Swahili, Yoruba and Zulu.
Austronesian: Malay/Indonesian, Filipino, Malagasy, Māori and Hawaiian.
Dravidian: southern India, e.g. Tamil and Telugu.
Turkic and Uralic are further families.

Counting speakers depends on whether you count only native speakers (those who learned it as a first language) or second-language speakers as well. That is why different languages come first on different lists.
Mandarin Chinese has the most native speakers.
English has the most speakers in total, about 1.5 billion counting second-language speakers.
Spanish has the second-most native speakers. Hindi is also very widely spoken.
Arabic is the language of the Qur'an (the holy book of Islam) and an official language in over 20 states of the Middle East and North Africa.
