Languages move when people move or when one group gains power over another. Four main routes explain the present world map of languages.
Migration, conquest and empire spread languages: Latin with the Roman Empire, and English, Spanish, French and Portuguese with colonialism.
Trade and religion spread languages too: Arabic spread with Islam, because the Qur'an is in Arabic.
Today globalisation (the growing links between countries) and the media spread dominant languages.
Most European languages belong to the Indo-European family, which divides into branches. A sketch map of the branches is a useful diagram in an exam answer.
Germanic: English, German, Dutch (including Flemish, the Dutch spoken in Belgium), Danish, Swedish, Norwegian and Icelandic.
Romance, from Latin (the language of the Roman Empire, so these languages descend from it): French, Spanish, Portuguese, Italian, Romanian and Catalan.
Slavic: Russian, Polish, Czech, Slovak, Ukrainian, Bulgarian, Serbian, Croatian and Slovene.
Celtic: Goidelic (Irish, Scottish Gaelic and Manx) and Brythonic (Welsh, Breton and Cornish).
Hellenic: Greek. Baltic: Latvian and Lithuanian. Albanian is a separate branch.
Non-Indo-European languages in Europe: Finnish, Estonian and Hungarian (Uralic); Turkish (Turkic); Maltese (Semitic, written in the Latin alphabet).
Basque is an isolate (a language with no known relatives), unrelated to any other language.
The EU has to manage many languages in one union. Irish has gained official status there, while English has become the language most Europeans learn as a second language.
The EU has 24 official languages, so documents and debates may be needed in each.
Irish became an official EU language in 2007, with full working-language status from 1 January 2022. Do not say 1973: that is when Ireland joined, not when Irish became official.
English is Europe's main second language, and language learning is supported by programmes such as Erasmus exchanges (study periods abroad).
The mass media (television, film, the internet and other means of reaching large audiences) now spread dominant languages, and English is the language most carried by them.
Television, film, music, the internet, social media and streaming are dominated by English, through Hollywood films and US and UK music.
About half of all websites are in English.
Young people adopt English words and English-language culture, because that is what they see and hear online.
Minority-language speakers consume most media in the majority language at home, so even in a Welsh or Irish-speaking household, most of what is watched is in the majority language.
The spread of English through the media and business changes other languages and puts pressure on them.
English loanwords (words borrowed from another language) enter other languages, such as the French le weekend (a feature of Franglais, French mixed with English).
English is the language of business, science and the internet, so people need it for work and study.
The pressure falls on small national languages as well as on minority languages.
Some states have used law to protect their language from English and other dominant languages. France, Quebec and Iceland are the examples.
France: the Académie française, founded in 1635, works to protect the French language.
Toubon Law (1994): French must be used in advertising, product labels, workplace documents and public signage.
French music radio stations must play at least 40% French-language songs (a quota, or fixed minimum; law of 1994, applied from 1996).

Quebec's Charter of the French Language (Bill 101, 1977) made French the sole official language of Quebec, a French-speaking province of Canada, and requires most immigrant children to attend French-language schools.
Iceland coins new Icelandic words for new things, e.g. tölva (computer), so it does not need to borrow English words.
A minority language survives better if people can hear and see it every day. Broadcasting in the language gives it a public presence and helps young people use it.
Raidió na Gaeltachta began broadcasting in 1972, so Irish was heard on the radio every day.
TG4, originally Teilifís na Gaeilge, launched on 31 October 1996 and is based in Baile na hAbhann, Conamara.

S4C, the Welsh-language television channel, launched on 1 November 1982, after Plaid Cymru's former leader Gwynfor Evans threatened a hunger strike in 1980 when the government backed away from its promise.
BBC Alba, the Scottish Gaelic television service, launched in 2008, so Scottish Gaelic gained its own screen presence.
EITB, the Basque public broadcaster, began television in 1982.
Social media and online content also let small languages reach young people.
Many languages are under threat, and it is the minority languages that are most at risk.
A minority language is spoken by a minority of a state's population, e.g. Irish, Welsh, Breton, Basque, Scottish Gaelic and Sámi.
About 40% of the world's languages are endangered, meaning they may stop being spoken.
Languages rarely die for one reason. Pressure from outside combines with decisions made inside families, and each cause below is a separate point you can use in an essay.
Conquest and official suppression, because a ruling power can ban a language from schools and public life.
A dominant language is needed for jobs, education and emigration, so people see the minority language as less useful.
Famine and emigration, and the in-migration (arrival) of majority-language speakers, reduce the number of speakers in the heartland.
Urbanisation (movement to cities), mass media and globalisation all expose people to the dominant language.
Parents do not pass the language on, so inter-generational transmission (passing a language from one generation to the next) breaks.
Extinct languages can sometimes be brought back, which shows that decline is not always final. Manx and Cornish are the examples.
Manx: the last native speaker, Ned Maddrell, died in 1974. The language has since been revived, with a Manx-medium primary school (a school that teaches through Manx).
Cornish: the last traditional speaker is usually given as Dolly Pentreath, who died in 1777. Cornish was revived in the 20th century.
The Cornish were recognised as a national minority in 2014.
A language survives when the state, schools, media, employers and families all support it. Exams ask for these strategies by heading, so learn each one as a heading you can develop.
Official status in law, such as Article 8 for Irish, which gives the language public standing.
Education through the language: immersion and medium-of-instruction schools (where lessons are taught in the language), and compulsory study of the language.
Media, such as broadcasting and online content, so the language is heard daily.
Jobs and economic development in the language's heartland (the area where it is strongest), and planning and housing controls, so speakers can afford to stay.
Language commissioners (officials who enforce language rights) and public-service rights.
Community and family support, culture and festivals, because a language lives only if people use it socially.
Cross-border and EU recognition, so the language has support beyond one state.
Possible future measures, such as language conditions for housing in the Gaeltacht or more online content, count alongside measures already in place.
Irish is Ireland's national setting for this topic. Its legal status is strong, but the number of people who use it every day is small.
Article 8 of the 1937 Constitution makes Irish the national language and the first official language; English is the second official language.
Census 2022: about 1.87 million people (about 40%) said they could speak Irish, but only about 72,000 spoke it daily outside the education system.
Census 2022: the Gaeltacht (the Irish-speaking regions) had a population of about 106,000, of whom about 20,000 spoke Irish daily outside education.
Census 1851, the first count: about 1.5 million Irish speakers (about 23%), which shows how far the language has fallen.
Gaeltacht areas lie in seven counties: Donegal, Mayo, Galway, Kerry, Cork, Waterford and Meath.

Main areas: Gaoth Dobhair (Co. Donegal); Conamara and the Aran Islands (Co. Galway, the largest); Corca Dhuibhne (Co. Kerry); Múscraí and Oileán Chléire (Co. Cork); An Rinn (Co. Waterford); Ráth Chairn and Baile Ghib (Co. Meath).

The State has created a set of bodies, laws and plans to support Irish, especially in the Gaeltacht. Each is a point you can use under the strategies of official status, commissioners, planning and economic development.
The Gaeltacht Areas Order 1956 and the Department of the Gaeltacht (1956) are the founding state measures for the Gaeltacht.

Údarás na Gaeltachta (1980) is the Gaeltacht development authority. It grant-aids firms in the Gaeltacht, such as on the Gaoth Dobhair industrial estate, and supports Irish-language community projects, so that jobs exist locally.

Official Languages Act 2003 (amended 2021): the public has the right to deal with public bodies in Irish. The 2021 amendment sets a target that 20% of new public-service recruits be competent in Irish by 2030.
An Coimisinéir Teanga (Language Commissioner), set up in 2004, enforces the Act, so the public can complain if their right to Irish is ignored.
Foras na Gaeilge is an all-island body, so it works in both parts of Ireland, set up in 1999 under the Good Friday Agreement to promote Irish.
Gaeltacht Act 2012: 26 Gaeltacht Language Planning Areas, each with a language plan; Gaeltacht Service Towns; Irish Language Networks outside the Gaeltacht.
The 20-Year Strategy for the Irish Language 2010–2030 aims to raise daily speakers to 250,000.
Northern Ireland's Identity and Language (Northern Ireland) Act 2022 gave official recognition to Irish and Ulster-Scots and created an Irish Language Commissioner.
Schools and cultural events give people the chance to learn and use Irish. They matter most for children, because a language survives only if the young learn it.
Irish is a compulsory subject, so all pupils learn it, through primary and post-primary school, with exemptions.
Gaelscoileanna are Irish-medium schools (schools teaching through Irish) outside the Gaeltacht; their umbrella body was founded in 1973.
Gaeltacht summer colleges (coláistí samhraidh) bring learners to live with Irish-speaking families, so they hear Irish in daily life.
Seachtain na Gaeilge is an annual Irish-language festival around St Patrick's Day. The Oireachtas na Gaeilge festival was first held in 1897.
TG4 broadcasts Irish-language drama, sport and music programmes.
Despite state support, Irish is weak as an everyday community language. The 2007 study set the figure that shows how fragile the Gaeltacht is.
The Comprehensive Linguistic Study of the Use of Irish in the Gaeltacht (2007) found that Irish is viable as a community language only where at least 67% speak it daily.
Its 2015 update warned that Irish could cease to be the community language in most Gaeltacht districts within about ten years.
Evaluation: Irish has high ability, meaning many people can speak it, but low daily use.
The history of Gaeltacht boundaries since 1850: there is more on this in The complexity of regions (ii).
Welsh is the international setting for this topic. Its history shows how law, industry and a government decision each weakened the language.
The Laws in Wales Acts of 1535 and 1542 annexed (took over) Wales to England and barred Welsh speakers from public office unless they used English.
The 1847 government reports on education in Wales, known as the Treachery of the Blue Books, blamed Welsh for the people's backwardness.
Coal and iron industries in the 19th century drew large numbers of English and Irish workers into south Wales, spreading English.

The flooding of the Welsh-speaking village of Capel Celyn in the Tryweryn valley in 1965, for a reservoir to supply Liverpool, went ahead despite almost all Welsh MPs opposing it, and became a symbol of Welsh powerlessness.
Welsh speakers did not accept decline passively. Campaigners pressed the government for rights and services in Welsh.
Cymdeithas yr Iaith Gymraeg (the Welsh Language Society) was founded in 1962 after Saunders Lewis's radio lecture Tynged yr Iaith (The Fate of the Language).
The society used civil disobedience (deliberately breaking rules in protest), e.g. painting over English-only road signs.
The campaign that secured S4C, described under media that protect minority languages, was part of the same activism.
Activism was followed by a series of laws that gradually gave Welsh equal standing with English.
The Welsh Language Act 1967, a first step, gave Welsh limited equal validity.
The Welsh Language Act 1993 gave Welsh and English equal treatment in the public sector and created the Welsh Language Board.
The Welsh Language (Wales) Measure 2011 gave Welsh official status and led to a Welsh Language Commissioner from 2012.
The National Assembly for Wales (1999), renamed the Senedd in 2020, makes laws through Welsh and English.
The Cymraeg 2050 strategy (2017) sets a target of 1 million Welsh speakers by 2050.
As with Irish, schooling and youth organisations are how Welsh is passed to the next generation.
Welsh is compulsory in all schools in Wales up to age 16, and Welsh-medium schools are found across Wales.
Urdd Gobaith Cymru (a youth movement founded in 1922) and the National Eisteddfod (a Welsh festival of culture) promote Welsh among the young.
The Census 2021 figures show a decline in Welsh speakers, and the heartland faces pressures such as second homes.
Census 2021: about 538,000 people aged 3 and over (17.8%) could speak Welsh, down from 19.0% in 2011. Wales has a population of about 3.1 million.
The highest shares are in Gwynedd (about 64%) and the Isle of Anglesey (over half), in the north-west heartland.
Second homes and English in-migration push up house prices in Welsh-speaking rural areas, so local Welsh speakers struggle to afford homes.
From April 2023 Welsh councils may charge up to a 300% council-tax premium on second homes, as a response to this pressure.
Evaluation: Welsh is often cited as the most successful Celtic-language revival, but its decline in the heartland shows the limits of revival despite statutory support (support set out in law).
There is more on Welsh political history in A European regional case study of identity.
Basque, spoken in northern Spain and south-west France, was suppressed under Franco and has been strongly supported since. It is the main comparison with Irish and Welsh.
The Statute of Gernika (1979) created the Basque Autonomous Community, a self-governing region of Spain, where Basque is co-official with Spanish.
The school models are A (Spanish-medium, with Basque as a subject), B (both languages) and D (all through Basque, with Spanish as a subject). Model D is now chosen for most pupils.
Ikastolak are Basque-medium schools that began as a clandestine (secret) movement under Franco.
Euskaltzaindia, the Royal Academy of the Basque Language, founded in 1919, created standard Basque, Batua, from 1968, so that speakers of different dialects share one written form.
Basque television is provided by EITB, described under media that protect minority languages.
Evaluation: use of Basque is rising among the young, which suggests the school models are working.
Breton, the Celtic language of Brittany in France, shows what happens when the state gives little support. It contrasts with Wales and the Basque Country.
Brittany was united with France in 1532, so it has long been part of a state where French dominates.
Article 2 of the French Constitution, added in 1992, states that the language of the Republic is French.
Since 2008 Article 75-1 states that regional languages belong to France's heritage.
France signed the European Charter for Regional or Minority Languages in 1999 but has not ratified it (formally approved it so that it becomes binding).
Diwan: Breton-medium immersion schools (where pupils are taught entirely in Breton), the first opened in 1977, run as a voluntary association, so they depend on volunteers rather than the state.
In 2021 France's Constitutional Council struck down parts of a new law, the Molac Law, that allowed immersion teaching in public schools.
Breton has declined sharply, and most of its speakers are elderly, so few young people are learning it.
Māori shows that a language can be revived with state backing and early-years schooling. It is a brief non-European example.
Te reo Māori became an official language of New Zealand in 1987 under the Māori Language Act.
Kōhanga reo (language nests), preschools run entirely in Māori, began in 1982, so children learn the language from the earliest age.
Beyond individual states, Europe-wide bodies also recognise minority languages.
The Council of Europe adopted the European Charter for Regional or Minority Languages in 1992, which gives minority languages recognition across Europe.
Irish's EU status is set out in Irish and the EU, and English as Europe's second language.
This is a data skill from the Ordinary-level examination: a bar chart of languages spoken in Ireland by age group. If you practise it, invent clearly labelled illustrative data.
Find the tallest bar to identify the age group that speaks the language most.
Add the percentages for one language across the groups to find its combined share.
A promotion idea for Irish should target the group where the chart shows the lowest use, and link the language to jobs, travel or culture.
An advantage of speaking another language is access to jobs with multinational companies, to travel, and to understanding another culture.

A cultural indicator is a feature that helps identify and map a cultural group. Religion is one of the strongest, because it affects how people think, live and look, and it leaves visible marks on the landscape.
Religion shapes beliefs, values and moral codes (the rules about right and wrong), and so it often marks group identity more strongly than nationality does.
It shows in the landscape, so a place's religion can be read from what is built there: churches, mosques, temples, synagogues, holy wells, wayside shrines and cemeteries.
It shapes diet, such as halal (permitted under Islam), kosher (permitted under Judaism) and Hindu vegetarianism, and dress, such as the headscarf, the turban and the kippah (the Jewish skullcap).
It shapes the calendar and festivals, such as Christmas, Easter, Eid, Diwali and Yom Kippur, and it also shapes names, education and law.
Census questions on religion (a census is the official count of a population) make it easy to map, because the results can be compared place by place.
Religion rarely stands alone. It is tied up with other indicators of culture, which is why it helps define a cultural group.

Religion is linked with language, because holy texts and worship use particular languages: Arabic and the Qur'an (the holy book of Islam), Latin and the Catholic Church in the past, and Hebrew and Judaism.
Religion is linked with nationality, so that faith becomes part of national identity: Catholicism with Irish or Polish identity, and Orthodoxy with Serbian identity.
Religion is also linked with politics, because religious groups often seek influence over laws and government.
Secularisation is the decline of religion's role in public life and personal practice (a secular state or society is one not run by or tied to religion). The trend is uneven across the world.
Religious practice and church influence are declining in much of Europe, including Ireland and France.
Religion stays strong in many other parts of the world, such as Indonesia, so the trend is not global.
Migration brings new religions into Europe, which means Europe is becoming more religiously varied even where older churches decline.
These are Pew Research Center figures for 2020, published in 2025. They describe 2020 and should not be presented as current.
Christians: about 2.3 billion, about 29% of the world, so this makes Christianity the largest religion.
Muslims: about 2 billion, about 26% of the world.
Religiously unaffiliated: about 1.9 billion, about 24%. The unaffiliated are people with no religion, not a religion in themselves.
Hindus: about 1.2 billion, about 15%. Buddhists: about 320 million, about 4%. Jews: about 15 million.
Islam was the fastest-growing major religion from 2010 to 2020.

A hearth is the place where a religion began, before it spread outwards. Judaism, Christianity and Islam began in the Middle East, while Hinduism and Buddhism began in the Indian subcontinent (the region of India and its neighbours).
Judaism is the oldest of the three Abrahamic faiths (Judaism, Christianity and Islam), so the other two grew after it, and Jerusalem is its holiest city.
Christianity began with the life of Jesus in Roman Palestine, so its hearth is in the Middle East, for example Jerusalem.
Islam was founded by the Prophet Muhammad in Mecca, Arabia, in the early 7th century. The Hijra (the move of the early Muslims) to Medina in 622 begins the Islamic calendar.
Hinduism has no single founder; it developed gradually in the Indian subcontinent.
Buddhism was founded by Siddhartha Gautama (the Buddha) in north-east India around the 5th century BC. Bodh Gaya is where he is said to have gained enlightenment (spiritual awakening).
Sikhism was founded by Guru Nanak in Punjab in the 15th century. The Golden Temple (Harmandir Sahib) at Amritsar is its holiest site.
Religions moved out of their hearths through five main routes: empire, missionaries, trade, colonialism and migration. Each route explains why a religion is found where it is today.

Empire: Christianity spread through the Roman Empire, which made it the official religion in the 4th century. Islam spread with the Arab conquests from the 7th century, across the Middle East and North Africa and into Spain within about a century.
Missionaries (people sent to spread their faith): Irish monks, such as St Columba on Iona and St Columbanus in continental Europe, spread Christianity in the early medieval period.
Trade: Islam spread to Indonesia and West Africa, for example along trade routes.
Colonialism (rule over overseas territories by a foreign power): Christianity spread to the Americas, Africa and the Philippines.
Migration: Islam, Hinduism and Sikhism spread into Europe as people moved there.
Christianity split into three main branches, and each is strong in different regions. Two events, the Great Schism and the Reformation, created these divisions.
Roman Catholic: southern Europe, Ireland, Poland, Latin America and the Philippines.
Protestant, which began with the Reformation: northern Europe, the UK and the USA.
Orthodox, which grew from the Great Schism: eastern Europe, Russia, Greece and Serbia.
The Great Schism (the split) of 1054 divided the Catholic West (Rome) from the Orthodox East (Constantinople).
The Reformation (the break from Catholicism that created Protestantism) began in 1517 with Martin Luther in Germany, and Calvinism spread from Geneva.
Christianity is growing in sub-Saharan Africa (Africa south of the Sahara).
Islam is spread across a broad belt of the world, and the largest Muslim population is not in the Arab world. It has two main branches, Sunni and Shia.
Islam is strong in the Middle East, North Africa, Central Asia, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Indonesia, and parts of West and East Africa.
Indonesia has the world's largest Muslim population, which shows Islam's centre of numbers is not in the Arab world.
Sunnis are about 85–90% of Muslims. Shias are the majority in Iran and Iraq.

Mecca and Medina, in Saudi Arabia, are Islam's holiest cities, because Islam was founded in Mecca and the Hijra went to Medina. The Hajj pilgrimage to Mecca is a duty for every Muslim able to make it.
Islam is growing in Europe through migration, so it is a new religion for many European countries.
These four religions are more concentrated than Christianity or Islam. Each is tied to a homeland, with a diaspora (a population living scattered outside its homeland) elsewhere.
Hinduism is found in India and Nepal and in the Indian diaspora. About four in five Indians are Hindu, and Varanasi on the Ganges is a major pilgrimage city.
Buddhism, which began in India, is now found in Thailand, Myanmar, Sri Lanka, Tibet, Japan and Vietnam.
Judaism is found mainly in Israel and the USA, because most of the world's Jews live there.
Sikhism is found in Punjab, with a diaspora in the UK and Canada.
A sketch map of the major religious regions is expected in an 80-mark answer.
Label the major religious regions and the holy cities: Jerusalem, Mecca, Varanasi and Amritsar.
Census results show how the religious make-up of both parts of Ireland is changing. The Republic is becoming less Catholic, and in Northern Ireland the balance has shifted.
Census 2022, Republic of Ireland: about 69% Roman Catholic, down from about 78% in Census 2016.
About 14% have no religion, so the share saying no religion is rising as the Catholic share falls.
Orthodox Christians and Muslims are growing groups, through immigration.
Census 2021, Northern Ireland (religion or religion brought up in): Catholic about 46%, Protestant and other Christian about 43%.
This was the first census in which Catholics outnumbered Protestants, though Catholics were not a majority.
There is more on religious issues arising from migration into Ireland in Ethnic, racial and religious issues arising from migration.
Countries differ in how far religion and government are joined. The four types run from religious rule to strict separation.
Theocracy: religious leaders rule the state, so religious authority is also political authority.
An established or state church (an official church recognised by the state): the Church of England is the established church in England.
Strict separation of church and state: France's laïcité (the French principle of secularism) and the USA's First Amendment.
States in which one church had a dominant influence without being the official church: Ireland in the 20th century and Poland.
In a theocracy, or where religion and state are fused, religious law and religious leaders hold political power. Iran, Vatican City and Saudi Arabia show this in different ways.
Iran has been an Islamic Republic since the 1979 revolution. A Supreme Leader, a senior cleric (religious leader), has the highest authority.
Vatican City is an independent state ruled by the Pope, created by the Lateran Treaty with Italy in 1929.
Saudi Arabia's law is based on Sharia (Islamic religious law), and the public practice of other religions is not permitted.
The Church of England shows an established church, and the USA and France show separation. France's version is the strictest, and it has led to laws on religious dress.
The Church of England is the established church. The monarch is its Supreme Governor, and 26 bishops sit in the House of Lords (the UK's second parliamentary chamber).
The First Amendment (1791) to the US Constitution bars an established religion.
France's 1905 law separated the churches and the state. Laïcité, or secularism, is a core principle of the Republic.
A 2004 law banned conspicuous religious symbols, including the Islamic headscarf, in state schools.
A 2010 law banned face coverings, including the burqa and niqab (veils that cover the face), in public places.
A constitution can be secular while religion still presses on politics. India is the example of a secular state facing religious-nationalist pressure.
India's constitution describes it as a secular republic, so the state is not tied to any one religion.
Hindu nationalism, such as in the demand for a Hindu temple at Ayodhya (politics that treats India as a Hindu nation), has grown in Indian politics since the 1990s.

Bunreacht na hÉireann (the Irish Constitution) reflected the Catholic majority's influence. Its religious content shows how close church and state were, yet it never made Catholicism a state religion.
Bunreacht na hÉireann was approved by referendum (a vote by the people) on 1 July 1937.
The preamble begins: In the Name of the Most Holy Trinity.
Article 44 originally recognised the special position of the Holy Catholic Apostolic and Roman Church as the guardian of the Faith professed by the great majority of the citizens.
Article 44 also recognised the Church of Ireland, the Presbyterian Church, the Methodist Church, the Religious Society of Friends (Quakers) and the Jewish congregations.
Article 44 guarantees freedom of conscience and practice and says the State shall not endow (fund) any religion. Its special position clause did not establish a state church.
Article 41 originally banned divorce, so civil law followed Catholic teaching.
The Eighth Amendment (1983) gave the unborn a right to life equal to the mother's.
In the 20th century the Catholic Church shaped Irish schools, hospitals and social policy. The Mother and Child Scheme showed the limits it could set on government.
Most primary schools, about nine in ten, are under Catholic patronage (the Church is the school's patron, which controls its running), and the Church controlled many hospitals.
The Church influenced social policy on censorship and contraception.

The Mother and Child Scheme (1950–51), a free health-care plan for mothers and children, was dropped after opposition from the Catholic hierarchy (the bishops) and doctors. The Minister for Health, Noel Browne, resigned.
Pope John Paul II visited Ireland in 1979, which shows the Church's standing in Irish life, and Pope Francis visited in 2018.
From 1972 onwards, referendums removed or reversed much of the Church's constitutional influence. Abuse reports in 2009 weakened its authority, and school patronage is now debated.
Fifth Amendment referendum, December 1972: removed the special position clause and the list of named churches (about 84% Yes).
Divorce referendum, November 1995: passed by about 50.3% to 49.7%.
Marriage equality referendum, 22 May 2015: about 62% Yes. Ireland was the first country to allow same-sex marriage by popular vote.
Referendum of 25 May 2018 repealed (cancelled) the Eighth Amendment (about 66% Yes).
Referendum of October 2018 removed the offence of blasphemy (insulting religion) from the Constitution (about 65% Yes).
The Ryan Report (May 2009) examined abuse in residential institutions run by religious orders. The Murphy Report (November 2009) examined the Dublin archdiocese's handling of abuse allegations.
Educate Together is a multi-denominational school patron, founded in 1984. Its first school, the Dalkey School Project, opened in 1978.
The debate on school patronage includes the State's aim to divest (hand over) some Catholic schools.
Religion is seldom the only cause of conflict, but it often deepens it. Four factors recur.
Competing claims to holy sites and territory, for example in Jerusalem, because each side may see the same place as sacred.
Religion overlapping with national identity and political power, so that a religious divide also becomes a divide over who governs.

The conflict was about national identity and political power as much as theology. Civil rights, national identity and power were central, not religion alone. The roots lie in settlement, history and partition.
The Plantation of Ulster began in 1609, so settlers and natives became divided by religion; it settled English and Scottish Protestants on confiscated land.
The Battle of the Boyne (1690), when William of Orange defeated James II, is commemorated by Orange Order parades on 12 July. The Orange Order was founded in 1795.

The Government of Ireland Act 1920 led to partition (the division of Ireland). Northern Ireland was established in 1921 with six counties and a Protestant/unionist (supporting union with Britain) majority.
Catholics faced discrimination in housing, jobs and local voting, including gerrymandering (drawing boundaries to favour one group), e.g. in Derry.
There is more on partition of Ireland as a boundary change in The complexity of regions (ii).
The Troubles was the period of violence that followed the civil rights movement. It ran from the late 1960s to 1998.
The Northern Ireland civil rights movement began in 1968, campaigning against the discrimination Catholics faced.
The Troubles, from the late 1960s to 1998, killed over 3,500 people.
British troops were deployed in 1969, and internment without trial (imprisonment without a court case) was introduced in 1971.
Bloody Sunday, Derry, 30 January 1972: British paratroopers shot dead 13 civil-rights marchers. A 14th man died later.
The 1981 hunger strikes: ten republican (seeking a united Ireland) prisoners, including Bobby Sands, died.
The Good Friday Agreement of 1998 set up power-sharing, but Catholic and Protestant communities are still separated by peace walls, and few pupils attend integrated schools.

The Good Friday (Belfast) Agreement, 10 April 1998, set up a power-sharing Assembly and Executive, North–South bodies and the consent principle (no change in Northern Ireland's status without the consent of its people).
The Omagh bomb, 15 August 1998, killed 29 people, showing violence continued after the Agreement. The Real IRA was responsible.
Peace walls (peace lines) separate Catholic and Protestant areas of Belfast. The first was built in 1969, and some still stand.
Lagan College, Belfast (1981), was the first planned integrated (mixed Catholic and Protestant) secondary school. Integrated schools still teach fewer than one in ten pupils.
There is more on the Agreement's institutions and Brexit in The complexity of regions (i).
Religion decided the borders of the subcontinent in 1947, and religious tension has continued in India and Kashmir since.
Partition of India, August 1947, created Hindu-majority India and Muslim-majority Pakistan, which included East Pakistan, now Bangladesh.
Because the border followed religion, around 15 million people were displaced and hundreds of thousands were killed.
Kashmir is a Muslim-majority region claimed by both India and Pakistan and divided by a Line of Control. India and Pakistan have fought wars over it.
Hindu nationalists demolished the 16th-century Babri Mosque at Ayodhya on 6 December 1992. Riots followed in which about 2,000 people died.
A Hindu temple to Ram was consecrated (made sacred) on the Ayodhya site in January 2024.
Operation Blue Star, June 1984: the Indian army stormed the Golden Temple, Amritsar, to remove armed Sikh separatists.
Prime Minister Indira Gandhi was assassinated by two Sikh bodyguards on 31 October 1984, followed by anti-Sikh riots in Delhi.
Jerusalem is sacred to three religions, and the dispute over land there mixes religion with territory and national identity.
Jerusalem contains the Western Wall (Judaism), the Al-Aqsa Mosque and Dome of the Rock (Islam), and the Church of the Holy Sepulchre (Christianity).
The State of Israel was declared on 14 May 1948. About 700,000 Palestinians fled or were expelled in the 1948 war, an event known as the Nakba, meaning catastrophe.
In the Six-Day War of 1967 Israel occupied the West Bank, East Jerusalem and Gaza, so these became the territory later contested.
Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank are illegal under international law in the view of the UN and most states.
The Oslo Accords of 1993 brought mutual recognition between Israel and the Palestine Liberation Organization, and limited Palestinian self-rule.
On 7 October 2023 a Hamas-led attack from Gaza killed about 1,200 people in Israel and took about 250 hostages.
Israel's military campaign in Gaza killed tens of thousands of Palestinians and destroyed much of Gaza. A ceasefire began in October 2025.
Ireland recognised the State of Palestine on 28 May 2024, with Spain and Norway.
Shorter examples show religion feeding conflict in other regions. Each needs only a line or two.

Lebanon shares power by religious community (a confessional system): the President is a Maronite Christian, the Prime Minister a Sunni Muslim and the Speaker a Shia Muslim. Civil war from 1975 to 1990 was ended by the Taif Agreement (1989).
Nigeria has a mainly Muslim north and a mainly Christian south. Boko Haram's insurgency (armed rebellion) began in 2009, and in April 2014 it kidnapped 276 schoolgirls from Chibok.
Iraq and Syria saw Sunni–Shia violence after 2003 and in the Syrian civil war. The Islamic State group declared a caliphate (a state ruled by a religious leader) in 2014.
There is more on the Rohingya in Racial groupings, and on Bosnia in A European regional case study of identity.
Culture and identity are the broad concepts. Everyday expressions are the visible parts of culture that people practise, and they are what an essay on this topic is built from.
Culture is a group's shared, learned way of life: its beliefs, customs, language, arts, food and dress. It is learned, not inherited, so each generation has to be taught it.
Identity is a person's or group's sense of who they are and where they belong, for example as Irish, Catalan or a member of a county club.
Everyday expressions are the visible, practised parts of culture: people choose them, repeat them and pass them on.
The main everyday expressions in this option are sport, traditions, costume, food, music, art and festivals.
Customs are not just pastimes. They do real work for a group, and these five functions give you the points to explain in an essay.
They mark belonging: taking part in a shared custom shows that a person belongs to the group.
They pass culture from one generation to the next, because children learn the games, songs and customs by taking part.
They assert identity when a culture is under pressure, as Irish games and music did during the Gaelic Revival (a movement to bring Irish games and music back into everyday use).
They attract tourists and bring income to the places where they are practised.
They can also mark division: parades in Northern Ireland and football rivalries separate groups as well as unite them.
Globalisation (the growing connection between countries through trade, media and travel) spreads the same products, sports and customs to many countries, so cultures can become more alike.
Fast food, Hollywood films, global sports and global brands are the main channels of Americanisation (the spread of American culture to other countries).
McDonald's opened its first Irish restaurant on Grafton Street, Dublin, in 1977, an example of a global brand entering everyday Irish life.
Halloween customs returned from the USA in a commercial form, although the festival itself has Irish origins in Samhain (the Celtic festival of 31 October to 1 November).
Communities do not simply accept cultural change. Three responses try to keep traditional expressions alive.
Revival movements, such as the Gaelic Revival, promote Irish games and music to keep them in everyday use.
UNESCO's list of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity (living traditions and skills rather than buildings or objects) was created by its 2003 convention. Irish harping was added in 2019.
State support for traditional music, sport and arts events helps keep these expressions in practice, because funding lets them continue and reach new audiences.
Migration (people moving to live in another country) also changes everyday culture, because migrants bring their own customs with them.
Migrants bring new food, festivals, religious celebrations and sports, which become part of everyday life in their new country.
New and existing expressions blend: multicultural festivals and fusion food (dishes that mix cooking traditions) combine traditions from different groups.

The Gaelic Athletic Association (GAA) promotes native Irish games, chiefly hurling and Gaelic football. It is the strongest example of sport as an expression of Irish identity, so be ready to treat it in depth.
The GAA was founded on 1 November 1884 in Hayes' Hotel, Thurles, Co. Tipperary, by Michael Cusack and others, to preserve and promote native Irish games.
Maurice Davin was the GAA's first president.
Players are amateurs, so the games stay rooted in the community, which means they play for their club and county without being paid.
Clubs are based on parishes and teams represent counties, so the GAA reinforces local and county identity.
The GAA is organised on an all-island basis and has clubs among the Irish diaspora (Irish people living abroad).
Camogie, the women's form of hurling, is run by the Camogie Association, founded in 1904. Ladies' football is the women's form of Gaelic football.
Hurling was added to UNESCO's list of living traditions in 2018. It is a cultural symbol and is not Ireland's national sport by law.
Croke Park is the stadium behind the GAA's best-known rule changes and events, so you can use it to show how sport and national history are linked.
Croke Park, Dublin, holds about 82,300 spectators and is one of Europe's largest stadiums.
Members were banned from playing "foreign games" (soccer, rugby, cricket and hockey), which kept the GAA focused on native Irish games. The ban was removed in 1971.
A rule barring members of the British security forces from the GAA was removed in 2001.
Bloody Sunday, 21 November 1920: British forces opened fire at a Gaelic football match in Croke Park, killing 14 people.
This is a different event from Bloody Sunday 1972 in Derry, and there is more on it in the notes on Religion as a cultural indicator.
From 2007 Croke Park hosted rugby and soccer internationals while Lansdowne Road was rebuilt. England played Ireland at rugby there in February 2007.
Other sports express identity too, and in Northern Ireland the team a person supports can signal which community they belong to.
The Ireland rugby team represents the whole island, including Northern Ireland, so it is an all-island expression of identity.
Sporting loyalties in Northern Ireland are divided between Irish and British teams, so the choice of team can express national identity.
Traditional music is played informally, and sessions are the main setting in which it is shared.
Traditional instruments include the fiddle, uilleann pipes (Irish bellows-blown bagpipes), tin whistle, flute, concertina, accordion, bodhrán (a hand-held frame drum) and harp.
The harp is Ireland's national symbol and appears on coins and the presidential seal.
Sessions are informal gatherings where musicians play together, which is how tunes and playing styles are passed on.
Uilleann piping was added to UNESCO's list of living traditions in 2017.
Traditional music has an organisation behind it and a yearly festival, and it has a singing and dancing side too.
Comhaltas Ceoltóirí Éireann was founded in 1951 to promote traditional music.
The first Fleadh Cheoil na hÉireann (a national music festival) was held in Mullingar in 1951. It is now held in a different town each August and draws hundreds of thousands of visitors.
Sean-nós ("old style") is unaccompanied traditional singing in Irish, strongest in Conamara.
Sean-nós dancing is the traditional informal dance form that sits alongside the singing tradition.
Irish music and dance also reached a world audience, which shows an Irish expression spreading outwards through globalisation.
Riverdance began as the interval act (the performance between entries) of the Eurovision Song Contest, performed in Dublin on 30 April 1994.
It became a worldwide touring show, carrying Irish dance to audiences abroad.
Irish popular music with traditional roots combines the traditional instruments and melodies with modern styles.
Festivals bring a community together on a fixed date. These points cover national and religious occasions, and St Patrick's Day shows Irish identity in the diaspora.
St Patrick's Day, 17 March: parades are held across the world, for example in New York, and landmarks are lit green.
St Patrick's Day is a global expression of Irish identity in the diaspora. Dublin's St Patrick's Festival began in 1996.
St Brigid's Day (Lá Fhéile Bríde, around 1 February) became a public holiday in 2023, the first named after a woman.
Samhain (31 October to 1 November) is the Celtic origin of Halloween.
Local festivals and fairs tie a place to a custom, and each of these is held at the same time every year.
Puck Fair, Killorglin, Co. Kerry, is held every August (10-12 August), when a wild goat is crowned king.
Lisdoonvarna Matchmaking Festival, Co. Clare, is held every September.
Ballinasloe Horse Fair, Co. Galway, is held every October and is one of Europe's oldest horse fairs. It is also important to Travellers, a group with a distinct everyday culture.
Some festivals look outwards to the diaspora, and others celebrate writing and the arts.
The Rose of Tralee, Co. Kerry, has been held since 1959 and is open to women of Irish birth or descent worldwide, so it links Ireland with its diaspora.
Bloomsday, 16 June, celebrates James Joyce's Ulysses, which is set on 16 June 1904.
The Galway International Arts Festival has been held since 1978. Wexford Festival Opera has been held since 1951.
Some customs go back much further than the modern festivals above.
Wakes (gatherings held when someone has died), holy wells and pattern days (feast days held at holy wells) are older Irish traditions that are still practised in some places.
What people wear and make can show where they come from. Irish costume and craft range from a handknit jumper to a team jersey.
The Aran sweater is a knitted wool jumper from the Aran Islands, Co. Galway.
The Claddagh ring shows two hands holding a heart with a crown. It is named after the Claddagh area of Galway city.
Irish dancing costumes are worn for performances and competitions.
GAA jerseys are everyday dress that shows county identity: supporters wear their county colours.
Food is an everyday expression of identity, and several Irish dishes are tied to particular places.
Traditional dishes include soda bread, Irish stew, colcannon, boxty, coddle and the full Irish breakfast.
Boxty is a potato pancake associated with the north midlands and Connacht.
Coddle is a Dublin dish, so some Irish foods are tied to a particular place.
Guinness has been brewed at St James's Gate, Dublin, since 1759, so it is a long-standing Irish drink.
Irish food is not fixed. Immigration has added new foods to the traditional ones.
Census 2022 recorded Polish as the most common home language after English and Irish.
Polish shops and Polish food are now common in Irish towns, so new foods sit beside traditional dishes.
Irish art and monuments from the distant past are still expressions of identity today.
The Book of Kells is an illuminated gospel manuscript (a hand-written book of the gospels with decorated pages) made around 800. It is kept at Trinity College Dublin.
High crosses, such as Muiredach's Cross at Monasterboice, Co. Louth, are carved stone monuments of early Christian Ireland.
Newgrange (Brú na Bóinne, Co. Meath) is a passage tomb (a burial mound with a long entrance passage) built around 3200 BC and is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
Sunlight enters the chamber at Newgrange at the winter solstice (the shortest day of the year).
Writing is another way in which Irish identity is expressed, in English and in Irish.
Irish Nobel Prize winners for Literature are W. B. Yeats (1923), George Bernard Shaw (1925), Samuel Beckett (1969) and Seamus Heaney (1995).
Irish-language literature and songs express identity through the language itself. There is more on this in the notes on Language as a cultural indicator.
Irish Travellers are a group with a distinct everyday culture of their own.
Irish Travellers have a distinct everyday culture, traditionally nomadic (moving from place to place) and based on strong extended family ties.
Horse fairs are important to Travellers, for example the Ballinasloe Horse Fair in Co. Galway.
Travellers have their own language, known as Cant, Gammon or Shelta.
There is more on their recognition as an ethnic minority in the notes on Racial groupings.

In Northern Ireland, parades and painted symbols express two opposing identities: unionist (wanting to remain in the United Kingdom) and nationalist (wanting a united Ireland). Here you need only the expressions, not the conflict.
Orange Order parades on 12 July commemorate the Battle of the Boyne (1690). Bonfires are lit on the night of 11 July in loyalist areas (areas of strong unionist, pro-British identity).
Parades express unionist identity and can divide communities. There is more on the conflict itself in the notes on Religion as a cultural indicator.
Painted gable-end murals (pictures on the end walls of houses) in Belfast and Derry show loyalist and republican identities.
Kerbstones are painted red, white and blue or green, white and orange to mark territory.
Spain is the first European example. Its festivals range from religious processions to a tomato fight, and some express regional identity.
San Fermín in Pamplona, Navarre, runs from 6 to 14 July and includes the running of the bulls through the streets.
La Tomatina in Buñol, near Valencia, is a tomato fight held on the last Wednesday of August. It has been held since 1945.
Semana Santa (Holy Week, the week before Easter) features religious processions, especially in Seville.
Flamenco, the song, guitar and dance of Andalusia, has been on UNESCO's list since 2010.
Castells, human towers built in Catalonia, have been on UNESCO's list since 2010 and express Catalan regional identity.
Football, bullfighting and food in Spain show how regional identities are expressed, and sometimes contested.
FC Barcelona's motto, "Més que un club" ("More than a club"), reflects its role as a symbol of Catalan identity, especially under Franco (Spain's dictator, who suppressed regional identities).
Athletic Bilbao fields only players born or raised in the Basque Country, or trained in Basque clubs, which makes the team an expression of Basque identity.
Catalonia's parliament banned bullfighting in 2010, with the ban in force from 2012. Spain's Constitutional Court overturned the ban in 2016.
Paella comes from Valencia. Tapas are small dishes shared in bars.
Scotland offers a second example, with distinctive dress, music and festivals.
The kilt, worn with tartan (a woven pattern of crossing coloured stripes), is the best-known Scottish dress.
Bagpipes are played by pipe bands and at Highland Games.
Highland Games are traditional sports such as the caber toss (throwing a long wooden pole) and hammer throw, held with piping and Highland dancing.
Burns Night, 25 January, celebrates the poet Robert Burns with haggis, whisky and poetry.
Hogmanay is the Scottish New Year celebration, so Scotland marks the new year in its own way.
In Glasgow two football clubs carry religious and national identities, which is why their rivalry is more than a sporting one.
Celtic FC was founded in 1887 in Glasgow's East End by Brother Walfrid, a Marist brother (a member of a Catholic religious order), to raise money for poor Irish Catholic immigrants.
Rangers was founded in 1872 and was traditionally supported by Protestants and unionists.
The rivalry between the two clubs, known as the Old Firm, carries religious and Irish or British identity.
Germany's examples combine a long-running festival, regional dress and food shaped by migration.
Oktoberfest in Munich, Bavaria, has been held since 1810. It began with a royal wedding.
Visitors to Oktoberfest wear lederhosen (Bavarian leather shorts) and dirndl (a traditional Bavarian dress).
Christmas markets are held in German cities.
The döner kebab became popular in Germany through Turkish immigrants, an example of migration adding to everyday food.
France's examples include a national day, a cycle race, food and a film festival.
Bastille Day, 14 July, commemorates the storming of the Bastille in 1789 and is marked by a military parade in Paris.
The Tour de France cycle race was first held in 1903 and takes place each July.
The "gastronomic meal of the French" was added to UNESCO's list in 2010.
The Cannes Film Festival is held each May, which makes film one of France's expressions of culture.
French public life is shaped by a principle of keeping religion and the state apart.

Laïcité, the principle of state secularism (keeping religion out of government and public institutions), shapes the debate over religious dress in public life. There is more on this in the notes on Religion as a cultural indicator.
Italy's expressions are strongly tied to local districts and regions.
The Palio di Siena is a horse race around the Piazza del Campo between the city's districts, the contrade, held on 2 July and 16 August.
Venice Carnival, with its masks, takes place before Lent (the period of fasting before Easter).
Neapolitan pizza-making was added to UNESCO's list in 2017.
Regional food is central to Italian identity, with pizza from Naples and pasta as the main examples.
Football is also a major Italian sporting expression, for example alongside the Palio.
These shorter examples can be used when you need extra European material, one point each.
Norway's Constitution Day, 17 May, marks the constitution of 1814 with children's parades and the bunad, a regional folk costume.
King's Day in the Netherlands, 27 April, sees people dress in orange, the colour of the royal House of Orange.
The Festival Interceltique de Lorient in Brittany has been held every August since 1971 and brings together musicians from the Celtic regions.
Fest-noz, the Breton night dance festival, has been on UNESCO's list since 2012.
The National Eisteddfod of Wales is an annual festival of Welsh music, poetry and culture held entirely in Welsh.
There is more on festivals in Switzerland and the Balkans in the notes on A European regional case study of identity.
Eurovision is a European-wide event, and Ireland has a strong record in it.
The Eurovision Song Contest is a European-wide event in which countries present national acts, so it also expresses national identity and politics.
Ireland has won the contest seven times, including three in a row in 1992-94.

Nationality and the nation state are political entities placed on the physical and cultural landscape. Three words that sound alike, state, nation and nationality, each have a precise meaning, and the rest of this option depends on keeping them apart.
A state is a sovereign political unit (one that governs itself and answers to no outside ruler) with territory, a permanent population, a government and recognition by other states.
The Montevideo Convention (1933) set out the criteria for a state: a permanent population, a defined territory, a government, and the capacity to enter into relations with other states.
The United Nations has 193 member states, which shows how many sovereign units the world map is divided into.
A nation is a people who share a culture, history and often a language or religion, and who see themselves as one community. A nation is defined by identity, not by a government.
Nationality is membership of a nation or, legally, citizenship of a state, so the word can mean either belonging or a legal status.
A nation state is a state whose people largely form one nation, for example Iceland, Portugal or Japan. Here the nation and the state match.
A multinational state contains several nations, for example the UK, Belgium, Switzerland or Spain.
A stateless nation is a nation without its own state, for example the Kurds.
Ireland is close to a nation state but has minorities, such as Irish Travellers; the UK is a multinational state.
The idea that every nation should have its own state is fairly recent, and it spread in two main waves. Even so, it has never been fully achieved.
In Europe, nationalism (the belief that a people sharing a culture should govern itself) held from the 19th century that each nation should have its own state.
The break-up of empires after the First World War and after 1989–91 created new nation states in Europe.
Elsewhere, decolonisation (colonies winning independence from the European powers that ruled them) after 1945 created most of the new states.
Most states are not pure nation states, because they contain more than one cultural group (a people sharing a language, religion or way of life).

A boundary is the line that marks where one state ends and another begins. Boundaries can be classified by what they follow on the ground and by when they were drawn relative to the people living there.
Physical boundaries follow natural features, such as mountains, rivers, lakes or seas.
Geometric boundaries are straight lines, often lines of latitude (lines running east-west around the globe), so they ignore the landscape.
Cultural boundaries follow a language or religion, so they separate peoples rather than landscapes.
Antecedent boundaries are drawn before settlement; subsequent boundaries are drawn after settlement and follow cultural divisions, so they fit the people already living there.
Superimposed boundaries are imposed by outside powers regardless of culture, as in colonial Africa (Africa when European powers ruled it).
Relict boundaries no longer function but remain visible, for example the line of the Berlin Wall.
Mountains, rivers and seas are the most obvious places to draw a border, because they are easy to see and hard to cross. Whether they match the cultural map is another matter.
The Pyrenees, the Alps, the Rhine, the Rio Grande and the Himalayas are major physical boundaries.
The Treaty of the Pyrenees (1659) used the Pyrenees as much of the France–Spain border.
The Rhine forms part of the border between France and Germany; the Rio Grande forms part of the USA–Mexico border.

Physical boundaries often fit cultural divides but can also cut through a cultural group: the Basques live on both sides of the Pyrenees, so a mountain border still splits one people between two states.
Where boundaries are drawn as straight lines on a map, they take no account of the people on the ground. This matters most where outside powers drew them.
The 49th parallel forms most of the western USA–Canada border, agreed in 1818 and extended in 1846.
The Berlin Conference (1884–85) set rules for the European division of Africa, so European powers carved up the continent among themselves.
Many African borders are straight lines that ignore ethnic territories (the lands of different peoples), splitting some groups and joining rival ones.
These colonial borders are a cause of later conflict and secession (a region breaking away to form its own state), because rival groups were forced into one state and single peoples were divided.
A boundary does more than mark territory. It shapes who people feel they are, and it can unite, divide, harden or soften depending on how it is managed.
Boundaries create a shared national identity within them, through citizenship, schools, media, sport and symbols (such as flags), which all treat everyone inside the border as one people.

Boundaries split cultural groups and create minorities (smaller groups living within a state dominated by another group): partition (dividing a territory between two states) in Ireland, the Kurds and the Basques.

Boundaries can harden into barriers: the Berlin Wall stood from 1961 to 1989, and the Cyprus Green Line, the UN buffer zone (a neutral strip separating two sides) through Nicosia, has divided the island since 1974.
Boundaries can also soften: the Schengen Agreement, first signed in 1985, removed passport checks between most EU states.
Ireland is outside Schengen because of the Common Travel Area with the UK, in place since 1923; the border has been open since 1998.
Boundary disputes can cause war, and changing boundaries create new identities and new minorities.
The island of Ireland is a clear physical unit, but its political border divides it. This is the national example of a boundary that does not follow the landscape.
The Government of Ireland Act 1920 created two administrations on the island.
The Anglo-Irish Treaty was signed in December 1921; Northern Ireland was established in 1921.
Northern Ireland consists of six of Ulster’s nine counties: Antrim, Armagh, Down, Fermanagh, Londonderry (Derry), and Tyrone.
Cavan, Donegal and Monaghan, the other three Ulster counties, went to the Irish Free State in 1922.
The Boundary Commission of 1925 (a body set up to review the border) was not published and the border was left unchanged.

The border is about 499 km long and follows old county boundaries rather than physical features, so it cuts through communities and farms, and through the Erne and Foyle catchments (the areas of land drained by those rivers).
There is more on the partition boundary history in The complexity of regions (ii).
Partition did not just draw a line. It created two states, each with its own majority and its own minority, and Ireland’s constitution had to respond.
Partition created two states, two majorities and two minorities, so each state contained people who identified with the other.
Ireland became a republic and left the Commonwealth (the association of states once part of the British Empire) in 1949.
Articles 2 and 3 of the Constitution originally claimed the whole island as national territory.
After the Good Friday Agreement referendum of May 1998, the Articles were changed to an aspiration to unity by consent, in force from December 1999.
Everyone born on the island of Ireland is entitled to Irish citizenship; under the Agreement, people in Northern Ireland may be Irish, British or both.
Since 1998 the border has been open, so most people cross it without noticing. Brexit, the UK’s departure from the EU, made that openness an issue again.
The border has been open since 1998, and its openness became an issue after Brexit because leaving the EU could have meant checks on the line.
In the UK referendum on EU membership on 23 June 2016, Northern Ireland voted about 56% Remain.
The UK left the EU on 31 January 2020, which is why the status of the border mattered.
The Windsor Framework (2023) keeps the land border free of checks, so the border stays open.
Few states are made of one people. Three historical processes explain why almost every state holds more than one cultural group.
Historical conquest and union brought different peoples into one state, as one people took over or joined with another.
Boundaries drawn without regard to culture placed groups in the wrong state, leaving them as minorities under a government of another group.
Migration added new cultural groups to existing states, as people moved in from elsewhere.
States respond to cultural diversity in very different ways, from sharing power to denying a group’s existence. The responses form a range.

Federalism (power divided between a national and regional governments) and autonomy (a region controlling its own affairs) give regions control of their own affairs, as in Belgium, Switzerland and Spain’s autonomous communities.
Devolution gives regions their own parliament or assembly while the state keeps overall power, as in the UK in 1999.
Power-sharing gives each main group a role in government, so no group is shut out, as in Northern Ireland and Lebanon.
Multiculturalism recognises several cultures within one state, as in Canada.
Assimilation requires minorities to adopt the dominant culture, as in France.
Suppression denies a group its identity: historically the Kurds in Turkey, and today the Uyghurs in China.
Spain is a multinational state whose Basque and Catalan regions each have a distinct identity. It has answered with autonomy rather than a single national model.
Basques and Catalans have their own languages, autonomy statutes (the laws setting out each region’s powers) and strong regional identities.
The Basque Autonomous Community (Statute of Gernika, 1979) and Navarre collect their own taxes, a sign of how much power they hold.
Catalonia’s autonomy statute dates from 1979 and was revised in 2006; Barcelona is its capital.
Basque and Catalan were suppressed under Franco (1939–1975), the period of dictatorship before the 1978 constitution.
Independence movements arose in both regions: the ETA campaign in the Basque Country and the 2017 referendum in Catalonia. There is more on these in the conflicts blocks below.
The UK is a multinational state of four nations. Devolution since 1999 gave three of them their own elected bodies.
The UK is made up of England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland.
Devolution in 1999 created the Scottish Parliament, the National Assembly for Wales (renamed the Senedd in 2020) and the Northern Ireland Assembly.
The Scottish independence referendum of 18 September 2014 voted about 55% No, so Scotland stayed in the UK.
The 2016 EU referendum was a different vote: the UK voted about 52% Leave, but Scotland voted about 62% Remain. There is more on Northern Ireland’s result in The island of Ireland and partition.
Quebec is the clearest example of a distinct cultural group inside a state that has stayed together, though narrowly.
Quebec is French-speaking, so its identity is distinct within Canada.
Quebec’s Charter of the French Language (Bill 101) was passed in 1977, to protect the French language.
Quebec held sovereignty referendums (votes on whether to become independent) in 1980, when about 60% voted No, and in 1995, when about 50.6% voted No, a very narrow result.
In 2006 Canada’s House of Commons recognised that “the Québécois form a nation within a united Canada”.
Belgium and Switzerland are two multinational states that are full case studies elsewhere in this option, so only a pointer is needed here.
Belgium has several language groups and federal regions, so it is a multinational state. There is more on this in the Belgium option of A European regional case study of identity.
Switzerland has cantons (the member regions of the Swiss federation) and four national languages. There is more on this in the Switzerland option of A European regional case study of identity.
Ireland is close to a nation state, but it has a recognised ethnic minority and new communities formed by recent immigration.
Irish Travellers were recognised as an ethnic minority on 1 March 2017 and number about 33,000 (Census 2022).
Census 2022 recorded about 20% of residents born outside Ireland, creating new immigrant communities.
Indigenous peoples (the original inhabitants of a region) often now live as minorities inside states. The Sámi show how one such people can span several states and still have its own elected bodies.
The Sámi are the indigenous people of the far north of Norway, Sweden, Finland and Russia’s Kola Peninsula (Sápmi), traditionally reindeer herders.
The Sámi have their own elected parliaments, for example in Norway (1989), Sweden (1993) and Finland (1996).
Aboriginal Australians and Māori are also indigenous peoples within states. There is more on them in Racial groupings.
China is a state with large minority peoples who have no state of their own. Two of them are treated as stateless groups below.
China’s minorities include the Tibetans and the Uyghurs, both dealt with under cultural groups without a nation state below.
The Kurds are the main case study of a stateless nation: a large people with a shared language and homeland, split between four states.
The Kurds are commonly estimated at 30 million or more, the largest ethnic group without its own state.
Most Kurds live in a mountainous region, Kurdistan, divided between Turkey (the largest number, in the south-east), Iran, Iraq and Syria.
Kurdish is an Indo-European (Iranian) language, so it is one marker that sets Kurds apart as a people.
A Kurdish state was promised after the First World War and then withdrawn. Turkey, home to the largest Kurdish population, then suppressed Kurdish identity, and that led to armed conflict.
The Treaty of Sèvres (1920) provided for a possible Kurdish state.
The Treaty of Lausanne (1923) replaced it and drew the borders of modern Turkey with no Kurdish state.
Turkey long denied a separate Kurdish identity and banned Kurdish in public life and broadcasting until the early 1990s.
The PKK (Kurdistan Workers’ Party), founded in 1978, began an armed campaign in 1984; the conflict cost about 40,000 lives.
The PKK announced its dissolution in May 2025.
In Iraq and Syria the Kurds have fared differently from Turkey: Iraqi Kurds suffered an attack but won autonomy, and Syrian Kurds fought the Islamic State group.
On 16 March 1988 Saddam Hussein’s forces attacked the Kurdish town of Halabja with chemical weapons, killing about 5,000 people.
After the 1991 Gulf War a no-fly zone (airspace closed to Iraqi aircraft) protected Iraqi Kurds.
Iraq’s 2005 constitution recognised the Kurdistan Region as autonomous, with its own government and parliament in Erbil.
On 25 September 2017 about 93% voted for independence in a referendum that Iraq’s government rejected; Iraqi forces then retook Kirkuk.
In Syria, Kurdish-led forces fought the Islamic State group, including the defence of Kobani (2014–15), and ran an autonomous area in the north-east.
A people without a state keeps itself together through shared culture. For the Kurds, language and a national festival do this work.
The Kurdish language and Newroz, the Kurdish New Year on 21 March, are major expressions of Kurdish identity.
The Palestinians are a second example of a people without a fully sovereign state, with many living as refugees (people forced to flee their homes) in neighbouring countries.
About 700,000 Palestinians fled or were expelled in 1948. There is more on the events of 1948 and 1967 in Religion as a cultural indicator.
Palestinian refugees and their descendants live in Jordan, Lebanon, Syria, the West Bank and Gaza.
The Oslo Accords of 1993 created the Palestinian Authority, with limited self-rule, so Palestinians gained some government but not a sovereign state.
Ireland, Spain and Norway recognised the State of Palestine on 28 May 2024; the UK, Canada and Australia did so on 21 September 2025, and France on 22 September 2025.
The Roma are a people spread across Europe with no territory of their own. Their history shows both migration from India and long-running persecution and discrimination.
The Roma number about 10–12 million in Europe (European Commission estimate) and have no territory of their own.
Their Romani language is related to languages of northern India, showing that their ancestors migrated from India; they reached south-eastern Europe by the 14th century.
Large Roma populations live in Romania, Bulgaria, Hungary, Slovakia, Spain and Turkey.
Roma were targeted for extermination in the Holocaust, the Nazi genocide of the Second World War.
In D.H. and Others v Czech Republic (2007) the European Court of Human Rights ruled that placing Roma children in special schools was discrimination.
Tibetans are a people whose homeland has been under Chinese control since 1950, with their leader in exile.
China’s army entered Tibet in 1950, which began Chinese control of the region.
After a failed uprising in 1959, the Dalai Lama (Tibet’s spiritual and political leader) fled to India; Tibet’s government-in-exile is based in Dharamsala.
The Tibet Autonomous Region was set up in 1965.

Tibetans see Han Chinese migration (settlement by China’s majority ethnic group), controls on monasteries and Mandarin-medium schooling (teaching in China’s official language) as threats to their culture.
The Uyghurs, a Muslim people of north-west China, are a recent example of a state acting against a cultural group.
The Uyghurs are a Turkic-speaking, mainly Muslim people of Xinjiang in north-west China.
Since 2017 an estimated one million or more Uyghurs and other Muslims have been held in detention, or “re-education”, camps.
A UN human rights office report of August 2022 found “serious human rights violations” that may amount to crimes against humanity.
Not every stateless nation is in the same position. Basques and Catalans show a nation without a state that nonetheless has real self-government.
Basques and Catalans are nations without independent states that have strong autonomy, which contrasts sharply with the position of the Kurds.
Groups without a state have a limited set of ways to respond, and the results vary widely.
Groups without a state keep their identity through language, festivals and diaspora organisations (groups of people living abroad who keep ties to their homeland).
They pursue peaceful political campaigns, demand autonomy, or in some cases use armed struggle.
Outcomes range from autonomy, as in Iraqi Kurdistan and Catalonia, to repression, as in Tibet and Xinjiang.
Conflicts between a state and a cultural group tend to have the same underlying causes, whichever country they happen in.
Boundaries cut across cultural groups, so one people divided between states or minorities inside another group’s state.
A dominant group controls the state, so other groups feel excluded from power.
The language and religion of a group are suppressed.
Economic inequality between regions or groups creates grievances.
Two groups make competing claims to the same territory.
Northern Ireland is the national case study of a state built around one cultural group while another lived within it. This led to civil rights protest and then the Troubles.
The state of Northern Ireland was created around a unionist majority (people wanting to stay in the UK) with a large nationalist minority (people wanting a united Ireland).
Discrimination against nationalists fuelled the civil rights movement from 1968.
The 2021 census recorded Catholics at about 46% and Protestants and other Christians at about 43% (religion or religion brought up in).
The Good Friday Agreement redesigned Northern Ireland’s political structure so that both cultural groups had a place in government.
The Good Friday (Belfast) Agreement was signed on 10 April 1998; referendums on 22 May 1998 returned about 71% Yes in Northern Ireland and about 94% Yes in the Republic.

The Agreement redesigned the political structure for two cultural groups: a power-sharing Assembly and Executive, a North/South Ministerial Council (a body linking both parts of the island), and the consent principle (no change in status without majority agreement).
The Agreement did not move the border.
The Assembly was restored in February 2024, with Michelle O’Neill as the first nationalist First Minister.
Brexit challenged the Agreement’s arrangements. There is more on this in The island of Ireland and partition.
In the Basque Country, one wing of the independence movement turned to violence. Spain responded mainly through autonomy.
ETA (Euskadi Ta Askatasuna, “Basque Homeland and Freedom”) was founded in 1959.
ETA killed over 800 people in its campaign for an independent Basque state.
ETA declared a definitive end to violence in 2011 and dissolved in 2018.
Spain responded through the autonomy granted under its 1978 constitution. There is more on this in Spain under cultural groups within nation states.
Catalonia’s conflict with Spain was fought mostly through courts and votes rather than violence, and it escalated after a court ruling in 2010.
In 2010 Spain’s Constitutional Court struck down parts of Catalonia’s 2006 autonomy statute, including its description of Catalonia as a nation, fuelling the independence movement.
On 1 October 2017 an independence referendum was declared illegal by Spain’s courts and police tried to stop voting; about 90% of those voting backed independence, on a turnout of about 43%.
Spain imposed direct rule (central government taking over the region’s powers) using Article 155 of its constitution, and the regional president Carles Puigdemont fled to Belgium.
Nine leaders were jailed in 2019 and pardoned in 2021; an amnesty law (a law forgiving those convicted) was passed in 2024.
Yugoslavia was a multinational state that broke apart, and it is a full case study elsewhere in this option.
Yugoslavia was a multinational state that broke up into separate states. There is more on this in the Balkans option of A European regional case study of identity.
Other examples show the same causes at work in different parts of the world.

Sri Lanka: civil war from 1983 to 2009 between the government, led by the Sinhalese majority (mainly Buddhist), and the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE), who sought a Tamil state in the north and east; the LTTE was defeated in May 2009.
Chechnya, a mainly Muslim republic in Russia’s North Caucasus, fought Russia in wars in 1994–96 and 1999–2009; Grozny was largely destroyed.
Cyprus has been divided since 1974, so one island holds two separate communities. There is more on this in The complexity of regions (ii).
Rwanda’s ethnic conflict is another example. There is more on this in Racial groupings.

Identity is layered: local, regional, national and European identities coexist, and each is shaped by several cultural factors. Choose one region and use only that region's facts, because a mixed answer cannot be developed in depth.
The cultural factors are language, religion, ethnicity (belonging to a people with a shared ancestry and culture), nationality (belonging to a nation or state), culture and shared history.

The six headings are: historical developments (physical and political boundaries), ethnicity and race, religion, music, art and festivals, the role of migration (people moving in or out of a region), and new boundaries.
Choose about four factors as the aspects of the essay, and develop each with the region’s dated facts, so that every point is backed by a specific example.

Finish with an evaluation of how the factors combine, or cut across one another, in the region. Cutting across means that two divisions do not line up, for example a language divide that does not match a religious divide.
Switzerland's landscape shaped where people live and how separate its communities stayed. Mountains divided the country into valleys, while the lowland carries most of the population.
About 60% of Switzerland is in the Alps (Europe's great mountain range); the Jura mountains, a lower range, lie in the north-west.
Most people and cities are on the Swiss Plateau (Mittelland), the lowland between the Alps and the Jura, because the mountains are hard to settle.
The mountains isolated valleys, which helped preserve local dialects and Romansh (a small Swiss language), since communities had little contact with one another.
Switzerland is landlocked (it has no sea coast); Lake Geneva (shared with France) and Lake Constance (shared with Germany and Austria) form parts of its borders.
The Rhine and Rhône rise in the Swiss Alps, so the mountains are the source of both rivers.
Switzerland began as a small alliance of mountain communities and grew by adding members. Its independence, neutrality and borders were later confirmed by European treaties.
The Federal Charter of 1 August 1291 was an alliance of Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden (three founding cantons, the member states of Switzerland); 1 August is the national day.
The Confederation (a league of self-governing members) grew as further cantons joined, so it was built by agreement rather than imposed from above.
The Peace of Westphalia (1648) recognised Swiss independence from the Holy Roman Empire, the loose German-centred empire that had claimed authority over it.
The Congress of Vienna (1815) recognised Switzerland’s permanent neutrality (staying out of other countries' wars) and fixed its borders; Geneva, Valais and Neuchâtel joined as cantons.

After a short civil war, Switzerland became a federal state, one where power is shared between a central government and the cantons. Its political system gives ordinary citizens and each region a strong say.
