The Sonderbund War of November 1847 was a short civil war in which a league (Sonderbund means separate alliance) of Catholic, conservative cantons was defeated.
The federal constitution of 1848 created the modern federal state, so it settled the dispute that had led to war; it was revised in 1874 and fully revised in 1999.
There are 26 cantons with wide powers over schools, police, taxes and churches, so local differences can be managed locally.

Direct democracy means citizens decide laws themselves: they vote in referendums (votes on a single question) several times a year, and a popular initiative (a citizens' proposal for a new law) needs 100,000 signatures.
The Federal Council (the national government) has seven members from the main parties, who govern collectively, so no one party rules alone; language regions are represented by custom.
Switzerland keeps its distance from European and world organisations, and its unity does not come from one language or one ethnic group. This is why it is described as a nation by will.
Switzerland is not in the EU; it joined the UN only after a referendum in 2002, and it joined the Schengen area (the European zone with no routine passport checks between members) in 2008.
Willensnation means a nation formed by the will of its people rather than by a common language or ethnicity, so Swiss identity rests on shared institutions and choice.
Switzerland has four national languages, each concentrated in particular cantons. The rule that each area has its own language keeps the system stable.
The main languages are German (about 62%), French (about 23%), Italian (about 8%) and Romansh (about 0.5%); people may give more than one language, so the shares do not total 100%.

There are 17 German-speaking cantons, 4 French-speaking (Geneva, Vaud, Neuchâtel and Jura), 1 Italian-speaking (Ticino), 3 bilingual German–French (Bern, Fribourg and Valais) and 1 trilingual (Graubünden: German, Romansh and Italian).
The territoriality principle means each canton or commune (local authority) has its own official language or languages, used in its schools and administration.
German-speaking Swiss speak Swiss German dialects (Schweizerdeutsch) in daily life but write Standard German, the written form shared with Germany.
Children learn a second national language at school, so the language groups can understand one another.
Even the smallest language has official recognition, and the language groups have their own media. Yet the groups still vote differently, and this divide has its own nickname.

Romansh became a national language by referendum in 1938 and a partly official language in 1996; Rumantsch Grischun, a written standard, was created in 1982 so that the language could have one shared written form.

The Röstigraben (the “rösti ditch”, named after a potato dish) is the cultural divide between German- and French-speaking Switzerland, often visible in referendum results; it runs roughly along the River Sarine (Saane) in Fribourg.
The public broadcaster SRG SSR runs separate services in German (SRF), French (RTS), Italian (RSI) and Romansh (RTR), so each language group has its own radio and television.
Language divides Switzerland, but it does not break it apart, because people identify first with Switzerland itself.
No language group wants to join its neighbouring country: the French, Italian and German speakers each identify with Switzerland rather than with France, Italy or Germany.
Shared Swiss institutions and the cantonal system allow four language groups to coexist within one state, so national identity sits above language.
Switzerland was split between Protestant and Catholic cantons after the Reformation (the 16th-century movement that broke from the Catholic Church). That split still shows on the map.
Ulrich Zwingli led the Reformation in Zurich from 1519; John Calvin led it in Geneva from the 1530s–40s, and Geneva became known as the “Protestant Rome”.
Historically Protestant: Zurich, Bern, Basel, Geneva, Vaud and Neuchâtel, so the Protestant cantons include both German-speaking (such as Zurich) and French-speaking (such as Geneva) ones.
Historically Catholic: the central cantons (Lucerne, Uri, Schwyz, Zug and Unterwalden), Fribourg, Valais, Ticino and Jura, so Catholic cantons also include German- and French-speaking ones.
The Sonderbund War was a religious-political conflict between Catholic and Protestant cantons, which shows that religion once divided the country.
Because the religious map does not match the language map, no single division splits the country in two. This is a key reason for stability.
Religion cuts across language: both German- and French-speaking Switzerland contain Protestant and Catholic cantons.
There are Protestant and Catholic German speakers, and Protestant and Catholic French speakers, which reduces conflict between the language groups.
Religion in 2022: Roman Catholic about a third, Reformed (Protestant) about a fifth, no religion about a third, and Muslim about 6%, so the mix has changed since the Reformation.
Two popular votes, one in 2009 and one in 2021, put religion-related questions to Swiss voters. The 2021 vote passed narrowly.
On 29 November 2009 a popular initiative banning the building of new minarets (the towers of mosques) passed with about 57.5%.
In March 2021 a ban on face coverings in public passed with about 51%; it came into force on 1 January 2025.
The minaret ban concerned the building of mosque towers, so it is an example of religion becoming a subject of a national vote; the 2021 ban was a second popular vote.
Alpine traditions give Switzerland a shared national culture that does not depend on language.
Yodelling (singing that switches rapidly between chest and high voice) and the alphorn (a very long wooden horn) are traditional Alpine music.
Schwingen is Swiss wrestling in sawdust rings, held at Alpine festivals, so it is a sport tied to the mountain regions.
1 August is the national day, marked with bonfires and fireworks, and recalls the Federal Charter of 1291.
Each region has its own festival, and several are recognised by UNESCO (the UN body that lists world cultural heritage). They show local identity inside the national one.
Basel Fasnacht is a carnival beginning at 4 a.m. on the Monday after Ash Wednesday (the “Morgestraich”); it has been on UNESCO’s intangible heritage list since 2017.
Sechseläuten in Zurich (April) features a parade of the guilds (old trade associations), and the Böögg, a snowman figure, is burned to mark the end of winter.
The Fête des Vignerons in Vevey is a winegrowers’ festival held only about four or five times a century, most recently in 2019; it has been on UNESCO’s list since 2016.
Switzerland's identity also draws on world-class arts events, food, and a role in international affairs, especially through Geneva.
The Montreux Jazz Festival has been held since 1967, the Locarno Film Festival since 1946 and Art Basel (an international art fair) since 1970.
Fondue, raclette, rösti, chocolate, Gruyère and Emmental cheese are typical foods, so food is another shared symbol such as the national day.
The International Committee of the Red Cross was founded in Geneva in 1863 by Henri Dunant, so Geneva's international role is part of Swiss identity.
Geneva hosts the UN’s European office and many international organisations, which links Swiss identity to neutrality and humanitarian work.
Migration has made Switzerland a country with a large foreign-born population. Many workers also cross the border daily rather than live in Switzerland.
Foreign nationals make up about a quarter of the permanent resident population (about 27% in 2023).
The largest groups are Italians, Germans, Portuguese and French, plus large communities from Kosovo and elsewhere in former Yugoslavia, Spain and Turkey, so the foreign population is itself varied.
Most Swiss Muslims have roots in former Yugoslavia (Kosovo, Bosnia and North Macedonia) or Turkey, so migration brought Islam to Switzerland.
Almost 400,000 cross-border commuters from France, Italy and Germany work in Switzerland each day, many in Geneva, Basel and Ticino, which are cantons that border France, Germany and Italy.
After the Second World War, Switzerland recruited foreign labour, and later it opened its labour market to the EU.

After 1945 many Italian guest workers (temporary workers invited to fill labour shortages) came, often on a seasonal-worker permit that restricted family reunification (bringing relatives to live with them); this restriction was abolished in 2002.
Free movement of persons with the EU has applied since 2002, under bilateral agreements (separate two-sided treaties between Switzerland and the EU).
Immigration has repeatedly been put to the voters, with very different results over time. Switzerland was also once a country that people left.
The Schwarzenbach Initiative of 1970, which sought to cap the foreign population, was rejected by about 54%, so voters at that time refused a limit.
The “against mass immigration” initiative of 9 February 2014 passed with about 50.3%, a very narrow majority.
Historically, Swiss men served abroad as mercenaries (soldiers hired by foreign rulers); the Pope’s Swiss Guard, in service since 1506, is a survivor of this tradition.
Switzerland's boundaries have changed within the country as well. The canton of Jura was created when French-speaking Catholics broke away from the canton of Bern.

The canton of Jura was created on 1 January 1979 after referendums from 1974, in which the French-speaking, mainly Catholic northern districts voted to leave the German-speaking, mainly Protestant canton of Bern.
The southern French-speaking districts, mainly Protestant, chose to stay in Bern, so religion as well as language shaped the new boundary.
The town of Moutier voted in 2021 to move from Bern to Jura, and the move took effect on 1 January 2026; an earlier 2017 vote was annulled and is not the decision.
Boundaries of identity can also be political: between Switzerland and the EU, and between those who may vote and those who may not.

On 6 December 1992 voters rejected joining the European Economic Area (about 50.3% No); relations with the EU since then rest on bilateral agreements, a boundary of identity between Switzerland and the EU.
Women gained the federal vote (the vote in national elections) only in 1971, so who belongs politically changed.
Appenzell Innerrhoden, the last canton, was forced by a federal court ruling to allow women to vote in cantonal matters in 1990.
Switzerland holds together despite its diversity because its political system and its divisions work in its favour. Use these points to close the essay.
Federalism gives the cantons control over schools, police, taxes and churches, so diversity is managed locally.
Direct democracy and consensus government give each language and religious group a voice, so no group feels shut out.
Neutrality and wealth reduce external pressure on the federation.
Cross-cutting language and religion mean that divisions do not line up, which reduces conflict.
The Balkans, the south-east European region that was once Yugoslavia, has rugged relief that made it hard to unite. Its rivers are major routes.
The Dinaric Alps run parallel to the Adriatic coast, and their rugged relief fragments settlement, so communities were separated by mountains.
The Danube and Sava rivers are major features, so cities such as Belgrade and Novi Sad stand on them; the Danube flows through Belgrade, where the Sava joins it, and through Novi Sad.
“Balkanisation” is a term for the break-up of a region into small, hostile states.
Two empires ruled the region, and the line between them became a line between faiths and peoples.
The Ottoman Empire (a Muslim empire based in Turkey) ruled Serbia, Bosnia, Macedonia and Kosovo for centuries, from the 14th and 15th centuries.
Austria-Hungary (the Habsburg empire) ruled Slovenia and Croatia and annexed Bosnia (took it over formally) in 1908.
The Ottoman–Habsburg frontier ran through the region, and the Great Schism of 1054, the split dividing Catholic and Orthodox Christianity, ran roughly along the same line.
The Battle of Kosovo (1389) against the Ottomans is central to Serbian national memory, which is why Kosovo matters to Serbian identity.
A killing in Bosnia set off a world war, and after it the South Slavs were joined in a single state.
On 28 June 1914 Gavrilo Princip, a Bosnian Serb, assassinated Archduke Franz Ferdinand in Sarajevo, triggering the First World War.
The Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes was proclaimed on 1 December 1918 and renamed Yugoslavia (“land of the South Slavs”) in 1929.
The Second World War left deep wounds between the peoples, and Tito's communist state tried to hold them together under one identity.
The Croatian fascist Ustaše state ran the Jasenovac camp, where Serbs, Jews and Roma were killed, so the war left memories of group against group.
Serbian Chetniks (Serb nationalist fighters) also killed civilians; Tito’s communist Partisans won the war, which is why he could then lead the new Yugoslavia.
Socialist Yugoslavia under Josip Broz Tito (1945–1980) had six republics: Slovenia, Croatia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Serbia, Montenegro and Macedonia.
Two autonomous provinces (areas with some self-rule) lay within Serbia: Kosovo and Vojvodina; the official slogan was “brotherhood and unity”, which aimed to stop ethnic rivalry.
After Tito's death, leaders who stressed national identity gained power, and this began the break-up of Yugoslavia.
Slobodan Milošević rose to power in Serbia from 1987, so nationalism became a force in Serbian politics.
Kosovo’s autonomy was removed in 1989, which increased tension with its mostly Albanian population.
The main peoples of the former Yugoslavia are closely related. Their differences are of religion, script and history, not of race.
The South Slav peoples are the Slovenes, Croats, Serbs, Bosniaks, Montenegrins and Macedonians; they are of similar ancestry and largely speak one language.
That language, Serbo-Croatian, is now standardised as Serbian, Croatian, Bosnian and Montenegrin; the groups mostly understand each other.
Serbs use Cyrillic (the alphabet used in Russia) as well as Latin script (the alphabet used in English); Croats use Latin.
The groups differ in religion, script and history, not in race: ethnicity is defined largely by religion.
Not every group in the region is a South Slav. Census figures from Bosnia show how its population mix changed.
Albanians, a non-Slav people, are about nine-tenths of Kosovo’s population, so Kosovo is the main exception to the South Slav pattern.
Hungarians form a minority in Vojvodina, so this autonomous province within Serbia has a non-Slav minority too.
Bosnia’s 1991 census (population about 4.4 million) recorded Muslims (Bosniaks) at about 44%, Serbs at about 31% and Croats at about 17%.
The 2013 census (about 3.5 million) recorded Bosniaks at about 50%, Serbs at about 31% and Croats at about 15%, so the total population was smaller and the Bosniak share larger than in 1991.
Bosniaks were counted as “Muslims” (a nationality) in 1991; the term Bosniak came into general use during the war.
Religion divides the South Slavs more clearly than language does. Religious buildings show both coexistence and conflict.
Catholic Slovenes and Croats, Orthodox Serbs, Montenegrins and Macedonians, and Muslim Bosniaks and most Albanians (many of whom converted under the Ottomans) make up the religious groups.
Sarajevo has a mosque, a Catholic cathedral, an Orthodox cathedral and a synagogue within a short walk of each other; the Gazi Husrev-beg Mosque dates from the 1530s.
The Ferhadija Mosque in Banja Luka (16th century) was blown up by Bosnian Serb forces in 1993 and reopened in 2016 after rebuilding, which shows religious buildings were war targets.
Medjugorje, Bosnia and Herzegovina, has been a Catholic pilgrimage site (a place people travel to for religious reasons) since reported apparitions (visions) in 1981.
When Yugoslavia broke up, the new borders did not match where each group lived, and war followed. The wars in Slovenia and Croatia came first.
Slovenia declared independence on 25 June 1991, and a ten-day war followed.
Croatia declared independence the same day; war from 1991 to 1995 pitted Croatia against Croatian Serb forces backed by the Yugoslav army.
Vukovar was besieged (surrounded and attacked) and destroyed in 1991, which makes it an example of a town ruined by the Croatian war.
In Operation Storm (August 1995) Croatia retook the Krajina (an area held by Croatian Serb forces), and about 200,000 Serbs fled.
Bosnia, where Bosniaks, Serbs and Croats lived mixed together, was at war from 1992 to 1995. Groups were forced out so that areas would become uniform.
The Bosnian war of 1992–95 killed about 100,000 people, and about half the population was forced from their homes.
“Ethnic cleansing” means forcing out other groups to make areas ethnically uniform.
The siege of Sarajevo by Bosnian Serb forces lasted from April 1992 to February 1996, the longest siege of a capital city in modern warfare.
Mostar’s Old Bridge (Stari Most, 1566) was destroyed by Croat forces on 9 November 1993 and rebuilt in 2004; it became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2005.
In July 1995 about 8,000 Bosniak men and boys were killed at Srebrenica by Bosnian Serb forces; international courts ruled this a genocide (the deliberate destruction of a people).
The Dayton Agreement of 1995 ended the war.
The Kosovo war of 1998–99 followed the Bosnian war, and an international court later tried the leaders responsible.
NATO (the Western military alliance) bombed Serbia for 78 days (March–June 1999) during the Kosovo war of 1998–99.
About 800,000 Kosovo Albanians fled or were expelled during the Kosovo war.
The International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia (ICTY), a UN court for war crimes, sat in The Hague from 1993 to 2017.
Milošević died in custody in 2006 before a verdict; Radovan Karadžić and Ratko Mladić were convicted of genocide.
Music and festivals show identity in the Balkans: some come from tradition, and some were created to oppose nationalism or war.
EXIT festival, held at Petrovaradin Fortress in Novi Sad, Serbia, began in 2000 as a student movement against Milošević.
The Guča Trumpet Festival in Serbia is a brass-band festival held since 1961.
The Sarajevo Film Festival was founded in 1995, during the siege, as an act of cultural defiance.
Sevdalinka (sevdah) is a traditional Bosnian love song; the kolo is a circle dance, and the Serbian kolo is on UNESCO’s list (2017).
Sport and popular culture reflected the changing mood, from shared Yugoslav success to open rivalry.
Divers jump from Mostar’s Old Bridge each summer, a tradition linked to the bridge that was rebuilt after its destruction.
On 13 May 1990 fans rioted at the Dinamo Zagreb–Red Star Belgrade match in Zagreb’s Maksimir stadium; the riot is remembered as a sign of the coming war.
Yugoslavia won the Eurovision Song Contest (an international song competition) in 1989 and Serbia won in 2007; Croatia reached the football World Cup final in 2018.
People have left the region for work since the 1960s, and young people are still leaving today.
West Germany signed a guest-worker agreement with Yugoslavia in 1968; many Yugoslavs also went to Austria and Switzerland, from the 1960s.
Large-scale emigration of young people is causing population decline in Serbia, Bosnia and Croatia.
The wars forced people to move, and in 2015 the region became a transit route for refugees from elsewhere.
The 1990s wars displaced large numbers of people within the region and from it, making many areas ethnically uniform.
In 2015 hundreds of thousands of refugees crossed North Macedonia and Serbia on the Western Balkans route (the overland path towards northern Europe).
Hungary built a border fence in 2015 to block the route.
The break-up of Yugoslavia produced a series of new states, each with new boundaries, over about fifteen years.
Slovenia and Croatia became independent in 1991; Macedonia in 1991, renamed North Macedonia in 2019 after an agreement with Greece; and Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1992.
The Federal Republic of Yugoslavia (Serbia and Montenegro) was formed in 1992 and renamed Serbia and Montenegro in 2003; Montenegro became independent in 2006.
Two cases show that the new boundaries are still disputed or divided: Kosovo, which is only partly recognised, and Bosnia, which is split into two parts.
Kosovo declared independence on 17 February 2008; Serbia does not recognise it.
Over 100 states recognise Kosovo, including Ireland, but five EU states (Spain, Greece, Cyprus, Romania and Slovakia) do not.
Under the Dayton Agreement, Bosnia and Herzegovina is divided into the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina and Republika Srpska, with a three-member presidency (Bosniak, Croat and Serb).
Brčko District is a separate self-governing unit since 2000.
The EU offers the region a new kind of boundary: membership of a union with open borders.
Slovenia joined the EU in 2004 and Croatia in 2013; Croatia adopted the euro and joined Schengen (the area with no routine passport checks) in 2023.
Montenegro, Serbia, North Macedonia, Albania and Bosnia and Herzegovina are candidates for EU membership (December 2022).
The Balkans case shows how boundaries and identity can pull against each other. Use these points to close the essay.
Boundaries drawn along the old republic lines left large minorities on the wrong side, so many people lived in a state dominated by another group.
The Dayton structure ended the war but fixed ethnic divisions in place.
EU accession (joining the EU) is a hoped-for softening of borders, which would reduce the importance of the boundaries that divide the region.
The Celtic regions share a history of language survival on the edge of Europe. They split into two branches of Celtic language.
The six Celtic regions usually counted are Ireland, Scotland, the Isle of Man, Wales, Cornwall and Brittany, on Europe’s Atlantic fringe.
The Goidelic languages are Irish, Scottish Gaelic and Manx; the Brythonic languages are Welsh, Cornish and Breton.
Celtic peoples were pushed west by the Romans and the Anglo-Saxons.
Britons migrated from south-west Britain to Armorica (which gave Brittany its name) in the 5th and 6th centuries, as Anglo-Saxons settled eastern Britain.
Peripheral (far from the centre), mountainous or coastal locations helped the languages survive.
Manx’s last native speaker died in 1974, and Cornish’s last traditional speaker died in 1777; both languages have since been revived. There is more on this in Language as a cultural indicator.
Wales has a long-standing border with England, drawn by early earthworks and strengthened by conquest and law.
Offa’s Dyke is an 8th-century earthwork (a bank and ditch) along much of the Wales–England border.
Edward I conquered Wales in 1282–83, and Llywelyn ap Gruffudd, the last native Prince of Wales, was killed in 1282, so Welsh rule by its own princes ended.
Edward I built castles, such as Caernarfon, Conwy, Harlech and Beaumaris, to hold the conquered land; Beaumaris has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1986.
The Laws in Wales Acts of 1535 and 1542 annexed Wales to England; the border with England has remained unchanged since.
Devolution means that a national parliament passes some powers to a regional body. In Wales, the border stayed the same while self-government grew.
In the devolution referendum of 18 September 1997 about 50.3% voted Yes, a very narrow majority.
The National Assembly for Wales opened in 1999, was renamed the Senedd (Welsh Parliament) in 2020, and is enlarged to 96 members from the 2026 election.
Wales has about 3.1 million people (Census 2021); its border with England is unchanged, but its political powers have grown.
The Welsh language is the core of Welsh identity, and its strength varies sharply from place to place.
Census 2021 recorded about 538,000 people (17.8%) who could speak Welsh.
Welsh speaking is highest in Gwynedd (about 64%) and Anglesey (over half), and lowest in the industrial south-east.
The north-west heartland is Y Fro Gymraeg, and the south-east is English-speaking.
Language policy includes the Welsh Language Measure 2011, S4C (the Welsh-language television channel) from 1982 and Cymraeg 2050. There is more on this in Language as a cultural indicator.
Religion in Wales was closely tied to language: Nonconformist chapels, not the Anglican church, were the centre of Welsh life in the 19th century.

The 1851 religious census showed that most worshippers in Wales attended Nonconformist chapels (Protestant churches outside the Church of England: Methodist, Baptist and Independent) rather than the Anglican church.
Chapels were centres of Welsh-language education, singing and community life.
The Church in Wales was disestablished (separated from state support) in 1920, and chapel-going has declined since.
Welsh festivals and music are held in Welsh and keep the language and its traditions alive.
The National Eisteddfod of Wales is a week-long festival of poetry, music and literature held entirely in Welsh, alternating between north and south Wales.
The Gorsedd of Bards holds ceremonies at the Eisteddfod, such as the chairing of the bard (the honouring of the winning poet).
The Urdd Gobaith Cymru (Welsh youth movement, 1922) holds its own Eisteddfod, one of Europe’s largest youth festivals.
Male voice choirs grew in the mining valleys, so they reflect the industrial communities of south Wales, and the harp is a traditional Welsh instrument.
Sport, symbols, an anthem and food all give the Welsh a shared national culture.
The Welsh Rugby Union was founded in 1881; the Principality Stadium in Cardiff opened in 1999 as the Millennium Stadium.
St David’s Day, 1 March, is the national day, so it is the one date when Welsh identity is celebrated nationwide.
The anthem “Hen Wlad Fy Nhadau” (“Land of My Fathers”) was written in 1856.
Symbols include the red dragon (Y Ddraig Goch), the daffodil and the leek.
Foods include cawl (stew), Welsh cakes and bara brith.
Migration has both weakened and spread Welsh culture. Workers came in during industrialisation, Welsh people left for new lands, and today incomers raise tensions in rural areas.
19th-century coal and iron industries drew English and Irish workers into south Wales, spreading English there.
Welsh settlers sailed on the Mimosa in 1865 to found a colony in Chubut, Patagonia, Argentina, where some Welsh is still spoken.
A campaign of arson attacks on English-owned holiday homes, attributed to Meibion Glyndŵr, began in 1979.
English retirees and second-home owners have moved into rural Welsh-speaking areas, while young Welsh speakers have moved out.
From April 2023 Welsh councils may charge up to a 300% council-tax premium on second homes, a response to second-home ownership.
Newer immigrant communities live in Cardiff, so migration continues to make Wales more varied.
Brittany is the second Celtic region. Its link with France led to strong pressure to use French, and the Breton language declined.
Brittany was united with France in 1532.
After the Revolution of 1789 the provinces were abolished and France was governed centrally through departments (the standard units of local government).
French was promoted as the only language of the Republic, and the Breton language declined as a result.
Article 2 of the French Constitution and the Diwan schools from 1977 are part of the language policy. There is more on this in Language as a cultural indicator.
Brittany's boundary is itself disputed, because a wartime decision removed one of its historic cities.
In 1941 the Vichy government (the French government that cooperated with Nazi Germany) separated Loire-Atlantique, including Nantes, the historic seat of the Dukes of Brittany, from the region.
Nantes is outside the official Brittany region, and campaigners still seek its reunification.
The 2016 regional reform left Brittany’s boundary unchanged.
Catholic tradition and a lively music revival define Breton culture today.
Catholic pardons are processions and pilgrimages to local saints.
Bagadoù (pipe bands), the biniou (bagpipe) and the bombarde (oboe) are traditional Breton instruments.
The fest-noz, a night dance festival, is on UNESCO’s list since 2012.
The harpist Alan Stivell led a Breton music revival from the 1970s, so traditional music was brought back to a wide audience.
The Festival Interceltique de Lorient has been held every August since 1971.
Costume, food and a flag give Brittany visible symbols of its separate identity within France.
The tall lace coiffe (headdress) of the Bigouden area is the best-known Breton costume.
Crêpes and galettes (made from buckwheat), and cider, are typical Breton foods.
The Gwenn-ha-Du flag, black and white, was designed in 1923, so it is a modern symbol of Breton identity.
The Celtic regions are linked by shared music and by cooperation to protect their languages.
The Festival Interceltique de Lorient, held in Brittany, brings musicians from the Celtic regions together.
Irish and Welsh cooperation on language, and EU support for minority languages, link the Celtic regions in their efforts to preserve their languages.
Belgium's main division is cultural, not physical. Its history shows how language became tied to power.
Belgium is mostly low and flat, and the language border crosses open country: it is cultural, not physical.
Belgium became independent in 1830 after a revolt that began after a performance of the opera “La Muette de Portici” in Brussels on 25 August 1830.
French was long the language of government, courts, the army and universities, which left Dutch speakers at a disadvantage.
The language border was fixed by laws of 1962 and 1963.
Belgium responded to its language divide by sharing power between regions and communities, a process of federalisation (turning a central state into a federal one).
The first state reform came in 1970, so the move towards federalism began more than twenty years before 1993.
Belgium became a federal state in 1993, with three regions (Flanders, Wallonia and Brussels-Capital) and three communities (Flemish, French and German-speaking).
The language divide is an example of cultural regions (areas defined by a shared language or culture). There is more on this in Cultural regions.
Belgium has two main language groups, the Dutch-speaking Flemings and the French-speaking Walloons, with a bilingual capital between them.
Belgium’s population is about 11.8 million (2024): Flanders about 6.8 million, Wallonia about 3.7 million and Brussels-Capital about 1.2 million.
Dutch speakers are about 6 in 10 and French speakers about 4 in 10; the German-speaking Community in the east, around Eupen, has fewer than 80,000 people.
Brussels lies inside Flanders geographically but is its own region; it is officially bilingual, but mostly French-speaking in practice.
The language divide runs through universities, parties and media, so the two communities live largely separate public lives.
The Catholic University of Leuven split in 1968; its French-speaking section moved to Louvain-la-Neuve in Wallonia.
Belgium has no nationwide parties; parties, media and schools are separate by language.
Belgium went 541 days without a new government in 2010–11, which shows how hard it is to agree between the two sides.
The Flemish nationalist N-VA has been the largest party since 2010; its leader, Bart De Wever, became Prime Minister in February 2025.
Unlike in many divided regions, religion in Belgium did not add to the language divide.
Belgium is traditionally Catholic in both Flanders and Wallonia, so religion did not reinforce the language divide.
Historic conflicts between Catholics and liberals were fought over schools; secularisation (the decline of religion in public life) has since reduced religious practice.
Islam grew through Moroccan and Turkish migration.
Belgian culture includes famous Flemish art, a comic-strip tradition and festivals, and some events express the identity of one language community.
The Ghent Altarpiece by Jan van Eyck was completed in 1432 and is in St Bavo’s Cathedral, Ghent.
Pieter Bruegel the Elder and Peter Paul Rubens (Antwerp) are Flemish painters, so Flanders has the older tradition of famous art, such as van Eyck's altarpiece.
Hergé (Georges Remi) created Tintin in 1929, so Belgium has a strong comic-strip tradition.
The Carnival of Binche in Wallonia features the Gilles in costumes and wax masks; UNESCO proclaimed it in 2003.
Tomorrowland, an electronic music festival in Boom (Flanders), has been held since 2005.
11 July is the Flemish Community holiday, marking the Battle of the Golden Spurs (1302), when Flemish militias defeated French knights.
Food and drink are shared symbols of Belgium that both language groups claim.
Belgian beer culture was added to UNESCO’s list in 2016, so it is recognised as heritage worth protecting.
Chocolate, frites and waffles are national symbols.
Labour migration from southern Europe, Morocco and Turkey made Belgium, and especially Brussels, ethnically diverse.
A 1946 agreement with Italy sent Italian workers to Belgian coal mines in exchange for coal.
The Marcinelle mining disaster on 8 August 1956 killed 262 miners, 136 of them Italian, so it shows how much of the dangerous mine work migrants did.
Labour agreements with Morocco and Turkey were made in 1964.
Brussels hosts the main EU institutions and NATO’s headquarters, so it is one of Europe’s most international cities.
On 22 March 2016 Islamic State suicide bombings at Brussels Airport and Maalbeek metro station killed 32 people, which exposed tensions around migration and security.
Money and power moved from Wallonia to Flanders, and this fed the Flemish demand for more self-rule.
Wallonia’s coal and steel industry, in Liège, Charleroi and the Sambre–Meuse valley, declined.
Flanders grew through the port of Antwerp, Europe’s second-largest port, and modern industry, so its economy became the stronger of the two.
This reversed the historic balance of wealth and power between the two regions, feeding Flemish nationalism.
Belgium's internal boundaries are the ones that shape identity today, and they are still debated.
The language border, the federal regions and Brussels’ position as an enclave (an area surrounded by another region) are the boundaries that shape identity today.
Debate continues over further devolution or separation. There is more on the present-day politics in The complexity of regions (i), and on the boundary changes in The complexity of regions (ii).

Soil is the thin layer of loose material on the earth's surface in which plants grow. Its formation is called pedogenesis, and it starts with the rock or deposit the soil forms from, known as the parent material.
Soil is made of four components: mineral matter (particles of weathered rock), organic matter (living and dead material), water and air. Every later block looks at how one of these shapes the soil.
Residual soils form from rock weathered in situ, meaning in place, directly beneath them, so the soil and the rock below are closely related.
Transported soils form on redeposited weathered material that has been carried and laid down by ice, water, wind or volcanic activity, so they can differ from the rock beneath.

Transported parent materials include glacial till (boulder clay), fluvio-glacial sands and gravels (laid down by meltwater from ice), alluvium (river deposits), loess (wind-blown silt), wind-blown sand and volcanic ash.

Weathering (the breakdown of rock at the surface) produces regolith, the loose layer that soil develops from. Freeze-thaw, carbonation and hydrolysis are among the processes involved. There is more on this in Weathering processes, in Rocks, Weathering and Mass Movement.
Named places make the residual and transported types concrete. Remember that the same area can look residual on a map of rock types but be transported in fact.

Residual examples: the limestone of the Burren and the granite of the Wicklow Mountains, which gives acidic, sandy soils. Most Midland soils formed on boulder clay over the limestone, so they are transported, not residual.
Transported examples: the boulder clay (till) plains of the Irish Midlands, and alluvium on the floodplain of the Shannon Callows, meadows beside the River Shannon that flood in winter.
Loess (wind-blown silt), called limon in France, covers plateaux of the Paris Basin, such as the Beauce. There is more on this in A Core European Region: the Paris Basin.
Soils take time to develop, and in Ireland the clock was reset by the ice. This is why Irish soils are young and why they often do not match the rock beneath.

Most Irish soils formed on glacial deposits laid down during the last (Midlandian) glaciation, which ended about 10,000 years ago. There is more on this in Glacial processes, patterns and associated landforms.
So most Irish soils have developed in about 10,000 years or less, since the ice melted, and they often differ from the solid rock beneath them because the glacial deposits came from elsewhere.
A soil profile is a vertical section from the surface down to bedrock, divided into layers called horizons. A soil pit or road cutting shows it, and the horizons are named by letters.
O horizon: organic litter (undecomposed plant and animal remains) and humus (the dark, decomposed organic material) on the surface.
A horizon: topsoil, with mineral matter mixed with humus.
B horizon: subsoil, which receives material washed down from above.
C horizon: weathered parent material, the rock or deposit the soil forms from.
R horizon: bedrock, the solid rock beneath.
There is more on the full profiles of named soils in Soil processes and the global pattern of soils.
Soil is mostly mineral matter, with small shares of organic matter, water and air. The figures below are the textbook values for a good loam, a balanced, fertile soil.
A typical good loam has about 45% mineral matter, 5% organic matter, 25% water and 25% air, by volume.
These proportions describe a well-structured loam. They are not fixed values for every soil, so don't present them as true of all soils.
Water and air share the pore spaces (the gaps between particles), so when one rises the other falls. A wet soil is poorly aerated for this reason.
Diagram: a pie chart of the four components.
Mineral matter is the largest component, and the parent rock decides what kind of mineral matter a soil gets. It is the first of the four components to know for an essay on soil development.
Mineral matter is particles of weathered rock, from stones down to clay. It forms the soil's skeleton and decides its texture (the mix of particle sizes).
As it weathers, mineral matter releases nutrients such as calcium, magnesium and potassium, which plants then take up through their roots.
Parent rock controls the result: limestone gives base-rich, less acidic soils (bases are the chemicals that neutralise acid).
Granite gives sandy, acidic soils with quartz grains and clay from weathered feldspar.
Sandstone gives sandy, acidic, free-draining soils.
Clay particles are the chemically active part of the mineral matter, because they hold on to nutrients and water.
Organic matter is a small share of the soil by volume, but it gives soil its dark colour, its crumbly structure and much of its fertility. The key is the difference between litter and humus.
Organic matter is living organisms (bacteria, fungi, earthworms, insects and roots) plus dead plant and animal remains.
Litter is undecomposed material. Decomposers (organisms that feed on dead material) break it down into humus, a dark, sticky, jelly-like substance, which is the end product of decomposition.
Humus darkens the soil, binds particles into crumbs, holds water and nutrients, releases nutrients slowly, and is the main store of nitrogen in the soil.
Earthworms mix and aerate the soil, drag litter down into it, and their casts (droppings) improve structure.
Charles Darwin's last book (1881), The Formation of Vegetable Mould through the Action of Worms, showed how earthworms mix and enrich soil.

Nitrogen-fixing bacteria (bacteria that turn nitrogen from the air into a form plants can use), such as those in the root nodules of legumes, add nitrogen. Clover is the standard example of a legume in Irish grassland.
Humus comes in different forms depending on the vegetation above and the organisms below. The forms are named mull, moder and mor, and each is linked to a soil type.
Mull humus is mild, crumbly, well decomposed and well mixed by earthworms. It is slightly acidic to neutral and forms under deciduous woodland and grassland, giving brown earths.
Mor humus is acidic, fibrous and poorly decomposed, with few earthworms because the acidity does not suit them. It forms under coniferous forest and heath, giving podzols.
Moder is intermediate between mull and mor.
Water enters the soil as precipitation and is held in its pores. It exists in three forms, and only some of it is any use to plants.
Water dissolves nutrients to form the soil solution, from which roots absorb them.
Gravitational water drains down through large pores after rain and carries nutrients away. This is the cause of leaching (the washing of nutrients down out of the soil).
Capillary water is held in small pores by surface tension. It is available to plants and can move up as well as down.
Hygroscopic water is a thin film bound tightly to particles, so plants cannot use it.
Field capacity is the water a soil holds after gravitational water has drained away.
Wilting point is reached when only water that plants cannot extract is left, so the plants wilt.
Which way water moves depends on whether rain or evaporation wins. This decides what the soil loses or collects, and it leads into the soil processes.
Where precipitation exceeds evapotranspiration (water lost by evaporation and plant transpiration), water moves down and leaches the soil. This is the situation in Ireland.
Where evaporation exceeds precipitation, capillary action raises water to the surface and leaves salts and lime there, as in deserts and grasslands.

Too much water fills all the pores and causes waterlogging, which leads to gleying (the grey, rusty-mottled soil of waterlogged ground). There is more on this in Soil processes and the global pattern of soils.
Air fills whatever pore space water does not. Living things in the soil need it, and whether it is plentiful or scarce changes how the soil forms.
Air fills the pores not occupied by water.
Soil air supplies oxygen for root respiration and for the aerobic organisms (those that need oxygen) that decompose litter, and nitrogen for nitrogen-fixing bacteria.
Soil air is richer in carbon dioxide than the atmosphere. This forms weak carbonic acid in soil water, which aids chemical weathering.
Poorly aerated (anaerobic, meaning without oxygen) soils decompose slowly, so organic matter builds up as peat.
In poorly aerated soils iron is reduced (it gains electrons and changes chemical form), giving grey colours.
The four components do not act separately: each changes how the others behave. Showing this interaction is part of a full answer on soil development.
Humus improves crumb structure, which opens pores for both air and water.
Clay holds water but reduces air, because its tiny pores fill with water and leave little room for air.
Organisms need both air and water to work, so a soil that is too wet or too dry supports less life and less decomposition.
Texture is the proportion of sand, silt and clay in a soil. It is set by the size of the mineral particles, so it is one of the most basic characteristics of a soil.

Sand has particles 2 to 0.05 mm across; silt 0.05 to 0.002 mm; clay under 0.002 mm. Particles over 2 mm are gravel or stones. Some textbooks put the sand and silt limit at 0.06 mm, which is also acceptable.
Clay is the smallest particle and sand the largest.
Field test by feel: sand is gritty, silt is smooth and silky, and clay is sticky and can be rolled into a ribbon when moist.
Texture is shown on a soil texture triangle, a triangular graph. There is more on this method in Figure interpretation, in Tables, Graphs and Data Skills.
Particle size decides how water, air and nutrients move through a soil and how easy it is to farm. Each texture has strengths and weaknesses, and loam balances them.
Sandy soils are light, free-draining, well aerated, warm quickly in spring and are easy to plough. They hold little water and few nutrients, and they are easily leached.
Clay soils are heavy and hold water and nutrients. They drain slowly, become waterlogged and cold, crack and harden when dry, and are hard to work.
A loam is a balanced mix, roughly 40% sand, 40% silt and 20% clay. It combines good drainage with good water and nutrient retention, and is the best for farming.
Silty soils are fertile but form a surface crust and erode easily.
Structure is the way particles are grouped into clumps called peds. Two soils with the same texture can behave very differently if their peds differ.
Crumb: small rounded peds, typical of humus-rich topsoil, and the best structure for farming.
Granular: a further type of ped structure.
Platy: flat, horizontal plates that hinder drainage and root growth.
Blocky: angular cubes, common in clay subsoils.
Prismatic or columnar: vertical columns, found in some clay subsoils.
Structureless soils are single-grain (loose sand) or massive (solid clay), because their particles are not grouped into peds.
Structure matters because it sets the pore spaces that water, air and roots use. It can be built up by natural agents and destroyed by pressure.
Structure controls the size and number of pores, so it decides drainage, aeration and how easily roots penetrate.
Humus, clay, earthworms, roots and freeze-thaw build peds.
Compaction (squashing the soil together) by heavy machinery, and trampling by livestock on wet ground (called poaching in Ireland), destroy peds and so close up the pores.
Colour is a clue to a soil's composition and conditions, so reading it tells you what the soil contains and how well drained it is. Each colour below is linked to a cause and a named soil type.
Black or dark brown: rich in humus, as in chernozems and peat.
Brown: humus plus iron compounds, as in brown earths.
Red, orange or yellow: iron oxides in a well-aerated soil, as in tropical latosols and terra rossa.
Ash-grey or bleached: heavily leached (washed of its nutrients and colouring), as in the E horizon of a podzol.
Grey or blue-grey with orange (rusty) mottles: waterlogged, with reduced iron, as in gley.
White: lime or salt crusts, as in desert soils.
Dark soils absorb more heat, so colour also affects soil temperature.
How much water a soil can hold, and how fast it passes through, depends on its other characteristics. Two similar-sounding terms, porosity and permeability, must be kept apart.
Water retention depends on texture (clay retains water, sand drains), structure and organic content. Humus holds several times its own weight of water.
Porosity is how much pore space a soil has. Permeability is how easily water passes through it.
Clay soils have high porosity but low permeability, because their pores are tiny, so they drain slowly.
Organic content is the amount of humus in a soil. It varies a lot between soil types and affects several other characteristics.
It is high in chernozems and peat, moderate in brown earths, and low in desert soils, which have little vegetation.
Tropical latosols are surprisingly low in humus, because litter decays so fast that little humus builds up.
Organic content affects colour, structure, water retention and fertility.
pH tells you how acidic or alkaline a soil is, which affects which organisms and crops can live in it. It is shaped by climate, parent rock and vegetation.
pH is the measure of acidity or alkalinity, on a scale of 0 to 14, with 7 neutral.
Soils become acidic where heavy rain leaches out bases, and where acid litter such as conifer needles or heather builds up.
Soils are alkaline on limestone and chalk and in dry climates.
Most crops and earthworms prefer slightly acidic to neutral soils.
Teagasc, the Irish agriculture and food development authority, advises a soil pH of about 6.3 for grassland and about 6.5 for tillage crops. Liming corrects lower values.
Farmers spread lime, which is ground limestone, to raise pH.
A fertile soil holds nutrients in a form that roots can reach and rain cannot wash away. This depends on tiny charged particles in the clay and humus.

Clay particles and humus form the clay-humus complex. Its tiny, negatively charged particles, called colloids, hold positively charged nutrient ions (charged atoms) such as calcium, magnesium and potassium.
Held nutrients are not washed away, and they are exchanged with roots, so plants can take them up.
Base-rich soils are fertile; base-poor, leached soils are not.
NPK (nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium) are the main nutrients farmers add.
The characteristics above work together to decide which soil processes dominate and which soil forms. Each link below is one step of the argument an essay needs.
Texture and structure control drainage, so they decide whether leaching, gleying or capillary rise dominates.
pH controls which organisms live in the soil, so it decides whether mull or mor humus forms and how fast humification (the breakdown of litter into humus) happens.
Organic content controls structure and fertility, so it decides how well the soil supports the vegetation that feeds it.
Water retention and aeration together decide whether decomposition is aerobic, as in fertile brown soils, or anaerobic, as in peat and gley.
Use brown earth, podzol, gley, latosol and chernozem as illustrations by name.
A soil is shaped by its surroundings, so five factors decide what it becomes. The first three are the rock it forms from, the climate above it and how long it has had to develop.

Parent material (the rock or loose deposit the soil forms from) supplies the mineral matter and sets the texture, the base content (the supply of nutrient bases such as calcium) and the starting pH (acidity). There is more on this in Soil composition and characteristics.
Climate is the most important factor at a global scale, because it controls both how fast rock breaks down and which plants grow.
Temperature controls the speed of weathering (the breakdown of rock) and of decomposition (the rotting of dead plant matter). Warmth speeds both, while cold slows both.

The balance of precipitation and evapotranspiration (water lost from the soil by evaporation and from plants by transpiration) decides whether water moves down through the soil (leaching) or up (capillary rise, water drawn up through tiny pores). This is why soil belts follow climate belts.
Time: a mature soil has had long enough to develop distinct horizons (layers), while an immature soil has thin or missing horizons.
The shape of the land and the living things on it also change a soil. Relief (the height and slope of the ground) decides where water and material end up, and organisms add or mix the organic matter.
Steep slopes have thin, well-drained soils, because material moves downslope.
Hollows and valley floors collect water and have deep, wet soils.
A catena is the sequence of soils down a slope developed from the same parent material, so the differences between them come from slope and drainage.

Altitude brings cooler, wetter conditions, which mean more leaching (washing of nutrients down through the soil) and more peat. Aspect (the direction a slope faces) affects soil temperature and moisture.

Vegetation supplies litter (fallen leaves and plant debris) and decides humus type (humus is the dark, decomposed organic matter in soil): deciduous woodland gives mull, a mild, well-mixed humus, while coniferous forest and heath give mor, an acid humus that builds up in a layer.
Roots bind soil and recycle nutrients, and animals mix the soil. For example, earthworms mix the soil as they burrow.
Humans change soils. There is more on this in Human interference with soils.
If you dig a pit, a soil shows distinct layers called horizons. Together they make the soil profile, and each is named by a letter.
O horizon: litter and humus, which may be split into L, F and H layers. It sits at the top because it is made of fallen plant matter.
A horizon: dark topsoil, with humus mixed with minerals. It is dark because of the humus.
E horizon: eluvial (material has been washed out of it), a pale, washed-out layer found in leached soils such as podzols, because leaching has stripped its colour.
B horizon: illuvial (material has been washed into it) subsoil, where washed-down iron, aluminium, clay or humus accumulate.
C horizon: weathered parent material. R horizon: bedrock. The C horizon sits below the B horizon, so it is the least altered layer.
Eluviation is the washing out of material from an upper horizon. Illuviation is its deposition in a lower one. This is why a leached soil has a pale E horizon above a richer B horizon.
Diagram: a labelled soil profile showing depth and horizon letters.
Weathering is the breakdown of rock where it lies, and it is the first step in making soil. How fast it works sets how deep a soil can get.
Physical and chemical weathering break parent material down into mineral particles and release nutrients. This is why weathering is the first step in making soil.
Hydrolysis (a reaction between minerals and water) forms clay, and oxidation (a reaction with oxygen) gives red and brown colours.
The rate of weathering sets soil depth. Soils are deep in the hot, wet tropics, where chemical weathering is fastest, and thin in cold or dry regions.
There is more on the processes themselves in Weathering processes, in Rocks, Weathering and Mass Movement.
Soil can be lost as well as made. Erosion removes it, and the loss changes the characteristics of what remains.
Soil erosion is the removal of soil, especially topsoil, faster than it forms.

Erosion by water takes the forms of rain-splash (raindrops knocking soil particles loose), sheet wash (a thin sheet of water carrying soil away), and rills and gullies (small and large channels cut into the soil).
Erosion by wind is deflation of dry, loose, bare soil, which means the wind lifts the particles away.
Natural geological erosion is slow and balanced by soil formation. Accelerated erosion follows the removal of vegetation, which no longer protects the soil.
Erosion thins the profile, removes the humus-rich A horizon and its nutrients, and exposes infertile subsoil.
It also worsens structure (how the particles clump together) and water retention. The eroded material is redeposited elsewhere, as alluvium (river-laid deposits) or loess (fine wind-blown silt).
There is more on human causes and responses in Human interference with soils.
Where rain is heavy, water carries nutrients out of the upper soil. This washing is leaching, and it makes soil more acid and less fertile.

Leaching happens where precipitation exceeds evapotranspiration, so there is surplus water. Gravitational water (water pulled down by gravity) moves down through the soil. For example, it is common where rainfall is heavy.
The water dissolves soluble minerals and nutrient bases (calcium, magnesium, potassium and sodium) and carries them to lower horizons or into groundwater.
The upper soil becomes more acidic and less fertile, and material may be redeposited in the B horizon.
Leaching is common in Ireland's wet climate. Mild leaching gives brown earths, and intense leaching gives podzols.
Humification is the making of humus, the dark organic part of soil. It depends on how quickly the organisms that rot litter can work.
Humification is the decomposition of litter by bacteria, fungi and soil animals into humus. It has nothing to do with humidity. The nutrients in dead matter are locked up until it is broken down.
It is fast in warm, moist, well-aerated, base-rich conditions, which produce mull.
It is slow in cold, acid or waterlogged conditions, where partly decomposed matter builds up as mor or peat.
It releases nutrients for plants, as part of the nutrient cycle (the repeated passing of nutrients between soil and living things).
Podzolisation is an intense form of leaching that produces the podzol. It strips iron and aluminium from the upper soil and deposits them lower down.
Conditions: a cool, wet climate where precipitation is well above evapotranspiration; acid parent material such as granite or sandstone; coniferous forest or heath vegetation giving acid mor humus.
1. Acid litter releases organic acids into percolating water (water seeping down through the soil).
2. The acids combine with iron and aluminium (chelation, or cheluviation) and carry them down, along with bases and humus.
3. The A/E horizon is left as a bleached, ash-grey, sandy layer of quartz, because the coloured minerals have been removed.
4. Iron, aluminium and humus are deposited in the B horizon, which turns dark reddish-brown.
5. A thin, hard iron pan (a cemented layer) may form in the B horizon. It blocks drainage and roots, so water lies above it and peat may form on top.
Result: the podzol, which is acidic and infertile, with sharply defined horizons. It is infertile because bases and nutrients have been washed out of the upper soil.
Laterisation occurs in hot, wet tropical climates. Intense weathering and leaching remove silica and leave a soil rich in iron and aluminium.
1. High temperatures and heavy rain cause intense chemical weathering to great depth.
2. Silica and bases are leached out, since silica is soluble in warm water under these conditions.
3. Insoluble iron and aluminium oxides (sesquioxides) are left behind and concentrated, giving a deep red or yellow colour.
4. Litter decomposes so quickly that little humus accumulates.

5. Where the forest is removed and the soil dries out, the iron-rich layer can harden into a brick-like crust called laterite. A laterite crust forms only when the soil is exposed and dries out, not under intact forest.
Extreme laterisation of aluminium-rich rock forms bauxite, the ore of aluminium (the rock aluminium is extracted from).
Bauxite is mined from laterised rock in tropical countries such as Guinea, Jamaica and Australia (north Queensland).
Result: latosols (oxisols). It is infertile because the silica and bases have been leached away.

Calcification occurs in dry continental climates where evapotranspiration roughly equals or exceeds precipitation, as in temperate grasslands and semi-arid areas. Little water moves down, so calcium stays in the soil.
1. Rain penetrates only part of the way down, so leaching is weak.
2. Calcium carbonate is dissolved and carried a short distance down, then deposited in the B horizon as nodules (small lumps) or a lime-rich layer.
3. In dry periods, capillary action draws water and calcium back up.
4. Deep grass roots take up calcium and return it to the surface in litter.
Result: an alkaline or neutral, base-rich, fertile soil with a thick, humus-rich A horizon, the chernozem. It is fertile because calcium and humus stay in the topsoil.
Gleying happens when a soil is saturated with water and has no air. The lack of oxygen changes the colour and behaviour of the iron in it.

Gleying happens in waterlogged soils: heavy clay, impermeable till (boulder clay that water cannot pass through), a high water table (the level below which the ground is saturated), hollows, or soils above an iron pan.
Pores fill with water, air is excluded, and conditions become anaerobic (without oxygen).
Bacteria reduce iron from its red ferric form to its grey or blue-grey ferrous form, which is why the soil turns grey.
Where air enters along roots or cracks, iron is re-oxidised and forms orange or rusty mottles (patches).
Result: a gley soil, which is grey, mottled, sticky and cold, slow to warm, and slow to decompose.
In hot, dry areas, water moves up through the soil rather than down, and it leaves salts behind.
In hot, dry areas, evaporation draws water up by capillary action and leaves soluble salts at or near the surface, sometimes as a white crust.
Poor irrigation (watering land artificially) makes salinisation worse. There is more on this in Human interference with soils.
Salt crusts link this process to desert soils. This is why desert soils often carry a white crust of salt.
Soils are classified by how much of their character comes from climate, from a local factor, or from lack of time.
Zonal soils are mature soils whose character is set by climate and vegetation, so they form broad belts matching the world's climate and biome (major plant and animal community) belts.
Intrazonal soils are dominated by one local factor, such as drainage (gley, peat) or parent material (rendzina, a thin lime-rich soil on limestone).

Azonal soils are immature, with poorly developed horizons. Examples are alluvium, scree, sand dunes, fresh volcanic ash and recent glacial deposits. They are immature because they have had too little time to develop.
Because climate and vegetation set zonal soils, the world's soils form belts. Going from the poles to the equator, each belt has its own soil.
Tundra soils are thin and gleyed, with permafrost (permanently frozen ground) below.
Podzols lie in the boreal (taiga) coniferous forest belt of northern Canada, Scandinavia, Finland and Siberia (Russia).
Brown earths lie under temperate deciduous forest in Ireland, Britain, much of western and central Europe (e.g. France and Germany), and the eastern USA.
Chernozems and chestnut soils lie under temperate grassland. Chestnut soils form on the drier margins of the grasslands.
Red Mediterranean soils, called terra rossa, form on limestone in Mediterranean lands, e.g. southern Italy. There is more on this in A Peripheral European Region: the Mezzogiorno.
Aridisols, or desert soils, lie in the hot desert belt, including the Sahara, Arabian, Australian and south-western USA deserts.
Latosols lie under the tropical rainforest of the Amazon Basin, the Congo Basin and South-East Asia (e.g. Indonesia, Malaysia).
Diagram: a world map of soil belts, or a pole-to-equator transect (a line of sections across the belts).
Climate changes with height, so soils on a mountain change in the same way as they do across the world.
Soils change with altitude as climate does, a pattern called vertical zonation. Upslope they become thinner, more leached and peatier. This is because altitude brings cooler, wetter conditions.
Ireland's soils follow relief and drainage. Lowlands, uplands, wet clay and limestone each have their own soil.
Brown earths and grey-brown podzolics dominate the lowlands. Mild leaching under woodland gives brown earths.
Podzols and peaty podzols occur on the uplands.
Gleys are found on poorly drained clay till, especially in the drumlin belt. Water cannot drain through the clay, so the soil is gleyed.

Peatland covers about a fifth of Ireland's land area. Peat is intrazonal: blanket bog lies in the west and on mountains, such as Co. Mayo and Connemara, and raised bog lies in the Midlands, such as Co. Offaly.
Thin rendzinas, which are dark and lime-rich, occur on the limestone of the Burren.
Brown earth is the default choice for an Irish soil. It forms under mild leaching beneath woodland.
Brown earth is Ireland's main lowland soil, and the most widespread soil of the Irish lowlands, especially in the south, east and Midlands.
Fertile grassland and tillage (crop-growing) soils of the Golden Vale (Co. Tipperary and Co. Limerick) and the south-east are brown earths. The soil is fertile, which is why it suits farming.
Grey-brown podzolics, which are slightly more leached relatives with clay washed into the B horizon, are typical of the limestone-rich till of the east Midlands, e.g. Co. Meath and Co. Kildare.

It formed under Ireland's mild, wet, cool temperate oceanic climate and the deciduous woodland of oak, ash, elm and hazel that covered most of Ireland after the Ice Age. There is more on the climate in Physical regions.
Annual rainfall is roughly 750 to 1,000 mm in the east and over 1,200 mm in much of the west.
Parent material is usually glacial till, and the soil is slightly acidic, at roughly pH 5.5 to 6.5.
Processes: mild leaching carries some iron and clay down, and mull humus is mixed into the soil by earthworms.
The brown earth profile is mixed by earthworms, so it has no bleached layer. That makes it fertile and easy to farm.
O: a thin mull humus layer.
A: dark brown, loamy, with crumb structure (small, rounded crumbs), roughly 20 to 30 cm deep.
B: lighter brown, with some iron and clay washed in. The boundary with A is gradual because earthworms mix the soil.
There is no bleached E horizon, because earthworms mix the soil. Depths are rough illustrative values only.
Characteristics: loamy texture, crumb structure, slightly acidic and fertile, because mull humus and earthworm mixing keep nutrients in the topsoil.
Uses: grassland and tillage in the Golden Vale and the south-east, because the soil is fertile.
Improvement: lime is applied where pH falls below the Teagasc targets. There is more on this in Fertility and nutrients, in Soil composition and characteristics.
Podzols are the soil of Irish uplands. Cool, wet, acid conditions there drive intense leaching.
Podzols occur on Irish uplands such as the Wicklow Mountains, which are granite, and on other mountains with heather moorland and high rainfall.
Many lie under conifer plantations, notably Sitka spruce, whose needle litter feeds the acid mor humus.
Many Irish upland podzols are peaty podzols, with a peaty O horizon above an iron pan.
Formation follows the podzolisation steps given earlier, under acid mor humus from heather or conifers in a cool, wet climate.
The podzol profile shows the effect of leaching clearly. A bleached layer sits above a dark, enriched layer, so the horizons are sharply defined.
A/E: ash-grey, bleached sand. It is bleached because iron and humus have been washed out.
B: reddish-brown, enriched with iron and humus. It is reddish-brown because the iron is deposited here.
Characteristics: strongly acidic, at about pH 4 to 4.5. Acid mor humus and leached bases cause this.
Uses: rough grazing for sheep, and forestry, because the soil is too acid and infertile for crops.
Improvement: deep ploughing to break the iron pan, heavy liming and fertiliser.
Gleys are the wet soils of Ireland. They form where water cannot drain away.
Gleys occur in the drumlin belt of Co. Cavan, Co. Monaghan and Co. Leitrim, on impermeable boulder clay in the wet hollows between drumlins.
Heavy clay soils of the north Midlands and Co. Clare are also gleys, because the clay holds water.
Formation follows the gleying steps given earlier: waterlogging, reduction of iron, and grey, mottled colours.
Water sits in a gley for much of the year, which decides how the land can be farmed.
Profile: a waterlogged upper layer that is grey or blue-grey with orange mottles, sitting on impermeable clay.
Characteristics: wet, sticky and cold, with a short grazing season because wet ground is easily poached (trampled into mud by animals).
Improvement: field drains and arterial drainage (large-scale drainage of rivers and channels). There is more on this in Human interference with soils.
The latosol is the tropical red soil. It is a choice for the continental soil in an essay.
Latosols form under the tropical rainforest of the Amazon Basin, the Congo Basin and South-East Asia (e.g. Indonesia, Malaysia).
The climate is hot, about 27 °C all year round, with over 2,000 mm of rain. There is more on this in One major biome in detail.
Formation is laterisation, as given earlier.
Latosols look rich because of the lush forest above them, but they are infertile. The nutrients are in the living plants, not the soil.
Latosols are deep, often many metres, much deeper than Irish soils. This is because chemical weathering is fastest in the hot, wet tropics.
Profile: a thin O layer; a thin, leached A horizon; a very deep red B horizon of sesquioxides; deep weathered rock below (C).
They are red or yellow from iron and aluminium oxides, clay-rich, acidic, and have very little humus. They have little humus because litter decomposes so quickly.
They are low in nutrients. Nearly all nutrients are held in the living vegetation and recycled quickly from the thin litter layer.
Shifting cultivation (slash and burn) traditionally used the soil for a few years before moving on.

When the forest is cleared, the soil loses fertility within a few years, erodes under heavy rain, and can bake into laterite crust. Without the forest, nothing recycles the nutrients or shields the soil from rain.
The chernozem is the soil of the temperate grasslands. Its climate and grass cover explain why it is so fertile.
Chernozem is the Russian name for black earth.
It lies on the steppes of Ukraine and southern Russia, the Prairies of North America (the Great Plains of the USA and Canada), and the Pampas of Argentina.
The climate is continental, with hot summers, very cold winters and low rainfall of roughly 250 to 500 mm a year, mostly in late spring and summer.
The natural grassland of steppe or prairie has dense, deep roots that die back each year, supplying large amounts of organic matter. This is why the soil is so rich in humus.
Calcification, along with burrowing animals, builds a deep black soil with a lime-rich layer below.
Snow melt in spring gives a short burst of downward water movement. Calcium is moved within the soil as in calcification.
Burrowing animals mix the soil: ground squirrels, called susliks in the steppe, and prairie dogs in North America.
Their filled-in burrows show as darker patches called krotovinas.
A: very thick, black, humus-rich topsoil, commonly about 1 m deep, with crumb structure. It is black and thick because of the humus from the grass roots.
B: calcium-rich, with white lime nodules. It is calcium-rich because calcification deposits dissolved calcium carbonate there.
C: loess, fine wind-blown silt, in much of the steppe and prairie.
The chernozem is among the most fertile soils on earth, so it supports intensive farming.
Neutral to slightly alkaline, and very fertile. It is fertile because of its humus and calcium.
Uses: some of the world's main wheat and maize lands, with sunflowers in Ukraine. They suit these crops because the soil is fertile.
Ukraine has been called the breadbasket of Europe.
Ploughing the prairie soils for wheat, followed by drought in the 1930s, caused the Dust Bowl. There is more on this in Human interaction: mass movement, in Rocks, Weathering and Mass Movement.
Two other soils are valid choices for the continental soil. Each has its own full treatment elsewhere.
India's black soil, or regur, of the Deccan is formed from Deccan Traps basalt. It is clay-rich, so it holds moisture, cracks when dry, and is used for cotton. There is more on this in India.
The aridisol of the hot desert is another valid choice. There is more on this in One major biome in detail.
Soil is the thin layer on which almost all land plants and farming depend. People can protect it or damage it, and the damage is hard to undo.
Soil forms very slowly but can be lost quickly, so on a human timescale it is a non-renewable resource: once it is gone, it will not be replaced within our lifetimes.
The Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO, the UN food agency) has stated that it can take up to 1,000 years to form 1 cm of soil. This was quoted for the International Year of Soils, 2015.
Human activity can degrade soil, which is a negative impact, or conserve and improve it, which is a positive impact.
Overcropping happens when farmers take more from the soil than they give back. It changes the soil's characteristics (its nutrients, humus, structure and water-holding ability) in a series of steps.

Overcropping is growing crops on the same land too intensively, without fallow (leaving land unplanted to recover), rotation (changing the crop each year) or enough organic matter returned, so the soil is exhausted.
Nutrients are removed faster than they are replaced, so humus content (the dark, decayed organic matter in soil) falls and crumb structure (the small stable clumps of soil particles) breaks down.
The soil becomes dusty or compacted, holds less water, and is easily eroded by wind and rain, so yields fall.
Monoculture, one crop grown year after year, takes the same nutrients each time and encourages pests.
In the Sahel, cash crops (crops grown for sale) and shorter fallow periods exhaust soils.
The Dust Bowl shows how ploughing up natural vegetation, followed by drought, can strip away a whole region's soil.
Place and time: the Great Plains of the USA, including Oklahoma and Kansas, in the 1930s.
The natural grassland was ploughed up for wheat, which removed the roots that had held the soil together.
Severe drought then left bare, dry soil that strong winds blew away in huge dust storms. Many farming families were forced to leave.
The prairie soils are chernozems (deep, dark, fertile grassland soils).
Response: the US Soil Conservation Service was set up in 1935. Shelter belts of trees, contour ploughing and crop rotation were promoted.
Overgrazing damages soil by removing the plant cover that protects it. Animals add a second problem by trampling the ground.
Overgrazing is keeping more animals on land than its vegetation can support, which exceeds its carrying capacity (the number of animals the land can feed in the long term).
Vegetation is eaten down and roots die, so the soil is exposed to rain-splash (the impact of raindrops that knocks soil particles loose) and wind.
Trampling compacts the soil. On wet Irish ground this is called poaching. It reduces infiltration (water soaking in) and increases runoff (water flowing over the surface).
Sheet, rill and gully erosion (washing away of a thin layer, then small channels, then deep channels) remove topsoil and humus. Less litter (fallen leaves and plant remains) means less humus.
On peat, bare surfaces erode quickly, because loose, light peat is easily washed and blown away.
International examples: in the Sahel, livestock concentrated around wells, and in Iceland, sheep grazing prevented birch regrowth.
A change in farm payments, not a change in the land, caused overgrazing of Irish hills. Commonage is hill land that farmers use together for grazing.
From the 1980s, EU (CAP) headage payments paid farmers per animal, so sheep numbers rose sharply on hill commonage in the west of Ireland.
The affected areas include Connemara, Co. Galway, and the mountains of Co. Mayo, Co. Donegal and Co. Kerry.
Overgrazing stripped heather and grass, exposed and eroded blanket peat (a thick peat layer covering hills), and sent silt into rivers.
The silt harmed salmon and trout spawning grounds, because it smothers the gravel where the fish lay eggs.
Response: payments changed from per-head to per-area. Commonage Framework Plans, from the early 2000s, set lower stocking rates (fewer animals per hectare).
Response: REPS, the Rural Environment Protection Scheme introduced in 1994, paid farmers to farm in environmentally friendly ways.
Desertification is often misunderstood. It is about land losing its productive soil, and it has both natural and human causes that usually work together.
Desertification is land degradation in arid (very dry), semi-arid and dry sub-humid areas, resulting from climatic variations and human activities.
It is the degradation of land on desert margins, not the advance of sand dunes from an existing desert.
Physical causes are drought, unreliable rainfall, high temperatures and evaporation.

Human causes are population growth, overgrazing, overcropping, cutting trees and shrubs for fuelwood, and poorly managed irrigation causing salinisation (salts building up in the soil as irrigation water evaporates).
The two usually act together. Human pressure leaves the soil bare, then drought and storms remove it.
Desertified land loses the qualities that make soil useful, and the people who farm it lose their living.
Loss of topsoil and humus, and lower fertility, because the nutrient-rich surface layer is the part that is removed.
Surface crusting, so rain runs off rather than soaking in, and water retention is reduced.
Wind-blown sand and dust, because bare, dry soil has nothing to hold its particles down.
Salt crusts where irrigation is poorly managed (salinisation). In extreme cases the ground becomes bare and sterile.
Human effects: falling yields, food shortages and famine, loss of livestock, and migration to cities and abroad.
The Sahel is the main example of desertification. Its climate explains why its soils are so vulnerable.
The Sahel is the semi-arid belt along the southern edge of the Sahara. It stretches across Africa from Senegal and Mauritania in the west, through Mali, Burkina Faso, Niger and Chad, to Sudan.
Annual rainfall is roughly 200 to 600 mm. It falls in one short summer wet season, when the ITCZ, the rain belt, moves north.
Rainfall is highly unreliable from year to year, so a run of dry years can strip the plant cover.
In the Sahel, human pressure and drought combined: people left the soil bare, then drought and heavy rain removed it.
Population growth led to more cattle, goats and sheep concentrated around wells and boreholes (drilled water sources), shorter fallow periods, more cash crops and more fuelwood cutting.
Cash crops such as groundnuts (peanuts) in Senegal and cotton took the best land, pushing food crops and herders onto marginal land.
Nomadic herders, whose movements once let pasture recover, became more settled, so land around their camps was grazed continuously.
Droughts, notably in the 1970s and 1980s, left bare soil that was eroded by wind and by the heavy rain of the short wet season.
The Sahel shows the soil damage of desertification and its effect on water supply.
The soil effects are loss of topsoil and humus, lower fertility, surface crusting, reduced water retention, wind-blown sand and dust, and salt crusts where irrigation is poor.

Lake Chad, on the Sahel's border of Chad, Niger, Nigeria and Cameroon, has shrunk dramatically since the 1960s, through drought and water use for irrigation. A widely quoted UN figure gives a shrinkage of about 90%.
Because desertification crosses borders, governments have tried to respond together.
The UN Convention to Combat Desertification (UNCCD) was adopted in 1994. 17 June is World Day to Combat Desertification.

The Great Green Wall was launched by the African Union in 2007. It is a planned band of restored land about 8,000 km long across Africa, from Senegal to Djibouti, aiming to restore 100 million hectares of degraded land by 2030.
Progress has been slow and well short of target. The project has shifted from a line of planted trees towards a mosaic of local land-restoration projects.
Some of the most effective responses come from farmers using low-cost methods that fit dry soil.
In Burkina Faso, in the Yatenga region of northern Burkina Faso, farmers such as Yacouba Sawadogo revived the traditional zaï technique.
Zaï are small pits dug in hard, crusted soil and filled with manure or compost. They catch rainwater and concentrate nutrients around the seed.
Farmers also built stone lines, or bunds, along the contours (lines of equal height) to slow runoff and trap soil.
In Niger, farmers rebuilt tree cover without planting. They simply protected what was already growing.
