In Niger, farmer-managed natural regeneration (FMNR) means farmers protect and prune tree shoots that regrow from old stumps and roots in their fields.
FMNR has regreened about 5 million hectares since the 1980s, especially in the Maradi and Zinder regions.
Trees shade the soil, cut wind speed and add leaf litter. Species such as Faidherbia albida also add nitrogen.
Comparing the Sahel's responses shows what works.
Local methods have restored land at scale in Niger, but the Great Green Wall has been slow to meet its targets.
Conservation works best when farmers gain from it and take part, as the Niger FMNR and the Burren results-based payments show.
Beyond overcropping, overgrazing and desertification, several other human activities damage soil.
Deforestation exposes soil to erosion and stops the supply of litter, which is the source of humus.
Heavy machinery and livestock on wet ground compact the soil and destroy its structure.

Excess fertiliser and slurry let nitrates and phosphates wash out of the soil into rivers and lakes, causing eutrophication (nutrient enrichment that makes algae overgrow). Some fertilisers also acidify the soil.
Salinisation and waterlogging (soil saturated with water) occur under badly managed irrigation. Canal irrigation in Punjab and Haryana, India, has caused both.
Peat extraction removes an entire soil, as in Irish bogs, because the peat itself is the soil being cut away.
Urban sprawl and roads seal soil under concrete and tarmac, so it can no longer grow plants or absorb rain.
On slopes, water and wind carry soil away. These methods slow the water or wind so the soil stays in place.
Contour ploughing means ploughing across a slope along the contours, so that furrows trap water instead of channelling it downhill.
Terracing cuts steep slopes into level steps, such as the rice terraces of Banaue, Luzon, Philippines, which are over 2,000 years old.
Strip cropping alternates strips of crops and grass. The grass traps soil washed or blown from the cropped strip.
Shelter belts and windbreaks of trees and hedges cut wind speed and reduce wind erosion.
These methods keep nutrients and humus in the soil and keep the surface covered.
Crop rotation, fallow, cover crops and green manure, such as clover, restore nutrients and humus.
Adding manure and compost builds up humus, so the soil holds more nutrients and water.
Reduced or zero tillage (little or no ploughing), and mulching, leave crop residue on the surface to protect the soil.
Protecting soil from grazing animals means letting plants recover and using roots to hold the soil.
Controlled stocking (limiting animal numbers), rotational grazing (moving animals between fields), fencing and reseeding allow vegetation to recover.
Afforestation (planting trees where there were none) and replanting bind the soil with roots.
Dry regions need methods that capture scarce rain and protect soil from wind.

Stone lines (bunds) along contours, zaï planting pits, and farmer-managed natural regeneration of trees are the dryland methods used in the Sahel, because they capture scarce rain and protect soil from wind.
Conservation protects soil that already exists. These methods go further and improve poor soils, or even create soil.
Liming raises the pH of acid soils, so they become less acidic and suit more crops.
Field drainage and arterial drainage improve gleys (waterlogged soils). The Arterial Drainage Act, 1945, began state schemes to deepen and straighten Irish rivers to drain wet farmland.
Deep ploughing breaks an iron pan (a hard layer in the soil), as in podzols.
Irrigation with proper drainage avoids salinisation, because the drainage carries away the salts instead of letting them build up.
Building soil where none existed: on the bare limestone of the Aran Islands, Co. Galway, islanders layered sand and seaweed, and later manure, on the rock inside stone-walled fields.
Government schemes pay farmers to protect soil, and EU rules limit pollution from farming.
REPS was followed by GLAS (Green, Low-Carbon, Agri-Environment Scheme), from 2015, and ACRES (Agri-Climate Rural Environment Scheme), from 2023.
The EU Nitrates Directive (1991) limits how much organic nitrogen can be spread per hectare and bans spreading slurry during a closed period in winter.
The Burren is the syllabus's Irish example of human interference with soil. It is thought that its bare rock is partly a result of early farming.
The Burren, in north-west Co. Clare, lies on Carboniferous limestone, with extensive limestone pavement of clints (blocks) and grikes (gaps between them).
Its soils are thin, dark, lime-rich rendzinas, found mainly in the grikes and hollows.
Plants from Arctic-alpine and Mediterranean environments grow side by side, e.g. spring gentian and mountain avens.
Poulnabrone, a Neolithic portal tomb (dolmen) over 5,000 years old, is evidence of early farming communities.

It is thought that the Burren once had thicker soil and woodland cover. Clearance and grazing by early farmers, followed by erosion of soil into the grikes and underground, helped expose the bare pavement.
On the Burren, grazing is part of the solution. The problem today is too little grazing.
Winterage means cattle are grazed on the upland limestone in winter, because the rock stores heat and the ground is dry.
Grazing keeps grass and scrub down and maintains the flower-rich grassland.
From the late 20th century fewer farmers grazed the uplands in winter, because of farm changes, supplementary feeding and labour shortage.
Hazel and blackthorn scrub (low woody bushes) then spread over grassland and pavement, because nothing grazed it back.
On the Burren the main threat is undergrazing, not overgrazing.
Conservation projects on the Burren led to a payment system that rewards farmers for the quality of their land.
BurrenLIFE (2005 to 2010) was an EU LIFE-funded project led by Dr Brendan Dunford, with local farmers, the National Parks and Wildlife Service and Teagasc.
It tested scrub removal, better feeding systems and grazing plans.
It was followed by the Burren Farming for Conservation Programme (2010 to 2015) and the Burren Programme (from 2016), funded by the Department of Agriculture.
These pay farmers by results. Each field is scored for habitat quality, e.g. on a scale of 1 to 10, and a higher score earns a higher payment, so farmers decide how best to manage their land.
The model has been copied in other Irish agri-environment schemes.
Iceland shows how settlers can strip a landscape of trees. Their cutting and their sheep removed the cover that protected the soil.
Iceland was settled by Norse people from about AD 874.
At settlement, birch woodland and scrub covered a large part of the island, an estimated quarter or more. Today native birch woodland covers only about 1 to 2%.
Settlers cut and burned birch for fuel, for charcoal used in iron working, and for grazing land.
They kept large numbers of sheep, which grazed the year round and prevented regrowth.
Iceland's soil and climate made the damage worse, because the soil is easily blown away and plants recover slowly.
Iceland's soils are andosols formed from volcanic ash. They are light, loose and low in clay.
Once the vegetation cover is broken, they are easily blown away by strong winds and washed out by rain.
Erosion escarpments (rofabörð in Icelandic) are steep banks of soil being eaten away from their edges.
Volcanic eruptions add ash that smothers vegetation, so plant cover is lost again after each eruption.
A cold climate and a short growing season mean vegetation recovers very slowly.
Iceland also shows the positive side: over a century of work to hold and rebuild its soil.
The Soil Conservation Service of Iceland (Landgræðslan, now part of Land and Forest Iceland) was founded in 1907. It is one of the oldest soil conservation services in the world.
Methods include fencing off eroding land to keep sheep out, and sowing lyme grass (Leymus arenarius) to stabilise drifting sand.
Other methods are sowing grasses with fertiliser from the air, and replanting birch.
Nootka lupin fixes nitrogen (turns nitrogen from the air into a form plants can use) and binds soil, but it has become an invasive plant that crowds out native species, so its use is controversial.
Farmer-led reclamation projects, called Farmers Heal the Land, began in 1990.
Sheep numbers have fallen from their peak in the late 1970s, which means less grazing pressure on the soil.
Iceland shows both sides: over a century of positive impact through conservation and reclamation, after centuries of negative impact through deforestation, overgrazing and erosion.
Positive and negative impacts can occur on the same land at different times.

A biome is a large world region with a distinctive climate, soil and community of plants and animals adapted to those conditions. In the hot desert option, everything you write follows from one starting point: the climate.
Climate is the main control, because it shapes the soil, and climate and soil together shape the vegetation, which in turn determines which animals can live there.

Biotic inter-relationships (the links between living things) include food chains and webs, which run from producers (plants, which make their own food) to herbivores (plant eaters) and carnivores (meat eaters), with decomposers (organisms that break down dead matter) returning nutrients to the soil.
Plants and animals also compete for scarce water, which is the key shortage in a desert.

The hot desert is one of the biome belts that follow the world climate belts: tundra, boreal forest, temperate deciduous forest, temperate grassland, Mediterranean, hot desert, savanna and tropical rainforest.
On mountains, biomes change with altitude in vertical zones, because temperature falls as you climb.
Hot deserts are the driest places on earth outside the poles, and they sit in predictable bands. Learn the rainfall limit, the latitudes and a set of named deserts with their continents.

Annual rainfall is under 250 mm, which is the limit that defines a hot desert. Hot deserts lie roughly between 15 and 30 degrees north and south of the equator, mainly on the west sides of continents and in continental interiors (the middle of large landmasses).
The Sahara, North Africa, is the world's largest hot desert, at about 9 million km², crossing Morocco, Algeria, Libya, Egypt, Mauritania, Mali, Niger, Chad and Sudan.

Other hot deserts: the Arabian Desert; the Thar (India and Pakistan); the Namib (south-west Africa); the Atacama (Chile); the Sonoran and Mojave (south-west USA and north-west Mexico); the Great Victoria and Simpson Deserts (Australia).
Map cue: sketch the desert belts on either side of the equator, and label the west coasts of the continents where they reach the sea.
Aridity (extreme dryness) has five separate causes, and different deserts get different combinations. Give each cause its own explained point, with the mechanism and a named example.
1. Subtropical high pressure: air that rose at the equator sinks at about 30 degrees north and south (this circulation is the Hadley cell). Sinking air warms and dries, so clouds cannot form.
2. Offshore trade winds blow from the dry interior of the land out over the sea, so they bring no moisture to the coast.

3. Cold ocean currents off west coasts cool the air above them. The cooled lower air is stable (a temperature inversion, with cold air under warmer air), so it cannot rise to form rain, and fog forms instead.

Examples of cold currents beside deserts: the Canary Current (western Sahara), the Benguela Current (Namib), the Humboldt Current (Atacama) and the California Current (Baja California and the Sonoran coast).
4. Rain shadow: mountains force moist air to rise, so it cools and rains on the windward side (the side facing the wind), then descends dry on the leeward side (the sheltered side).
Rain shadow examples: the Andes shelter the Atacama from the east; the Sierra Nevada shelters the Mojave, including Death Valley, from Pacific moisture.
5. Continentality: the interior of a large continent is far from the sea, so winds have lost most of their moisture before they arrive.
Desert temperatures are extreme in two ways: very hot by day in summer, and with a huge swing between day and night. Both come from the lack of cloud and moisture in the air.
Summer daytime temperatures often exceed 40 °C, because little cloud blocks the sun.
Clear skies and dry air give intense insolation (incoming solar radiation) by day and rapid heat loss by night. So the diurnal (daily) range is very large, and nights can be near freezing in winter.
A diurnal range of 20 to 30 °C or more is common.
The annual range (the gap between the warmest and coolest month) is larger than in the tropics.
The highest air temperature officially recognised by the World Meteorological Organization is 56.7 °C, at Furnace Creek, Death Valley, California, on 10 July 1913.
Rain in a desert is rare, and when it comes it behaves differently from rain elsewhere. Evaporation, humidity, wind and fog complete the picture.

Rain is scarce and unreliable. When it falls it is often short, intense convectional downpours (rain from warm air rising rapidly) that cause flash floods, because the hard, dry ground cannot absorb it quickly.
Potential evaporation (the water that would evaporate if it were available) far exceeds rainfall, and humidity is low.
Strong, hot, dusty winds blow across the bare surface, because there is little vegetation to slow them.
Coastal fog deserts: the Namib, among the oldest deserts in the world, receives much of its moisture as fog from the cold Benguela Current.
The Atacama, Chile, is the driest non-polar desert on earth; some of its weather stations have recorded no rain for years at a time.
The picture of endless sand dunes is misleading. Knowing the three surface types and the dry river bed word wadi lets you describe the landscape accurately.
Most of the desert is rock and gravel, not sand dunes.
Hamada: a bare rock plateau. Reg: a stony gravel plain. Erg: a sand sea with dunes.
Wadis are dry river beds that flow only after rain.
Wind erosion landforms are taught separately. There is more on this in Erosion by wind.
The soil of the hot desert is an aridisol (a dry-climate soil). Its features follow from the lack of water and the lack of plants, and it is a classic contrast with the rainforest.
Aridisols are thin and immature, because weathering (the breakdown of rock) is slow without water and is mainly physical.
They are coarse, sandy or stony, with very little humus (decayed plant matter), because few plants grow. This is why they are pale grey, yellow or red in colour.
Little leaching (washing of nutrients down through the soil) takes place. Capillary rise (water drawn up through the soil, then evaporating) brings salts and calcium carbonate to the surface.
This forms salt crusts (salinisation) and lime hardpans called calcrete or caliche (calcification).
Wind removes fine particles from the surface, so the stones are left behind as a desert pavement.

The soils are alkaline. Where irrigated they are fertile, because nutrients have not been leached out; they are farmed in the Nile valley in Egypt and in California's Imperial Valley, irrigated from the Colorado River.

Alluvial soils (deposited by rivers) from rivers that rise outside the desert, such as the Nile, are an exception to the aridisol pattern, because the river brings fresh sediment from outside the desert.
Contrast with rainforest: desert soils are poor in humus but can be fertile when irrigated, whereas rainforest soils stay infertile beneath lush forest.
With so little water, plants cannot form a continuous cover. The pattern of where they grow is itself a response to drought.
Cover is sparse, with much bare ground, so biomass (the total mass of living matter) and diversity are low.
Plants are widely spaced so that they do not compete for the same scarce water.
Creosote bush in the Mojave and Sonoran Deserts limits competitors with evenly spaced plants, roots and chemicals, and individual bushes can be very long-lived.
Vegetation is concentrated, because water is there, along wadis (dry river beds that flow after rain) and at oases (places where groundwater reaches the surface).
Xerophytes are plants adapted to drought. The first strategy is to store water when it rains, as succulents do in their stems or leaves.
Succulents store water in their stems or leaves, such as the cacti below, so they can survive the long gaps between rains.

Saguaro cactus, found only in the Sonoran Desert of Arizona and Sonora, Mexico: its pleated stem expands to store water after rain, and it has spines and shallow roots spread widely just below the surface.
The saguaro can grow over 12 m tall and live over 150 years. Its white flower is the state flower of Arizona.
Cacti are native only to the Americas. Euphorbias in African deserts look similar through convergent evolution (unrelated plants developing the same features in similar conditions).
Spines in place of leaves cut water loss (less surface to evaporate from) and deter animals; a thick, waxy cuticle (the outer coating of the plant) reduces evaporation.
Other plants cut water loss or reach water by their roots and leaves. Each feature below solves a different part of the drought problem.

Few, sunken stomata (the pores through which leaves lose water vapour); in many succulents they open only at night (Crassulacean acid metabolism, or CAM, photosynthesis), so less water is lost in the heat of the day.
Long tap roots reach groundwater: mesquite, in the south-west USA and Mexico, has tap roots that can reach tens of metres down.
Shallow, widespread roots catch brief rain before it evaporates or drains away, so the plant can take in water quickly.
Acacia trees in the Sahara and Arabian deserts have deep roots, small leaves and thorns.
Small or light-coloured leaves, or leaves shed in drought, reduce water loss because less leaf surface is exposed to the sun.

Welwitschia mirabilis, Namib Desert, where fog is the main moisture: it has only two leaves, which grow throughout its life; it absorbs moisture from fog; some plants are thought to be over 1,000 years old.
Halophytes (plants that tolerate salty soils) cope with the salts that rise to the surface. Some plants in coastal deserts harvest moisture from fog.
Some desert plants do not endure drought at all. They avoid it, by surviving as seeds until rain arrives.
Ephemerals (short-lived plants): their seeds lie dormant for years, then after rain germinate, flower and set seed within weeks, producing a desert bloom.
In the Atacama, Chile, a flowering desert (desierto florido) appears in unusually wet years, often linked to El Niño (a climate pattern in the Pacific Ocean).
Death Valley had a widely reported superbloom in 2016.
The dromedary (one-humped) camel of the Sahara and Arabia is the standard desert animal, with a whole set of adaptations to heat, thirst and sand. Name the feature and the reason for each.
Its hump stores fat, not water. It can go many days without drinking, then drink over 100 litres in a few minutes.
It lets its body temperature rise by several degrees during the day, saving the water that sweating would use, and thick fur on its back shades it from the sun.
It has long eyelashes and closable nostrils that keep out sand, and broad, padded feet that spread its weight on sand.
Very concentrated urine and dry droppings reduce water loss (dromedary camel; kangaroo rat).
Other desert animals escape the heat by being active at night or underground, find water in food or fog, or breed fast when rain comes. Pair each animal with its adaptation.
Fennec fox, Sahara: the smallest fox, with very large ears that radiate heat so it stays cool; nocturnal (active at night); burrows by day; fur on the soles of its feet for hot sand.
Kangaroo rat, North American deserts: gets water from its seed diet and from its metabolism (the chemical reactions in its body); nocturnal; seals its burrow by day to keep humidity in.
Namib fog-basking beetle: stands head-down on dune crests at dawn so that fog condenses on its back and runs to its mouth.
Thorny devil lizard, Australian deserts: grooves in its skin channel water to its mouth, so it can drink from any damp surface.
Spadefoot toad, Sonoran Desert: estivates (lies dormant) underground through the dry months and emerges after summer rain; its eggs and tadpoles develop extremely quickly, before the pools dry up.
Addax antelope, Sahara: pale coat, which reflects sunlight; gets most of its water from plants; now critically endangered.
Desert locust: breeds rapidly after rain, when food is available, and can form huge swarms.
Even in a sparse biome, species depend on each other. Desert food chains are simple, but there are close partnerships around the cactus.
Lesser long-nosed bats pollinate (carry pollen between) saguaro and agave flowers at night.
Gila woodpeckers dig nest holes in saguaros; when the holes are abandoned, elf owls and other birds use them.
Food chains are short, because there are few producers; seed-eating rodents are prey for snakes, owls and foxes.
People adapt to the desert as well as plants and animals do. The syllabus also asks for a European example, and Spain provides one.
Tuareg (Sahara) and Bedouin (Arabia) are pastoral nomads (herders who move with their animals) who herd camels and goats.
Oasis farming grows date palms, whose roots reach groundwater, so they can grow where rain cannot support crops.
Tabernas Desert, Almería province, Andalusia, south-east Spain: often called Europe's only desert, a semi-arid area in the rain shadow of surrounding mountains.
Its dry, open landscape explains why the Tabernas Desert was used as a film set for spaghetti westerns in the 1960s and 1970s.
A climate graph shows temperature as a line and rainfall as bars for each month. The values below are invented to show the method.
Annual range: the warmest monthly mean minus the coolest, for example 34 °C minus 12 °C gives an annual range of 22 °C (invented illustrative values).
Total rainfall: the sum of the twelve monthly rainfall bars, for example 150 mm (invented illustrative values); a total under 250 mm points to a hot desert.
Seasonality: describe when the rain falls and when temperatures peak, for example a single short wet season in late summer (invented illustrative values).

The tropical rainforest is a biome: a community of plants and animals adapted to a hot, wet equatorial climate and to nutrient-poor soils. This set of blocks stands alone, so you can answer any biome question from it.
Climate is the main control, because it shapes the soil, and climate and soil together shape the vegetation, which in turn shapes the animals.

Biotic inter-relationships (the links between living things): food chains and webs run from producers (plants) to herbivores and carnivores, with decomposers returning nutrients to the soil. Species compete for light, and many pollinators and seed dispersers depend on the plants they feed on.
The rainforest is the biome of the equatorial belt, one of the biome belts that follow the world climate belts.
Mountains show vertical zones of biomes instead, because temperature falls with altitude.
Rainforest is found in a belt on either side of the equator, in three main regions plus some smaller areas. It covers little land but holds a very large share of the world's species.
A dense, evergreen, broadleaved forest in the hot, wet equatorial climate, mainly between about 10 degrees north and south of the equator.
Amazon Basin, South America: the largest, covering about 5.5 million km², with roughly 60% of it in Brazil.
Congo Basin, Central Africa: the second largest, including the Democratic Republic of the Congo.
South-East Asia: Indonesia (including Sumatra and Borneo), Malaysia and Papua New Guinea.
Smaller areas: Central America, West Africa, eastern Madagascar and north-east Australia (the Daintree, Queensland).

Rainforests, though small in area, cover only about 6% of the earth's land surface but are widely estimated to hold over half of the world's land plant and animal species. This is a widely quoted estimate.
Map cue: shade the equatorial belt, then mark the three main basins and regions.
Temperature in the rainforest is high and almost constant, because the sun stays high in the sky all year. The daily swing is bigger than any seasonal one.
Mean monthly temperatures are about 26 to 28 °C all year, so there is no cold season.
The annual range is only about 2 to 3 °C, because the sun stays high and day length barely changes.
The sun is overhead at the equator twice a year, at the equinoxes in March and September.
The daily range is greater than the annual range, and there are no seasons in the temperate sense (no summer and winter).
Rain falls in every month, and the cause is a daily cycle of heating and convection (warm air rising). The equatorial low-pressure belt drives it.
Annual rainfall is over 2,000 mm, falling throughout the year and in places far more. Manaus, in the central Amazon, Brazil, receives about 2,300 mm a year.
Stage 1: because the sun is high, intense morning heating warms the ground and the moist air above it, which rises.
Stage 2: the rising air cools and cumulonimbus clouds (tall rain clouds) build up.
Stage 3: heavy afternoon thunderstorms follow, almost daily.
The low-pressure belt of rising air along the equator, the ITCZ (Inter-Tropical Convergence Zone, also called the doldrums), drives this; some areas have a short drier season when it shifts.
Relative humidity (the amount of water vapour in the air) is often over 80%.
A large share of the Amazon's rain is water recycled from the forest by evapotranspiration (water given off by plants and evaporated from the ground and leaves).
The lush forest grows on poor soil. It survives because nutrients are locked in the living plants and recycled very quickly, rather than stored in the ground.

Latosols are deep, red or yellow, laterised (leached of most minerals except iron and aluminium by heavy rain), acidic and infertile, with little humus. There is more on this in Soil processes and the global pattern of soils.
Litter (fallen leaves and dead matter) decomposes within weeks in the heat and humidity.
Shallow roots and mycorrhizal fungi (fungi growing on the roots) take up nutrients almost at once and pass them to the trees.
Most nutrients are held in living vegetation rather than the soil, so the nutrient cycle is rapid and closed.
Rainforest soils are infertile despite the lush forest; hot desert soils are infertile in humus but can be fertile when irrigated.
The forest is arranged in layers, each with different light and conditions. Learn each layer with its approximate height.
Emergents rise above the canopy, at about 45 to 60 m and more: kapok, the Brazil nut tree in the Amazon, and dipterocarps in South-East Asia.
The canopy, at about 25 to 40 m, is a dense, continuous layer that intercepts most sunlight and rain and holds most of the animal life.
The understorey of young trees and palms reaches up to about 15 m.
The shrub layer grows in the dim light below.
The forest floor is dark and humid; only about 2% of the sunlight reaching the canopy arrives there.
Diagram cue: a labelled vertical profile of the layers, with approximate heights.
Rainforest plants are adapted to heavy rain, thin soils and competition for light. Each feature below answers one of those pressures.
Buttress roots (wide, wall-like roots at the base) support tall trees such as kapok (Ceiba) and the Brazil nut, which have shallow roots.
Shallow roots catch nutrients from the litter layer, because that is where the nutrients are.
Drip tips and waxy leaves shed heavy rain, so the leaves do not stay waterlogged.
Large leaves in the understorey capture the little light that reaches it, because the canopy above blocks most of it.
Thin, smooth bark, because the trunk needs no thick insulation in the constant warmth, and a smooth surface makes it harder for epiphytes to cling.
Evergreen, with leaves shed and replaced all year. When a tree falls it opens a light gap, and young trees grow rapidly upwards into it.
In a crowded forest, many plants reach the light by climbing or growing on other plants, and some cope with poor soil by trapping insects or living as parasites.
Lianas are woody climbers, rooted in the soil, that climb trees to reach the light, so they do not need to build thick trunks.

Epiphytes (plants growing on other plants) such as orchids, bromeliads and ferns grow on branches and take moisture from the air and rain. Bromeliads hold pools of water in their leaf rosettes, which tree frogs use.
Strangler figs start as epiphytes high in the canopy, where there is light, and enclose their host tree.
Pitcher plants (Nepenthes) in the nutrient-poor soils of South-East Asia trap and digest insects.
Rafflesia arnoldii, a parasite on vines in Sumatra and Borneo, has the largest single flower in the world, about 1 m across, and smells of rotting meat to attract flies.
Rainforest has extremely high species diversity of plants and animals. The pattern is many species but few individuals of each.
Hundreds of tree species can grow in a single hectare of Amazon rainforest, compared with a handful in an Irish wood.
Many species grow in each hectare, but each species is represented by few individuals, so a tree's nearest neighbour of the same species may be far away.
The climate is warm and wet all year with no cold or dry season to survive, so plants grow all year round and many species can coexist.

The layers of the forest create many separate niches (ways of living, each with its own light, food and shelter), from the sunny emergents to the dark forest floor, so more species can live side by side.
This richness depends on the closed nutrient cycle: when the forest is cleared, both the species and the nutrients stored in them are lost together.
Most animals live in the canopy (arboreal, meaning tree-living), where the food and sunlight are. Their adaptations suit life in the trees.
Spider monkeys and howler monkeys, Amazon: prehensile (gripping) tails used as a fifth limb; howler monkeys are among the loudest land animals.
Three-toed sloth: its very slow metabolism suits a low-energy leaf diet; algae growing in its fur give camouflage; it descends to the ground only about once a week.
Toucan, South and Central America: its large, light bill reaches fruit at the tips of branches and helps it lose heat.
Orangutan, found only in Borneo and Sumatra: the largest tree-living mammal, with long arms.
Harpy eagle, Central and South America: hunts monkeys and sloths in the canopy.
Beyond the canopy, forest animals rely on camouflage, warning colours and swimming. Place each animal on the correct continent.
Poison dart frogs, Central and South America: bright colours warn predators of their toxic skin, so predators learn to leave them alone.
Jaguar: the largest cat in the Americas, with a spotted coat that breaks up its outline in the dappled light of the forest floor; a strong swimmer that hunts along rivers.

Many animals are strong swimmers or live in water, because rivers flood the forest for months each wet season: the anaconda, a huge snake, hunts in flooded forest and rivers, and the Amazon river (pink) dolphin swims among the flooded trees.
Capybara, South America: the world's largest rodent, a semi-aquatic grazer that escapes predators by diving into water.
Many animals are nocturnal (active at night), which avoids daytime predators and competition, and some canopy animals glide between trees rather than climbing down.
Okapi, Congo rainforest: a forest relative of the giraffe, with striped legs for camouflage in the dim forest.
Gorillas and bonobos live in the Congo Basin; bonobos are found only south of the Congo River.
Rainforest plants and animals depend on each other closely. Pollination and seed dispersal link them, and some partnerships are mutualism (both partners gain).
Pollination by insects, birds and bats, and seed dispersal by fruit bats, birds and other animals link plants and animals closely.
Mutualism: Azteca ants live inside Cecropia trees, which give them shelter and food; in return the ants attack herbivores and clear climbing plants from the tree.
Leafcutter ants cut leaves to grow the fungus they eat, so the leaves are food for the fungus, not the ants.
Brazil nut: pollinated mainly by large orchid bees and dispersed by agoutis, rodents that bury the nuts; trees produce poorly in plantations away from intact forest.
Indigenous people have long lived in the forest by methods that let it recover.
The Yanomami (Brazil and Venezuela border), the Kayapó (Brazilian Amazon) and the Mbuti (Ituri forest, Democratic Republic of the Congo) are hunter-gatherers.
Hunting, gathering and shifting cultivation (slash and burn, clearing a patch and moving on) at low density, because small numbers of people take little, let the forest and soil recover.
There is more on commercial felling in Human alteration of biomes.
The syllabus asks for European examples where appropriate, but this biome has none.
There is no tropical rainforest in Europe. There is more on Europe's role in the trade that drives felling in Human alteration of biomes.
A climate graph shows temperature as a line and rainfall as bars for each month. The values below are invented to show the method.
Annual range: the warmest monthly mean minus the coolest, for example 28 °C minus 25 °C gives an annual range of 3 °C (invented illustrative values).
Total rainfall: the sum of the twelve monthly rainfall bars, for example 2,400 mm (invented illustrative values); rain falls in every month, with no dry season.
Seasonality: describe the pattern as even, with temperatures near constant through the year (invented illustrative values).
A biome (a large natural community of plants and animals, shaped by climate) has a natural state. People have changed almost every one, and the exam asks how.
Natural (climax) vegetation is what would grow if the land were left undisturbed. Very little of the earth's land remains untouched, so most biomes now show some human influence.
Humans alter biomes by removing, replacing or degrading vegetation, changing soils and water, introducing or removing species, and polluting.
The effects reach every part of the system, because the parts are linked: climate, soil, plants, animals and people all change together.
Before people changed it, Ireland's natural vegetation was forest. The forest spread as the ice retreated.
After the last glaciation (the last ice age) ended about 10,000 years ago, Ireland was colonised first by birch and hazel, then by pine, oak, elm and ash.
By about 6,000 years ago forest covered almost all of the island. This was the temperate deciduous forest biome (broadleaved trees that lose their leaves in winter).
The first big change came when people stopped hunting and gathering and began to farm. Farming needs open land, so forest had to go.
Mesolithic hunter-gatherers (the Middle Stone Age, people who lived by hunting and gathering) had little impact on the forest.

Farming (the Neolithic, the New Stone Age) reached Ireland about 6,000 years ago, about 4000 BC. Farmers cleared forest with stone axes and fire to grow cereals and graze animals. This was the start of human alteration of the Irish biome.

A sharp fall in elm pollen (found in layers of old soil and bog) around this time, the elm decline, is seen across Ireland and Britain. Clearance by farmers and elm disease are both thought to have contributed.
The Céide Fields show what clearance did to Irish soils. Farmland created by clearance was later buried by bog.
Neolithic farmers built stone-walled fields here, about 5,500 years ago. The fields are among the oldest known field systems in the world.

Blanket bog (a thick peat cover over wide areas of upland and west-coast land) later covered the fields. Forest clearance, a wetter climate and leaching (nutrients washed out of the soil by rain) turned the forest soils into bog, and peat grew over the walls.
A local teacher, Patrick Caulfield, found the stone walls under the bog while cutting turf in the 1930s. His son, the archaeologist Séamas Caulfield, later studied the site.
Clearance went on for thousands of years, but the greatest loss of Irish forest came much later, under conquest and trade.
Earlier clearance continued through the Bronze and Iron Ages and in early Christian and medieval farming.
The great clearance came in the 16th and 17th centuries, during the Tudor conquest and plantations. Woods were felled for timber exports, shipbuilding, barrel staves and charcoal for ironworks.
Woods were also felled to remove cover used by Irish resistance, because forest gave fighters places to hide.
By 1900 Ireland was among the least wooded countries in Europe, with about 1% of the island forested.
Forest cover is now about 11%, mostly conifer plantations (cone-bearing evergreen trees grown in rows), so most new forest is not the original woodland.
Clearance did not just remove trees. It changed the land cover, the wildlife and the soils.
Native deciduous forest was replaced by farmland, hedgerows, bog and grassland, which is why little of the original forest remains.
Woodland species declined because their habitat was lost. The wolf was hunted to extinction, the last one generally said to have been killed in the late 1700s.

Soils under heath (open land of low shrubs such as heather) were leached and podzolised (made acidic and infertile, with a pale layer where nutrients have washed out), and blanket bog spread across the uplands.
Ireland has tried to bring trees back, but the new forests are not the old ones.

State afforestation (planting trees on land that had none) has mostly used fast-growing, non-native conifers, chiefly Sitka spruce (native to western North America), because they grow quickly for timber.
Sitka plantations form a new, species-poor habitat, with few kinds of plant and animal, and acidify soils and water.
Native woodland survives in remnants, such as the oakwoods of Killarney National Park, Co. Kerry, and the Reenadinna yew wood on the Muckross peninsula, a rare pure yew wood.
Forests around the Mediterranean Sea have been cut since ancient times, so the damage there is a clear European example.
Deforestation since ancient times, for shipbuilding, fuel, farming and goat grazing, degraded the evergreen oak and pine forest to maquis (dense scrub) and garrigue (low, open scrub on thin soils).
Soil erosion on the cleared slopes followed, because tree roots no longer held the soil. There is more on this in A Peripheral European Region: the Mezzogiorno.
The cedars of Lebanon, prized by the ancient Egyptians and Phoenicians for shipbuilding and temples, survive only in small groves, such as the Cedars of God grove, a UNESCO World Heritage site.
Global example, Iceland: birch woodland was cleared and grazed after settlement. There is more on this in Human interference with soils.
The Amazon in Brazil is the main case study for felling (cutting down) tropical rainforest. Satellites measure how fast it is being cleared, and the rate has risen and fallen sharply.
Brazil's space agency, INPE, measures annual deforestation in the Brazilian Amazon by satellite (the PRODES programme).
Clearance peaked at about 27,800 km² in 2004, fell to about 4,600 km² in 2012, rose to about 13,000 km² in 2021, and fell again from 2023 under renewed enforcement.
Close to a fifth of the original Amazon forest has been cleared, so a large share of the biome is already gone.
Forest is cleared to make money from the land. Farming and timber are the first group of causes, and cattle ranching is the biggest.
Cattle ranching is the largest single cause and accounts for most of the cleared land in the Brazilian Amazon. It is the cause, not soya or logging, to name first.
Soya farming, for example, spread north from Mato Grosso. Much of the soya is exported as animal feed, including to Europe and China, which links the forest to distant demand.
Logging of hardwoods: selective logging (taking only chosen valuable trees) opens roads and gaps in the canopy that lead to further clearance.
Government policy and debt, together with global demand for beef, soya, timber and minerals, drive clearance.
Big building projects open the forest up. Roads bring settlers, mines need power and fuel, and dams flood land.
Road building and planned settlement: the Trans-Amazonian Highway (BR-230), begun in the early 1970s by the military government, opened the Amazon to settlers from the poor, drought-prone north-east.
BR-364 into Rondônia, paved in the 1980s with World Bank support (the Polonoroeste programme), led to a fishbone pattern of clearings along its side roads, which shows up on satellite images.
Mining: Carajás, Pará state, is one of the world's largest iron-ore mines, operated by Vale and opened in the 1980s. A railway carries the ore to the coast.
Charcoal-fuelled pig-iron smelters (furnaces making crude iron) near Carajás used forest wood, so mining cleared forest beyond the mine itself.
Illegal gold mining (garimpo) on Yanomami land pollutes rivers with mercury.

Hydroelectric dams: the Belo Monte dam on the Xingu River, Pará, completed in 2019, is one of the world's largest hydroelectric schemes by capacity. It flooded forest and land, diverted the river past the Volta Grande (Big Bend), and displaced thousands of people.
The Kayapó and other indigenous groups strongly opposed Belo Monte. There is more on river impacts in Human interaction: river processes.
Removing the trees affects the animals, the soil, the water cycle and the climate. The effects feed into each other.
Loss of habitat and species, many of them endemic to the region (found nowhere else), so animals that depend on the forest lose their homes.
Fragmentation of the remaining forest (breaking it into patches) creates edge effects, as the forest edge is drier, hotter and more exposed.
The nutrient cycle is broken: cleared latosols (the deep, nutrient-poor red tropical soils) lose their fertility within a few years, and pasture is abandoned.
Soil erosion and a hard laterite crust (an iron-rich layer that bakes hard) form on the exposed land, and rivers silt up.
Less evapotranspiration (water given off by plants into the air) means less rainfall downwind and longer dry seasons, and fires become more frequent.
The forest stores huge amounts of carbon; burning and decay release it to the atmosphere as carbon dioxide.

Scientists, notably Carlos Nobre and Thomas Lovejoy, have warned that losing about 20 to 25% of the forest could push parts of the Amazon past a tipping point (a threshold after which change cannot easily be reversed) towards degraded savanna.
People live in the rainforest, and clearance harms indigenous peoples (the original inhabitants) through loss of land, disease and conflict.
Indigenous peoples lose their land, suffer disease, and face violence and conflict with ranchers and miners, for example the Yanomami and the gold miners.
Chico Mendes, a rubber tapper and union leader who campaigned to protect the forest, was murdered by a rancher's family at Xapuri, Acre, on 22 December 1988.
In 2023 the Brazilian government declared a public health emergency in Yanomami territory after illegal gold mining caused malnutrition and disease.
Brazil has laws, markets and monitoring to slow clearance. How well they work has changed with national policy.
Brazil's Forest Code requires landowners in the Amazon to keep 80% of their land as forest, the legal reserve. The code was revised in 2012.
The Amazon Soy Moratorium (2006): major traders agreed not to buy soya grown on newly deforested Amazon land, which removes the market for that soya.
The Amazon Fund (2008), with Norway the largest donor, pays for forest protection, so money from abroad supports enforcement.
INPE's PRODES annual figures and DETER near-real-time alerts guide enforcement by IBAMA, the federal environment agency, so illegal clearing can be found and acted on.

Protected areas, indigenous territories and extractive reserves, where local people harvest rubber and nuts sustainably, were set up after Chico Mendes's death; the Chico Mendes Extractive Reserve in Acre is one example.
Evaluation: the falls and rises in clearance show that protection depends on political will and enforcement.
Rainforest in Borneo and Sumatra is a second example. Here the main driver is palm oil, a vegetable oil from oil palm trees.
Indonesia and Malaysia together produce about 85% of the world's palm oil, so these two countries dominate world supply.
Lowland rainforest and peat swamp forest (waterlogged forest growing on thick peat) in Borneo and Sumatra are cleared for oil palm plantations and timber.
Drained and burned peat causes regional haze (smoke pollution), notably in 1997 and 2015, affecting Singapore and Malaysia.
The Bornean orangutan was listed as Critically Endangered by the IUCN in 2016, making it the flagship threatened species (the animal that stands for the wider loss) of this clearance.
European consumers drive some of the clearance, and the EU has begun to act on it.
Europe's demand for beef, soya (as animal feed), timber and palm oil drives felling.

The EU Deforestation Regulation (adopted 2023) will require firms selling beef, soya, palm oil, cocoa, coffee, rubber and timber in the EU to prove they were not grown on land deforested after 2020. Its application has been delayed.
Intensive farming tries to get as much food as possible from each patch of land. This changes the habitats on and around the farm.
Intensive farming uses high inputs of capital (money), machinery, fertiliser, pesticides and water to get maximum output per hectare.
It creates monocultures (one crop grown over a large area), larger fields and drained wetlands, so habitats become fewer and simpler.
Irish farming has intensified in both dairying (milk production) and tillage (growing crops on ploughed land). The changes removed habitats and polluted water.
EU milk quotas (limits on how much milk each farm could produce) ended on 1 April 2015, after which Irish dairy herds expanded.
Hedgerows were removed and fields enlarged; wetlands and callows (wet meadows beside a river) were drained; species-rich meadows were reseeded with ryegrass, a single grass grown for feed.
Silage (grass cut and stored for animal feed) replaced hay. Earlier, mechanised cutting destroys the nests of ground-nesting birds such as the corncrake.
The corncrake has declined to a small population mainly in north-west Donegal, west Mayo and the Shannon Callows.
Wild bees and farmland birds have declined, because the hedgerows and meadows that fed and sheltered them were lost.
Heavy use of fertiliser and slurry (liquid animal manure) affects water and the atmosphere. Policies now try to reduce it and help wildlife.
Heavy use of fertiliser and slurry raises nitrate levels in rivers and estuaries, especially in the south and south-east.
The extra nutrients cause eutrophication of lakes (an overgrowth of algae that uses up the oxygen in the water).
Agriculture is the largest source of Ireland's greenhouse gas emissions, over a third of the total, according to the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA).

Responses: the Nitrates Directive (1991); agri-environment schemes (payments to farmers for farming that helps nature) REPS (1994), GLAS (2015) and ACRES (2023); and the All-Ireland Pollinator Plan, begun in 2015.
The EU's Common Agricultural Policy (CAP, the EU's system of farm payments) shows how policy can drive intensification across a continent.
The Common Agricultural Policy began in 1962. Guaranteed prices encouraged farmers to remove hedgerows, enlarge fields and drain wetlands, notably in the arable east of England (East Anglia).
Food surpluses, the butter mountains and wine lakes, followed in the 1980s, because guaranteed prices encouraged farmers to produce more than was needed.
Later reforms, from 1992 onwards, began paying farmers for environmental farming.
Intensive farming has also replaced grassland biomes, and it overlaps with rainforest clearance.
The tallgrass prairie of North America (temperate grassland) has been almost entirely converted to farmland; only a few per cent survives.
The Dust Bowl, when ploughed grassland soils blew away, is an example of the soil loss that followed. There is more on this in Human interference with soils.
Cattle and soya in the Amazon are also intensive agriculture; the impacts are those listed under the felling of tropical rainforests.
Irrigation (supplying water to crops by channels) can destroy a whole lake. The Aral Sea in Central Asia is the case study.
The Aral Sea lies on the border of Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan. In 1960 it was the world's fourth-largest lake.
From the 1960s Soviet planners diverted its feeder rivers, the Amu Darya and Syr Darya, to irrigate cotton and rice in the desert, so less water reached the sea.
The sea shrank to a fraction of its former size and split into separate parts. Its salinity rose and the fishing industry collapsed.
Former fishing ports such as Moynaq (Muynak), Uzbekistan, were left far from the shore, with ships stranded on the dry seabed.
Dust storms carry salt and pesticide residues from the exposed seabed onto farmland and people, with health effects.
Salinisation (build-up of salt in the soil) and waterlogging damaged the irrigated soils.
The Kok-Aral Dam (2005), built by Kazakhstan with World Bank funding, raised the level of the small North Aral Sea, and fishing has partly recovered there.
Factories and power stations release gases that make rain acidic. The pollution travels, so it damages forests and lakes far from its source.
Sulphur dioxide and nitrogen oxides from coal- and oil-burning power stations, industry and vehicles form acids that are carried downwind, often across national borders.

Acid rain acidified thousands of lakes in southern Norway and Sweden from the 1960s to the 1980s; fish died out in many of them. Its source was largely the emissions of other countries, so the countries that suffered were not the ones that caused it.
Effects on coniferous forests include needle loss, dieback (trees dying from the top down) and nutrient leaching from the soil.
Effects on lakes include fish being killed and aluminium being released into the water.

The Black Triangle, where the borders of Germany, Poland and the Czech Republic meet, had lignite-burning power stations, so large amounts of acid gases were released (lignite is a low-grade, dirty brown coal).
Large areas of spruce forest in the Ore Mountains (Erzgebirge) and neighbouring ranges died in the 1970s and 1980s, a process known as Waldsterben (forest death).
Because acid rain crosses borders, countries had to act together. The same fixes were applied at home.

Responses: the Convention on Long-Range Transboundary Air Pollution (1979); EU limits on power-station emissions; flue-gas desulphurisation (removing sulphur from chimney gases); and liming of lakes in Sweden and Norway, which neutralises their acidity.
Sulphur dioxide emissions in Europe have since fallen by well over half, and many forests and lakes have partly recovered.
Moneypoint, Co. Clare, on the Shannon Estuary, was Ireland's only coal-fired power station, opened in the 1980s.
Flue-gas desulphurisation was later fitted to cut its sulphur emissions, so less acid rain formed. ESB ended coal-burning there in 2025.
Industry changed the raised bogs of the Midlands. A raised bog is a dome of peat that formed over thousands of years, and it was harvested for fuel.
Bord na Móna, a state company set up in 1946, harvested milled peat on a large scale from the Midland raised bogs for power stations and briquettes (peat fuel blocks).
The peat-burning power stations at Shannonbridge (West Offaly) and Lanesborough (Lough Ree) closed in December 2020. Bord na Móna ended peat harvesting in 2021, under its Brown to Green plan.

Its cutaway bogs (bogs where the peat has been removed) are being rehabilitated and rewetted. Lough Boora Discovery Park, Co. Offaly, is cutaway bog converted to wetlands, woodland and amenity land, so land damaged by harvesting gains new habitats.
Clara Bog, Co. Offaly, is one of the largest relatively intact raised bogs in Ireland, and is a nature reserve and Special Area of Conservation, so it shows what an undamaged raised bog looks like.
Peatlands cover about a fifth of Ireland, so changes to them alter a large share of the country's land.
Getting oil out of sand needs huge areas to be dug up, so the boreal forest above is destroyed.

The Athabasca oil sands, around Fort McMurray in northern Alberta, Canada, are mined by surface (open-pit) methods that strip away boreal forest (northern coniferous forest) and muskeg (peatland) to reach bitumen-soaked sand.
The mining produces large tailings ponds (ponds of polluted waste water) and high greenhouse gas emissions per barrel.
Companies must reclaim mined land (restore it), but little of it has been certified as reclaimed.
Oil extraction can pollute a whole delta, where creeks, mangroves and farms are close together.
Oil has been produced in the Niger Delta, Nigeria, since the late 1950s, by Shell and others.
Repeated spills from pipelines, and theft, have polluted creeks, mangrove forest (coastal forest growing in salt water) and farmland.
A UNEP study of Ogoniland (2011) found pollution so widespread that a clean-up could take 25 to 30 years.
A nuclear accident killed a forest, and then the absence of people let wildlife return.
The Chernobyl nuclear power station in Ukraine, then part of the USSR, exploded on 26 April 1986.
Radiation killed a nearby pine forest, because the trees absorbed it, whose needles turned reddish-brown, the Red Forest.
A 30 km exclusion zone was evacuated. With people gone, so that wildlife is undisturbed, wildlife such as wolves, elk, wild boar and the reintroduced Przewalski's horse has become common there.
Industry affects biomes beyond the factory site, through the atmosphere and through the spread of towns and factories.

Greenhouse gases from industry shift climate belts and stress biomes, through coral bleaching, thawing tundra permafrost (ground that stays frozen all year), and more drought and fire. There is more on global warming in Option: Global Interdependence.
Urban and industrial sprawl (the spread of towns and factories over open land) replaces habitats and seals the soil beneath.
Human activity can also repair biomes, so a balanced answer weighs benefits against losses.

Not all alteration is negative. Protected areas, rewilding, rewetting of bogs, results-based farming (farmers paid for the wildlife results they achieve, as in the Burren) and pollution controls can restore biomes.
The central evaluation is the balance between economic gain and the loss of biomes.
People disagree about what 'development' means, and so about what counts as progress and who gets to set the standard. Every model in this subsection starts from a different answer.

Economic development means growth in a country's output and income (the goods and services it produces and the money earned), usually measured by GNP per head (gross national product, the total income of a country's people, divided by the population).
Human development means health, education, freedom and choice: people's ability to live lives they value, whatever the size of the national income.
Sustainable development means meeting today's needs without harming the future, so growth must not use up resources or damage the environment that later generations will need.
Who defines development matters: definitions are usually set by rich countries and international institutions, which decides which goals and measures count.

Measures follow views: GNP per head reflects the growth view and the HDI (Human Development Index, a score built from health, education and income) reflects the human view. There is more on this in the Economic Development notes.

'Underdevelopment' is itself a loaded word with two meanings. It can mean 'not yet developed', the modernisation view (poor countries are behind on a common path), or 'made poor by others', the dependency view (poor countries were held back by richer ones). Both meanings must be explained.
Ideas about development have not stood still. Each era produced its own model and its own goals, usually reacting to the failures of the one before.

Colonial era: colonies were treated as suppliers of raw materials for the ruling country, so their wealth flowed out, and colonial rule was justified by a 'civilising mission' (the claim that Europeans were bringing progress to others).
1950s–60s: growth and modernisation. Because the aim was catching up, development meant GNP growth and industrialisation, following Rostow's model (covered below).
1960s–70s: dependency theory emerged in Latin America, arguing that poverty was caused by the structure of the world economy rather than by the poor countries themselves.
1970s: the basic needs approach, a reaction to growth that left the poor behind, put food, water, shelter, health and education ahead of GNP growth.

1980s–90s: the neoliberal Washington Consensus (neoliberal means trusting free markets over state control). The term was coined by the economist John Williamson in 1989 for market reforms promoted by the IMF, World Bank and US Treasury.
These reforms were privatisation (selling state-owned firms to private owners), free trade and cuts in state spending.
From 1990: human development, measured by the HDI, and the idea of development as freedom.
From 1987: sustainable development, which links growth to environmental limits because resources are finite.
2000s–2010s: goal-based views (the Millennium and Sustainable Development Goals, sets of targets agreed by the UN) and rights-based views of development (development as people's entitlement).
Environmental determinism is the oldest idea here. It holds that the physical environment, especially climate, decides how far a society can develop.
Temperate climates (mild, moderate temperatures) were said to produce energetic, advanced peoples, while tropical climates were said to produce poor and backward societies.

The theory was developed by 19th- and early 20th-century geographers. Ellen Churchill Semple, in Influences of Geographic Environment (1911), and Ellsworth Huntington, in Civilization and Climate (1915), argued that climate determined how 'civilised' a people could become.
It was used to justify colonialism and racial hierarchies (rankings of peoples), presenting European rule as the natural order.
Critique: it ignores history, including colonialism, slavery and trade rules, as well as politics and people's choices.
Critique: it is contradicted by Singapore, which is tropical yet one of the world's richest countries, and by poverty in temperate places.
Critique: its assumptions about the abilities of different peoples were racist, and they are rejected today.
Reply: possibilism, associated with the French geographer Paul Vidal de la Blache, holds that the environment offers possibilities and people choose which to use.
Few geographers now say the environment decides everything, but some still argue that physical geography shapes development. This version keeps the idea without the racism.
Jeffrey Sachs, in The End of Poverty (2005), stressed malaria, poor soils and a landlocked location (no coast, so no easy access to sea trade) as obstacles that aid could help overcome.
Jared Diamond, in Guns, Germs, and Steel (1997), argued that geography (crops, animals and the east–west axis of Eurasia) explains why some societies gained power first.

Botswana is landlocked, yet it became independent in 1966 as one of the world's poorest countries. Diamonds and stable government made it an upper-middle-income country, so physical limits can be overcome.
Physical factors raise the costs of development without fixing its outcome, which is why Botswana could succeed.

Modernisation theory holds that all societies pass along one path from traditional to modern, as Western Europe and North America did. Poor countries are behind and need investment, technology, industry and Western values to catch up.
Walt W. Rostow, an American economist and adviser to Presidents Kennedy and Johnson, set out his five-stage model in The Stages of Economic Growth: A Non-Communist Manifesto (1960).
Stage 1, traditional society: because output is low, people live on subsistence farming (growing food mainly for the family's own use) and limited technology.
Stage 2, preconditions for take-off: investment in transport and education, new ideas, and trade opening to outside contact.
Stage 3, take-off: investment rises to over 10% of national income and a few leading industries grow fast.
Stage 4, drive to maturity: growth spreads across the economy and diversifies into many industries.
Stage 5, age of high mass consumption: because the economy is mature, most people enjoy cars, durable goods (long-lasting items such as appliances) and services.
Rostow dated Britain's take-off to the late 18th century (about 1783–1802). He is not used to date any other country's take-off.
Applying Rostow to Ireland is a textbook interpretation, not Rostow's own work. The model can be applied to Irish development as follows.
Traditional stage: a farming economy with heavy emigration, including net emigration (more people leaving than arriving) of about 400,000 between 1951 and 1961.

Preconditions: T. K. Whitaker's Economic Development and the First Programme for Economic Expansion (1958), and an opening to foreign investment, with the IDA (the Industrial Development Authority, which attracts foreign firms) set up in 1949.
Take-off: industrial growth in the 1960s and 1970s, free secondary education from 1967, and EEC (the European Economic Community, now the EU) membership from 1 January 1973.
Drive to maturity: growth in the 1980s and 1990s led by multinational companies (firms operating in many countries).
High mass consumption: the Celtic Tiger, from the mid-1990s to 2007.
Limits of the model: the crash from 2008 and the EU–IMF bailout of November 2010 show that the stages can be reversed.
South Korea is an East Asian success story whose industrialisation seems to fit Rostow's stages, because it climbed from poverty to wealth within decades.
The Korean War (1950–53) left South Korea among the world's poorest countries.
Export-led industrialisation (building factories to sell goods abroad) was planned under Park Chung-hee from the 1960s.
Large family conglomerates (chaebol), such as Samsung, Hyundai and LG, led the growth, and heavy investment in education supplied skilled workers.
South Korea joined the OECD (a club of mainly wealthy countries) in 1996 and was reclassified as a developed country by UNCTAD (the UN body for trade and development) in 2021.
Its rapid industrialisation seems to fit Rostow's stages, which is why it is used as evidence for the model.
Modernisation has been widely criticised, because many countries did not follow the predicted path. Each criticism below is a separate point to make in an evaluation.
Eurocentric (judging everything from a European viewpoint): it assumes the Western path is the only path and that Western society is the goal.

Linear and stage-bound: countries can skip, stall or go backwards. Zimbabwe, with land seizures from 2000 and hyperinflation (prices rising out of control) peaking in 2008, and Syria, where civil war from 2011 reversed decades of progress, show this.
It ignores colonialism and unequal trade as causes of poverty, treating poor countries as simply late starters.
It assumes wealth will trickle down from growth to the poor, which often does not happen, because owners and governments keep most of the gain.
It is growth-centred and environmentally unsustainable: mass consumption for everyone is impossible on current resources.
It ignores culture, inequality and gender, so growth alone can leave women and minorities behind.
Many African states that followed modernisation advice did not take off.
Modernisation was not only an idea. It shaped what governments and international bodies actually did, and it was top-down: decided from above rather than by local people.
Large prestige projects, such as dams and steelworks, were built to bring industry quickly, and were often built with little local participation.
The Washington Consensus described above applied the same top-down thinking through markets, imposing reforms from outside.
Debt and aid followed these policies, because poor countries borrowed to pay for such projects. There is more on this in the Empowering People notes.
Dependency theory turns modernisation upside down. It holds that poor countries are poor because of how they were drawn into the world economy, not because of their own backwardness.
The rich core (metropolis) countries develop by draining wealth from the poor periphery (satellite) countries.
Development of the core and underdevelopment of the periphery are two sides of one process, because the core's wealth and the periphery's poverty are linked.
Origins: Latin American economists and thinkers. Raúl Prebisch, an Argentine economist, headed the UN Economic Commission for Latin America (ECLA), set up in 1948.

With Hans Singer, Prebisch argued in 1950 that the terms of trade (the price of exports compared with the price of imports) of primary-product exporters (sellers of raw materials and farm produce) tend to decline. This is the Prebisch–Singer thesis.
Andre Gunder Frank, in The Development of Underdevelopment (1966), argued that Latin America was underdeveloped by its links with the core, through metropolis–satellite chains.
Dependency is structural, through trade, investment and debt. It is not the same as dependence on aid.
Dependency theorists point to specific mechanisms that keep the periphery poor. Each one is a separate point you can make.
Colonial extraction of raw materials, using slavery where needed, moved wealth from colonies to the ruling country.
Dependence on one or two primary exports (raw materials or farm produce) whose prices are low and unstable, so incomes are low and hard to plan.

Tariff escalation, where rich countries tax processed goods more heavily than raw materials, which keeps poor countries exporting raw materials, and rich-country subsidies (government payments to their own producers) that undercut producers elsewhere.
Profit repatriation: multinationals send profits home, so the money does not stay in the host country.
Debt repayments drain income, so less is left to fund development.
Brain drain: skilled people leave for the core, which means the periphery loses the doctors, engineers and teachers it trained.
Local elites who benefit from the link with the core and resist change.
Commodities are raw materials and farm products sold on world markets. These examples show countries tied to the core through one or two of them.
For example, Brazil's colonial economy moved through export cycles of brazilwood, sugar, gold, coffee and rubber, each tied to demand in the core.
Côte d'Ivoire and Ghana grow over half of the world's cocoa, mostly exported as beans rather than processed chocolate, so the higher-value processing happens elsewhere.
Zambia depends on copper, which is most of its exports, so its income rises and falls with one commodity.
Sudan's Gezira Scheme, from 1925, grew cotton for the Lancashire mills, so the farmland served the core's factories.
Wallerstein developed dependency ideas into a three-part picture of the world, which allows for countries that change position.
Immanuel Wallerstein's The Modern World-System (first volume 1974) divides the world into core, semi-periphery and periphery.
Core countries control high-value production and finance, so they keep the biggest share of the profit. Periphery countries supply cheap raw materials and labour.
Semi-periphery countries sit between the two, and countries can move between zones. South Korea and China have moved up.
China began reforms in 1978, joined the WTO (World Trade Organization) in 2001 and has been the world's second-largest economy since 2010.
Dependency theory explains some poverty well, but later events exposed its weaknesses.
It cannot explain how the Asian Tigers (South Korea, Taiwan, Hong Kong and Singapore) and China developed through trade with the core.
Countries that cut their links with the world economy through self-reliance (depending on their own resources) stayed poor.
It blames outside forces, so it can excuse corruption and poor government at home.
The remedy, withdrawal from world trade, has rarely worked, because countries lose markets and technology.
In the 1970s some thinkers turned away from GNP growth and asked what poor people actually needed, and what technology would suit them.
The basic needs approach of the 1970s put food, water, shelter, health and education first, not GNP growth.
The ILO World Employment Conference (1976, held by the International Labour Organization, the UN body for work) put basic needs at the centre of development policy.
E. F. Schumacher's Small Is Beautiful (1973) argued for small-scale, appropriate technology that local people can afford, use and repair.
Schumacher founded the Intermediate Technology Development Group in 1966, now called Practical Action.
The human view judges a country by how people live, not by how much it produces.

Amartya Sen, an Indian economist and Nobel Prize winner in Economics (1998), argued in Development as Freedom (1999) that development means widening people's choices and capabilities (what people are able to do and be).

The first Human Development Report (by UNDP, the UN Development Programme) appeared in 1990. The HDI was created by Mahbub ul Haq with Sen. There is more on how it works in the Economic Development notes.
The human view judges progress by people's lives, not by national output alone.
Two further alternatives change who decides and what is protected: local people take part in planning, and growth stays within environmental limits.

Bottom-up (grassroots) development puts participation, co-operatives (businesses owned by their members), NGOs (non-governmental organisations, such as charities) and women's groups at the centre, in contrast to top-down projects. There is more on this in the Empowering People notes.
The Brundtland Report, Our Common Future (1987), set out sustainable development. There is more on its application in the Sustainable Development notes.
The Sustainable Development Goals are 17 goals adopted in 2015, with a target year of 2030.
If development is more than money, then GNP is the wrong ruler. These two proposals measure or describe progress differently.
Bhutan's Gross National Happiness was put forward in the 1970s by King Jigme Singye Wangchuck as a goal ahead of GNP.

Hans Rosling, a Swedish doctor and statistician, with Ola Rosling and Anna Rosling Rönnlund in Factfulness (2018), argued that dividing the world into 'developed' and 'developing' is out of date and replaced it with four income levels. Most people now live in the middle-income levels.
The pictures people see shape what they believe about a place. Media and charity images of Africa have been narrow, and that has consequences.
Famine, war, disease and helpless victims, especially children, dominate media and charity images of Africa. Good news and ordinary life are rarely shown.
Stereotypes follow, such as the belief that 'Africa is a country', when it is a continent of many different countries.
Donors can take a 'saviour' view of themselves, and the people shown can come to see themselves as helpless.
Investors and tourists may lose confidence in countries shown only as crisis zones, so the images can cost those countries income.
Audiences can tire of the same images, leading to donor fatigue (people giving less because the appeals feel repetitive).
Coverage of this famine shows both the power and the cost of one image of Africa. It raised huge sums but also shaped how a whole continent was seen.
A BBC television report by Michael Buerk in October 1984 brought the famine to world attention.
Band Aid's single 'Do They Know It's Christmas?' (1984) and the Live Aid concerts (July 1985), organised by Bob Geldof, raised huge sums.
The famine came during civil war in northern Ethiopia, and government policies worsened it.
The powerful coverage fixed an image of Africa as helpless and dependent, and hid the political causes: civil war and government policy.
Aid agencies, writers and speakers have pushed back against the single story of crisis.
Dóchas, the Irish association of development NGOs, drew up a Code of Conduct on Images and Messages that its member organisations sign.
The code requires images to respect the dignity of the people shown, avoid stereotypes and tell the full context.
NGOs use dignified images and the people's own voices in their appeals, so the people shown speak for themselves.
Kenyan writer Binyavanga Wainaina's satirical essay 'How to Write About Africa' (Granta, 2005) mocked Western clichés about the continent.
Nigerian novelist Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie's talk 'The Danger of a Single Story' (2009) argued that a single story about a place distorts it.
Positive examples from sub-Saharan Africa (the part of the continent south of the Sahara desert) replace the image of helplessness with specific achievements.

Rwanda: after the genocide from 7 April 1994, in which about 800,000 people, mostly Tutsi, were killed in about 100 days, the country rebuilt. Since the 2013 election women have held over 60% of the seats in the lower house of parliament, the highest share of any country.

Kenya: M-Pesa, a mobile-phone money transfer service launched in 2007 by Safaricom (part-owned by Vodafone), lets people without bank accounts send, receive and save money by text message. Most Kenyan adults use it.
Botswana: its growth from diamonds under stable government is the counter-image to the landlocked-state argument above.
Words used for poorer countries carry hidden assumptions. A loaded term suggests a judgement while sounding neutral.
'Underdeveloped' and 'backward' imply that poor societies are lagging behind a normal path.
'Primitive' implies that poor societies are at an earlier stage of human history.
'Developing' implies one direction of travel, towards the Western model, so it assumes every country wants the same goal.
'Less economically developed country' (LEDC) still measures other countries against the developed norm.
'Global South' groups countries by their position in the world economy rather than by wealth.
'Majority world' is a term popularised by the Bangladeshi photographer Shahidul Alam, because most of the world's people live there.
The UN created the 'least developed countries' category in 1971. Most of its members are in sub-Saharan Africa, and it is an official term.
These labels began as politics, not as a ranking of wealth. Their meaning drifted after the Cold War (the rivalry between the USA and the Soviet Union) ended.
'Third World' was coined by the French demographer Alfred Sauvy in 1952, by comparison with the 'Third Estate' of the French Revolution (the ordinary people, outside the clergy and nobility).
It was originally a Cold War political term, not a ranking of wealth. The First World was the USA-led capitalist West and the Second World the Soviet-led communist bloc.
The Third World was the rest: mostly newly independent former colonies that did not align with either bloc.

The Bandung Conference, Indonesia, in April 1955 brought together leaders of newly independent Asian and African states. The Non-Aligned Movement (countries refusing to join either bloc) was founded at Belgrade in 1961.
The Soviet Union dissolved in December 1991, ending the Second World and leaving the terms without their original meaning.

The terms became a ranking, with first meaning best, and a byword for poverty, because people forgot their Cold War origin. They lump together very different countries, from Singapore to the poorest states.
The North–South model divides the rich, industrialised North from the poor South. It replaced the three worlds as the main way of picturing global inequality.
The Brandt Report, North–South: A Programme for Survival (1980), came from a commission chaired by the former West German Chancellor Willy Brandt.
The Brandt Line runs roughly along 30°N and dips south to include Australia and New Zealand in the North.
The Brandt Line is a 1980 concept, not a current UN or World Bank classification.
The gap in income, health and power between most of Africa and Europe remains very large, which is why the idea still has some use.
World Inequality Report 2022: the richest 10% of people own about 76% of global wealth, and the poorest half about 2%. Poverty and deprivation also exist within the North.

Global institutions remain weighted towards wealthy states: the five permanent members of the UN Security Council (the body with power to decide on international action) are the USA, the UK, France, Russia and China.
Since 1980 many countries south of the Brandt Line have grown rich or powerful, so a simple two-part split no longer fits the world.
Many 'South' countries are now high-income or industrial powers, such as Singapore, South Korea, Taiwan and Hong Kong, so 'South' no longer means poor.
China is the world's second-largest economy, and India is among the five largest.

The BRIC term (Brazil, Russia, India, China) was coined in 2001 by Jim O'Neill of Goldman Sachs, and the first BRIC summit was held in 2009. South Africa joined in 2011, forming BRICS. Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran and the United Arab Emirates joined in January 2024, and Indonesia in January 2025.
The G20, set up in 1999, includes China, India, Brazil, South Africa, Indonesia, Mexico and Saudi Arabia, giving the South a stronger voice.
Most of the world's people now live in middle-income countries, as Hans Rosling showed in Factfulness, so a rich/poor split misdescribes them.
In 2016 the World Bank announced that it would stop dividing countries into 'developing' and 'developed' in its main data tables, keeping its four income groups.
Eurocentric thinking sees the world from a European point of view and judges other societies by European standards, as if Europe's path, values and history were the norm. Maps show it clearly.

The Mercator projection (a way of flattening the globe onto a map) was designed by the Flemish map-maker Gerardus Mercator in 1569 for navigation, because lines of constant compass bearing are straight on it. Its effect is to place Europe at the top centre of the world map.
On the Mercator projection, Africa is about 14 times the area of Greenland, yet the two look similar in size.
The Peters (equal-area) projection, presented by the German historian Arno Peters in 1973 (the Gall–Peters projection), shows true areas and challenges this distortion.
Greenwich (London) was chosen as the prime meridian (the line of 0° longitude from which other places are measured) at the International Meridian Conference, Washington, in 1884.
Regional names such as 'Middle East' and 'Far East' are measured from Europe, so they only make sense from a European position.
Eurocentrism also shaped how history was told and how development was defined, with Western experience treated as the standard.
Christopher Columbus reached the Caribbean in 1492. Describing the Americas as discovered treats lands that were already inhabited as if they were empty.
