At the Berlin Conference of 1884–85 European powers set the rules for claiming Africa, which they then divided among themselves. By 1914 only Ethiopia and Liberia were independent.
African and Asian achievements are ignored in European histories, so Europe appears to be the only source of progress.
Edward Said's Orientalism (1978) showed how Western writing portrayed the East as exotic, backward and inferior.
'Developed' was defined as becoming like Western Europe, with industry, urbanisation (growth of towns and cities) and mass consumption.
Traditional knowledge and ways of life were dismissed, so Western experts designed projects without local input.
The balance of economic power is shifting, and with it the idea that Europe is the model.
China's Belt and Road Initiative, launched in 2013, and the growth of South–South trade and aid (between developing countries, including China in Africa), show a shift away from European-led models.
The rise of Asia and the voices of local people now challenge Eurocentric models of development.
No country makes or grows everything it needs, so countries depend on one another. The key idea is the effects that follow when a decision is taken in one place and the results land in another.

Countries and regions rely on each other for raw materials, components (parts used to make a product), markets (places to sell), investment, labour, food and a shared environment, so a decision in one place has effects elsewhere.
Globalisation (the growing links between countries), through trade, multinational companies (firms operating in many countries), communications and migration, has deepened this interdependence.
It has an economic form (trading patterns), an environmental form (shared global issues) and a political and social form (decisions on refugees, migration and human rights).
A global product is made in some places and bought in others. Geographers call these producer regions and consumer regions, and the gap between them explains who gains most from trade.
Producer regions supply raw materials, components and assembly (putting the parts together). These are often developing countries with low wages, which is why firms locate this work there.
Consumer regions buy the finished product. These are mostly rich countries, and increasingly China and India, because their people have the income to buy it.

Value added (the extra worth created at each stage of making and selling a product) is shared very unequally along the chain: most of it is captured by design, branding and retail in consumer regions.

Apple is the main case study of a multinational whose product is designed in one country, built from parts made in several others, and sold worldwide. Following the iPhone shows how many regions one product links.
Apple was founded in 1976 by Steve Jobs and Steve Wozniak, with headquarters in Cupertino, California (Apple Park, 2017). The iPhone launched in 2007.
Apple designs in California, where its headquarters are. Its packaging states: 'Designed by Apple in California. Assembled in China.'
TSMC in Taiwan makes Apple's A-series and M-series chips (the processors inside its devices). Samsung and LG in South Korea supply screens, so no single country makes the whole phone.
Other components come from further suppliers around the world. Minerals include cobalt (a metal used in batteries), most of which is mined in the DR Congo.
Foxconn (Hon Hai Precision Industry), a Taiwanese contract manufacturer (a firm that builds products for other companies), assembles most iPhones in China, at Zhengzhou and Shenzhen.
Foxconn and the Indian Tata group assemble iPhones in India near Chennai and Bengaluru, so assembly is spreading beyond China.
Apple's largest sales regions are the Americas, Europe and Greater China, so its customers are spread across three continents.
For the regions that make and supply the parts, Apple's orders bring real benefits but also costs. A good answer gives both sides, with named places.
Positive: assembly and supply firms provide jobs for millions of people, bringing skills, industrial growth and export earnings to China.
Positive: supplier firms grow because of Apple's orders, as TSMC and Foxconn show.

Negative: a 2011 study by Kenneth Kraemer, Greg Linden and Jason Dedrick estimated that Apple kept about 58% of the sale price of an iPhone (2010 model) as profit, while Chinese assembly labour received under 2%. This shows how unequally value is shared.

Negative: a cluster of worker suicides at Foxconn's Shenzhen factories in 2010 drew attention to long hours, strict discipline and pressure. Foxconn raised wages and put up safety nets (nets fixed to buildings to stop people falling), a response to the attention.
Negative: in November 2022 workers at Foxconn's Zhengzhou plant protested over pay and COVID-19 lockdown conditions, delaying iPhone supplies worldwide.
Negative: producer regions depend on Apple's orders, which can move. Some assembly has shifted to India, which shows that the orders can move.
Negative: Amnesty International (2016) documented child labour in the DR Congo's hand-dug cobalt mines, which supply the metal for batteries.
Rich consumer regions gain the product and keep the most valuable parts of the chain, but they also send problems back to poorer countries.
Consumers in rich countries gain access to new technology and services, paying high prices for products whose assembly is cheap.
Most profit and the high-paid design and marketing jobs stay in the USA, because the company is based there.
Electronic waste from discarded devices is exported to poorer countries.
Ireland is both a place where Apple employs people and a country affected by decisions taken elsewhere about Apple. This is a good example of how one firm links a small economy to the EU and the USA.
Apple opened at Hollyhill, Cork, in 1980, its first manufacturing plant in Europe. It now has about 6,000 employees in Cork and its European headquarters there.
Apple's Cork campus does not assemble iPhones. Its role is European headquarters and support, not the Chinese assembly chain.

In 2016 the European Commission ruled that Ireland had given Apple illegal tax benefits worth €13 billion. This was the recovery of illegal State aid (help from a government that breaks EU competition rules), not a fine, and Ireland argued against collecting it.
The General Court overturned the decision in 2020. In September 2024 the EU Court of Justice reinstated it, and Ireland received about €14 billion, including interest.
A decision in Brussels therefore affected both Ireland and the USA, where the company is based.
US tariffs (taxes on imports) on many Chinese goods from 2018, and higher tariffs on most countries' imports in 2025, have pushed Apple to move some assembly to India.
Cadbury shows how a long-established British brand became part of an American multinational, and how Irish plants fit into its chain. It is a food company, so its chain begins on farms.
Cadbury was founded by John Cadbury in Birmingham, England, in 1824, so its origins are British. Its Bournville factory and model village for workers opened in 1879.
The American firm Kraft Foods took over Cadbury in 2010. In 2012 Kraft's snacks business, including Cadbury, became Mondelēz International, headquartered in Chicago.
Because Mondelēz is American, Cadbury is no longer a British-owned company.
Cadbury Ireland has a chocolate factory at Coolock, Dublin, and a chocolate crumb plant at Rathmore, Co. Kerry.
Rathmore uses milk from local dairy farms to make chocolate crumb (milk, sugar and cocoa), which is sent to Cadbury factories in Britain. It makes crumb, not finished bars.

The cocoa in chocolate comes mainly from West Africa, where small farmers earn little and face serious problems. These points cover who grows cocoa, how their incomes are supported, and the child labour in the trade.

Côte d'Ivoire is the world's largest cocoa producer, with about two-fifths of world output. Ghana is second. Together they grow over half of the world's cocoa, mostly exported as beans, so these two countries depend on one crop.
Most cocoa is grown on small family farms of a few hectares, so individual farmers have little power over the price they are paid.
From the 2020–21 season Côte d'Ivoire and Ghana added, because farm incomes were low, a Living Income Differential of 400 US dollars a tonne to cocoa sales to raise farmers' incomes.

A study for the US Department of Labor by NORC at the University of Chicago, published in 2020, found about 1.56 million children in child labour in cocoa growing in Côte d'Ivoire and Ghana (2018–19).
The Harkin–Engel Protocol (2001) committed the chocolate industry to end the worst forms of child labour in cocoa. Deadlines have been missed repeatedly.
Irish dairy farms supplying Rathmore are also a producer region for the company.
Cocoa growing also changes the land, and a country that depends on one export is exposed to price swings. Most of the profit from processing is made far from the farms.
Côte d'Ivoire has lost most of its forest since independence (1960), much of it to cocoa farms, because farmers clear forest to plant more cocoa.
In 2024 cocoa prices rose to a record above 10,000 US dollars a tonne after poor West African harvests, caused by bad weather and the cocoa swollen shoot virus.
Farmers gained far less than the world price, because their governments fix farm-gate prices (the price paid to the farmer) in advance.
Value is mostly added outside Africa. The Netherlands, through the port of Amsterdam, is the world's largest cocoa-processing centre (where beans are turned into cocoa products).
The company has made several choices about how it buys cocoa. One of them has been disputed.
Cadbury Dairy Milk carried the Fairtrade Mark (a label guaranteeing farmers a fairer deal) from 2009.
Mondelēz launched its own sustainability programme, Cocoa Life, in 2012, to improve cocoa farming, with about 400 million US dollars committed over ten years.
In 2017 Cadbury Dairy Milk in Britain and Ireland replaced the Fairtrade Mark with the Cocoa Life logo. Fair-trade campaigners criticised the decision.
Chocolate is bought mostly by richer countries, which also keep most of its price. Their shoppers and governments can in turn pressure the producers.
Europe and North America consume most of the world's chocolate. Brands, marketing and retail take most of the price, because they add the most value.
Consumer campaigns and EU rules pass pressure back to producers, so a decision in a consumer region changes how farms are run.

The EU Deforestation Regulation (adopted 2023) will require firms selling cocoa, coffee, beef, soya, palm oil, rubber and timber in the EU to prove the goods were not grown on land deforested after 2020. Its application has been delayed.
Intel is a shorter alternative case study of a multinational, useful if you studied it in the economic option. Its chain runs from design in the USA to factories and customers around the world.
Intel was founded in 1968 in Mountain View, California, and is headquartered in Santa Clara. Research and design are based in Oregon and California.

Wafers (thin discs of silicon from which chips are cut) are made in fabs (chip factories) at Hillsboro (Oregon), Chandler (Arizona), Leixlip and Kiryat Gat (Israel). Leixlip makes processor wafers, not computers.
Assembly and test (the final stages, away from the wafer fabs) take place in Penang and Kulim (Malaysia), Ho Chi Minh City (Vietnam) and Chengdu (China).
Customers are computer makers, such as Lenovo, HP and Dell, which sell worldwide.
Intel's Leixlip fab has operated since 1989, and over €30 billion had been invested by 2023. Fab 34 opened in 2023.
49% of the Fab 34 joint venture (a business shared between two firms) was sold to Apollo Global Management for about $11 billion (2024).

Decisions elsewhere affect Intel: the US CHIPS and Science Act 2022 (about $50 billion, US support for chip making), about 15,000 global job cuts announced in August 2024, and a US government stake of about 10% (2025).
Ireland is a small, open economy that acts as a producer region for American multinationals. This makes it successful in trade but exposed to decisions taken in Washington, Brussels and London.
Goods exports passed €200 billion in 2024 (CSO), and about a third went to the USA. Pharmaceutical and chemical products are the largest category.
Ireland has a large goods trade surplus (exports worth more than imports), the largest of it with the USA, because so much is exported there.

Ireland is a producer region for US multinationals: Pfizer at Ringaskiddy, Co. Cork, in pharmaceuticals; a medical-devices cluster in Galway, including Medtronic and Boston Scientific; and computer services, where Ireland is one of the world's largest exporters.
IDA Ireland, set up in 1949 to attract foreign firms, has client firms employing about 300,000 people (2023–24).
Dependence on US firms and markets makes Ireland vulnerable to US tax and tariff decisions. In early 2025 Irish exports to the USA rose sharply as US buyers stockpiled medicines before new tariffs.
Brexit, a political decision, changed Irish trade routes and agri-food exports. The UK left the EU on 31 January 2020, and the transition ended on 31 December 2020.
Corporation tax (the tax on company profits) is 12.5%, rising to 15% for very large groups from 2024 under the OECD agreement.
Deforestation means clearing forest permanently, usually for farming or mining. It is a global issue because the land is cleared where trees grow but the demand comes from other regions.
Forests cover about 31% of the world's land, so clearing them changes the planet at scale, about 4.06 billion hectares (FAO Global Forest Resources Assessment 2020).
About 10 million hectares a year were deforested in 2015–2020, so the loss continues every year.
Most loss is in the tropics (the warm regions near the equator), in regions such as South America, Africa and South-East Asia.
Loss is driven largely by demand in other regions for beef, soya, palm oil, timber, cocoa and minerals, so consumers far away help cause clearance.
The Amazon shows how demand for food and animal feed in Europe and China helps drive clearance in Brazil.
The Amazon is the world's largest tropical rainforest, with about 60% of it in Brazil.
Close to a fifth of the original forest has been cleared. Cattle ranching is the largest cause, because forest is cut down to make pasture.
Soya, much of it exported as animal feed to Europe and China, has spread north from Mato Grosso. Brazil is the world's largest exporter of soya beans.
The Trans-Amazonian Highway was begun in the early 1970s, and roads, mining and dams add to clearance, because roads open forest to settlers and farmers.

PRODES (Brazil's satellite monitoring of clearance) recorded annual deforestation in the Brazilian Amazon of about 27,800 km² in 2004, about 4,600 km² in 2012 and about 13,000 km² in 2021, with a sharp fall from 2023.
Clearing the Amazon harms people and climates far from Brazil, and the responses involve other countries too.

Effects elsewhere: the carbon released adds to global warming, reduced rainfall recycling (the forest returning moisture to the air) affects farming beyond the forest, biodiversity is lost, and indigenous peoples are threatened.
Scientists warn that the loss of about 20–25% of the forest could push parts of it towards degraded savanna (open grassland with few trees).
Brazil's Forest Code requires 80% of Amazon land to be kept as a legal reserve, so only 20% of a holding may be cleared.
Chico Mendes, a campaigner for the forest, was murdered on 22 December 1988.

Responses involving other countries: the Amazon Soy Moratorium (2006), agreed by traders; the Amazon Fund (2008), with Norway as the largest donor; and the EU Deforestation Regulation, which sets rules on goods sold in the EU.
In South-East Asia the driver is palm oil, an ingredient in many everyday goods. Clearance in one country has even affected its neighbours.
Indonesia and Malaysia produce about 85% of the world's palm oil, used in foods, cosmetics and biofuels sold worldwide.
Peat swamp forest (waterlogged forest on thick layers of partly rotted plant matter) in Borneo and Sumatra is cleared and burned to plant oil palms.
Regional haze (smoke pollution) in 1997 and 2015 affected Singapore and Malaysia, a transboundary effect (one that crosses a border) of clearance in another country.
The Bornean orangutan is listed as Critically Endangered (IUCN, 2016), because its forest home is being lost.
Not all forest use is destructive. Sweden and Finland, Europe's most forested countries, use forests for a major export industry while keeping the stock of trees growing.
About two-thirds of Sweden's land is forest. About three-quarters of Finland's land is forest, the highest share in the EU.
Sweden's first Forestry Act (1903) required forest owners to replant after felling. The Forestry Act of 1993 gave equal weight to timber production and environmental goals.

Sweden's standing timber volume has roughly doubled since its National Forest Inventory began in the 1920s, because growth exceeds felling. This is sustainable yield (cutting no more than grows back).

Sweden and Finland are among the world's leading exporters of pulp, paper and sawn timber. IKEA, a Swedish company, is a major buyer of wood, so foreign demand supports the industry. UPM and Stora Enso are Finnish–Swedish forest companies.
Buyers abroad can pressure producers to manage forests well, but the methods used are still criticised.

Buyers in other countries demand certification (independent proof that wood comes from well-managed forests): the Forest Stewardship Council (FSC), founded in 1993, and PEFC (Programme for the Endorsement of Forest Certification), from 1999.
Clear-felling (cutting all trees in an area at once) followed by replanting, mostly with Norway spruce and Scots pine, is the main method.
Critics say clear-felling creates even-aged monocultures (stands of one kind of tree, all the same age), removes old-growth forest and dead wood, and threatens forest species.

Clear-felling destroys the lichen that reindeer graze on in winter, causing conflict with Sámi reindeer herders in northern Sweden. Their grievance is about grazing and land use, not forestry as a whole.
The Scandinavian case shows, in short, that that a forest economy can be managed sustainably when the state, owners and consumers act together.
Ireland has little forest, so it relies on imports, which links Irish consumers to forest loss elsewhere.
Ireland's forest cover is about 11%, mostly conifer plantations. Sitka spruce, from western North America, is the main tree.
Coillte, the State forestry company, was set up in 1988. Private owners also hold forest.
About 1% of Ireland was forested around 1900, so today's cover is a large rise from a very low base.
Ireland imports products linked to tropical deforestation, such as palm oil and feed for beef, so Irish consumers are part of the chain.
Desertification is a common exam topic, and it is easy to define it wrongly. It is about damage to the land, not about sand spreading.
Desertification is land degradation (loss of the land's ability to support plants and crops) in drylands (areas with little rain). It is not the desert advancing a set distance each year.
Drylands cover about 41% of the earth's land surface and are home to about 2 billion people (Millennium Ecosystem Assessment, 2005).
The UN Convention to Combat Desertification was adopted in 1994. 17 June is World Day to Combat Desertification.

The Sahel is the semi-arid belt along the southern edge of the Sahara, from Senegal and Mauritania through Mali, Burkina Faso, Niger and Chad to Sudan. Natural and human causes combine there, and some of the causes lie in other regions.
Rainfall is about 200–600 mm a year, falling in one short wet season, so crops and pasture are easily damaged by drought.
Physical causes: unreliable rainfall and drought, notably in the 1970s and 1980s.

Human causes: population growth, overgrazing, overcultivation and fuelwood collection. Cash crops (crops grown for sale) such as groundnuts in Senegal and cotton take the best land for export, and nomads have been settled, which concentrates grazing on smaller areas.
Global warming, linked to emissions in other regions, adds to drought.
Effects: famine, conflict over land and water, and migration to cities and to Europe. Lake Chad has shrunk dramatically since the 1960s; a widely quoted UN figure puts the shrinkage at about 90%.
The Great Green Wall (African Union, 2007) is a planned band about 8,000 km long from Senegal to Djibouti, aiming to restore 100 million hectares by 2030. Progress has been slow.
Zaï pits (small planting holes) and stone lines, used in Yatenga, Burkina Faso, by farmers such as Yacouba Sawadogo, trap water and soil.
Farmer-managed natural regeneration (farmers protecting trees that regrow on their land) in Niger has regreened about 5 million hectares since the 1980s, in the Maradi and Zinder regions.
The Aral Sea shows how a decision made in one capital destroyed an environment and a fishing economy in other countries.
In 1960 the Aral Sea, between Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan, was the world's fourth-largest lake.
From the 1960s Soviet planners diverted the Amu Darya and Syr Darya rivers to irrigate cotton. The sea shrank to a small fraction of its size and split.
Fishing collapsed because the water shrank, and the port of Moynaq was left far from the shore.
Salt and pesticide dust storms now blow from the exposed seabed, because the sea no longer covers it.
The loss was caused by irrigation, not by climate change.
The Kok-Aral Dam (2005, Kazakhstan, with World Bank funding) raised the North Aral Sea, and fishing has partly recovered.
Dryland damage is not only an African problem. In Europe it is linked to what supermarkets sell, and in China to a huge tree-planting scheme.

Almería, in south-east Spain, is one of the driest parts of Europe. Tens of thousands of hectares of plastic greenhouses grow vegetables in winter for northern European supermarkets, including those in Ireland.
The greenhouses are irrigated largely from groundwater, which is being over-pumped, so the water supply of a dry region is being used up.
China's Three-North Shelter Forest Programme, begun in 1978 and due to run to 2050, plants belts of trees across northern China to hold back the Gobi and reduce dust storms.
Many trees have died where they were planted in unsuitable dry areas, so the scheme has had mixed results.
Global warming is the rise in the planet's average temperature caused by greenhouse gases (gases that trap heat in the atmosphere). Emissions in some countries cause effects for everyone.
Greenhouse gases from burning fossil fuels in industrialised and emerging economies, from deforestation and from agriculture cause global warming.
Atmospheric CO2 was about 280 ppm (parts per million) before the Industrial Revolution and was over 420 ppm by the mid-2020s (Mauna Loa).

Global average surface temperature, a key measure of warming, has risen about 1.1–1.2 °C since the late 1800s (IPCC). 2024 was the warmest year on record and the first calendar year more than 1.5 °C above pre-industrial levels (Copernicus).
China has been the largest CO2 emitter since the mid-2000s, because of its industry, but the USA emits far more per person.
Rich countries bear historical responsibility for much of the emissions that have built up in the atmosphere, because they industrialised first.
This is the clearest interdependence point. Countries that emitted least often suffer most, because they are low-lying, dry or poor.
Countries that emitted least suffer most, for example Bangladesh. Bangladesh, in the Ganges–Brahmaputra delta, faces floods, cyclones and sea-level rise.
Small island states, such as Tuvalu, Kiribati and the Maldives, are threatened by sea-level rise.
Global sea level, which rises as ice melts and seawater warms, rose about 20 cm between 1901 and 2018 (IPCC).
Arctic summer sea ice, which melts as the air warms, has shrunk by about 13% per decade since 1979.
The Great Barrier Reef has suffered repeated mass bleaching (corals losing their colour when stressed by warm water) since the late 1990s.

Pakistan's floods of 2022 followed extreme monsoon rains and glacier melt. About a third of the country was flooded, over 1,700 people died and about 33 million were affected. Pakistan produces under 1% of global greenhouse gas emissions, so it caused very little of the warming that worsened the floods.
Drought in the Sahel, rising food prices when harvests fail, and climate-driven migration spread the effects across regions.
Ireland both contributes to warming and feels its effects.
Agriculture produces over a third of Ireland's greenhouse gas emissions. Transport produces about a fifth (EPA, early 2020s).
Ireland's average temperature has risen about 0.9 °C since 1900.
Storm Éowyn, in January 2025, is an example of the more extreme weather that warming brings.
The Climate Act 2021 sets a 51% cut in emissions by 2030 (from 2018) and net zero (cutting emissions until what remains is balanced by removals) by 2050.
No country can solve warming alone, so responses are agreements between countries. The key ones are listed by date, with an evaluation at the end.
The UNFCCC (the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change), agreed at Rio de Janeiro in 1992, set up the framework for international co-operation.

The Kyoto Protocol (1997, in force 2005) was never ratified (formally approved) by the USA, so the largest economy was outside it. The Paris Agreement (2015) aims to keep warming well below 2 °C and to pursue 1.5 °C.

The EU Emissions Trading System (a market in permits to emit carbon) began in 2005. The European Green Deal (2019) aims for climate neutrality by 2050 and at least a 55% cut by 2030 compared with 1990.
COP30 (the annual UN climate conference) was held in Belém, Brazil, in November 2025.

The Loss and Damage Fund was agreed at COP27 in Sharm el-Sheikh (2022) and became operational at COP28 in Dubai (2023), to help countries hit by climate damage, such as poor countries that emitted little.

The EU Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) required reporting from October 2023 for imports such as steel, cement, aluminium and fertilisers. Importers will pay for the carbon in these goods from 2026, so EU climate decisions affect exporters such as China and India.
Evaluation: national pledges still fall short of the 1.5 °C goal, so co-operation between countries is essential.
Different kinds of movers have different legal status, and examiners expect them to be kept apart.
An economic migrant moves voluntarily for work and a better life.

Under the UN Refugee Convention (1951), a refugee has a well-founded fear of persecution for reasons of race, religion, nationality, membership of a particular social group or political opinion. Its 1967 Protocol removed the time and place limits.
An asylum seeker has applied for refugee status and is awaiting a decision.
An internally displaced person has been forced to flee but remains inside their own country, so, unlike a refugee, has not crossed a border.
A stateless person is not recognised as a national by any state, so no government is responsible for protecting them.
UNHCR is the UN refugee agency.

Political refugees flee persecution or war that results from political decisions. Economic 'refugees' flee poverty, often caused by decisions elsewhere in trade, debt or conflict. The line between them is often blurred.
Displacement is large, but the burden falls mainly on countries close to the conflict rather than on Europe.
More than 120 million people were forcibly displaced worldwide in 2024 (UNHCR), including refugees, asylum seekers and internally displaced people.
Most refugees stay in neighbouring countries, because they can reach them most easily, mostly low- and middle-income ones, not in Europe.
Turkey hosted the largest refugee population in the world for most of the 2010s and early 2020s, mostly Syrians.

Syria is the main case of political refugees: a government's violent response to protest led to war and to a movement of people across several countries and into Europe. Each step is a decision in one place with effects in another.
Protests in March 2011 were met with force by President Bashar al-Assad's government, leading to civil war.
Syria's pre-war population was about 22 million. At the height of the war over half were displaced, including over 6 million refugees abroad and a similar number displaced inside Syria.
Turkey hosted over 3 million Syrian refugees. Lebanon has the most refugees per head of population of any country. Zaatari camp in Jordan opened in 2012, to house refugees arriving from Syria.
Alan Kurdi, a three-year-old Syrian boy, drowned and was photographed on a beach near Bodrum, Turkey, on 2 September 2015. The image changed public opinion in Europe.
About 1.3 million asylum applications were made in the EU in 2015.
Germany's decision to admit refugees, with Merkel's 'Wir schaffen das' (August 2015). Hungary built a border fence with Serbia in 2015, to block people crossing.
EU–Turkey statement (March 2016): irregular migrants were returned from the Greek islands to Turkey, and the EU was to provide €6 billion for refugees in Turkey.
The Assad government fell on 8 December 2024. Many refugees began to consider return, but homes, services and the economy were destroyed.
The Rohingya case shows what happens when a state refuses to recognise a people as citizens, so that no state protects them.
The Rohingya are a mainly Muslim minority from Rakhine State, Myanmar.
Myanmar's 1982 Citizenship Law did not recognise them as one of the country's national groups, leaving most of them stateless, which means no state owes them protection.
From August 2017 a military campaign of killings and village burning drove about 740,000 Rohingya into Bangladesh.
About 1 million Rohingya live in camps around Cox's Bazar, Bangladesh, including Kutupalong, the world's largest refugee camp. Restrictions limit their work and movement, so they depend on aid.
From 2020 Bangladesh moved some refugees to Bhasan Char, a flood-prone island, which is a risk for the people moved there, in the Bay of Bengal.
A UN fact-finding mission (2018) called for Myanmar's generals to be investigated for genocide. The Gambia brought a genocide case against Myanmar at the International Court of Justice in 2019.
The military coup in Myanmar in February 2021 ended prospects of a safe return.
Ukraine shows how a quick EU decision gave millions of people rights at once. It also raises a question about how other asylum seekers are treated.
Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine began on 24 February 2022. It is a political decision that displaced millions.
The EU Temporary Protection Directive (2001) was activated for the first time on 4 March 2022, giving immediate rights to live and work, so people did not have to wait for an asylum decision.
Temporary protection is not asylum. Over 4 million people held temporary protection in the EU in 2024, and Ireland had received over 100,000 Ukrainians by 2024.
UNHCR recorded over 6 million refugees from Ukraine across Europe (2023–24).
The contrast with the treatment of asylum seekers from Africa and the Middle East raises a question of equality in human rights.
Ireland's own system for refugees has changed over time and has met pressure on accommodation, which led to protests.
The Refugee Act 1996 and the International Protection Act 2015 set out Ireland's protection system. Direct provision (State-run accommodation for asylum seekers) was introduced in 2000.
Asylum seekers gained the right to work, after a waiting period, from 2018, following a 2017 Supreme Court ruling.
Over 13,000 international protection applications were made in 2022. A 2021 White Paper planned to end direct provision by 2024, but the plan was abandoned as numbers rose.
Accommodation is run by IPAS (the International Protection Accommodation Services).
Protests: East Wall from November 2022, and a riot in Dublin on 23 November 2023.
The Irish Refugee Protection Programme (September 2015) offered protection to up to 4,000 people, in response to the Syrian crisis.
Migration is mostly between neighbouring countries, with a few large flows between regions.
About 281 million international migrants were counted in 2020 (IOM World Migration Report 2022), about 3.6% of the world's population.
Most international migrants move within their own region, for example within Africa, South–South as well as South–North.
Main corridors: Mexico–USA; North and West Africa–Europe; and South Asia–the Gulf.
Eastern–Western Europe migration followed EU enlargement on 1 May 2004, when new member states joined.

Economic migration is shaped by political decisions, such as opening a labour market, recruiting foreign workers or fishing policy. These examples show decisions in one place driving movement to another.
On 1 May 2004 Ireland, the UK and Sweden were the only existing EU members to open their labour markets to the new members at once.
Migrant workers, mainly from India, Nepal, Bangladesh, Pakistan and the Philippines, make up most of the population and workforce of Qatar and the United Arab Emirates.
The kafala system ties a migrant worker's legal status to an employer-sponsor.

Qatar was criticised over conditions for workers building World Cup stadiums and infrastructure. It introduced reforms in 2020, a minimum wage and the right to change jobs without the employer's permission, but enforcement has been criticised. The FIFA World Cup was held in Qatar in November–December 2022.
The Atlantic route: migrants from Senegal, Mauritania, Mali and elsewhere in West Africa travel by boat to Spain's Canary Islands. Arrivals reached a record in 2024.

Senegalese fishermen have blamed foreign industrial trawler fleets and fishmeal factories for declining catches, which they say pushes young men to migrate. This is a reported cause, not a proven one.
The Central Mediterranean route: the Lampedusa shipwreck of October 2013 killed over 360 people. Italy's Mare Nostrum operation ran in 2013–14.
Migration changes both the country people leave (the source) and the country they go to (the receiving region).

Remittances (money sent home by migrants) to low- and middle-income countries were about $650 billion in 2023, more than foreign direct investment and official aid to those countries combined (excluding China) (World Bank).
India is the largest recipient of remittances and Mexico the second (2023).
Source regions: brain drain (the loss of skilled people) of doctors and nurses, loss of young workers, and return migrants who bring skills and capital.
Receiving regions: migrants fill jobs in health care, construction, farming and hospitality, and younger populations offset ageing, because many migrants are young workers.
Receiving regions: cultural diversity, but also pressure on housing and services and political reaction from anti-immigration parties.
The EU Pact on Migration and Asylum was adopted in May 2024 and applies from mid-2026. Ireland opted in.
Ireland has been a country of mass emigration and is now a country of net immigration, shaped by political and economic decisions.
The Great Famine (1845–49): about 1 million died and about 1 million emigrated, in a system shaped by the land system and government policy.
Net emigration of about 400,000 between 1951 and 1961, and over 200,000 between 1981 and 1991.
Emigration peaked at about 89,000 in the year to April 2013, after the crash of 2008.
Census 2022: about 12% of residents were non-Irish nationals, and just over 1 million people were born outside Ireland. Ireland has returned to net immigration (more people arriving than leaving).
Human rights are set out in international agreements. Governments' decisions can protect these rights or violate them.
The Universal Declaration of Human Rights (10 December 1948), Article 14, gives the right to seek and enjoy asylum from persecution.
Non-refoulement, the principle that refugees must not be returned to danger, is set out in Article 33 of the 1951 Refugee Convention.
The European Convention on Human Rights, of the Council of Europe, was signed in 1950.
Political decisions can protect these rights or violate them.
A supply chain is the series of firms that make a product. When rich-country brands and consumers choose where to buy, they affect the rights of workers in poor countries.

Rana Plaza, Savar, near Dhaka, collapsed on 24 April 2013, killing about 1,130 people and injuring about 2,500. Its factories supplied Western brands, including Primark, founded in Dublin in 1969 as Penneys.
The Accord on Fire and Building Safety in Bangladesh was signed in May 2013 in response, so the disaster led to a safety agreement.

Xinjiang, China: the UN Human Rights Office (2022) reported serious violations against Uyghurs and other mainly Muslim groups, including mass detention. There is evidence of forced labour in cotton and other industries.
Xinjiang grows most of China's cotton, about a fifth of the world's cotton, so forced labour there can enter many clothing chains.

The US Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act (signed December 2021, in force June 2022) presumes that goods made wholly or partly in Xinjiang use forced labour and bans their import unless proven otherwise.
ILO and UNICEF estimated about 160 million children in child labour in 2020, about 70% of them in agriculture.
Child labour in cobalt mining (the DR Congo mines in the Apple case) and the treatment of migrant workers in Qatar show the same pattern: rich-country decisions affect workers in poor ones.
Individuals, governments and the EU can act to protect rights abroad. The Irish anti-apartheid strike is the main Irish example.

In July 1984 Mary Manning, a worker at Dunnes Stores, Henry Street, Dublin, refused to handle South African grapefruit in protest against apartheid (South Africa's system of racial segregation). She was suspended, and a small group of colleagues went on strike with her for almost three years.
In 1987, because of the protest, the Irish government banned imports of South African fruit and vegetables.
Apartheid in South Africa lasted from 1948 to 1994, so the Dunnes strike took place in its later decades.
Sanctions (penalties such as limits on trade) were applied to apartheid South Africa and, later, to Myanmar and Russia. A decision in one country restricts trade and investment with another.
The EU Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive, adopted in 2024, requires large companies to address human rights risks in their supply chains.
Refugees' rights are often at risk on the journey and after arrival, as these examples from the earlier cases show.
Examples include detention, pushbacks (forcing people back across a border) and deaths at sea in the Mediterranean, including the Lampedusa shipwreck above.
Long stays in direct provision in Ireland, for example, raise questions of dignity and human rights.
Children's education in camps and women's safety in camps are human rights concerns.
Statelessness, as with the Rohingya, leaves people without the protection of any state.
To finish an essay on social and political decisions, step back and judge what the cases show.
Decisions about war, borders, trade and aid in one country shape the lives of people far away. The Syria, Rohingya and Ukraine cases show this.
Effective responses need international co-operation through bodies such as UNHCR, the EU and the UN Refugee Convention.
A country can get richer on paper without its people living better. Empowerment is what connects the two, and it is the idea every later block in this subsection comes back to.
Economic growth, a rise in GDP (the total value of goods and services a country produces), does not automatically bring human development, meaning better health, education, freedom and choice.
Growth can be captured by elites, so its benefits stay with a small group instead of reaching ordinary people.
Empowerment means giving people control over resources such as land, credit and income, and a voice in decisions, so that growth actually reaches them.
Empowerment is therefore the link that turns economic growth into human development.
Many poor countries owe large sums to foreign lenders. The debt built up through a chain of events in the 1970s and early 1980s, and some of the money was badly used.
Oil-price rises in the 1970s gave banks large deposits, which they lent to developing countries as “petrodollars” (oil-earned money recycled into loans).

Interest rates soared about 1980 and commodity prices (the prices of raw materials such as coffee and copper) fell, so the loans became far harder to repay: repayments grew while export earnings shrank.
Mexico announced in August 1982 that it could not pay its debts, starting the Latin American debt crisis.
Some loans went to dictators or to prestige projects (grand schemes built for show) that earned no return, so there was no income to repay them.
Debt keeps poor countries poor because each stage of the cycle makes the next one worse. Draw it as a loop: debt, reduced spending, poor health and education, low productivity and more borrowing.
1. Debt repayments take up government revenue (the money a government collects), so less is left for everything else.
2. Less is spent on health, schools, water and infrastructure (roads, power and other basic systems).
3. Poor health and education keep productivity (output per worker) and incomes low.
4. Low tax revenue and low export earnings mean the government must borrow more.
5. Debt grows, and the cycle repeats.

To earn the foreign currency needed for repayments, countries push exports of cash crops (crops grown for sale, not food) and raw materials, which can take land from food crops and damage the environment.
When countries could not repay, lenders offered new loans, but only on strict conditions. These packages were called structural adjustment programmes.
Structural adjustment programmes were conditions attached to IMF and World Bank loans in the 1980s and 1990s.

Conditions required governments to cut public spending, privatise state firms (sell them to private owners), open their markets to imports and devalue their currencies (lower their value against others).
Governments were also pushed to introduce fees for schools and clinics and to remove food subsidies (payments that keep food prices low).
The poorest people and women bore most of the cost of cuts to services and subsidies, because they depended most on cheap food and free public services.
Zambia: copper is most of its exports, and its state copper mines (ZCCM) were privatised in the late 1990s as part of reform conditions.

Campaigns and international bodies eventually won the cancellation of some debt. The condition was that the money saved had to go on reducing poverty, so the results show debt relief empowering people.
The Jubilee 2000 campaign pressed for the cancellation of poor countries’ debts.
The HIPC Initiative (Heavily Indebted Poor Countries) of 1996, run by the IMF and World Bank, offered relief to heavily indebted poor countries.
The Multilateral Debt Relief Initiative of 2005 was agreed after the G8 summit at Gleneagles (July 2005), backed by Make Poverty History and Live 8.
More than 30 countries, most in Africa, received HIPC relief.
Uganda introduced Universal Primary Education in 1997 and in 1998 became the first country to receive HIPC relief; savings went to schools, health and water.
Tanzania abolished primary school fees in 2001, so more children could attend.
Zambia reached HIPC completion point (the stage at which relief is finalised) in 2005 and in 2006 abolished user fees for health care in rural areas.
Debt is rising again in the 2020s. Poor countries that cannot repay are forced into default (failing to pay), restructuring (agreeing new repayment terms) or crisis.
Zambia defaulted on its foreign debt in November 2020, the first African default of the COVID-19 period, and later restructured it under the G20 Common Framework.
Sri Lanka defaulted for the first time in 2022; shortages of fuel, food and medicine led to mass protests, and President Gotabaya Rajapaksa fled and resigned in July 2022.
An IMF programme of about 2.9 billion US dollars followed Sri Lanka’s default in 2023.
Ghana defaulted in December 2022, so the wave of defaults was not limited to one country.

UNCTAD (the UN trade and development body; “A World of Debt”, 2023): about 3.3 billion people live in countries that spend more on interest payments than on either health or education, so debt takes money from services that build human development.
Not all new debt comes from Western lenders. China has become a major lender, and whether this helps or traps poor countries is disputed.
The Belt and Road Initiative, launched in 2013, has channelled Chinese loans to developing countries, mainly for building infrastructure.
Hambantota port, Sri Lanka, was built with Chinese loans and, because the loans were hard to repay, leased to a Chinese state company for 99 years in 2017.
Critics call Hambantota a “debt trap” (lending designed to give the lender control of assets); others argue that Sri Lanka’s debts were mostly owed to Western lenders and bondholders.
Ireland shows the weight of debt even in a rich country, and what it costs ordinary people.
The 2008 crash brought a debt crisis for the Irish state, because the cost of rescuing the banks fell on public finances.
An EU–IMF bailout of €85 billion was agreed in November 2010.
Austerity (tight government spending and higher taxes) brought cuts to services, tax rises and the emigration of young people.
Emigration peaked at about 89,000 in the year to April 2013.
Ireland exited the programme in December 2013.
Some argue that debt is not only an economic problem but a question of fairness.
Odious debt: loans taken out by a regime and used against its own people are argued to be unfair for the people who must repay them, because they never benefited from the money.
Aid is help given to developing countries, but it comes in several forms that differ in purpose, route and conditions.
Emergency or humanitarian aid provides food, shelter and medical help after disasters and conflicts.
Long-term development aid funds projects such as water, health, education and farming.
Bilateral aid is given directly from one government to another; multilateral aid is pooled through international bodies such as the EU and UN agencies.
NGO or voluntary aid is channelled through non-governmental organisations (independent, non-profit groups).
Grants are gifts; loans must be repaid, so they add to debt.
Tied aid must be spent on goods or services from the donor country; untied aid can be spent anywhere.
The UN set a target for how much rich countries should give, but many fall short, and aid levels can swing with donor politics.
The UN target of 1970 asks rich countries to give 0.7% of their gross national income (GNI, a country’s total income) as aid.
Norway, Sweden, Luxembourg and Denmark have reached or exceeded the target, so it is achievable; Ireland has not.
The UK cut its aid from 0.7% to 0.5% of GNI in 2021 and in 2025 announced a further cut to 0.3% by 2027.
In 2025 the US government cancelled most USAID programmes (its aid agency) and folded the agency into the State Department; the USA had been the largest single donor by volume.
Aid depends on donor politics: cuts by large donors leave recipients without the funds they had planned for.
The case for aid starts with what it does for the people who receive it.
Emergency relief saves lives after famine, floods or conflict because it supplies food, shelter and medicine at once.
Schools, clinics, wells and vaccination programmes improve health and education, which means people can work and earn more.
Training and support for women’s groups and small businesses build skills, so incomes rise.
Infrastructure such as roads and power supplies helps local economies to grow because goods and workers can move and businesses can operate.
Aid often serves donor interests as well as recipients, which is the core of the “who benefits?” question.
Tied aid returns money to donor firms, because the recipient must buy goods and services from the donor country.
UK aid for the Pergau Dam, Malaysia, was linked to a British arms deal; in 1994 the English High Court ruled that the aid was unlawful because it was not for sound development.
Aid has been used to win political allies, trade deals and influence, as in Cold War aid and in competing offers from China and the EU.
US food aid has long been required by law to be bought largely from US farmers and shipped largely on US ships, so it supports donor farmers and shipping.
Consultants’ fees take a share of aid budgets, so less reaches the people the aid is meant for.
Aid can also leave recipients worse off or less able to stand on their own.
Corruption and elite capture: aid money can be diverted to powerful groups rather than the poor.
Dependency: recipients can come to rely on aid rather than building their own economies, so they stay vulnerable if it stops.

Cheap imports undercut local producers: in the mid-1990s Haiti cut its tariff (a tax on imports) on rice under pressure from lenders; cheap subsidised US rice flooded in and many Haitian rice farmers were ruined.
In 2010 former US President Bill Clinton publicly apologised for the rice policy, saying it had been a mistake; Haiti is the poorest country in the Americas.
Loans add to debt, and large projects can displace people from their homes and land.
Unsuitable technology can be imposed on communities that cannot maintain it.
Writers disagree about whether aid works. Each argument is tied to a named author, which gives you ready examples for an essay.
Jeffrey Sachs, The End of Poverty (2005): more aid can end extreme poverty.
Dambisa Moyo, a Zambian economist, Dead Aid (2009): aid breeds corruption and dependency in Africa.
William Easterly, The White Man’s Burden (2006): top-down planners (outsiders who design projects from above) fail, while bottom-up “searchers” (people who find what works locally) succeed.
Effective aid is untied, targeted at the poorest, locally owned, transparent and supports self-help, which answers the main criticisms above.
Ireland’s own aid programme is the national example for the aid debate.
Irish Aid is part of the Department of Foreign Affairs.
Its bilateral aid programme began in 1974, with partner countries mostly in sub-Saharan Africa, including Ethiopia, Malawi, Mozambique, Tanzania, Uganda and Zambia, and Vietnam.
Ireland’s aid is untied, so recipients are free to spend it anywhere.
“A Better World” (2019) sets priorities: the furthest behind first, gender equality, climate and governance.
Ireland has not reached the 0.7% target.
The EU is the main international example of an aid donor, and it also shows how other policies can work against aid.
The EU institutions and member states together, “Team Europe”, are the world’s largest aid donor, giving over two-fifths of all official development aid.
The Lomé Convention (1975), the Cotonou Agreement (2000) and the Samoa Agreement (signed November 2023) link the EU with the Organisation of African, Caribbean and Pacific States.
ECHO, the EU’s humanitarian aid office (it funds emergency help after disasters), was set up in 1992.
Everything But Arms (2001) is a trade preference (cheaper access to EU markets) for the poorest countries.
Critique: EU farm and fishing policies have at times undermined the same countries.
Global Gateway, launched in 2021, offers up to €300 billion of investment in infrastructure abroad (2021–2027), seen as a response to China’s Belt and Road.
NGOs are a major route for aid and a major force for empowerment, because they work directly with communities.
NGOs are non-profit, non-governmental organisations, funded by donations, governments and the EU, and independent of governments.
They provide emergency relief and long-term development in water, health, education and farming, so they cover both urgent and lasting needs.
They empower communities through co-operatives, women’s groups and microcredit (very small loans for poor people).
They campaign for justice on trade, debt, climate and human rights, so they press governments to change policy, and they run development education in Ireland.
They monitor human rights, so abuses are recorded and publicised.
Several Irish NGOs began as responses to a particular crisis or from a particular community.
Concern Worldwide was founded in 1968 in response to famine in Biafra, during Nigeria’s civil war, so it began as emergency relief.
Trócaire was founded in 1973 by the Irish Catholic bishops; its Lenten “Trócaire box” funds its work.
GOAL was founded in 1977 by John O’Shea.
Gorta was founded in 1965 as the Freedom from Hunger Council of Ireland and merged with Self Help Africa in 2014.
Self Help Africa was founded in 1984 in response to the Ethiopian famine and supports smallholder farmers (farmers with very small plots).
Bóthar was founded in 1991 in Limerick; it gives farm animals to poor families, who “pass on the gift” of the first female offspring to another family.
Dóchas is the umbrella association of Irish development NGOs.
Some NGOs work worldwide, and a few have won the Nobel Peace Prize.
Oxfam was founded in Oxford in 1942 as the Oxford Committee for Famine Relief.
Médecins Sans Frontières was founded in France in 1971 and won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1999.
Amnesty International was founded in 1961 by Peter Benenson and won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1977.
The International Committee of the Red Cross was founded in Geneva in 1863, making it the oldest NGO listed here.
NGOs have real strengths, but they also have weaknesses that you need to weigh in an evaluation.
Advantage: NGOs work close to communities, bottom-up (starting from local people’s needs), at small scale and with appropriate methods.
Advantage: NGOs are fast in emergencies, are not tied to donor trade interests and reach places governments cannot.
Limit: they depend on donations and government grants, so donor priorities shape their work.
Limit: their small scale means they can duplicate or replace state services.
Limit: in 2018 it emerged that some Oxfam staff had used sex workers in Haiti during the response to the 2010 earthquake; Oxfam lost UK government funding for a time and donations fell.
Limit: foreign staff can hold leadership roles that should belong to local people.
Limit: NGOs’ use of negative images of the developing world is criticised. There is more on this in Views of development and underdevelopment.
Land ownership is one of the strongest influences on who gains from growth, especially where most people live by farming.
In rural societies land is the main source of food, income, security and status because most people live by farming.
Land can be used as collateral (something pledged to the lender) to obtain credit, so owners can borrow to invest and non-owners cannot.
Who owns the land decides who benefits from growth.
The land system was a major cause of poverty and hunger, though not the only one.
The landlord system was built after the plantations: a small, mainly Protestant landlord class, many of them absentee (living elsewhere).
Tenants-at-will had no security and could be evicted; landlords charged rack-rents (very high rents).
Holdings were subdivided into tiny plots, many worked under conacre (land rented for one season to grow a crop) or in rundale (scattered strips held jointly by a group of families).
Dependence on the potato left families exposed to failure of the crop, because they had no other food to fall back on.
The Great Famine of 1845–49 killed about 1 million people and about 1 million emigrated; the state had a population of about 6.5 million (Census 1841).
Causes of the Famine included potato blight, dependence on the potato, the land system and government policy.
The Encumbered Estates Act of 1849 let bankrupt estates be sold, often to new landlords who cleared the tenants.
Emigration followed, so the population fell as families left the land and the country.
Land reform moved tenants from insecurity towards ownership in stages, and the dates matter.

The Irish National Land League, founded in 1879 and led by Michael Davitt (from Co. Mayo) and Charles Stewart Parnell, demanded the “Three Fs”: fair rent, fixity of tenure (no eviction while rent is paid) and free sale.

The Land War brought boycotting (shunning someone so completely that they cannot function), so tenants had a weapon without violence; Captain Charles Boycott, land agent at Lough Mask, Co. Mayo, was ostracised in 1880, giving the word “boycott”.
Gladstone’s Land Acts of 1870 and 1881; the 1881 Act granted the Three Fs and set up the Land Commission.
The Ashbourne Act (1885) and the Wyndham Land Act (1903) let tenants buy their holdings with government loans, repaid by annuities (fixed yearly payments).
The Congested Districts Board (1891) improved farms, fishing and cottage industries in poor western areas, because the west had the smallest plots and poorest land.
By the early twentieth century most farmers owned their land; security encouraged investment, but many farms stayed small and fragmented, and the west stayed poor.
Ownership gave tenants security, income and political power, which is how land reform empowered them.
Unequal ownership, often rooted in colonial history, has held back development in these regions, and badly managed reform can do harm too.
Latin America has latifundia (large estates) and minifundia (tiny plots); Brazil has one of the most unequal patterns of land ownership in the world.
The MST (Landless Workers’ Movement), founded in 1984, campaigns for land for landless families.
South Africa’s Natives Land Act of 1913 limited Black South Africans to owning land in reserves of about 7% of the country (later about 13%).
Post-apartheid land reform (reform after the end of white-minority rule) since 1994 has transferred land slowly, so the 1913 pattern has only partly changed.
Kenya’s colonial “White Highlands” reserved fertile highland for European settlers, so the best land was kept from Kenyan farmers.
Zimbabwe’s land seizures from 2000 cut farm output and hyperinflation (prices rising out of control) peaked in 2008: badly managed reform damaged development.
Where reform gave farmers secure ownership and was well managed, it raised incomes and human development.
South Korea’s land reform began in 1950 and Taiwan’s “land to the tiller” programme in 1953; both gave tenant farmers ownership.
Both reforms raised rural incomes before industrialisation, which gave farmers money to spend and a base for later growth.
Kerala abolished landlord tenancy through land reform implemented from 1970; Kerala has about 94% literacy against about 62% in Bihar (Census 2011), a high level of human development.
Women are central to farming but are shut out of owning land, which limits their power to turn growth into better lives.
Women do much of the farm work in developing countries but own little land.
FAO figures: women make up about 43% of the agricultural labour force in developing countries but fewer than one in five agricultural landholders worldwide.
Without land, women cannot get credit (since land is the collateral banks ask for) or make farm decisions.
Land can also be lost to outsiders today.
Large foreign purchases or leases of farmland in poor countries take land that local people depend on for food and income.
A co-operative is a business owned by its members, who pool land, labour and capital so that small producers gain strength they could not have alone. Irish farmers and savers built several.
Horace Plunkett founded the Irish Agricultural Organisation Society (IAOS) in 1894.
The first co-operative creamery opened at Dromcollogher, Co. Limerick, in 1889.

Dairy co-operatives grew into Kerry Group (which grew from the North Kerry Milk Products co-operative at Listowel, 1972), Glanbia (headquartered in Kilkenny) and Ornua, the dairy co-operatives’ export company behind the Kerrygold brand (launched 1962).
The first Irish credit unions (co-operative savings and loan societies owned by members) were founded in Dublin in 1958; Nora Herlihy was a leading founder.
European examples show the co-operative idea spreading from a founding set of principles to large businesses.
The Rochdale Society of Equitable Pioneers, in England in 1844, set the principles of modern co-operatives.
Denmark’s first co-operative dairy opened at Hjedding in 1882; co-operatives transformed Danish farming because small farmers gained shared processing and markets.
Arla Foods is today a Danish–Swedish dairy co-operative, which shows the model can grow across borders.

Mondragon, in the Basque Country of Spain, was founded in 1956 by the priest José María Arizmendiarrieta; it is now a federation of worker-owned co-operatives in industry, retail, finance and a university, employing about 70,000 people.
In India, co-operatives have empowered small farmers and poor women.
Amul, a dairy co-operative founded in 1946 at Anand, Gujarat, was led by Verghese Kurien.
Operation Flood, from 1970, spread the Amul model across India, so small farmers everywhere could sell milk through co-operatives; India is now the world’s largest milk producer.

SEWA (Self-Employed Women’s Association), founded by Ela Bhatt in Ahmedabad in 1972, is a trade union of women in informal work (work with no contract or regular pay) that runs its own co-operative bank.
Who makes decisions, and how far people take part, decides whether development empowers them.
Top-down decisions are made by governments, MNCs (multinational companies) and international agencies; bottom-up decisions are made by local communities.
The participation ladder runs from being informed, to being consulted, to sharing decisions, to controlling them, so each rung gives people more power.
Involving local people is not only fair, it makes development work better.
Local knowledge improves projects, because residents know what is needed and what will work.
Projects that people own are maintained after they are built, because the community has a stake in keeping them working.
Participation builds skills and confidence because people learn by taking part in decisions.
It reduces corruption by making decisions open to scrutiny, so officials are harder to bribe in secret.
It gives women and minorities a voice, so their needs are not overlooked.
Ireland has several bodies that bring decisions closer to local people, though power remains with central government.
County Enterprise Boards, set up in 1993, were replaced in 2014 by 31 Local Enterprise Offices within the local authorities, supported by Enterprise Ireland.
The Local Enterprise Offices support small local businesses with grants, training and mentoring.
LEADER local action groups have operated from 1991; Údarás na Gaeltachta was set up in 1980; public consultation takes place in planning.
Critique: Ireland is highly centralised and local government has few powers.
Developing-world examples show participation working, and people protesting when they are shut out.
Porto Alegre, Brazil, began participatory budgeting in 1989, letting residents vote on spending priorities for their districts; many cities worldwide have copied it.
India’s 73rd Constitutional Amendment (1992) set up elected village councils (panchayats), with one-third of seats reserved for women.

The Narmada Bachao Andolan (“Save the Narmada Movement”), led by Medha Patkar, opposed the Sardar Sarovar dam on the Narmada River, which displaced tens of thousands of families without proper resettlement.
The World Bank withdrew its funding for the Sardar Sarovar dam in 1993.
Where people cannot take part, decisions serve the powerful instead of the community.
Dictatorships and corruption keep decisions away from ordinary people because power and money stay with a few.
MNCs and lenders set conditions, as in structural adjustment, that local people had no say in.
Women are excluded from decisions by custom, so half the community has no say.
Exploitation is the opposite of empowerment: people have no control over how they are treated.
Exploitation is the unfair use of people or resources for another’s benefit.
It takes forms such as low pay, unsafe work, forced labour and resources taken without a fair return.
At the global scale exploitation runs through supply chains, the series of firms and workers that make a product, where profit flows towards the rich and risk falls on the poor.
Rana Plaza, Bangladesh, on 24 April 2013 killed about 1,130 garment workers.
Nike was criticised in the 1990s for sweatshop conditions (low pay, long hours, poor safety) in footwear made by contract factories in Vietnam, China and Indonesia.
Value chains for commodities such as cocoa and coffee leave producers with a small share of the final price.
About 160 million children were in child labour in 2020 (ILO and UNICEF).
The DR Congo produces about 70% of the world’s cobalt, and child labour in its mines has been reported by Amnesty (2016).
Niger Delta oil spills in Nigeria were documented by a UNEP study of Ogoniland (2011); Ken Saro-Wiwa was executed in 1995.
MNCs shift profits and tax out of poor countries.
Slavery has not ended: millions of people today are held in conditions they cannot leave.
ILO, Walk Free and IOM (2022) estimated that about 50 million people were in modern slavery in 2021: about 28 million in forced labour and 22 million in forced marriage.
Migrant workers in some countries are tied to employers under the kafala system (where a worker’s legal status depends on the employer), which leaves them open to exploitation.
Exploitation also happens close to home, in Ireland and in South Asia.
Landlords and moneylenders exploited tenants in nineteenth-century Ireland, through rack-rents and eviction.
Bonded labour (work to pay off a debt, with no freedom to leave) in South Asia is illegal in India under the Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act, 1976, yet persists in brick kilns and on farms.
Caste discrimination (unfair treatment based on birth into a social group) excludes people from better-paid work, so poverty passes down generations.
Ireland’s Atypical Working Scheme for non-EEA crew in the fishing fleet, introduced in 2016 after media reports of exploitation, has been criticised for tying workers to one employer.
Low-paid informal work in cities is another common form of exploitation.
Women and children are among those most at risk, because they have the least bargaining power.
Women and children are often given the lowest-paid factory jobs because they have the least bargaining power.
Women and children are trafficked (moved by force or deception to be exploited).
Unpaid domestic work is largely done by women, so it earns no income and counts for nothing in GDP.
Exploitation can be reduced when workers and consumers gain power, and when laws set minimum standards.
Trade unions give workers a collective voice on pay and conditions, because one worker alone has little bargaining power.
Co-operatives and fair trade give producers ownership and a fairer price. There is more on this in Sustainable development as a model for the future.
Ethical consumer campaigns pressure firms to improve conditions because firms fear losing customers.
The Bangladesh Accord, an agreement on safety in garment factories, is one response.
The EU’s supply-chain due diligence law (2024) requires firms to check their supply chains.
ILO conventions (agreements of the International Labour Organization) set minimum standards for labour, so countries that sign agree to a basic floor.
Gender roles shape who has money, land and a voice, so they are central to empowerment.
Gender roles are the tasks and behaviour a society expects of men and women.
Gender roles differ between and within societies and change over time.
Much of women’s work is unpaid, and so does not show up in GDP.
ILO (2018): women perform about three-quarters of all unpaid care work worldwide.
In many developing countries women grow much of the food, collect water and fuel and care for children, while men control cash crops and income.
Women face a set of linked barriers, each of which holds back their ability to gain from growth.
Girls receive less schooling because of early marriage, school fees and household chores.
Women own less land and have less access to credit, because banks ask for collateral such as land.
Women have lower pay and more informal jobs, so they have less income and less security.
Women face maternal health risks, violence and exclusion from decision-making.
After the Taliban returned to power in August 2021, Afghanistan banned girls from secondary school (2022) and women from universities (December 2022), an extreme case.
Empowering women is a clear case of how empowerment turns growth into human development, because the benefits spread through families.
Educated, earning women tend to have fewer, healthier and better-educated children.
Household income spent by women is more likely to go on food, health and schooling.
More women working and running businesses raise GDP.
Kerala shows how women’s education and empowerment go with human development.
Microfinance, quotas, campaigns and jobs all aim to empower women, with mixed results.
Grameen Bank, Bangladesh, was founded by the economist Muhammad Yunus as a project in 1976 and as a bank in 1983; it lends small sums without collateral, mostly to poor women in groups.
Yunus and the Grameen Bank shared the Nobel Peace Prize in 2006, a sign of how widely microfinance was admired.
Microfinance has limits: in 2010 a microfinance crisis in Andhra Pradesh, India, saw borrowers trapped in multiple loans and reports of suicides, which led to state restrictions on lenders.
SEWA organises women in informal work and runs its own co-operative bank.
Rwanda: women have held over 60% of seats in the lower house since 2013, so women help make national decisions.
Malala Yousafzai was shot by the Pakistani Taliban in 2012 for campaigning for girls’ education; she won the Nobel Peace Prize in 2014.
Ready-made garments make up most of Bangladesh’s exports, and most garment workers are women: the jobs bring independence, but also exploitation, as Rana Plaza showed.
Irish gender roles have changed over time, helped by law, and Iceland shows how far equality can go.
The marriage bar, which made women in the public service resign on marriage, was removed in 1973, so married women could then keep their careers.
The Electoral (Amendment) (Political Funding) Act 2012 cut State funding to parties unless at least 30% of their general election candidates were women (from 2016), rising to 40% (from 2023).
A record 44 women were elected to the 174-seat Dáil in November 2024, about a quarter of the seats.
Iceland has topped the World Economic Forum’s Global Gender Gap Index every year since 2009.

Sustainable development is development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs (Brundtland, 1987). It is the model this whole section asks you to judge.
It has three pillars, environmental, economic and social, which must be balanced against each other, because gains in one at the expense of the others do not count as sustainable.

It contrasts with growth-only models, which measure development by rising output (the total goods and services produced), such as Rostow’s stages ending in mass consumption. There is more on these models in Views of development and underdevelopment.
The idea grew over several decades, from a warning about limits in 1972 to global targets in 2015. Knowing the sequence lets you give a dated origin for the model.
“The Limits to Growth” (1972), a report for the Club of Rome, used computer models to warn that unchecked population and economic growth would exhaust resources within about a century.
The Brundtland Report, “Our Common Future”, was produced by the UN World Commission on Environment and Development in 1987. It gave the definition above.
The Earth Summit in Rio de Janeiro (1992) produced Agenda 21 (a global action plan) and the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (a treaty on tackling climate change).
The Millennium Development Goals (eight goals, 2000–2015) were followed by the Sustainable Development Goals: 17 goals adopted in September 2015, with a target year of 2030.
The Paris Agreement (2015) committed countries to tackle climate change.
The world is off track to meet most of the Sustainable Development Goals, so the targets are not being reached on time.
The case for making sustainability a priority rests on the fact that today’s growth can undermine tomorrow’s. Use these reasons when an essay asks whether it should be a priority.
Resources are finite (there is a fixed amount) and are being overused, so they cannot support unlimited use.
Climate change, biodiversity loss (the decline of plant and animal species) and inequality between and within generations threaten future development.
The poorest people suffer first when resources are degraded, because they depend most directly on land, water and fuel and have least to fall back on.
Growth that destroys the resources it depends on cannot last, because the base of that growth is used up.
The model is widely accepted but hard to apply. A good evaluation says where it falls short as well as where it works.
It is vague and open to greenwashing, where firms and governments claim sustainability without real change, because nobody can say exactly what counts as sustainable.
The pillars conflict: jobs can be at odds with protecting the environment, so balancing all three is difficult.
Poorer countries argue that rich countries grew without limits and now ask them to slow down, which they see as unfair.
The costs of change fall unequally, and progress on the Sustainable Development Goals is behind schedule.
If development is not just rising output, it needs other yardsticks. Two alternatives measure wellbeing and environmental pressure instead.
Bhutan’s Gross National Happiness, put forward in the 1970s by King Jigme Singye Wangchuck, measures wellbeing beyond income.
The ecological footprint measures the land and resources a population needs to support its consumption.
Sustainable resource use means using resources so that they last. The principles below differ for resources that regrow and those that do not.
Renewable resources (those that regenerate, such as fish and forests) should be used no faster than they regenerate. This rate is the sustainable yield.
Non-renewable resources (those that cannot be replaced, such as fossil fuels) should be used efficiently and replaced by alternatives where possible.
Reduce, reuse and recycle waste, so that fewer resources are taken and less waste is dumped.
Protect biodiversity (the variety of living things).
Involve local people in decisions about resources, since they live with the results.
Fish are a renewable resource, but only if catches stay below what the stock can replace. Irish fishing policy has been shaped by what happened when this was ignored.
Irish fishing has been shaped by past overfishing in EU waters, which is why rules now limit catches.

The Common Fisheries Policy of 1983 was reformed in 2013, introducing maximum sustainable yield (the largest catch that can be taken without shrinking the stock) and a landing obligation (a discard ban), phased in during 2015–2019.
The Sea-Fisheries Protection Authority was set up in 2007.
Killybegs, Co. Donegal, is Ireland’s largest fishing port.
The North Sea herring fishery was closed from 1977 to the early 1980s and recovered under quotas (limits on catch), showing that management can work.
The Grand Banks cod moratorium (a ban on fishing) of 2 July 1992 cost about 30,000 jobs off Newfoundland and is the warning for overfishing.
Bord na Móna has moved from burning peat to renewable energy under its “Brown to Green” strategy. Peat is partly decayed plant matter dug from bogs, once burned for electricity.
Bord na Móna was founded in 1946.
The Lanesborough and Shannonbridge peat stations closed in December 2020, and peat harvesting ended in January 2021.
Cutaway bogs (bogs where the peat has been removed) are being rehabilitated and rewetted, and peatland is valued as a store of carbon.
Lough Boora Discovery Park, Co. Offaly, is one of the rehabilitated sites.
Bellacorick, Co. Mayo, has wind farms on cutaway bog.
Moving electricity generation from fossil fuels to renewables is a central part of sustainable resource use. Ireland has set targets in law.
Wind provides about a third of Irish electricity, and renewables about two-fifths (early 2020s).
The Climate Action Plan targets 80% renewable electricity by 2030 and at least 5 GW (gigawatts, a measure of power capacity) of offshore wind by 2030.
The Climate Act 2021 requires a 51% cut in emissions by 2030 (from 2018) and net zero (no more greenhouse gas added than removed) by 2050.
The East–West Interconnector (2012), a cable that lets electricity flow between countries, links Ireland and Britain, and the Celtic Interconnector to France is due in the late 2020s.
Farming shapes most Irish land, so how it is run matters for sustainability. Schemes reward good practice, but dairy expansion pulls the other way.
BurrenLIFE (2005–2010) and then the Burren Programme pay farmers according to habitat scores for each field, so they are paid for results.
Agri-environment schemes (payments to farmers for protecting the environment) have included REPS (1994), GLAS (2015) and ACRES (2023).
Origin Green, Bord Bia’s sustainability programme, began in 2012.
Milk quotas (limits on how much milk each farm could produce) were abolished on 1 April 2015, and the dairy herd grew strongly afterwards.
Agriculture produces over a third of Irish greenhouse gas emissions.
Only about half of Irish waters are in good or high ecological status (EPA, 2016–2021).
Dairy expansion is therefore in tension with water quality and emissions targets.
Sustainability also depends on changing everyday behaviour. Two Irish measures show how charges and deposits can cut waste.
The plastic bag levy (a charge on each bag) began in March 2002 at 15 cent, and plastic bag use fell by over 90%.
The Deposit Return Scheme (Re-turn) began on 1 February 2024.
Only about 11% of Ireland is forest, and much of that is not native. Forestry is a final Irish example of resource use.
Forest cover in Ireland is about 11%, mostly conifer plantations of Sitka spruce.
Coillte was set up in 1988 to manage state forests.
Remnants of native woodland, such as the Killarney oakwoods, show what Ireland has lost.
Ireland needs more native broadleaf woodland, because plantations of one conifer support less variety of life than native woods.
Managed Scandinavian forests are another example of forest use. There is more on this in An interdependent global economy.
Costa Rica, in Central America between Nicaragua and Panama, shows how a country can reverse resource loss.
In the 1970s and 1980s forests were cleared for cattle pasture, and by the late 1980s forest covered only about a fifth of the country.
The Payment for Environmental Services programme, started in 1997 and run by the national forestry fund FONAFIFO, pays landowners to protect and replant forest, so keeping trees earns income.
The programme is paid for largely by a tax on fuel.
